This game tends to get dumped on a lot, but I have to say that it probably doesn't deserve a lot of the hate it gets. I admit, the story is wafer thin, the framerate chugs and any story choices you make feel really insignificant. Some combat classes also feel more useful than others, so you'll likely spend the entire game with just Recon and Engineers. Perhaps the game's most glaring flaw however is it's nearly brain-dead AI, who you need to micromanage lest they run out into the open or directly into a group of enemies. However, combat is extremely busy and highly stimulating, and it will force you to juggle managing your team, your abilities and your own combat at the same time.
By far the game's greatest strength is its combat system. A lot of people probably won't like it at first, because they'll try to run in guns ablazing and get completely wrecked. This isn't that sort of game, and once you get the hang of Battle Focus, it really does start to feel like a real time Enemy Unknown. You'll be constantly popping in and out of focus to check the status of the battlefield, evaluate whether to move from cover or to take a few pot shots, and manage your team. Each of the weapons in the game also have interesting effects, from your standard rifle to plasma burn.
That said, is this game worth 20 dollars? I'd say it's a bit of a stretch, and you'd really have to work to get your money's worth at that point. Now drop the price to 10-15, and I would absolutley reccomend this game. Although the story is awful and the game feels somewhat half-baked, the meat of the game, the combat, is sweet and satisfying; easily good enough to sustain you through a 8-10 hour campaign- longer with side missions. It's tough, it's stimulating, and it's something different the shooter genre hasn't seen before. 7/10

So I'm one of the original people who bought this game. I used to hype about this game so much, used to watch the gameplay videos pre-release and was absolute crazy over it. I used to live somewhere I could never get the game, so the first instance I got when I moved to University in another country, I bought the game instantly. My first bought game ever. I was so thrilled.
What I got completely demoralized me. The game was good, sure, but there was almost no multiplayer at all, given that I'm not in one of the major countries there's bound to be players in, such as NA or KR. I could never, ever, find an online match so I played the expedition mode a lot. I liked the game, it had great potential, but it died out and I moved on.
When I saw that it went f2p, I was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in a way. I had starved myself a bit to save money from my student budget to be able to buy this game and now this happens? I didn't touch the game for a long time until today, as I write this review.
Honestly, I just gave it a shot and I'm falling in love with it all over again. I had a huge bonus to the 'silver keys' the game uses as currency for being a 'founder', and although I'm still a bit frowny over my money, it was an okay consolation and I let it slide. I do, however, miss the Evacuation mode. That mode was really fun. The multiplayer; finally, I get to play online. And boy, is it everything I hoped for. Sure, it could use some balance tweaking here and there, with a few monsters/hunters being too weak or too strong, while some just have no clear strengths or weaknesses, and are therefore pretty dull. But the game is still absolutely amazing and I give the Devs all my hope that they'll continue to groom this game into something even better. If they keep updating the game with balance patches [better if they include patch notes so we see who gets buffed/nerfed] and the occasional new map/monster/hunter/skin, this game could get up to be absolutely stellar.  I wish the Devs of Evolve good luck and hope that they won't let me or the others who play this game again. Just like the game got a 'Stage 2', it's also on it's second chance for most people, and I doubt majority would be willing to spare a third chance.
Cheers and happy hunting.

I never played Evolve before it became free to play so i have nothing to compare it to.
As it currently stands, Evolve is the best free to play game on the market. I have been so surprised by Evolve that i decided to write this review in an attempt to stem all the hate coming from butt hurt "Founders".
In my own experience i have found Evolve to contain the following
-Friendly, interactive community
-Excellent match making system
-Daily incentives to keep the player engaged and motivated
-Very few bugs for a free to play game that just had a huge overhaul
-Excellent graphics (I play on ultra)
-Balance seems to be spot on between the hunters and monsters
Overall this is a game i will continue to recommend. It only gets better with every update that also adds free content, there is no pay to win feature like in so many free to play games out there and has a very active community.
In conclusion, it's a very solid free to play game with a heavy emphasis on cat vs mouse gameplay.

I love this game so much that even after taking close to 50 hours to finish the main campaign, I wished the game was a bit longer, just so I could spend some more time immersed in the world of Dunwall. It's a beautiful game that I simply couldn't get enough of.
When someone mentions artistic games, they most likely are talking about indie games such as Firewatch. In fact, some might even frown upon anyone mentioning a AAA title. So it might surprise some people when I say that Dishonored is one of the most artistic games I have ever laid my eyes on. You can take screenshot of almost any place in the game and it would look like a beautiful oil painting, even when Dunwall is a dark and dreary place to be in, infested with rats and plague. Its atmospheric look evokes a sense of mystery and suspense. The world is so well done that I wanted to learn the history of the city. When, say, I passed by an abandoned building, I wondered about the people who used to live there. That is how well done Dunwall is, pardon the pun. I was so immersed in it that it felt real. It made me curious. I wanted to know more. I wish they written novels about Dunwall. I would definitely read it. There is plenty of lore, if you're interested in it, to learn the backstories of some of the characters, and places. But I wished there were more.
Lot of people love to look down on AAA games for being violent and crass and shower praise on indie titles such as Undertale for going the opposite route. "You can finish the game without killing anyone", they would say. Well, guess what? In Dishonored, you can finish the entire game without killing anyone too! In fact that's encouraged. And there is an achievement if you happen to not kill a single person in the game. And it's not easy not to kill. The game makes you work for it. Sometimes killing is so tempting. Especially because, in this game, apart from your regular weapons such as the sword and gun and crossbow, you also get special abilities such as super vision, ability to stop time, ability to possess other people etc.  If you don't mind a darker ending, you can unleash all your powers on your enemies. But the game rewards you with a better, brighter, more positive ending if you exercise restraint.
Dishonored has a decent main story plus lots of interesting side stories. There are a lot of literature lying around in the world for you to read to discover the back stories of the places and the people. That makes the game even more immersive. You can even ignore all of it if you want, even though I wouldn't recommend it.
All in all this is a great game and it's a must play for anyone who loves playing immersive games.

When you first start playing, it is hilarious of course - the premise is silly, it's full of over the top characters and goofy puns, and just lots of laugh out loud moments.  But then, as you start to progress and go through multiple play-throughs, you will start to unlock more situations, and learn more about the world and story you are playing in - and it's actually a really good story, with depth and mystery and meaning and all of those important things.  It's so much more than it first appears - and knowing anything about it would ruin the fun, so it's hard to review.
Obvious down sides of the game are the silly-bad graphics (the whole game is mostly the same photographs of birds standing statically above a text box), and it can get a bit repetitive after several playthroughs (I'm on my 11th and no regrets!) - but there is a nice fast-forward feature which helps with that a lot.  There are also some big plays on words that don't make as much sense in English as they would in Japanese (especially the title), and also they are inconsistent about changing the order of people's last and first names (you might be Smith John or John Smith... usually Smith John though).  But that sort of thing should become decipherable as you play, especially if you are vaguely familiar with Japanese culture and/or language, and there are also a lot of puns that are translated very well too.  At the end of the day, I actually really like the shabbiness of it, and the fact that the culture isn't "translated out" of it.
You will play through the whole game for the first time in probably about half an hour - it will be a silly lighthearted dating sim that is funny, and strangely touching at the end (unless you go for one of the really weird characters first).  You can easily play through the whole game several more times, and get a similar vibe, but pursuing different characters as your love interest... but by the second or third time through you will probably start to get a hint of something bigger going on underneath.  Keep playing and experimenting!  Don't read about the story on the internet!  The mystery is a lot of fun.  The only thing I will say is this - After a while, I created a save just before the first decision you have to make, because there is a lot of decision-less intro at the beginning.  While that's okay for your first few play throughs, DO try playing from the beginning once in a while, as there may be something different that happens there.

A very good yuri VN that requires the player to be observant and apply some detective skills. One of my favourite things is the score, especially the piano-driven tracks that play at certain times. It compliments the art style so well too.
The characters are also well written and (for the most part) likeable. The protagonist is quite timid, but she's clever and empathetic. I never really found her behavior frustrating. The romance scenes take some work to get to, but they're very nice.
If I had to give some complaints, there's still a few typos and errors in the translation at the time I'm writing this. Also, some of the choices don't make a whole lot of sense. For example, choosing option 1 at a certain point might improve the relationship potential for character A, despite there being no logical reason why it's relevant at all.
Another thing people may not initially realise - this is actually just part 1 of a 4 game series. The game still follows it's own dramatic arc, but the ending doesn't come with total closure.

I now completed the game, took me 33 hours and I loved every minute of it.

The entire Flower series is broken into four games and while each game is complete in itself, they are connected, let's hope they come to Steam in the next year.

I never write reviews despite spending a good chunk of my life playing video games, but I beleive that right now Hearts of Iron deserves it. Roughly 99% of these reviews are angry at the whopping ten whole dollars for something that you can easily download a mod for. God forbid paradox is at least offering official DLC. Why complain about it if A: It's pretty cheap and B: You can easily get a free mod for the skill trees. Almost every new core feature that's added with the DLC's such as impassable areas (great addition IE The saharah) and the new air force system are patched in for free. I personally only bought the first dlc and later refunded it due only to lack of interest in playing the colony countries to start with, but after spending so much time in HOI I later went back and gladly rebought it. I believe that even at $15 it's still a great value if you have the money to spare for the true way Paradox wants the trees to be, This is a fantastic game that's a dream come true for history fans. Any focus tree you feel is missing (including fantasy joke ones such as Hundland, pupper empires) is almost certainly a free mod. I'd like to thank Paradox for being so supporting of what in my opinion is the best modding community of any game rivaling Skyrim especially for is much smaller player base and age. People my compain about stupid AI, but imo it only seems slightly dumb sometimes and even then it's when you've spent a lifetime, like me, playing this game. It first appears to have a steep learning curve, but in reality is quite simple. It's a game best learned by tiny reddit tips, and watching youtubers just have fun like Isorrowproductions and the Yogscast. I'm not without minor complaints, such as the fastest speed slugging down later in the game during long battles such as against the Soviets, but even then my minor complaints are just that, minor. I love this game, and would easily give it a 9 or 10/10.

Pros:
* Great artwork. Very unique.
* Challenging. Initially I strugged to take on waves of zombies but the game rewards strategizing and learning.
* Mostly wel balanced. This is Early Access so I expect balance to be improved in the future.
* Tight design. There are a set number of units and all of them make sense.
Cons:
* I'm not too sure I love the maps too much. Could use some improvement.
* Could use some UI improvements but mostly it handles well.
If you want a single player RTS that delivers on strategy this is it. Great premise. Great art. A lot of time spent thinking and making choices!

This is a hard review to write, because I like this game. I like the mechanics, graphics, game play and it is challenging. However, I am convinced the game cheats.  My thinking is that instead of creating an AI that reacts and uses straight forward tactics to play against the player, all the computer does is at a certain point, search for the weakest part of the player's defenses and send enough units to overwhelm the player's defenses. That is not to say the player can't react and successfully repel the attack, but that it all seems very contrived and unnatural.

Do you like Age of Empires?  Do you like zombies?  Do you like tower defense?  If you answered "yes" to all 3 of those, get this game.  It is still a bit rough around the edges, but overall is one of the most addictive games I've played in quite a while, even if it can be very frustrating.

"From the makers of Terraria..."
Terraria is one of my favorite games and since I was armed with a coupon for 25% off Pixel Piracy, I decided to try it out. I've put on about 15 hours now, and despite a few technical problems, I'm having a blast with the game. You start off as a lone pirate with a sword and wood to build a ship. Once you build a raft you can set off to start exploring, discovering islands or coming across merchant/pirate ships and plundering them. When you come across cities you can buy new skills for your pirate, food, weapons, ship parts, or hire more pirates to join you. You can level up anyone on your team, or use the same points to teach them new skills, like how to parry. The further away you get from your starting point, the harder the island inhabitants and pirates get. You also get to buy better equipment to keep up with the difficulty.
The game is still in early development access, and not "officials released. Due to that, there are still some technical problems with the game that will hopefully get ironed out before version 1.0 hits. When you attack level 4 pirate ships, the enemy pirates will shoot their cannons at you even if you are already aboard their ship. This will destroy their boat and anyone who happens to be on it. The island inhabitants level up with your character, but seem to level up faster. Your pirates and birds will Poop on the deck of the ship, which can be cleaned up by to teaching someone the "cleaning" skill. However, if the poop hits one of the Pirates it will hurt them and knock them back, and I've lost a few pirates who have been standing on the bow of the ship get knocked into he water and drown.
Despite the technical issues, I would recommend this game as it is a lot of fun, and hopefully those bugs will get squashed in time.

And the game becomes boring and repetitive even before buying cannons. And the story is also repetitive even at the first hour. Attack islands, kill the treasure guards, loot the chest. Attack ships, loot the treasure, plunder them if you manage to not sink them if you have cannons. Or if you are really high level, attack towns and take the gold. Nothing else, except for the events which are either you getting exp or crew wanting money.
The graphics are at the level of some basic flash game but is too resource heavy for non-gaming computers, which is why I bought this at the first place. And mind you, it can run games (at low specs) like Minecraft, M&B, Bioshock etc.  smoothly but not this. So don't buy this thinking it is easy to run.
The combat is also too boring. It is essentially random and also stupid: a turtle or a chicken can deal more damage than a sword...

It is funny in a silly way at the first couple of hours but gets incredibly annoying with the repeating sounds (poop+kick) and places and missions.

So I'm one of the original people who bought this game. I used to hype about this game so much, used to watch the gameplay videos pre-release and was absolute crazy over it. I used to live somewhere I could never get the game, so the first instance I got when I moved to University in another country, I bought the game instantly. My first bought game ever. I was so thrilled.
What I got completely demoralized me. The game was good, sure, but there was almost no multiplayer at all, given that I'm not in one of the major countries there's bound to be players in, such as NA or KR. I could never, ever, find an online match so I played the expedition mode a lot. I liked the game, it had great potential, but it died out and I moved on.
When I saw that it went f2p, I was pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in a way. I had starved myself a bit to save money from my student budget to be able to buy this game and now this happens? I didn't touch the game for a long time until today, as I write this review.
Honestly, I just gave it a shot and I'm falling in love with it all over again. I had a huge bonus to the 'silver keys' the game uses as currency for being a 'founder', and although I'm still a bit frowny over my money, it was an okay consolation and I let it slide. I do, however, miss the Evacuation mode. That mode was really fun. The multiplayer; finally, I get to play online. And boy, is it everything I hoped for. Sure, it could use some balance tweaking here and there, with a few monsters/hunters being too weak or too strong, while some just have no clear strengths or weaknesses, and are therefore pretty dull. But the game is still absolutely amazing and I give the Devs all my hope that they'll continue to groom this game into something even better. If they keep updating the game with balance patches [better if they include patch notes so we see who gets buffed/nerfed] and the occasional new map/monster/hunter/skin, this game could get up to be absolutely stellar.  I wish the Devs of Evolve good luck and hope that they won't let me or the others who play this game again. Just like the game got a 'Stage 2', it's also on it's second chance for most people, and I doubt majority would be willing to spare a third chance.
Cheers and happy hunting.

I originally wanted to like this game, having liked the concept of the first one and wanting a good open-world driving game. I heard all the negative feedback but decided to get it (two years after release) while it was cheap. Let's just say I'm glad I got it on sale.
To start off, the game REALLY likes showing you the cutscenes and letting you hear the voice acting. The problem is that the human(oid) figures look like a high school student's class project and the voices sound like an obscure anime dub. I bought this game to drive, NOT to watch ReBoot. The terrain looks passable and didn't seem to be TOO distracting. As for the cars themselves, they look good for their time, but seem a bit too "plastic-y" and matte-finished. Normally you'd expect the driving to be the best attribute of a racing game, right? Well the driving here feels really stiff, more like the 2002 Test Drive iteration, and less like a game made in 2011. Cars either grip perfectly at insane speeds, or barely turn at all, which is a very bad business model for a car manufacturer.
Soundtrack is a purely subjective thing, I know, but I personally don't think you could get more obscure, ear-violating, and volume-lowering music if you tried. The only saving grace is that one of the TWO stations plays electronic music that's actually tolerable as background noise.
It's hard for me to say much about the optimization since I have newer hardware that could power through it, but I did get slight stutters every now and then on a GTX 670.
Hindsight being 20/20, if I'd known that most of my 10 or so hours played would be spent tabbed out, I probably wouldn't have bothered.

Ever wondered how it would be if you didn't just command your XCOM troops in battle, but you actually played one too? I have asked myself that question quite a few times. The Bureau is here to answer it. In this continuity the aliens invaded early, you play an agent of XCOM and as usual your goal is to show those aliens why they should have stayed out of earth to begin with. Set in the American 60s, the Bureau is an action-tactical game. Your role is not only to fight the enemy but to command a squad. And here lies the major problem of the game. Unlike other similar games, your squad is practically helpless without your guidance, but you will be too busy trying to keep your own character alive. There is just too much happening to bother giving accurate direction for long. The game bites much more than it can chew. Despite the beautiful setting, the intriguing atmosphere and interesting characters, the whole experience is more frustrating than enjoyable.
So to my earlier question, how would it be if you played an XCOM trooper too? The answer is... "not that fun". Unless you are an XCOM fanatic, or someone with too much time to waste micromanaging, this title is not recommended. And what a pity that is.

Don't read online critic review of this game, as they tend to focus more on how it compares with other XCOM titles. Judging this solely as an individual game, I thoroughly enjoyed the approximate 12 hour campaign. The story was very interesting and I'm sure I would have enjoyed it even more if this were not my first game of the XCOM universe. Gameplay wise, this game was even better. The battle focus thing is one of the core features of the game, which allows you the ability to command your agents in an almost XCOM Enemy Unknown feel to strategize your opening moves whenever you encounter enemies on a mission. After you plan your moves/actions, you can return to the 3rd person shooter than defines this game. It feels similar to other tactical shooters, but there is so much more control over your AI teammates (like who to focus on or what abilities to use and in what order).
Another great feature that I was totally not expecting was the inclusion of this sort of central hub that your player returns to in-between missions. I was totally expecting a completely linear storyline similar to Call of Duty or Battlefield. I was wrong. Between missions you can sort of partake in side "mission" and talk to people of XCOM while chosing different questions/replies (RPG like...Fallout?), making the game feel more of an experience than just a game. You can also recruit more agents (4 different classes: Recon, Medic, Commando, Engineer) at the base to swap between missions and level up individually on missions. Speaking of leveling up, each level gained provides perks to be used and usually you can only pick one of two, like would you rather take less damage or do more...etc. This gives the game so much more customization since you can take missions differently depending on who you decide to take into the field with you and what perk that have (like is your medic tailored to help fight or is he solely built around supporting others). The fact that once your fellow agents die in the field, they will never return forces you to play tactically and not that lone wolf thing you do in other shooting games.
Mission-wise, you choose what you want to do at a mission select screen. You can do minor operations which are proper side missions or major operations which moves the main storyline along. Also, there are missions that you can send your other agents (whom you don't take into main missions with) to do. This reminds me of the Assassin's Creed guilds and such (Kenway's Fleet except it doesn't take like a whole real life day for them to complete). There are plenty of collectibles to find to bolster both yourself and your agents throughout all 3 missions types.
Overall, I really liked the game (doesn't hurt that I got this off of Humble Bundle for very cheap) and would recommend it based upon its classic shooter feel mixed with almost a hint of RPG element. There's a pretty big and surprising plot twist at the end with a couple of decision based endings, which made things even more memorable. Also, you don't know what it feels like to go from shooting aliens with a 1911 pistol at the beginning to destroying them with their own advanced alien weaponry until you play this game.

Pros:
- the retro setting mixed with sci-fi elements works very well
- music and visual effect are good
- the combat system is well designed (clean and nice UI) and battles are exciting
- abilities are varied and effective
- levels are usually  polished and a joy to move around in (but very linear)
- the enemies are sometimes surprisingly sneaky and use covers/terrain well
Cons:
- some unexplainable stuff in level design (air strike possible in closed areas, conveniently placed weapons and random resupply crates in enemy territory)
- you can carry very little ammo
- the XCOM base is dull, there is little to do and you have to run around a lot (a joykiller between missions)
- the weapons are adequately flashy and effective, but unimaginative (laser gun A, laser gun B, plasma gun A...)
- rather one dimensional characters and a storyline that falls apart at the end
- despite being an XCOM game, there is NO research whatsoever. In the beginning they explain how we have to reverse engineer alien stuff before being able to use it, yet in the game you can just pick up any alien blaster you find and use it right away. This hurts a lot.
- there is little incentive to use different squads for different missions
- squad mates stop leveling up at rank 5 which you can get to very quickly
Conclusion: 6.5/10. There are no game breaker flaws and I had much more fun than annoyances, but I won't replay this game.  Get it if you feel like blasting alien b@tt (it feels awesome to clear a tough wave of enemies) or if it's part of a good bundle (which is how I bought it).

-
- that's the thing, these buildings are useless after you upgrade everything. You're forced to kill all the enemies to progress, which I normally don't have a problem with, but normally, killing enemies is fun. This isn't fun. Your attacks don't have any knockback or interrupts, so you'll constantly take damage as the enemies can still attack you while you're hitting them; you also have no block.
So as a free, student project, this is quite good, particularly on the visual side (even if the protagonist has way too much jiggle physics), but I can't recommend it as a game.

Pixel Piracy is probably one of the most prime examples of the pitfalls of early access. Pixel Piracy is nowhere near finished. It's startlingly low on content, depth, and polish. It has a well thought out conept, and it has the solid groundwork of an enjoyable and well-executed game, but that's it. The result is a semi-enjoyable, yet extremely repetitive and frustrating, prototype of a game.
The actual game is a strange but creative mixture of FTL and Dwarf Fortress, as you manage the various needs of a group, which you need if you want any hope of survival, namely health, hunger, and moral. You do this by managing them in combat, feeding them, paying them or supplying drinks. They level, you teach them important skills, and spec out their stats. The macro management is relatively fun, as you choose to teach what to your various crew. Do you want to invest in teaching one guy fishing, cooking, and cleaning, or are you too worried that he'll die too easily in some wayward skirmish, or would you rather not overburden one super-crew member and rather disperse the work? Having a large crew is nice, but also expensive, in gold and in food. This form of management and gameplay, along with watching your ship grow to be larger and larger and more functional as you personally design it, is the meat and potatoes of Pixel Piracy, and they are enjoyable and well done. The base game is there, and it's good. The graphics and audio are also charming and polished. The problem, however, is virtually everything else.
Pixel Piracy suffers from four primary issues. First let's just talk UI and general control. It's terrible. Shockingly so. Controlling your bundle of haphazard pirates is an absolute pain, and the AI is attrociously bad. There seems to be no rhyme of reason to how your crew wobbles about, as you cannot seem to get them to prioritize and enemy and move in one motion. They need to be heavily baby-sitted through every single command and action, and if you cannot coordinate this collection of bumbling idiots, one of them will die. Very rarely do you feel responsible for any of the deaths, either you have not the slightest clue of what's going on, or the AI just decided that it doesn't want to play along. The fact that it takes about three or four clicks to get the entire crew and their captain to prioritize a certain enemy is just downright idiotic, I'm honestly confused how Re-Logic messed this up as bad as it is, and the simplest aspects of the game and genre, no less. I applaud them for trying to break the mold, but they have to do so with some confidence that it's bareable, which the controls of the game are just simply not. You eventually get used to it, but it's still an infuriatingly awkward design, to describe it briefly and crudely, it's like someone tried to combine elements of 2D point-and-click adventure games with typical top-down RTS games, and no, it did not work out. Oh, and don't even get me started on the map movement and menu setup, it's just as frustrating. You learn through experience not to use the menu or customize your ship while your captain's in a shop.
The second issue is how the game adapts to the rogue-lite genre. First of all, there are three modes, normal mode, hardcore mode, and for some reason an arena mode, which showcases by far the weakest aspect of the game --the combat, which I have already explained-- in a typical horde-like fashion. The normal mode gives you the option to save before every movement on the world map, which basically removes any weight from any mistake you make, unless it's a macro mistake. You can die as much as you like and just reload, no problem. No decision carries any importance. Okay, you may think, then just play on hardcore, which has no save feature. There in lies the rub. Due to all of my previously stated greivances about the controls and AI, combined with the game's incredibly random and confusing nature, it's near impossible to play the game feelings as if it's anymore than the roll of the dice. All the time, some tiny detail with go wrong, and literally everything will be ruined. A good rogue-lite/like will wear you down, kill you over a serious of misfortunate events, will make you pay for many little mistakes building up. In Pixel Piracy, the AI just messes up once and everything's over. Just once, the rest of your crew just decides not to follow their captain into battle regardless of their given orders, and next thing you know the game's over. Not to mention that the game has certain checkpoints, namely surviving until you get a sustainable three-person crew with cleaning and cooking abilities and when you intergrate cannons into your combate, that so suddenly kills you that it feels like your efforts meaning nothing in the palm of the RNG gods. Especially during cannon fights, which lack any option of escape after commitment, you can die so quickly and easily it makes everything seem pointless.
The third issue is just pure lack of polish. The game is incredibly repetitive, and it's buggy. Pirates falling through blocks, feces hovering inobtainable in the air, a cook who apparently just forgot how to cook, so on and so forth. And the entire game is just the identical "throw all your crew at once at the enemies' face and see how has the larger numbers" over and over and over, with only slight various in enemy type. Except when you get cannons, then it's just resource management mixed with spamming and RNG. Oh, and there's like two events, both just boring text across a blank open sea, which boils down to extra XP or paying gold instead of fighting an uncooperative swabbie. It's mind numbingly dull, just busy work in order to get resources to manage. The game desperately needs more meat on the bone.
The last issue is just the general confusion and unnecessary learning curve. It's not a matter of discovery of cryptic items and attributes like Binding of Isaac or Dungeons of Dredmor, it's a matter of just figuring out how to play the game. Learning the backwards idiosyncrasies of the AI, or how to cook food, or how to just manage your crew, is not fun, but frustrating. There is no direction, and almost everything is head-scratchingly unintuitive. This is the early action problem, the core aspects of the game, aspects it desperately needs to be enjoyable, are just not there yet.
My suggestion, wait on it. The game is currently not worth $15 in the slightest. Maybe it's worth the grind if it's half off or less, but even then, I would suggest waiting. I expect this game to get a lot better, as Re-Logic has proven itself to be a good developer, but right now, it's just not in an enjoyable state, not even truly in a playable one. I would suggest against impulse buying Pixel Piracy, in it's current state, it's just not worth it. Wait a few months, watch its development if you're interested. When the game fixes it's AI and UI issues, and more seriously designs it's the meta of the game and genre, I could see it being fantastic. Until then, put it back in the oven.

I wanted to put some time into this before writing a review. I'm not even finished with the Locksmith's story after 5 hours (the first story in the game, there are 4-5).
This is one of the funnest stealth games I have played. The theme, music, and style are really appealing. The screenshots don't do the game justice. Most of the missions consist of a heist. Stealing certain objects and getting out alive. Every level you play will have multiple floors which can take some time to scope out and get an idea for the best way to approach the mission.
The character design has been done really well. I think the best compliment I can give regarding this game is that me and my friends simply can't decide who to choose each time we play. Every single character is useful in some way or another. And depending on who you choose, you will be playing the mission very differently.
This game realllllyyyyy shines in multiplayer. Don't get me wrong. Singleplayer is a lot of fun, and is actually probably easier to pull off a clean mission. But playing with some friends or random people, it makes it REALLY feel like a heist. Get someone playing the hacker to disable the security, get someone playing the cleaner to knock out the guards, get someone playing the gentleman to simply walk in and steal the loot. Sounds easier right? WRONG! It's a lot more difficult with other people playing. Considering if someone gets caught, the whole floor basically freaks out. It makes it more fun because there is a much bigger risk.
The only complaint I have about this game is when you are using gear / weapons. See at the beginning of each mission, there will be boxes with different things to choose. Crossbows, shotguns, EMPs, TNT, etc. A lot to choose from. But it is rediculously confusing. Playing as the cleaner? Well if you pick up something, you'll be using that weapon instead of your knock out ability. I've still yet to figure out how to cycle between things you pick up.
Overall it feels kinda bad that I got this game for free. This is my type of game, and I would have paid $15 for it had I known about it. I highly recommend it

MONACO: WHAT'S YOURS IS MINE
is a heist game focused around stealth, which in itself is not exceedingly common nowadays, though there are others out there.
Its top-down rectangular graphics may not appeal to all, but the gameplay is where this game excels.
Your screen is comprised of a large rectangular map, zoomed in and blacked out until you explore it. When exploring, you find guards, guns, and gold. The guards will chase after you if you dash past them suspiciously, but if you casually walk past, more often than not, they'll pass it off as nothing important.
Having up to four-player co-op and up to eight playable characters each with their own primary, secondary, and occasionally tertiary skillset that may be accessed by others, but not nearly as well as the masters.
For example, the Locksmith is adept at picking locks on doors primarily, but also safes and cash registers. He picks locks 2 to 3 times faster than any other character.
The Gentleman puts on a simple disguise while hidden from view and applies disguises found around extraordinarily quickly. While others can put on disguises, none do it as fast as he and neither do they do it while hidden.
The Lookout knows where enemies are all over the map, and can additionally climb stairs and ladders faster.
The Pickpocket has a pet monkey that snatches cash undetected, and can stow himself away in bushes almost instantly.
The Cleaner can knock out unsuspecting witnesses and utilize medkits more efficiently.
The Mole breaks through walls. Yeah, that's about it.
But I could go on and on about this game's many merits--it has a level editor that was used to make every level in the game, for goodness' sake--but I think I can sum up this game's sense of humor and hilarity by saying that it's got a special gamemode called "ZONACO: YOUR FLESH IS MINE" in which all enemies are replaced by quick-moving small zombies or gigantic, slow, explosive zombies.
If you like stealth and/or heist games at all, get this. You won't regret it.

This game gets a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥for not being what it obviously isn't. It's not your standard XCOM fare. It similarly is not a regular third person shooter. Maybe I'm just a sucker for the 1960s "deniable ops" sort of feel to the game, but I've been having a blast with it.
The most common complaint that I've seen is that the AI squaddies are infants in diapers who, for some unknown reason, have been selected as the "best of the best" -- their training manifesting as a propensity for standing in direct fire while shouting "HALP. GIVE ME ORDERS. HALP." They do that. It's the game's cute way of saying maybe you should actually give orders to the infants. Play the game like the tactical shooter it is and idiot AI is more than manageable throughout the engaging and (at times) brilliantly designed firefights.
As it stands, there's a lot missing from the game that would have otherwise bumped it over an 80 Metacritic score. Linear level design, a lack of base customization, poorly compressed cinematics, no laboratory research projects, and a weird combination of player/AI control over squadmates ultimately hold back what otherwise would be a stellar game.
It's still a fun game. It shines at times, albeit through occasional graphics glitches and infrequent crashes. Just don't let yourself think of how magnificent it could have been if it drew more inspiration from other XCOM games.

The first paragraph is a rant on the silly negative reviews that really put the game down even though it’s good so I want to get that out of the way so here it is:
I really don't understand why this game is 'Mostly positive' so I looked at negative reviews to see why, and they are just awful, one I saw was just disgusting and it basically got a negative review because the person though it was like Project Zomboid, so because it didn’t live up to his/her expectations they rated it bad/down. Disgusting.
EDIT: I just saw another negative review because someone thought it was supposed to be like diablo 3, really? Idiot. (As you can tell stupid review trigger me.)
Now that 'rant' is out of the way I’ll review the game, now please bare in mind am not a reviewer, I just want to say my opinion on the game and I’m rating it up to 'fend off' all the silly negative reviews because it is a good game and deserves a better rating.
Let’s start off, people saying it’s just a ‘Point A to B’ and ‘Collect this and bring it back’ type of game, well yeah that’s true, but if you think about it, just about all games revolve around that same ‘schematic’ I look at their profiles and they have 2k hours in DOTA 2 and say this game is repetitive, I swear some people, but really don’t take that as a negative point, because all games are like it in some way or another, in DOOM you just run from room to room killing sh*t but that’s still a good game right? Exactly so why can’t this be?
Pros –
The game has a really cool concept that I personally really like, you have a camp and a big map to build said camp anywhere you want, and you have loads of ‘crafting stations’ that all do separate things, like the Kitchen workshop for food, and Armoury for weapons etc. simple stuff, and you can build defences because every so often your camp will get raided by hordes of zombies for you to fend off which is also really fun, that in that aspect is a base building tower defence game.
Also just like the first one there are Food and Water gauges, but no sleep in this one, which Is fine, the sleep was rather pointless on the first one to be honest, I only used it to skip night.
Also the Skills you buy with Experience points is a lot better than the first one, a lot more skills that do many different things, more in depth if you will.
The graphics are good, I’m not one who really cares about graphics so to some it may be bad, so I suggest you judge for yourself by the screenshots.
Fairly big map to build your camp, but also every quest has a different map which is good for keeping the game fresh.
Cons –
The Aiming can be really fiddley at times, sometimes I will run up to a zombie to do a running charge attack and my character will just do a 180 degree turn away and hit the air rather than the zombie, and the zombie will just turn around and hit me, keep in mind this doesn’t happen all the time and I’ve only gotten killed once by it.
Also the Aiming for guns and bows will sometimes just make you have to restart the aim even though you didn’t take it off, this can be really annoying at time when in panic situations and zombies are closing in on you.
The UI for transferring items is really fiddley too, you can’t shift click the items and so therefore you have the click and hold the item drag it over and then select how much of said item you want to move, and you have to click the ‘okay’ button, pressing enter will not work, so this con could be removed if the Developers implemented a shift click.
Lastly the game has crashed on me twice but it’s in early access and they weren’t hard crashes, just alt+tab and close with no lag, no progress lost either.
End -
That’s about it I think, like I said I’m not a reviewer so this isn’t going to beat the better ones, but really I wrote this just to like a said before ‘fend off’ those silly ones that make no sense and should be removed because they’re just putting the game down on the ratings side of things.
Edit: Also want to say I have 7.6 hours as of writing this and I’m still really enjoying it and feel like I’m a long way off ‘completing’ the game, the reason completing has been highlighted is because you don’t just do all the quests to complete the game, you can make your camp bigger and better and perhaps play with friends amongst other things so its defiantly worth the price.
Thank you for reading and I apologise for any spelling mistakes. :) – Old Gregg

TL:DR at the bottom...!
Great game so far! I don't understand the negative reviews though. If you don't like grindy games, this game isn't for you.
This game is much more polished than the first one, even in early access. It has much more content than the first one, which was so linear compared to this one. There's a much more in depth crafting system, which just adds stuff to do. The quests can be done over and over to grind for experience, especially if you don't want to to do the longer ones. The game plays out really smooth and is very well optimized - surprising for an early access game. Honestly, it doesn't feel like it's in early access at all.
I got this game on sale for 70% off. I paid like $5 CAD for this. I feel like a game this cheap has already exceeded my expecations. I enjoyed the first one quite a bit, so I took a chance on this, even with a 72% (at the time of writing) review from users. The first one took me about 12 hours to complete, since it was pretty linear. I've already put in about 12 hours (at the time of writing) and there's just SO much more to do.
Overall, if you don't mind a casual zombie/isometric/diablo-esque styled game, give this one a try. I don't know if it's worth full price (it probably is - only about $20 CAD) but the $5 is a freakin' steal. My logic is that if you can put in an hour for every dollar you spent on the game, it's paid itself off.
Game itself = I would give an 8.5/10. Really solid game, good sound effects and decent music. Only thing I wish could be improved a bit is movement, but then again, it's supposed to feel a bit clunky.
TL:DR? Do yourself a favour and get this game. It's much better than the first one and the regular gamer would probably enjoy this too.

This is the RTS we all wanted, but didn't know we needed. It's the sort of difficulty you want on a comp stomp - and it's very unforgiving. Leave any part of your base undefended, and the zombies will know. And they'll get in, and everything will get destroyed.
There is no do overs, no save scumming, you just get to try again. Some might find that frustrating, others might find that refreshing. For an RTS game, I think that was a bold decision and what keeps this game fresh and exciting. Every move you make, every attempt at expansion, can be costly.
I've never seen something I've taken so long to build fall so quickly. It only makes me want to try again.
So many other reviewers have said it better, but I just had to add my own recommendation here. As a long time RTS fan, this is a breath of fresh air that is crushingly difficult and very unforgiving. But so much fun.

Let's face it, the market is glutted with Free-2-Play MMO's. And for the most part, very few of them really bring anything new to the table. This is not the case with Rift. On the surface, one could be excused for thinking this fantasy MMO is just another WoW clone (but isn't that what *every* MMO gets accused of, eventually??). However, those who dig a little deeper into Rift will find a refreshing departure from tired class conventions, lackluster player housing and pay-to-win item shops.
For starters, a player can literally create their own character classes. There is virtually no limit as to the kind of build one can create using Rift's extremely robust 'souls' system. And here is the very best part - players can switch between multiple classes on the same character at will. Want to play a healer for that dungeon? Piece of cake. What if your group needs a tank? No problem. A character can switch between any soul at the click of a button, providing they have spent points in the skills needed. Show me another MMO that lets you do *that*!
Secondly, there is Rift's 'Dimension' system. Instead of giving your character a single house to occupy, Rifts throws the doors wide open and gives you an entire (instanced) slice of the game world itself to build in, decorate and host parties and events in. Combine this with literally hundreds of thousands of building items available in the item shop or via questing, and one can literally create almost anything they can imagine.
Lastly, there is the in-game item shop. You will find no nickel/diming pay-to-win shakedowns here. Almost everything in the item shop can be found via questing or participating in game events in one way or another. The few items that are available exclusively in the item shop are purely cosmetic, and are not needed to successfully play the game at all. Finally, someone has struck just the right balance between value, selection and sanity for a cash shop!!
So that is my review. If you are looking for your next MMO, you really owe it to yourself to at least give Rift a try. I think you will be very pleasantly surprised.

A month or two ago, I had "Gamer's Block", despite having a good amount of games to choose, so I decided to browse the F2P section. Evolve Stage 2 is the game I chose, and I do not regret getting this game at all. Some may get bored of the repetition, some won't, because what you do is either have a team of four that hunts down a large and dangerous monster, or you play as the monster and try to destroy the power relay (a way to win the match) or kill the hunters, and that's the only game mode for now, as other game modes besides "Hunt" may be added.
The game is very fun, especially with teamwork and co-op, they are encouraged. You really get a thrill when you play or fight the monster, there can be some intense battles and situations. At first the game seems complex and takes some getting used to, but eventually you'll realize how simple the system is.
There are four classes to choose from, Assault, Trapper, Support, and Medic. Each have a large variety of characters to choose from, which all have unique weaponry and tools to use against the monster or to assist your team. Such weapons and tools include an orbital drill to rain a giant laser upon the monster, a flamethrower gauntlet to melt the monster's face, and a pet Trapjaw that tracks down the monster and revives teammates, but this is not even a fraction of the current arsenal.
Monsters, on the other hand, have special abilities, and the current monsters are Goliath, a muscled brute that breathes fire, Kraken, a long range electrical beast of destruction, Wraith, a stealthy assassin like monster, Behemoth, a tanky and ginormous juggernaut, Gorgon, a spider-like monster that hide and attack from above, from poisonous spits to struggling traps, Meteor Goliath, a direct upgrade to Goliath but with longer cooldowns, and Elder Kraken, a heavily CQC AoE monster. Monsters have different tactics, you can choose to either sneak your way to devour small prey, and build up your armor and eventually evolve, while still thwarting the hunters from your position, or to just go beserk and attempt to obliterate the hunters.
The graphics are outstanding, there's multiple, large-scale maps that really have an alien-world feeling to them, I usually run a smooth 60fps, not sure how it is for other computers, but just know it's not choppy at all on a beefy computer. I'd just look at the system requirements and judge from there.
The sound in the game really makes the atmosphere unique and eerie, as you hear nature with it's bizarre alien like noises. The soundtrack is good, it only plays in the main menu, lobby, and loading screens.
Replayability is fine for me, but as I said before, "Some may get bored of the repetition, some won't, because what you do is either have a team of four that hunts down a large and dangerous monster, or you play as the monster and try to destroy the power relay (a way to win the match) or kill the hunters, and that's it for now, as other game modes besides "Hunt" may be added," so you'll have the play a couple matches and see for yourself." I don't get bored of the repetition, mainly because of how unique the game is, mostly because of the alien landscape, that sucks you in, making you feel like you're in an unknown world with unknown dangers.
In conclusion, I'd give this game a go, It's a great game to play with friends, and it's free, so why not give it a try?

A minimalist game in which Alice is depicted as a cube falling through Wonderland, passages of the novel would be read out as you play and words would form up as obstacles inhibiting your progress. A creative take on an otherwise old formula that’s been done plenty of times on Steam. What was initially a fun concept turned into a mighty struggle against repetition, it was a chore in exercise when I was barely minutes into the game.
First of all, this game only contain parts of the novel and not the entire thing, I fail to grasp why that is the case besides laziness. Secondly, the stages will always play out the same since it was fixed in stone by what was written in novel, so you’ll hear certain lines so often that you’ll come to hate them and Lewis Carroll (no offence to the great author). Lastly this game only featured a practice mode (stage select) and a ranked mode (leader board), which is the same thing in reality, thus there is no replay value what so ever.
The biggest bane of this game came from its atrocious controls. Tapping the arrow keys moves too slow in the faster stages, but holding the shift key moves way too fast. The animation would also turn jerky as you move, so the game essentially forces you to hug the top or bottom lane for much of its duration and to limit movement unless absolutely necessary.
Camera angles also worked against you in the worst manner possible, most evident when the game decided to make sharp corners just to spite you. By the time the next word (obstacle) appeared on screen, you will be too late to react but to start anew from the beginning. In fact, I beat the game solely by writing down the key sequence I used to dodge, and beat it on trial and error alone.
I really wanted to say something good about this, but the concept was its only saving grace, which is nowhere near enough for me to recommend a purchase. If you see this on sale with a huge discount, you’ll still be better off with some other game.

Buyer must ALWAYS be wary of Early Access games, as developers tend to get lazy when they are given money for lack of work. Just an early warning for those looking into this.
This game is very simple; you control a little pirate captain, kill other pixel pirates, recruit more pirates to fight with you, and so on. It's a side-scrolling game that goes at your pace, and it's an extremely casual Real Time Strategy as you have to make the choice; "Should I go pillage these landlubbers, or run away like a wimp?" every time.
The controls are limited, only needing the mouse for controlling your movement and your team movement, and the left and right arrow keys or A and D keys to move the camera left and right. You can literally play this game to its full extent with just one hand, so it is friendly to the disabled players out there.
Combat may seem lacking, as it's just motionless cardboard  cutouts smacking each other, but the entirety of the game has nothing doing any sort of movement except for wobbling. This is akin to South Park, where detailed movement is kept to a bare minimum. This may be a turn off for some, but for others it may provide just the right kind of amusement.
Music is exceptional. The pirates all sound like kids with an overdose of helium, save for a few satanic-sounding options, and they all sing these hilariously child-friendly pirate songs at times. Even if you just leave the game sitting and have the music play, it's relaxing and enjoyable.
Graphics may not seem important, especially since this game has far less detail than even Terraria (Published by the same group), but they are simple and to the point. There is no unnecessary detail, and you can tell what everything is without straining your eyes to figure out if the pirate is smiling, frowning, or constipated. By the way, the pirates love to poop on your ship, and it's even animated.
Depth of gameplay, as of the current build (0.7.2.1), is rather shallow. Items only go so far up, making later fights near impossible. Money becomes an issue after so long, and you have to either hope you find exceedingly good items in uninhabited island chests, or throw away your pirates to take down a ship and get 50 gold. Legendary Ships are even more tedious, as they can utterly destroy your ship in 3 shots, ending your game.
Again, Early Access should ALWAYS be "Buyer Beware", but I would recommend this game simply because it is enjoyable as-is, and is fully worth the low price during the sales.

Dishonored evokes the steampunk aesthetic and gives you a huge dose of stealth and cool gadgets and powers to use. The plague is penetrating Dunwall and you are on a mission of revenge. Throughout you meet some interesting characters and very cool locations. While the story won't win awards, and you can tell they were on a budget, the game is still top tier and has a lot of heart behind it. Everything is fairly pollished, though dated in some parts graphically, the mechanics are very well done. You definitely do not have to stealth your way through the game, but I do at least recommend playing on hard for a moderate challenge.
Like the old Hitman games, this one lives off its choices and gear. There are a lot of tools to play with in the game. Your powers like teleport, stopping time, and calling rats on people or even possessing others are a huge boon to the creative direction. You can tell this wasn't made with the largest budget, but the stylized nature of the graphics fits in perfectly with the world they built. There is plenty of DLC to keep you busy as well.
Nvidia AA codes work for SGSSAA and so does a Hawken HBAO code. You can't beat the visual quality here. On consoles the "definitive" edition was just released and it pales in comparison. Not even close. I play this game with Input Mapper and a DS4 and I'd never go back to anything less than 60FPS with 4xSGSSAA. It makes the moody and atmopsheric visuals all the more immersive. Sound is also very good in this game. You can always hear little extra details in the soundfield, and the music fits the game well. Highly recommended for anyone that wants a great "stealth" game with impressive visual and sound direction. Fire that crossbow up if you haven't already.

I have to say I really enjoyed this short game, possibly only because I also have SAD and her experiences (if not her entire attitude) match some of mine almost exactly.
That said, this might not be a game for people who can't relate to it.  I've seen several negative reviews from people that weren't able to relate in the slightest, and it's unfortunate that the game wasn't able to make some of those people realize how crippling SAD can be in its worse forms.  I remember being in college and never once eating decent, hot food  in the main cafeteria, grabbing the to-go cold meals instead and getting back to my room as quickly as possible to hide.
Yes, it really IS hell to go down the hall to make oatmeal sometimes.
But it's hard to decide on recommending this or not.  I think some people will relate to it as I did, some will learn a little about social anxiety, but some will dislike her personality and others will be completely unable to understand what's happening at all.
In the end, I recommend it because I think there ARE things to learn from it, and because I was looking into a mirror at the person I was in college (although my sarcasm was less bitter!).

I am primarily a PS4 player. I'm not upset they went F2P. I think it's a good thing since the PC playerbase was so low, it could get more people to play. It's not really as big of a problem on PS4, but I was looking forward to it on PS4 as well. Bigger playerbase is always better. However, the other changes they made are horrible. Everyone being able to place a dome is awful. This cuts out a major part of being a trapper. They dumbed it down so much. Use satelite and walk in that direction than anyone can trap it. Okay.
As for monster, there was no point in changing it so that they start with 4 points and then 3 and then 2. There was nothing wrong with the 3 3 3 system before. I guess they did this to offset the fact that the game is now essentially arena instead of hunt. Domes last a while now if you don't knock one of them out or take enough damage. If you have a fairly equal match where no one is losing health because everyone is good at dodging (or sucks at aiming) then the dome will just be there for five minutes.
Speaking of how the game is basically hunt arena, what happened to all the other game modes. I know they are supposed to be adding them in later, but why not just put them all in now? They already have them from the base game, so there's no reason to leave them out. I personally preferred hunt, but the other modes were occassionally fun too. I liked arena as it was, but if I want to play hunt then I want to play hunt, not some weird mix of hunt and arena where it's basically 90% dome time.

I've never played a dating sim before, but I'm not sure how much this represents the genre. It's a little bit more like an adventure story with a romantic touches of varrying degrees in each arc. But then again, all the other characters are birds so you can't really take it too seriously. It starts out simple enough just going to school, but just about every ending turns into weirdness. In a good way however, although a couple endings become disturbing and the bonus story for unlocking all the other endings is madness (but very interesting). In general I wouldn't recommend this game for anyone wanting a light hearted dating sim, though it has some light hearted moments. The only change I would make to this game would be if the dialog boxes could change color or otherwise indicate who's talking because it can get confusing in multiperson-pigeon conversations or before you've memorized everyone's names.

Costume Quest is a fun little indie game about two siblings on their quest to save Halloween which is mainly directed towards a younger audience. The game itself is very easy and should be able to entertain most children around the age of 10 for the same number of hours.

Costume Quest is my "go-to"' game when the Halloween season comes around. I originally owned a copy back on PS3 when it was first launched.  I was more than happy to pay for it again here on Steam (my new preferred platform for gaming).  The PC version includes the extra Grubbins on Ice content for free that was originally sold as DLC on consoles. The game is a fun, short and sweet RPG title that takes place on Halloween night where you play as a kid and his friends who have to "trick-or-treat" houses in order to earn enough candy to save your sibling who was stolen by goblin like villains. The combat system revolves around the type of Halloween costume you wear.  For example... When you wear the Robot costume into battle it will give you a critical strike move where the robot costume fires a missile barrage at your opponent(s) in a slick animation cut scene. There are lots of costumes to find throughout the game that you can wear into battle. Each will give you a different attribute when fighting. In addition, there are a bunch of side quests to complete as well. It may seem like a lot to do but the entire game goes by very quickly and can be completed in a couple of sittings which is why I tend to play it (or the sequel) just about every year. Overall, this game is a must play for anyone who is looking for something that will get them into the Halloween spirit.

This game is better than the original HTS in many ways. There's a camp building/levelling dynamic that wasn't in the first game. You level up your character, their abilties, your camp as well as each different building. Your main character level and abilities are levelled up using XP. Levelling up the camp also uses your XP points, so there's a lot going on. You can't level your character or buildings past your camp level. At different intervals of camp levels you have to complete a zombie wave challenge to test your camp defenses and survive the countdown timer. It's extremely fun.

The devs of this game captured lightning in a bottle, and then smashed it for some reason.  The game is amazing.  It is the first RTS I have played in … hell … years and years.  I have 14 hours clocked and played 11 games…and lost every single one.  Finally I turned the difficulty down to 55 percent and got to the end game.  The final rush is insane and counter to the entire game up to this point.  You need to expand to find the space to build your base and have the resources to field an army that can stand against the in game hoards.  But at the end they are billions, from every direction.  Wait, what ?  How does this make sense.  The best way to defend against something like that would be short, tight defensive choke points where you can stack your defenders, but I cannot do that because my base is large and sprawling with many access points.  I cannot be strong enough everywhere to defend against the billions.  Either I suck (and hey, let’s not discount that) or the game is fundamentally broken.  It is an early release.  I am going to put it away and hope the devs work out what sort of game they are making because right now it is all over the shop and outrageously frustrating.  Oh, and the lack of a save feature makes the pain all the more acute.  You have to fix that fellas, come on.

The Bureau is a game with a lot of baggage. It was first announced as the way 2K was choosing to revive the X-Com franchise, a decision that was understandably received with a considerable amount of bafflement and ill will. Yes, people wanted a modern X-Com, but that meant a turn-based strategy game of research and tactical battles, not some shooter. The fact that, as shooters went, it actually looked pretty interesting and ambitious was largely lost in the outpouring of disgust over the brand they chose to attach to it. Then it faded from view, and in the meantime Firaxis' much more faithful franchise reboot was announced and even released before The Bureau came back into view, now branded with that name. Unfortunately, it was clear that some ambition had been lost along the way, and its development was revealed to have been troubled and fraught with drama. It came out to a general wave of indifference, and was promptly dismissed.
Having now completed it, I believe this indifference was unwarranted. It's true that it's not X-Com. And the game originally previewed might well have been a better one. But the end result is a rather enjoyable melding of squad tactics and quality shooting, with light RPG elements; attached to a fairly compelling scenario of apocalyptic alien assault. Both major and side missions have interesting things to show you, and reveal more about the nature and motivations of your foe, and there's even a pretty spiffy late game twist. And I really appreciated the sequences where you walk around the XCOM base between missions. The various people you can converse with are all fairly well drawn as characters, if not horribly deep, and there are additional story tidbits and several layers of ambient conversations and announcements throughout, changing after every major mission.
Mind you, it's not perfect, either. The notion that all of this is a secret that's been covered up for decades is, well, just not plausible at all, especially when the rest of the time they want to give you a sense of the appalling scale of events. Some of the conversations are a little prone to repetition. And there are some disappointing technical issues, some of which seem to be specific to AMD cards from what I've read, but others seem more generally problematic. I had severe framerate issues with either PhysX setting on and active (i.e. if I was around PhysXed cloth or effects), and on settings above Medium (at least in the DirectX 11 client), the shadows were prone to very distracting and glitchy flickering. I've also read some people have had issues with crashes, although I personally did not experience these.
The technical issues were pretty easy to work around, and if you're prepared to quietly ignore the premise that any of the game's events are covert, that's not the biggest deal in the world either. So I don't feel either of these things should put you off The Bureau. I quite enjoyed myself all the way to the end, and I would definitely recommend it.

My primary criticisms will be focused on the combat.
The controls and animations are inconsistent and floaty/sluggish.
It's hard to identify when the window for combo inputs are. I think the inputs are queued, but its hard to tell when the attack animations seem to cut each other off one active hit detection is complete. I think the light swing was like an upwards swing then a sideways swing into downward swing, but when I pressed light attack three times in quick succession the middle sideways swing animation seems to be extremely short.
There is also little consistency to how long pauses are and which attacks get pauses. Most attacks seem to have no pause on hit while some of the specials get pauses of wildly varying length. The pauses also occur regardless of a hit connecting with an enemy or not.The visual flash, vibration, and sound effects are good feedback, but combat feels too quick and light. It feels like I'm flailing around with a wet noodle rather than cutting into the enemies with a sword. Every attack should have a bit of a pause or dramatic slowdown to give it more of a meaty feel when connecting hits on an enemy.
Also, enemy models should have more visual feedback with a stagger as well. The gunners and the armored enemies give no stagger or reaction to attacks making it seem like I'm not hitting them at all.
It's also dificult to judge the range of the swings, especially since the camera is directly behind the character. Either naturally angle the camera or give a little homing nudge to all the attacks.
A mini-map or an enemy counter would be very useful given the arena format of the encounters or give the AI a larger player detection radius. It sometimes very easy to miss an enemy and have to run around to find them.
There's a lot of potential in this build and I hope the developer team gets a chance to show off what they can really do in the future.

Despite the lack of explanation, story, and really anything of substance, The Lost Mythologies has the flavor of a great game. The foundation of something amazing is here, I can feel like when you hit F and jolt forward toward the rifle enemies, or how quickly you'll need a strategy for taking down the small mini-bosses that shoot rockets at your feet. The framework is here, but the lack of translation and story will prevent most people from going further than the first heavy boss.
Put it this way: There's more in the "About this game" section, than is EVER listed in the actual game itself. Again, the controls and mechanics are fantastic, and the graphics are out of this world good, but it needs more. It requires a bit of imagination to figure out why you're running from these traditional Chinese landscapes into the back alley of current movie sets. I'd like to know why.
Try it. It's small and worth the time.
Oh, and if you're here just for the achievement, check out how to get it by downloading the Chinese-only version through the console.

A month or two ago, I had "Gamer's Block", despite having a good amount of games to choose, so I decided to browse the F2P section. Evolve Stage 2 is the game I chose, and I do not regret getting this game at all. Some may get bored of the repetition, some won't, because what you do is either have a team of four that hunts down a large and dangerous monster, or you play as the monster and try to destroy the power relay (a way to win the match) or kill the hunters, and that's the only game mode for now, as other game modes besides "Hunt" may be added.
The game is very fun, especially with teamwork and co-op, they are encouraged. You really get a thrill when you play or fight the monster, there can be some intense battles and situations. At first the game seems complex and takes some getting used to, but eventually you'll realize how simple the system is.
There are four classes to choose from, Assault, Trapper, Support, and Medic. Each have a large variety of characters to choose from, which all have unique weaponry and tools to use against the monster or to assist your team. Such weapons and tools include an orbital drill to rain a giant laser upon the monster, a flamethrower gauntlet to melt the monster's face, and a pet Trapjaw that tracks down the monster and revives teammates, but this is not even a fraction of the current arsenal.
Monsters, on the other hand, have special abilities, and the current monsters are Goliath, a muscled brute that breathes fire, Kraken, a long range electrical beast of destruction, Wraith, a stealthy assassin like monster, Behemoth, a tanky and ginormous juggernaut, Gorgon, a spider-like monster that hide and attack from above, from poisonous spits to struggling traps, Meteor Goliath, a direct upgrade to Goliath but with longer cooldowns, and Elder Kraken, a heavily CQC AoE monster. Monsters have different tactics, you can choose to either sneak your way to devour small prey, and build up your armor and eventually evolve, while still thwarting the hunters from your position, or to just go beserk and attempt to obliterate the hunters.
The graphics are outstanding, there's multiple, large-scale maps that really have an alien-world feeling to them, I usually run a smooth 60fps, not sure how it is for other computers, but just know it's not choppy at all on a beefy computer. I'd just look at the system requirements and judge from there.
The sound in the game really makes the atmosphere unique and eerie, as you hear nature with it's bizarre alien like noises. The soundtrack is good, it only plays in the main menu, lobby, and loading screens.
Replayability is fine for me, but as I said before, "Some may get bored of the repetition, some won't, because what you do is either have a team of four that hunts down a large and dangerous monster, or you play as the monster and try to destroy the power relay (a way to win the match) or kill the hunters, and that's it for now, as other game modes besides "Hunt" may be added," so you'll have the play a couple matches and see for yourself." I don't get bored of the repetition, mainly because of how unique the game is, mostly because of the alien landscape, that sucks you in, making you feel like you're in an unknown world with unknown dangers.
In conclusion, I'd give this game a go, It's a great game to play with friends, and it's free, so why not give it a try?

- Multiplayer works well so far (I've only done private universe with a friend)

Cons:
- Menu options can be a bit cludgy - it took my friend and I about 10 minutes to figure out how to invite each other to our private universes.

- Limited graphics settings, but the basics are there and I expect this to change as development continues
- No linked inventories, which makes it a pain to drag the right resources from one piece of crafting furniture to another.

Costume Quest trades in item management and statistic tracking to focus more on mood and comedy. That's not to say there isn't an engaging RPG experience to be had here, it's just played a bit differently. You play as one of two siblings about to trick or treat on Halloween night. Whomever you pick, monsters mistake the other as a piece of candy because of their costume.
Thus begins a quest against the crusty Grubblins to rescue your own flesh and blood to avoid being grounded. These goblin-like Grublins are attempting to steal all of the candy from the houses in the neighborhood. So, to progress, you guessed it, trick or treat your♥♥♥♥♥off! It's a gamble, sometimes theres a friendly neighbor looking to rid themselves of late night sweets, while other doors open to a battle against the grubblins.
The battles are what set it apart from other RPGs. The various costumes you collect give you different abilities when worn into battle. They each have unique attacks and specials that charge during the battle. In addition, you collect Battle Stamps that give you various attacks and stat boosts for characters, which you may only equip one at a time. Despite how simple this system may sound, you are given a lot of freedom to create some interesting, fun, and dangerous combinations between costumes and stamps over the course of a full game.
It's short though, clocking in at about ten hours for me after finishing up all of the loose ends. I had a good time. Running from house to house along jack-o-lantern lit streets really made it feel like October and I was reminded of my own childhood experiences.
