Costume Quest is a cute, funny and short RPG where your abilities come from the costumes you wear and not the kids themselves. The cartoony visual art style just adds to the Halloween feel and has aged pretty well for a almost 7 year old game. The game is pretty easy and simplified with a battle system that kinda reminds me of a Mario RPG, as in you press some buttons or move a stick to make the moves stronger or take less damage when defending. The writing is pretty funny and adorable but the plot is pretty simple, not that it's a bad thing. The main game can also be beaten in just a day, it took me about 9 hours to complete it. It also comes with a mini adventure that happens after the main story that only takes about 2 hours. I recommend playing that after the main story because you keep all your items/costumes from the main game.
I only have a few issues with the game but nothing too terrible. Your character's movement is a bit stiff when outside of battle, kinda like tank controls but better. Like I said before dialog is really charming but the text auto scrolls pretty fast sometimes and it wasn't until I tried skipping a cutscene that I found out that you could pause it by pressing X/Square (if you're using a controller). Now my biggest issue with the game is the menus, at least with a controller. It's kinda annoying to move around the settings menu to change things. Instead of just pressing up/down to get to the next setting you have to press left/right, pressing up or down will for example raise or lower volume or what ever it is you're currently on.
Those are really my only issues with the game other than it being pretty easy, but even that isn't that bad seeing as it feels like it would make a good game to introduce someone younger into the RPG genre. For whatever reason this game makes me nostolgic even though I've only found out about it and it's sequal last year. This is definitely a game you'll want to play on October/Halloween, maybe with someone younger as well to share a fun memory with. The game is pretty easy to 100% as well if you're into that, the only achievement I have yet to get is the one where you have to play it on Christmas. The game is relatively cheap at only $10 and I say it's a must play if you want to play a Halloween game that isn't about the spooks. If you're still unsure about buying a short RPG for that much then wait for it to go on sale, I picked it and the sequal for about $5 and can't wait to play the second one next year!

Dishonored is broken at the most fundamental level; the player character is too overpowered. I don't mean this in a story context, where the player is a one man army God who decimates everyone (which he is.) I can forgive this style of gameplay for the sake of fun. What I mean by overpowered is that the abilities given to the player are so powerful you can ignore enemies and sprint/blink through every level, even on higher difficulties. This is enabled by level design that allows you to abuse your blink ability to cross vast distances and scale walls that make the game a cakewalk. Why bother killing/downing enemies when you can run past them all anyway. There is no downside to alerting guards when you can blink away from them. Couple that with a wallhack-type ability and you find yourself never in any danger. This completely kills any sense of suspense you're supposed to have in a "stealth" game.
I began my playthrough of the game attempting to do a pacifist playthrough. However, there is was a glaring flaw right off the bat: There are only two ways to takedown enemies without killing them. You can do a stealthy takedown, or use a sleep bolt from the crossbow. This is infinitely more boring than the dozens of abilities and weapons they give you to kill. This is coupled with the fact that you are incentivized to not kill in order to get the "good" ending. Not that you'll care about the story. Dishonored's motto is "tell, not show." None of the plot points that might make the player actually care about any of the characters are even shown, and those that are don't have any build-up.
I would only reccomend this game to those who want to go on a killing rampage with dozens of different methods to do so. Anyone looking for a story based game, or somthing akin to the original Thief, look elsewhere.

I wasn’t quite sure what to think of
when I first saw it on Steam. The artwork was decent and it was tagged as a visual novel so I decided to give it a try because it was free. When I got into the game I immediately regretted my decision. Playing as Samantha was very annoying and throughout the whole game I wanted to slap her.  All this over a bowl of oatmeal.
When you start the game you’re put into the shoes of a young college student named Samantha Browne who is hungry, however due to her social anxiety she has yet to feed herself and now has to grab a late night bite by going to the kitchen. Simple, right? Wrong. For some reason every choice Samantha makes causes her anxiety, from choosing which flavor of oatmeal to using the microwave. What makes matters worse is her inner monologue comes off as annoying and pretentious, the whole time spent trying to get her to feed herself all I could wonder was how she ever made it to college and how does she plan on making it in the real world. Some of her anxiety I could understand and relate to but most of it just made me roll my eyes, and there really isn’t any story besides her trying to eat.
Controls are easy, you use your mouse to click to make choices as you try to get Samantha fed. You have a anxiety meter at the top right that fills with each choice you make. Some choices only add a little bit while others add more, your goal is get your oatmeal and get back to your room without your anxiety meter filling up. I found the feature interesting, however, I didn’t like how every choice, no matter how small, gave Samantha anxiety. Choosing the wrong oatmeal flavor, waiting for water to boil, trying to use the microwave all made her anxious. My first playthrough I managed to easily feed her and get her back safely but couldn’t not do so without some anxiety building up. If your meter fills all the way up there are a variety of ways to lose; Samantha locks herself out of her room, Samantha doesn’t even leave her room and I imagine starves, Samantha drops her oatmeal and many others.
The artwork in the game is rather simplistic but still visually pleasing, the graphics help put a visual aspect to how anxiety feels. There is also some animation in the game which is a nice touch. I was quite fond of the mug Samantha used to make her oatmeal, it had a cat on it! The music isn’t bad, it fits the game and the sound effects were nice.
While I know everyone has different levels of anxiety and things that trigger it, I really just couldn’t relate to most of what Samantha was going through. I found it dumbfounding how she had such trouble just trying to feed herself, and I’m not even talking about the anxiety she felt having to maybe see people in the kitchen. I imagine some people can find this game relatable which I think is good and I applaud people using video games as a medium to tell emotional stories. Other than it being free and having Steam achievements I find it hard to recommend
, however if you have social anxiety or just want to see what it can be like then give it a shot, it’s very short.

I think what gets to me more than just an awful game is a game that could NOT have been awful. A game with potential to actually be fun and difficult and full of smooth techno dance music that helps you get into the jam. But this game just wasn't it. I can't say much about a game I've loggeed barely an hour on. But I promise there is a reason for that.
The premise of Rabbit Hole 3D is similar to games like Velocibox or to some extent Impossible Game, Geometry Dash, and Super Hexagon. They consist of one stagnant object (that you control) juxtaposed with a constantly moving surrounding area. These areas have tons of walls and colors and twists and turns that you as the poor afixed object must dodge while jamming out to hardcore techno. A lot of the times what makes these games so enticing isn't the challenge (and boy, can they be challenging) but the progression of the music as you go deeper and deeper into...the rabbit hole.
A lot of these games are made to be really hard--they're made to keep you pressing to keep going and jamming to that hardcore dubstep. You want to find out what happens next in the song or the space around you. And this time you'll get passed that hard jump...or turn...or whatever it is you just. keep. running. into.
And all of the above games I've mentioned would probably be way more fun than Rabbit Hole. Because a lot of the previously mentioned games don't have the one problem that Rabbit Hole DOES have: A shoddy camera.
Rabbit Hole's camera is presented behind you almost directly behind the box. You can't really tell your position on the plane--nor the position of the words. Everytime you move the camera jerks disorientingly with you--changing the angle to one that is even harder to differentiate. Am I in front of a hole or a letter?  Will I make it through or will I be forced to fall flat on my face and start ALL the way over? You can move what feels like infinitely left and right--but when it comes to up and down you can only move twice: once up and once down. It just feels awkward. You FEEL like you should be able to move similarly on the y axis as you do the x but you just can't. Why did you do this
...

The Bureau is a very different take on the XCOM universe... it was set in 1960's, height of cold war, when a jamming wave blanketed the nation, and aliens invaded Earth. With comm blackout, information is slow to trickle in, but it appears the nation's military had been crippled, and only XCOM, a command setup to take control in case of full war, is mankind's last hope.
At its heart Bureau is a tactical shooter where you control two other agents to deploy where you want them as well as deploy their special abilities, such as sniper hit, deploy turret, and so on. As the senior agent, you have abilities too, and you'll get more as time go on.
Graphics are quite good and the desolation in the middle of 1960's America is quite evocative. Agents were wearing suits and appropriate hairstyles, esp. the ladies.
There is also quite a bit of dialog, with choices you have to make (and they will affect the outcome, at least a little) a bit like Mass Effect series. Talk to other people in the base, for additional clues, expositions, notes, and whatnot that tells you more about the people you meet. Characterization is quite nice.
Managing the agents during a sort of "Matrix-like super-slo-mo" mode known as "Battle Focus" is the key here, where you place the agents at vantage points so they can engage the enemy effectively is key. Flanking is often the best way, as are using the environment such as explosive barrels (yes, that too).  As agents gain "rank" they also gain special abilities they can deploy. The key is to deploy them at the right place at the right time, and that's your job as commander.
The Aliens are nicely animated and sprints into and out of cover and will attempt to flank if possible. However, they are not very bright can can be outsmarted. Later you'll run into bosses, like Mutons and Sectopods (walkers), though most are just Greys. There are occasional elites and commanders. Commanders are tough as they can give shields to other units, but that just makes them vulnerable to strikes when they do that. Add drones, turrets, and you can be in a tough fight.
This alternate history is a lot of fun to play in. It is highly recommended if you like the genre.

The Bureau – XCom Declassified was announced before XCom – Enemy Unknown and so – as many other all-time fans of the XCom/UFO-series - I was quite disappointed that 2K is going to make the sequel of one of the milestones of turn-based strategy games a shooter. With XCom – Enemy Unknown released and being a worthy successor to the series my initial rage faded away. So now that I don't have to treat The Bureau as a sequel but rather a spin-off, curiosity made me buy this title. And to my surprise I was quite pleased with the approach 2K took on the theme – at first.
The XCom setting is transferred into the late 1950ies with the USA suffering from anti-communist paranoia. The first abductions, alien attacks and UFO sightings are misinterpreted as a soviet invasion by authorities.
If you played any XCom titles you will get familiar with your enemies, weapons and abilities quickly. Also in the XCom-HQ, which you can roam and explore between field missions, you will find all the well-known departments like Engineering, R&D, Hangars and Infirmary. Merging the 1950ies with the XCom theme breathes new life into the franchise and works quite well. I liked to see my sniper wearing a vest and tie while aiming for a hostile commander or my Tech/Engineer wearing some ordinary janitor jumpsuit while blasting Sectoids into smithereens.
During missions you control your own character and via the command interface, which significantly slows down the time and allows to scan the surroundings, you can issue orders to two additional agents. Even though it's a 3rd person view you will use well-known tactics you would use in the strategy games as hide and cover, flank the enemies and focus fire. Success heavily relies on the use of those tactics as well as yours and your agents special abilities like mind-control, critical strike and deploying additional equipment as turrets, mines and drones. So The Bureau actually is a tactical shooter and run and gun will get you killed.
Unfortunately the game constantly prevents you from using these tactics. The missions are (as the whole game) heavily scripted and linear. Approaching a hostile encounter is always announced by a checkpoint save and a cliff, high boxes or another obstacle you have to jump off down into the battlearena. In the first half of the game these battlearenas are so small and the provided possibilities for cover so few, that you don't have much choice where to deploy agents and what tactics to use. In fact it feels like a longwinded tutorial.
In the second half of the game the battlearenas get much larger and you have a lot of possibilities to flank enemies and can diversify your tactics. Unfortunately your character has a very restricted area of command. So I have my heavy gear guy flank the enemy on the right side while sending my sniper to a vantage point. But as soon as I move my character and any of my agents aren't covered by the area of command anymore, they start closing in to me ignoring any enemies or any order given beforehand.
The poor technical optimization is the second major annoyance. Even though I have a decent gaming rig, I wasn't able to play with DX11 but had to turn down to DX9 and even then I had <30fps until I turned off the PhysX features. This game devours system resources without giving much back.
But even more annoying than the above-mentioned are all the inconsistencies of the plot. You will find dialogues missing, making some answers given by NPCs meaningless. And despite the story has a nice twist in the later part of the game, you will feel there are parts missing and obviously the world and the plot were meant to be more fleshed out in the first place. At least the german voice acting is quite good.

As of 1/22/2017:
I've been really impressed with what's been put together so far. The developer's description of the game as in early beta is fairly accurate. The game is plenty playable, with a lot of core elements already in place, although the content can be burned through fairly quickly. At the current state, once you've built all the essential structures and crafted a space ship, you're pretty much done. That said, it's still plenty fun to roam around, and currently I'm busy getting a colony on the second planet built.
There are a lot of improvements that could be made. For example, the game world is pretty small, and it's not procedurally generated, so there's not really a lot to explore. Also, it's a little too easy to craft everything and become self-sufficient. It would be a bit more engaging to have limited access to crafting, using the skill tree to gradually climb the tech tree.
It also feels like surviving should be more of a struggle. In particular, oxygen is a bit too much of a free resource. Suits only lose it when they're ruptured, and inflatable domes and airlocks provide unlimited supply. Food and water are similar. Once you have a bio-dome, berries provide unlimited food, and water reclaimers provide unlimited water. I feel like both should need at least an occasional resupply of oxygen and hydrogen.
The skill tree system also needs work. I get the sense the current system is sort of a proof of concept, but still, the system for gaining skill points is awkward and sometimes tedious. The proficiencies system also doesn't seem to have any real function beyond being a way to get skill points, making it a bit redundant.
That said, this is all just constructive criticism. The game is looking really great so far, and I'm looking forward to future developments.

TL;DR- Good game, lots of potential, 7/10.
Gameplay----- This game truly is amazing in terms of gameplay, but could be a lot better. Building and finding resources is kind of a grind. Mineral placement definitely needs to be improved, but otherwise, it's great. The feeling that comes with being able to build things is extremely rewarding. I wish you could interact with satellites that you haven't built, but that's okay for now. Space travel is easy and can be done in a jiffy.
Combat----- Combat is kind of iffy, but easy if you're good at aiming at things. Some creatures really need to be nerfed/changed up a bit. For example, the Parasyte really needs to be removed or nerfed. I was mining rubber from a tree and suddenly blood splattered onto my screen and my character's view shot up to the sky. I pulled out a pistol and looked around, but couldn't see anything(it was nighttime on Proteus 2, the moon that you start off on). I finally found a Parasyte scuttling around and trying to eat me. I couldn't get a bead on it, so I ran back to my base with a quarter of my health remaining. I had to boost jump onto the top of my biodome and camp there while I used a medkit and my ground turret took the Parasyte out. Skeliopods are annoying, but not too overpowered if they're not in a group with other skeliopods. Giant crabs are really easy to kill. Colossi are weird, because I didn't know whether they were hostile or not. Apparently they're not, but the colossus that I found broke away from its herd to come over to me and splatter blue liquid all over me. I didn't know whether it was trying and failing to kill me or if that was just its way of greeting me. I ran away, and eventually I lost it. Aziel is a lot worse, though, because there are hardly ever any Cow Giraffes visible and a lot more Salamanders than there needs to be. I wish the developers could increase its health but decrease its speed, and at least add some animation when the Salamander notices you and starts zipping through the ice at supersanik speed. I would rate combat a 7/10.
Graphics/Visuals----- This game has BEAUTIFUL graphics. Only thing about visuals that I would suggest is making it easier to see on Aziel at night. I crashed so hard I lost half my spaceship's health because I couldn't distinguish between the ground and the sky. I rate graphics a 10/10.
Bugs/Glitches----- The bugs are truly the worst thing about this game. There are two specific game-breaking bugs that I would like to address. One of them is losing your spaceship in some remote part of the world when your game crashes. My game crashed for the first time in my 11 hours of playing it a few days ago. I was reentering Proteus's atmosphere when my game crashed. I reloaded the game to find I had respawned in the middle of nowhere in Proteus. The same thing happened to my friend shortly after. We had to craft two whole new spaceships because we went in our other friend's ship into space to look for our ships, but we found them in the skybox, unreachable. Later, I went back to space in my new ship and saw my old, lost ship in reachable range, hurtling towards the blue gas giant with rings, so I couldn't reach it. One day on Proteus, I equipped my locator tool and eventually I found BOTH of our spaceships lying in the dust, in perfectly good condition, next to a giant Indlewrath skeleton. Now we have 5 ships, two of which we don't need. Another bug happened when my friends stored their belongings in repairdroids and hoverbikes, since we were too lazy to go all the way to our depositories on the other side of Proteus 2. We all left the game and rejoined later to find that all of our items were gone, along with the droids and hoverbikes which we couldn't find even with a locator. Nobody had access to our universe except us, and it was a private universe. Please fix these ASAP. I rate the bugs a 2/10.

First impression: concentration game
I have played 5/42 (?) levels. The premise of this game is to make all squares the same color. There are 6 colors, and you can change them in a circular fashion (both ways): Red-Yellow-Green-Cyan-Blue-Magenta-Red. The game adds difficulty by having a "time bomb" (10 second timer on a changing square) in some levels, and in some levels squares also add their colors to neighboring squares where indicated. (There may be other mechanics in later levels.) The puzzles are not really that hard, but they take concentration because if you mis-step, your score suffers.
I did not like that the game offers 6 changes on each color when only two of them work; and I missed keyboard shortcuts for the changes. Otherwise, the interface is doing its job well.
The game was not able to hold my interest for long because I found it more tedious than challenging.

This game is pretty damn hard. It looks really simple but you have to memorize which combination does what and then be able to do that in a timely manner for the timed levels and be able to see a couple of moves ahead to complete the levels with the arrows in them (from the trailer.)
Something that isn't in the game or at least not explained that well is how the combinations work. Here they are:
Starting with the block followed by what it is combined with then what that ends up making. Colors stay in their teirs (additive and subtractive) and do not combine with each other. It took me a while to figure that out to be quite honest and I think this will help you out if you're interested:
blue w/red=megenta
blue w/green=cyan
green w/blue=cyan
green w/red=yellow
red w/blue=magenta
red/wgreen=yellow
magenta w/cyan=blue
magenta w/yellow=red
cyan w/yellow=green
cyan w/magenta=blue
yellow w/cyan=green
yellow w/magenta=red
So basically you have different worlds that have a base block color that all the puzzles will require you to turn all the blocks in to. The first is red. You can see the first level in the trailer if you need more of a detailed explanation:
Click on a block.
6 colored wheel comes up that you can choose from (even though only two work)
Choosing a color from the wheel combines the two colors into whichever one I said it would above this.
Repeat until they're all the color you want.
Sounds simple in principle, but I did not find it to be. The difficulty spiked pretty fast. As another con, there is no settings button I could find. It's fullscreen only with the ability to silence the music or not and the ability to view the credits (do people do that?).
Honestly, this game seems pretty damn great and the only real reason it could be such a challenge is because the color combinations are not what I learned. I learned red, blue and yellow were the main three colors of the world, with blue and yellow making green instead of red and green making yellow. It's all pretty backwards to me and goes against what I was taught since I was a kid.
I'll update this if I find anything horribly wrong in the later part of the game but since all the reviews are hidden currently I figured I'd throw this one out there with such little playtime. This game seems to be worth $3, no doubt. However, as previously stated, I think this is a really challenging puzzle game and will definitely not be for everyone. Get this if you think your a puzzle god or if you want a challenge.

Enjoyable HOG with a solid soundtrack and artwork that verges on the surreal. This one has a different system to any other HOG I've played. In the adventure game portion, you usually need to combine multiple objects to progress, and the objects you need are shown in an inventory group per puzzle. Most of the objects you need are hidden in the landscape rather than being gated behind a puzzle or lock, effectively making every screen a hidden object scene. There are also a lot of nice touches that make the game stand out: fast travel, collectibles that you can backtrack to if you miss, and an inventory pane that stays locked open. There are a couple of negatives: sometimes it doesn't register clicks, and the bonus adventure is pretty ordinary but mandatory to unlock many of the achievements. Anyway, this is one of the best HOGs, I reckon.

The animation is appallingly "my face is pasted on".  The story railroads you through puzzles; you can't start a puzzle until you have clicked on exactly the right object to trigger it, even if you're constantly finding objects that are obviously clues.
Pass on this one.

Even though Artifex Mundi works with various developers, their game have a very coherent taste. I played a couple of them and I currently have pretty low requirements put in their Hidden Object games - I assume the graphics of visited areas are going to be charming, puzzles are going to re-use the same mechanics I've seen in the other games, music and sound effects are going to have a quality of a royalty-free asset stores, voice acting and the general plot are going to be cheesy and silly without a single drop of originality and the game is going to be a fun experience... as long as you are ready for some "so bad it's good" moments.
Be ready to laugh at some points. Not with the game, but at it. I was surprised that there was no specific McGuffin to chase this time, but for some reasons the games related to Artifex Mundi keep cutting budgets for writers. This time the "writing" is bad, but not terrible.
However, the general interface is very friendly this time. In most Hidden Object games you are gathering items and putting them wherever you can, what sometimes resembles old-school adventure games with absurd puzzles following no logic whatsover. In The Beanstalk, however, requires you to first look around, activate some areas, and then gather around listed items needed to overcome the obstacles. It's difficult to describe it to someone who hasn't played other games from Artifex Mundi yet, but generally the game has much more of "looking for hidden objects" elements and less "solve puzzles" elements. What is definitely welcome in this case, since our character is basically a wizard and often solves her problems with out-of-this-world objects such as talismans, spell books or magic powders.
Beanstalk was one of the better hidden objects game I've played and I would give it probably a 5, maybe 6/10. But I have to recommend it anyway - these games just have such a relaxing feeling for me and no matter how dumb I find them, I like to play a one or two of them every couple of months. If you find yourself to share my taste, you should be satisfied with Fairy Tale Mysteries 2.
However, If you don't like hidden object games at all, this one would be a waste of time for you.

In Fairy Tale Mysteries 2: The Beanstalk you're once again asked by the Grimm Brothers to help them investigate. This time you need to help a young boy named Jack who, of course, comes across magical beans. The story is much more interesting than the first one, in my opinion it just feels much more magical than the first one did as well.
Where the first game tried to follow the usual HOG formula and did it (in my opinion) well, this sequel tried to add something new. From the very first interactive screen you can already tell that something has changed: every item has turned into its own hidden object puzzle!
Each item you need to interact with now has its own inventory where you first have to collect certain parts all over the world before you get that item. This also means you can't collect anything until you've unlocked the inventory it belongs to. In my own opinion, this is incredibly annoying and forces you do to much more backtracking than necessary.
But the game, of course, also features the regular hidden object puzzles. Contrary to the first game, this time you also have interactive hidden objects as indicated by their green names. I feel like HOGs with interactive items are generally easier since they don't have to rely on having their items blend into the background. The first game definitely had this problem.
If I could, I would give this game a mixed review. I was definitely frustrated by the changes it made, but I'm sure other players will appreciate the extra layer of hidden objects. Just know what you're getting yourself into.

This game is amazing. Admittedly, my experience with visual novels is a bit lacking (consisting mostly of Analogue: A Hate Story, Hate Plus, and various Twine games), but I have a feeling that Hatoful Boyfriend is probably not quite representative of a typical Japanese dating sim VN (and not just because of the birds).
I don't want to spoil too much of the story, but it frequently veers pretty far off the beaten path. Japanese High school dating sim VNs have never really appealed to me too much as a general concept, but this game is much, much more than just a dating sim. The stories are wildly varied depending on your choices and what ending you're going for. There is thankfully a fast-forward button to get right to different choices to see how they play out, as well as ample save slots for saving before important choices.
And I'd
recommend playing through every ending (don't be afraid to use a guide after your first playthrough). Each ending is interesting and varied on its own, but also because it unlocks a special epilogue story that's actually much longer than a normal playthrough. And the epilogue is
worth playing through - it gives a lot of background information on how the (evidently post-apocalyptic) society came about, and explains a lot of the backstories of the birds and the world you inhabit. It does drag on a bit near the end, but I'm really glad I played through to the end.
If you like visual novels you'll love this game. If you don't like visual novels you'll still love this game because it's hilarious and weird and delightful. It certainly delivers a silly tongue-in-cheek bird dating parody, but it's so much more than that. Buy it.

I'm not entirely sure why people dislike this game. If it was before the SWAT update, maybe, but I've been having an absolute blast with this. I played the first game a bit and I had some fun with it but I never really got into it. Fortunately for me, this game is quite different from the first. This game is kind of reminescent of Hell Divers. You level up, you unlock (craft) new weapons/armor/food/meds/etc, you have a hub world, and the story progression consists of quests from a variety of sources. One of the coolest things, though, is the hub world. You're placed in what seems like a small area but the more you explore the larger and larger it is, it's actually pretty damn huge. In this world you are able to build what starts as a measly camp, but can be built up to a full blown zombie proof fortress. This game can get very intense when your friend accidentally runs into a horde, attracting 20+ zombies, not all of which are slow and incapable. Some zombies can keep up with your sprinting speed and there is no outrunning them. Night time is dark and atmospheric, leaving you partially dependant on your flashlight.
The combat mechanics aren't perfectly polished, especially melee, but it's not bad. I enjoy how the ranged combat is set up. You are required to aim/focus on an enemy in order to get a headshot, otherwise you don't do nearly as much damage. Melee is very simple but can be very satisfying at times. It consists of 2-3 press combos and different attacks modified by movement as well as the option to finish of stunned enemies with a variety of different fatalities.
Something pretty unique that this game does is how your characters and camps work. You can have a total of three characters. You can have a Local, Public, and Private character. Each character can only play in camps of corresponding permissions. Public camps are run on dedicated servers and are always open for anybody to join. The camp Admin can decide whether or not to have friendly fire and how much, change player default permissions and raise (or lower to ♥♥♥♥ with) friends permissions or ban whoever.
----------
* Fight zombies and other creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥
* Hunt zombie animals for food and hides (soon to have non zombie animals as well)
* Loot and fight in towns, swamps, and forests.
* Explore a good variety of maps and a large hub world.
* Craft weapons, ammo, attatchments, armor, a large variety of medicines and tinctures, cook food, and create a variety of drinks.
* Turkeys.
* Build a base with many different resource and crafting structures, defenses, and traps.
* Upgrade structures, many of which change appearance as they progress.
* Test said base with survival horde challenges.
* Level up your camp as well as yourself and a quite large list of skills.
* Kick complete♥♥♥♥♥with your friends tag teaming zombies or get tag teamed by zombies and other creepy♥♥♥♥♥♥
* Have complete multiplayer freedom. Players in a camp are not confined to playing the same quests at the same time. Some people can be at camp, some people can be doing multiple quests all at the same time.
* Probably starve and suffer of dehydration.
* Most likely die because of said suffering.
* Grind.

So They Are Billions is an addictive base-defense RTS, with great visual polish and a good concept.
However, I feel it suffers from some issues that ultimately all form to make a really annoying experience:
1: The AI pathfinding is horrendous. Units will just run on the spot and fail to get to their destination. This gets your units killed more than I'd like to admit.
2: The game often generates near-impossible maps even on very low difficulties, where enemy doom-settlements are so close that if you build any defenses they just start spawning out fast zombies earlier than they should (And if you wait, they do it and you can't win due to lack of defenses)
3: The game seems to be built strictly for just one effective strategy. If you do anything it doesn't want you to, you will lose. If you even use your starting soldier, you will lose due to zombie aggro, if you don't only build rangers for weeks, you will lose due to horde aggro, if you build a single defensive tower before it wants you to, it will spawn the mini-hordes early and you will lose.
I can completely forgive the usual early-access stuff like how it will freeze very rarely from time to time, or how it hangs if you alt-tab, but the few things above really do make it an annoying experience.
When the game manages to spawn a forgiving map and you make it past like day 20, you can have an insanely great time with this game. I feel the problem is the game hasn't found the balance between bad implementation and being actually difficult. I'd like to note I've beaten the game's maps a couple of times and I've lost a few times too. The final mega hordes of zombies are actually insanely fun. Getting to the point where you can play past the opening 5 minutes is legitimately unfair though.
When its issues are fixed, my negative review will become a positive one ASAP, but for now it suffers from some design and implementation issues that it should take this opportunity of early access to fix.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a third-person squad-based tactical/cover shooter recommended for its excellent atmosphere and storytelling - as long as you can look past some really glaring gameplay, technical, and franchise continuity problems. Broadly, this is an XCOM game set in the 1960s, and stripped of all strategy elements in favor of a hero-driven storyline and real-time combat elements. Does it work? Sort of. Is it fun anyway? Yep.
If you haven't played XCOM before, the basics are pretty simple: Earth faces an invasion by hostile and technologically superior alien forces. An American secret government agency (XCOM, or here, "the Bureau") scrambles to confront the threat. Unlike the XCOM strategy games, here you control a single character - Agent Carter, a prototypical troubled hero, as he leads three-man assault squads on guns-blazing missions through numerous portions of the alien-infested USA and beyond, spending time between each mission trooping around the Bureau's secret underground headquarters uncovering backstory.
Always remember, this isn't XCOM like you know and probably love. It's not a strategy game. It's a single-player shooter campaign that is almost entirely linear and provides little or no replay value. The campaign is broken down into six major combat missions, each of which takes about an hour to play through. There are also about seven minor combat missions (depending on DLC), which take 20-30 minutes each and pop up at defined points along the way. The remainder of a 15-20 hour playthrough consists of time spent at the Bureau's base between each major mission, during which time you can chat with a few NPCs; manage your roster of agents; and discover ever-changing expository info-drops (recordings and texts). Completing investigations unlocks "dispatch" missions, which are essentially NPC missions  that allow you to level up agents that you don't take with you on Carter's missions. That's it. There is NO STRATEGY ELEMENT: if you want tech research, base building, tight budgeting, and intel ops, play the real XCOM.
That said, the game does a few things right. First: world-building, both stylistically and through story-telling. As for style, it's the 1960s - the conversative '60s that wish it was still 1945. The stars are the guys that thought the Vietnam War was a really good idea. They are the suits, the G-men, with top-secret files, fedoras, cigarettes and flasks, helicopters and machine guns. They run the country, keep civilians in the dark, cover up their mistakes, torture their prisoners, drop untold billions into weapons R&D, obviously discriminate against women and minorities, and, of course, work to save the world. They'll be darned if they're going to be licked by some bug-eyed aliens. This is fun, the way Mad Men is fun, largely because people used to have some frickin style, despite their many other faults.
Beyond style, there is also a pretty great B-movie sci-fi story underlying everything, if B-movie sci-fi had better special effects. The missions themselves have a lot of memorable story moments - the first major mission in a sleepy college town stands out for me, as does a later mission involving a dam - but the story really develops back at the base. Through talking to other Bureau staff and perusing the numerous photos, short texts, and recordings, you really start to get immersed in the effort to fight the alien threat. Which is great.
The other thing they did right was the game's combat. It is FUN. I was blasting aliens, and I really, really like blasting aliens. As a third person tactical/cover shooter, its mechanics will be familiar. They are stolen almost entirely - and pretty successfully - from the Mass Effect games. Cover is easy to handle, and the camera is solid. The mission setup is "arena" staging, meaning you run through basically linear levels, going through empty parts that build atmosphere, and arriving at areas that are set up for game combat, with lots of ammo lying around, cover to hide behind, and enemies waiting to get blasted. I played with a gamepad, DX11 with Vsync enabled. The controls felt a little soft at first but I eventually got used to them. The graphics are very nice and my machine stuttered a little bit when things got really hectic, but this did not detract from gameplay. The fights felt really kinetic and hectic but not out of control, with solid enemy AI at the higher difficulties, fast pace, and a sense of danger. Good stuff.
But all was not perfect. The squad combat, sadly, kind of sucks. Backing up a moment, you take two teammates with you on each mission. There are four types of soldier to choose from, with each class having a few unique abilities to unlock. There is minimal customization: you can decide which weapon to give them (which isn't very helpful, because each class can only use a few of the available weapons, and you always just want to give them the best one you've unlocked), and choose them a bonus buff (a bizarre "backpack" mechanic). Not great, but fine for what it is. In the field, you have control over where your mates set up, and where and when they will unleash their special abilities. You control them via a popup rotary menu that slows time - all very Mass Effect - and it is SO CLOSE to not sucking. The problem is your squaddies are suicidal idiots. They don't stay where you put them, so flanking is practically impossible. They get killed constantly unless you keep them behind you. AND they don't do much damage. So you basically babysit. The game would have been better without them, frankly. Nonetheless, once you figure out how to manage them combat goes back to being fun - just a little more broken than it should be.
The problems really start up once you get back from missions and have to wander around the base, which is about a third of the game. Notwithstanding the story elements and a couple of nicely atmospheric rooms, the base really feels sterile. I think this is because they felt compelled to render it in 3D and it suffers from the same problem a lot of 3D environments have - it's really hard to make them feel alive. Most of your time there is spent walking (annoyingly, sprinting is disable in-base) from place to place. This is BORING. Then, when you find somebody to talk to, you are forced into a dialogue prompt setup that again is stolen from Mass Effect, but this time badly. There are dialogue options, kind of, but it is totally pointless because it has no larger impact on the story, and there is really just one conversation that the developers want you to hear. The "investigations" that characters give you consequently end up feeling like pointless make-work, rather than fun story elements. Also, the lip-synching is comically bad, which is a shame because the voice acting is actually pretty good. Perhaps showing my age, I found myself wishing for the TCS Tiger's Claw from the first Wing Commander game. Just put the people I need to talk to in front of me and let me click on them! Something more streamlined and not 3D would have been a daring move and probably would have saved the otherwise poor base situation. Oh well.
Finally, I have to mention the continuity thing. The idea is that this is an XCOM origin story. So there is a massive alien invasion, with basically the same tech, and mass deaths worldwide, and the government makes huge strides toward understanding it all, and (sarcastic spoiler alert here), wins (duh), and then in the "future" XCOM games nobody has heard of any of this. There is some hand-waving about blacking out the files and misdirecting the public, but... really? It's unfortunate that they had to shoehorn the XCOM stuff into what would have been a perfectly fun game (probably more fun) without it.
And that's it. Verdict: a memorable and entertaining once-through adventure with some flaws that probably get more attention than they deserve. I largely enjoyed the game, despite its flaws.

I have played all of the XCOM games and love the series, so being able to play a third-position shooter take on the XCOM universe was very nice and refreshing.
If you like the series, alien themes, third-person action shooters, and squad-based tactics, you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are fantastic with lots of special effects in the form of mutons (mutations taken from the alien technology). The music fits very well with the theme and setting - it is appropriately intense whenever the action calls for it.
The controls are fairly straightforward, and the tutorial mission is great at helping you understand both the controls and how to issue orders to your squad without being too long or too boring. The learning curve is moderate, however, the game can be extremely unforgiven in the commander (hardest) difficulty. There is permanent death if your squad members are downed and not revived in time on commander difficulty; furthermore, reviving them only stabilizes them - meaning they are out of combat until the instance is cleared of all enemies. I am playing on this difficulty, and have had many situations where I had to slow-play and defeat all the enemies on my own. Your squad members are heavily reliant on your orders, especially in the harder difficulties.
The story is pretty good, and there is a lot of extras provided in the form of audio recordings and files if you choose to look for them.
The gameplay reminded me a lot of Mass Effect, down to the very first muton power you unlock for your character - lift. The feedback is very good, showing the enemy's health at the top center of the screen, and having large grenade icons warning you of the blast radius. During battles, you can go into battle focus, which slows down time to a crawl and allows you to issue your orders. There is a range where you can order your squadmates to move/do actions, which I found to be very nice. You can have two weapons equipped at a time, and you will slowly unlock new equipment (the first being a bag that increases your headshot damage). You may have only 2 other active squad members at a time.
Cover is extremely important, as the enemy will try to actively flank you and can become very aggressive. Most combat instances will have a few ammo drops to refill your weapons, and explosive barrels are littered in many areas to help you kill mobs of enemies quickly.
As you gain experience, you will level up and can choose different perks for both you and your teammates. There is a decent variety of customization - you can change every agent's clothing color (pretty basic), and their background changes the type of perks that can be unlocked. You can recruit new agents, and when you do this you will be given an option to choose both their class and their background (ex: engineer class with technical expertise, leading to faster cooldowns on abilities).
The XCOM base is not as explorable as I'd like, but it is still fun to walk around and talk to people - or read the extra content like agent dossiers.
There are a number of side missions for you to play and unlock more mutons. Completing these help you gain levels and increase your psychic arsenal to defeat the alien invaders.
Very good game, especially if you are a fan of the series.
Definitely recommend!

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a science fiction video game in the X-COM series, developed by 2K Marin and released by 2K Games for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.
The Bureau is a third-person shooter with an emphasis on squad-based tactics.
The player controls the agent William Carter and commands two additional agents in each mission. Carter has his own unique abilities, but other agents are divided into the Commando, Engineer, Support, and Recon classes. By entering "Battle Focus Mode", which slows time significantly, the player can order their agents to move to strategic positions and activate class-specific abilities. Agents have customizable outfits, weapons, equipment and abilities. As in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, soldiers will suffer from permanent death and if Carter is unable to revive agents who have taken too much damage, they will die (variable difficulty levels also determine whether or not it is possible for downed agents to become battle-ready when revived, or if replacement agents will appear during a mission).

A quite interesting short choice making game based on social anxiety and a college girl dealing with it. Very simplistic, however conveys a great, although subjective, "adventure" of a girl who faces choices to combat or avoid her anxiety provoking actions. Very interesting, definitely worth a quick playthrough as it won't take too long to finally cook her oatmeal correctly. A linear game, but that doesn't take away from the main concept that it is portraying, the struggle with anxiety in even the most lackluster of actions.
The story itself had a charming appeal, realistic as well. Don't expect any "action" or adventure, this is like a "choose your own ending" game where you just try to make your way to a happy ending.

Sometimes I think I get more out of short, free indie games than I do out of fifty hours playing a big title smash hit.
I think the point of this charming point-in-click is not to make the player feel pity for Samantha Browne because of her difficulties with social anxiety disorder, but instead to generate greater empathy and understanding. People live this way. All the time. It's not really an illness needing to be cured or fixed or pitied. Just to be better appreciated.
Also, probably, to some degree or another, the majority of gamers can relate to, or have been, or are Samantha Browne.

Costume Quest is not revolutionary or cutting edge. It doesn't reinvent the wheel. What it is, however, is a lot of fun. It's very charming and brings back the childhood nostalgia of Halloween. The combat is similiar of games like Mario RPG or South Park the Stick of Truth. It is turned based RPG with timing based attacks. Different costumes have different abilities both for puzzle solving, and for combat. It is not a game that is intensely deep, it's just a blast to play. Lighthearted good fun. I would recommend it to anyone, especially during October.

Costume Quest has it's fair share of flaws such as a simple and repetitive combat system, unimagitive enemy designs and a preference to a offensive playstyle.
Thankfully, most of these issues can be overlooked because of the game's heart and charisma, which drips from every inch of it's writing and visuals.
If this game was a generic fantasy RPG, it would be considered a failure. However, thanks to the comedic talent of Double Fine, Costume Quest is instead a fun Halloween romp that you won't forget anytime soon.

Graphics are very nice, background music is very mood setting, lots of puzzles, repetative combat but unique costumes to try in each battle, not too short of a game just about the right length for me. Overall a very fun little game.

There's nothing about Costume Quest that makes it extremely impressive. It's not the sort of game to end up on a game of the year list, and it's not the sort of game you show off to all your friends. Unlike most games i play, there isn't any super unique or innovative mechanic that really makes the game stand out from other rpg's, but it does enough to be above average.
The story is that on Holloween night you are a boy/girl who goes trick or treating with your brother/sister until he/she is kidnapped by monsters. Goblins not only want to eat your family member, but they want ALL OF THE CANDY. However you can stand up to them, thanks to the powers given to you by your Holloween costumes! Your goal is to go on an adventure meeting new kids and going all around town in order to chase down the monsters and save your sibling!
The actual combat is the classic turn based combat formula. You take to the field using the power of whatever costume your wearing to tear down those ruthless baddies! This time it has been has been given a twist, badges and quick time events! This reminded me a lot of Paper Mario TTYD (like my #1 game of all time), but the quick time events are less precise than paper marios and if you don't use more than the basic moveset it becomes extremely repetetive. This is where badges come in to add variety to your game, except the badges are mostly uninteresting stat boosts that do very little to change up how you play (unlike Paper Mario where the badges completely defined your playstyle). I found the combat engaging enough to hold my interest throughout the game; it falls into the same pitfall most turn based combat does where all your abilities feeling too similar and achieve the same goal. Combat is not Costume Quest's strong suit.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. There's this childrens bedtime story vibe to the whole game that i found really fitting because the entire story feels like a kid playing pretend. From the costumes giving you powers to the adults not seeing monsters, the game has this make-believe quality where you half think the whole game is a facade but you're caught up in sillyness of it all so you don't care.
What i enjoyed most in the game was just exploring the world. Throughout the multiple zones you have a costumes and candy (and monsters) to discover through exploration and use of your super powers. The game makes good use of the Holloween setting. Every zone has houses to trick or treat at, and each house can either give you a candy giving adult or an evil monster who will want to fight. If you pick this game up pay attention to the dialog and talk to as many NPC's as you can because it'll give you a good chuckle. There's all sorts of cute characters to talk to, all of whom set a contrast to the spooky monsters.
The game isn't going to do anything to blow your mind, and that's ok. With everyone running around the indie market trying to be the next Bastion, i enjoy these games that focus on being cute and fun. If what i've written sounds pleasent, give Costume Quest a try and see if you'll like it.

I played a lot the first part and of course the driving physics are nothing to write home about, but there was a certain feeling to the free roaming going 300km/h in a cabrio Lamborghini or such cars in a huge island, and simply (and very sadly) there is no other game like this, that you can buy houses and nice cars in nice locations. So i didn't hesitate much when i purchased the second for like 20 euros or so. After investing 30 hours in it i realized the developers concentrated and tryed to improve on the wrong aspects of the first game to make this sequel. Which resulted in a worse game than the first.
The cop chases are downright broken. I like challenge, but the police cars coming straight at you with 200+km/h in a one direction road, and every few seconds. I think this is a major fault in this sequel. I remember the first TDU and there was nothing like this, the cop chases were fun and challanging in the same time. In a driving game this is important for me.
Also collecting points for making facial surgeries? Are you kidding me? I can get past this, as you can just ignore this feature, but this kind of mentality is visible throughout the game. Even if you dont want to, the game reminds you that you should be wanting to become the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of all time. Some cars have their gear rations mixed up. I realized in a few cars,i think they were Lotuses, that their 3rd gear is higher than their 4th. Basically these two gear ratios are swapped.
I understand they couldn't implement proper collision physics into the game with real life cars. But this is as far from test driving as possible nowadays. But at least the first TDU could somehow make me forget this. I was eager to get all the nice cars, and get some villas in nice locations. But the more i discovered and tryed out in the second part the more i got disillusioned. I just deleted it and i can not reccomend it to anyone, especially at this price. Maybe at a massive discount, but even then, you should stick with the first part in my opinion.

A lot of people are complaining about stupid things, but I will be honest with you.
Going free to play is hands-down the best move that the people working on Evolve could have made. The game from what I could tell was dying harshly before going F2P, with only a couple hundred players being online at a time at peak hours, so it was very difficult trying to get a game going, especially for new players.
Post-F2P release, they changed quite a bit about the game that does affect the balance and how matches play out. Some are good and were pretty much required to prevent certain cheeky tactics from working whilst other changes are simply awful.
What I'm going to discuss are the changes that should have never been implemented.
The first change being that there are now round timers in place. The round timers force monsters to be on the back foot at all times, applying pressure where it is not necessary and causing them to make mistakes or force them into their deaths (because this timer will freeze whenever the monster enters combat).
Something to take note of is that
as they did not destroy the objective in time. That alone is bull because it is up to the hunters to be able to hunt the monster quickly and effectively. Why shouldn't it be that when the timers runs down that the Hunters lose because they didn't kill what they were hunting in time? It begs the question why it is even there to begin with which is what I'm trying to get at - do not think I am trying to argue for the timer to be changed to be in the Monster's favor. I'm going to be blunt before people start strawmanning:
This timer, as you may have already seen in negative reviews, completely decimates the "sneaky monster" strategy that some monster players employ to avoid confrontation with hunters at all times (myself included). Because of the round timer, monsters can no longer take as much time as they have to to sneak around the map and hunting wildlife when they see opportunities to. Instead, they now have to rush faster than they are used to even if it means getting caught by an Arena (where it can be avoided easily by taking your time).
While playing sneaky is still possible, it's not a viable strategy anymore as the meta has changed to rush down wildlife as quickly as you can, getting Arena'd and surviving (or taking out the Trapper/hunter that placed the Arena), then dashing out and hunting more, repeat until you win or lose. It's pretty silly that this is the meta we're in right now, which brings me to my next point.
For asymmetrical games, it's not good to have a meta strategy for one side - one "go-to or be crippled" strategy. The biggest thing about asymmetrical games is to have a variety of tactics you can use to gain whatever advantage you can. Hunters have this in stock since they can build a team and chain perks together to synergize well. Monsters don't get this opportunity at all. It's either stack damage, cooldown reduction, or traversal cooldown perks and that's it. With only one strategy that works so well and trumps all others, you can't really use any other perk to synergize with the strategy you want. Again,
A third point that I wasn't really happy with was the Planet Scanner. This is another thing that kind of defeats the "sneaky monster" strategy since it points in the exact direction you are in, no strings attached. This issue isn't too bothersome and it's pretty easy to play around
Unless they changed this and I missed the patch notes about it: If you are within a certain range (I think 50 meters?) of the hunters and they use the Planet Scanner, it will actually highlight you. That last bit is my biggest issue that I have with it. It should not highlight you when you are close to the hunters when they use PS.
Other than the issues I stated, any issues I have had that I would have mentioned here were actually fixed in the most recent patch, so it's great that they are constantly working on quality-of-life stuff. I highly recommend this game and I always have since the beta days until they started doing their DLC and Access Pass bull. Evolve was never a bad game and it is constantly being added onto to give more to the experience so people don't bored of it too quickly, something that Dead by Daylight seems to suffer from as of late (2 months since release as of the posting of this review and no big additions).
It's free, so give it a try and see how you like it. They have a good thing going and it all falls to us hoping that they don't somehow screw it all up like they did on release.
EDIT 11/6/2016: Nevermind, RIP game, it is no longer being worked on by Turtle Rock Studios.

Released on October 10, 2007 by the beloved Valve tells a story about a test subject going through a series of experimental rooms involving the use of portals and other various accessories produced in the fictional company of Aperature Science. Solve each room's increasingly challenging puzzles as you learn more about the current conditions of Aperature Science and the twisted pasts of what has happened ever since the inclusion of GLaDOS, an artificial intelligence that maintains the entire facitility.
Portal is presented with a combination of sleek grey and white architecture with contrasts of black, in which enables the industrialized facility tone in which the developers strived towards. The use of lighting from the portals and various other Aperature Science items creates the sci-fi aesthetics that is recognizable very easily. Very polished and refined from the previous iterations seen through the trailers, and is maintained throughout the testing facilities. However, this changes to a very rustic and worn-down tone of bright red and black as the plot progresses to a new section of the game, in which is quite reflective of the change in enviroment. Overall, a very fitting and interesting stylistic choice from the game.
Rating: A
The music used throughout the game goes along well with the entire sci-fi atmosphere that Portal has created for itself. Each of them creates a sense of unease yet also calming feeling, which is quite interesting to say the least. The sound effects used are consistent and matches up with the action that is happening. Some of the sound effects are quite memorable and easily recognizable, as with many aspects of this game. Although the soundtrack is great, it's not used much throughout the game is mostly remained to silence. This might be decided from the developers to further cement the fact that the player is basically trapped inside a testing facility, with no signs of any humans nearby, but I still felt like it could have been used more frequently instead of being in a couple test chambers. The final song in the credits, "Still Alive", performed by Ellen McLain and composed by Jonathan Coultan is catchy and a nicely concludes the game.
Rating: A-
The story seems to be non-existent in the beginning. You're a test subject going through one test chamber at a time, solving puzzles and learning about different mechanics. However, as the game progresses, you learn pieces and parts of what Aperature Science actually is and the history behind it. Still, the story is kept quite simply for the player to learn more about it in the sequel, Portal 2. As a puzzle game, there's not much of a comprehensive story like other games would have, and that is fine. With the amount of story Portal has it's already quite satisfying and makes the player want to learn more about the history of the game they're playing.
Rating: A
As a part of the puzzle game genre, Portal is a rare inclusion as it's a 3D game rather than most puzzle games, revolving around 2D. This gives the game much more potential and the mechanics that the game includes are phenominal. Each aspect revolving around portals are fun and interesting, combined with the other puzzle aspects of this game, creates an enjoyable experience from beginning to end. The developer commentary that can be accessed after playing through the entirety of the game explores more upon how each chamber is altered and created based on previous testings and a progressive learning structure that Portal is based upon. The amount of work put into each puzzle is quite astonishing, and the synergy of difficulty and enjoyment is balanced well throughout. There are also two side modes in addition to the main story, advance maps and challenge mode. Advance maps takes previous test chambers and alters one or two factors of the map to make it much more difficulty. Each of them were quite enjoyable and nicely challenging to go through. The challenge mode on the other hand place the same chambers from before and put goals such as steps taken, portal used, or time taken, to see the performance of each aspect on each individual map. I found this mode to be way too difficult and honestly detracts from the calming atmosphere of Portal, making in quite uneccessarily stressful throughout each map. With that aside, since it's an optional mode, it didn't have much of an impact to the main game.
Rating: A
Portal is an extremely well developed game that has the right amount of difficulty, enjoyment, and interests for me to keep on returning to this game. It's almost flawless upon all aspects and I would say my complaints are only small nitpicks that are quite based on my personal taste. This is definitely one of my favorites of all time, along with the rest of the fantastic line-up developed by Valve. High praise for this company and high praise for this game. If you have not bought or played this game yet, I would recommend you do as soon as possible. It's an experience that is quite hard to put into words, and will keep you engaged right to the end.
Final Rating: A

It all looked very promising, but failed at execution.
There are many elements lifted from Enemy Unknown, but none of them really made an impact. There are still full cover, and half cover, but it doesn't make any difference, not that I've noticed. You get shot when you peek out or when flanked anyways. So why bother.
Slow down time is cool, and a kind of throwback to original - you prepare your strategy, how to attack, what abilities to use etc, but once that first surprise attack is over, it's back to cover shootings. Trying to control the battlefield and flank the enemies rarely works as they move in real time and react to your movement. The only strategy is to shoot until they all fall down, starting from biggest threat (obviously).
However, the biggest disappointment for me is enemy variety. XCOM was always brimmed with it. Here, you have sectoids, outsiders (a bit different design - ok, whatever), muton, drone and that's it. Turns out Outsiders are main antagonists, as a whole alien race. There are technicians, psy, ghosts, elites blah blah... even bosses look just like regular foot soldiers with a bit more variety in armor. Where are chrysalids, Thin men (Which would work well in story as the ones that take human or agent form) Uber Etereal as final boss? So disappointing...
Oh, and no matter what squad mates you bring with, it always ends up with you killing the most of bad guys - so, another fail.
They each have their set of abilities, and more as they level up, but rarely do they turn the tide. Maybe on highest difficulty - but what I've played, it was all about me.
Running around XCOM HQ is tiresome, conversations sequences rarely have any outcome no matter what you chose to say, and weapons go through ammo fairly quickly. You often run around looking for ammo - during the battle!
As for good things - graphics really made an impact on me. It really looks nice. The scene where alien ship exits space portal is wow, and the 60s settings is spot on. However facial impressions are bland, and lip sync is almost comical.
Story is OK, but lacks a bit more depth. No one explained to me what that thing on my arm is...
As for recommendation. Hard to say... It was disappointing, but in the end I enjoyed playing it - sort of. Maybe someone who knew nothing of XCOM before and how much potential this game had, he may view it for what it really is. 6/10

Eventually you get to the point where you have cannons and lvl.3 computers don't, so you just hit one after the other racking up gold, BUT until that point, you are constantantly resetting games either because of too few crew members trying to take on too many enemies, or a LOT of unexperienced, untrained, combat-feeder crew members who sit around, poop, and eat you out of house and home (ship).
It took me a bit to find a nice balance, but it first had to start with...
2. Starting Captain
Would you believe me if I told you that, in my 2nd game, I started out with a Captain who had 1 strength and 1 vitality?...Completely worthless. I even tried to make it work. Couldn't 1v1 a crab.
If the developers were going for truly random stats, CONGRATS. You did it.
It took me until my 4th game to get a character with balanced enough stats to run with.
3. Cannons are OP.
Can anyone tell me a legitamite reason to why I have to train my seafears how to swim? Let's just say someone can convince me there is legitimacy to this game mechanic.... My point still stands. Even with the knockback on the lowest of settings, my crew are flying off my ship and drowning. If it's my captain, well I'm screwed. I get that cannons are powerful, as they should be, but something about the knockback just feels so off. "So, how'd you die?" "I was hit by a cannon....which made me fly into the water and I can't swim..." Something seems off. Explosions do knockback, but when the ratio of person/ship size is as miscalculated as this game, you can kill people at 75% of their health but just pushing them into water.
4. I decided just to try my luck against a LEGENDARY boss when I KNEW I was FAR too underleveled to go against (I could barely beat level 4 CPU's) because, heck why not! The game asks me to save every other second (autosave feature? anyone?) so I knew that even when I failed I could still go back to the very second before I decieded to do it.
I won. Wasn't even hard.
The enemies had lower health than the enemies in level 4 ships and I only lost 1 crew member...And my ship was perfectly intact. There is something fishy about it, no doubt.
Not to mention, I then steal the legendary ship and get 5/6 free cannons. With Gold as hard to get as it is, that's a HUGE boost for me.
5. LASTLY, I get that this game is 2 dimensional in that it's a 2d scrolling game. But does the gameplay have to be so....two dimensional? (Sorry, bad pun) While playing this game I ACTUALLY had this thought, "Man, this game is so fricken fun, even though It's the same thing over and over again...oh...."
There needs to be another aspect to this game. Building shops on Islands to get revenue? Taking over FORTS on islands? Getting several ships to make a FLEET? SAVING HOT BABES?
This game is fun, well worth the money...but by balancing some of the things I've mentioned and adding just ONE more aspect to this game would go from me telling my friends about this game to forcing them to buy it.

"Rabbit Hole 3-D" is essentially a slapdash flight simulator. You attempt to pilot a little pixellated cube around the words of the first chapter of "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" as they come rushing toward the screen. Unfortunately, the awkward camera angle robs the player of any reliable sense of depth, or even the ability to see what's coming around corners until it's too late. This is, shall we say, kind of a game-killer where precision and timing are supposed to be crucial to the player's survival.
To make matters worse, by the time level 4 or 5 rolls around, the screen starts to spin but the controls don't spin along with it, so that left becomes right and up becomes down and so on and so forth, over and over as the screen continuously spins. Meaning that you will die a lot (which isn't so bad) and unfairly (which is). I think this was originally a mobile game, so maybe it controls better on a phone, but on a PC it's just tedious and a waste of time.

This game took me completely by surprise.
Everything about Hatoful Boyfriend suggested that it wasn't anything more than a joke. I expected to play this game for an hour, show it to my friends, have a good laugh, and move on. What I didn't expect, was just how much this game would impact me on a deeper level.
The story starts off slow, gradually introducing you to each bird. This is the part of the game where the concept is at its most ludicrous. Bird puns are thrown around with reckless enthusiasm, and you'd be forgiven for assuming that the rest of the story would follow in the same comedic vein. However, there's a much darker tale lying just beneath the surface.
I don't want to spoil anything here, but suffice to say that these birds have issues. Tragic pasts, entertwining dramas, bleak outlooks, sinister plans, and a caveat of other unexpected elements in their lives.
The sad part is, it's entirely possible not to witness ANY of these plot threads on your first playthrough, and there will undoubtedly be people who miss out on these awesome stories because they were unlucky enough to get a generic, predictable story on their first playthrough, which might turn them off to exploring relationships with the other birds. If you stick with it, and go back through the game seeking different outcomes, you will not be dissapointed.
Hatoful Boyfriend is full of surprises, and you'll be rewarded for getting to know its twisted universe, and the characters within it. I can't believe I'm saying this, but I highly recommend this game. It definitely isn't for everyone, which is understandable given the ridiculous concept, but if you can get past that, there's some very memorable, touching, and hilarious moments just waiting to be discovered in this unexpected gem.

Fairy Tale Mysteries 2 shows strong, creative mechanics by mixing hidden and fragmented object scenes, plus it has an interesting (but short) take on the familiar Jack and the Beanstalk story.
When a hidden object game gets a sequel three years after its release, it is usual to see that the two games have barely anything in common. Still, this can be a good thing—case in point, Fairy Tale Mysteries 2: The Beanstalk.
Whereas its predecessor was a fairly forgettable HOG, this one brings something new by mixing up the usual mechanics: every story screen is turned into a fragmented object game, replacing the traditional point ‘n’ click parts, but keeping the standard hidden object scenes intact. So, if you like to search for items, you are in luck, because this game has plenty of it—but not to the point where it gets tiresome.
As for the story, the title mostly says it all: someone is trying to grow a new beanstalk to let the giants escape from their cloud prison, and our protagonist, freshly from the Brothers Grimm Institution, must prevent this by getting the help of the Guardians of four magical realms. Episodic, straightforward, a little too short, but fun for a hidden object game.

I always suggest driving around and unlocking 75% of the roads in Ibiza's area 2 before you get into the racing scene as this helps with car selection and gives you level 3 performance upgrades for the first few cars you will need (C4, A7, A6 and B4). It takes a decent amount of time just to drive around and unlock roads, but atleast for me it's worth it in the end and you will notice a good diffrence having that level 3 or 4 performance upgrade in those harder races. Level 1/2 upgrades are rarely worth it imo so spend the time and get atleast 75% in Ibiza area 2 right off the bat, then Ibiza 1 and Hawaii 1 (for the high end A1 car's like the Veyron and CCX) later.
In the end this is a very addicting racing game that can be intense at times and laid back in others. If you like open world racing games with a plathora of cars from silly hatchbacks to Bugatti's, this one is a no brainer!
