A lot of people are complaining about stupid things, but I will be honest with you.
Going free to play is hands-down the best move that the people working on Evolve could have made. The game from what I could tell was dying harshly before going F2P, with only a couple hundred players being online at a time at peak hours, so it was very difficult trying to get a game going, especially for new players.
Post-F2P release, they changed quite a bit about the game that does affect the balance and how matches play out. Some are good and were pretty much required to prevent certain cheeky tactics from working whilst other changes are simply awful.
What I'm going to discuss are the changes that should have never been implemented.
The first change being that there are now round timers in place. The round timers force monsters to be on the back foot at all times, applying pressure where it is not necessary and causing them to make mistakes or force them into their deaths (because this timer will freeze whenever the monster enters combat).
Something to take note of is that
as they did not destroy the objective in time. That alone is bull because it is up to the hunters to be able to hunt the monster quickly and effectively. Why shouldn't it be that when the timers runs down that the Hunters lose because they didn't kill what they were hunting in time? It begs the question why it is even there to begin with which is what I'm trying to get at - do not think I am trying to argue for the timer to be changed to be in the Monster's favor. I'm going to be blunt before people start strawmanning:
This timer, as you may have already seen in negative reviews, completely decimates the "sneaky monster" strategy that some monster players employ to avoid confrontation with hunters at all times (myself included). Because of the round timer, monsters can no longer take as much time as they have to to sneak around the map and hunting wildlife when they see opportunities to. Instead, they now have to rush faster than they are used to even if it means getting caught by an Arena (where it can be avoided easily by taking your time).
While playing sneaky is still possible, it's not a viable strategy anymore as the meta has changed to rush down wildlife as quickly as you can, getting Arena'd and surviving (or taking out the Trapper/hunter that placed the Arena), then dashing out and hunting more, repeat until you win or lose. It's pretty silly that this is the meta we're in right now, which brings me to my next point.
For asymmetrical games, it's not good to have a meta strategy for one side - one "go-to or be crippled" strategy. The biggest thing about asymmetrical games is to have a variety of tactics you can use to gain whatever advantage you can. Hunters have this in stock since they can build a team and chain perks together to synergize well. Monsters don't get this opportunity at all. It's either stack damage, cooldown reduction, or traversal cooldown perks and that's it. With only one strategy that works so well and trumps all others, you can't really use any other perk to synergize with the strategy you want. Again,
A third point that I wasn't really happy with was the Planet Scanner. This is another thing that kind of defeats the "sneaky monster" strategy since it points in the exact direction you are in, no strings attached. This issue isn't too bothersome and it's pretty easy to play around
Unless they changed this and I missed the patch notes about it: If you are within a certain range (I think 50 meters?) of the hunters and they use the Planet Scanner, it will actually highlight you. That last bit is my biggest issue that I have with it. It should not highlight you when you are close to the hunters when they use PS.
Other than the issues I stated, any issues I have had that I would have mentioned here were actually fixed in the most recent patch, so it's great that they are constantly working on quality-of-life stuff. I highly recommend this game and I always have since the beta days until they started doing their DLC and Access Pass bull. Evolve was never a bad game and it is constantly being added onto to give more to the experience so people don't bored of it too quickly, something that Dead by Daylight seems to suffer from as of late (2 months since release as of the posting of this review and no big additions).
It's free, so give it a try and see how you like it. They have a good thing going and it all falls to us hoping that they don't somehow screw it all up like they did on release.
EDIT 11/6/2016: Nevermind, RIP game, it is no longer being worked on by Turtle Rock Studios.

This is a fantastic game. Sleeper hit of the year for me.
On the label, this looks like an RTS game with zombies, and neither of those things appeal to me anymore. RTS games have felt rote and stale for more than a decade, and zombies, well, we hit the zombie media saturation point years ago too. The label is deceptive though - They Are Billions combines elements from many different genres and the resulting mix feels decidedly fresh. There's a ton of potential here, not just for TaB but also for something like a new genre: The Part-Time Strategy Game.
I'm going to try to list the different unique features of this game to bring out why it feels so interesting and engaging.
So this is a turtling PvE RTS where you can pause anytime you like. This gives the players complete control over the APM aspect of the game - rather than an anxiety inducing manic clickfest all the time where the fastest finger always wins, you can play at exactly the speed you want and no faster. In pause mode the buildings you place don't cost money yet so you can make building mistakes without penalty, and even more importantly - in pause mode zambee's can't eat your face. Yet. (They will tho).
This isn't just PvE RTS though, it's also got timed waves to beat like tower defense. And unlike most RTS's where everything mostly boils down to a war of attrition between competing production chains and the bigger number usually wins, in TaB all it takes is one zombie to destroy an entire base. This is because in expanding and growing your colony, you are also making lots and lots of humans, aka future-zombies. When a building gets destroyed, all the workers staffing it immediately decide they want to eat your face, and the snowball effect ripples across your entire base very quickly. No matter how big and powerful your base gets, you are always exactly one zahmby away from losing.
And there are a LOT of zombii. At least dozens.
So even though you can play at the speed you want, the stakes and the tension are always at maximum. You are also locked into ironman mode, so every decision you make matters. It doesn't take very many suboptimal decisions before zombores are eating your face either. They will definitely your face too, and there are a lot of them. Hundreds maybe. If I had to count.
So you need a lot of troops and defenses to survive, and you need a lot of resources to make that♥♥♥♥♥♥ so you have to expand. And you have to expand defensively, because anything you build that isn't defended is basically just enemy reinforcements. The loop goes something like this - scout, clear out walkers (without alerting too many of them at once), pick out defensive points, expand to said points and set up prelimary defenses, convert new land into resources, convert resources into troops and D, keep scouting and clearing. And you're gonna be doing all of those things at once, all of the time, or, well, face-eating. Every part of the loop has failure potential, and with the stakes at maximum all the time, the ebb and flow of the game is incredibly satisfying and exciting.
The random map generator keeps the loop feeling fresh and interesting, because you're never going to be faced with exactly the same situational parameters twice. Sometimes you have a couple of easy chokes to defend but not enough space to convert into resources, sometimes you've got tons of space but not chokes or resources, sometimes you're wedged in between zumbai cities, sometimes you've got tons of wood but no food or stone, and sometimes a lot of zombies eat your face. I think like thousands? Probably. You have to adjust to your circumstances and do the best with what you've got. There's never going to be an optimal build order for this game.
The survival waves add increased pressure to maintain your defensive levels, because the waves can come from any direction and you only get a brief warning as to where the face-eating is gonna happen from. All it takes is one weak point at a bad time and well, you know. Nom nom nom.
And did I mention how many ♥♥♥♥ing zubzubs there are? At any given time there gonna be 10s of thousands of the ♥♥♥♥ers on the map, and the game engine really does an incredible job of conveying the scope of the conflict and maintaining frames for maximum face eatage. The starting zomboos act like an environmental deterent, and navigating and clearing them even has some stealth elements to consider. Too many guns in the wrong place making too much noise and you could pull too much aggro for you to handle. The zoomba hordes kind of have fluid mechanics, and tend to flow in and around your♥♥♥♥♥♥like nasty face-eating goo. I've never seen anything like it in an RTS before and it is very impressive. The final wave does tend to lag a lot, but the metric ♥♥♥♥♥on of face-eaters on the map at that point means you're going to be pausing like a schizoid on acid anyways. It really is a lot of zompers. More than several.
The end result is something totally unique - part RTS production buildup, part tactical high-stakes RNGesus navigation, part tower defense planning, part horde-survival nightmare, part learn-through-failure training, part getting your face et. It's quite polished for a recent EA release, and has already been patched several times. It's very addicting and punishingly difficult. Somehow the only thing I want to do after yelling and swearing at a screen full of recent-humans all up in my♥♥♥♥♥♥is re-roll the next base. Die again, die better.
There are definitely some flaws and annoyances though. If any of these things sound like deal breakers you might want to give it a few patches before trying:
-unit pathing is abysmal. you will have to have some patience for some dumb micro. the good news is idiot units tend to get eaten quickly, like they deserve.
-the map isn't rotatable and things behind other things don't have outlines. you will have to put up with having some difficulty finding and selecting certain things.
-arbitrary space and building limitations make building more awkward than it needs to be. a blueprint tool or copy/paste functionality of some kind would be really nice, but do not exist yet.
-the UI has some weird glitches and is sometimes unresponsive. most of the time it's ok, other times you accidentally delete all your walls. so it goes.
-units and defenses aren't all that balanced yet. once you've explored the tech tree you're going to be building a lot of snipers, thanatos, and executor towers.
Overall though, for me the rough edges are totally worth it. This game is a blast and I don't know of anything quite else like it.

Even at the lowest possible settings, this game is a challenge when first starting off. Once you get the strategy down a little bit, it gets easier. Walls and Turrets are your friends. You will die a lot in this game, the AI in this game punishes every mistake, every opening. Protect your houses. Once Zombies reach a row of houses, the game is over.

Currently 30 hours in and enjoying myself.  Got my moneys worth.  I even hate nearly everything that is zombies (movies, shows, games) but this is enjoyable.
For people who are having issues with balance, it's really not too hard (won 100% first map, 120% second map first try.)  It does require quite a bit of pausing and also planning based on the immediate surroundings.  If you do it wrong you will lose, but as long as you build and plan even a small amount you should be able to win.
Pros:
- Easy to learn
- Tons of fun
- Balance is ok but some units are useless (IMO)
Mix between Pro/Con:
- No saves.  I like it so there's no save scumming.
- The jumping zombies are annoying and killed me on a great run.  They can jump across rivers or through trees.  What I thought blocked all movement still allowed a single jumper to get into my (unprotected) residential and command center area.
Con:
- No key rebinds.
- Unit movement needs work.  If you trap a unit in the middle of a group and try to move the group, they'll move the unselected unit in the middle.  Same if you make a wall and make them move through a unit.  They can also block entries/walkways.
- The upgrade buildings can't be demolished.
- The mayors you get seem to have random attributes.  For tier 3 mayors (which I think is 1k pop) you may get an offer for +80 gold/turn or you may get -50% sniper upkeep or 2 free titans (the research to even build a titan is 6k gold, not counting the cost to build.)
- Some buildings don't seem to be useful.  The radar one for instance.
- The shock tower could use some extra functionality to "link" it with other shock towers.  Right now if a zombie is in range they will both shock at the same time.  "Linking" them so they wait half the cooldown would be nice.
Other things to note:
- The "Survive X days to win" is a bit misleading.  You expect the billions on X day, not several days beforehand.  On the 100 day setting the final wave is at day 91.
- From start to finish on a 100 day map is about 4-7 hours.  Lots of pausing.
---
Edit: After writing the review I went to play the third map, the snow level.  Beat that first try as well on 140% (challenging / challenging).  Even though I almost lost at the final wave (a single weak wall) it was beat.  Please do ignore the reviews saying it's too hard even on easy, it's not hard.

This game has a lot of potential. Keep in mind that this is an early-access game. It's a lot of fun during your first playthrough.
However, the game has an awful difficulty curve that massively limits replayablity. Once you understand the mechanics, the first 90% of the game is pretty easy. The game tells you in advance when a zombie horde is coming, and it is straightforward to repel. Then, for the last 10% of the game time, a very seriously impossible horde is sent at you from all sides. To my knowledge, only an extreme few have survived this on normal or higher difficulty, and victory is often impossible for many starting map geometries. Losing and watching your colony burn is fun, but every game is the same.
Ultimately, I loved this game for about 10hrs straight, but in its current state there is no replayability.
I have high hopes but I would not recommend this game to most people in its current state; better to wait to see how it evolves for now.

Billions is a very well executed merger between a slightly watered down base building/management game (like Banished) with influxes of unexpected danger in the shape of increasingly larger hordes coming from off the map (like invaders in Planetbase).
Couple this with the ever present danger of completely random trains from zombie cities or small roaming groups and you have a recipe for vast potential.
The combat units currently in live have a slight StarCraft 1 feel to their behaviors and animations, which is not a bad thing at all.
The procedural start system does need a little bit of attention. Perhaps one of every 20 games or so I've experienced a start that is literally impossible. A friend experienced being surrounded by impassible terrain on 2.5 sides and a zombie town that generates a train of aggro if they see a wall, building, or you fire a shot at them, the game was over inside of a few days.
That is the only problem I've seen or experienced thus far. Great game, highly recommended, and cannot wait to see the roadmap develop.

The Bureau surprised me - It really was not what I was expecting.  But it was enjoyable, nonetheless.
While The Bureau obviously takes place in the XCOM universe, it isn't an XCOM game.  There's none of the familiar turn-based, squad-based, tactical combat.  Instead, it's a fairly straight-forward third-person squad shooter.
You control your protagonist, and issue orders to a small squad of soldiers, while engaging the enemy in various '60s-era battlefields.
The setting is beautifully realized.  It genuinely feels like I'm walking through a little slice of 1960s Americana that's been assaulted by Alien invaders.  And the clash of Alien high-technology with small-town USA creates a wonderful aesthetic.
The gameplay is solid, with lots of nods to traditional XCOM mechanics.  You've got a squad of team-members you can individually train and specialize...  And you can dispatch team-members on missions without you...
But, like I said, the core gameplay really is a substantial departure from the XCOM franchise.

I picked this up from the Humble 2K Bundle as the sole reason for purchasing a "Below the Average". I already had Bioshock and Darkness 2 looks like a bad JRPG had sex with Deus Ex - Human Revolution while it was sleeping and tried to raise the baby as it's own and it turned into a crippled ward of the state child welfare nightmare.
The Bureau was good. I would absolutely not have paid full price for it. The gameplay is 3rd person shootery rather than top down tactical turn based combat. I read this before I bought it but I never really digested it because I was so used to X-Com's format. It works well, it's very different without being terrible. The environments work well with the format despite being very linear and small, I rarely felt I was being constrained to a single path because I was almost always hammering in some alien's face with a M14. The environments are good looking as are the characters, weapons etc.
The "Press space to massively slow down time and order your doods about" system works well also. In lieu of a turn-based interface to queue things up it's actually very good. The way the AI moves around you based on "Defend this" and "Follow me" and also fluidly around avoiding grenades and retaking cover is also good. I never found myself thinking "Stupid f-ing bots!" which is great in a small team focused game like this.
The dialogue is awful. The voice acting is great but the dialogue is awful. The writing is terrible. Some of it is genuinely laughable, the rest is choppy. More than once I have been tasked with doing something I have no idea about what it is, or a character has referred to something or someone that has not been introduced. Due to the "roam around the base before your next mission and talk or explore or whatever" interval missions I imagine this dialogue gap is because I simply didn't speak to the right people and therefore missed out the introductions. One of the dialogue options was "What do you think about Faulke's paranoia?" when my character had literally never heard any mention of paranoia regarding Faulke, ever. It feels very strange and even making an effort to talk to everyone and explore all areas I still found myself being introduced to things like "Use the Venn Brace to capture the target." when I had never heard of a Venn Brace before, even less knew it was the techno gadget attached to my arm. It literally just appeared one mission - no "I am a scientist here is your new piece of kit" or "I see the white-coats (scientists) fitted you out with their latest contraption." it literally was just there one mission and got named several missions later.

Aliens attacking earth I can stretch to, biological weaponry that's very advanced, that's fine. We see alien gunships that are badass. We see alien spaceships and other flying badass looking things in the sky attacking earth. Fantastic!  This game had it all.
1. Rich lore and world building from the start.
I loved the care taken to explain the whale oil economy, scrimshaw,  and debaucherous holidays.  Take a moment to read the tomes and notes scattered around, they go a long way toward building a fleshed out breathing world.  Pointing the "heart' at someone can sometimes gives you insight on someone's true nature or simply tell you that their family has been taken by the plague.  Good stuff.
2. A myriad of creative ways to execute and incapacitate your foes.
Dishonored offers you a dozen tools that can be combined for a rewarding combat experience.  Lay razorwire traps on alarms, fire your gun in the air to alert the guards and watch as they get shredded when they reach for that alarm button.  Possess guards to remove explosive whale oil barrels, drop the barrel in a group of enemies and then fire an explosive crossbow bolt from your hidden position.  If anyone survives, summon a swarm of carnivorous rats to finish them off or let them dispose of the bodies and erase any trace of your dirty work.
3.  Great level design and layout.
Run across rooftops, jump through windows or duck into sewers, under tables, hide atop rafters.  Most areas are accessible and allow you to go through or around your enemy.   The setting is a city in economic and social decay but is still quite beautiful.
I loved this game from start to finish and wish I hadn't passed it over for so many years.

Osiris: New Dawn holds a special place in my Sci-fiction heart. The developers wanted the player to "FEEL" their game's emotional impact. Rather than some of the other crop-ups in response to No Man's Sky, Osiris takes the detour away from merely exploring. Now it's for survival. Now it's for investigation. Now it's for a better understanding as to why our lives will be forever changed because we are unable to return to Earth.
I don't know how many, but some people will say, "I'd rather play Astroneer" or "I'd rather play Empyrion." You know what? That's up to them. Osiris brings to the table AMAZING graphical content. AMAZING animations. AMAZING models. and AMAZING in-game feeling. Ultimately, if you set the table for the hardest gameplay possible, you experience a new realm.
Osiris gives you the tools to explore, build, defend and destroy. Content has been intermittant, but a game that delivers this amount of quality is seeking to make it last. NMS burned because the content couldn't last. Here in Osiris, gameplay is meant to be adventurous and challenging. With the realistic conditions of thermal dynamics, oxygen, and legitimate "building" or "crafting," you can expect a change of depth in your otherworldly dreams.
Is there stuff missing? Yes.
Do the developers listen? Yes.
Should you help them live their dream too? ABSOLUTELY!
Look, this game deserves at least 100hrs in a year from everyone. You can watch it from others, but the experience of being in this realm really opens your eyes to what is possible in games now. (and don't quote me, but I think the devs have a secret storyline that we haven't heard about.)
So, go ahead. Play the game!

If your not a fan of the human excrement, perhaps this game is not for you. However, once you get the hang of the game, that problem ceases to be all that problematic, and you can go back to sailing the high seas plundering or capturing everything in your way in wonderous 2d pixel paradise.
Indeed, after you get past the admitably problematic begining to your adventure (Dying horribly, learning that you can not swim, having a ship full of exvrement, etc...) this game opens up alot of unique gameplay that you are unlikely to find in other games. You can chose to utalize the 2d envornment to have your enemies float dreamily to the bottom the the sea, obsess over the allocation of your precious training points, storm enemy ships with a barrage of kamakazi pirates, or just teach a bunch of pirates how to fish and have them catch fish after fish in the tavern, of all places. Really there is quite a bit of content to explore.
However, as it was almost certainly mentioned several times before, this game is still in development, being an early access game and all. Glitches come and go with alarming frequency and you will have to watch as your pirates fall of the ship for no legidiment reason (along with, say, having half of your ship all move one tile downwards, just to annoy those perfectionist types). If you are not willing to put up with the occasional glitch, then this game may not be for you.
However, all things considered, this is still a great game that is worthy of your time, and 8/10 at the very least. And if you get it now, you can appricate the game as it evolves to the point where it can score a 9 or even a 10. But, your choice...

Hoo boy, I have gotten a LOT of flack from my friends when playing this game.  And to some degree, I agree with them.  A great deal of this was only mildly entertaining and I did not understand why people (especially close friends of mine) loved this game.  The game begins with the main character (a female...  yes, you play a female in a dating sim...) starting her sophomore year [unsure if right or not] and during the next year dates several bird-boy-people-things...  NOW, you must be wondering, "Why is a girl dating birds!?  How can she develop intimate feelings for these avian creatures!?  HOW CAN THE BIRDS FRICKIN' ACT LIKE HUMAN BEINGS!?!?!?"  Put those questions aside when you play the story, but just don't forget about them entirely.
Each character's dating route got progressively more funny and interesting the more I played it, EXCEPT FOR ONE which made me feel like I was mashing my head against a wall for doing something so inanely stupid as it was not a good route to take...  If you play the game, you will know the one because you will think the main character is dumb.  After playing through just about every route at least once, I unlocked a new route that was only available to begin in the beginning.  THIS FINAL ROUTE, HOO BOY IT WAS A DOOZY!
This final route made the entire game so much more worth it, and answered soooooooo maaaaaannyyyyyy quuueeestions!  OH, and if you want to do the epilogue, you need to get all endings before doing the Final Route (There are some characters with TWO endings, one being a normal ending and the other being a TRUE ending...).
I am not really going to talk about the final route too much, but let me just say that this game was a rollercoaster of funny moments and intense plots.
I TOTALLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME, but it sometimes felt annoying to play through a route again JUST for the epilogue...  Good thing this game has a skip function to speed through text...  Saved me MUCH MORE TIME than I would have done, if that function wasn't in the game.
In short, if you love games with fantastic stories, GET THIS GAME NOW!

The ridiculous, flat story won't inspire you to greatness, but the innovative take on the hidden-object game genre is fun and exceptionally well presented.
The hidden-object concept is not just limited to specific scenes, but indeed the whole point-and-click adventuring is hidden-object based. As times, it is a bit silly, but for fans of the genre it can be a lot of fun to be constantly hunting for objects.
In case you're worried, it's done in a way that keeps things very simple indeed. Even at "expert" difficulty, I found this game to be very easy for the genre. Oddly, the bonus chapter falls back to a more traditional hidden-object style. It's quite long, too, almost a game in itself.
The graphics, voice acting, and music are all lush, and the game engine is buttery-smooth, just as you would expect from Gogii Games.
The Grimm Brothers branding, though, is an insult to our intelligence. I doubt they would recognize this dumb narrative as a "fairy tale" of any kind. Come on, Gogii! You have a great engine. Stop pumping out this drivel and try to invest in some serious storytelling.
Finally, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

Day 17. T-Day
Got a solid base camp set up. My friend and I hfound a very easily fortifiable spot. One way in and a couple drops off and a Kovac Tunnel nearby. We've done a few missions for Kovac. Met up with a man named Kenji. Seemed like a cool guy.
That's when we got the call. Something guy out in the swamps. Said he was trapped and needed help. Something about his turkey's? I didn't know. "Turkeys are dinner back in the day. Nothing more." If only I knew what my friend and I were getting into. So I headed that way and told my friend to meet me there. When I arived I realized I had forgotten my bow. "Oh well," I thought, "I'll just play it safe keep my distance unless necessary."
So I went on. I hopped a fence and noticed a 'fatty' as we've come to call them. I stealthily made my way around him. That's when I heard it, a Turkey gobble. I won't lie, it startled me. The man said we'd have a reward for killing 100 or more of the fat things. I figured that sounded pretty good. I readied my machete and started keeping an eye out. Then I saw it. This ugly, red, brown, and purple thing come bounding through the grass. I readied my swing. Then another came bouncing and gobbling. All of the sudden there's at least 5 flying towards me and 4 more pecking at me. I run, hopping a fence and climbing on a car screaming on the radio for my friend to help.
"JON!" I screamed.
"What?" He spoke nonchalantly.
"HURRY THE F*CK UP!" I yelled slashing wildly at the fat ugly things. "I'M GONNA DIE TO THESE GOD D*MN TURKEYS! THE B*STARDS ARE EVERYWHERE! JESUS CHRIST!"
About a minute later and 8 more infected turkeys later my friend arrives to find me covered in blood, feathers, a few eggs, and scratches surrounded by 16 dead turkeys.
The next 3 hours were spent slowly moving through these god forsaken swamps as my friend and I cleared out wave after wave of turkey.
I moved ahead, we had finished clearing an area and my friend was regathering his arrows and some feathers.
I hopped another fence and made it about 5 steps, I heard a twig snap and turned. A sigh of relief came from my lips, just a zombie. No turkey in sight. Then I heard one. Then another. I look down the path and see 10 coming at me I turn to run and notice another 6 moving in from the sides I screamed and ran I seee atleast 10 more Cutting me off. "JESUS CHRIST! WHAT THE HELL? THEY'RE LEARNING MAN! THEY'RE LEARNING!" I scream through the radio.
"What do you mean they're learning? I'll come help don't worry." HE states a slight bit of urgency. He's seen the horror of these things now. "How many?"
I do a quick headcount noting more have appeared as I trip over the fence feeling a few pecks and scratches on my legs. "F*CK AT LEAST 30 GIVE OR TAKE?" I get up fast as I see them start to hop the fence. "HOW FAR AWAY ARE YOU!?"
"Holy sh*t? 30?" He says his urgency picking up, "I'm out past the summoning circle man. I don't know whether I can make it."
I sigh, I can feel my legs starting to give out. I haven't eaten in almost 2 days, water has been scarce too. But I'd be damned if I'd die to Turkeys. I said something that I never thought I'd said. "OH LORD IN HEAVEN (if there is one) PLEASE SHOW MERCY ON ME I CONFESS TO YOU MY SINS PLEASE SAVE ME SWEET BABY JESUS OH LORD SAVE ME! PLEASE SAVE ME TOM CRUISE!" I close my eyes, sprinting as hard and fast as I can.
I finally see the summoning circle thing appear. "Oh thank you." I let out a bare whisper as I see my friend set up with the bow as I come around the corner. Then I see him pale. A LITERAL HORDE OF THESE F*CKS IS BEHIND ME!
That's when it happened. I realized it a moment sooner than it did. "Save yourself." I whispered as I felt my leg buckle in the wet mud, "I'm done for."
-10% xp.

Fantastically thrilling game. Even though it is a deceptively repetitive concept; (find the monster and kill it), every game feels different and unique. You need teamwork and good co-ordination as hunters, and each role is important in their own way, and their abilities quintessential for the team. The medics keep you alive, the support buffs and protects the team, the assault deals the damage and the trapper finds and crowd controls the monster. Playing as a monster? Well, your job is to eliminate the entirety of the hunters. You win when all of them are incapitated, but it is not as easy as it sounds. Choosing your target is essential and it is what seperates most good monsters from bad ones. Different situations require you to focus different targets. Each monster has 4 skills, and after you've eaten enough wildlife, you get to put more points into the skill of your choice. The perk system also allows you to choose perks to suit your playstyle, there is an array of perks, for monsters and for the hunters alike. I've been having mad fun with this game, and the only downside to it, in my opinion, are the lack of players. If you've read this far, I highly recommend you to give the game a try. Have fun, and happy hunting :)

You will be challenged if you buy this game, in a fun way.

- i don't think i've played a single rts that made me plan my base layout in a manner which satisfies troop mobility, resource, inter-building relationship and security requirements... well done devs.

- while the currently available survival mode is the only one available... and a lack of a save/load functionality make some sense.. i don't see why i can't replay the same map again from the beginning... even at a score penalty.
- tech trees would be nice. maybe chosing different branches, allowing for mutually exclusive bonus options.
- the game atmosphere if gloomy and dark... i quite enjoy it. ... it would be nice more gritty/gloomy decisions... such as a random events in which to choose whether or not to increase the food production output by 1/building at the expense of 10% troop hp or something similar... but with a cool story-driven reason...
- it was fun the first time when a single zombie managed to wander into my base, whereby making me lose the game by managing to infect a house, and fractallically multiply itself by infecting everything in the base ... not so fun the 20th time it happens.
... here's my point... if a house/tent gives 4 workers... then it should stand to reason that in the event it is infected... you should have to deal with 4 zombies... right? ... no. ... because some of those workers should be working away in other areas of the colony. ... some of those workers are soldiers... etc.
... a zombie infecting 10 houses, creating a horde of 40 zombies ... in a town with 40 colonists which has 10 soldiers... makes no sense. (random numbers... still... this is what it feels like.) ... one could argue that they have families... but it's a zombie apocalypse... ... retirement/child labor would be the least of our concerns when an impending horde of brain-hungry zombies is expected to arrive in less than a year.
- wall placement restrictor algorithm needs work. it seems to refuse 3x3 wall grids for some reason, unless there's a tower there, or something else is going wrong. it's a useless feature.
- missing awareness of used grid squares when placing resource buildings.
- needs better and more detailed descriptions of buildings and units. ... (also a revision... i.e. "executor rower" ). knowing whether a tower does AoE or Single target damage would prevent frustrations.
- should make buildings transparent when entering build mode.
- should add camera rotation functionality as well.
- should add key mapping customisaiton feature.
- maybe should have some time controls (speed up/ slow time)
- etc. ... small tid-bits... but the game is still solid. definitely worth preordering... and definitely worth the wait until v1.0. great job.
-... ah... last but not least... when things get realy rough... ... and i mean... REALLY rough... the game lags like ♥♥♥♥.

I'm still a bit on the fence about this game.  On the one hand I love the concept and a single-player fully fleshed out RTS city defense game is a grea idea.  There are just a few things that I found that took away from the game experience enough to make it unfun for me.  For starters, you're managing 7 resources, so I constantly found myself at a point where I would want to build something but would need more of 3 or 4 different resources.  Or, I would find this chain of missing resources.  I need more workers for this building, but then I need more food to get more workers, and now I need more wood to build food structures, and now I've spent so much on all of those that I don't have the gold to build what I wanted to in the first place.  This might sound like the general struggle of all RTS's, but there's just too many resources for my liking.
The other point that I didn't quite enjoy was that the general gameplay routine was very repetative: exand, build, defend, and once you figure out what works and what doesn't, there just isn't much more depth to the game.  It was fun when I was dying, but once I figured it out, it lost its luster for me.
All in all, this is a soft "no" for me.  There are certainly people who will enjoy this game, but until there is more variety, say for instance another race to play as or something that shakes up the zombie attacks, and a finetuning of the resource process, I won't be returing to They Are Billions.

This could have been a great game, unfortunately the game has three major flaws that make it just an average game.
Firstly, all of the ai are garbage. The teammates, the friendlies, the civilians, and the enemies. They are worse than ai from 10 years ago.
Your teammates can be set to either never fire or to kill everything. If set to never fire then they just aren't helpful and might aswell not exist. If set to kill everything then they either get themselves killed, or leave nothing for you to do and make the game really boring.
The friendlies are uncommandable and kill everything when they happen to show up, but usually appear after you have killed everyone. They could be removed from the game and I wouldn't even notice.
The civilians only exist to get killed by you accidently, and they're pretty good at it. They will often run straight into your gunfire and because its an Ubisoft game you get penalized for killing them. If you kill three friendlies and civilians in succession then you basically just die, because thats fun.
The enemy ai would be fine if this were an average shooter or open world game, but this is supposed to be a tactical shooter so then the enemy ai are subpar. They are horrible at searching and give up if you run a quarter mile away.
Secondly, the engine for this game is by far the worst part of it. Boats and water don't really work and none of the ai can use boats. There are no tanks, only an apc with eight wheels that drives and turns like a car with four wheels and is as well armored as your mom's minivan.
I also think it is worth mentioning that the game is not optimized at all so it runs like trash (like all ubisoft games) and that the graphics are...strange. Like if a car back window is cracked alot and you look inside the car through that, then you can see the cracked glass texture sort of moving with the passengers inside. Its hard to describe.
Lastly there aren't as many tactical cosmetics as anyone would like, just the bare minimum. The devs release a little cosmetic dlc about each month or week and a lot of them look kind of silly and everyone wants more military guns. Also, the teammates dress like hipsters that walked through a military surplus store and there is no way to customize them or their equipment.
If you want an open world shooter with a military theme that leans towards the casual side then this is your only option so buy it. If you want a good game then do not buy this.

Osiris New Dawn is on it's way to being one of the great games we've been waiting for. It's still in development so there are still some bugs that need to be addressed. I've put hundreds of hours playing this game and  I find myself not being able to put it down. Note: This Game was given to me by a friend
When I first saw the trailer for Osiris: New Dawn, I thought, "WOW! This game looks like something I could play for hours on end and might be something I will play for a very long time!" Well here's my experience when I started playing the game.
When I first launched the game, some friends and I were able to get onto a server with the concurrent player count of 6. However, when we tried to build a base, the structure limit was reached. We were a bit bummed out but then thought, "Let's just try to find a new server that is less populated." We proceeded to join another server, and for awhile, we had a magical time. One of the best first time moments ever was seeing the hugest worm gliding over our heads almost ready to devour us whole, however we escaped with our minds filled with awe and wonder. We were able to set up a small base in around 1.5 hours and we logged off for the day. The next day we log on to find out that all our stuff is gone without a trace, which was pretty disheartening. However, we decided to move on and we soon found a place next to the lair of one of the huge worms. We played for ~11 hours in two days to get a base with some ships and all the structures that you could build. We even had a Shower and Garden! We then proceeded to procure 3 turrets in order to defend the base from what destroyed our stuff last time. The very next day, on a non populated server, *poof*, all our stuff is gone without a trace. Eleven hours of hard work gone to waste. That was my experience with the game. I thought the turrets we worked so hard to create would defend our base, ultimately did nothing. We were nowhere near others and we took the closest inspection to decay. I mean I would understand if the server had more than just us at the current time, but it was virtually empty, with the occasional pop in of one or two people. Well this is turning in a rant XD. Heres a pro con list of this game.
Truthfully, I like this game alot. It is fun to me and many others I'm sure. However, I feel this game has amazing potential, especially with the unique skill web and stat system, and the part I didn't talk about, but really is in the game, factions and classes. Overall, if you want to buy this game to support the developers, PLEASE DO, but if you want to get a fun game that you can play for hundreds of hours, I wouldn't pick up this game just yet.

I fully admit that the "hidden object" adventure genre ranks somewhere between free to play mobile games and a piece of toast jammed into an NES in terms of "things I want to spend my time playing". I don't understand the appeal of the genre, and while I've seen some friends play some from time to time, I never really got into them myself. Then, a couple of weeks ago, one of those bundle websites had a deal where you could get like a dozen of these for the price of however many cheetos you could find in your couch, and I was dumb and decided that for such a low price it would be worth finally checking out the genre myself. If Fairy Tale Mysteries 2: The Beanstalk is any indication, though, I'm going to want my cheetos back.
Like I've said, I've only ever seen people play these sorts of games before, but from the little I've seen I can already tell this is the exact same game. All of these are not so much new titles as they are the same title, again, wearing a costume and pretending it is someone else. You walk around and find hidden objects, solve rudimentary puzzles, and try not to fall asleep. There are really two types of hidden objects in this game: actual hidden object scenes and hidden objects that are scattered throughout the various background environments. Occasionally you will run into something you can't quite get to yet, like a locked chest or an elevated door, and the game will tell you "hey, you need to find the code to this chest, chump". You'll then be shown the objects you need to find to proceed and can go around to all available areas and try to find the pieces you need.
The problem is neither of these hidden object types works very well. The scenes themselves are fine, but there are only fifteen in the entire game, at least eight or so of which are in the bonus final chapter that is only half an hour long or so. For a game that is a "hidden object" game, there aren't a ton of hidden objects to find. The worst part is the game never does a good job of actually hiding these objects, opting instead to just sort of drop them on the ground and knock off early for a cigarette break. The issue is that after you click on an object, it will disappear to show that you've picked it up. The game doesn't want to just leave a blank outline where it once stood as that would look stupid, so instead what they've done is draw the background first and placed the hidden objects on top of them. This might not sound like a big deal, but sometimes the objects look like they were drawn by a different person at a different time and also they were not aware the objects were supposed to be hidden. I was finding things I knew were hidden objects without even knowing I was looking for them most of the time. I'd get to a scene and go "oh, yeah, I'll need to pick up those six things huh" and then a couple of screen later the quest would pop up and I'd walk back and grab exactly what I needed.
The story is ridiculous and might as well not even be there. There is supposed to be what I think is a BIG TWIST in terms of who is trying to free the giant, but the game literally goes "HM ISN'T THAT PERSON SUSPICIOUS HMM HMM HMMMMMM" and you're like, well not really, but I guess he is now. Characters show up for two lines before disappearing, and there just isn't any sense of narrative flow at any point in the game. Maybe I'm dumb for expecting a decent plot from a hidden object game, but then what else am I supposed to be playing this for? The puzzles are mindless, the hidden object scenes are easy and bad, and the characters all sound like they are voiced by the first five people they found wandering the parking lot. Even at a reduced price, this isn't worth it.
It's appropriate that I feel swindled out of my money for a game about magic beans, I guess.

Fans of this genre should already be a familiar with Artifex Mundi, a prolific and well regarded  casual adventure game developer. It should come as no surprise that this is a recommendation. This is your second mission as a Brothers Grimm detective in this Artifex Mundi series. Your mission this time is to  find the last of the giants, defeat him and save the world. You think the Grimm Brothers would help a rookie detective more....
The voice acting was passable and the artwork is the excellent standard expected of Artifex Mundi. The best art work in this game is in the Magical World locations. My personal favourite artwork location was Moon World but I think this is the best location artwork in Desert World:
I did not enjoy having to click continue on my mouse every line in the voice acting. Listening to the cut scene uninterrupted is preferable. Needing to pause the game is the only possible and useful reason. If so a pause button instead of continue is suffice.
The achievements in this title are easier as you can 100% this game on easy, advanced and expert. Collecting all 40 collectibles would of been a good achievement to add. To get all achievements you must play the bonus game. In previous titles playing the bonus game it has been just one achievement but in this game you will be missing four;
Currently based on the Artifex Mundi games I have played I feel that this is a weaker entry for three reasons.
1.	The Mini games in this title are on the easy side and I would of liked more .For the more experienced casual adventure gamer you may not find much challenge in this one.
2.	 The game feels like constant Hidden Object scenes. This is because as well as the traditional Hidden Object Scenes there is Hidden Object Pieces  game play in all locations. This means having to find items before you can use them on objects.
3.	The story wasn't as engaging as for me personally. This is really down to a matter of personal taste/themes but I felt like this wasn't the strongest writing.
If you like the idea of easier game play,
, in my opinion is a better game that I recommend for more experienced adventure gamers even if the artwork in the this game is superior.Despite my criticisms of this particular title I still look forward to trying the first game in this series, the first detective mission, recently released on steam which I will still be making time to play this year...

The name alone caught my attention, I love fairy tales! The game proved to live up to my expectations and was a lot of fun.
The story is simple, you're on a quest to stop an evil force from bringing Giants back down to Earth and also save Jack. Jack is a young boy who traded his cow for magic beans, when one of the beans grows into a huge beanstalk he is captured. You proceed to meet the Guardians and aid them on your journey and they help you to stop the evil one and free Jack. With the giant destroyed everyone is happy! The bonus chapter is basically you finding the remaining magic beans so the same thing doesn't happen again.
There aren't many surprises in the story, even the identity of the evil one isn't a shock. The game play is solid hidden item fare, though items are scattered around main areas for you to find so it all feels like one big hidden item game with a few puzzles thrown in. Oddly enough, the bonus chapter does not follow the same formula, it's more traditional. Either way, it's fun and offers some challenge. Though the game is a bit easy, especially if your a veteran of this genre.
It's fully voiced with lovely artwork but it's short and easy. It's still a great game and would be a great one for young children. Older players may want to wait for a sale price, however.

The Lost Mythologies is a student project that exists as a psuedo-game jam, where they sought to see how much they could make in how little time.
On that metric, and that metric alone, they did well. Most game-jam games are 10-15 traditional minute-long titles that aren't worth playing. These devs made a fairly ambitious hack n slash with a decent half hour's worth of content. There's some stuff here that's worth seeing. A fantastic set of assets from the bottom-up, for one. A great boss soundtrack, for another.
Most criticism is easily rendered moot by pointing out the the previous. It's a student project. They didn't set out to create a massive, indepth combat system, or a set of incredible believable levels with heavy exploration, or anything along those lines. And that's fine. But there's some basic stuff here that just makes this game not that much fun, and not something I see myself replaying.
Enemies have so-so hitstun that procs less often than it should. Which is always. They'll gladly ignore any opening if they momentarily think about it, regardless of whether or not you've baited their attacks. Their telegraphs are pathetic, more often than not just limply reaching out and your health bar decreases, rather than the exaggerated motions that a fast-paced game demands. 2/3 of the special attacks are absolutely terrible, doing about as much damage as a single heavy attack which doesn't do that much to begin with.
There's no way to really punish far-ranged enemies who'll gladly bank it and run, even that they only die in two hits, they'll still give you a solid 10 seconds of cat and mouse to just waste your time.
Even the boss comes down to just dodging through boring attacks and then running off to deal with the mobs he summons. Although to a undeniably great piece of BGM.
The rest is fine, whatever. Hell, the apple-shaped assets under the skirt give you something to look at during the chase. But a hack and slash where you can't reliably avoid damage and includes enemy types that aren't fun to fight isn't really fighting for the highest echelons of design.
Still, it's half an hour long. It's free. It's in Unreal engine, so it doesn't look bad. It's fairly ambitious for what it is and not just typical game jam garbage. If you're just after something casual to spend half an hour with and forget about, this is here for you.
Also the single achievement for launching the game has been broken for over a year, which I'm not sure how that even works.

This is one of my favorite games of all time. It's short by today's standards but that's because the game itself is more of a fleshed out tech demo than a AAA title.  That said, the premise of using portals to solve platforming and physics puzzles is SO good that it doesn't NEED to be more.  They didn't need to tack on an 80 hour epic storyline, level up system with skill trees, endless procedural crafting or whatever else companies think a game needs to be good.
That didn't stop Valve from going the extra mile, though. Instead of making a set of solid puzzles and calling it a day, they gave us the BEST antagonist I have ever seen.  At all.  The fact that the game is pretty repetative doesn't even sink in when GLaDOS's quirky chatter keeps you entertained.
While these days (oh god, is this game really 10 years old already?) it seems like a small game with not enough meat on its bones, what's there is SO good it doesn't NEED more.  Besides, they expanded the concept in Portal 2 if you REALLY need a game with a bigger scope.

Portal is a first person 3-D puzzle platforming game released by Valve. While it's relatively short, and definitely is lacking in content, the adventure of Chell is well worth your time and money.
The story (no major spoilers):
You wake up in an empty box with a radio playing, and nothing much else. You here a robotic voice that guides you out, and then you begin your adventure.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is by far, the most unique gameplay I've seen in a long time. It's similar to Half-Life 2, but with portals. You have to play it to believe it.
Verdict:
Considering Portal turns 10 years old this year, I can surely say it is one of the best games of the last decade, and set the new standard of single player games. While it is short and isn't the most inavative game out there, it holds a special spot in my, and plenty other gamers, heart.
Portal gets a solid 8/10.

First off, I have absolutely no experience with the XCOM franchise, so I can't say how the plot stands with the other games, or how faithful the universe is.
Besides, I haven't played a tactical TPS in a long time, which means that I may overlook some aspects that avid players of the genre look forward to.
But here are my general thoughts. I'll try not to be too detailed, since AAAs have such a bigger scale compared to what I'm used to playing.
So. The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a tactical third person shooter, set in the 60's, in the first alien invasion of Earth. The best of the best are united in the XCOM to fight this invasion, and cover it up to protect the population.
You'll go through several missions (some minor, some major), and you'll get to know the people you're working with between each, in the base.
You have a squad of 3 people (you, and 2 AI partners), that you have some control over, during the fights. There are different classes in the game, and with each come different skills to aid you in battle. Some are support focused (providing shields, damage buffs, etc.), engineers (focus on tech, turrets, etc.), artillery (with long range deadly shots), you get the drill.
Each of them can be leveled up to rank 5, and you go as far as rank 10. With each rank you choose 1 of 2 perks (sometimes, 1 of 1... tough choice, there).
Let's start with the
.
It's a AAA game, and that's very clear. Everything looks really nice, and it felt the theme surprisingly well, with the lighting effects giving the game an
! Other parts of the game looked more generic, unfortunately. But overall, it certainly looked great, with good particle effects, lighting, and physics.
The
also fit the theme very well, both the 60's feel, and the sci-fi. Unfortunately, it was very far apart. I don't feel like they've used the music very effectively, specially in the tense and emotional moments, the music in those was simply underwhelming.
Overall, it didn't really feel as unique as it could have. As a AAA, it did very little to standout, despite being pretty good aside from that.
One thing it did well in the beginning, was portraying the time setting well, using posters, and even the conversations with the different people.
Moving on.
The
started out pretty good, but the probems soon started to reveal themselves. I chose to play in Commander Difficulty at first. The problem with that, was the friendly AI. They died within 4 seconds of the start of the fight. And I'm not exaggerating!
If I sent someone to revive them, they'd just stand in the middle of the shots and would die as well. And that was pretty much the experience. That kind of challenge wasn't welcome at all. I spent way more time trying to keep my squad alive than fighting!
So... after about 5 missions I decided I had enough with it, and turned it to Veteran. I died twice in the whole game after that. Once in the last mission, with throws wave after wave of enemies after you.
There's just such a big discrepancy between Hard and Very Hard... that's not a very good balance, in my opinion.
Commander mode could have been really strategic and tense, if the AI was worth something.       Unfortunately, it was really bad. And you could see in the end, comparing their kills to yours. You alone did about 95% of the job, so yeah...
Other than that, it wasn't bad. You had several different weapons at your disposal, different enemies had to be taken out in different ways (not too different, but a bit different nonetheless), the skills lead to some nice teamwork... I wasn't bad!
It was not spectacular, but I was fairly enjoyable.
As I said before, between missions, you'll be in the
. Here, you can talk to the scientists, engineers, pretty much everyone, and get their view on the invasion. You'll also know why they're there, and what they're working on. That was cool. It didn't blow my mind, but it's good that it's there, if you feel like exploring a bit more.
There are also Notes, Photos, and Audio"Logs" spread out, during the breaks between battles. These also give you a bit more insight into the world, which is always good!
Something that really bothered me though, was the Audio Logs. You had to stand near to listen to it. ... Why? The whole point of audio logs is to keep the player exploring, while being presented with the backstory. And they managed to screw it up, and have you stop your playing to listen to it... It makes no sense! Might as well give you a note instead of an audio log... I don't understand.
There's not much else to say about it, really. The cover system works fine, for the most part. One complaint I have, is that you can't roll into cover! That's really important, in my view! You can roll out of the way fine. But if you roll into cover, it doesn't connect, so you'll stand up, fully vulnerable, after rolling. And you'll take unnecessary shots. I don't see why it's not in there either, but oh well...
I may seem overly negative about the game, for a positive review. The fact of the matter is, that it mostly functions very well. The gunplay is solid, movement in fluid, combat involves some level of tactic, while ordering your squad members, ...
It's not a bad game at all. It's simply not a very good one either, and for full price, I definitely do not recommend it. But if you're curious about the setting, or you're a fan of XCOM, I don't see a problem in getting in a sale, or something along those lines.
The character interactions, though, were really bad in my opinion. And so was the way they handled the ending.
SPOILERS HERE.
Overall, I expected more. But for the price at which I got it, it was a fine game. Won't change the world in any way, but it was enjoyable.

Costume Quest is one of the amazing games that came out of Double Fine's Amnesia Fortnight. A traditional turn based RPG with a Halloween concept and smart writing, Costume Quest is perfect for all ages. This game comes with a free DLC called Grubbins on Ice.
Depending on who you choose, you play as either Reynold or Wren. The twins are hyped to go out and trick-or-treat but a monster ends mistaking one of the siblings as a large piece of candy and kidnaps the child. With the help of a cat(?) who may or may not have given your character special powers through his/her costume, your character goes off on a quest to save his/her sibling with friends he/she makes on the way, and maybe, in the process of doing so, end up saving Halloween.
Costume Quest's story is fairly adequate but it is bolstered by stellar writing filled to the brim with traditional Double Fine humour. Expect to chuckle often while playing this game.
Costume Quest is a turn based RPG lite. It's very simplistic in execution, and gets the job done. Do not expect huge skill trees or deep mechanics - there are none in this game. You can do additional damage or reduce damage taken by doing QTEs with very generous timings, and you have 'Battle Stamps' that give you passive bonuses like dealing additional damage. Your characters are also healed automatically after every battle. There are no random encounters in this game (aside from the monsters that you encounter while trick-or-treating). Costume Quest has boss battles that are quite fun indeed.
Outside of combat, you play in fixed camera hub worlds, trick-or-treating at various houses or bashing various environmental objects to get candy. You can use candy to buy new Battle Stamps to make your character even stronger, however, each character is only allowed to equip one Battle Stamp at a time. After you trick-or-treat all the houses in a given hub, you are allowed to pass through the Monster Gate that blocks your progress to the next hub and this repeats several times till you reach the end of the game.
Each costume your characters wear provide them with various powers in battle. The Statue of Liberty costume plays a traditional healer role while the Space Warrior is a pure melee character. Some of your costumes also have environmental effects - the main character can use the Shield ability to block falling debris while wearing the Knight Costume, while the Robot costume can allow you to quickly Boost yourself so that you can dash around through the environment. You'll need your costumes to not only fight, but also make it through the various obstacles you encounter in each hub, all the while collecting candy and Creepy Treat cards, doing quests, and finding various pieces of costumes that will help you in your adventure.
This is a very easy game, and one should expect a playthrough to be between 4-6 hours. The additional DLC chapter, Grubbins on Ice, is another hour or two of gameplay.
Costume Quest has a very charming art style and is definitely easy on the eyes. The small scenes that precede battes where your character transforms into a giant sized, realized version of the costume he/she is wearing is really good and well animated.
However, the game doesn't run all that well technically. It's sufficient but a game like this shouldn't be having difficulties running at a solid 30 or 60 FPS. There are bits of slowdown, most noticeably in the scene where you are trick-or-treating. This is not a big deal in battles, fortunately.
On the aural front, Costume Quest is not a winner. None of the music in this game is memorable or even good.  I can't comment on the voice acting in this game because it has none. Sound effects do their job.
Costume Quest is a must-play, fun game that is perfectly paced - just before the signs of repetition even kick in, the game ends. Clever writing and tons of heart make this game perfect for every age. If you see this game on sale, be sure to snap it up. My only regret is I didn't play this game on Halloween. Oh well.
The game was an ~600 MB download on Steam.
Costume Quest works on Windows 10. Word of caution : DO NOT ALT+TAB OUT OF THIS GAME; Alt+Tab will result in a crash, almost always.
Costume Quest has Steam Trading Cards.
PRO TIP : You can skip the short scene that plays when you get into a battle by pressing Shift.

XCOM's return to prominence has been an interesting one, originally an FPS with little to do with the original series, it was scrapped, and it's side project, Enemy Unknown, became an unexpected hit.
Following in the wake of it's success is The Bureau, kind of a half way house between the original FPS concept and the popular strategy remake. Many of the original concepts from the scrapped FPS return here, such as the 1950s setting, the 'silicoids' and the investigative themes.
What on the surface looks like a shallow cash-in, is actually a very deep and enjoyable hybrid TPS/RTS game, but in order to really enjoy The Bureau you have to be willing to give it a chance and excuse some of it's shortcomings.
It's story is paint-by-numbers, it's characters are shallow, the levels are linear, it's everything you'd expect from a mediocre shooter, but for those willing to invest in the game, there's a deep and tactical experience to be had, not to mention some genuinely clever plot twists that most people won't see coming.
The Bureau boasts many of the features of a 'true' XCOM game, you'll unlock better equipment as the game progresses, you'll recruit and train soldiers who can die permenantly, and you'll need to be strategic and use your assets creatively in order to win against increasingly grim odds. What sets it apart from the traditional XCOM games is the story driven campaign and the more personal perspective of being a soldier in the field.
It features quite nice graphics at times, and the 50s setting and aesthetic is charming, reminiscent of Bioshock and Fallout. The cover-based shooting is simple but tight, and using the tactical view, which slows time and allows you to issue orders and use skills, is a joy to use, you'll get immense satisfaction from pulling off combos.
For those fans of the XCOM universe, old and new, this is a must have game, and for fans of third person shooters and strategy games, this is a solid addition to your library.

I've enjoyed my first hour and find it to be very much like a cross between Ark, and Space Engineers, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoyed either.
My first hour and a half of the game started with me beginning the tutorial phase of the game after what appears to have been a Master Chief style entry onto a desert-like planet.
After fumbling around with my controls I fixed up the breach in my space suit with duct-tape (yes...duct tape). But it was too late to save my oxygen supplies and I was now slowly dying.
Frantically, I scavenged from some nearby crates and was able to find enough resources within them to arm myself and fulfill the tutorial mission of, "build a inflatable dome". I placed the dome and was stumbling my way to it as black spots started to appear in my vision.
I then promptly collapsed and died mere feet away from the airlock...
After re-spawning nearby, and in full health, I looted my body and proceeded inside where I saved the game at the bed and found a laptop. I clicked on the laptop and found I had a few "encryption locks" available. I clicked on one and it started the decryption process which was like one of those pipe games, where you have to rotate the tiles to make the flow of water go from one point to another, only I only had a set amount of moves within which to complete it.
I failed the first attempt, but had one more which I finished and was rewarded with a "floor light" schematic, which I had no idea how to build yet so decided to continue with the tutorial missions.
My next step was to head out and find resources so that I could build a depository. Upon stepping out however I found myself being welcomed to the neighborhood by a giant sand worm.
I patched up the hole it had just made in my suit while my friendly drone began shooting at it. I armed myself with the assault rifle I had found earlier and made short work of the alien monster.
I then switched my assault rifle for a more humble pickaxe type thing and went looking for resources.
Unlike other games such as Ark or Space Engineers, the resource harvesting was a little more simplified, although I found out later that resources also had their own nodes, there was also two more common nodes called "precious metals", and "base metals", which gave you random resources within a certain selection, which was a perfect way to find resources needed to build the more basic things.
After finding enough materials, and a few battles with some "skelepod" aliens, I made my way back and built a depository where I...well deposited my stuff.
After getting a level up notification, I went into the skill web where I had points to spend in each branch of military, engineering and science.
My next mission was to build a forge which would prove a bit more challenging as it required plutonium which, although found in the base metals nodes, it showed up a lot more infrequently.
It started to get dark and a sand storm had rolled in, so I went back to base and deposited the resources I did manage to find.
Still lacking the appropriate amount of plutonium, and no way to advance time, I discovered I had a headlamp which made things a little easier, however the sandstorm had not eased up so I ordered my drone buddy to follow me.
After some walking I found an area which held an abundance of resources, however before I could strip the place bare I become over-encumbered, so I ordered my drone to set a patrol route and mine anything it came across between our location and the depository.
On my way back to the depository the sun began to rise and I was greeted by a message that congratulated me on my survival of the first day.
After some more resource collecting, alien monster killing and exploration, I got enough resources to build my forge which unlocked a whole new set of materials and objects enabling me to build my first proper structure, the Habitat.
This is where the Space Engineers sort of gameplay comes in, because you have to set down a frame and build the objects piece by piece, each consuming a small amount resources as you go.
Each wall is customizable in both colour and design, allowing a selection between a normal wall, a windowed wall, or a coupling which allows you to link other building to it via a hallway piece.
This was my first hour and a half experience with the game and as I said I rather enjoyed it. The game flows at a decent pace so there is a good balance between building, gathering and fighting, while leaving you with a mostly unfettered ability to explore at your own pace. While this is my experience alone, the game clearly has a lot of potential and could easily benefit from a few more people playing together weather they are friends or enemies.

I know a girl quite like Samantha. She's the sweetest thing, but really, really introverted. I've tried to understand how come she "makes" everything so damn difficult - I mean, everybody sometimes think "what do they think about me?" about other people, but I never understood just how much introverted people keep themselves under the magnifying glass. This game was not just a fun point-and-click story with cutesy drawings, but a real eye-opener about how it feels to be an introvert. Edit: I also noticed that some people whom suffer from SAD have interpreted Samantha as "mean" or "spiteful". I think I can relate to that. When you're scared, and hungry on top of that, you tend to think or even say things you don't really mean, or usually even have the guts to say. It's part of how adrenaline affects us. The "you may have your precious kitchen back" might not have been said with a spiteful tone, to add to that. Imagine her thinking/saying that with a sigh of relief... "The Beanstalk," is the second installment of "Fairy Tale Mysteries." Previous game from this series is called "The Puppet Thief."
There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're nicely done. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are three different game difficulty modes to choose from: Casual, Advanced and Expert.
The notebook keeps tracks of the events that had happened in the game.
There are interactive items in the game, they're marked with a symbol, but sometimes these interactive items do require extra items before they can be interact with.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates there are tasks that needs to be done at certain locations.
Most of the hidden object scenes consists of traditional word list and picture items. Some of them do require little or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are rather easy to solve without much difficulty. For most of these puzzles there's a reset button. However, there's definitely a skip button, for all of the puzzles. These two features are only present in "Casual" game difficulty mode.
There are eleven different achievements to unlock during gameplay. Each of these achievements comes with certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
There's at least forty decorative egg collectibles in-game, they're scattered throughout the game, most of them can be cleverly hidden in plain view.
Since this is a collector's edition game, there's a bonus chapter, but it can be unlocked only after the main story of the game's completed.
The bonus chapter continues where the main story had ended.
There are total of five different trading cards. You only get the three of those cards from the game. There are several ways to get the rest of the trading card: Purchased from Steam’s Market; Trade with friends; Booster Packs and it’s Booster Pack Creator. Badge can be crafted and upgraded with these trading cards. This feature is only available for Steam’s version of this game.
Final thoughts, I definitely enjoying playing this game all the way through to the end. The gameplay wise is very different from the previous game "Fairy Tale Mysteries: The Puppet Thief." I want to point out in order to  clear up some confusion that some might've about this game. Gogii had developed this game completely themselves. Artifex Mundi just published it.
The replay value I would say for this game is low as in every once in a while. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Another inferior Artifiex Mundi game not developed by Artifex Mundi.
There are some minor egg collectibles to search for, and, in the main, game, very few hidden object searches (about 5-7), which seems odd for a hidden object game.  There's also an odd inventory system where, in order to do anything, you need to find multiple objects throughout the environment to build any object needed.  It essentially makes the inventory system into mini-hidden object games, and becomes the primary gameplay of the game.  What's strange is that this system is abandoned in the bonus chapter for a conventional inventory system, and makes it feel somewhat arbitrary, as if the game developers ran out of money to program the entire game as intended.   The bonus chapter also features more hidden object scenes than the full game.
It's not a bad game, and some of the inventory/hidden object puzzles are pretty tough.  But for whatever reasons, perhaps as a result of a rather thin and uninspired storyline, the game feels pretty underwhelming.  It's also a short game.  I have 6.3 hours clocked, and that's for both the main game and the bonus, and a good chunk of that was the game being left on during The Leftovers, The Affair, and Homeland where I wasn't playing the game much, if at all.
5/10

I didn't play the first one because I didn't realise that it was on Steam and already in my library. I wanted to try this one, published (it's the keyword) by Artifex Mundi on Steam. And you can't see that it's not them that developed it.
Your role is to search who is the hooded man that is trying to bring back giants on Earth (or into that magical world, choose what you want). Based on the fairy tale "Jack and the Beanstalk", you're going to search for beans, guardians, a traitor and a way to save Jack and stop that terrible plan.
While the story is good - I enjoyed it, the gameplay only suffers of some well-hidden objects. But that's where the frustration begins. I rarely hit the hint button during a HO game. In fact, I refrain myself to do it in a game with achievements included. Unfortunately, I was forced here to do it because of these needed items to advance in the story. And it's the same for the HO scenes. There is also a lot of objects that need to be "repaired", making you go slower for the achievement where you have to find everything under a minute. You will probably unlock it in a second playthrough, after keeping somewhere in your head their locations.
And while the graphics are really correct, though not transcending, I was disappointed in the soundtrack: I already heard it in another HO. Yet, well, it's a good track.
Another thing with the gameplay is that it's different in the main game and in the bonus chapter. The main game is showing you a list of items to find from a scene to another to build what you need - and these items become clickable when you find the use for them. The bonus chapter is more behaving like any other HO game: you don't need to find that this item will help you to click on it, you can collect it without the knowledge.
While I'll recommend the game, I'll advise you to get it with a discount - I don't think it's worthy of 10 bucks. The -40% discount for the launch was already a better price but this game will probably drop lower, so I suggest you to wait until it's 2 or 3 bucks.

I bought this game because I was looking for a new challenging RTS, and although this game only has one mode at this time which is survival, I have not been disappointed.
I have played 8 survival games and have only managed to complete 2 of them on easiest and easy difficulty.
Every time I play it my base is more efficient and I feel more confident to take land from the zombies.
My 8th base had roughly 15 Titans defending the 6 entrances, and it was ONLY JUST enough for the final hoard.
This gives the game a lot of replay value, as you are testing your building and management skills every time.
The units and buildings all have a charm, as much as you would find in Command & Conquer.
I would like to see more options for sound and gameplay, at the moment you can't turn off the noises for when you click on a building. I would also like to see more options for units and their skill progression.
It would also be nice to be able to see the health for the units on the hud when they are all selected (they are all in one portrait of each type with no health bar) although pressing Alt will suffice for now, maybe even have a "Units" button on the HUD
So far, for the fun I have had on this game already I would easily say its one of the best RTS I have played. keen to see how it the development continues.
