A brief notice is required up front if you are not yet aware: The Bureau is NOT an XCOM game, has nothing to do with the XCOM series, and contributes nothing to its lore.  It is a fantasy "what-if" spinoff scenario that has just as much relevance to the franchise as the C-3PO's cereal
had to Star Wars.  Having said that, even if it did not have XCOM in its name, Bureau is still a poor attempt at turning Mass Effect's blend of over the shoulder shooting and command wheel tactics into a pure action game.
The developers obviously want you to use their fancy Battle Focus feature to issue orders and devise brilliant plans to thwart your alien enemies, but made several baffling decisions which frustrate any efforts to take it seriously.  Enemies recieve large amounts of damage reduction while in cover, requiring a large number of shots to kill.  Complicating this is your low ammo reserve, which does two things: 1) It strongly encourages you to flank the enemy, removing the enemy's damage reduction and offering a better angle to headshot them, and 2) keeps you on the move so you can constantly pick up the weapons of your fallen enemies to replenish your ammo.  While this certainly does work on paper, this core gameplay feature undermines itself in practice.
Frankly, your agents do not listen to you and must constantly be babysat.  Ordering them to hold a position does entirely nothing, as they will not only abandon this position as soon as they feel like it, but even if they don't, their health bars vanish rapidly as they are quickly gunned down.  Their reluctance to stay in place and propensity for being wounded limit any kind of tactical manuvering you can actually do.  Even when they ARE following your orders, they are terrible shots and do little damage on their own.  Giving them the orders to move while you lay fire on the enemy does not seem to make a difference, and since your health bar is not much stronger than your fellow agents, isolating yourself just puts you at risk.  The end result is a stop-and-pop game where your weapons are woefully underpowered due to an unusable cover/flanking mechanic, interspersed with frustrating moments of scrambling for more ammunition by sprinting through a hail of gunfire and hoping that you or your allies aren't brought down.
Outside of the gameplay, the story and setting are well done and intriguing for the majority of the game.  Despite the bland-ish protagonist, the characters are designed and performed well enough to make the plot enjoyable.  The usual tropes associated with atmospheric world building are here as well: lots of improbable notes and "audio logs" are present.  Apparently reel-to-reel tape can generate its own audio.  It's all rather harmless fun and nothing really rubbed me the wrong way until the very last mission where some extremely corny drama had me thinking that I had not only seen the same thing in the Gangstas In Space ending for Saints Row the Third, but that Saints Row actually did it *better*.  Ouch.
Even if you're looking for some popcorny cold war sci-fi, I cannot recommend this game at all.  The gameplay is frustrating, working against you in every battle.  Even if the AI worked well and your weapons were more effective, I very much doubt that the process of issuing individual orders for every single meaningless battle would hold a player's attention for long.  Strategy games offer much deeper options for deployment, maneuver, and attack and give more substantial consequences for each battle.  For the amount of effort that would go into this battle system, even if fully functional, you get nothing in return except the privilage of doing it over and over again just to progress through an otherwise standard Call of Duty style level layout.
Because there are some aspects of this game that are done competently, I cannot give it less than a 4 out of 10.  As far as my personal satisfaction with it, however, I must rate that a 2.  I pressed on to the end only to watch the ending so I could say I've seen it.  I see no reason to ever play this again, or recommend it to anyone.  Better luck next time.

When I bought this game I thought, "Well, it doesn't have anything like X-Com gameplay at all, but maybe it wont be too bad."
I was wrong. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥where do I begin, how about gameplay. It plays like a bad, uninspired Mass Effect, the only cool feature being the slow-mo that comes up when you're selecting which skills to use and deciding where to put your AI partners. Theres not much in the way of team management outside of combat. Your AI partners by the way are essentially blank slate goons whose skills and appearance you can customize, and they show up in cutscenes, and thats about it. No dialog aside from stuff they yell in combat. Equipment wise all you got are guns and backpacks, and there are about a thousand god damn backpacks, all with different bonuses, but after you get the straight damage increase or defense increase ones you probably wont bother experimenting, because the bonuses themselves are pretty lack luster. You get most of those backpacks from side missions you send AI dudes to go handle solo so they can get a free level up.
Story wise it's a mess. Without getting into spoilers the gist of it is a "SAVE THE WORLD FROM THE ALIENS" plot like you'd expect, but aside from the angle of the mass cover up, it's pretty forgettable. Speaking of forgettable, I honestly cant recall the name of the protagonist, he's that bland. With a backstory of "SOLDIER/AGENT BADASS" you'd think they'd think of something more interesting that "He's seen some♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. There are side plots that are straight up dropped, there are moral choices that dont actually matter (aside from one I think, and its not even one at the end) and the general theme of censorship and "NO ONE MUST KNOW" is pretty much not there aside from the occasional dialog snippet from NPCs. You dont burn or hide evidence yourself, its more or less just an alien murder ride from start to finish. The game tries to connect itself with the Enemy Unknown/Within game, I wont go into spoilers but it doesnt do it very well, and there are a lot of "What" moments.
The setting is Americana/Cold War, and while you can sort of see it in the levels and loving on characters, the actually COLD WAR, even though it would be rightly overshadowed by the wide scale alien invasion, only comes up like twice.
And besides all that, heres some nit picking!
Why are there audio logs everywhere? EVERYWHERE.
How does everyone already know the names to each of the alien enemy types? Theres never any "What do we call it?" moments, its just "MUTON! SECTOPOD!"
Why does the artillery skill work indoors?
Why does this game try to force itself into the EU/W story when it doesnt want to be consistant? "Nah, we bulldozed all that sick plasma tech and got rid of the info we had on the aliens, have fun starting from scratch while fighting off a second invasion, but its cool, you can have a fedora."
WHY IS IT SO EASY. I played on the hardest difficult and it doesnt make the enemy AI any smarter, just harder to kill.
Final verdict: Wasted Potential/10, do not buy.

I recommend this game to anyone who likes easy achievements, or likes connecting personally with a character/ experiencing things that you are unfamiliar with.
Samantha is a college student that overcomplicates everything on account of her social anxiety. Things that you think are easy to achieve aren't as simple to Samantha because she doesn't have the ability to tolerate social instances that are commonly simple. Almost everything she does feels like the wrong thing to do (Simulating that she is worried about every little thing no matter what; which perfectly expresses her anxiety) so it causes her to slide into anger and bitterness with herself. Your job is to make choices that make her feel comforted with doing a daily task.
This game places the player inside of the mind of a young girl who tries to avoid social conflict. It's an almost perfect simulation, for people who don't suffer with social anxiety, to experience the worried thoughts that can cross their mind over simple matters. In this instance, Samantha overcomplicates cooking herself a small meal because she is worried what others think.
If you have never felt social anxiety, this is basically it. "Will they think I'm weird" "should I talk to them, or ignore them, but will that make them think I'm awkward?". It doesn't put in a lot of factors, but it comes surprisingly close; and at the low cost of .00 cents I'd say this is a good "purchase" for a few hours of interesting dialogue and beautiful scenery. I'm serious, the art is fantastic and simply cute, how can you NOT love this game. The music also rises perfectly in certain instances that can induce the player to feel anxiety while Samantha feels anxiety, and it lowers down to a softer tune when she is comforted by being alone. It's all-together absolutely perfect.
(Some of the other reviews make an opinion that social anxiety doesn't force you to be angry, but they missed the point that Samantha isn't angry at others- she is angry with herself for not being able to do things without worrying, therefore making her interactions a bit detached. In the scene where Samantha says to the girls at the kitchen that they could have their precious kitchen back, she didn't actually say that, she merely thought it in her head. She isn't angry or bitter towards them, she's just annoyed that she didn't get a proper response from them. The proper response probably being to leave politely. Which is a perfect representation of social anxiety; she can't examine the fact that they probably don't think anything of her being in the kitchen, so she worries that they think she is weird. Then she becomes annoyed that they think she is weird. Most of the people making reviews haven't taken into consideration that other people react to social anxiety in different ways, so don't pay too much attention to their opinion if they don't recommend the game because it's "A bad representation of social anxiety".)
Thanks for reading and I hope you enjoy the game as much as I do!

Hatoful Boyfriend is a visual novel video game about a high-school age Japanese human girl who lives in a cave and attends a very prestigious prep school for pigeons. Very early on, the game offers you the option to see "human portrait" versions of every male pigeon when you meet them and from there on, you must decide which pigeon to date. With that all in mind, believe me when I say that this game will suprise you with just how insane it is, and I love it all the more for that reason (among others).
My first introduction to the genre of Japanese visual novels was with Sakura Spirit, and that really only had tons of fan-service and an adorable story about cute yet desperately horny furries and their friends. While I enjoyed the fan-service, I felt Sakura Spirit was pretty hollow as a visual novel as it only gave the player one choice to make in the entire game. So when it came time for me to give Hatoful Boyfriend a try, I was hooked immediately by the web of choices waiting to be discovered in the game. Where Sakura Spirit had a single choice that would only partially change the game, Hatoful Boyfriend has a string of multiple reactions that will end up in different endings. Where Sakura Spirit had badly translated sensuality and fanservice, Hatoful Boyfriend has full blown insanity with extremely well-written plot twists. The only other game I've played where I was this desperate to replay the game in hopes of seeking out different endings was the Stanley Parable, and believe me when I say that this game is so much more worthy of a multiple ending gag game.
While the premise and initial setting for the game is pretty absurd and quirky, you are given several indications through gameplay of what type of world you live in that condones human-pigeon relationships and are given several possible endings, depending on which male bird you choose and HOW you choose them (i.e. submissively, dominantly, romantically, accidentally, etc.). Some of these endings range from the sad, to the silly, to the absurd, to the horrific, to the gut-wrenchingly insane (the "Fallen Anghel" ending blew my mind), to the downright non-canon. Like so many other visual novels and multi-ending video games, Hatoful Boyfriend's appeal lies in discovering each new ending and all the options hidden away in the game. Overall, the music is fitting, the translation is superb and the risk of actually dying all give the game that much more appeal.
If you like insane Japanese exports, visual novels, bizarre stories of interspecies love and the support/shame it gives rise to  or a combination of all three of these things than you should definitely check out Hatoful Boyfriend!
100% COMPLETION EDIT: I just finished playing the final ending. The game definitely gets deeper and darker the more endings you uncover. It make start out silly, cute and quirky, but it gets pretty grim. Very well-written, though.
YEARS LATER EDIT: Yep, still a great game.

Horrible controls kill this game.
I can get behind the concept, and the music is fitting, but the only supported inputs are the arrow keys. Even if you try to map a controller in the Unity options, the game ignores it.
Gameplay in a nutshell: you are glued to either the top or bottom of the screen, and need to pass through the gaps between letters in order to collect them to form the word shown at the bottom of the screen. Unfortunately you have very little time to react, and combine that with a tilting camera that makes it extra unclear where exactly your block is located compared to the upcoming letters, and this game becomes less about skill and more about luck.
This game either needs to get rid of the tilting camera, or give some kind of indication where exactly your cursor is, by a shadow or light in front perhaps. In its current state it only serves as a source of frustration.

Remember that old flash game where you guide a missle down a tunnel and try to avoid crashing by flying through holes in the walls? This game is basically that. And that's fine! I like that kind of game. But the controls here kill it.
You fly through the holes in letters and avoid touching the letters themselves. While you're free to move whereever you want horizontally, there are only two vertical planes: top and bottom. So you can't fly through the center of the letter O; you have to fly around the upper or lower corners of it. So that takes getting used to.
But the WORST thing, by far, is the camera. The whole game is about lining up your block to make it through the empty spaces. But every time you move, no matter how small of a move it is, the camera violently whips around so you can't see straight. Imagine trying to thread a needle while shaking your head back and forth. It's nigh unplayable when you can't figure out where your block is going in a game about percision.
You know what would fix this ENTIRE game? Lock the camera behind the cube you control. That way you can actually see what's going on. The way this game is now, it's an unplayable mess.

While no particular aspect of
is earth shattering, the overall experience is quite enjoyable and makes for a solid addition to the fairly niche tactical shooter lineup.
Given the fantastic games that get made by 2K, it is strange to me that their development process can so frequently be described as problematic, as was the case for
.  This title had some interesting features planned such as detective work and stealth based gameplay, but those unfortunately got cut as the game underwent repeated revisions and delays.  It sounded promising.  As is, The Bureau fails to inspire much passion but nonetheless contains plenty of fun and is without question worth a play.
I have to admit I was very excited about The Bureau prior to getting my hands on it, and even now have a certain amount of bias favoring this one, because of:
I love speculative, historical fiction.  I loved the
IP and was ready for more such action, and of course like everyone, I love convincing science fiction.  The Bureau delivered in some regards and not others.
The story expands upon what's already established by previous titles in the IP.  The plot had some clever ideas that I liked, and some that baffled, none of which I can describe without spoilers, so I won't go there.  I didn't play the classic series back when it came out in the mid '90s, so as story and gameplay go, I - unlike the core fans - am blessedly free of the urge to decry any deviations from what made those games great.  My impression is that XCOM is one of those rare IP's that just doesn't need an overly involved story; it is enough that aliens are here wreaking havoc on Earth and humanity must pull together to survive and conquer.
Combat is fun.  It didn't get old before I reached the end, not even after I attempted a new playthrough on the Commander difficulty.  On standard difficulty you can play it all tactical, all shooter or anything in between.  It all works and satisfies.  Putting around the base between missions is okay and rewards the player with bits of background story and unlockable side missions.  Most of the campaign is linear, which is fine by me.  The bugs were few and far enough between that they don't merit mention.  The visuals with graphic settings maxed are excellent and the audio does its job.  My only technical complaint is that the actual movement and placement of your agents (and targeted abilities) with the ground cursor feels a bit console port.  You use skills and reposition often in combat encounters, so this might get tiresome.
I don't have the DLC's and have no knowledge of
.  My thoughts on this game included how a cooperative or competitive mode might work: the player pauses to access skills and issue squad orders in a tactical mode.  So, instead of being able to pause and use that interface indefinitely, start players with only a few seconds of the tactical mode but reward them (jointly in co-op, individually in competitive) with extra seconds of tactical time for skillful play (flanking and exposed attacks, environmental kills, combo and skill kills, etcetera).
After finishing the game, I went and read some major reviews.  In my opinion they're a bit unfair.  My advice is to judge the game on its own merit and decide for yourself.  It may or may not feel like an XCOM title but at the end of the day
that I recommend to anyone who shares the tastes I listed here.
TIP: Avoid Rookie difficulty; it is trivial and will bore you.
TIP: Don't jump straight into Commander difficulty - instead get a feel for the mechanics first.
TIP: Once you are at Commander, remember the game punishes even slight deviations from ideal tactics.  You will consistently have to use everything at your disposal including skills, environment, rapid repositioning and your own sharpshooting.  If you don't, be ready to restart checkpoints a lot..
TIP: If you're digging the story and setting, there are side activities to hunt down in base and also letters and audio clips both at base and in the field.  Plus, if you stand near people they will have some funny conversations.

What do you get when you combine Interstellar, The Martian, and Alien? Osiris: New Dawn
Pros:
- great visuals, lighting and character movements
- breathtaking atmosphere that immerses you all on its own.
- customizable public and private servers allowing modification of alien presence and resource respawn among others.
- intuitive crafting and building. Not too complex but enough to let you do what you want to.
- sense of threat without being discouraging. Just enough to make you second guess venturing out at night alone, but not enough to stop you if you have enough suppies, ammunition, or even better - an armored rover.
Cons:
- as with any early release game, there are small things that are undoubtably being fixed
- some animations are simplified for other players onlooking vs how they look on your screen
- sometimes unclear point allocation for skill tree progression
- space flight can be confusing when trying to travel to the other moon
- player and monsters can occasionally clip and and out of structures.
Conclusion: The game is still evolving and will undoubtably get better. Even with the few bugs (that keep getting fixed) it's not nearly enough to turn you off. As for right now, it's absolutely worth the price and is garunteed to keep you and your fellow sci-fi fans busy and having a great time. 9/10

Each costume has only one attack and one charged attack which builds up every three turns. So combat is basically choose target, attack, press the right button, enemy attacks, press the right button, repeat repeat repeat. The quicktime event for attacking and defending doesn't feel rewarding, it feels mandatory. If you miss any of the quicktime events it's basically a major loss for the team.
One thing about this game that sparked an idea is the False RPG. This game has exp and levels, but it's meaningless.  Most enemies are unskippable and you don't select new skills with new levels. This is a lot like an action game where you just pick up new weapons or items over time. You didn't earn those weapons or items by killing enemies, you just got them because it was time to. Take Final Fantasy X-2 as a comparison, three women with different outfits that do different skills, as you level you choose different skills to unlock, different grids for outfits that allow for super outfits. It's a much more fleshed out system that isn't the exact same the next time you play it.
Pros: Great idea for a game. Exploration is fun.

Costume Quest easily became one of my favorite turn-based RPGs.
It's Visuals are really amazing to look at, the cartoonish cute graphics with the halloween theme combined really fits well.
The Story is simple but also unique, you play as one of the twins getting dressed up to trick or treat around the neighborhood, but the other twin gets kidnapped by a bunch of monsters and you need to rescue him/her. The game also has some pretty good dialouge for some of the interactions.
The Gameplay is something you don't see every so often in other turn-based RPGs (again, it's simple and unique). Since it's a halloween game, the game has a clever mechanic when you go trick or treating in a door, you have a 50% to get a battle (Trick) or someone who gives you an amount of candy (Treat). Instead of getting different party members like in most RPGs, you collect Costume Pieces in which you need to complete the set to get the full costume. Each costume gives you different abillities for battle or exploration, you can switch costumes for the 3 characters in the game which basically switches their roles. There's also Battle Stamps that you can buy with candy which enhances your characters with special atributes. The battles are basically what you get in other RPGs; you have Attack, Super, Special Abilites if you have specific Battle Stamps, and Run Away. The combat system is similar to those in Mario RPG games but much easier, where you can do a specific command to do more damage than your normal attack or to lower your damage taken. After battles, you gain XP, Candy to buy more Battle Stamps and sometimes Creepy Treats Cards.
While the game is great, it also has it's downsides. Game is locked at 30 FPS and there is no available way to disable that, combat can be a bit repetitive, some parts are really dark and can't see really anything (even though some of those parts you need the Space Suit), there's only one Minigame: The Apple Bobbing one, Candy can only be used for Battle Stamps,
the maximum level is 10 (Main Game) and 14 (Grubbins on Ice Expansion), and the game is a bit short as i beat the game 100% in just 7 Hours (5 in Main Game, 2 in Grubbins on Ice Expansion) with no Replay Value.
Even though it has it's problems, i have to say that with it's nice-looking artstyle, good story and unique gameplay mechanics, this game is a must-buy for RPG fans that want something fresh and simple, and if you're new to RPGs, pick up this game, it's short but it's still a great game to enjoy.

Story of overpowered and overnerfed classes aside, this is quite an entertaining game.
Best equipment is still acquired via tedious grinding, but at least you get a lot of stuff to do before your next dungeon. Finding all the hidden mountain cairins for example. Or completing all the quests after returning to appropriate character level. Or killing 500 boars because you want that title. Or running around the less frequented parts of the world, hoping to find that last missing item for your artifact set. Or decorating your lair to show off to friends you might potentially have. The list goes on.
While it still boils down to the old "Kill ten wolves to get new pants" formula, it feels that authors actually put effort in creating the world and making it... "fun"?
Still, because it is a F2P MMO, and aged one at that, the community has been on somewhat of a decline. The number of servers has decreased and the ones that remain feel populated only in peak hours. But because of the cross-shard PvP system and dungeon finder, it's not hard to find other people. The community itself is fairly nice, split between Really Nice People, people who aren't sure what they are doing and that one guy that messes everything up.
Pay to win system used to be practically non-exist, but ever since the first expansion Trion has added special souls (player classes) that are unavailable untill you purchase them. While in itself this hardly affects balance of the gameplay, this does remove specific class combinations from non-paying players. And then there are water-capable mounts, that are also restricted. Add currency boosts to that and that's pretty much it.
It starts off a bit confusing, but I've found it quite enjoyable. And considering it's free, I do recommend to at least try it out.

This is Dark Souls meets Seven Days to Die in a neat RTS package.
Summary -
You must build and aggresively expand your settlement, as you fight off periodic hordes of zombies and clear the map of undead denizens.  Every map is randomized, so it always feels fresh and unique.  However, the real draw here is - you are inevitably going to fail.  Failing never felt so satisfying though.  As the days pass, the zombies hordes that periodically attack get bigger.  You must find new ways to expand while scouting out the best choke points to funnel the zombies to your walls, turrets, and a hailstorm of bulletly death.  Victory is measured in surviving more days than you did last game.
It is actually possible to win, but once the game countdowns to day 100 (or whatever you have it set at), the entire map of any undead that you have not killed plus brand new hordes from every direction charge your base.  You have to be a very efficient player resource-wise to possibly beat the map, and you will need a little bit of luck too.
But just like dark souls, every failure feels like an accomplishment because you truly learn something valuable, which will greatly assist you for the next zombie apocalypse.
Frankly, a game like this is sorely needed for the Real Time Strategy genre, as it often lags behind the other genres.  This is a truly unique and refreshing game.

Players will need to eat and drink to survive, a kitchen allows them to cook better food, allowing for a better recovery of those needs, if a player is thirsty they will face longer times to aim at the enemy and if they are hungry they will have a hard time to hit an enemy strong enough to give a good damage.
The enemies are no different, zombies that wants to kill you, but the nice thing is, a normal zombie is only normal until you provoke them, a zombie can be either slow or fast, very fast, and you can find yourself in deep trouble if a fast one starts to run at you and you are still reloading your rifle or you crossbow. Oh, and don't forget that your weapons produces loud sounds when you shoot, so use your rifle/pistol wisely, in a time you won't bother too much with that, firepower is needed to kill those zombies, just make sure to know your enemy first.
Want bullets? Craft them with gunpowder and lead pellets. Want some good food? Cook them at the kitchen using foods you find on your quest, mixing those poor quality foods to make a high quality one!
How to Survive 2 is, so far, nice and comfortable to play, so far the game proved to be interesting as you can defend your base with barricades and even traps, because killing zombies with bullets and arrows isn't enough when you can put some zombies heads at some good spike traps. Remember, this review is being made at the early access so things can change, but so far so good as they say, or Kovac says...

Dishonored is a stealth action game where you play as Corvo Attano, the Royal Protector of Jessamine Kaldwin, the empress of the city of Dunwall.  First of all, the story is great and the campaign is INCREDIBLE.  The game gives the player total freedom over what they can do.  You can choose to be stealthy and lethal, stealthy and nonlethal, chaotic and lethal, chaotic and nonlethal, or a mixture of any of these.  The campaign had unlimited playability and for the five times I have played it, I have always enjoyed it.  The character movement is fluid and the controls are completely customizable to your preferences.  The "quick access wheel" in the game is magnificent and effective.  Players can bind abilities and items to all numbers 0 - 9.  As old as Dishonored is, the game runs very well and the graphics aren't too bad.  There are even a couple of funny ragdolls.  Takedown animations are magnificent.  Overall, I would give this game an 11/10!

Costume Quest easily became one of my favorite turn-based RPGs.
It's Visuals are really amazing to look at, the cartoonish cute graphics with the halloween theme combined really fits well.
The Story is simple but also unique, you play as one of the twins getting dressed up to trick or treat around the neighborhood, but the other twin gets kidnapped by a bunch of monsters and you need to rescue him/her. The game also has some pretty good dialouge for some of the interactions.
The Gameplay is something you don't see every so often in other turn-based RPGs (again, it's simple and unique). Since it's a halloween game, the game has a clever mechanic when you go trick or treating in a door, you have a 50% to get a battle (Trick) or someone who gives you an amount of candy (Treat). Instead of getting different party members like in most RPGs, you collect Costume Pieces in which you need to complete the set to get the full costume. Each costume gives you different abillities for battle or exploration, you can switch costumes for the 3 characters in the game which basically switches their roles. There's also Battle Stamps that you can buy with candy which enhances your characters with special atributes. The battles are basically what you get in other RPGs; you have Attack, Super, Special Abilites if you have specific Battle Stamps, and Run Away. The combat system is similar to those in Mario RPG games but much easier, where you can do a specific command to do more damage than your normal attack or to lower your damage taken. After battles, you gain XP, Candy to buy more Battle Stamps and sometimes Creepy Treats Cards.
While the game is great, it also has it's downsides. Game is locked at 30 FPS and there is no available way to disable that, combat can be a bit repetitive, some parts are really dark and can't see really anything (even though some of those parts you need the Space Suit), there's only one Minigame: The Apple Bobbing one, Candy can only be used for Battle Stamps,
the maximum level is 10 (Main Game) and 14 (Grubbins on Ice Expansion), and the game is a bit short as i beat the game 100% in just 7 Hours (5 in Main Game, 2 in Grubbins on Ice Expansion) with no Replay Value.
Even though it has it's problems, i have to say that with it's nice-looking artstyle, good story and unique gameplay mechanics, this game is a must-buy for RPG fans that want something fresh and simple, and if you're new to RPGs, pick up this game, it's short but it's still a great game to enjoy.

I'm usually not a fan of all of those main-streamed RPGs. There are alot of reasons for that, but to keep this short - I absolutely loved "Costume Quest".
If you're anything like me, let me tell you - this game has a very big heart. The story, although not sophisticated at all, is very relatable. The fighting system is quick, easy and responsive. The Costumes, which are the main point of the game, work exceptionally well, and often times add a great deal of variety to the entire package. And it's just a joy to play overall.
It's a game you should play. And you could also use it to inroduce your younger kids, siblings, nephews or nieces to the world of video games. I recommend it with all of my heart - and now that the second one is finally out, I would definitely be coming back for a second round.

The bit of the game that bothered me the most was, as she's leaving the kitchen, she says out loud "You can have your precious kitchen back now." leaving the two chatting girls behind her with confused expressions. I'm sorry- but WHO with SAD would ever do something like that? 1) It's rude and forward. 2) It's way too embarassing. Come on.
I would hope this game doesn't give anyone the impression that people with SAD avoid people out of some sort of uncalled for anger and bitterness. I've never felt anger towards people, who are simply minding their own business, just because their presence makes me nervous.
That said, there were small bits of the game that I related to tremendously, like the pretending to clean up the kitchen to waste time and avoid looking odd. The increased heart rate as the microwave goes on and on, fearing that it will disturb the others.
Overall, I can't say I reccomend this game. It had a lot of potential, the art and music was cute. The overall message that something as simple as getting oatmeal can be a nerve-wracking task for someone with SAD, is a good one. Unfortunately, the attitude and personality of Samatha completely ruined it for me- it's not her social anxiety that makes her unlikable, it's the fact that she's a bitter person with rude thoughts.

The game features the story of Samantha, a girl who has social anxiety and is laying in her dorm peacefully.... until she notices she's hungry. Very hungry. So, she needs to go to kitchen and try to make a cup of oatmeal, but due to her condition this will not be a simple task.
This short non-kinetic Visual Novel had potential, since it demonstrates accurately how a simple everyday task may be an impossible thing to do for a person with social anxiety. Sadly, it develops too little the main character, which may pass the impression that people with social anxiety are all about their paranoias - and they aren't. A game that addresses such a delicate matter like social anxiety should have done a deep development of their protagonist, in a way she could look more like an individual person rather than a generic character with social anxiety.
Also, after one or two playthroughs, the story gets very repetitive as most of the endings are the same with just a small little variation.

My wife & I have pounded our way through torchlight 2 and Grim Dawn and wanted a different take on 3rd person RPG's.  This was on sale for $4 so we figured that if it was as bad as the original it was still less than the price of one movie ticket.
It is redundant but we knew that going in.  There isn't really a story, just pure survival.  We project that once we get to a certain level there will be no point in playing because once you've arrived at the top of the tech chain, why keep playing.  But until then we're going to enjoy the journey.
However, we played for 4 days in game and found a total of 2 food items... I've been at 0 water and she has been at 0 satiation for more than a day.  We've covered a LOT of ground and hacked our way through a lot of houses.  Basically no food or water.  It went from being an awesome game in our minds to tanking and not being fun.
We don't want to level too much to get access to more missions because we can barely survive now thanks to literlly having nothing to eat or drink.  So you figure if you run around long enough you'll find a stash, right?
Someone complained that food was too plentiful and too overpowered in a previous build.  So, unfortunately, the reaction has been a pendulum swing that really ruins it.  We'll be restarting a camp and saving all the food we get in the beginning until we can build a kitchen so we can make quality food that'll last longer since we know we'll just stop getting it at a certain point.

Most people have heard of the infamous 'bird dating simulator' because the premise is... well, seemingly ridiculous. You play as the only human in a school of birds and the object of the game is to form meaningful relationships with them. Yep, that's right, you're gonna pull yourself some sweet pigeon booty. Coo Coo. It seriously feels like a parody on the dating sim genre at best.
The writing is mediocre at best with most of the birds being just as much as an oddball as the main character. The birds personalities do fall flat at time, but what really ties the game together is the 'true ending' which can only be obtained by playing through every bird's route. The true ending manages to effortlessly weave the links between all of the birds and Hiyko together leading to a story that has twists, surprises and tearjerking moments. The conclusion is satisying and enough to convince me that although this is a game with a ridiculous concept, it's meant to be taken seriously and not as the joke as it seems.
Overall, Hatoful Boyfriend is a quirky game with a colourful cast of birds to romance and with enough twists and turns to remain fresh for every playful. The ability to fast forward through scenes is much appreciated and the game isn't a joke, no matter how hard it seems like one.

This was, very unexpectedly, a really awesome game. I first started playing expecting a hilarious and absurd story just for the fun of it, but the game really sucked me in and kept me fascinated. Hell, I even bonded emotionally with the birds (especially those with more heartbreaking endings).
The bonus ending (the BBL route) was one of the more compelling game (and VN) stories I remember reading made from such seemingly simple and ridiculous premises. I don't even know how they made all the story parts so intervowen, when at first they seemed so random. It was worth unlocking all the slightly repetitive playthroughs to get to it. For anyone wondering why this game is interesting - wait until you get to the last part.
I'd recommend it to anyone who lacks prejudice against the obvious ridiculousness of the game and wants to try someting different. It's really funny, sad, and awesome all at the same time.

I'm a huge fan of the X-COM franchise since the beginning and was very satisfied with the remake 2K published in 2012.
When The Bureau was announced as part of this franchise and the first pics were shown, I couldn't wait to see its release. But several things (mainly the third-person-perspective and the combat mechanism) kept me from buying it then.
But thanks to the latest summer sale I decided to buy it and all of its DLC.
Easy part first: the DLCs aren't worth it. One gives you an extra alien weapon, one gives you a short extra mission and the Hangar 6 R&D gives you a bit of a pre-story to the main game and some new - only (!) in that DLC available - weapons to fight through some simple 'survival' levels.
A bit complicated is the main game. While in many other cases I have problems with the third-person-perspective, it worked well in this game. Also the combat system is working good and most time satisfying, but way to simple to fullfill the tactical needs of an old X-COM veteran.
The graphic, the sounds and the characters really helps to create the right atmosphere for the game and also the different settings for the missions making it fun to play, even with a too much repetitive gameplay. And that gameplay is also the biggest issue of the game. You walk trhough the 'tunnel' maps knowing nothing will happen, until you come to a 'battlefield' (easily identified thanks to the huge amount of cover for your men and the aliens), where you fight some waves of enemies and then continue to the next 'battlefield'.
The only thing that keeps me playing was the story, which had some weird twist and gets very unsatisfying in the end. But for me, the game was worth money and I didn't regret it any minute to have bought it.

Even when you attempt to move your AI partners to flank an enemy, half the time they just get downed almost instantly by pinpoint accurate enemy fire. Add to that horrible weapons with small ammo capacity yet a LAUGHABLY abundant amount of ammo crates littered across the battlefield. The combat is just not fun in ANY way, shape, or form.

I could forgive a game with solid and fun gameplay but a weak story, i would still have a fun time albeit with some regrets. This, however, is just a painful and frustrating experience.

I want to be able to recommend this game.  It is free, after all, so anyone can try it.  But it just isn't good.
Lost Mythologies is short, simplistic, and honestly a bit annoying.  The models look pretty.  Individual animations are basic, lacking real follow through or impact, but acceptable for a free title.  While your character is normally grounded, it is hard to miss that she floats rather high above the steps in the starting area.
Combat uses light and heavy attack buttons, which each having a short chain.  However, there is no impact or feedback from hits, nor do different hits carry any different effects (pushback, knockdown, stun, etc).  You can dash out of anything, which is necessary as there doesn't seem to be a block.  There is a jump, but it appears useless, and you can only do a single weak attack while airborne.  You have three special attacks, but all three are too slow to use mid-combat, which makes the two close-range specials useless.  The only useful special appears to be the long-range projectile, which appears to do little damage, but does let you hit targets from outside their attack range.
There are only a few enemy types, and you'll fight them over and over across a map that is too big for its little bit of content.  Enemies feel like damage sponges, even though some die in a few hits.  The boss is a major damage sponge.  Combat mostly consists of mashing a button around three or four times, then dashing away from anything still alive before it hits you.
The boss has an attack that hit some distance beyond its graphical effect.  The camera becomes an issue whenever there is more than a few enemies around, and remains an issue throughout the boss fight.
On a side note, the game has a single achievement that should be awarded simply by starting the game.  This achievement does not get awarded.  It apparently only worked for a few days after release, being broken with the English user interface update.

Ship building seems cool at first, but there's really only a few ways that they can be made to be effective.  Decorations don't do much, though some improve morale.
Fighting is terribly limited as your only commands are basically "go here" and hope they start attacking. Islands currently scale off of your captain, so it's one of the few times where you actually -don't- want to level.. because at a certain point, islands are just pointless to ever bother attacking because your crew can't handle them without taking tons of casualties or expending all of your cannon balls. Deaths seem more common than in X-Com (for you that know that game's infamy of crew murder).
All of these issues are still in production for being fixed.  The company only has a few people working for it at this time.  Ultimately, I think it'll be a great game.  But as with any early release, it really does need that work.

Costume Quest is a silly roleplaying game with a Halloween theme. You play as either Wren or Reynold, a young kid who needs to rescue their kidnapped sibling and stop the invading monsters from stealing all the Halloween candy.
The visuals are rather cute and adorable. Unfortunately the game has a lot of technical problems. First of all, the game has an extremely annoying 30 FPS lock that doesn't even work properly and that makes all the animations look choppy.
Furthermore, the game does not properly support 16:10 resolutions and some of the UI elements will appear partially outside the screen.
The game has a decent enough sound track and the sound effects are pretty good too. There's no voice acting.
The gameplay in Costume Quest is pretty dreadful. The exploration aspects are passable but rather repetitive. You wander around the maps, looking for houses to trick and treat and simple quests to complete.
It is the combat, however, that is truly terrible. This is probably the worst RPG combat I have ever seen. It's the traditional turn-based JRPG combat with all the depth and choice removed. And to add insult to injury, every single action will require you to complete a tedious QTE. To make matters even worse, the encounters are extremely repetitive and even the bosses are generally quite simple.
The ability to change your Halloween costume (and unlock different special powers) is a nice touch, but not nearly enough to make up for the otherwise weak gameplay.
The game is quite easy and only a couple of the bosses provide any real challenge.
The controls are passable on a gamepad but by no means great. The constant QTEs in combat are extremely tedious and the fixed camera can be a major pain while exploring.
The story is rather silly and childish. This wouldn't really be an issue by itself, but unfortunately the quality of the writing is quite low, especially for a Double Fine game.
Overall the game was reasonably bug free. However, the quest for recovering your stolen costumes appeared quite glitchy and it took quite a few attempts to complete.
I found Costume Quest a pretty bad game overall and it is easily my least favorite Double Fine game so far. The cute visuals are nowhere near enough to make up for the utterly dreadful and repetitive gameplay. Definitely not recommended.

This game can be perfectly described by a single word: Fun!
It's a relatively short RPG where you play as a young kid who goes trick or treat with your twin, who very soon gets abducted by candy eating monsters, on Halloween Night. Now you gotta fend off the monsters from your town in order to save your sibling!
The battles are not your typical recipe though, instead it employs simple QTEs for both attacking and defending, which in my opinion makes the game even more kid friendly since practically any age can accomplish that, so if you got young kids this can definitely prove a great game for them.
What you can do in battle depends on the costume you're using. You can dress any of your party members in any costume you have acquired, each with it's own strengths, weaknesses and ability. Want to have an astronaut, a giant robot and a ninja fighting? Great! Want to have a Unicorn, the Statue of Liberty and a serving of McFries fighting? Yes, that can happen.
The game can get a bit repetitive but thanks to its length it doesn't really wear you out. All in all a very entertaining experience!

What can I say. I've been waiting for a truly awe-inspiring sci-fi survival for a while. Though the content is rather limited currently, this absolutely fits the bill.
PROS:
- Phenomenal graphics, holy cow. The landscapes and views (When it's clear) are
- The weather systems are truly immersive. Nothing quite like losing your bearing in a sudden sandstorm whist being hunted down but bloodthirsty aliens.
- The music is grade-A for an early access. It always seems to fit the mood, whether tense and high strung during fights to melodic sci-fi during down times and stifling silence when floating out in space. Certainly helps to contribute to the immersion.
- Alien AI are pretty smart. They always seems to find the paths over boulders to sneak attack you and even retreat once wounded.
- New leveling system and skill web are a great addition and make crafting feel less grindy.
- Materials are sparse enough to make it a challenge to find and survive before your starting supplies run out.
- Playing single player truly makes you feel like a lone survivor on a hostile planet. Just how Matt Damon must have felt in the Martian but with less potatoes.
- Have not played PVP but PVE multiplayer is definitely fun, especially now that they have private servers that you can use for you and your friends. Connection issues seem non existent after the last few patches as well.
- Detail levels on material nodes, tools, weapons, vehicles, etc are very detailed. You can tell they put a lot of work into making this game look good. Animations are pretty great too for being in such and early stage.
- The new
planet is fantastically different from the main starting planet but, if anything, feels more hostile and much tougher to survive. I love it.
CONS
- Building limits. Right now You can only build 10 buildings and two vehicles, even locally. I can understand public servers but they should allow local games to up those counts.
- Again, building limits. You can only build one Habitat within, maybe, a 500m range of each other, which means they can't be connected. Being able to build them closer to create a large compound would be great.
- Still some bugs with structures. Clipping through windows sometimes, no lighting at night in the barracks. The biggest breaker is that you can have an uncapped hallway off a habitat that's opened up to the outside air and it still considers your hab as pressurized. Certainly immersion breaking.
- Power. Currently everything runs without being powered, except for the Fabricator in the hab as far as I can tell. Would be more of a challenge to have to Macgyver some nuclear generators from plutonium or solar arrays earlier in the game to power your structures
- Skill web is very basic. Would also like to have items I can't craft yet not show in the menus until they're unlocked.
WOULD LIKE TO SEE:
- Larger solar panel arrays
- Bring large gas storage tanks back
- More structures and larger building limit
- Walls snap together much better
- More creature types on the new planet, especially making sure they would fit in that type of environment
- Space station base building would be AMAZING
- Larger variety of droids, even if its for mundane things around the base
- Parts from your downed ship at start to cannibalize
FINAL THOUGHTS:
For a 25$ early access game, it is amazing. The world is beautiful and immersive. The music is on point. The devs are clearly passionate and dedicated (The Aziel patch, WOW) and even though there are only a handful of them (Three I believe when Osiris launched) they update regularly and are engaged with the community which is vital to an early access' survival.
This game as insane potential and I can't wait to see where it goes! Sort of reminds me of Ark and the technical stages it was in a year ago. I certainly urge people to try this out, and if the content if too sparse for you currently, come back in a few months, I guarantee there will be much, much more!

Okay, i decided to write a review for this game, and oh boy is this a tough one...
On one hand I love the game. It has a beautiful world, fairly challenging for a survival game without being unfair and a very active dev team working on the game.
But i have come to the decision of saying this.
Do i recommend Osiris? No, Not yet
The good has been fun but the bad is REALLY bad, so let me bring up some things that are frustrating about this game at the moment.
Nothing beyond the initial 5 missions is explained, i don't know how many times i heard "What is ____?" or "How do i get ____?" and my only response is "Check the wiki"
I'm not meaning the tutorial needs to be redone (even though i think it should be tweaked slightly) but i think there should be an in game Info PDA or something that can tell you about certain things after encountering it once (Kill an enemy and learn about them/gather resource and figure out where to find more of it)
Flight mechanics are absolutely horrible, going to space is straight forward but the way the ship handles is awkward, unconventional and very very limited. i feel it needs to be taken back to the drawing board early on before they add in more insentive to go to the other moon Aziel, which will lead me on to the next point.
The switching between moons is very buggy, you can lose your ship, if you are playing multiplayer you can crash while trying to switch to the other moon, and there isn't too much to warrant going to Aziel besides a tougher experience.
And finally, content is very limited at the moment but as people will say "It's Early Access" but some of the issues in the game cannot be justified under that statement.
Will this game be better in the future? I don't know, if they keep up their consistancy then yes, but that could change.

Of course, it is flawed. The graphics are fantastic but not the framerate, nor is the fluncy of the controls. It plays a lot like Mass Effect 3 but it doesn't have that game's slick controls. The controls also isn't very intuitive, especially regarding grenade throwing and the battle HUD. The AI isn't terribly smart and likes to die a lot due to silly moves, and the gameplay is fairly difficult even in Normal.
However, I like the game settings, and being XCOM you're treated with a huge feast of alien graphics. The base is the equivalent of The Citedal on Mass Effect 3, albeit without much interaction with NPCs nor does it have as much events. You can send your squads to seperate missions while you handle the main ones, and it hits me as such a good idea that I wonder why Mass Effect 3 doesn't do this. Then there's the gameplay, which again plays a lot like Mass Effect 3, but one thing that it handles well is cover. In ME3 it can be difficult to know whether you managed to send your squad to cover or just standing before it, but this isn't a poblem here. You can even issue a chain of commands for them to execute sequentially, which is a huge plus.
Try this out before judging it. It is flawed, but still a must have for XCOM fans.

I almost feel bad for not joining the love the people - including friends and family - share for Double Fine and so also for this game, because I don't think this is perfect. I think its the best looking Double Fine game to date, with its very refined cell-shaded graphical style, but I think it's just too easy, and too short. Perhaps that's what this game is not
, as it seems that the festive atmosphere and the charm the world inherits from what Double Fine games are known for.
My problem is that it's a short game that feels long, in a bad way. Of the 7 hours I spent playing this game (including the DLC), I felt like I was watching the same 3 battles play over again and again, without any feeling of commitment since the battles are so easy and simple. Each character has one  basic attack and a special attack that is usable in the 3 turn. But by the time I can use it, I most likely don't even need to use it, since one basic attack is enough to be succesful. You do get the option to add another action, like stunning or poisoning, but I found those not necessary, even after using them. In fact, I used the buffs that would increase attack power and the ability to counterattack so the fights are over within 2 or 3 turns.
Another small quirck, that some other reviewers also mentioned, is the fast-crolling, automated dialogues (though, mostly just in cutscenes). The is no voice-acting, but only texts. The problem that you can easily miss parts of the text when you're destracted at all. I don't read fast or slow, but I was still somewhat annoyed with this text speed.
Despite the lack of difficulty and the monotonous combat, I still enjoyed the game for the look and character. Try it out when you feel like taking a break a night or two from the stress you might endure from your regular life.
Edit: during a sale you can get this game (including the DLC) for a mere 1 buck. Though I wouldn't recommend this for a full 10 bucks, I do think it's definitely worth it for such a low price.

This game offers a hard-scifi survival and breathtaking audiovisual experience and atmosphere. You won't find anything else better to fulfill your nerdy stranded astronaut in distant world fantasies.
Survive! Gather materials, build your habitat piece-by-piece. Expand it with garden and living quarter modules. Build furniture and utilities to help you become self-sufficient. Pros:

- Beautiful weather effects

- Building system
- Creepy enemies and a giant sand worm
- Spacewalks
- Vast amount of potential
- Fun, even more with friends!
Cons:
- Standard early access disbalance, griefing and offline raiding (there are public and private PvP and PvE servers)
- Bugs that make you start over
- Not much to do after building everything, but that doesn't stop you from enjoying the experience

Overall, it is a above average, but I cannot recommend it right now. Some people say "this is Dark Souls for RTS", in my opinion that expression is over-used and to be honest, doesn't apply to this game a bit. Putting TL;DR here for the impatient, followed by a bit longer version.
TL;DR: ○
+
-
- Maps are randomly generated, and the generation is very poor/bad right now
- Ironman only?!? For a game where a slight mistake can end the game, this is unacceptable
- Needs "x2" "x4" game-speed buttons, any game that has pause button should have game-speed buttons as well
- Basic, staple RTS mechanics are missing. No order-queues, for example
- Too many resources to manage. It doesn't add anything to the game, save for frustration
○ There is only one game type available right now; Survival Mode
+ You can pause the game any time you want
They Are Billions is a RTS game where you build and manage a colony of survivors against the unending zombie threat. Right now, only Survival mode is available, and the Campaign will arrive at a later date.
For Survival, the map generation is very poor right now, and has a huge impact on your chances of victory. Sometimes you don't have access to some resources, sometimes there isn't enough room to build properly, sometimes an infested building is right next to you, sometimes there are no good choke-points to hold off even the early-mid aggression. It is really bad, and needs much more work.
You cannot load a previous save if you make a mistake; game plays only in Ironman mode. Given that the RNG map generation plays a big part on your chances of success, having Ironman as the default and the only option is unacceptable in my opinion, especially when even a slight mistake can end your game. Rather than flat-out destroying a building, zombies infect them which can lead to a cascasding effect, quickly overwhelming your colony in a matter of minutes, if not seconds.
Pathing could use some work. Some classic RTS mechanics are missing, you cannot queue orders for example, or you cannot set a unit to follow another. I hope they'll be implemented later. You can pause the game by pressing a button (or hitting space), which is a nice thing to have. In my opinion any game that has a pause function should have game-speed options as well. There is not much to do in between building, cleaning, and defending and I really hope they'll add a game speed button or two (like x2 speed, x4 speed) as it gets boring when you are waiting for something to happen or be done.
Base-building and resource-management are somewhat meh. To be honest, I don't like the amount of resources that needs to be managed. Gold, wood, stone, iron, oil, worker, food, power, citizen. Most of the time you end up waiting for another building to finish because you've run out of -insert resource- or you need to demolish/disable a building or two.
Overall, as I've said, it is a above average. It'll get better in time, and definitely be worth checking it out, but for now I don't recommend it. It's too rough on the edges.

They Are Billions feels like one of the good old survival game modes in Warcraft 3 taken to a quality that makes it into its own game.
The main focus is to build a city as condensed as possible and as secure as possible. You'll find yourself packing everything in behind secure walls or perhaps doing risky expansions early on. You'll use units to fight the zombies consistently throughout the game. Early on zombies are slow, stupid, unorganized and easy to take out. Later on they get faster, have special units, get ranged attacks and more. The difficulty can be changed between how many zombies will come at you and over what amount of time they will do so. This ranges from 80(Hard) to 150(Easy). Survive until the days run out and you'll have killed the zombies. A typical playthrough will take a couple hours if you survive the start.
Currently the only mode is a survival mode on a randomly generated map which feels like a complete game by itself. Everything is random. You could spawn next to cities packed with zombies or in a nice green field full of minerals. Keeps the game very interesting as your tactics will change from game to game. You might start with low space, but great bottlenecks. You could also start in a large open area giving you tons of room to build up a city. There are currently four different maps with differences in style and with special modifiers. If you like hardmodes the fourth map is currently ridiculously hard and tons of fun.
You start with a colony of only a few people. And grow it into cities of hundreds/thousands. Your goal: Survive the zombie apocolypse. Great game full of replayability. You can try to rush out a military and clear the map as much as possible or rush economy and hope you fill in all the gaps from zombies. Or do both and be golden. If you like city building survival games you might just wanna give They are Billions a try.
Addition:
After making it to day 90+ in a 100day medium pop game...the game is just tons of fun. What a gem. And no I did not survive =P
Addition:
After finishing the first three maps and failing at the fourth I give They Are Billions a 9/10. Its a really fun game. Well worth the price.

In an alternate timeline: The year is 1950. Donald Draper never joined Sterling Cooper to work as an ad man, he remained in the army and rose through the ranks. Eventually recruited by the CIA, he becomes involved with The Bureau, and helps fight off an alien invasion of Earth. Thats this game in a nutshell: Donald Draper shooting aliens.
The gameplay is fun, at first. The Third person shooter + squad combat is neat on the first mission, when you get agents with all their abilities unlocked. But then it takes that away and you have to -slowly- level them up again. Gameplay is largely the same, fighting the same 2 aliens over and over again, except when they occasionally throw in a muton or sectopod battle. Also, one of the big bosses froze up on me and just sat there as my squad gunned it down. Long set peices showing off the devestated cities lead up to cover based combat sections in a predictable pattern. For some reason, there's more ammo than you can carry in the areas without enemies.
The characters suffer from a bad case of rubber face, and the shot-reverse-shot dialogue trees become tedious very fast. Which sucks, because apparently a bunch of content is hidden in the speech you go through in the base.
It's a cool game in premise, but it doesnt quite live up to what it could have been. A few tweaks and a little more though into varying gameplay would have gone very far in making this better. Although it is a totally different game, XCOM Enemy Unknown does a better job at Squad based alien killin fun. I got this in the Humble Bundle, so its okay for the price, but I wouldnt recommend buying this game straight up, unless it's on sale.

So far this game has been one the strangest gaming experiences of my life, but also one of the most intriguing. I have only uncovered 4 of 12 possible endings, so I am nowwhere near done (as I definitely plan to uncover them all), but already it has transpired that the story is a lot more complex and nuanced than I was led to believe in my first playthrough.
I have never played any dating sims, so I can't compare it to any other games in the genre, but I imagine it is already vastly different from the bulk of the genre by virtue of being about human-bird relationships. Which isn't nearly as creepy as it sounds, believe it or not. The characterizations of the different birds (and thus romance options) are surprisingly complex and   feature well put-together twists. I can't wait to find out what the next one has in store.
I am also beginning to believe that one has to play all of the different paths in the game to fully understand the story. Each playthrough takes only about 30-40 minutes, so this is completely doable. Some endings appear to only be available after a couple of PTs, which further increases replayability.
The music is also worth mentioning. Each character has their own theme that usually plays while the main character is having any interaction with them, and it consists of a wide variety of tunes, some known, some, I presume, specifically written for the game. Given the game's complete lack of voice acting, the music is a great way to give the characters some "audible personality".
To sum it up, even if you are not a fan of visual novels or dating sims, this game is worth it for the incredibly strange setting and the great charactererization alone.

This is not a game. It's a choose your own adventure book with pictures. You can read it, not play it. There is no gameplay. How can a book being marketed as a game get so much praise? I am flabbergasted.
The book is about you, a human girl, dating birds in a pigeon high school. If you happen to be in the market for a book about dating birds, then you are in for a treat. But why would you be on Steam looking for a book?
If I were a bookworm in the habit of reading books, I would have read all the branching storylines and given a more in-depth review. And maybe then I would have found that there is more to this book than just a few laughs. Maybe it's a very good book, as far as books go. But I wouldn't know. I'm a gamer, not a reader. And while I don't regret reading this book (it only took one hour of my time and was somewhat enjoyable), I do regret buying it even at its low price, as I would rather have bought a game which is what I thought I had done.

The first part is simply too short to be entertaining.  Any route can be read in about an hour going at a relaxed pace, but there is significant overlap between routes, including sections that have no effect on the particular route you're playing, so I found myself skipping more and more as I replayed.  This also caused me to inadvertantly skip content I hadn't read before, because some sections have multiple outcomes but start out the same way regardless of route.  There is no way to go back to content accidentally skipped without reloading or starting a new game and it simply wasn't interesting enough to worth bothering to find out why I was faced with the choice of telling Okosan "convenience store" or "grocery store" and I could infer it had something to do with pudding anyway.
Consequently, there just isn't enough time to give any character depth and there's no challenge to complete a route.  By the time you finish a route, you feel like you were merely introduced to the character.  Picking routes are also very obvious and there is never any difficulty in seducing the various birds, unless you can't figure out that picking every opportunity to spend time with your desired bird is necessary to romance them.  The routes I enjoyed most, Okosan, Shuu, and Anghel, stood out because they were simply the most oddball.  For a game that is billed as a comedy, most routes utilize stereotypical melodrama.  Bird puns and pop culture references abound, but there's really nothing laugh out loud funny in Hatoful Boyfriend and at best you'll smirk a lot.
There is a very simple stat system, raised by choosing between three elective classes at regular intervals and in a couple of events that likewise present three choices which raise a stat.  The stats serve one purpose, which is to determine whether you get a normal ending or an extended ending.  Extended endings require you to raise one stat to maximum and reward you with an extra scene that was implied in the normal ending anyway.  Each ending has a separate achievement and you can't get both the normal ending and extended ending achievements in one go, so you have to play the same route twice in order to get all the achievements and unlock the Bad Boys Love extended ending.  I wasted part of my life to get the BBL extended ending and it was just as disappointing as the other extended endings.
The second part of the game, the Bad Boys Love secret route is much more interesting, but by the time I unlocked it I was already tired of the game.  I trudged on in hopes that it would be good and it was, kind of.  The game suddenly takes a much darker tone, reveals how the world came to be dominated by talking birds, and becomes a mystery story.  It seems interesting for a while, but as all the threads come together it becomes a soap opera for the ages.  Characters are revealed to be secret brothers, secret childhood friends, secret enemies, secret agents, secret terrorists, secret weapons, secretly superpowered, secretly alive, but, alas, there are no secret comas to complete the cliche pantheon.  I got the distinct impression that the first half of the game was written primarily to introduce the characters so that the meandering mysteries wouldn't simply baffle readers.
All in all, Hatoful Boyfriend wasn't an altogether terrible game, but it just wasn't worth the money and I got it in a 50% off sale.  I will likely never read it again and would forget about it entirely if Steam didn't keep it in my library forever.  As some consolation, the trading cards were surprisingly valuable and I was able to quickly sell them for about $1.50.
If you don't mind a lot of repetition, love every visual novel no matter what, and really love silly gimmicks, then buy this game.  Otherwise, pick up just about any other visual novel on Steam.  Even some of the free ones are more entertaining than Hatoful Boyfriend.

Osiris: New Dawn
As an avid Space Engineers lover, a recent 7 Days to Die Fan, and a long time player of minecraft I like to think that I know what I do and do not like in a survival game. While first impressions wise I really enjoyed Osiris, within 20 minutes into the game I found it unplayable.
Pros:
-Graphics
-Massive worlds
-Multiple planets
-Variety of enemies
-Challenging environment and resource management
-Character classes (Yet to be released)
-Modular base building
The negatives are not game breaking by any means but they were just annoying enough to make me drop this game.
Enemies:
-Enemies are in a wide variety which I really enjoyed, crabs, worms, you name it. However when a 10 foot tall giant crab sneaks up behind me with no alert system or sounds, I had gotten ambushed nearly 5 times before even able to break a single rock. Games such as the ones I mentioned initially all have key sounds when enemies are approaching. In the Forest you are so intune with the environmental sounds that even the steps of the cannibals rings loud when they approach. Sure they have stealth mechanics and sometimes get the suprise on, but hulking giant mindless crabs should not be able to sneak up on anything. The only tip off that there was an enemy at all was the quiet still sound of being hit as the damage indicator upon being hit. It makes players who otherwise pride themselves on being aware of their     surroundings and environment almost feel like a joke knowing they are repeatedly ambushed.
Drone:
The drone command from what I could tell did absolutely nothing along with the fact that my last con specifically targets the fact that there was no indicator of enemies approaching or even when they were in the base. The drone stood idle when an enemy nearly trampled it. I would expect at the least for the drone to send alerts, help to defend, or at the veey least distract the enemies. I got the feeling that the drone wanted me to die at times with its neglagent disregard for the enemies that would pop up.
Combat:
When I actually knew an insect was attacking, I actually found the critical hit system enjoyable. It made sense that shooting the soft looking spots or joints would do excess damage. Thats about it though, avoiding the enemies was futile as attempting to run would get you hit in the back and flying would only have the enemy sit underneath you until you landed. When you are hit the entire screen shifts and there is a delay before you can move again. While understandable I found it annoyig that I could not switch weapons or reload when flying. Combat is an endless cycle of shoot, duct tape, heal, repeat. It gets old very quick.
It has potential sure,and im sure there are pleanty of people who  love this game. I am not one of those people however.

Back in the mid-90s i came across a game named UFO: Enemy unknown. It was a one-of-a-kind experience, so well planned and played i have warm spot for it in my heart ever since.
When the new XCOM reboot came out i was quite dissapointed - to say the least. So, when "The Bureau" came along i truely hoped it would fare better.
So far, it looks good. The story is much better, and gives an fresh twist to the original plot. Battle mechanics and interface are kind of strange, but in a good way.
Altogether, i like it.

NOTE: Reviewer's game difficulty was set to Commander, finishing the game with no deaths.
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a squad-based third-person tactical shooter not unlike the Mass Effect Series. Although it does not quite reach the heights of Bioware's Magna Opera, it still delivers moments of greatness throughout its 10-hour campaign.
--
CAMPAIGN
The storytelling is well-paced, although some cutscenes can use some work with regards to its fluidity. These cutscenes attempt a more filmic look, but it transitions poorly once control is handed to the player. The characters themselves could have had a more fleshed-out backgroud, but as it stands, most of the them fall under recognizable tropes.
Lore can be found scattered throughout the world, and they greatly contribute to the atmosphere of the game. Of course they don't directly contribute to the game itself, but for players who enjoy getting themselves immersed in such world-building, they are certainly a neat touch. The locations for each level are also highly varied and colorful. Hyper-modern games have a tendency to look really brown or greyish, but The Bureau breaks away from the pack and surprisingly manages to convey a sense of desperation even amid the richness of the color palette. The developers could have certainly put more effort into the battle areas though--an organic and subtle approach would have gone a long way into keeping the player engaged. Boxes and railings suddenly take on a symmetrical form, walls and cars inexplicably appear in positions that don't make much sense except as cover. Still, it is only a minor gripe and it doesn't take away from the presentation of the game.
--
MECHANICS
The gameplay is akin to many third person cover-based shooters. It patterns itself closer to Mass Effect--one button is highly contextualized, from sticking to cover to sprinting, or vaulting objects. It works for the most part, although having individual buttons for different things could have allowed the game to be more precise.
The shooting aspect is enjoyable, and the ability to issue commands to your squad is an exercise of thinking. Running and gunning is not a viable option, especially on higher difficulties. As such, patience and a quick mind is integral to the success of your team. Each encounter is similar to a puzzle begging to be solved: do you distract the enemy with a diversion and plant a mine behind them? Or should you force them to scatter and pick them off one by one? Nothing is binary within a firefight. Everything is dynamic, and it is the player's responsibility to constantly assess and reassess the situation. Friendly AI could definitely use some tuning though (mainly on autonomous cover choices), but it does not detract from the overall usefulness of the squad AI.
RPG aficionados also have some options in tinkering with their squad composition. Differing playstyles can easily be accomodated by the game, with each agent being highly customizable from their perks right down to their equipments , although changeable outfits would have been a welcome inclusion in the game.
--
CONCLUSION
All in all, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a welcome addition the XCOM franchise. It may not be on the same level as the Mass Effect Series (which it seems to have patterned itself to) but it is definitely an enjoyable game. Critics and naysayers alike have been too quick to dismiss the game without actually paying attention to it, just because of the silly notion that it is NOT XCOM. Well, it isn't, its The Bureau--it's simply its own game within a larger XCOM universe.
