This game, for me, is addictively frustraiting and I can't recommend it highly enough for others who like the build 'em up genre.
Resources :
Gold - Earnt by having colonists and by the sale of other resources when the Market has been unlocked. Also found on the map for your army (Defenders) to pick up. This pays for building upkeep and army upkeep, spent when building and recruiting.
Wood - Produced by the Sawmill and used in building and on certain units.
Stone - Produced by the Quarry and used much like Wood.
Iron - Also Produced by the Quarry, again, like Wood.
Food - Produced by the Hunter's Cottage (Place near woods for higher 'income'), Fishing Hut (Needs to be placed adjacent to sea tiles to work) and by the Farm (Unlockable, needs green grass tiles to work). This is used to maintain colonists and to feed the units.
Oil - Produced by the Oil Well and used on something... I honestly don't know as I keep dying before getting to use this stuff, I would guess it is used like Wood but who knows.
Workers - Used to maintain buildings and to be employed by the army.
Power - Used to run buildings. Generated by the Mill and the Power Plant (Unlockable, uses stone and wood to generate power)
Not quite a resource buuut pretty important, Space - Used by buildings and extended into by Tesla Towers (Use power to expand the area you can build in.
You start off with a soldier (Mid range, quick attack, mid damage, loud and mid speed) and 4 rangers (Low range, slow attack, low damage, silent and fast) and a handfull of gold. Your HQ produces a little food, gold, power and has some workers too. It also gives a large area to start your base in. Protect it at all costs, you lose this, you lose the game.
I normally find myself trying to start off in an enclosed area, woods cliffs and sea tiles are impassable by the zombie menace (And by me) so I use them to naturally protect my starting spot. I use the rangers to scout around a little before starting work on my base, there are guides for how to set up a good base but I don't read them, I learn it for myself.
Graphically it has that steampunk edge that gives the game a character that is, for me, very endearing, I don't find myself growing tired of looking at the buildings nor the units. The game fills the space between buildings and around your colony with the odd worker *unable to be attacked* so that even though you are waiting on resources to come in it isn't a dull screen. The zombies have a good mix of looks giving the hoard something rarely seen in most hoards, variety.
The only issues that I found are that double clicking selects all of the thing you clicked on, so it highlights everything across the map not across the screen. I also dislike that last clicking does not unselect what you have chosen. Other than that I have not found any bugs or issues.
I give this game a solid 8 out of 10 and hope that others buy this game to play.

There may be a few things that you may consider "Spoilers" in this review.
In all honesty, this is an.. "Decent" game.  This coming from someone who's never played the first game, I have mixed feelings, and thoughts about the differences between the two products.  Anyway, I will give you my honest impressions on this game after having it for a year or so.
This game greets you with absolutely beautiful graphical detail, and very accurate vehicale models.  This game simulates modern, and classic vehicles in a very accurate manner, along with accurate prices too. (Most of the time.)
There are many ways to earn money in this game, some more convenient than others, some more fun than others.  One is by completing the Solar Crown Championships, which require certain vehicle types to participate in.  Now, let me say this... I DO NOT recommend attending the championships, unless you enjoy completing some of the most repetitive, monotenous acts I've ever seen.  I mean, most of them are common in a lot of racing games today, however, I just feel they are just wasted potential here.  I would have enjoyed seening the type of racing like in Midnight Club 3, which is an amazing game made by Rockstar if you didn't know.
A more convinient way of earning a bit of cash is by using F.R.I.M. F.R.I.M is a system that gives you a small amount of money for doing simple things, such as having a near miss with another driver, or constantly drifting. (It gives you $100 dollars when you start, and the money increases then.  I believe the maximum you can get in one run is $10,000.)
Another way to earn money is to race other drivers you find around the area.  The will have a random name, and flashing you headlights at them will allow you to race them instantly.  You can race the same person until you grow tired of it, so if you find that one person that has no chance of winning, you can make VERY easy money for as long as you please.
Now, for those of you who enjoy driving you valuable vehicles like a sane human being, the cockpit view is very detailed, and flows well with the overall control scheme, and graphical style.  Although, if you hate slow AI drivers, than here's something to note.  TDU2 has some of the dumbest civilian AI I've ever seen.  The are just about the slowest driver AI as well.  You just need to play the game to see.
Another note, if you want to play this game with a friend, I have some bad news.  Because of the developer studio shutting down, the multiplayer servers went with them.  It's worth searching whether a multiplayer mod will be made for this game, like the one made for Just Cause 2.  (If you have any information on that, please tell me.  I'd be willing to play online with someone.)
With all that aside, I can't help but go back to this game because of the sharp visuals, and lovely selection of vehicles to choose from.  The sounds are wonderful, the thrill of have a 1.6 million dollar car keeps you playing, exploring the island(s), and finding landmarks.
With that said, I do recommend this game, just be aware of some of the "Moments" that the AI has, and some of the short- comings of the physics engine.
I give this game a Seven out of Ten, and I do recommend it to anyone who wants a good-looking, mixture of arcade fun, and realistic simulation.
Thank you.

I love this game, and unlike many, also like the DLC policy.
The game was good on release, and I played many hours of it at that time. I got my money's worth. But it contniues to grow, getting better and better. This requires money.
Most released games quickly fade away, or are left to the community to try to fix. A patch or two and then they are gone, with many known issues left. There is simply no budget to continue to pay anyone to continue to work on it. With the continue-to-release-paid-DLC model, work on adding features and fixing bugs can and does continue, both paid (DLC) and unpaid (bug fixes).  Yes, the eventual total price is expensive, but I find it akin to an online game, where constant income means constant development (and people are quite happy to pay literally a thousand for their years of say EVE online).
I certianly find this method more honest than keeping a game in endless 'early access' (and even releasing DLC for said game which surely is a contradiction in terms) and love that I can expect new features, better AI and cosmetic changes for a game that I know I will still be playing for several more years.
An often given argument is that feature x should have been in the base game, and thus Jonny Gamer resents having to pay for it. My thinking is that feature x only exists at all because of the continuing paid development model. Perhaps they hadn't even thought of it at base release, or simply did not have the time or money. In any other game, feature x would never come to exist, or you would still pay for it, just in Game II, released several years later! Yet here, you can actually expect feature x to arrive, sooner or later (air units handled more like the way ground are is on my wishlist, and I actually am confident that it will happen).
I can only dream of what could have happened if games such as Vampire Bloodlines had been released by Paradox, with work continuing for several years after release.
TLDR? If you like WW2 strategy, you will love this, buy it. But you already have if you do, so thus the question is should you continue to support its development by buying DLC or not? Well, I feel it is the same question as should you subscribe to an online game. Play without for a while, but if you love it and will continue to play, support the game!

Well what makes me come back to this game time and again? Interesting story... no, great driving physics...no, interesting characters.. dont let me start on that, voice acting?.. you could say that if you were entertained by the repeating announcement that apparently the Wilder brother are squabbling with Stewart again (who-tf is Stewart I can only guess).
However this game has something. You have you car and the freedom to travel around two islands full of nice sights and sunny vistas. You can drive for hours, buy cars, houses or just explore at your leasure.  You can challenge other people whos worlds seamlesly intersect with yours like in Dark Souls. Or you can explore the world without invisible bounds around the roads, a bit like Skyrim in Cars. But even if you stop, the environment doesn't look as generic as for example in Need for Speed or Driver series, so you are really motivated to visit new places.
The graphics are great, there is a weather and day/night cycle. The views you get out of some of your Flats/Houses are amasing. The challenges a varied and exciting. There are also a pair of races around the Island, that can take nearly a real-world hour to complete. I mean if I think about it a bit more, this game is the opposite of what I really don't like about other racing games whith dumb driving on the same track over and over again with an extreme example being american Nascar where you just drive in a circle.
Sure the characters look like dorks and sound even worse, but then you see the attention do detail the developers put into the game and it's amazing.  Just try to explore the starting location. You will not see it any more after the first minute or so in-game but the effort put into it speaks for itself. If you take your time and look around at the nicely textured babes, whose breast actually bounce around a bit (in a racing game!), the bar with actually some bottles stuffed behind the counter, then you really get into this holiday Ibiza mood. Did I mention  I really appreciate that detail? There are also many cars each with detailed interior, which you can admire.
This game however is not without its (many) problems, to name a few:
- the characters are just plain silly and the story even more so
- you have to set the controls just so, or the driving experience will be awfull
- the driving physics could be much better (I miss dirt 2)
- there are no pedestrians (to drive over :)  ) anywhere!
- the developer is not in business any more
Well thats my 2c, you can get this game really cheap for less tha $10 on steamtrades, so if you just like to drive around, explore and do an occasional race, this is a game for you!

Alright, here we go. Here goes my rant...
Pixel Piracy is being published by Re-Logic, the devs behind one of my personal favorite Indie games: Terraria. Do they get cut slack because I love Terraria so much? Nope. The gameplay is a bit repetitive, even for a roguelike. I'm a big fan of roguelikes and enjoy playing them a lot. However, this one isn't that good. The exploration thing is alright, but it could've used more detail. Managing your ship is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥due to being overwhelmed with food, crewmembers, poop, ship upgrades, health, and more. It overwhelms me even more than FTL does. The graphics are average at the most, and there isn't much to it. YES, I understand this is pixelated graphics, but to the people out there who lack intelligence, I DON'T LIKE THE WAY THE PIXELATED VISUALS WERE USED. There.
The audio, oh god, the dang audio. It is so ANNOYING listening to "Me hardy har!" every three seconds. Yes, I'm well aware of this thing called 'mute' and it ruins the game, too.
The game, which I do understand, as it is in Early Access, has very little content. If it were the full game, I would rate this lower, but seeing that it isn't, I won't even bother with that. However, on the bright side of this, Pixel Piracy does have a pretty good future ahead, but it wouldn't be one of the greatest roguelikes of recent memory, like Dungeons of Dredmor and FTL. Also, for an Early Access game, I discovered little to no bugs. I've played many Early Access games, and this one was probably the best running of all of them. One other thing I saw is that it does have quite the replayability, and that it is one of those games that you dislike, but you can't help but play it anyway.
So, in conclusion, I understand the game is in Early Access, but I've played better games that came out with less content, more bugs, etc etc. If you buy it and like it, then great. I'm happy for you that it was worth it. However, I would approach this game with caution. I'm afraid that I cannot recommend this game.

As a game, it's... not bad. As a narrative about social anxiety, it's reasonable; a lot better than many depictions found in games and television. It gives a basic rundown and is sympathetic to the character.
I can certainly empathize; as a kid who grew up hiding assignment papers and computer screens from supervising teachers, I have some idea of how irrationally cautious and/or anxious everyday things can be to people with anxiety disorders. To this day, I still occasionally avoid kitchens when there are other people in them. I also tend to choose my seats in cafeterias carefully so I can either see anybody approaching, or hide myself eating, depending on whether I'm more self-conscious or anxious that day. I also don't fix hair or apply deodorant in washrooms if anybody else is present. Sometimes people will go great lengths to avoid ordinary facts of life.
Honestly, while I appreciate the depiction of the character, the game itself defies one of the unspoken rules of interaction: if the player gets a game over,
. In this game, many of the ways to fail come from seemingly unrelated decisions. Your first playthrough of the game is blind and you will probably fail by no fault of your own. In games that follow this rule like Dark Souls, failing is a consequence of poor decisions. In this game, seemingly innocuous and ordinary decisions carry severe consequences. I would say that this is the major failing of the game.
As far as this goes, I'm inclined not to recommend it as a game. It's a cutesy story to experience for 10 minutes, but navigating the multiple endings isn't all that rewarding when most of them are failures. This game is an obstacle course of torture dressed up in a vibrant oatmeal-coloured package. For the price of free, by all means play it, but it's about as interesting as one might find a new meme to be.
Before this review becomes longer than the game, I bid Adieu.
EDIT: And why in the world does this need a 2 GHz processor!? That's like saying you need a Ferrari to drive to your Grandma's home 5 blocks away...

I appear to be the first negative reviewer to have completed the game in its entirety.  This game has two distinct parts, the dating sim and the Bad Boys Love secret route unlocked by romancing every bird possible.
The first part is simply too short to be entertaining.  Any route can be read in about an hour going at a relaxed pace, but there is significant overlap between routes, including sections that have no effect on the particular route you're playing, so I found myself skipping more and more as I replayed.  This also caused me to inadvertantly skip content I hadn't read before, because some sections have multiple outcomes but start out the same way regardless of route.  There is no way to go back to content accidentally skipped without reloading or starting a new game and it simply wasn't interesting enough to worth bothering to find out why I was faced with the choice of telling Okosan "convenience store" or "grocery store" and I could infer it had something to do with pudding anyway.
Consequently, there just isn't enough time to give any character depth and there's no challenge to complete a route.  By the time you finish a route, you feel like you were merely introduced to the character.  Picking routes are also very obvious and there is never any difficulty in seducing the various birds, unless you can't figure out that picking every opportunity to spend time with your desired bird is necessary to romance them.  The routes I enjoyed most, Okosan, Shuu, and Anghel, stood out because they were simply the most oddball.  For a game that is billed as a comedy, most routes utilize stereotypical melodrama.  Bird puns and pop culture references abound, but there's really nothing laugh out loud funny in Hatoful Boyfriend and at best you'll smirk a lot.
There is a very simple stat system, raised by choosing between three elective classes at regular intervals and in a couple of events that likewise present three choices which raise a stat.  The stats serve one purpose, which is to determine whether you get a normal ending or an extended ending.  Extended endings require you to raise one stat to maximum and reward you with an extra scene that was implied in the normal ending anyway.  Each ending has a separate achievement and you can't get both the normal ending and extended ending achievements in one go, so you have to play the same route twice in order to get all the achievements and unlock the Bad Boys Love extended ending.  I wasted part of my life to get the BBL extended ending and it was just as disappointing as the other extended endings.
The second part of the game, the Bad Boys Love secret route is much more interesting, but by the time I unlocked it I was already tired of the game.  I trudged on in hopes that it would be good and it was, kind of.  The game suddenly takes a much darker tone, reveals how the world came to be dominated by talking birds, and becomes a mystery story.  It seems interesting for a while, but as all the threads come together it becomes a soap opera for the ages.  Characters are revealed to be secret brothers, secret childhood friends, secret enemies, secret agents, secret terrorists, secret weapons, secretly superpowered, secretly alive, but, alas, there are no secret comas to complete the cliche pantheon.  I got the distinct impression that the first half of the game was written primarily to introduce the characters so that the meandering mysteries wouldn't simply baffle readers.
All in all, Hatoful Boyfriend wasn't an altogether terrible game, but it just wasn't worth the money and I got it in a 50% off sale.  I will likely never read it again and would forget about it entirely if Steam didn't keep it in my library forever.  As some consolation, the trading cards were surprisingly valuable and I was able to quickly sell them for about $1.50.
If you don't mind a lot of repetition, love every visual novel no matter what, and really love silly gimmicks, then buy this game.  Otherwise, pick up just about any other visual novel on Steam.  Even some of the free ones are more entertaining than Hatoful Boyfriend.

So after playing a few hours alone, I can say I like it! And so begins the list of why
PROS AND CONS
-Much better graphics than the first game, and much bigger areas to explore. No more claustrophobia or "Why cant i mount this ledge or move past this thing" Anything that sensibly could be traversed in reality can now be mounted or jumped off. While inside buildings, you see through a "Hole cut" system where the forground disappears, which is great because now the game can have interiors and other sequences the first didnt have, these all lead to super pleasing environments.
-Every mission has its own environments and you can replay them all for loot or fun
-Much more "Walking dead" and much less "Dead island' feel to this game, the forests and cities are much more friendly to my idea of what a zombie game should be like. Night no longer brings creepy lunatics who are afraid of light (At least not constantly, they however can occasionally appear), clearing cities at night is spooky and can make you jump, the amount of zombies is reduced from 1 but they are more lethal and you have to play smarter, which I prefer. In the first game it was always a "How many times can you empty the clip on your nerf gun" feeling, wheras in this one its like "Pick and choose your targets and sneak, and be ready for a zombie behind every door"
-Kovac.... Just... Kovac
-After playing till i got a gun, i can confirm they are no longer air powered, long story short, they are handmade guns that sound like guns and take bullets and hurt things, not a supersoaker that magically shoots bolts and nails. and yes, they are loud and will attract walkers, very Walking dead feel to using your gun in this game. The guns are all homemade and as such have "Interesting" appearances, but not "Silly" anymore. The other weapons, bows and such, also got a sexy new look and upgrade that I love.
Now, on to what I DO NOT like so far.
-The menus are an utterly horrendous mess, hopefully this will be fixed later, you have a seperate menu on seperate keys for every single menu you can access, this needs to be replaced with hotkeys to parts of a central menu with subsections.
-The camp system is cheesy and feels really pointless considering you are camping about 4 feet from Kovac's massive safe bunker, This could really use some expansion and more "Reason" to do it rather than because kovac told you to do it and wont share his bunker, Id prefer having environments to choose from rather than just putting it up in the generic woods you start in, give us options to use that dont make it so its a 20-mile jog to kovacs bunker and by proxy literally 90% of the quests.
-Farming for materials is what will be the death of this game, the monotomy is toxic, enter mission, look for random drops, find 1 or 2 of your item, redo mission, repeat. This needs to be made more fun.
And Last, what I want to see develop as the game moves out of early access.
-The customization menu needs to be much more comprehensive and have many more options. Instead of having "male body A" and "Male body B" have the same look but different pants (I assume this is planned anyway)
-While I love the fact every mission environment is now its own Cell and you dont have to walk to each of them, having more places to explore when not in missions would be nice, the forest is beautiful but it has like, 4 landmarks to explore.
-A menu to select already done quests so you dont have to remember/run to the guy who gave it every time you want to redo it for materials.
-If more areas are added in the future, instead of making us build near the bunker entrances, just let us place one in the environment?
-Current finishing moves have three choices, 1 and 2 are generic and dont care about the weapon, and 3 is weapon specific (Some weapons have more, such as the bat) but expanding on these and making it so the weapon finishers happen more would be nice! Also, I cant get my arrows back when i use my bow in a finisher, i assume this is a bug.
-In a game like this, modding support seems like it could be both possible and potentially amazing, Id love to see this happen with custom missions and gear. (I assume this would be possible because the Cells you do missions in Feel like they were created by a mapmaker type software, instead of each being "hand made")
-I really REALLY like the creepiness some of the night missions give, adding a thicker more terrifying horror element to these missions would be amazing. Im not talking H2S style "Creepers in the dark" Im talking somethat that legitimately will make you sit in a building and not want to open a door, or go back outside or things of that nature. (All the pictures of slenderman on the walls help with the mood!)
All in all this game is an improvement on the first in almost every regard, and is supposed to just get much better, I look forward to seeing where it goes! Im gonna hop into the beta branch and Put what I find below and try to update it

Don't let the early access title scare you on this one. There are plenty of hours of fun, challenging content.

This game has a lot of potential, however, there are two major flaws with the current release.
Auto pathing is horrible: You have to be very careful with how you set up your base, and pay close attention to where your units are going. In tight base setups, its pretty often that units will get confused and start running the opposite direction to get to where you click to walk all the way around some terrain in the fog of war, to get to the other side of your base, instead of just walking through a clear path. This can easily be a game ender if you aren't careful.
Also, It's too difficult to tell the infected from your own vilagers. There is a warning system like with all RTS games that tells you when your base is being attacked, but it only actually works half the time. Just suddenly notice a couple of my houses are grey, and there are 10 infected in my base. This has only happened to me within the early stages of the game.
That being said, the frustrations I'm experiencig can be avoided as you learn to build bases the AI can navigate, and in general to "git gud" at watching over your base before you get some walls up.
I'm digging the art style and am having a pretty great time in general with this game. I haven't gotten anywhere near the end yet, and am looking forward to my next try.
Overall, I'd reccomend this game if you are looking for an interesting and unique RTS to play.

Firstly...the community in this game is absolutely awful. "Filthy casual", "carebear" these are things that are said to those who have mentioned they disliked the 100% clear rate for the next map. They need to grow up. Making the game more accessible to everyone isn't a bad thing, no one forces people to play easier or harder so really they are just idiots.
The game is difficult yes, the mode released though is survival and I personally like the 100% difficulty, although have chosen a smaller one to learn the game on as I couldn't get past day 50 on map 1 to begin with. The main constraints are space management, resources can fairly easily be managed, but one poorly placed building can quickly ruin you later. Pausing and planning is a necessity, as is losing and retrying. Trial and error to learn the game is best.
People have compared it to Dark Souls. I think it's a poor comparison. Dark Souls is built around its difficulty, in map design, loot locations and enemy placement etc. This is a random generated RTS, nowhere near the same except trial and error gameplay.
If I could change one thing it would be how quick the in game hours pass. Keep building and research speeds the same etc, but a little extra time per day to micromanage repairs and such wouldn't be a bad thing imo. Yes it can be paused and managed, however sometimes in a state of urgent expansion you can't pause otherwise you won't be ready for the next wave, meaning having to micromanage both defenses and units advancing. Or perhaps a "retreat" unit option that when a unit is hit would move a 5 tile radius back to make sure you can safely take eyes away from units for more than a minute.
Overall a very enjoyable game and I look forward to future updates and campaign mode also. (Really looking forward to the tavern to hire mercs)

Similar to Terraria but in a pirate world and a lot more interesting mechanics; Pixel Piracy is shaping up to be a fantastic game and one, that if you love pirates, you will want to play.
For my full first impressions review, go to:

Pixel Piracy holds much potential, that's what I wanted to say first. However, the game is currently in beta and it is far from completed. The interface is rather confusing and there are game-breaking bugs which only a restart and reload of an old save will solve. The game balance is very off, especially when the AI can easily be defeated by a single person. You can beat an army of enemies with just your captain by
. There are several other annoyances, such as missing scroll bars if you collected many items, and the weird interface for your crew, as well as poop. So much poop on your ship! Pirates need to eliminate from time to time and will do so on your ship. You can teach your people to clean, but for some reason, the cleaning rate is lower than pooping rate, so you will end up having a ship full of poop.
Nevertheless, I can not only list the bad stuff, can I? I love the art/graphic style. It's simple, yes, but it's very beautiful. I also like the sound and the smooth animations and transitions of the interface. The game's core concept is great, I want to play this, just explore one more island and fight one more legendary boss. But right now, there is little to be explored. I hope they will add much content (or modding support?).
All in all, I had and still have fun with this game, even in the current state, so I can recommend this game to people who want to support the developers and can take a peek into the game, but not to people who want to have a finished game.

I was immediately taken by the menu screen's music and small visuals in the backdrop of palm trees swaying at an angle. I created my world and was off.
Moving was confusing at first because I assumed W-A-S-D would work but instead I had to click. I caught on quickly and bought crew members and food (and accidently attacked shopkeeper). Then I made my ship, had to watch a video to learn how to sail, and began my grand adventure.

Map appears to be pretty small, at least the map with resources on it. If you go beyod a certain point there are no more resources or environment, just empty polygon ground texture. Seems like someone took a bunch of prebuilt code libraries and put them into a game which sure added some nice things like weather effects, a planet, a movement system, etc, but it doesn't feel like there was much done with the actual coding of the game itself.
The worst part is that it took a while to figure this out because when you first start playing, the game seems alright, the small area isn't so small when your on foot, but once you invest 4 or so hours you get a hover bike, then, once you get your base set up to the point where you want to go exploring outside of the local resources (~10 hours in), you find out there's nothing to explore, space is crap, and finding and raiding others is pointless.

First let me state that to enjoy this game the most, I recomend playing the evil campaign first doing what you want and gettig used to the powers and having fast paced fun, and then playing a good guy campaign to challenge yourself and take different routes and admitadly have less fun becouse the most enjoyable way to play is as a power fantasy like bioshock, which the developers don't seem to grasp. I played this game before on xbox 360 and the pc is definately the superior version for having quicksave, more on that below.
1. Visuals, the game is exellent in this regard and uses a unique artstyle to bring you into it's own world. Admitadly it's a bit offputing at first, and for some reason all the major characters tend to look and sound the same despite having very distinct features and voices since almost everyone speaks in a low sad monotone voice that makes them sound identical through repeated levels. But overall the game drew me in well enough and runs well enough that even through quicksaving and quickloading the pace was not interrupted too much.
2. Story, the story is very compelling and well thought out when written down or in the wiki, which is what I recomend you do. In my first playthrough all the characters sounded the bloody same and even when important plot points like kidnapping the scientist were introduced I had no Idea who he was or why I cared. So I got the bad ending first becuse the game is centered around killing people and killing people is very fun and all the characters explaining how this was not what I was supposed to be doing and that I was damming the city felt like the buzzing of flies around my lunch. Things went better in the second and third playthrough when I did a non-lethal run and forced myself to listen to the god-awful voice acting that makes the npc's in Skyrim look like shakesperian characters. Overall I'd say the story brings down an excellent game into just being good, because your actions have consequences, and you are discouraged from the cathartic and fun action and herded into slow sneaking which doesn't suit the gameplay as well as murder sprees.
3. The gameplay. It is by far the best part about the game and the only thing I remeber even years after finishing it. It's quick paced and tactical and some other good words. However, to get the most out of it one has to colect all the bone charms and runes, and stupidly there is no new game plus, which means that you can't just ignore some hard to get runes because you will get more in the next playthrough. I played through the game three times and through the dlc campaign twice, all things considered it's about eight hours on a bad killer campaign and about sixteen hours on a saint campaign, and surprisingly it's still entertaining to take different aproaches with more skill and thoughtfullness the second time around.

If the enemy gets through your main defences, you have basically lost. The rapid spread of zombie infestiation means you have no chance to recover. Pulling every solider you have off the defences and into the base can save your main building, but then you are doomed anyway.
This needs to change. There needs to be some mechanism to recover after this huge loss, or some alternatives to fight it (Order a purge of all citizens? Otherwise, every game will play pretty much the same, and games that have been expertly played can be lost on one random zombie.

I love this game, and unlike many, also like the DLC policy.
The game was good on release, and I played many hours of it at that time. I got my money's worth. But it contniues to grow, getting better and better. This requires money.
Most released games quickly fade away, or are left to the community to try to fix. A patch or two and then they are gone, with many known issues left. There is simply no budget to continue to pay anyone to continue to work on it. With the continue-to-release-paid-DLC model, work on adding features and fixing bugs can and does continue, both paid (DLC) and unpaid (bug fixes).  Yes, the eventual total price is expensive, but I find it akin to an online game, where constant income means constant development (and people are quite happy to pay literally a thousand for their years of say EVE online).
I certianly find this method more honest than keeping a game in endless 'early access' (and even releasing DLC for said game which surely is a contradiction in terms) and love that I can expect new features, better AI and cosmetic changes for a game that I know I will still be playing for several more years.
An often given argument is that feature x should have been in the base game, and thus Jonny Gamer resents having to pay for it. My thinking is that feature x only exists at all because of the continuing paid development model. Perhaps they hadn't even thought of it at base release, or simply did not have the time or money. In any other game, feature x would never come to exist, or you would still pay for it, just in Game II, released several years later! Yet here, you can actually expect feature x to arrive, sooner or later (air units handled more like the way ground are is on my wishlist, and I actually am confident that it will happen).
I can only dream of what could have happened if games such as Vampire Bloodlines had been released by Paradox, with work continuing for several years after release.
TLDR? If you like WW2 strategy, you will love this, buy it. But you already have if you do, so thus the question is should you continue to support its development by buying DLC or not? Well, I feel it is the same question as should you subscribe to an online game. Play without for a while, but if you love it and will continue to play, support the game!

Played this on PC for a while, was amused but the game is more broken than fun. Now returning after updates I find that it is less broken, but also absurdly less fun. Let us review..
The difficulty of this game shifts wildly from easy to the point of boredom to how-the-hell-am-I-supposed-to-do-anything. Often times this shift doesn't even require you to begin a new game, rather you just have a small stroke of bad luck and suddenly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t abounds. The easiest example of this are the islands that are everywhere. You explore them at the beginning and find but a few enemies, if you're lucky they are pirates with similar health and weapons, luckier still its just a group of monkies with a chest. Those are not typical encounters. Rather the vast majority of the time you will find the island literally infested with more enemies than you have crew, each with better weapons than you can buy, and each indivudually having more health than your entire crew combined. That's not a challenge, that's locking off an entire section of the game.
Ok, you might think to yourself, I guess I can come back later with more pirates/weapons/skills/etc and do this. You can, but only for those islands that you have explored and thus locked down their difficulty. The more you grow your crew the more the absurd scale of the island difficulty tries to be vertical. I'm at the point where I effectively ignore them unless I feel like watching my crew get slaughtered by BOARS.
Now with a signifigant portion of the game rendered effectively gone lets address the pirate ships. Those are definitely fun...for a while...which is to say up until danger level 4. Once the idiots start getting cannons it become an exercise in frustration as you bumrush the cannoneers to stop them from blowing up and sinking their own ship and killing everyone. You would think that those who carry explosives aboard their ships would provide more than a single layer of wood between them and a watery death. This also raises serious questions about the usefulness of cannons aboard your own ship, since a few shots from you might cause the same destruction leaving you with nothing for your troubles except some debt since you now need more cannonballs. That's fun.
OH, I almost forgot about the AI, though intelligence is rather a strong term for what I've seen my pirates do. Lets say you're going to try and be tricky to take an island you explored that has less than 15 enemies with 300 health that hit for 20+ damage. You notice they are spread out and figure you can mob them individually without losing everyone. So you land, you drag the attack icon to a guy and watch as everyone proceeds to sprint past them and die...Ok reload and try again, maybe you misclicked or something. Nope, attack icon doesn't seem to actually direct anyone...right click? Nope. Hrm...
I should also mention that getting all of your pirates to actually do anything is a miracle in itself. I can't count the number of times I've ordered my men to board a ship only to find that 3-4 just decided "Nah" and are hanging around my ship causing unnecessary losses. Even better should you spam right click to get the lazy buggers over there it is entirely possible that a few of your pirates already on the enemy ship decide that your orders mean they should go back home. Now since new targets have opened up some of your own pirates may gleefully decide to run the gauntlet of every other enemy on the ship and die.
There seem to be new features being added, which is good, like the bounty/wanted boards...buuut you can't seem to put them off until later? Yeah sure my and my one other crewmate will go after this dude, that makes sense. If you tell it to♥♥♥♥♥♥off, like you probably will 99.99% of the time, then it mocks you and will never activate again.
Don't even get me started on the voices...for the love of god the voices. I would rather they not even be there instead of listening to the same damn line over...and over...every time I take an action or just because they happen to be talking to the crew. ♥♥♥♥ hearing my captain say "Loser" or "Land HO" about 2000 times just makes me turn the sound off entirely. That's disappointing because the sound is actually pretty good.

Costume Quest is a game that unexpectedly won me over completely. While I still have not played all of Double Fine's games yet, this particular game is near the top for me, and also one of my favorite games in general for recent years.
There is a lot of heart in the design and story of Costume Quest, which is a wonderfully funny kids' adventure. You begin the game on Halloween night for a brother and sister, which quickly evolves into a gigantic quest beyond any normal realm, as you must fight monsters that sweep in to take over the night.
As a whole, Costume Quest is indeed a quest. As you control a set of kids going on their adventure throughout the game, you will do a variety of things from actual trick-or-treating to exploration for hidden items to performing role-playing battles. The game is indeed an RPG with main and side quests, special equipment and power-up items, along with general collectibles. Most fitting to the game is that candy is your currency.
Each new area that you enter, you generally must trick-or-treat at a set number of houses or doorways. When doing so, you will literally get a trick or a treat. The treat is simply candy, as expected. The trick, however, is a fight with the monsters that are the main enemies of the game. When battles launch up, your characters have mini-cutscenes where they turn into the beings that they are wearing as costumes, e.g., a robot will suddenly stand up very tall and be prepared to fight.
The style of the battles are turn-based, though you only have three options - normal attack, special power, and Battle Stamp power. When you perform normal attacks, each costume has a different style of "timing" that you can use to perform extra damage if you hit the right buttons in the proper manner. Special powers cannot be used until enough energy (essentially MP) is accrued, which will generally happen after a few turns in battle. Battle Stamps are part of the equipment of the game, where each character can wear a single stamp to add extra strength or a new capability. Some of the Battle Stamps just affect stats, like increasing attack power. Others will give an ability for that third battle option, such as stunning enemies temporarily.
As can be seen both in and out of battle, the game has a very interesting, 3D cartoon art style showcasing the environment and characters. As already mentioned above, the battles have mini-cutscenes related to the costumes, and there are also special effects for the power attacks or for certain bosses that you fight along the way. Altogether, everything truly screams Halloween. Even the costumes that you are wearing will allow you to perform different capabilities in the "real" world, as you will need to switch between them to access certain areas or complete side quests on the map.
The story itself is also very well-done, having both a cheesy style but also a mapped-out purpose. As you continue through the game, you will learn more information about the beings that you are fighting against and what their end goal is. Take note that once you finish the game, the story is not done. The game has a free "Grubbins on Ice" DLC which continues from the end of the game. And even further, there is a Costume Quest 2 which continues from the endpoint of that DLC.
I highly recommend this game to just about any person. The adventure of the children is filled with fun, charm, humor, and a number of other qualities, combined into a very enjoyable game.

I really enjoyed this game because it really captures a lot of the fun of the Halloween spirit that can be so easily ignored in favor of Christmas, especially for us adults who don't get much to do on Halloween unless we want to go to a bar or club.  Starting off, I'd say what builds this Halloween concept so well is all of the different nods to Halloween activities throughout.  This ranges from the bobbing for apples mini-game, collectible cards you can trade and swap for, gathering random household objects to build different costumes, going throughout different areas in town to attend various events (costume contest, various neighborhoods, etc.), dealing with a random bully/jerk, and of course going Trick-or-Treating.  I thought it was fun going to random doors, not knowing if you would receive a treat, in the form of gobs of candy, or a trick, in the form of a random battle.  A nice variation on the random battle aspect you normally get in RPGs.
Battles are fairly straightforward and simple, with different costumes providing the player with options on which combat style and ultimate move they prefer to use.  Don't like trying to time your attack or hit the right button prompt once it appears on screen?  Then you will likely have an alternative to use instead, once you unlock enough costumes.  Sometimes different combat situations will require the player to mix and match to get the right combination, but since this game lacks grinding (since enemies don't respawn) there is always some way to get through your current fight.  Early and mid-game fights were sometimes hard to get through since I'd need to avoid making any mistakes (especially when going against 3 baddies at once), since it was so easy for them to just kill off one of my guys and make it so I couldn't win the fight at all.  Otherwise though, I saw nothing wrong in the combat as it had just the right balancing, for me at least.
The game has fun and witty dialogue, which compels the player to explore and talk with various NPCs.  Sometimes navigating the map can be a bit annoying, but once you get the hang of it it's not too bad.  It does help having the robot roller skates on to zip around at turbo speed, a thankful addition since most games like this have you plod around at a constant speed.  You even get to pick between being the boy or girl, without one or the other being obvious eye "candy." *pun intended*
Overall, I would recommend this game.  It doesn't offer much for replayability, but it's worthy of a full playthrough.

I would rather vote 'neutral' or 'not as good as the first one' if there were options.
The first 'How To Survive' was simple, a little odd and seemed quite challenging to just manage your inventory... but that gave it the charm!
Although local co-op and base-building were things that would have improved the first game incredibly, in this, they seem needed to just keep the balance...
Upgrading each building, the base in general, yourself and your skills is very time-consuming and requires a LOT of resources (some, rarer than rocking-horse dung!) and most of the time I spend gathering resources leaves me with more EXP than I'll ever need (maxxxed every skill and XP-related thing to level 10 before upgrading my base)
I am not too happy with the gun crafting system as the first game had a massive customisable feature. You had this bit, this bit and this bit... now depending on which of the next three changed the weapon. Or you replace the first bit and get a whole new set of options!
Now, it's all levelled hard-craft choices. build 'this item' with 'these stats' and deal with it.
Ammo is all bullets. Loud and attention-grabbing. so there's another step down.
Upgrading your gear should make killing enemies easier... not say 'hey, i killed one of you. all rush me!' so it seems to be forcing you back towards the bow and crossbow.
Melee weapons are much the same. Can't mess up 'hit them until they stay down'.
The buildings allow for great new recipies, but could do with the option to MOVE ONCE PLACED! My biggest complaint about the base-building is that once it's down, deal with it.
Put something down wrong? deal with it or destroy it.
Like many other things, once you've done it, it's stuck.
I feel that this game could do with some more features (like 'move buildings' or 'define camp area') and will gladly take back any of these comments if they're already on the drawing board and appear later.
I like the option to 'increase the difficulty' of missions. that's great for testing gear, grinding XP or keeping things interesting... but again, with hard-choice crafting, you don't get the customisability and have to carrry alternate options with you instead.
The inventory system is weight-based, no longer slot based (one of the better choices made) but with one glaring problem...
YOU NAVIGATE IT WITH A CURSOR!
With a mouse, that's perfectly fine and makes sense... with a controller (which is apparently the suggested method of play) a cursor is a nightmare to use!
Generally, I was far more impressed with the first game than this one.
Worth a play for fans of the genre (moreso if they havn't played the first) but I can't recomend this game to anyone full-price.

I'm probably going to be harsh on this game, but it seems to me like the core gameplay/mechanics are complete. I feel like the game tried to be a bit like Don't Starve. All the pieces are here for a really great game. Unfortunately, the execution leaves a lot to be desired.
Pros:
- Game is very stable.
- Crafting is not bad
- Combat is okay
Cons:
- Missions are awful. Exclusively fetch quests or "Go here and kill/collect X things"
- AI isn't. Everything runs at you in a straight line. Some things are faster than others.
- Thirst and hunger are ultimately pointless.
- For a game called "How to Survive," survival is surprisingly easy. I've found it really hard to die unless I crank the mission level to the max.
- Missions are meant to be repeated. Do a mission, collect resources, do it again.
- The game's key areas are swamps, forests, and an urban environment. Why there are so many zombies in the swamps and forests is a mystery, but ignoring that, the environments and textures are repeated ad nauseum. The environments aren't exciting to begin with, but are constantly re-used.
I'll keep my eye out for any significant updates, but I believe the game right now is a pretty good representation of what the finished product will be. It's not completely terrible, but... well, it's mostly terrible. Enjoy your swamps and forests.

This review is long. Read at your own risk.
TL;DR Not an isometric view guy, but this game has me by the balls. 10/10
I'm not really a top-down shooter person. Imagine my surprise when I snag this after purchasing something my computer can't run.
How to Survive 2 is an excellent title, and is preferable of those that are available, and here's why.
Start with a baseball bat, Smash some zombies' face in, then you start to find materials,  materials you can use to begin building a camp.
From you camp you build a variety of crafting stations from which you cook food, make weaponry from  bows to wooden firearms, work with metal and turns bits of lead into ammo, Take random junk you find and make armor, and take plants and rocks and make some gunpowder.
The beauty of this game is freedom. Sure, you need missions to gather food and whatnot, but as for your camp? You have a large woods area and can build your camp literally Anywhere. Want a tunnel to access Kovac more easily? Done. Wanna live out of a train car on abandoned tracks? done. wanna live in a ditch? Also done. You can build, create, and fight waves of zombies, and the beauty is you don't even have to stick to one spot. Bored with your camp? Build a new one!
As for zombies, welll...they're very....varied. There are different types of zombies, and as you progress in levels, more type will present themselves, and in greater numbers. FIrst, they walk...then jog...bows are fine for these, but whaat to do when they run at you, 10 at a time? Haha. Yes, zombies can run, you also have bloated ones that explode, deer, turkeys, pelicans, zombies that only come out at night, and run faster than anything.
As for a story, it's actually quite interesting. Exploring the woods your camp is set in provides an interesting backstory into the universe. Kovac, Survival enthusiast, assists you in beginning to survive. THe brothers, who live in the woods just away from kovacs tunnels, bicker back and forth, but reward you for your assistance. Kenji, from the first game, has burning hatred for Kovac and his fans, and wants your help in undermining them...and I imagine more will present themselves.
Now, remember, I'm not an isometric person, and I LOVE this game. So yeah, the viewpoint can be daunting for me, but the game itself is way worth it.

Once you unlock all the endings, including the death ending, you then can play Hurtful Boyfriend. Which I honestly liked a lot because all the stories the love interests have, all run into each other and has a very nice conclusion for everyone. There are choices but they don't really mean anything since its impossible to get a game over. Its just meant to tell the back story of the world they live in as well as the characters in it, while leading it to an ending that was very touching.
Overall, if your open minded this game will surprise you. You'll laugh, you'll cry, and you'll fall in love over and over again with these awesome characters and story.

I've had a few friends in my time. Shocking, I know. And therefore, I'm well-acquainted with a certain type of friend. Let me paint a picture here. He's always had your back, always been there when you needed him, but he has a couple of really, really painfully annoying quirks. For instance, remember that time a fly entered your flat? He just wouldn't shut up about it. It's always something small, something minor, but he ensures you pay the closest attention to it, regardless of how meaningless it actually is.
Well, today I made such a friend in The Bureau: XCOM Declassified. Agent Carter is the kind of guy who's the first to let you know he won five bucks in the lottery, there's a strange car going by, or a slightly interesting sesame seed happens to be on his burger bun. How do I know this, you ask? Because that's the Bureau experience! Pass the 100th enemy craft in the past five minutes? Carter's right there, with an, erm, clever "WHAT IS THIS THING?" He always brings along two of his best friends who are personified in exactly the same way, fear not.
"Biggles," I hear you cry. "We get it. He's lame. But a character does not a game make! How can you possibly justify this negative review on one thing?"
What a rude line of questioning! I found Carter unlikable from moment one, making, as I play through, it very hard for me to find him sympathetic enough to NOT walk him into enemy fire if only so he'll stop talking for one bloody second. But, okay. You want more complaints? Oh, I was picking out the mildest one and hoping this review could turn out somewhat nice.
I suppose I do have one nice thing to say: the plot has a few mildly compelling elements.
Erm, that's about it.
Really? I have to do this? Fiiiine.
Let's start with the most glaring sticking point: optimization. This game supposedly runs on Unreal Engine 3, which is a downright shame. I've never encountered an instance before where UE3 results in optimization this bad. It maxed out my reasonably high-end system despite looking like a 4-year-old console title. Even worse, despite this, it lags comparably to me on an early morning. I had to turn settings down considerably on a GTX 770 and hyperthreaded quad-core CPU to get the blasted game to stop stuttering. I could understand this if the title presented an interesting aesthetic or impressive visual fidelity, but it just... doesn't. It's going for 50s sci-fi, but missing the mark. A grain filter and some art deco font doesn't sell me on the concept, and that's all we have going here.
The gameplay sadly doesn't make up for any of this. It's the most very boring and generic of shooters, masked by a faux-squad-strategy "mode". Sounds cool enough, sure, but it just doesn't work in practice. The game doesn't actually pause, rather slow down upon entering its "command mode or whatever", which means you're often left directing the game's AI to do tasks while you sit behind cover simply to avoid getting hit. Your own squadmates fail to take cover on their own, leading to a lot of stop-start gameplay, with no real payoff. Even worse, the enemy AI is as clever as your team. Nothing here provides a glimmer of interesting challenge.
I simply can't recommend this game. I'll finish it, I'm stubborn like that, and this is very much a first impression, but I can't see this game lifting itself out of the rut it's so totally committed to burrowing. Whatever elements it introduces from this point, it will remain a buggy, poorly-optimized, generic shooter-with-a-gimmick. And to make matters wor-

In many ways, I still want the XCOM FPS that was annoucned way back in 2010.  I thought the 1950s setting combined with the horrific alien blobs that apparently killed people by forcing themselves down their victims throats, essentially drowning them, and the shape-shifting geometric space ships combined into what looked like a very interesting game.
You probably don't remember the trailer...or if you do, you probably remember the Internet rage that came out around it as gamers rioted at the idea of an XCOM game that wasn't a tactical game.
The newly announced XCOM FPS faded from the radar, and was almost forgotten with the announcment and release of the amazing XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  In 2013, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is released with relatively little fanfare after being in what can only be called "Development Hell" for 3 years.
Despite this, I still had fun with The Bureau.  It doesn't break any new ground (many aspects of the game are clearly inspired by the Mass Effect games), but it does what it does well.  It is easy to move your AI teammates into the position you want them to be, and to use the abilities you want them to do.
I found the combat to be fun, and the controls to be nice.  If you played Mass Effect, you will likely recognize the ability wheel that lets you control what you and your agents do.  Your agents a chosen from a roster, and they level seperately.  But be warned, if your agent goes down and you don't save him, he and his experience are gone.  This adds a bit of tension to your orders as you try to keep your boys in cover while trying to drive your alien opponents from theirs.
However, I can't help but think this game suffers from being released in the shadow of the absolutely amazing XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  While the Outsiders are nomially in charge of the invasion, other XCOM opponents, such as Sectoids and Mutons, are arrayed against you, with little rhyme or reason why they are there.  Really, the story of Bureau doesn't really jive with the story that was in Enemy Unknown, but on it's own it works alright.
Still, I can't judge a game to harshly on "what might have been".  While I would hesitate to call it great, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a solid game, and I don't regret buying it at all.

TL;DR: If you like turtling and sustaining in RTS games, this will definitely be worth your money. If you like strategy games with a simple yet difficult concept, you will probably enjoy this game. I bought it fully ready to give the two-hour try and refund it if it wasn't fun, but then I ended up playing for four and a half hours in one sitting without realizing it.
Bought this game more or less on a whim. Had a couple friends ask to watch while I played.
Four and a half hours later I finally turned the game off, though none of us really wanted to stop. In that time I went through three playthroughs - lost the first two and stopped with 25 days left on the third.
If you enjoy RTS games I think you'll be pleased. The game isn't incredibly deep - there are no unit-specific abilities, hero units, or any sort of special abilities you can do - but I think that suits the game just fine.
Your objective is to survive for a set number of days. You pick from a few different options for length, map, and infection severity. You start with your command center and a small squad of troops. From there on out it's your job to explore and expand while preparing for horde attacks. They happen infrequently at first and become both larger and more frequent as the game goes on. The map is also constantly populated by infected, and they do wander, so you can't just leave yourself completely open then turtle up right before a horde.
The maps are procedurally generated once you select a region, so every game is different. Some of your seeds will be unlucky (my first one in particular was almost right next to a doomed colony, so I got attacked constantly), but that's part of the game and something I didn't see as a problem like some other reviewers did.
Research/tech tree is pretty standard RTS - build a research building and use it to tech up and unlock new buildings. I think the real fun of the game comes from crossing the halfway point. Once you start NEEDING to upgrade your defenses, the tension and resource crunch the game puts on you is very fun.
I will say as a final note that this is a very difficult game. The first game I lost within thirty minutes and I was on normal spawn with easy time limit and the standard map. The second game I lost in about forty-five minutes and I was on easy. So, don't go into this game expecting to clump a bunch of units and tear everything up no problem. The game will probably frustrate you, and you'll feel like things are unfair. But that's part of the fun, and I can't wait to see more added over time.

Okay, so I was shown this game because, guess what, I have generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and situational anxiety. AND guess what, I'm an American who lived in this exact kind of flat/dorm during my time in England. The only thing we shared was a kitchen, and everything was communal from the pots to the forks to the table and chairs. Of course, maybe not all flats were like this. I was in the graduate student housing. Maybe we were spoiled.
While this short little thing does capture social anxiety pretty well (the fear a woman has, for many reasons, of not wanting to eat around other people [related to body image]; the fear of forced interaction with relative strangers; the fear of being seen at all), most things depicted in this little thing are just weird.
I never played passed the "forgot my keys whoops" moment because I just couldn't take it anymore. The parameters of this situation are just, basically, ridiculous.
1) Instant oatmeal is instant. It cooks instantly. Does this lady not know what boiling water looks like? Water boils. Poor on instant oatmeal. Voila, it's edible. No waiting needed! QUICK! Run back to the room and eat in solitude! Problem solved, right?? No, we have to wait for it to "cook". ????? No. I can understand that a person might be so out of their skull from anxiety that they are to the point of delusion and can't tell when INSTANT oatmeal is cooked... but is that even the norm?? Have mug. Have spoon. Can eat. SO, the issue of being locked out of her room is only an issue an hour or two AFTER she eats her oatmeal when she has to maybe use the loo, which is not communal, but in her locked room. She can still eat the goddamn oatmeal, which was cooked before she microwaved it.
2) Why for the love of monkeys does this lady not have food INSIDE her room??? She is living on her own. Are there really rules against this? Unlikely. I have lived with anxiety for, well, ever, and I CHANGED MY ENVIRONMENT to cope. So what if she has to stock up on ready to eat, no-cook foods. If her SA is that bad, she'll have figured out how to cope. She'll have figured out long ago that eating in private is the way to go. Buy some Digestives, some pre-cooked Heinz beans, and have yourself a dinner. That's about as healthy as a pack of instant oatmeal anyway, if not healthier.
3) I get that this sort of SA situation is probably new to this lady, but environmental adaptation can happen very quickly. What's more, if her SA was really so bad to the point of being incapable of adapting to her SA (i.e., changing her environment and keeping food in her room), then she probably would have never gone to England in the first place, or applied to a school that would not be even remotely cheap for her. I can understand a person may have reasons for wanting to go to another country (I mean, I did it, after all), but I also survived 3 years of US dormitory life, which is far, FAR worse than just having a communal kitchen!! Did this poor creature leave her high school life to immediately attend school in the UK? That's enough of a harsh situation (culture shock, even when it's the same language) to kick anyone's butt. Is this her first night in the flat? Didn't seem like it. Maybe it was? Maybe I missed that. Even so, the complete ineptitude of this person was alarming. Maybe that's the point.
4) People with anxiety issues or OCD or any modicum of intelligence probably shouldn't play this little thing as it will just make them angry and want to throw things.
I dunno. I'm rambling now. I just can't get over the fact that someone didn't have the wherewithal to keep food in their safe place (private room) and not know instant oatmeal is instant.

Simple to play, free, and cute art make the game not too horrible. Other than that, the story it relies on is stupid - the anxiety of the main character is hyperbolic and almost makes her seem childish rather than relatable. The panic about others seeing her was very real, but when she started freaking out about things like the microwave being loud...yeahhh...no. Plus, there's hardly any moral learnt at the end or anything, making the whole thing pointless and kind of sad. Finding the correct ending is pretty tedious, too.

This may have worked in a different setting. For example, maybe she lives at home with a suffocating parent and going to the kitchen would draw attention and force you into a long conversation about "what are you going to do with your life" which makes me anxious just thinking about it. But in a college setting, I just kept thinking "how does she even get to class?" So what, there are people in the kitchen, none of them seem at all inclined to talk to her, which is how I prefer things with my social anxiety. If they had tried to force her into conversation, okay a little more believable, but not much. She's in college. Going to classes would be a lot worse for people with social anxiety.
Also, how do you undercook oatmeal? You put in hot water, then you wait. If it's not done after 30 seconds, microwaving it isn't going to "cook" it faster. You just let it sit for a while. This may have worked if she was making Cup Ramen or something, but she could have taken it back to her room and let it sit for a few minutes just fine.
Aside from many glaring setting and subject issues, as a person with severe social anxiety, this game didn't speak to me at all.

Well, what should I say. Since I bought HOI1 nearly 15 years ago in a shady shop somewhere on the other side on the globe I was a fan of HOI/Paradox. This "love" even survived the desaster which HOI3 was on launch. Fast forward to HOI4. The game does many things right, has some good ideas and neat gfx for a wargame. On the other hand it has an attrocious AI, a supply model which is really bizarre (you pay oil once you build units, then never again), a laughable naval system and an air war model with the depth of a puddle on a hot summer day.
If you into HOI, you could give it a try, there are many mods which make the game somehow enjoyable. But I'm giving a negative review anyway because of the wasted potential and the DLC policy which is extremly bad in this case. The game is out for one year now and received two lackluster addons which really added nothing too important and didnt really fix the core problems. Looks more like milking the cow (the customer) right now.
Some detail:
About the "AI": invasion spam, battle AI ignoring empty provinces, it is just a big mess. I've been using the battle planner and my units simply wouldnt attack or punch through weakened enemy units. How I won the war against the Soviet Union as Germany then you ask? I've marked some nearby units and rightclicked somewhere further on the map. Did the job with ease
About the naval model: you want a decent Pacific/Alantic war with this game? Forget it. I wasn't expecting War in the Pacifc from 2by3 Games but his is just junk. Sub war is broken, the rest also. Expect the UK to invade Germany in 1939
I think the airwarfare model is actually better than the old HOI "lets treat air units like ground units" model. The issue, apart from teleporting planes, which in bad cases ignore most of your defense (imagine a strike against Munich in 1943 where only the fighters in Bavaria scramble while the others in Northern Germany pick their noses). Also, there is no fuel nor is there any need in pilots. You just create air units out of thin air, yeah, that easy. So the strategy boils down how many planes you can produce. Maybe were you put them but thats it. Considering what broke Japans and Germanys Airforces necks- it wasn't the output of planes
There are many more issues, but these are the most annoying ones for me. And as I said: the wasted potential  pi**es me off mightily. Maybe also the fact that I made the mistake to buy a season pass and now have to stick with these crappy DLCs where I basically get Focus Trees for countries I never play.
Being able to control and create a different government in a country of your choice makes this game incredibly unique.

It's free, and you get what you paid for: it's a small, proof of concept-style hack-and-slasher in the vein of Dynasty Warriors done as a first effort by a bunch of Chinese programmers.

Please keep in mind that these are my opinions and constructive criticisms towards the game and that they should in no way shape or form be taken as a means of offense to the developers of this game.
For a free game this has quite a few high points. But as a game in general it has many more low points. The game itself has a great idea and visual style and impliments alot of its points fairly well. The visuals are decent though you can tell most of the work was put into the main character, main boss, and large enemy models, where the smaller enemies were very lack luster in their design and could really use a bit of touching up. Thats not to say that the level designs werent good or looked bad but you could definitely tell that majority of the terrain was copy/pasted with a staircase or stack of unbreakable boxes to hide easily distinguishable features that would give it away.
Now, lets talk about combat. The combat of the game absolutely needs a few tweaks to improve the overall gameplay. The combos are very appealing, well animated and pretty but dont have much in the way of having some kind of feeling of impact when attacking enemies. By that i mean when striking an enemy they continue their own attacks and do constant damage where one would usually think they would stagger or be slightly stunned from the attacks the player delivers. The damage dealt by enemies also needs to be tweaked, when the player has to constantly break away from combat to hunt down healing items just to have their health slapped back down by what few enemies decided to persue them it really makes the game hard to enjoy as well as breaking the flow of the game. No im not saying the game is too hard , im saying that it has an artificial layer of difficulty with the enemies damage amounts, constant attacks and their ability to not be stunned. This can be easily fixed by either adding a block ability, a better escape ability, or by lowering the enemies damage, and a MUST is to add stagger for when the enemies are hit so that the player doesnt have to stop fighting just to search for the rather scarce healing objects.
The level design isnt bad for an indie game. Though the game is obviously linear by nature the areas are wide enough for you to move rather freely during combat while being narrow enough to keep the player from getting lost while trying to find health items in between fights, or sometimes in the middle of them, and has a very nice variation of styles in the areas you go. You are rarely going to find yourself in a room that looks EXACTLY the same as a previous one which is a big high note for an indie game in and of itself.
Enemy AI leaves a bit to be desired in a rather surprising way. The smaller enemies meander around and will 'try' to find a way to reach the player when they get close enough but dont really follow you if you move too far too fast, this isnt a bad thing as the smaller enemies are the main bulk of what you find but pairing this with the larger enemies who hunt you down to the ends of the earth and sport a ranged attack that can hit you twice and momentarily stun you, it doesnt make alot of sense in my honest opinion. the only thing that helps you when theyre after you is how slow they are so you at least have some breathing room when youre looking for health items, which you WILL be looking for when fighting the larger enemies no matter how hard you try.
The movement and overall speed of the player character is great, not too fast and not too slow but paced just enough to allow the player to take in the visual style and scenery of the level designs. The dash however may need a few tweaks to make sure it can be used in combat more effectively without leaving the player open to an enormous amount of attacks.
Unfortunately i cannot recommend this game in its current build if you are looking for a fully fleshed out indie game. my hope is that the devs will continue working on this game and really make it into something as awesome and fun as it feels like they were trying to accomplish. the game itself shows an enormous amount of promise and i look forward to seeing how it progresses if the devs continue working on it, which i genuinely hope they do.
RLDR; game shows great promise, but still needs A LOT of work

In the following I reference a few puzzles and a few methodologies through which they were built, so those might constitute a very light sort of spoiler. However, I do my best to preserve the mystery of the game, so hopefully that worked out.
It's not a terrible game. I haven't finished it, but I don't know if I will. The puzzles are *occasionally* good, but more often they suffer from a fatal flaw. Often, 'puzzles' are nothing more than 'find the pixel.' This isn't really intellectually satisfying. Othertimes, the puzzles can be brute forced very easily -- which, in one case, is the *only* way to solve it; as far as I can tell, it's the intended method, and I say this after having read a few walkthroughs to see what the intended solution was. One or two puzzles I solved *accidentally* by just twiddling with the elements of it to figure out how it worked, and it just ... unlocked. A *lot* of puzzles are contrived; there's one where you have an aparatus that's free-standing, which you could very reasonably walk around, but that has an item you need in a bracket facing away from you. Instead of just walking around the device and collecting it, you must solve a small puzzle so that it hands it to you. It's ... weird. The context of the game is also strange; you go there as a repairman, and ... then immediately leave all of your tools in the boat that took you there, and instead proceed to break into this home and steall a large quantity of his stuff (coins, figurines, paintings -- without *any* reason or rationale). There is alos a lot of backtracking, which actually I like, but I know some people have problems with. As usual, there's a sort of implication of believability that is harmed by the presence of some of the stranger puzzles, which do not seem to fit into a real worldspace. There's also 'clues' to puzzles that are hidden in books; for absolutely no reason, the main character will flip to some random page in a random book in a whole room full of books, find some random number or word, and that random bit of information will be the crucial code for some absolutely unrelated puzzle.
This isn't to say that it's all bad. Some puzzles offer a little bit of interest, and you are rewarded for really exploring your environment. The plot so far seems intriguing enough that I actually want to play it to the end, and -- with the exception of the way they highlight doorways and such -- the graphics and atmosphere are solid. There isn't any voice acting in it so far, though again, I haven't gotten to the end, so maybe there's something.
I will grudgingly recommend this game, but ... it's no Myst, not so far as I can tell.

But, towards the end, there are things like numerical codes where--as far as we could tell--you simply had to try all the numbers you encounter in order to know which one works. And you encounter quite a few. Also, 100% completion requires some pixel-hunting for collectibles.
We recommend that you keep a walkthrough handy and use it whenever you spent however long your comfort-limits are on a phase, then just look. The game was a lot of fun, and the use of a walkthrough helped make that so, for us. Without one, we think some of the puzzles would have simply been impossible or else require monkish devotion to looking for candidate solutions that would only be effective after a lot of trial-and-error.
