It's trendy to hate on The Bureau because it's not XCOM but I quite liked it. The combat is really fun and I didn't find the friendly AI too dumb. Yes you have to babysit a bit but that's the tactics part. Carter's movement and shooting are solid and responsive and the abilities are interesting and can synergize often. The voice acting is good and the characters memorable enough. The graphics and art style are very nice and the busted up 50s locales are a lot of fun to romp around in.
I did find it rather easy though even on Hard in the last half when every member of your squad is a badass and nothing really poses much of a threat. But facing the first few mutons and sectopods with a sniper rifle was challenging. The plot is also half finished swiss cheese but has a nice tangy twist. The buggy visuals and plot add to a kind of B-movie feel that fits well with the art style and period but I can't tell if that is intentional.
Don't let the haters who have never played it ruin this better than average game.

Disclaimer: At the time of writing, I'm 6.1hrs in, and have up to the Laser SMG
If you forget the fact this carries the X-Com badge, and just want a shooter similar to Mass Effect (with AI Squad mates that have the lifespan of a gnat), but without any of the conversation depth, exploration, or moral choices, then it might be worth playing....
However, it does have the X-Com badge, and it's the worse for it.   I can understand the enemies carrying a slightly different appearance (like a muton the size of a small pickup truck, or a Sectopod with a Sectoid in it), but unless there's some glorious retcon later in the plotline, there's absolutely no rationale for why your team (at a very low level) gets abilities like Group Heals, Shield Spheres, or the ability to.... telekinetically(?) Lift enemies and allies by waving your hand.
On top of that, one of the classes gets the ability to... summon?  an automated laser turret, yet another piece of tech that the "real" X-Com games never had.
So, again, if they didn't call it X-Com, it might be okay...
Except for the squad AI.    They have absolutely no sense of self-preservation, or peripheral vision.   I was playing on "Commander" (Maximum) difficulty, and had to lower it because the Squad would just do the most asinine things, causing them to be incapacitated, focusing more fire on me and causing my death as well.
Couple examples that stick out.
1. We were both in cover behind a wall, sort of a bracket ( ] ) shape, with a gap in the middle.   I got taken out, and ordered him to revive me.   What'd they do?  Rather than take the one additional step to the side so they could run behind reasonable cover, they vaulted the wall, and made it about two steps before the enemy cut them down as well.
2. I had positioned both squad members in a building that was gloriously defensible, Explicitly Moved them by the windows shooting at the enemies.   I Lifted one of the enemies, told them both to focus fire on that target.   Target dies, and suddenly one of the squad starts whining about healing, I look, and he is OUTSIDE, UNDER THE WINDOW, completely flanked.  The AI was so busy focusing on keeping Target A in the line of fire, it took cover in such a way that it left it's flank exposed, to the bulk of the enemies (which, BTW, both the main mass, and the target it was going after were accessible from the window cover)
Incredibly frustrating, and just not worth dealing with.   Maybe if you pick it up on the Humble Bundle for a couple of bucks, but not worth more than that.

Good stealth games don't come around that often. Games like the Metal Gear Solid Series, the original Thief, and Splinter Cell Chaos Theory truly set the bar on what stealth games should strive to be. In my eyes, Dishonored is another game that all stealth games should learn from.
Dishonored puts the player in the shoes of Royal Protector Corvo Attano who seeks revenge on those who are responsible for the assassination of the Empress and the kidnapping of her daughter, Emily. The story, while ending on a bit of an anticlimactic note, was good and it kept me invested in the world till the end. While the overall story wasn’t anything groundbreak the game does a great job at making the world feel like a real lived in place. The characters woven into this tale of revenge are great. Almost all of them have interesting back stories and personalities that makes it feel like they are real people. The levels are also packed with books and Audio logs that flesh out the world's lore in interesting ways if you care to take your time look through it all. Overall, the game has a fantastic story and it will keep you interested for the 12 to 20 hours it takes to complete.
The gameplay is where Dishonored truly becomes a staple of its genre. The level design is excellent giving the player multiple ways to approach each objective. Whether you go guns a blazing or decide to take a more stealthy approach you will have fun getting through all the unique challenges the game has to offer. The limit of 100 saves and the occasional AI glitch did annoy me but it never fully ruined the fun I had sneaking through each of the levels. When the credits rolled I was itching to play through it again with a different approach.
Overall, Dishonored is a great stealth game and is a must play for those who love open ended gameplay. It isn’t a perfect game, but the mechanics and level design made it a joy to play through. It is truly a game that all future stealth titles should look up to.

- As of this writing there is no way to adjust the volume within the game.  I suggest alt-tabbing out of the game, right clicking the speaker icon in the windows taskbar tray, and selecting Mixer. I don't understand how this game has anything to do with anxiety or any psychological disorder. The only image resembling mental distress was the hallway blurring. The empty hallway. The protagonist got upset when people were in the kitchen, but it didn't blur her vision or have any effect. She just walked into the room like they weren't there. So... people are what she fears and dislikes the most, but they don't bother her as much as an empty hallway?
The game is full of these charming little inconsistencies.
At two points, you're forced to watch
a kettle warming up to boil. There is a timer on the screen forcing you to wait until it's done. Then there's another timer while you're "cleaning." Of all the things one might've chosen to skip in game design, they didn't choose to skip these? It adds absolutely nothing to the experience.
There's more waiting as the game forces you to stir the oatmeal intermittently, so it doesn't overflow in the microwave. So you're handling the cup, which is presumably getting warmer and warmer? Yet somehow, when it's done, she burns her hands on the hot cup. SHE'S BEEN HANDLING IT THIS WHOLE TIME.
Then you return to the room, only to discover that you've locked yourself out.
This is where we reach another charming example of game design: if you restart from a bad end, it brings you back to the point at which you're just exiting the room. At first I thought, oh great, I don't have to play through the whole intro again. WRONG. Wrooooong.
The intro is where you're given the decision to take your key. But if you get to a dead end, the game automatically brings you back to a point AFTER you could've made this choice. Unless you do a full restart, you're doomed to keep coming back to a locked door...
The game doesn't have a save option, or any way to easily return to a previous choice-fork. You have to replay it from the beginning each time. You'd think it's not a big deal, but try sitting through two counters of watching grass grow more than once...
This is the most pointless game I've ever played. It's not cathartic, insightful, or engaging. It's not even that visually attractive, which I thought would be a saving grace. The main character is a lazy, under-socialized, privileged jerk. It has nothing to do with anxiety, and it's offensive that it tries to portray itself as if it did.
Not even I was this autistic in freshman year.

As a lover of challanging games, survival games and rts games this game complements them all.  I never thought a rts game could be difficult against Ai but this game is one brutal and unforgiving.  Its like the Dark Souls of Rts.
Pros:
-Difficult
-Pace.  The games starts out slow and picks up the pace allowing you to expand fairly fast if you want.
-High Replayability due to random spawn locations and new stratageys to win
-Zombies
-Graphics look great
-Game can handle lots of units on screen.  I haven't experinced any lag.
-Building and Tech progress is easy to understand
Cons:
-Unit pathing is buggy.  I've lost a few games due to units running into a wall or going the long way.
-No Tutorial (not really a issue, as you can pick up on what to do really fast).
-You can Spawn fairly close to a village of doom which can be a game breaking loss, no real way to counter.
FInal Thoughts:
I really enjoy this game, Not many like it.  I've always been a fan of survival based games, zombies and base building.  This game combines all three into one.  It's a unique experince for a game getting to build up your base and try to survive against waves and waves of zombies.  It can feel a little overwhelming at first it has a intresting learning curve to it.  What makes the game great to me and a truly challanging experince is the way you have to build.  You can't just spam defense on one side and hope it'll hold.  Hordes can come from everywere making how you expand important.  The map has lots of choke points and is very uneven.  You won't be able to just make a giant square.  You'll have to build out in sections.  No one base you create will ever look the same.  Only thing that I don't like about the game is the unit pathing just doesn't feel great.  It's still early access so I can't wait to see what they add and fix.
Should I get this game?
-Yes, if you enjoy a challanging game and want a dark souls style experince with rts.
In its current state I give the game a 9/10

Crazy fun,great mix between being an RTS and a tower defense really. The art style is fantastic as well gives me a Factorio vibe. Definitely recommend if you enjoy RTS's or Tower Defenses. If you're a huge city builder fan not sure there's enough for you to do here quite yet.

This game has TONS of potential and I absolutely hate to not recommend it. However, there are waaaaay too many balance issues and other factors that need to be reworked before this game will be worth playing. Some of the more notable issues:
- Requiring a specific structure to expand the area you can build. This adds nothing to the strategic depth of the game and just serves as one extra nag factor while you're managing the rest of your base.
- The overall number of workers required for everything is MUCH higher than it needs to be. As a result, bases end up clogged with worker structures (tents, cottages, etc.)
- Too many different resources for a micromanagement-driven RTS. At present, you have Gold, Wood, Stone, Iron, Oil, Energy, Food and Workers. This causes build orders to become very linear and makes it difficult to keep from a single resource becoming overly valuable (and thus a choke point for growth).
- The use of space for resource structures is awkward. The amount of resource you produce from, say a lumber mill near some trees, is dependent on how many forest tiles fall within a NxN area around the lumber mill. What's more, resource structures can't overlap AT ALL. This means you'll almost always be leaving resource deposits partially unused (or wasting precious space on structures that aren't producing much).
Despite the frustrating and clunky decisions, there's still fun to be had here. The music is FANTASTIC, The combat is very satisfying (when you win you feel like a boss and when the zombies break your line and eat your base, there's a certain satisfaction in watching them break all your toys). Exploration in a zombie wasteland is fun for its own sake, but also very necessary for early-game information and resources.
I hope before launch, the devs rethink some of the mechanics. With some tweaks, this title could be a must-play for RTS fans.

If you want single player offline cruising, get TDU2. (for $5 when it's on sale)
If you want anything else (responsive controls, racing, challenges, story mode, good overall sound track, etc) do NOT get TDU2.
PROS:  two huge islands to drive around on for the sake of casual cruising.  That's it. This is the sole only reason worth playing this. If you want this and this alone in offline mode, go for it.
CONS:..........  I'll just write a whole book here......
"Do I want quality or quantity?"
Well, this game offers a high quantity of low quality content.
It has been a disaster since day 1. It was never finished (this is confirmed), what you will play is a beta profuct.
- Basically no moderation. It's a cheater paradise. The few who get banned return instantly to ruin other people's games. CRC mode (challenges made by players for players) was made extinct because of this. There goes 33% replayability content of what this game was supposed to offer.
- The game is on life support and held together by dry tape. A mere skeleton crew is running the servers which goes down a lot, A LOT, without any warning; you never get noticed in advance or told when it will be back up like any other well-kept game does. This was common since the beginning when they dared charge $50 for this mess. I expect Atari to pull the plug on the server unannounced very soon and you end up with an unplayable game. Some say to play it in offline mode, but what is the point of promoting an MMO (or M.O.O.R. as Atari wanted to hype it) if it is so extremely unreliable and offline a lot?  Its online feature is supposed to be a big selling point, yet it fails; oh how it fails at this. The online feature of this game is very uncertain.
- Atari has behaved very unprofessional towards its customers this entire time, we get no proper feedback, no messages when the servers go down, the official forums have died a long time ago, support tickets go unanswered etc.
- Your save game file is stored LOCALLY on your PC, not online. It can go corrupt at any random moment due to faulty programming, so you are expected to make a manual backup everytime you play. Doesn't happen to everybody but it happens often enough to many people in general that this is a huge game-breaking bug that was never fixed.
- Difficult to play with friends due to the random 8-player session system. I had a 25% success rate to join my friends at all. Eventually they all left, I don't blame them.
- After you finish the game (I did this within 1 month after release) earning money is no longer fun. It's a tedious repetitive boring grind-fest. What were they thinking removing bomb mission after you do them? They gave the game diversity at least. (they weren't thinking really, I can't list all the many bad game design decisions but they are MANY!)
- No big secret here, the physics are awful awful awful. Some cars behaviour is just unexplainable. Collision reaction is just as buggy. This is an arcade car game, well it sure doesn't control as such. It feels like the air was let out of the tires. The Burnout series, the Midnight Club series, the
Need for Speed series, these are all CORRECT arcade physics games. Heh, even TDU1 has better physics. What the hell happened here in this sequel?
- The AI in single player races is a joke. Your rival AI opponent rubberbands around you no matter how good or bad you drive, the rest always stay far behind. This is a big contrast to the extremely hard (& pointless) driving school sessions which may block you early at the start of the game for the average gamer. Don't be fooled what others say, you will not become a better driver by finishing them, just relived that you passed those frustration-fests.
- The Sims elements is not a good meaningful addition. You will giggle about it at first, but soon it loses its luster and meaning. This is a car game, you won't be seeing your character or your houses indoors for most of the time. It was a waste of time and resources developing this Sims stuff. The time would have been better spent finalizing other more useful game features (which are broken or simply not there).
- What made TDU1 good has been removed from TDU2. (too many to list here). Many steps backwards were taken.
- Don't let the biased Metacritic score fool you.  That score is based on the launch condition the game was in (wasn't good back then either) and the positive thinking expectations of what it would become. Well, as time passed, the game got worse and worse. More errors/bugs were introduced instead of fixed. Force feedback got broken, innocent people getting marked as cheaters (their cars turn into Pink Mustangs), casino DLC getting more buggier, etc etc.
GOOD games promise XYZ, and deliver XYZ.
TDU2 promised XYZ, it delivered only X. (the goal-less cruising). The people who like X are the only ones who like this game and treat it like it's the best thing ever. That's a terrible way to review/recommend a product to others. You review THE WHOLE package, not just the part you like.
Not everybody plays an openworld game for the same reasons, since you know, openworld games offer a lot of varied gameplay. But like I said, this openworld only offers X, nothing more. That makes it a very limited openworld game. TDU1 did deliver all its promised XYZ.  So if you want to cruise offline, go play that instead. It has better working finished content. Atari, or what is left of it, doesn't deserve any money from TDU2.
I can only guess how many unfortunate people followed such biased misinformation and bought this thing only to rage-quit soon afterwards, having wasted their time and money. For every 1 satisfied player in this game, you will find 9 others who hate it. Just check twitter, facebook, etc etc (even these are practically dead). You will see a lot of hate, very little praise.

I was quite surprised by this game.
It has a lot of great things going for it and also a few minor issues here and there but no deal breakers.
Pros:
- Fun but challenging combat.
Awesome executions with melee and feel skilled with a bow and one shotting unsuspecting zombies. Also you have to be careful against stronger enemy types and large groups of zombies which adds to the excitement.
- Great crafting system.
You can make a lot of guns and armour but it doesn't give you them all at once, you have to progress and put XP into the right areas to do so.
- Good leveling system.
You can distribute XP into different areas and lets you adapt whatever playstyle/weapons you like. You can put all XP into character and base level and just make a base if you want but combat gets harder over time.
- Good balance between combat and building stuff.
Fight zombies to get supplies then make stuff to kill more zombies.
- Base building is awesome.
I loved making a camp in this game and it felt awesome to see it finished with guard towers, walls, weapons crafting area, armour crafting area and a cooking area. And later in the game you get traps which I'm looking forward to heaps!
Cons:
- Lacking in story a bit.
This game does have a story but the real interest in doing the missions comes from the item rewards rather than wanting to learn more about Kovac or help people. The story is alright but I found myself skipping dialogue a few times to get back to the combat and crafting.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
POSITIVE:
- Steam Achievements in such an early stage of the game!
- Steam trading cards in such an early stage of the game!
- Ability to adjust view distance and depth of field!
- The game has a working day/night cycle! When the game gets too dark, use your flashlight on 'F'.
- Interactability with in-game items / objects (though the area in which you can do so is very tight).
INDIFFERENT / MINOR BUGS:
- As far as I'm aware, in the current stage, Steam Achievements are unobtainable. I didn't scour every last building for an axe or a working car though. The door-breaking achievement wasn't awarded for the first door I kicked open, so I'm guessing it may be for every last door.
- Current bad Steam integration. I launch this game, and am presented with three different options. "Play The District", "Launch" and "Launch". Options one and two do exactly the same and launch the pre-loader, whereas option three gives me an error message from Steam saying it can't find the file it's trying to launch. This is *probably* going to be fixed with a bug patch, so take this with a grain of salt. I can easily see option one taking you straight into the game, option two launching the pre-loader configuration and option three being removed or replaced with a new game mode.
- The 'options' menus have no option to adjust or mute the audio. This will probably be implemented in the future.
- In the previous point I list two options menus. At this stage, the in-game options menu is different to the main menu option menu. Why is this? Presumably this is also an easy bug-fix for the future.
- No presented control scheme other than the one that is only presented the very first time you click the main menu options.  What's really strange is that this controls screen only appears the very *first* time you open the main menu options. If you clicked through them without reading them, you're left with no way of checking the controls.
- Even if you didn't miss the control screen, the functions listed on the main menu options control screen don't list all the controls. Yes, you can guess that walking would be WASD and looking would be done with the mouse, but this really should still be listed. Also, some things are completely overlooked in the controls that I have no idea about. For example, *something* comes up when you press F12. I have no idea what it is. As the Steam screenshot function uses F12, this really should be mapped to another button, whatever it is.
- If you are moving at *all* when you pause the game, the pause menu spins around uncontrollably.
- There's no ability to go back from the game to the main menu - The 'exit' button just closes the game.
- The flashlight is quite buggy in tight spaces, though even professional games seem to have this problem, so I can't hold this against the developer.
- The character has real difficulty going up stairs and moving smoothly around tight corners.
- You can walk right up the mountains and out of the game world. I know this is only Early Access, but hey, I can't be the only one who tried, right? :)
SERIOUS NEGATIVES:
- LAG. How can you lag in Alpha Stage? I have a top-of-the-line computer, and if mine can't handle it, something is seriously wrong. For that matter, there aren't any videos, there are few audio clips and (almost) stock assets, so *what* exactly is using up all that memory?
- IMPOSSIBLE play in some scenarios. There's currently a bug that seems to affect the entire game resolution. It scales along the height to match the native resolution, but not the width. This can lead to not only visuals getting terribly distorted, but an actual impossibility to play the game in certain resolutions. Go ahead and select any of the *top five* screen resolutions THAT ARE BUILT-IN-OPTIONS for your game resolution and you'll see what I mean - the main menu gets cut off.
- There is something HORRIBLY wrong with the movement that I cannot quite explain. You feel like you're walking in tar, getting 'dragged down'. Switching between walking and 'sprinting' (defined very loosely) can take anywhere up to three seconds. As this talks about 'elements of survival', I'm fairly certain there will be enemies at some point. I would not want to be fighting / running away from enemies with such a delay in the change between walking and sprinting. It even takes the same amount of time to toggle between standing still to regular movement! I don't know how the developer could get the movement system so wrong in a game that relies so heavily on it! I've tried my hand at Unity, and the *default* movement is much better than this!
- This 'game' is almost a direct clone of Unity's "Decayed State" pack
. The only difference is, this time you're not paying for the Unity assets, you're essentially paying for a poorly-assembled combination of them that you cannot modify in any way.
CONCLUSION:
Don't buy this game in the current stage. Perhaps it is a worthwhile buy in the future, once some of the core bugs have been resolved, but certainly not at this stage. At this stage, the developer really shouldn't have even released it for free. The concept is lovely, however, the developer sadly does not quite have the skills needed for the project they're trying to undertake. With a few extra developers working on this, it could turn into a great game. Until then, sadly, this game is best passed-over.

Just to get this out of the way - if you did not enjoy any of the Myst series or just genuinely dislike point-and-clicks, you might want to stay away. This game is right smack dab in that genre in every way.
And I ♥♥♥♥ing love it!
I saw the dev's booth at the indie game section of PAX Australia 2017 and was instantly drawn into the mystery in the 5-minute demo. Bought a game code right then and there (discounted price helped seal the deal, admittedly). This was day one of three of the con so the code was stashed in my wallet and promptly forgotten about.
A week later, I was wanting to try something new in my Steam library on a rainy day, and remembered that I had bought this game. Fired it up and instantly lost about 10 hours of my weekend - another 7 hours the following weekend and finally got to the end.
I'm not great at reviews so I'll just say why I think this game is absolutely perfect for the point-and-click puzzle genre:
-The difficulty of the puzzles. Obviously the main thing here. Things start pretty easy and you immediately feel brilliant as you piece things together, but damn do they get tough quickly. I admit that there were two times I looked up a couple hints for some of the mind-twisters near the end - but I don't regret it because I was spinning my wheels for a good hour at least. You feel a genuine sense of accomplishment as you progress and when you finally get through everything - what more could you ask from a game?
-The collectables. Lots of little things to find that aren't required to get to the end of the "story" but often they can be just as devious (if not moreso!) to uncover. I also like that once you complete the central path, you're left in the game world to 100% the game - and I really want to!
-The lore/story. In classic Myst-like fashion, there are no other characters or NPCs to interact with - you're dropped in with a vague prompt of why you're at this castle, but nothing else really. But there's a paper trail to follow of journals, letters, paintings, drawings, and environments that help build a surprisingly engrossing "post-narrative". The designer of this game did a great job with the various breadcrumbs, and you're left wanting a bit more at the end which I like.
-There's also some great philosophical excerpts to read within the book that not only discuss the themes of the game but also are often subtle hints for the puzzles.
-The graphics aren't anything to write home about necessarily, but they're pleasant and serviceable for sure.
-The sound and music is subtle and only ever enhances the experience. Just like I remember when playing Myst as a kid, it makes everything feel mysterious and waiting to be explored.
All in all, great game with a good 10-20 hours of gameplay depending on how quick you are with the puzzles (and how much of a completionist you tend to be!). I'll be keeping my "Eyes" out for future games from this dev!

You don't have to travel between worlds and trek across islands to use that new tool or piece of knowledge you just found ... your destination only about 20 or 30 seconds away. Hours and hours into the game, you can still get back to the very first room within a minute. I REALLY loved being able to do that.
As with all of these type of games, look high & low, and click on everything. There are achievements of collectibles, and some hidden areas as well. I had a fantastic time finding these secrets, as well as progressing through the game. There IS a decent story, but it's not as strong as found in similar games. The puzzles and exploration of the area aspect is top-notch, but I admit that I had problems in the 3rd chapter. After using a few notes from a walkthrough, I still think the solutions were a bit ambiguous.

This is a beautiful world to explore, with plenty of content and secrets. My only complaints are that some key objects are hidden in obscure places where I don't know I can click, and that many of the puzzles feel artificial, with no relation to the story. But it was certainly worth my time and money for the overall experience. You'll probably need a walkthrough...

With its glaring list of disputable issues that are more than just nitpicks, The Eyes of Ara could have emerged a disaster. It certainly doesn't start smoothly with its clunky controls, but you get used to that.
Then its very engaging first half gets muddied by an increasingly obtuse experience in the later chapters, due to lack of proper guidance against increasingly complex riddles, ultimately leading to a fair amount of guessing.
Yet, it's still a decent and enjoyable package overall. The game's challenges and engaging design construct a compelling arrangement, a thoughtful blend of familiarity and creativity, sufficiently rewarding to warrant its full exploration.
Full 3D environments are observed from a fixed point. Visually, the game looks alright, albeit perhaps a bit dated. Teleportation from point to point sometimes lands in unexpected angles that make reorientation more difficult than it ought to be, but you get used to that as well.
The game constantly challenges the player with multiple threads at once, including lots of optional puzzles and collectibles, ensuring that there is always something to chase or solve. There is so much to do and see, in fact, that it may even be difficult to get back into it if you take long breaks in between play sessions without feeling at least a little bit lost.
Solving puzzles require paying serious attention to details and taking down many notes from etchings, diaries, drawings, scribbles, sketches, book excerpts, posters, and tons of numbers scattered all over. An automatic log of meaningful discoveries would have been welcomed.
As comparable games I still prefer by far
and its sequels, with impeccable execution and cohesive style, but this game is nevertheless a good addition to a serious puzzle lover's library. Just don't be surprised that you may need a guide to reach its conclusion.

Dishonored is a stealth combat FPS. Your character can either sneak around without making a sound (ghost runs) or you slaughter everyone in your way (total chaos). Depending on how you play the game you will be presented with different endings. Going the chaos route also means a lot more combat, which on higher difficulty settings can spell disaster, so you need to pick your battles carefully. Corvo is not outfitted like the Doom Marine. Your main sources of damage are your sword, with which you can also block and parry, a very loud and not very accurate gun, as well as a sneaky and very accurate crossbow (headshot, baby). The more chaos you sow the more the city will go to hell, which also spawns more of a certain type of enemy, but you'll know this soon enough.
Of course there are a lot of things to collect and steal, but you can blaze through the game and just assassinate your targets and get out, once you know where they are and how to get there. Should be a feast for speed runners and completionists. My playthrough on easy took me 12 hours though, I got all the runes and just spent much time exploring the levels. And that's where the game is at its best, finding new routes, using abilities to create unique pathways and executions. Deciding who to kill and who to leave alive. Great game. Only issues I encountered were some pathing problems, as in your character would get stuck on terrain more often than should be the case...
There's also a small DLC pack with more missions. Well worth your money this game, unless you hate FPS and sneaking around.

Costume Quest is a cute little Halloween themed casual adventure game. This fun game had you teaming up with newfound friends to rescue your sister and save Halloween from candy-hunting monsters. The game feels like it was made for a younger audience, but certainly enjoyable by the young at heart.
were really nicely done. It was appropriately cartoony, which fit the game quite well. All the animations and movements felt really smooth. Each level of the game was set in a unique setting which the art represented well.
isn't the main focus of the game, but it is there. It's quite cute, fun and appropriate. There are certainly a couple of nods and winks in there and there's some enjoyable dialogue too.
was simplistic, requiring you to complete a number of quests on each level, all revolving around collecting candy, battle cards (which would give characters a boost in combat) and collectable trading cards. While each level was in a different setting, the gameplay felt a little too much like a copy of the level before it and that made it a tad boring. There were some unique activities on each level, I feel that more variety from level to level would have made it feel more fresh.
was very simplistic. Depending on which character's turn it was, it would either require a timed button press of one of four keys, a single button press or a mashing of one or more keys. Every third attack by a character had the options of choosing a special attack. Defence used a similar mechanic. I believe the simplicity of the combat can be attributed to a combination of the younger target audience as well as a relic of it being a console port. A Paper-Scissors-Rock style strength/weakness system would modify the damage given/received. The problem with this simplified approach is that after a while, it becomes rather repetitive. Given the number of battles you'll need to complete the game, the repetitive combat simply becomes boring and I found I was wanting to avoid combat rather than chasing enemies for extra candy and experience. This is compounded by the inability to skip special attack animations. While each animation isn't that long, you'll be seeing a lot of them, and if you're like me, you'll just want to skip it and move on.
for this game at quite simple to collect. If you examine them prior to playing, you should be able to pick them all up bar one in a single playthrough. That bar one is "Tisn't the Season", which can only be acquired on Christmas Day.
Costume Quest is really quite polished. I saw no bugs, screen artefacts, characters getting stuck, or the like. If I want to be really picky, the only thing I could bring attention to is that there are some minor signs that this is a port, combat mechanism for instance, but I don't think it would have been practice to have done anything about them.
Overall, Costume Quest is a beautiful fun game. If you like a casual, light-hearted adventure and can tolerate a little repetitiveness, you'll find enjoyment here.

I bought this game as it was made by the same group that helped with the Day of The Tentacle Reboot. Whether you should buy it or not kind of depends on what you're after. If you're wanting a mature in-depth game with vast arrays of landscapes, character development and difficulty this is NOT the game for you. This game is more of a kooky sweet family-friendly game to pass time with.
I'm a bit of a completionist and so I found this a fun simple game for completing the cute quests and unlocking the different outfits- it's not particularly difficult/complex but it can keep you engaged for a good 5-15 hours. I'd recommend it for when it's on sale at about $5-$10 as a cute game to whittle some time away with- but it's not something I'd want to pay $15+ for (as there are other more in-depth engaging titles for around that price instead).
People have complained that it involves childish jokes; however, to me it was no more childish than some of the original Dragon Quest games and so if you can put up with some of those jokes you can easily put up  with (or even appreciate) these ones.
I found the premises of the game (go door knocking at houses, fight monsters, collect candy, unlock outfits to progress further through), unique enough. It is somewhat repetitive, however I feel that they've balanced this by making the game a short one with three parts taking place in three different areas. To me the game length is perfect - you wouldn't want it to be much longer as you'd get bored of the lack of variety but it has enough different elements to keep you entertained for the length of the game. I'm someone who really likes playing side-quests and mini-games so I appreciated the card collecting, bobbing for apples, finding the hidden children quests, etc they had. And I appreciated playing Grubbins on Ice as whilst you could see it was made off of the same kind of gameplay ideas it was different enough to keep my interest.
I thought the battle graphics were endearingly sweet- although it does involve turn based combat and unskippable animations which may frustrate some players. So- if family friendly games aren't your thing I'd recommend skipping this game. If you're after something short, sweet, unique and like mini-games then this might be the game for you.
But if you're really not sure if it's your kind of game maybe watch a bit of a playthrough or a few cut scenes on the community board. I did like this game, I would recommend it, but I'm also wanting to write this review so that those who wouldn't find it appealing can be more likely to leave it alone and not come here complaining about having 'wasted their money on a kids game'.

This is a fun retro-style RPG that does not eat up all your time to finish, but that is completely rewarding for being so whimsical and full of interesting content.
I think you'll find that certain aspects are repetitive. For instance, the monsters one fights look similar and some of the minor quests are identical--e.g., apple bobbing. I think the turn-based fighting lacks strategy once you pick up a third friend. Also, you might want to adjust the in-game brightness because I had a hard time seeing at first. Still, all of these cons are mitigated by the fun content. I just loved collecting items, which was such a key component to playing the Costume Quest games. New costumes give you new powers. My favourite costume was the Eyeball from Grubbins on Ice. Hilarious!
I purchased the game in a bundle with Costume Quest 2 and Grubbins on Ice for $5 on Halloween. The price was unbeatable, although I would have probably accepted paying $20 for all three games. This won't be the game you'll be playing for an entire year, but it will be a game you'll look back on fondly for sure. For me, it filled in the void after I beat South Park's "Stick of Truth."

I almost bought Costume Quest 2 this past sale -- before playing Costume Quest 1, which I've had in my library for quite some time. I'm glad I didn't buy the sequel which is billed as much of the same. After playing Costume Quest 1 to 100% completion, I have no desire to ever revisit it or play the sequel.
Is it a bad game? No, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you're a fan of turn-based fights with QTE-like button presses. The art style is cute, the Halloween theme whimsical, the story is sufficient. However, the turn-based combat with unskippable animations gets
old
fast. In addition, the surprising lack of voiceovers is very disappointing; the game's story and interactions would have been much improved with spoken dialog.
If you're on the fence, watch a few Let's Play videos on YouTube in order to get a feel for the plot and the combat. My mistake was simply buying on the strength of the studio (Double Fine) and the majority of positive reviews. All-in-all, I'd say the game is like Halloween candy: it's sweet but ultimately will make you sick if you have too much of it.

Could've been, and should've been so much more.
Over all, I've been entertained by this game...but it seems like such a missed opportunity.  The idea of a squad-based third person shooter as an installment of XCOM is interesting, but ultimately it's poorly executed in this game...a pale reflection of Mass Effect.  Better AI, a bigger diversity of weapons, and more interesting passive/active abilities would've been a significant boost.  As it is, the game is quick to master, and as there's little else in the way of gameplay, it begins to make the game feel repetitive.
The  RPG elements provide hardly any depth, the items ultimately seem like nothing more than skin changes.  I have no idea why they decided weapons should be picked up in missions (instead of researched or built at your own pace) and nothing should have a clear representation of what effects are provided.  Does this backpack (your only other piece of equipment besides weapons) provide more damage resistance than that one?  Who can say, because the game sure doesn't.  More on the management side could've been a bit of a boost to gameplay as well.
The story is utterly disjointed...suddenly it will present information that I'm seeing for the first time as though I should be well versed in it.  It's poorly paced, characters can be a little bland and cheesey, all of which could be okay if the overall storyline and gameplay were more interesting.  As it is, it's just downright confusing at times.
All in all, it's an okay game.  I'm just disappointed that for whatever reasons (be it bowing down to exterior pressure, excessive development time, too many changes of direction) it feels like it could've been a lot more.  From the review, it probably sounds like I think it's a bad game.  I don't.  It's just passable, and it's not something that I would imagine that I'd ever pick up again after my first play-through.

Is this game a blatant rip-off of Mass Effect? Yes.
Does it have anything to do with the XCOM series? Not really.
But is it a good game? Yeah, it's half-decent.
I admit I'm not a veteran of the XCOM series but I played and enjoyed Enemy Unknown long before buying this. There's very little connecting the two games, but I don't really care. The game has a unique setting, does a good job of replicating the qualities of Mass Effect's combat system, has an alright story, and is decently challenging.
The game isn't without its problems though. The game lags horribly everytime it saves, the AI will get stuck on objects while trying to revive you, and at one point I had to restart a checkpoint because a cutscene never triggered after killing all the enemies. But for less than $5 it's a decent purchase.
As a full price game this review would be much more negative, but when you get it for cheap you won't regret it. The gameplay is solid and strategic and emphasises flanking more than Mass Effect did. It also allows you to use your stun abilities on even boss level enemies, which Mass Effect never would. The story kind of falls apart on the last couple missions, but it had me interested for the majority of the 10 hours or so it took me to beat it. It has a decent amount of side missions too which have unique level designs and don't feel like they're thrown in.
At the end of the day the negative reviews for this game boil down to two things: The gameplay rips off Mass Effect and it has nothing to do with XCOM. If you take it on its own it's a decent title. If you are at all interested in it and can get it for $5 or less, pick it up.

It is neither as technical as any Codemasters game, nor as friendly-driven and arcade like Burnout and last Need for Speed iterations. But it has somewhat that you may have very fun (maybe the european approach made the game seems like that).
It is an open-world driving game. As a valet driver, you basically do a bulk of events (including driving permission tests) from where you earn cash and experience. You have to win all the regional events (each one ends as a challenge against one of your rivals) in order to match a final "island grand cup", both in Ibiza and Hawaii islands (starting on first one).
The soundtrack and the scenario modeling are the superb things. It is a very nice environment, beautifully shaped. But the character modeling is pretty bad, although (both graphically and about dialogues).
The gameplay is reasonable. With a "PS2-like controller", you will have all the controls you need. The game is responsive and controlling the car is relatively easy. Maybe game menus are a little tricky sometimes, but it is a thing easily to be used to.
The game has a overall moderate challenging factor. The simulation factor is not high. You cannot make a turn reckessly with your car in some categories, but when you master that (it's a little hard), you beat all championships easily. Maybe the greatest difficulty of game is finding the right car for the right event. Besides each model and its features, you must find the brand's sellers through the HUGE scenarios. There are many of the great high-level car brands (some are missing, likely due lack of agreements with manufacturers). You must explore both islands to complete the tasks given to you, find shops, enter championships and even to find multiplayer spots.
You can customize your character (clothes and plastic surgery), your car (tuning, painting and so on) and the houses/manors you can buy.
By the way, multiplayer is gradually being abandoned, but you will find people doing some weird things (like races that the fastest lap was one second...).
The DLC's are not recommended. A couple of cars (not available in-game and has nothing effectively different from what you can purchase on the scenarios' stores) and a Casino that you may earn some cash to buy things. Both are expensive.
You may have some fun. It's not a mind-blow. The game has a soft and relaxing mood sometimes due it's soundtrack and the locations chosen. Maybe it was intentional.

The game has it's faults, sure.  But for a free game, it's actually pretty awesome!
This is not a very difficult game.  I mean, if I could potentially finish it (it crashed during the final boss fight on me ... I think it was the final boss fight, anyway) some people might consider it "too easy."  I don't mind the "lack of difficulty," however, as this is actually a selling point of the game.
The graphics are all right.  Your character is fixed and, as far as I can tell, completely uncustomizable.  Even so, she's certainly pretty to look at.  You can move the camera all around her if you like.  I suppose some where out there is a patch to make this more interesting, but I'm not terribly interested in looking.
The difficulty ramps up pretty smoothly.  That's a pretty unique feature for a modern game of any stripe.  Most games I play lure you in with a good and easy cruise for about four hours, than ramp up the difficulty to "off the charts" all of a sudden, but only after you've played too long to get a refund.
There are some complaints about the lack of options in the game, such as graphics and the like.  I don't mind this at all and it really doesn't bother me.  As I understand this was essentially a student project, I see nothing wrong with it's appearance or lack of options at all.
While I see reports that you can not configure the controls of the game, this isn't a bother for me, either.  It uses standard mouse and keyboard FPS controls.  If you're unfamiliar with those controls, or prefer to use a different control device, I don't know what to tell you.  In my opinion, they stopped making decent control devices for PC over ten years ago. O.O
All and all, it's a great game for the price!  Much better than anything you'll find in a mobile game, it has no microtransactions, and it's quite a fun little ditty to play when you just want to pass a littel time here and there.
Don't expect much replay, of course.  I suspect you'd just keep replaying it only to see if you can do it better, since the game is fairly short and nothing changes between game plays as far as I can tell.
But the game is free.  If it works for you, you'll probably like it for what it offers.  Especially if you read all my boring dull pointless ramblings about it. =p

The Eyes of Ara is a first person puzzle game with many clever and challenging puzzles to solve.  You must explore a castle and find the source of a strange signal coming from within.  This signal is disrupting everything in a 100km radius including TV, Radio, and WiFi so it's imperative that you succeed.  However, it soon turns into a mystery, “the mystery of the Eyes of Ara”.  What are they and why are they there?
Pros:
Decent graphics
Many areas to explore
Great mix of puzzles from easy to challenging
The developers are actively updating and answering questions
The game flows well from puzzle to puzzle
Many secret areas and rooms
A great deal of collectibles
Mysterious Story-line
Cons:
Point and Click format
A great deal of pixel hunting
Fairly Linear
I thought that most of the puzzles were clever and challenging.  A few were easy while one or two were very hard, but the vast majority were well balanced.  You must pay attention to detail, many of the hot spots are well hidden forcing you to pixel hunt, however, once a puzzle is solved or an item found, the hot spot goes away letting you know that there is nothing further to discover.
About the only thing I didn't like about this game (other than pixel hunting) is the fact that, strictly speaking, this is a point and click game.  There is no free roam that will allow you to go into a corner and see behind something.  Your character is rooted in the same place in every room.  There is only two or three exceptions where your position is slightly changed so be aware and alert.
At the time of this review, The Eyes of Ara was selling for $14.99.  Well worth it given that fact that it took me almost 16 hours to complete plus another 4 to obtain all of the achievements.  I wouldn't wait for a sale, I'd buy it now.

Before we start, keep in mind that this is an Adventure Game. Not an action or arcade type of nonsense.
Loved this game. I'm probably a little slower in the head than most people because it took me over 30 hours to finish this adventure but......It was over 30 remarkable hours!
There was only one part of the game for me that required looking up a cheat and that was a solar system puzzle thing which wrecked my mind completely. Even after looking up the cheat, I still couldn't figure out how in the name of anything holy that I could have ever figured it out. But, other than that mess, the rest of the game was intriguing. Every puzzle made sense and you always seemed to know what you had to do next.
MAKE NOTES!
Keep a pad and pen handy and make a ton of notes. Your welcome.
When you are coming to the end of the game you will notice that you can just do the last puzzle and finish the game. Done. The End. BUT....
You will realize that there were items that you probably missed during the game that you can go back and find 'if you want to'. And if you do, other little sections and puzzles open up for even more challenging enjoyment.
One such puzzle that you don't have to solve is in the cellar. I won't go into any detail and spoil it for you but if you decide to take it on, you will probably be just at the point of getting a rope and stool to hang yourself from your ceiling fan. But when you DO solve it....Oh boy....More puzzles and areas open up.
Anyway, I loved this game and it was Well Worth The Price of admission if you are an Adventure Game Loving Fan.

Dishonored is one of the finest examples of world-building on the market. Every environment is dripping with personality and intrigue. Meandering about the streets of Dunwall, I can't help but long for more of this world.
As far as the story goes, it's pretty cliche and even predictable at times but the stealth mechanics are tight and the mystical powers throw in some much appreciated variety. As for the straight up combat, it is horendously difficult, especially at first without any upgrades. Not that this is a bad thing. I would highly advise the stealth route until you get some better hardware. Be prepared to have to work hard for the "good ending" as killing people is definitely the easier route and usually less frustrating.
The graphics are also fairly impressive, even a few years later. The solid art direction helps the game look gorgeous without looking dated.
Overall, I would certainly buy Dishonored again. No question.

So, I played this game initially on a free weekend, and it scratched the open world shooter itch I had. It was fun, there was adventure, there were lots of items to get and play with.
So I bought the game, and I just 100% completed the base game. I won't be buying the DLCs because the base game experience was... underwhelming. Here's the good and bad:
- the game is pretty expensive for what you get
- it's really repetetive, and assets were clearly reused many times
- load times are SUPER long, especially when respawning after being killed
- the story was good, but not nearly as good as i had hoped
- there are quite a few bugs
- DEAR GOD THE GRENADE LAUNCHER BUG (caused me countless game overs)
- you have to play through ubisoft's uPlay, which caused my rather good computer to only be capable of a stable ~35fps. edit: may have* caused. regardless of the reason i was unable to get more than 35-40fps out of this game on single player, with occasional spikes down to <1fps
- the map is gorgeous, massive landscapes and beautiful scenery
- it seems like the game was definitely designed around playing multiplayer, both PvE and PvP. the single player experience was pretty meh
I can't in good conscience recommend this game at anywhere near full price. If it goes 50-75% off, it's worth the money for sure. But if you're looking for a great single player or even coop experience, you'll be better off looking elsewhere. I kind of wish that the PvP mode was locked into a DLC and the base game was priced much much lower.

Bought it on a whim because I had some spare change in my steam wallet and it was on sale for a dollar. If I had to describe this game in a single word, it would be "charming". The art of the world is gorgeous, the gameplay, while simple, is interesting and somewhat strategic. On a scale fo 1-10 with 10 being 1 being "warm blanket in front of the fire on a winter's night" and 10 being "white-knuckle rage-quit imminent", this game would sit at a pleasant 2. This is a very relaxing and humorous game to play. I sharply exhaled from my nose several times and even chuckled to myself a time or two.
Pros:
-The combat system is clever and unique. It vaguely reminds me of Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga, which was the game that properly introduced me to turn-based RPG.
-The writing is fantastic. The dialogue is clever and captures a certain whimsy that most other games either don't attempt, or do attempt but overdo it to the point of poor taste.
-The costumes and other collectibles are hidden, but not buried behind tons of filler. you can collect nearly everything without any backtracking.
-On a simillar note, the game doesn't require grinding to become a powerful player. You can play right through and have a great time with it.
Neutral:
-The game is short and linear. I beat the main game, the expansion, and completed all of the acheivements (except the achievement which requires you to play on Christmas) within eight and a half hours, and that includes me leaving for a lunch break and leaving the game on.
Cons:
-The game generally runs around 30 fps.
-21:9 support is mediocre. The menus and HUD do not scale properly. I ended up playing the 1920*1080 version and just making do with the stretch introduced.
Overall, this is a short, easy game that will be a welcome addition to any library

Since WOW is what I played before, and it is the reference most people make, I will use it as a comparison.
Pros:
Interesting and in depth soul trees - and combat is less boring when you can switch on the fly
Less reason to have a million alts to cover all classes and professions
Three professions slots, and you can purchase more (buying more character slots is actually cheaper)
'Free' but filled with paid goodies that you don't really need, but will probably want like bag slots
There feels like there is more stuff to do in Rift than WOW, but less pressure to do all of it
Better in game UI system
Better wardrobe system - collect an item, appearance is saved permenantly, you can get rid of item
In-game macro system
Chronicles for 1-2 player dungeons at lvl 50
Artifacts, puzzles, and treasures to promote exploration
Find a book but dont feel like reading lore right now?  Books are collected so you can read them later (love this feature)
Grinding for rep usually has multiple options, so if you dont feel like doing 50 daily quests, you dont have to  (thank god)
Optional dimensions for people who like to build things - can be completely ignored if you dont care, confers no benefit
Max level is 65, not 95.
Instant adventures for leveling with making the commitment of a dungeon
Mentoring and sidekicking systems - play with anyone at any level
Cons:
Soul trees are not balanced
Smaller following, less support
'Free' but filled with paid goodies that you don't really need, but will probably want, like bag slots
Characters, in general, are not as 'colorful' and feel flat compared to WOW
Professsions are a bit wonky comparitively
Lackluster support for addons like
An overwhelming amount of currencies
If you don't use macros, you probably aren't playing to your full potential - for some classes, I would consider it required
Minion system less fun than WOW's battle pets, but you get crafting materials
Important Notes:
If early on you like this game, buy the Rift game disc on Amazon for about $8, it opens up bag slots, character slots, selling on the auction,  and gives you patron status for a month.  Well worth the $8 price tag.
If you want expansions or soul packs, wait till they go on sale.  The Steam summer sale has them at 50% off.
Summary:
About on par with WOW, minus the subscription fee.  I still probably spend the same amount of money on it, but I feel like I control the amount of money I spend.  If I feel like playing something else for a month or two, I can without subscription fee guilt.  I like the combat and soul tree system much better, despite its imbalances.  I like having three solid characters which cover about 75% of the soul trees instead of needing 8 different characters to cover the same amount of combat variety in WOW.

I generally buy puzzle games to be challenged, and The Eyes of Ara provided a good twelve hours of challenge. Unfortunately, quite a lot of that was challenging me to find the tiny hidden hotspot.
tl;dr: Difficult, pretty, well-written, and the pixel-hunting elements are mostly optional. Yes, you should buy it.
Good things:
* Contains a lot of very good, original puzzles, and is much harder than the demo would suggest.
* Really, really pretty, and runs even on quite low-end PCs.
* Superb writing. The characters, though not appearing on-screen, are charmingly characterised through the notes they left behind.
* The game is divided up into five areas (although the first and last are very short), and you can't carry items from one area to another. This helps reduce the combinatorial nightmare that you might otherwise encounter from trying every object on every other object.
* Similarly, hotspots become inactive once they've served their purpose, which saves you wasting time on puzzles that have already been solved.
* If you don't like hidden-object nonsense, there are a few options you can turn on to make it a bit easier - making the cursor change when it's over a zoom-in spot, making collectible objects occasionally shimmer gold, and playing a chime when you enter a room with collectibles.
* If you like hidden-object nonsense, you'll find plenty of it here, but it's almost all optional.
Bad things:
* ALMOST all optional. There is at least one mandatory puzzle that requires playing find-the-hotspot.
* A common flaw in this type of game, but barely half of these puzzles have a good reason to exist. The in-game letters make a vague attempt to justify them - some were created as entertainment, for example - but unless your suspension of disbelief is particularly good, you will find yourself wondering why on earth you need to do all of this puzzle-solving just to make your way around a castle.
* There are a couple of moments where an item I wanted was visibly reachable, but access was blocked by a table that could easily be climbed over, crawled under, moved, or squeezed around. This was annoying.
* Some of the puzzles aren't that great; but there are enough hits that I don't mind the misses.
Other things:
* lake.kubilius has written a really good minimal-spoilers guide that will give you a hint to certain puzzles if you get stuck without completely solving it for you. It also lists the location of all the hidden collectibles.
* Content warning for suicide. Not on-screen, though.
* Arachnophobes may rest content in the knowledge that while this game is full of cobwebs, there isn't a single spider.
On the whole, though, The Eyes of Ara is a very enjoyable game.

This game is a mixed bag. It's got some great puzzles, a compelling story and very good music. If you like "myst" types of games as well as "click around a room to find items" types of games, it's right up your alley.
But the game does have some major design and playability flaws. For example, there are items that you find throughout the game, that at first SEEM like they're just additional parts, because you can go from area to area and your inventory is "cleared" each time you enter a different "zone" and you get a new set of these items to find, so you'd think "ah, this is just completionist stuff that doesn't really count". Until you get to the end of the game and realize that no, you actually needed all of those items. It's a design flaw that's startling to see because there's nothing indicating those items importance, as their permenance from zone to zone doesn't carry through, nor is it implied in the game play prior. If something is needed for the end game, make sure that the players understand that by carrying the total amount throughout the zones OR by making it so that you need to find all the items prior to moving on to the next area.
Also, there are areas in the game that are VERY difficult to get to, and have quite a bit of build up to their opening, just to have absolutely no payoff whatsoever once you've made it inside. Looking at you "Just Deserts"...all of that time and build up to open an area that's just devoid of any payoff whatsoever. Combine that with simple to avoid issues such as "when you walk into a room, have the door you just entered from be BEHIND you in every instance, and you come to realize that this project has some very sloppy game design. (For example, there are many times you enter a room through a generic "door" just to be standing in the next area surrounded by doors, some in front, some behind, which one did you come in from? who knows!)
Additionally, there are several puzzles that have absolutely no hints or clues within the game that would give a player any clue as to what to do or how they're connected. (eg-hallways statues)
It seems as if there were two teams on Eyes of Ara, a room design team and a puzzle team, and some days those two teams didn't really communicate with each other.
All of that being said, the game is quite good. The puzzles are difficult (some intentionally difficult, some because of the poor design choices) and the world is actually quite easy to lose yourself into. I found the puzzles to be more in-depth than games like "The Room" which, regardless of having easier puzzles, did have a much better puzzle solving gameplay.
With The Room & The Room 2 you understood that if you couldn't figure out a puzzle, it was because you hadn't looked at it from every angle. With Eyes of Ara, if you can't figure out a puzzle, it's probably because the devs didn't include the hint or they put it in another zone that has no other connection to the zone you're currently in.
Fun? Yes. Frustrating? Absolutely. Oh, and btw devs, take whoever designed the room that rewards the player with Just Deserts and beat them with a bag of oranges while screaming "Reward players who jump through your hoops, you trog!".

Firstly I'm not going to look a gift horse in the mouth, the game is free afterall. But with what few hours  I have on record I do want to review this game based off what I've seen of it's gameplay vs its story since I wasn't able to actually read it. My first biggest conundrum came when I first started the game as I couldn't find a settings menu to switch this game from windowed mode to full screen. But after getting through the prologue to the game I went straight to the settings and changed the settings to what I could, mid resolution and full screen, going back expecting the controls on the bottom of the screen to have remained there only to fall victim to the absence of said controls. So I ended up pressing every key on my keyboard to figure out the controls.
So I then got thinking to myself that "I got this, a bad beginning can't ruin this game for me. After all it is a game I got for free." I was proven wrong, so I get going and start fighting the baddies in front of me and I get to the last one in the beginning room and I'm killed off.
"What the ♥♥♥♥," I said to myself, "I didn't even get hit by anything until that guy."
I respawn, and turns out that there's no indicator that you're getting hit outside of just constantly monitoring your health bar. I get over my previous statement and I go on moving from area to area figuring out that the pots contain big health ups and the enemies drop almost insignificant ones. Until I get to a large area with cliffs and ranged enemies in addition to the normal cronies running about. And turns out there's no edge protection in this area where you have to use the special action key to move between platforms, making me fall to my death.
"No biggie," I say, "I surely got past a checkpoint on my way to this area." Yeah, no. I start right back at the beginning. And that brought me here to the review page. But hey, it's a fun game until it frustrates you, so give it a try. It's free.

I expected this to be quite adorable or maybe a bit funny. It ended up being awfully writen, very bad dialogue and also, it made me extremely uncomfortable, like experiencing second hand embarrasment.
The main character, Samantha, seems to have some anxiety disorder, and i assume the game tried to make awareness of how it feels to have it, but it ended falling flat on it's face. Samantha comes off as overly whiny, very self centered, nasty and, at times, unnecessarily cruel to people around her. Her holier than thou atittude is cringeworthy, not to mention how ridiculous is that she apparently can't make oatmeal and much less, handle a microwave. Considering she's already a young adult, and had a box of instant oatmeal in her room, it's not far fetched to think she has made oatmeal before without hassle and suddenly seems to forget how to prepare instant food. She makes a very nasty remark to the girls talking in the kitchen, which makes Samantha seem like a very bitter woman for no reason at all, and made me uncomfortable.
Speaking about game mechanics, it's just ''option'' after option, even though you're supposed to be in control, the game (in certain occasions) will force you to chose what samantha wants and override what you wanted, it's not like you're doing much, most of the supposed options are useless (Samantha talking to herself, i guess) and the ones that matter are often overrided, as above. This tendency tends to ruin the experience, it doesn't feel like a game anymore, it feels like someone's vanity project (which it is, pretty much). Also the music it's very loud and there's no option to mute it.
The only good thing is the artstyle, it's pretty cute and easy on the eyes.

Hatoful Boyfriend is more nuanced and compelling than it has any right to be.
Its outrageous concept is so over the top that it’s hard to view the game as anything more than a joke; something amusing but mostly held together by the mere fact of its existence. But these preconceptions, strung along by even its own marketing and description, are hiding the shockingly well written and emotionally stirring narrative underneath.
To be entirely clear, it is in part exactly what it appears to be: an otome dating simulator/visual novel, set in a world where birds have evolved to be the most intelligent species and humans have been mostly driven to extinction. Playing as the lone human student at Pigeonation Academy, you are tasked with going about your day, trying to scrape by in your schoolwork while wooing the bird of your dreams.
It’s an intentionally laughable idea, and one which at first can seem so ridiculous as to turn those less drawn to Japan’s stranger exports away, but its one which never dissolves into idiotic bird lover pandering (assuming that’s a thing that exists) or outright stupidity with its writing. Hatoful Boyfriend is entirely aware of its own absurdity, and treats it almost as an afterthought, to the point that the fact these characters are nearly entirely birds became irrelevant at least as far as being a very odd novelty.
Hatoful Boyfriend’s writing is exceptional, both hilarious and comical, and heart wrenchingly sad and contemplative. Though it begins as little more than a silly teenage romance, it spends this time crafting characters that you come to care about, before hurling them into a plot darker and more precarious than I ever could have imagine. While there are certainly parts (and entire storylines) within the game which are nothing but comedy, allowing the humorous and charming side of the game to take the spotlight for a moment and provide more than a few laughs, it was when the subject matter moved away from this silliness that I began to finally see the hidden brilliance of the game’s writer.
It’s shocking to even consider at first, and even now as I’m writing this I’m rather stunned at what Hatoful Boyfriend manages to do with its narrative, but it handles it's incredibly dark material with incredible grace and consideration. Calculated genocide, mass murder and biological experimentation, interspecies racism, and the value of family are not only touched upon, but discussed at length and in such a way as to not only allow you to take them seriously within the game’s context, but actually emphasize and become emotionally invested in the avian characters that once seemed so innocent and comical.
Hatoful Boyfriend made me laugh; it made me smile and appreciate its subtlety; and it made me cry. The spectrum of emotions I experienced throughout my handful of playthroughs (which should be considered a requisite, as you will miss the vast majority of the game’s content if you only go through it once) was something I never imagined this game to be capable of. It kept me playing for hours on end, up late into the night, and I’m still attempting to process all that I witnessed. It could very well be the apotheosis of a game you shouldn’t judge by its cover, and something that everybirdie ought to at least give a chance before writing it off as something it by and large is anything but.

Despite what the professional reviewers may say about this game, it is a solid third-person shooter. The game mechanics borrow heavily from Mass Effect 1, since you can give orders to squad mates, use alien powers such as lift or summon a friendly blob, and talk to NPC's between missions. Even the dialogue uses the multiple answer wheel from the game. The story is deserving of the XCOM title, contrary to what others may say. I'm not an XCOM elitest, so the fact that this game wasn't an RTS didn't bother me. Enemy Unknown was a great game, and to me The Bureau can proudly call itself an XCOM game as well. The final act has an interesting twist and the post-finale voiceover has a cool nod to EU. The game is not perfect though. Your squad mates are far from intelligent. Alyx Vance or Elizabeth, they are not. They are not completely useless either. Give them an order and they follow it just fine. The problem is that major baby-sitting is required. There are some graphical issues, such as ties clipping through the characters chest, or textures taking some time to load in. As well, there is a base hub you can walk around in-between missions to explore for documents, but there's not much in it. As I said already, The Bureau is a solid third-person shooter with an interesting story, good voice acting, and amazing looking locales. If it's on sale, give it a buy. As for the DLC, it can probably be left alone. Code breakers is a side mission that takes all of 10-15 minutes, the pistol is just that, a pistol, and Hangar 6 is a horde mode style game type that provides some background information on the game's plot. Overall I give The Bureau a  7/10.

The Bureau is a strange game. It's essentially a Mass Effect game without the plot choices (save for a few near the end). The squad controls like a Mass Effect 3 squad. You order them to cover and use abilities (like warp blast and lift...). There's a main mission hub where you talk to your companions with dialogue wheels. It's Mass Effect-lite.
It's pretty well made and the combat is engaging enough. I really enjoy the rare game that tries to capture cold war era America and I think The Bureau succeeds here quite well. Everything about this game is very 1962.
If you like the XCOM lore or are just looking for a decent third person squad shooter to spend some time with, you could do much worse. Skip the DLC though.

If you like tactical RPG shooting games, mainly Mass Effect, then you'll find this game to be an enjoyable, yet not amazing or incredible, game.
The story is alright, you defend 1950's-60's America from alien invaders who have better technology and numbers than you. It isn't as good as others in the genre but with a few twists here and there it doesn't drag down the enjoyment. The characters, an important part of these kinds of games since you will be talking to them so much, are only passingly enjoyable and many of them don't have enough going for them to make them memorable. Some of the main characters are fine but they aren't as good as the ones in other games.
The setting is a refreshing change from the norm of today's shooters. The clash between olden day America and the futuristic alien architecture is pleasing to look at as you see the destruction between the two. I liked the clash so much that I was a little disappointed when it changed to primarily alien bases later on in the game.
The graphics are nice, using the unreal engine 3 to a great extent. Character models look nice and the effects are fun to look at. The game has additional Physx support and so cloth and particles flow smoothly. I have AMD so I couldn't really use it. The graphics aren't spectacular to look at, but I enjoyed what I saw.
Gameplay is fun and challenges you to direct your team to victory. I played on the hardest difficulty, commander, and it wasn't too difficult once I got a handle on things. You can't take too much damage in this game, and unlike other games health doesn't really regenerate and you can't heal too often. This forces you to use your squad to its fullest capacity instead of going Rambo and doing everything yourself. The abilities are useful and directing your team in slow motion, since the game doesn't pause when you plan out your actions, is engaging and enjoyable.
The enemies are a little boring as many of them are just humanoid soldiers that don't act any different than any other game. The bosses, on the other hand, are fun and challenge you in tough fights. Things like Mutons, Sectopods, and Gunships become even scarier as they soak up damage and force you to rely on your team's abilities to slow down, damage, and distract the enemy. It really gives you an accomplished feeling when you can plan and take one down without anyone getting really hurt.
In the end, I enjoyed this game and recommend it to anyone on the fence on getting it during a sale like I did. It may not be the best of its kind in the genre, but you won't really have a bad time while playing it.

This game took me a bit by surprise... I was expecting something that played like Gears of War, but instead got a game more akin to Mass Effect 2.  It's a third-person shooter, but you can slow time to a crawl during the battle to plan your moves, give orders to your squad, and make use of your super-powers.  Between missions, you can walk around the XCOM base and talk to everyone to flesh out the story (and get access to extra side-missions).  It's also got some other "RPG-lite" elements (experience points, etc.) that can give you some different gameplay depending on your choices.
The game's biggest flaw, IMO, is that the between-mission talking dragged on a little too long, and it took too long to walk around the base.
Others have commented that they didn't like the story, or that it didn't make sense to them.  I actually enjoyed the story for what it was.  And there's a few moral choices near the end of the game that I thought about and fretted over for a while.
I would not recommend the "Hanger-6" DLC, since it's disjoint from the main campaign and mostly forgettable, but the other DLC mission integrates into the main campaign and it's actually a pretty fun mission.

Portal is one of the most quintessential games on Steam. From the beginning of the game to the very last cutscene, the game is steeped in a fascinating atmosphere. You wake up in the mysterious Aperture Laboratories testing facility, being spoken to by an unseen robotic voice who guides you through the various testing chambers of the facility. You'll quickly notice, of course, that she's far from an uninteresting character.
Early on, you are given a Portal Gun, which is the game's primary puzzle mechanic. With this tool, you're able to create two portals on most surfaces which you can step through. This opens up a huge variety of puzzles, which the game quite adequately explores.
There are a few other notable items at your disposal, notably the Companion Cube (and movable cubes in general) which also greatly assist the gameplay. You'll also find a number of secrets hidden around the many levels, contributing to the atmosphere and your understanding of the universe that the game has crafted.
The controls are quite simple, the graphics hold up fine today, and the soundtrack is fitting. Portal was probably one of the most influential puzzle games ever created; countless games have taken inspiration from it since its release. While it's a short game overall, it's definitely worth playing through.
