However the main reason is because, at least in my opinion, the game, since release, lacked content and deeper gameplay mechanics, and thus failed to grab the interest of most of the playerbase for a longer length of time as evidenced by the playerbase shrinkage in a single month. And even the move to f2p didnt gather enough of a playerbase for 2k to continue funding development for too much longer.
There were many suggestions on how to make the game better and deeper, for example from map based dynamic objectives through special skills and/or pickups to ways for both sides to hinder one another by using the map(by destroying parts of it creating paths and blockades and such) and unique gamemodes. Yet, the devs were mainly concentrating on adding new maps monsters and balancing, which isn't a bad thing but merely doing that won't keep your player base interested.
I myself would've liked to see complete server control(either in an ini file or through mutators) a server list listing dedicated and normal servers, and also the main thing that would give an enormous amount of longevity and interest to the game, modding.
I hope that in the future turtle rock will get the required support to continue development on the game and make it into the game they envisioned it to be. But until that happens, my review will stay negative, hovewer this doesn't mean i do not recommend the game, see for yourself if you like it or not, it is free to play after all.

Although I've enjoyed to play HoI II a lot and HoI III somewhat, I've been fairly reluctant to buy HoI IV. That's due to the bad reviews and Paradox obnoxious DLC policy.
Now that is has been on sale, I've bought the base game and enjoyed my first single player match. The series has made a huge leap from a stat manager to a WW2 simulator, which is nice. The army AI has been improved a lot. For the first time in a HoI game I feel comfortable to let the AI manage all fronts, finetuning it with order adjustments and an occasional direct order.
The Production system overhaul is a step into the right direction as well. You produce parts like artillery, tanks and weapons independently from divisions now, which just pick up the best equipment available in your stock upon recruitment. Old equipment gets gradually replaced once better equipment is researched and produced or salvaged from your enemy. That's nice and adds a great deal of immersion to the game.
Overall plenty of tedious micro-management aspects have been stripped and less new details have been added which increase the immersion. The base game is fun on its own, so I can recommend it. Like always with Paradox titles I can't help to feel ripped off though, when I see DLCs adding content, which clearly should have been included in the base game.

I was unsure if I would enjoy the game due to a couple of negative reviews but it is absolutely wonderful.
Likes:
> Thoughtful puzzles which, while unique, weren't obscure (meaning that, given time, I could figure them out).
> Smooth transitions of the "point and click" movements (poorly done 360 movement games make me ill).
> Well done graphics (as opposed to cubist backgrounds and surfaces with slapdash fillers).
> Interesting story line.  It avoided the tedious current trends of supernatural horror and violence.
> I had time to figure things out.  There was no urgency or deadline to solve the puzzles or game.  I hate to move at someone else's speed and not my own.
> I could wander back and forth in puzzle spaces.  Some games close off puzzle areas once you progress in the game.  This game does not leave any area off limits once you leave it.
> I could go back after completion to find things I've missed or wanted to look at again.
Dislikes:
>  Some areas were hard to get to as you could only be in one specific spot to to go there (e.g. I could see a table around the corner in views A, B, and C but couldn't inspect it unless I was in view C).  This made me think some areas were not available for inspection when they really were.
>  I wanted to be able to go into more areas and look at more of the building (call me strange but I really wanted to open that refrigerator).  Perhaps this is a testament to the developers as they made the spaces interesting and inviting to browse.
>  I see that a Halloween version was released but was not available when I purchased the game in February.  What a lost revenue opportunity for the game developers.
Overall - if you like quietly figuring out fun and unique puzzles while in an interesting game environment, this is the game for you.  I want more!  Can't wait for the developers' next game.

The Eyes of Ara:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

An unusual signal has been broadcast for the last few weeks from an abandoned castle and has disrupted every television, radio and local WiFi network within a 100 km radius. Strangely enough, no local technicians dare to enter the castle. Could it be because of the nonsense ghost stories that locals are spreading about this place?  Nonetheless, this signal has to be shut down as soon as possible. We thank you for taking this assignment on such a short notice and we look forward to resolving the issue promptly and efficiently.
The Eyes of Ara is a puzzle/adventure game in which you are a technician who ventures into a castle full of interesting puzzles.
But first you will arrive by boat and will enter the property via the back gate. From here, the first couple of puzzles are pretty easy to resolve until you reach the main hall.  The gameplay is very straight forward; simply move the mouse cursor all over each room. As soon as your cursor changes from a triangle to a circle it will mean that you can interact with a specific object or read journals and notes from the former owner of the castle.  These notes will give you more information on the story.
The Eyes of Ara is divided into three chapters and in each of them you have to look for a certain number of coins, photos, toys, orbs (blue and yellow) and a painting, but you must have your magnifying glass to find them. To be honest with you, it is just an additional feature in this game; with the exception of the yellow orbs, it will not get you further into the game whether or not you find them.
Puzzle-wise, this type of game is excellent if there is a good balance between the easy and hard puzzles. In that regard, this game nailed it perfectly! After resolving a difficult puzzle, you need to have a simple one to keep you going and vice-versa, and let me tell you there are some serious puzzles to do here!
Another aspect that makes this game as good as it is are the graphics. Splendid 3D graphics from one room to the next. A truly visual pleasure. I really like the soundtrack which adds immensely to the enigmatic atmosphere this game. My only negative comment is in relation to when you zoom out of an object or puzzle and the movement of the camera. The response is slow-ish, but this is me being very picky!
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Stunning graphics
-	Great range of puzzles, from simple to challenging
-	Additional objects to find
-	Great atmosphere
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Camera movement could have been better
If you like resolving puzzles then The Eyes of Ara is definitely a game worth a go!
8/10

Hello and welcome to my review of the relatively old game Test Drive Unlimited 2.
I am aware of the fact that the game was released in 2011, I've purchased it in 2013 and I will still review this title because the series are discontinued and I do still enjoy the game untill today.
Now something about me regarding the racing genre on PC.
I do not like racing games where you can race on a track, in a car which is almost unhandle-able ( in my opinion, ofcourse ).
With these games I mean Grid, and partially Dirt.
Okay, I did enjoy Dirt 3 and Dirt Showdown without a doubt but in the end, playing with a controller or a steering wheel, it didn't satisfy me enough to keep me playing these titles once in a week or more often.
So now back to what I do enjoy in a game of the racing genre.
I do really like the open-world idea, having a big map or several maps ( In Test Drive's case: Island ).
Driving around without anything forcing you do to anything, making speed and just drive all across the island on various landscapes with a nice sight does satisfiy me.
Buying a relaxing car, my Ferrari 458 Italia, Purple with black rims in this case: And just cruising around the island, on the roads with water to the right of me and the city to the left of me, hearing the engine doing it's work is what I like.
Not being forced to drive a track, do a race and aiming on finishing first without anything else you can do.
Just free-roaming in open worlds with customizable cars which you can upgrade and adjust to any specification you want.
And that's for the driving part, now for the experience in terms of sound.
The sound of the car, in various situations ( Driving in sand, dirt, or just a normal road ).
The sound is different every time, for every car in any situations ( weather too for example ) is just perfect in the game and these small things help me enjoy the game more than I already did.
Driving through a tunnel while It's raining in my custom white Nissan GT-R is what I can't do in any other game.
And these elements of Test Drive is what makes me want to play the game, the endless options to tune and adjust cars to exactly how I'd like to and then going on the road, hearing the right sound and feeling good when playing the game .. Yeah, that;
Now for the other part of the game:
Missions, Money, Houses and avatar.
Missions in Test Drive are tasks you have to complete which can be anything from getting a high adrenaline bar, but also could be driving above a certain speed and also opposite missions like driving really careful without the person next to you in the car getting sick.
These missions are pretty fun for the first few times but become boring quick, but they reward you with money to buy cars, houses and clothing.
Money in the game is pretty important ofcourse but I feel like you just have to keep grinding the repetitive missions to finally buy the car you have been wanting for a while.
So yeah, the method of money making within the game is something I don't like and that made me want to Cheatengine myself a couple houndred million instead of working for the money I want to buy the car I'd like.
Houses and Avatar: Besides the garage part to store your cars, I don't care about Houses or pimping your avatar ( Buying clothes, getting haircuts, etc ).
So yup, the car driving part is what I like the most of the game.
Okay, for some of you I might have not played the game in the right way, or not long enough but this was my final review of the game.
If I had to give the game a score from 0 to 100 I would give it a 85, some aspects could've been done way better ( Money making and missions ) but the driving itself is what makes the game a good open-world cruising game, and pretty unique in it's genre.
Okay okay, Grand Theft Auto is somewhat more bigger and to some also better but what I care about is the car driving.
In Grand Theft Auto the car driving is only fun when stunting and such with your friends.
So that's it for the review guys, I hope you have enjoyed reading my opinion about this game.

This is by far the first game i'd ever recommend to buy on early access.  It keeps well within the spirit of the first installment of the series and builds on that success.  I cant help but to feel some kind of "similar feel" to the old fallout games (i do mean the old ones, pre FL3).  Though its by no account a "rip off" or copy of said games.
The bad:
It is currently early access and, though its very playable at this date, my friends and I have had some frustrating times with our online camp. Desyncs, disconnects and crashes.  All of these are known issues and are currently in the works, so its not so much a bad component of the game, rather just something that we need wait for to get sorted.
Restrictive camera angles:  This does actually add to the gameplay, though there are a few out there who dislike it.  I gather there's actually talk going on about fixing this.  It doesn't ruin the game play in any event.
Again, this is early access, so my current frustration with the limitations of some resources will surely be something that will still be tweaked.  Fluids, for one, are quite annoying to keep stock of.  The main source of user-made drinks is berry juice and those shrubs are suprisingly tiring to get hold of (odd how you can't collect rain water in your camp).
It lacks the diverse "prey" animals from the first installment.  So far you are restricted to psychotic turkeys (and what a good laugh that level is), but you need to "farm" that instance which gets very boring very soon.  More wildlife is needed and hopefully not 'infected' kinds (fishing? deer hunting? what about those ostriches).
The controls may be a bit awkward for newcomers to learn, but once you get into the hang of it, its not so bad.
Inventory:  It becomes very annoying when you have to transfer items from you backpack to your trunk, having to click the "tick" when there's more than one said item in the stack.  It slows you down and becomes a drag.  I'd imagine this is something they'd get to work on as well
The good;
Incredibly addictive gameplay.   If you are a fan of "the walking dead' or any one of the survivalist zombie type series/movies then this will be your crack addiction.  It achieves what Day Z, dead rising and all those other quick-fix zombie apoc survival games does not.
You get to build a camp with 3 other friends (or alone) which can be tended to without everyone needing to be online at the same time.  Each person can just log on and do his/her part when time permits.  Playing together is obviously way more fun and lets you organise some seriously fun base building operations.
The "quests" or missions are rather well polished for something that is still in early access.  This deserves a special mention as mission/quest dynamics are usually the thing that suffers most during early access.  I've come to about level 14 and so far I've had one "somewhat" buggy mission to do (getting a package out of an undead pelican!).
The "main map" where you build your camp does appear like there will be exanded areas added to.  This area in itself is brilliant.  It's where you end up foraging for flint, medical herbs and all other kinds of stuff with friends (supply runs!).
Now if they'd just add a persistent city, much like the main area... just wow.

For me, this was a welcome return to the world of half walls. I haven't really been thrilled with cover mechanic games since Vanquish, but this I enjoyed. It shares a lot of similarites with Gears of War based on mechanics, all the same joys and ills. However, my biggest complaint with Gears, is the overly drab, too much machismo, stupidity that permeates the characters, the story and the gameplay. The sci-fi paranoia of this is much more engaging, and doesn't turn me off. The colour palette and retro feel is more refreshing, too.
Additionally, The Bureau distances itself from Gears with squad controls, and various perks. The perks are almost all fun and engaging to deploy across all the various classes, and there were a couple of missions where I just let my squad and their perks take charge. However, with every squad command game there are issues: here too, your squad will move from the cover you've placed them to freelance a bit, even if they've taken minimal fire, hopping into the open to get roasted. If they manage to survive this gambit out from cover, another issue comes into play. Whether its moving a squadmate, or deploying a perk, it must be steered across a path that a human can travel. This sometimes means you can't get your squad to quickly hop back over a wall they just jumped, and sometimes you can't trhow deployables over half walls.
Overall though, this is a very competent cover mechanic game with light squad strategies, playing somewhat similarly, but perhpas more robust than the later Mass Effects.
For those who dismiss it because it isn't XCOM, or XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you're right, it isn't, not even nearly, but that's gaming royalty, too. You'll see some familiar aliens from the franchise, and be told a decent narrative that is almost so disconnected from XCOM that it won't impact your experiences with that game either way. I say sit back, enjoy a fun, light romp through alien paranoia of the atomic age.

I'm just going to clerify this now. I love the original XCOM games. The ones that were hard as hell, and made everything into a exceedingly one sided game of Russian Roulette.
That being said, I can't honestly recommend The Bureau. While it is an XCOM game, it just lacks the feeling of XCOM. The chance to hit doesn't mean anything like it did in the old games, and as long as you have line of sight it's almost always a hit. There is strategy in it, and I do appreciate their attempt to make height and range a factor in battle. But the skills that your units gain from combat make it too easy to bulldoze through the aliens.
On the other hand, it does have a very interesting story. One that shows history in a stranger light, and almost seems like it came from a tabloid magazine or some conspiracy theorist's mind. It's interesting, but could have been so much more. XCOM is known as a world organization, yet in this game is only shown as a United States one. Yes, there is reasoning for it in the story, but that doesn't mean that you have to limit the game map to just the US. What about Canada? Or Mexico? Maybe Europe or Asia? What happened there? How did they fight? Did they fight?
Maybe thats just me asking too many questions. But there are plot holes that could have been filled. Overall, it is ok. Not good enough for me to recommend it to anyone, but still stable enough to be played and enjoyed by some. Graphicly, it looked nice. Explosions and blood was somewhat realistic, and the details in the aliens was nice. Gameplay wise, it could have been stronger, and less formulated like most 3rd person shooters.
I'd honestly give it a 3/5 rating, with a strong warning to anyone who wants to buy it.

Despite my initial hesitance toward the change of style for this game (from its initial showings), it's a surprisingly competent tactical TPS set in the early XCOM universe. It begins as your standard cover based shooter, but once you've moved onto the first main operation, opens up quite a bit as you unlock new abilities for both yourself and your squad mates. In some early game operations you can still sit behind cover for most firefights and take potshots at enemies, but a) that's *really* boring and b) doesn't work on harder difficulties (I played on "hard," I guess, but there's still one difficulty above that).
In many of the later operations, enemies will flank your position, throw grenades to flush you out, or rush you head on with cloaked enemies and mutons with jetpacks. The fun (and frustration) comes from flanking enemies with your squad mates (giving you a damage bonus) and using their abilites to funnel enemies into your line of fire, but I found myself in many battles to constantly be waiting for my heal ability to be on cooldown, or running around reviving my squad who have run out of cover for no reason. The game doesn't seemingly give you the ability to "keep" your squad in certain positions; sure, you can order them around, but it always felt that once I moved far enough away (far enough being not very far) they would move out of cover and subsequently die, forcing me to take a ton of damage to revive them and waste my heal ability on myself.
All that aside (and despite some minor quirks I had with the controls) I enjoyed my time with it. It's no XCOM UFO Defense or even Enemy Unknown for that matter, but it offers enough challenge and tactical options to be worth one playthrough.

I purchased the game not too long ago when it was in the 1.3.2 build, at a rather hefty price of S$34.99. With consideration of the game engine, I honestly believe the price should not have exceeded S$20, which would've been a rather reasonable price for a renowned game in the RTS industry. Regardless, I bought the game with high expectations and enjoyed the time I have spent on it especially with all sorts of mods. Recently, I noticed the price has shot up to an exorbitant amount of S$56.49 with DLCs ranging from prices S$13.99 to S$20.99. While DLCs are not mandatory to make the gameplay enjoyable, the lack of diversity in the base game is worrying. Without mods, I am certain a day worth of gameplay will surely bore me to death. Thus, seeing how Paradox has further worsened their marketing strategy by increasing the prices of all products exponentially, I continue to lose faith in their future games. Unless you're filthy rich, I advise strongly to not purchase the game at all. It is not worth at its current price level and will continue to be so.

The Eyes of Ara is a paradox, a dichotomy, a conundrum. It is both visually and audibly stunning. The progression from one area to the next is logical and clearly prompted, provided you're paying attention. But the puzzles, oh the puzzles. My brain hasn't had to work this hard playing a game since the Myst series. The benefit of this though, is that while some puzzles are frustratingly difficult to work out, there is a massive sense of satisfaction in completing a room, unlocking a door, and moving on to the next. Brilliance. Absolute brilliance.

The first two thirds of the game are challenging and fun, and set up an interesting little mystery.
Unfortunaly the last third of the game really fell apart for me. The puzzles stopped being challenging and became much more obscure, and the solutions didn't always make sense. They also became very non-linear which got extremely overwhelming. Some of the puzzle logic got pretty thin.
There's a couple of puzzles that aren't really deducable, but are instead a huge time sink of fiddling with matching pictures up. I much prefer a riddle that needs to be solved. Also, I would have appreciated the option to keep codes and notes in the inventory so that they are easier to refer to later, instead of relying on memory or taking hard-copy notes.
Unfortunatly the game got so irritating in the last third that I was just waiting for it to end, instead of being interested in the conclusion. And the end of the story is very lackluster.
I liked this game ok overall.
If you like Puzzles, this is the game for you.

Every now and then, the game threatens to pique your curiousity with its story, but that generally gets dropped quite quickly, lost among the extremely padded gameplay.
There's only really three positive things I think I can say about the game. The first, not many of the OBLIGATORY OBLIGATORY OBLIGATORY action sequences that we've all played in a dozen different games, and really the worst are wave-survival segments and boss segments. The game, aside from the boring third-person shooting and waist-high wall clinging, generally does its own thing. Additionally, at first, the game seems to have drawn a lot of inspiration from Cold War thriller novels and films, and create an identity for it. The third is that the game seems to tie into XCOM: Enemy Unknown much more than it needed to, although much of this is shallow. Unfortunately, the game uses neither of these positives very much, and contributes very little to the experience.
I must mention the major bugs and technical problems I also experienced. Sometimes, when you go through doorways, the floor hasn't spawned yet, and you fall under the map. Yes, THE FLOOR DOESN'T SPAWN, and it happened during every mission I played after the first one, and quite frequently at the base. Similarly, issues like doors not opening when they're scripted to (because heaven forbid they trust the player to open a door), or entire combat sequences being skipped over because the enemies don't even spawn. The game is fortunate to have a good checkpoint system, because you're going to be doing it often for how often these bugs occur. As for other technical issues, the game runs really quite poorly, embarrassingly so, with the framerate often tanking to below 10 FPS, whereas my system can run games that are significantly better looking without experiencing the same issues. Audio cuts out occassionally, especially during cutscenes. Many of the key commands have inconsistent responsiveness.
Just don't even bother playing this game. Its not even a game that is spectacularly bad that you can get entertainment from it that way. The only reason anybody remembers that the game exists is because "XCOM" was attached to the title. This is 12 GB of memory that can be put to better use elsewhere.

In general, there’s little to recommend as far as The Bureau goes. The game essentially tries so hard to be 60s Mass Effect, but really only succeeds on the former front, in that it’s 60s as hell. Seriously, it’s the sole shining point here; The Bureau is inundated with shirt-tie-and-vest combos, classic cars, transistor tube radios, and chrome as far as the eye can see, which really injects the proceedings with a much-needed sense of atmosphere. Unfortunately, everything else solidly falls within the realm of mediocrity; the blandly-written protagonist is your typical gruff “tormented past, seeks redemption through fighting the new threat” archetype, and the gameplay that you experience through him is a weird, somewhat tedious fusion of third-person shooter and XCOM-style strategy.
Don’t get me wrong, the visuals and effects of the abilities themselves are quite cool (especially in the late game, where you get access to turrets and airstrikes), but you have to hand-hold the inept AI that utilizes them so much that, in the end, you’re gonna be spending 50% of the time shepherding them through every action via Battle Focus (this game’s tactical view), and the other 50% running around and reviving them because they’re so goddamned fragile. Seriously, does the COM in XCOM stand for “Clothes Only, Men”? … (I’m so, so sorry.) Anyway, as a result there is a sort of franticness to the combat in that regard, but unlike its sister game Enemy Unknown, the management of lives is more frustrating than heart-poundingly tense due to the increased repetition and frequency at which “getting downed” occurs. In any case, if you end up purchasing this game (I personally wouldn’t unless it’s less than 7ish dollars), play on “Squaddie” difficulty or below, as there is less a focus on team micro-management, and more an emphasis on blasting aliens with space magic.

An excellent little game that's pretty hard to get into.
Naturally, this game is hard. For your first week of playing it, you'll do little more than flop onto the ground in a pile of limbs. Then, you get better at it. Much better. Suddenly, you're grabbing your opponent, reefing him towards you and breaking his torso open with your knee.
If anything, I'd wish for this game to become as big and competitive as CS:GO or Dota 2, even with international championships. If there's anything infinite about this game, it's room to improve, and I can imagine just how skillful these professional ESports players would get given a large cash prize and this game. There would some godlike skills at those championships.
Of course, that's never gonna happen, sadly. In the meantime, I'll settle for wrapping my legs around my opponent until his waist splits in two, or doing the inverted japanese schoolgirl pose to avoid an oncoming bullet.
So, now that all that is over, "What is Toribash"?
It's a martial arts combat game where you control every part of your body separately. Unlike other fighting games, you don't use pre-animated moves to fight. Everything is physics based, with you controlling each part of your body. Naturally, this leads to you being able to do any move you want, ever. You can perform all kinds of moves using your own skill. The game runs off a turn-based system where you and your opponent move their limbs within a set frame of time, once that time is up, the turn plays out with your intended changes having their effects.
The game does have multiplayer, of course, so now you and another player can battle, turn after turn, limb by limb trying to build up enough momentum to kick your foot through your opponent's torso.
The game also has mods, which don't require any downloads. You can merely go into this giant list, pick a mod and play it. Anything you could want is there, and if it isn't, you can use the handy inbuilt mod maker to create your own scenario to fight in. Certain mods add new weapons like swords, daggers, overwhelmingly massive Zweihanders and interesting situations such as the Jesus Copter, which puts one player holding onto a cross with a propeller on it, and the other player hurtling towards that cross so the two can engage in an interesting battle.
Or maybe you want one player riding down a zipline towards the other? Or how about a trapeze? Or do you wanna fight over a giant spinning blade so that the first person to fall will get diced? Maybe you want to try to skillfully navigate through a maze of lasers like a Mission Impossible laser grid, or attempt a Dishonored-like air assassination on one of your friends?
Whatever situation you want to fight in, there's likely a mod for it.
And lastly, the game is free. You know you wanna toss your friend into helicopter propellers and watch them explode, especially if you can do so for free.

Although I've enjoyed to play HoI II a lot and HoI III somewhat, I've been fairly reluctant to buy HoI IV. That's due to the bad reviews and Paradox obnoxious DLC policy.
Now that is has been on sale, I've bought the base game and enjoyed my first single player match. The series has made a huge leap from a stat manager to a WW2 simulator, which is nice. The army AI has been improved a lot. For the first time in a HoI game I feel comfortable to let the AI manage all fronts, finetuning it with order adjustments and an occasional direct order.
The Production system overhaul is a step into the right direction as well. You produce parts like artillery, tanks and weapons independently from divisions now, which just pick up the best equipment available in your stock upon recruitment. Old equipment gets gradually replaced once better equipment is researched and produced or salvaged from your enemy. That's nice and adds a great deal of immersion to the game.
Overall plenty of tedious micro-management aspects have been stripped and less new details have been added which increase the immersion. The base game is fun on its own, so I can recommend it. Like always with Paradox titles I can't help to feel ripped off though, when I see DLCs adding content, which clearly should have been included in the base game.

Preface:
For whatever reason, the steam timer says I have only a few minutes of playtime. I`ll include a screenshot at the end with my accurate playtime. Also, this review will feature slight puzzle spoilers.
Review:
This game has its high points but ultimately suffers from some major annoyances. Personally, while I did enjoy it for the first few hours, knowing what I know now, I wouldn't have gotten it. In essence, I cannot recommend it since it does cater to a more completionist mindset.
When it comes to playtime, I would say mine was around 6-7 hours when I got near to the end, I did go AFK plenty of times and left it on for a night (I currently have over 17 hours total.) Obviously your playtime will vary on how long you spend searching and analyzing puzzles. So from the price point perspective, you're getting decent mileage.
The one good thing I can definately say about this game is it's puzzles. The problems presented were logical in hindsight as opposed to other adventure games and do require a bit of thought. Each tougher entry always has a clue to be found, though some can be rather obtuse, but in my case I had zero to very little trouble working them out till the close end. That is not to say that everything was fine.
One of the weakest points of Eyes of Ara comes from its odd design. In the game, the puzzle scope is sectioned off, so you don't have to wonder around the whole house in order to progress... for the most part. This can be seen in practice as moving to a new loading zone will remove your current inventory. The kicker here is that the game allows you to progress not finding everything until when I realized I needed to go back and collect 2 early blue orbs in order to reach the final room. At that point I just facepalmed.
This reaction was propelled by the literal paper thin story. When you're moving from room to room and spending valuable time thinking about puzzles you need some sort of string to tie this thing together in order to keep you motivated. In my opinion the story was meh and the only reason I read/skimmed the few journal entries detailing the past was to seek clues for puzzles. By the time I got to the top part of the tower (planetarium) I was ready to row the boat back where I came from.
To add to injury, some of the items needed are really hard to spot and progression is halted when you know you're missing an item and you spend searching from room to room moving your mouse over everything. In one particular instance, in the planetarium, I found an item by accident that led me to find the clue needed. This inconvinience is compounded by another wonky design decision where in a close-up view the mouse icon does not change to signal that an item can be interacted with so you're left clicking on plenty of items just to be sure you've got everything taken care of.
Overall, the game seemed to drag on for me with ultimately no payoff due to the fact that I would have to go back and search god knows where for another 2 orbs in order to progress. With the previous faults stated, you shoud see my reluctance to accomplish this. Fortunately, at that point, I was simply too tired to give a damn and never looked back.

Costume Quest is one of my favorites - unique and dripping with the innocence of halloween most of us are too old to experience anymore, it's the type of game that makes you smile on its premise and presentation alone. Throw in fun - if simple - game mechanics, good humor, endearing characters and a plot out of a saturday morning cartoon: it's a really good package, and as something I can replay every year, it's more-than worth the TEN dollar asking price.
At its core it's a super simple turn-based RPG, but even its RPG mechanics have fun mechanics much like those from the original Paper Mario. You can fare better in battle with timed button presses to increase damage and defense. There are battle stamps that work like the badges from Paper Mario, which give each character a boost or a special command. It's really not that deep, but the fights are just difficult enough to require some kind of strategy. Not because they're complex or anything, but because the enemies will simply overpower you with force if you don't have a battle stamp equipped and aren't successful with the timed button presses.
For example - the Statue of Liberty costume has a special attack (which charge up through using regular attacks) that heals the party a small amount. It's a very small amount, but it can make or break a fight. The game is good about pitting you against enemies that are just a little bit tougher than your party, so you can't just breeze through them. There are also no random battles: all enemies appear on the screen, unless you meet them through trick-or-treating, and they don't regenerate - so there is a set number of battles per zone. This works well with the mechanics, as there are set items and experience you earn from the enemies you fight. That means you really must fight every enemy in the zone to get the full amount of experience, candy (currency) and items afforded to you.
You move between transitional dungeons and hub zones, where you have to trick-or-treat at houses or stores to progress through the story. You won't be able to do that all right away, though - you'll need to do random quests for kids around the zones, collect candy, bob for apples, trade stuff, and find parts to make new costumes which grant you new field abilities, so you can progress further. The zones are really detailed and oozing with character - they're fun to run around and don't usually outstay their welcome. My only gripes are without a map, it can be hard to find that one last house you need to trick-or-treat at to progress the story, or that one last enemy you need to fight. Also some of the dungeons drag on a little bit - but as I write below, if you're finding the game to drag, you probably just need to take a break.
The plot is simple - your sister is kidnapped and you have to find her. There are goblins running around, but the adults think they're just kids in costumes. The goblins want candy for some reason, there's a main villain witch, etc. etc. It's really cute, and serviced by some great humor. The game is almost south-parkian in the way that the kids have gotten over their heads in a very real situation to which the adults are totally oblivious. It makes it funnier when the adults names are all literally "grown up".
Costume Quest is a game to play in small spurts, as otherwise the mechanics will begin to get repetitive and you'll lose sight of the charm and atmosphere that makes the game so enjoyable. When I say repetitive, I mean the combat and actual field exploration can, yes, get really samey. It's best to play maybe half a zone at once and then take a break. You really owe it to this game and yourself to enjoy every minute of it, and that can't happen if you're just going through the motions.
Costume Quest is a gem. It captures the feel of Halloween perfectly and if you're in the right mood, it can make you feel like a kid again. Like you really are out trick-or-treating with some friends, in a world of make-believe. Buy this, play it (during halloween), and then play the Grubbins on Ice DLC (that comes with it) during Christmas.
I haven't actually played the Grubbins on Ice DLC yet, but I've heard great things about it. Albeit - it's a short little extra side-story that only take a few hours.

Costume Quest is very different from any other Halloween game I've ever seen. It's not a simple "BOO! Happy Halloween!" game that you find on Google's homepage. It's a full on RPG with a charming artstyle, great music, fun gameplay, and a lovable team of monster slaying children (seriously, the idea of putting on an adorable costume and then transforming into the the actual thing it was based off of was an epic idea :P). If you're sick of playing horror games during the Halloween season and just want a cute and fun game to play, look no further than Costume Quest!

I never knew that goats could be so violent - and so utterly indestructible.
In the beginning, I found that my goaty avatar could jump.  We jumped over things - boxes, fences... and then onto a handily placed trampoline!  This was fun!!!
Of course, jumping was just the beginning; my goat was quite horny, and so I wanted to make use of those vicious ivories.  Yes, my goat could smash boxes.  Break fences.  Explode cars?  WOW!  This was also a good means of getting around, as my goaty gamester was thrown some distance by the explosion.  We wandered some more, and found a group of protestors, protesting... something.  Time to give them a chance to get really upset - oh boy, did they scatter when my goat started in on the poor innocent protestors.
A little further in my wanderings, I found a petrol station.  Hmm... cars explode, I wonder what - OH BOY!  My goaty avatar was blown sky-high, and had a great opportunity to surveil the surrounds on the way down.  (Yes, he - or was it she? - survived this explosion as well.)
I soon learned that goats can climb ladders, and made my way to the top of a tall crane.  Great view, but goat lacks the opposable thumbs necessary to control this thing.  Oh well, time to get down.  Hmm - is that a pool below?  Or should I aim for one of those trampolines?  Turns out I am not good at steering goats from the top of towers onto small trampolines - but this goat was nothing if not resilient.
There is much, much more for me to discover and learn in this game.  For now, all I can say is it has my goat - I mean, vote.

I'd heard about Hatoful.  I'd laughed at the premise. "A DATING SIM ABOUT PIGEONS?! HA!"  I held out playing it for so long because it just seemed to hilarious to be true.  And then.... I downloaded the demo.  Let me tell you, at first, I was just, "Oh, this game is so cute!  Look at these adorable interactions!"  I completed the demo with Yuuya and was completely enamored.  I /needed/ the full version.  Enter Steam, releasing it in HD.
Dear Puddi, I never expected this game to give me what I got.  There's so much going on that you cannot glean from just playing one or two routes.  Play the whole thing.  Then play the BBL route and cry a million tears.  Cute game, yeah right.  More like vicious emotionally destructive game.  And I don't regret buying it--I regret laughing at it and putting it off as some dumb game.  Why there isn't more light on Hatoful is beyond me, because it's a beautiful game.  Does it have its errors?  Of course, doesn't every game?  It's well put together, though, and any errors in the script don't detract from the game (they may make you read the segment a few times, but it's definitely not game-breaking).  I've played a dating sim or two in my time, but this one is probably the best.  These are well-written characters, with feathers, of course.  It's easy to develop a connection with them because they are so well-written with hidden histories and pasts that you can find in Moa's mangas (available on Amazon!).
TL;DR: If you have any preconceptions about this game, FORGET THEM.  Buy it and try it for yourself.  Don't watch someone else play it, and don't just brush it off as some dumb game, because it's definitely worth the hours it takes to play it fully and completely.
Happy Birding ♥
P.S.: If you buy Hatoful and you enjoy it and want to put yourself through additional pain and misery, there is a sequel called "Holiday Star," available in English (i.e.: you don't need to patch it) for about $3, if I remember right.  Just visit Moa's wordpress and you can get it!
2016 Update:  I still love this game.  I still feel crushed every time I think about the true ending, and everytime I see an image of Shuu.  Definitely worth the money and time spent.

I originally bought this game for the lolz since the general idea for this game is "Oh it's a dating sim... for birds.. lol" So originally, I played it as such. But as I carried on through the different routes you could take, I found each story more and more compelling. So many twists and turns and things that just randomly straight up hit you in the feels or made you think "wtf just happened?"
The main story is really creative and the genre twist really takes you through a loop and keeps you hooked. And for birds, the characters are really well developed.
I think the makers of this game knew exactly what they were doing. I want to take the player into a false sense of "This is going to be hilarious and stupid" Which granted, at some points, that's what it does. Very well. It's really funny.
When really it's building you up for a huge unexpected story hit. All the different routes are just branches of character developments, readying you for the main plot. I applaud that.
Over all, I'd actually recommend buying this game and doing exactly what everyone else is doing. Go in while not taking this game seriously at all and let it change your mind. Because it seriously will. Then it'll leave you there to sit there and think about how unexpectedly brilliantly done it is. Mediatonic, Hato Moa... hats off to you, this was a great experience.

This game is alread looking to be the best of it's genre, and it's not even near complete.
The game looks wonderful, controls really well, and while there are a few glitches here and there, nothing is gamebreaking or majorly intrusive. The music and general atmosphere are spot on as well. A little short in singleplayer, but it's fellow survival/exploration games aren't much better in that aspect. Everything from exploring to combat to driving vehicles gives you a sense of awe and wonder.
A few complaints i do have is how enemies spawn. Trecking through so much ground with no life in sight, and then as soon as you whack a mining node you get swarmed is a little jarring and weird.
The other issue is how certain aspects of the game currently seem useless. There's virtually no need for the biodome, melee weapons, rover, and even the mech as of the time of this review. Hopefully that will change in the future with development.
Overall, this is a great game, and is going to be even better in the future, which is why i'm not recommending it now. Once this game is near completion or is completed, i will recommend it, because this is one title you really should not burn yourself out on early, and wait for its full glory.
If you do decide to get this game anyways, let me offer you four tips:
1. Water, rubber, and lithium are the most tedious resources to get or synthesize. Put all your effort into finding a Rubber Tree, making a water reclaimer, and finding the lithium/diamond cave early on. It'll save you a lot of time and pain later on when you get into advanced building and crafting.
2. Once you can make vehicles, make the Spaceship first. Don't bother with the rover or mech in singleplayer. Also, the spaceship will only successfuly land and let you get out of it on completely flat ground.
3. If you do not wish to die a horrible death to enemies, don't go far out at night or in sandstorms, don't become burdened, don't charge headfirst into craters, and if the three main hostiles do attack, just jump or stand on a raised platform to avoid their attacks. They CAN hit you through vehicles. Rushing enemies after their first charge will confuse their AI, but melee weapons have too small of a hitbox to make this tactic super effective. Do not cook or throw away any Crab Monster parts at first.
4. What item you are holding determines movement speed, and if you press E to holster your item, you can "sprint" with your boosters, making long distances or quick escapes on foot much faster.

Let me begin with these points:
It's a survival game - which means there WILL be some grinding.
It's early access - which means there WILL be bugs.
There are some reviews that complain about these 2 things but as of the date of this review it actually plays quite nicely in terms of stability.  I think there are some inefficiencies which drag the frame down a bit, usually I sit around 40 frames with a medium to high powered machine.
The grinding? Ok well I'll admit there is like 2 or 3 resources that are tricky to find the first time but once you found where they are, it's a piece of cake.  The resources in this game all respawn after some time and in the exact same position where they were, which in my opinion is a little sucky once you got the basics down.  Respawn = good, same place = meh, not my thing, I like to explore but each to their own.
The game is multiplayer (and single player if you prefer), both on public and private servers (private servers still use developer owned clusters), and for my experience has been pretty smooth.  I have a private server with some buddies in the US and we experience minimal lag, at least nothing noticable to me (being Australian) no matter who creates the server.  There are occasional disconnects but again nothing to excessive (could just be crappy Aussie internet).
NOTE: If you're going to play on public servers, it is no different than any other online game.  THERE WILL BE TROLLS - Learn to live with it or play a private server, don't blame the game for it!
I think at the moment the game strikes a reasonably good balance between single player and multiplayer (both PvE and PvP), although I think it is designed with a more PvP focus.  To elaberate: you can get some good game time and enjoyment for many hours in single player or a PvE server but in my opinion I think ultimately you'll want to migrate to PvP for replayability.  This could change in future as they add more planets.
Ok now to wrap it up!  Do I recommend? Yes, if you like survival games, science fiction and exploration it's a pretty sweet game.
As I mentioned there ARE bugs but nothing too great as far as I've experienced just minor things like creatures clipping through walls, items disappearing from inventory occasionally, textures not showing right, buggy AI's etc.  Nothing I would call "game breaking".
All in all I like it and I have fun with it NOW and it has much potential for the future!

Had XCOM: Enemy Unknown never been released and all we had was this game, I would say not recommend this game simply on principle. If this game was the reincarnation of the classic XCOM it would be sad. Like old Rainbow Six getting Vegas-ified.
However, since its not and classic XCOM still exists in some form, its safe to say this game isn't bad. In fact it was surprisingly good.
Gameplay
This is where this distinction between TB:XCOM and classic XCOM could have come into play. Minus the turnbase style of classic XCOM this is actually pretty close. Close enough, in my opinion, that this game might have replaced the classic style for many that were new to the series.
TB:XCOM is a squad-based TPS and its actually fairly well done. The controls are "slighty" clunky in areas, but still good. Your companion AI is useful, as are their skills. Overall its pretty fun, if a bit easy.
Story
Is meh. Its somewhat disjointed and the voice acting is pretty "blah" for the most part. It felt like there were parts missing. Don't buy this for an engaging narrative.
Visuals
Great for the most part, but un-optimized. It seems the Physx effects could have used work. I've played games with more Physx effect and they ran fine, but in this they seemed way too intensive than they should have been. It wasn't a "buggy" game, but it wasn't polished either.
Overall
It's actually a good game and an interesting take on XCOM and because it didn't replace the classic XCOM, I can safely recommend it.
EDIT: Game needs to be updated for 900 series cards. Since it evidently won't be, I can't recommend a game that can't work with updated cards it 2015, there's no excuse.

If you are upset about the Mass Effect series not being completely available on Steam due to EA's dickery, then The Bureau may be for you.  If nothing, it is Mass Effect-lite, and here is why (spoilers):
-Man vs. Aliens trope, which would be easily overlooked had it not been a copy of Mass Effect in every other regard except quality.
-Cover-based shooting with bad AI in your trio, but the AI here is FAR worse.  More on this below.
-Minor RPG elements, but not enough to feel noteworthy growth.
-Meaningless dialogue "choices."
-Needless weapons-only, no-actual-content DLC in addition to regular content DLC which could have been patched in instead of charged for due to how minor it is.
-Alien named Asaru.
-"Decontamination chamber" and elevator loading screens between parts of your base.
-One of your opening trio dies.
-There is indoctrination via The Bureau's Sleepwalking illness.
-Suicide mission!  Which you survive!
-The choice to kill a main character because he became furious with rage at the situation of working with a specific species, or to let him live.
-The choice within the same stretch to decide which one of two different characters gets to live while the other dies because you can only physically go to one of the two locations.
-Protagonist is the savior of everyone.
-To say nothing of the ending...
The Bureau would be an alright game if the AI were not so impossibly bad.  Your squadmates will run into their deaths and leave safe cover for no reason whatsoever, and if they ever get lifted by a drone and you did not see it, you may as well accept them as dead since it cancels the commands which you input for them--resulting in "default" AI behaviour.  The first major operation is when I realised just how bad this game would be because of it, and my opinion did not change throughout the rest of the game or in the Hangar 6 DLC.  If the AI worked, this game would work, and it is as simple as that.  Since the AI does NOT work for♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game does not work for♥♥♥♥♥♥  There was so much of this game to like if you actually play it (because of the series which it copied in form), but the AI will justifiably make people NOT want to ever finish it.
Also, it has PSOne quality cutscenes at times, which is just baffling when the rest of the game's graphics work just fine.  It breaks continuity because of just how 1990s the graphics become in those few scenes before returning to the superior gameplay graphics.  This seems like laziness on the part of the developers to not fully create the same cutscenes using in-game graphics, but that is just a strange creative choice more than a game flaw proper, as flawed of a choice as it is.  The game is really short, too, clocking ~25 hours for a complete playthrough when you watch all scenes and do all missions / sidequests.

I waited along time for this game, and after almost 400 hours of playtime I feel the need to share my thoughts to any potential buyers.
pros:
-alot of replayability
-each country provides its own opprutunities and challenges

cons:
-overly simplistic game mechanics

-AI is very stupid, for instance germany will declare war on the soviet union even if its losing the war with the allies, AI seems to follow national focus tree regardless of whether or not it makes sense to do so
-extremely over-priced DLC which adds very little to the game, the DLC is around 33% of the price of the full game and adds maybe 5% of the content, and the content it does add includes very minor features which were part of the base game in previous HOI titles.
-the base game is over-priced. when compared to other paradox titles such as eu4 or ck2 you get half the content and it costs alot more.
-no option to kick a country from your faction once they join, sometimes countries join your faction automatically meaning that world conquest is impossible if there are other nations in your faction. this forces the player to disband their faction if they want world conquest. basically this is a good example of a game mechanic that is so broken it actually makes sense for the player to avoid it completely in many cases, this undermines the value of what little content this game has.
Im sure the guys at paradox are good people but their business model is very exploitative to the consumer and this is unacceptable considering how loyal and dedicate the paradox fanbase is.

Probably the cutest game Double Fine has ever made, with a fantastic premise and decent execution. It's short but the length is nice for what it is, there are numerous laugh-out-loud moments with the dialogue, the environments are detailed and look quite nice, and the plot, while simple, is pretty enjoyable. The game is very easy in terms of its turn-based battles, so if you're looking for a challenge, look somewhere else. I do think it works very well as an "introductory RPG", though, and can be used to teach newcomers to the genre about basic RPG tactics like prioritizing enemies, diversifying your party's classes, making strategic decisions about abilities, and choosing when to use special moves so they will be most effective. A solid game that makes for a fun Halloween night.

It's no secret that people enjoy spooking themselves throughout October. Some may dabble into the horrific imagery, the classic monsters, the eldritch horrors or the psychological drama of fear. All of these qualities are what many would consider as connotations of Halloween.
Halloween for me, however, has never been about the scares. While I may sound to be admiring the commercialism itself, I've always been reminded of Trick-or-Treating, Halloween cartoons/specials, and of the creativity/love for the holiday, especially the costumes. These are the qualities adults and kids alike treat themselves to every year.
These sentiments are why I find myself revisiting Costume Quest as a tradition. It provides a light-hearted, four to six hour adventure (with the DLC and all the extra quests) that captures the qualities I enjoy the most. Its shortened length and kid-like spectacle perfectly shows the forgotten fondness we have for the holiday of fears.
CQ itself has nothing unique that hasn't been seen in TV specials, movies or games. Its set-up is that you play as the brother/sister of a family, and you must rescue your sibling from the clutches of an evil witch bent on taking over Halloween with all the candy. (Also possibly not to get grounded).
However, what the plot lacks in originality, the game's humor and execution provide something that shows its charm for being derivative of all the things kids and adults love about Halloween.
If you grew up in the '90s like myself, then you probably are familiar with the trick-or-treat game from Cartoon Network. You walked around an small map with magical costumes, collecting candy from doors and obstacles in a time-limit for high-scores.
Costume Quest shares the basic idea of a magical realism setting where the costumes themselves provide supernatural powers for kids. Instead of a competitive, high-score game, CQ is a traditional JRPG game with Paper Mario-like mechanics and various HUB maps to explore.
Compared to the Cartoon Network game, the maps are much larger along with providing mini-games and alternative quests for hidden rewards. Outside of combat, every costume provides an ability that varies in its utility. The quests are basic fetch or talk quests, and the level-design is a linear set of checkboxes given some player freedom to wander off. You won't be breaking the game's order of events or getting late-game costumes early.
When in combat, the kids transform themselves into a larger-than-life representation of their costume in what can be thought of as a Power Rangers mech fight. Enemies' designs are dramatized as well to make the combat more visually interesting than watching a blue-box robot fighting demons in bath-robes. That visual alone is how the fighting mechanics should be thought of: Absurd and simple.
Like Paper Mario, the turn-based battles are broken up by quick-time-events that add/lower the damage you deal. The player's team and the enemy's take turns trading hits, and while you are on the defensive you can block attacks to lessen the blow. Some costumes have unique abilities like the Knight's Shield (defense buff), the Robot's Missle Barrage and the Lady Libery's Anthem (healing skill).
To say that the combat system is basic would be stating the obvious. There are eleven costumes in the main game, and three new ones in the DLC. Each costume has its one-tailored playstyle and set of skills, separated by one of three costume types like rock-paper-and-scissors, and they each provide enough lasting appeal to keep the game from getting too stale with a limited roster. The game knows its combat isn't its greatest suit, so the variety and short length go a long way to keep the monotonous gameplay as low as possible.
As far as the game's other problems, if the game's charm doesn't sell you on it right away, then the gameplay, in and out of combat, won't sell you on the rest of the experience.
The writing isn't Double Fine's best as it relies a lot on tropes, especially the protagonist and his/her companions, but the subversions from the player's character towards not carrying about the plot helps mitigate that issue. (Kind of like how Doomguy doesn't care about the plot in his recent game.) This is something the DLC as well as CQ2 fail to grasp as the plot relies on characters explaining the techno babble of wormholes. Neither one captures the same charm as the original.
While Costume Quest is certainly not one of Double Fine's greatest successes it is an experience I would easily recommend to others. Usually I would have something more profound to say to end a review but CQ is simply a decent game.  It's nothing innovative in its gameplay, story or even its basic idea, but the way everything comes together nicely makes me longing for next Halloween to replay it again.
A short, but very enjoyable game that is perfect to play around the Halloween season.

In the initial release of 'Evolve', also known as Stage 1, it boasted a $60 price tag. Because of the selective gameplay shown by the developers and play-testers, the game looked like it was a masterpiece. Hype flew around the game for months while everyone waited for the initial release. Upon release, like other games, I refrained from immediately buying it, and instead seeing what others had to say about the game. Without a doubt, the community came across as dissappointed in the work done on the game. Months of development had seemed to prove nothing, and those who bought the game ran out of hope quickly. To make matters worse, all of the content that was added to the game, such as new monsters to play as, had a DLC price tag. The game saw little to no players daily, and there seemed to be no hope for Evolve.
However, years after its release, the Evolve team decided to make it free to play. Taking the community by surprise, the game had exactly 0 pay walls. Everything in the game is unlocked through playing. There is only one form of currency in the game: "Silver keys" which are only obtainable through playing games. There really isn't a reason to not get this game. The reason it's still mixed is because people who spent the full founders fee on the game are mad because it's free years later. They got their moneys worth for years, and most of the founders stopped playing the game anyway. After the game went F2P, founders came back to the game they had long abandoned and said, "Boo hoo, wipe my butt because I made a bad investment!"
Pros:
>Fully free to play
>No pay walls
>Hours of original content
>Insane fast paced battles
>High sense of reward when each team wins
>Feels like a constant Gears of War Raam boss fight
>Easy to learn, hard to master format
Cons:
>A large majority of the game consists of tracking the monster, and chasin it, leading understandably impatient players to dislike the game
>Not many monsters to choose from, this can feel repetitive and constant
>The game has a bad past, leading many characters to disregard Stage 2 as garbage
>18 GB file size
I recommend at least trying this game, if you are a patient gamer looking for rewarding content.

Early Access - early evaluation
-- please note game is constantly changing with multiple balancing and bug fixing patches along with less frequent but big content patches, this is not my final say but from what I can see this game can only get better --
TLDR: This is a true and unique gem of a game. To me, it stands strong among others like Gothic for example, in terms of being unique and sucking you in.
If you want to know what this game is: Ambiguous answer would be Dark Souls RTS, a better description would be very hard, survival, zombie, rogue like rts game.
The good:
+ soundtrack - catchy and fits the theme
+ I generally don't like steam punk settings but this game pulls it off beautifully
+ zombie game done right (it's hard to use something as overused as zombies and make it interesting
+ simple elements put together skillfully
+ randomization of maps
+ decent array of building and defensive options, with soldiers having advantages for different scenarios
+ excellent combination of tower defense, rts and rogue like
+ plenty of resources to manage, basic ones: wood, stone, gold, iron, oil etc., slightly more complex ones like population, food and then complex like space, you have to not only think how to secure resources but plan your expansion and optimise building cluster
+ some buildings have impact on other and should be built in proximity to boost benefits of the economy
+ simple rpg like mayor system giving you small benefits, but also forcing you to make a choice
+ clear, neat, good looking graphics
+ major and minor zombie waves
+ zombie towns - you can attack them and get extra rewards or avoid but this could have an impact later on if you dont have the map cleared properly
+ Dark Souls of rts genre
+ learning from your mistakes
+ hard, you won't win every time, but getting owned by the game is so much fun as you usually lose because of your mistakes
+ sometimes randomised map seed is stacked against you but even if I feel I am at a disadvantage I am giving it a go to see if I can adapt to adverse conditions
+ frequent updates
+ survival mode already providing hours of fun
+ price tag wasn't overly big and given coming to the game (40-50h campaign, new buildings and units, workshop to allow moding and possibly map making with potential coop or multiplayer maybe, its gonna be super worth it, I feel it already is)
+ devs are fairly responsive, despite being indie company
+ fairly helpful community, lots of players out there who are willing to give you tips, there are guides available
The neutral:
* some people report issues/bugs etc. but I haven't experienced any
* difficulty not aimed at beginners
* certain people can find this game repetitive - mostly because at this stage of the Early Access its just the survival mode
The bad:
- at this point in time Mayor choices are not really choices, I mean they are either too easy or both options you are presented with are just equally bad
I know, it looks like I am a total fan boy but I can't fault the game at the moment, I understand this is Early development, there are bugs and balancing issues to fix, features and content to implement. I will have a more critical approach once game leaves Early Access officially.
Hopes:
~ I am hoping the campaign won't disappoint
~ map editor (workshop confirmed)
~ new factions or maybe mods changing change would be cool
~ I would love to play a reverse version and control zombies XD
~ playable zombies to allow typical rts like games
I very rarely take interest in Early Access but I couldn't wait to jump and support this one, especially seeing as I have missed the Kickstarter campaign. With games like this one I am very happy for the Early Access option on Steam.
Numantian - you have done a great job, keep it up!

Okay, 25 hours and 2 default (challenging level) wins in, I feel like I can finally give a review that's not clouded by too much hype or frustration.
Summary Statement - The game has a solid foundation. I like what's here now. That's what I base Early Access on personally. If the company fell into the void tomorrow, would I feel bad about the money spent? The answer for They Are Billions, is nope.
Pros (in no particular order, just as they come to me):
- The game is aesthetically beautiful.
- It manages to maintain a tension. There are some units/strats that work that shift with any particular "meta", but there is always a sense of needing to be doing something and double checking any cracks or you will quickly find yourself staring at the AAR wondering what happened.
- You have to earn your base, and it feels good. Every tile you control beyond the first 20 or so around your command center, you probably fought or at the every least planned for. The undead are greedy and don't like to share map space.
- The music is really pleasant! I'm not one to really notice music in games, when I do, it's either really good or really bad.  This is the good kind of notice.
Cons (in no particular order, just as they come to me):
- Unit Balance is off. Some feel outright worthless and other are deities. From what I hear, who's in what camp changes per patch. Not unusual for this kind of game, but I can still wish for balance.
- There are some pretty significant bugs that work both for and against the player. An example of each: mayor bug that gives unholy bonuses, and "ghost" zombies infecting buildings even though if you catch it in time, the building is deletable (shouldn't be if it was actually under attack) and then the problem stops.  And some more minor ones. The good news here is that the devs are attentive. So things look good for that kind of thing being handled.
- Unit voicelines. I don't so much mind the content of the voicelines, they're cheesy but whatever, not my focus. They simply happen too frequently. If they're going to be cheesy GIVE ME LOTS OF CHEESE, SMOTHER ME IN CHEESE. Not just the same 2 or 3 bits of cheese.
- The devs either don't publicly document patch notes, or I simply haven't found where they do so.  Wish they were more transparent on that end.

MONACO: WHAT'S YOURS IS MINE
is a heist game focused around stealth, which in itself is not exceedingly common nowadays, though there are others out there.
Its top-down rectangular graphics may not appeal to all, but the gameplay is where this game excels.
Your screen is comprised of a large rectangular map, zoomed in and blacked out until you explore it. When exploring, you find guards, guns, and gold. The guards will chase after you if you dash past them suspiciously, but if you casually walk past, more often than not, they'll pass it off as nothing important.
Having up to four-player co-op and up to eight playable characters each with their own primary, secondary, and occasionally tertiary skillset that may be accessed by others, but not nearly as well as the masters.
For example, the Locksmith is adept at picking locks on doors primarily, but also safes and cash registers. He picks locks 2 to 3 times faster than any other character.
The Gentleman puts on a simple disguise while hidden from view and applies disguises found around extraordinarily quickly. While others can put on disguises, none do it as fast as he and neither do they do it while hidden.
The Lookout knows where enemies are all over the map, and can additionally climb stairs and ladders faster.
The Pickpocket has a pet monkey that snatches cash undetected, and can stow himself away in bushes almost instantly.
The Cleaner can knock out unsuspecting witnesses and utilize medkits more efficiently.
The Mole breaks through walls. Yeah, that's about it.
But I could go on and on about this game's many merits--it has a level editor that was used to make every level in the game, for goodness' sake--but I think I can sum up this game's sense of humor and hilarity by saying that it's got a special gamemode called "ZONACO: YOUR FLESH IS MINE" in which all enemies are replaced by quick-moving small zombies or gigantic, slow, explosive zombies.
If you like stealth and/or heist games at all, get this. You won't regret it.

Got this with a buddy of mine, sofar my experience is only in private coop, the review should be viewed as such. I assume you know its greenlight and will have some bugs.
Started out on the planet, seems like i may have been stranded since my suit is leaking O2 and i have supplies scattered around me. My buddy is nowhere to be seen, but fear not, we are only a few degrees latitude and longitude apart. A few minutes of walking later we come to a valley, one of us on either side, and start crossing to meet in the middle. All of a sudden a giant sand worm arcs out of the ground and we both scatter in panic, yelling over our microphones to GTFO. Soon after we are walking up a ridge together when a sandstorm hits, though we are but feet apart we quickly lose eachother in the dark. As the sand cleared up we saw that he had stumbled upon the motherlode, a large flat mesa ringed in all the resources we could ever want, and not a baddie in sight. We get to it, gathering resources, gathering the necessities for survival and surveying our surroundings. We both found the experience to be very immersive and felt compelled to explore more. From the little bit I've seen of this planet I am nothing but optimistic about seeing more.
The only bugs that I found to be problematic or gamebreaking:
You cannot reset or erase a private server after creating one and you cannot remove another players (ie, your first character on the map) buildings. This has already been acknowledge by the dev and should have a solution soon.
Enemies have killed me from outside of my structure while I've been in the center of my hab, I doubt that's the intent so it should also be fixed soon (or already if this review is old)
Get. This. Game.

* It runs incredibly well. My rig isn't great at the moment and I'm still not getting any performance issues on ultra.
* Aesthetic. The game is graphically impressive and it doesn't feel like anything you come across [or create] feels out of place.
* Combat. Weapons feel like they pack a punch and are fun to handle.
* Working multiplayer. Easy to set up a private game and there's been no latency issues. The fact that the host doesn't need to be online for someone to join their game is also a massive bonus.
* Enemies. They have their own behaviour and patterns of attack. Side note but they're also quite creepy.  Seeing an Arachnid-type creature rush towards you during the night-time is unsettling. All creatures also have their own weakness I.E if you attack a Crabs leg then it'll blow off thus adding a tactical element to the combat rather than the generic "Aim for the head!"
* Survival elements. They're pretty good. Having to manage hunger and thirst is well-implemented with it not being like other games requiring you to drink and eat every 3 minutes.
* Base building. You start with a small inflatable dome and can move on to a full habitat leading to chem labs, a barracks and even a dome in which you grow your own food. It's enjoyable to do and getting materials for all this isn't ridiculously hard or grindy like in other games.
* Weather effects. Going out and getting stuck in a massive dust storm is genuinely fun. Not being able to see 5 feet in front of yourself not only looks great but adds tension.
* There's not much in the way of audio when it comes to enemies. No piercing screeches or growls. The reason this is a problem is because if you're being chased then you literally need to change perspective or turn around to see what's actually hitting you and this can lead to you taking ever more damage.
* Level-up system. It's very basic and doesn't have as much as an effect as I'd like. I've put a lot of points into health but it doesn't seem to make as much as a difference as it should.
* Character gear. You'd imagine with the damage you take that you'd be able to craft new armour or upgrade what you have but that isn't the case here.
* Terrain deformation. This game isn't procedural or anything and it kinda takes from the experience when you're digging up dirt and the ground itself doesn't alter.
* Animation improvements. I've seen a lot of animations bug out in the 3rd person perspective and when this happens during combat then it leads to yet more damage for no reason. Animations for things like the shovel and repair-tool are also fairly weak.
* Structures. Me and my best friend are currently playing through this game and we both agree it'd be incredible to see some form of structures built by other civilisations or maybe even crashed ships just to add more of a feel to exploration.
* Armour. I would love for the ability to create some form of armour. Maybe creating a set for combat so you take less damage or a set for mining with bigger pockets so you can carry more.
* Events. I think this game would benefit massively from random events. Seeing a derelict ship crashing on the planet you're on for you to explore, getting a horde of aliens attacking your base because something has driven them out of their home and things like that just to make the universe feel more alive.
All in all I'm loving this game and I'm going to continue playing with my friend so I'll update this as I go.

Far Cry 3 was Skryim with Guns. Well, Pixel Piracy is Black Flag in 8 bit! In this game, you get to create your own ship, build your own crew with different PERSONALITIES and even background stories. There is no story, but at the start, you get this test, sort of like Fallout New Vegas, to choose what kind of map you want to play in. Full of monsters? Full of mysteries? Full of dramatic moments? It's all up to you. Don't think this game is easy just by looking at it. I have died a lot of times, but I learned from my mistakes and got better at it. The game has some contents that does better than AC4 which is amazing for a 15 dollar game!
The bads are that the combat is not as interesting. You just click at the opponent to order your crew to fight and the captain (you) himself. Watching pirates fall of the ship can be entertaining, but lacks strategy. Don't get me wrong, there is strategy in this game. There is a mediocre level up system and sets of weapons you can use with ship weapons as well (cannons). It's just that if there was maybe "Click as fast as you can to do a lot of damage" kinda thing, it would make you feel like you are in the battle and that you are motivated to make effort.
This is still early game and it's only 15 dollars; therefore, the game is amazing with great replayability and gameplay. Patches are coming and hopefully, they add multiplayer or coop cuz that would INSTANTLY make this game the perfect pirate game out there. If you are interested in creating a story yourself out in the sea with your own crew and your crazy ship design, this game is for you.
P.S. Go watch this video by HERO and it will help you out a lot in the beginning!

First things first.
