4, I´m fat and I have a bad haircut. Deal with it.
When The Bureau was announced, I was super excited, because the trailer looked amazing, the premise of alien attack situated in the USA in 60s as FPS with some tactical elements seemed great. We all know that there were some problems during the development and that the game was reworked many times. That sounds like a bad thing ( *cough* Colonial Marines *cough*), eh? Well it is NOT.

are stunning (I played on DX11). Seriously, I´ve never seen a game with better lightning of a scene. I often caught myself just staring on the scene and taking screenshots, because it simply looked beautiful. It required a decent hardware though on HIGH setting, I played on MID-HIGH. No cons. 10/10

The main part of the game are fights of course. Ever played Mass Effect? Imagine that, but better ( HERESY!). Far better. Yea, I said that. Here is the thing. On a mission, you can take two agents with you. Each agent can have one of four classes (Engineer, Recon, Commando, Support). I´ve ended up using Support and Engineer (Engineer can put a turret or mines on the battlefield, Support creates a shield, can give a stims to the whole team etc). You have a special class, called Agent. You can Heal, do some kind telekinetics, put a drone on a battlefield, and at level 9 out 10, you can use a mind control ( yea, those are not the agents you are looking for). You can give the commands to your team via command list (imagine KOTOR). When you press SPACE key, it will put you in slow motion mod and you have lot of time to think (not that much though, the game is not completely freezed). At the beginning of the game you will not use it that much, but when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hit the fan (that means when Sectopod or Muton introduce themselves on a scene), you will beg for mercy and most of the time, you will end up planning what to do, where to put your agents, and wondering how the ♥♥♥♥ you are supposed to kill them all. This game is challenging on a first walkthrough. Not THAT hard, but decently hard.
The weaponry of this game is not too big ( Colt 1911, M14, Springfield,  then laser and plasma variations, grenades), but nothing to complain, the main power of this game is within the abilities/perks of the team).

Edit: I'm not quite sure who the target market for this game is. MOBAs in general have much more lively and balanced pvp matches. And they are f2p as well. Raiding in general is a laggy low-fps jerkfest. My hardware isn't the top of the line, but it handled GTA5 at a decent detail level and framerate. Maybe people who like terrain puzzles and hunting artifacts? Maybe that's the real target market of this game still? Maybe the 5mans? Except that you'll be waiting for a 5man queue to pop maybe once an hour? The scintillating general chat?
Edit: The other thing that annoys me is how the expac souls are engineered to be so much better than the vanilla souls, so that you'll be forced to buy and play the new soul packs. So, if you are say, a mage, you will be forced to play harbinger, whether you want to or not, just because it does the required amount of dps needed to pass the content. Just one example of how f2p ruins a game over time. Another gripe would be how pvp rarely ever feels balanced, where almost every match feels like you're stomping the other team or you're getting stomped on. It's rare you see comebacks or even close scores at the end. It wouldn't matter except that they merged pvp and pve gear together, so that any change in pvp now affects pve, and if there's one thing pvp is always lobbying for, it's change, change, change.
Edit: The thing that really annoys me about this game is the lag. I'm sure that other MMOs do trickery to mask the underlying network latency, and perhaps Trion should look into that. That and the annoying little bugs related to the UI and display that have been in the game since launch. Their QA isn't nearly up to the level that Blizzard's is. And instead of fixing the bugs, Trion seems more interested in rolling out game after game after game. With probably the same sort of bugs in them too.
Edit: Not really pay to win, unless you're willing to shell out $100s. I'm guessing like all freemium models, they're relying on a few big whales to fund the playtime for everyone else. The current level cap 5man experts are decently hard. I can see where they tried to require teamwork, but all it has really done is make the tank shoulder an unequal burden in a PUG. Hence, players willing to tank are rather rare and you will be sitting in an expert queue for quite a while. The entry level raids are also decently hard too and do require even more teamwork to pull off. All in all, if you refrain from being a whale, it's a decent amount of content for not much money. PvP is rather laggy, if you ask me. I asked other people whether this sort of lag was normal and they said yes. So if you like crisp clear PvP, be prepared to be a little bit disappointed.
I played this game when it first came out. At the time, it was quite challenging, the 5man experts required quite a bit of teamwork to pull off properly. I left it when it was still hard, and still a subscription game, mainly because the internet I had sucked at the time. Can't really heal when you're lagging 5000ms. Not really fun either.
I decided to revisit it again, seeing as it's now f2p and subscriptionless, just to see what it's like these days. Everything is now easy mode, you're only in danger of dying if you get out of range of the healer. Otherwise the mobs just die in front of you and give you that sweet XP. The world is also ridiculously easy too, they've set the aggro radius on most mobs to be quite small, it's fairly easy to saunter in somewhere, hit a quest and then saunter back out.
I'm disturbed by the fact that you can now buy purple gear at the level cap. It may be a tier behind and the current tier you may have to play for, but it looks a lot like pay to win. I've no objection to paying for things, and in some ways, f2p makes for a nicer experience. Because nobody's on the clock (either you or the game designers) you don't feel that urgent need to zip through the levels to get to the cap, so you can get on with raiding. And the game designers (who you're really playing against) don't feel that need to slow you down, so they can get more money out of you. Time is money. You want to move fast, they want you to move slow.
But paying to win goes a bit too far. I haven't reached 65 yet (only 55 now), so we'll see.
Everybody (if you're willing to pay for it) can now do every role. Mages, can literally tank. Yes literally. The mage tank is no longer a joke. Warriors, can heal. No, not with bandages. They really can heal.
But if you just want something to kill time with, and all you care about is questing and 5mans, there's a lot of free content they're just giving away. Even if all you do is just dps with one of the original soul combos, it'll probably take you at least a month to get to 65. And then you can just move on to something else :P

"Costume Quest" is a fine opportunity to get into the Halloween mood. Or even deeper.
It is a one-player RPG game involving two twin siblings getting separated by candy-greedy monsters from Repugia and two friends of theirs. So one sibling gets kidnapped and the other three children (including you as the twin brother or sister) set off for the rescue while fighting monsters, bosses and having fun by collecting Halloween stuff (costumes, candy, candy cards, battle stamps) and solving quests that get in your way.
The gameplay: Most of the time you will walk around places like your hometown or the town's mall and search for items and quests. All of these help you progress in the story and getting stronger. One quest you must complete a couple of times in order to progress is to knock on every available door to ask for treats. Either you just get them or have to battle a monster (that has occupied this house).
So the other part of the game are the battles. The children use their costumes they've achieved (pumpkin, black cat, vampire, statue of liberty, etc...) and their special powers to fight the different monsters. And because it's an RPG you wait for your characters' turns and choose the actions they're suppoused to do now while the monsters get their turns, too. You can loose battles but never die. You just would have to try again. Every win is rewarded with experience points, candy and other items.
During all this you have your note book with you in which you have an overlook of your status, quests (and their status), costumes (with description), candy cards and a variety of battle stamps which can be used for battle by your characters.
I found "Costume Quest" very playable, the controls are easy to learn (and they're changeable if you really can't operate with them). I played with the keyboard and it worked just fine. It's a fun RPG with a good mixture of exploring, collecting and fighting. It's also easy to play, so also RPG beginners shouldn't have trouble to finish this game sooner or later.
The cartoonish 2.5/3D graphics are mostly sweet and lovely designed, that goes especially for the settings you go to.  They're colourful but not rainbow puking bright, they mostly match the Halloween season. When it goes to the characters, I find the children, their battle characters and the monsters were designed okay. I can't say that about the adult characters who either look like obese puppets, lifeless big-nosed humans or stick figures with grotesque heads and faces. They don't only look strange but also quite lifeless. I wished that a bit more effort would have went into their designs. But to the game's credit: the adults play a very minor role compared to the children.
The sound is so-so: I enjoyed the musical score very much. But the sound? It completely containts sound effects (which are fine), no voices (outside the occesional grunts of monster characters and human background mumbling in more crowded places). This means that the dialogues are all text bubbles and there are even no simple sounds expressed by the characters, wether a "Gasp!" or "Huh?" or "Ouch" or something. I find this negative since at least a bit of voice acting brings extra life to these characters but here, everybody is totally quiet.
What about extras? There are achievements, trading cards, one minigame about apple bobbing and there is also an additional chapter included called "Grubbins on Ice" that goes on right after the story of the main game. I can't say it's that exciting or so much fun, you practically do the same things and collect new costumes but without Halloween going on. Still, it's worth for a bit of fun and the achievements.
So, can I recommend "Costume Quest"? Yes, absolutely. It's a sweet, fun game all around Halloween and the fantasy of children celebrating it. If you can't stand Halloween or just don't care about it, then I guess this shouldn't stop you from trying but you might have less joy with that game.
And if you're into RPGs or starting this, you definitely should check it out.

The Eyes of Ara is a very good 3D puzzle game in the vein of Myst. You move around, click on suspicious objects and locations, collect items and combine/use them on others. The graphics are alright but very samey - you are in the inside of an old castle though so that is fine. The atmosphere is pretty good and the background story is also somewhat interesting, though the ending falls a little short in my opinion. Puzzles are usually very challenging, though there were a few puzzles (especially towards the end) that I found way too hard/where I found the solution to be way too "out there" and like 2 or 3 "picture puzzles" that take simple luck and trying out endlessly to solve without much strategy or finesse
EDIT: The developer now built in a function to "skip" these picture puzzles by finding a secret code. Very nice and a very responsive developer that really deserves his game being bought. Instead of just making them completely optional, he just makes you able to solve a different puzzle which is how it should be.
The game takes you about 10 hours if you take your time and try to find all the collectibles and secrets. It is well worth the investment even at the full price if you are a fan of games like Myst or puzzle games in general.
Very much recommended!

I've probably played this game more than I ever played any other. The graphics are a bit dated now and the driving is more arcade than anything meaning the cars handle and perform nothing like the real things or even similar representations in other games. The road design is often better suited to a Need for Speed franchise where wrecking is purposely added and part of the whole atmosphere of the game.
Some of the stuff you do in the game, things required to advance and otherwise, seem pointless and like "so what?" at best. Like clothes shopping and cosmetic surgery for a couple. Who really cares about either and most of the clothes are a joke and ridiculous beyond  belief. Many of the achievements needed to advance are very tedious and often require co-operation of other players. Good luck there both in finding enough players to help you and then finding enough good sports who'll actually help you. There's a casino DLC with its own blend of poker, slots, roulette and some players seem to prefer the casino to driving. Advancing through the different level cars requires a tiered licensing before you can buy the faster cars.
The story is thin- you basically work your way through a racing series called Solar Crown using various class cars from old classics to high dollar exotics to off-road. You win cash and sometimes cars from AI drivers you compete against. Warning here- this is another game where the AI cars can bump you off the road, spin you out and all that while they are about totally resistant to anything you do to them. A wreck may cost you 10 or more seconds to recover from but the AI cars hardly slow down when they wreck.
There are 'missions' you do along the way to earn money and some of them are kind of dumb, too. but they pay. There is an 'assist the cops' and 'run from the cops' ability that nets you special decals and a cop car at some point. A treasure hunt is included where you find pieces of cars that once assembled become yours. These include a Cobra Daytona Coupe, Cobra SC 427, a 70 Charger, VW Beetle, an Audi, and a few others. There are a number of DLC cars and motorcycles as well. There is a paint shop of sorts but you can't do any physical customizing like tires/wheels, window tint, wings, ground effects, etc. Only paint/stickers.
You can start a club and compete with other clubs and if you have enough money and reputation the club gets special cars to share with club members. But good luck there because there is no way to communicate with other club members unless you all happen to be on-line at the same time so event planning tends to fail and the clubs don't seem to last. My own few club interaction experiences were closer to demolition derbys and gang warfare than car races.
There are what are called Community Racing Centers with player created challenges in the game. Both are things you are supposed to do- make challenges and compete in them. Early on in the game they were so full of cheating it was a sad joke. They're supposed to be better now and the easy cheats fixed but I can't get psyched about trying them again and not messing with them has zero effect on the game being fun.  There are the player vs player and leade board challenges, too, both at spots throughout the map and immediately initiated by a flash of headlights. Again, in the early days of the game, one of the cheats had the ability to stop the clock during a race so all the leader boards show course times of 0.00.00 going hundreds and hundreds deep. It's not just impossible to beat such times, but the boards have never been cleaned off that I know of. so nobody stands a fair chance. Players used multiple IDs, set a time and never bring that record setting player back online to accept any challenges. If that's important stuff to you, I don't know what to say.
At the end of the game, it's just done in an anti-climactic sort of way. There are no more missions, no more 'new' races and there's nothing new to do. It's all "make your own fun" after that. There are still ways to make money- you can re-race every event you ran as often as you like. You can make money for driving semi-recklessly - right on the centerline - or some fields make money bouncing around in an off-road car. It's slow going but you can earn money to keep buying and modifying cars up to the limits of the garage spaces you have. Oh yeah, you have to buy houses with garage slots to store your cars... You get the idea.
Stiill, even with not a lot left to do, it is full open world and you do have some cool cars to cruise around in which is a ball in itself and why I keep playing it again and again.  All the fun of a driving game without the pressure to do anything but drive around!

Early Access review:
This game, in it's current state is very much playable and enjoyable, but definitely not fully developped yet... it feels like it might be close though.
I played both solo and co-op with 2 other online friends, we all enjoyed the game. But I noticed that a lot of important loot items in the game are extremely rare, so you pretty much have to do research in order to know where to look or spend an eternity searching. For instance, in order to get a wrench, there's only one known location in the game where you can find it (which makes no sense since it's realistically one of the most common household tools), and the worst part is that it's a hit or miss as to whether or not it'll actually be there. I did later find out that more show up as you pregress in the game, but it's still an issue that shouldn't exist. A lot of items are like that (including copper wire... I mean seriously, copper wire!?!?). I'm currently at lv 11 and I still haven't found a single strand of copper wire yet (I mean, what about all those computers and tvs and other electronics scattered throughout the game?). There's also a bit of grinding for loot by completing certain missions multiple times in order to progress further in camp development which is rather tedious, though not as bad when playing co-op since quest rewards go to each player rather than shared. There's also sections in the game in which we have no access to, I assume it'll either be DLC or the devs just haven't finished those sections yet (both within quests and main map). Aside from that, I did notice some random online latency issues and game freezing for a few seconds at a time during solo and multi-player for no reason at all, nothing too serious, but minor optimizations wouldn't go un-noticed. Melee combat seems to have a memory, so spamming the attack button is definitely never a good idea as it locks you in place while you finish the melee attack combination leaving you vulnerable from the back or sides. So just make sure not to spam the buttons and it'll work just fine.
The difficulty curve is set up really nicely overall. During quests, you can make them as difficult as you want and be rewarded with more XP if you chose to make them more difficult. I really like how they did that. I also like the camp building process, though I do wish it was a bit easier to do. Graphics are nicer than the first How to Survive, though I have very little accuracy or aim ability while indoors, so that needs a bit of tuning in my opinion.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the first How To Survive game. Sure I mentioned a lot more flaws than features in my review, as I do with most of my reviews, but you already knew what the features were when you read the game's description and watched the videos.

I loved the first game and How to Survive 2 is definately a nice addition to the series. However, after reading some of the over-enthusiastic reviews, I was also a bit disappointed.
Building your own camp is pretty cool and works great. Also the new city areas definately add to the fun, because indoors melee weapons are a much better choice than they ever were in HtS 1. But even outdoors melee is much more important now, because there is not that huge overflow of ammo from every second zombie you kill anymore. You will meet some familiar faces from the first game, which is pretty cool too. And the new types of zombies make things a little more interesting.
However, there were some things that I don't really like about HtS 2.
- The instance-based mission system may not be a turn-off for some people, but I really don't like it. You can accept missions in your camp and get teleported to the quest map to do your stuff and then return to the camp. HtS 1 had a much more open world-ish feel to it (it's not really open world but you can run around the islands all you want and don't get teleported somewhere else when you get a quest), which I liked better. Also, there are basically just 3 different types of missions: Kill X amount of zombies, collect Y amount of some resource or find person Z and talk to them.
- The level system is the worst part about this game though in my opinion. It is a very artificial limitation of progress and doesn't really fit into the game. You have to spend XP to level up your camp first, which does nothing except allow you to upgrade your buildings to the same level. Only after you have upgraded your camp can you level up yourself by spending XP, again changing absolutely nothing, except increasing your mission levels and allowing you to level your skills higher. You spend a large chunk of your XP on leveling up, which does absolutely nothing in itself, except making the zombies stronger (they level up with you or your camp depending on where you are). Meaning by leveling up, you don't become stronger, but actually weaker, because you don't gain anything but the zombies become stronger.
In HtS 1 at the beginning you just beat a few zombies up with a stick and at the end you killed massive hordes of zombies with the weapons you had earned by then, feeling absolutely godlike. In HtS 2 however, since the zombies level with you, the zombies are pretty much equally strong all the time, so you will face the same amount of them at any time pretty much all the time. This makes you feel like you are not really progressing that much after you get your first good gun or bow (whatever you prefer). All that changes is that higher damage-numbers pop up above the zombie heads when you hit them (yay ...).
- There are only very few types of different buildings in the city areas, making all maps feel pretty much the same. Sure this is still EA and I hope they will add more content. Just wanted to point that out.
- There are not enough missions to level up to max level, so you will have to start grinding missions you have already completed at some point. Again, this is EA and more will hopefully come.
- The story was MUCH better in HtS 1. Each NPC gives you some quests and they build up around some kind of storyline, but it's not really engaging and the different storylines aren't really connected all so much to each other. I'll wait what future quests add to the game.
- No boomerang :(
I don't mean to sound to negative, because this game is absolutely worth the money. I just think some people may like the more arcadey, story-driven, open world-ish HtS 1 more than this and could be a bit disappointed that HtS 2 is taking a somewhat different approach. As a final advice: Do play this with friends. It's just so much more fun that way. Gathering all the materials for your base can be a bit tedious when you have to get everything yourself.

I've seen some people describe this game as sweet. Depression and Anxiety are not sweet things, they are a darkness the creators of this game clearly do not understand. This game isn't just bad, it's borderline offensive.
As a real sufferer of Major Depressive Disorder, I am highly unamused by these armchair psychology adventure games about depression and anxiety on steam. Generally speaking, they portray self-diagnosed upper-middle class individuals who live lives of little to no adversity. In this regard, Samantha Browne is no different. The character absolutely suffers no actual anxiety or depression. The Samantha Browne featured in this game is simply lazy, unwilling to accept criticism, and views all other female characters in the story very misogynistically. At one point, she expresses no issue with venturing into general public, her "anxiety" only relates to talking to other young adult women in her dorm who might challenge or call into question her physical value to men. The themes at work here are oddly enough anti-feminist, and Sam is often times a straight up internalized misogynist. If I had to sum Samantha up with a spattering of adjectives, she's unskilled, overprivileged, ignorant, has an unwarranted sense of self-importance, has no common sense, and makes terrible decisions constantly.
Included below is a Stream-Of-Consciousness style play-by-play of a playthrough of this game so you can understand how horrifically banal, overprivileged, and logically absurd the whole thing is without actually contributing to its sales. Great works of feminist literature have been written about these topics, and for this or anything like it to be lumped in with them is absurd. This is feminism for people who have never sat through Roots or The Color Purple. Playthrough:
As I opened the game and gazed upon the 3-frame steam rising from the already-made oatmeal, I became overwhelmed with trepidation. Why was the oatmeal already made? In an attempt to access some kind of options menu to turn down the absurdly loud music, I entered a credits menu, and my fear turned to outright terror. There were no options. This was a game made in Renpy, and there were no options. I would be forced to play this game with its 7-key toddler keyboard soundtrack on max volume with clipping. I do not like my experience being restricted, so I alt-tabbed out of the game at this point, only to discover that the window was nowhere on my task bar. The music still poisoning my ears, I remembered to lower the volume in my OS, at which point the track started over. It was becoming abundantly clear to me that, somehow, somewhere, someone thought this music was worth playing at absolute max volume allowed via the engine.
Despite the ominous feeling deep within my bones, I soldiered on and returned to the game via alt-tab. As it turns out, Samantha Browne is the kind of girl who makes oatmeal in your grandma's cat coffee cup, how quaint. Mulling over Sam's bad decision making was getting me nowhere, the time to begin this Adventure(s) was upon me.
Only a few seconds into the game I was startled to learn that Samantha Browne is, in fact, not one of US, but one of UK. So Indie. I was introduced to Sam's "remote" 5-story, at least 70 room, dorm in the middle of campus. It's a flat, not because she's british, but because that's what the other students call it. Uh... Okay. We now learn that Sam has 0 friends. Bummer. Poor Sam, she truly lives a tortured existence of macbooks and iPhones that I'm sure only her mom calls her on. I was offered a chance to view the consequences of not obliging Sam's horrible decision to eat a high-carb food 6 hours into the night. "I'm sure she'll just ♥♥♥♥♥ on Tumblr," I thought, before clicking the top option.
I got introduced to Sam's desktop pretty quickly, upon which I learned that she was at least some degree of a furry, wonderful... In addition, she was illegally viewing copyrighted material on a TV Streams site. Samantha's power as a good role model for young women was only growing. The only word I can pick out of the Pirated TV dialogue is the male saying "♥♥♥♥ING" in a threatening manner to the female. How mature and progressive, I thought! I am now thrust into my first decision, do I lie to my furry boyfriend about my """crippling" "social" "anxiety""" (emphasis mine), or do I "make up some excuse"? I told the truth, because as we've already explained, my Sam is a smart furry role model who is working on improving her awful decision making. She quickly undoes my decision by spelling because "coz", much to my chagrin. We learn that Sam has no problem going to a Grocery Store, but can't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to walk downstairs because a person or two might be there. Sam continues saying and doing illogical things for 2 minutes. That was a joke, but the game immediately broke into 5 minutes being told to me not shown... after I wrote that joke. I can't make this up. After an official had declared Sam fully out of bed, choices once again forced themselves into the narrative. I could pick whichever oatmeal I liked. Joy! Upon my selection of Apples & Cinnamon, Sam spelled yes "YAAAAAHHHHSSS". I begin to lose energy to play the game. One man can only be expected to put up with so much tongue-in-cheek exaggeration. I picked a single oatmeal packet, but Sam overrode my decision and forced me to pick 2 because she isn't a bovine or something. "Look at me, making choices, like an adult," the adult character said. The toxic unchecked western privilege had begun to consume me. I am now playing a mini-game where I choose a spoon from a selection of one spoon while a 7 second jazz loop of royalty free muzak plays. This is a real game on steam, I chuckle to myself. Sam proceeds to complain about walking 10 feet. As she steps into the hallway, we learn that our introverted protagonist who "is scared of being seen" is wearing booty shorts that we had no option or inkling to change out of, probably because we're an overprivileged white womanchild who is afflicted with habitual whining instead of any real depression or anxiety, just a hunch. As it turns out, Sam's social stigma stems from someone trying to give her constructive criticism on her makeup, you know, the makeup that a character with introversion and social anxiety naturally wears all the time!
I am given the choice to talk to two friendly looking Stephen Universe fanfiction characters, both of the female gender. I choose to not speak to them as Sam has clearly established a dislike for women and only women because they may compete with her or criticize her. Sam has trouble using a kettle, but doesn't have the inkling to google a solution on her iPhone. Use of the iPhone is also not an option for wasting time, and for some reason we must stay in the kitchen while the oatmeal steeps. I am now in a stirring montage. This is on steam. Sam doesn't even know how to remove things from microwaves and also doesn't seem to understand simple Newtonian Mechanics relating to fluids. Despite previously refusing to talk to anyone, Sam makes a very snide remark to the other girls that they can "have their kitchen back". This level of frank misogyny shocked me. By the time I have made it back to introverted Sam's room she is baring her midriff and the artist has now decided to differentiate the cheeks of her butt with a line. Classy.
We've locked ourself out of the room and the furry boyfriend has become dismayed, whatever will we do?
I don't know because apparently I lost the game at this point, Sam can't complain about her hunger on Tumblr because she's locked out of the room, and we can't go talk to the other girls because as we've already covered, Sam is a raving misogynist, so we simply get a game over.

It's almost Halloween so I decided to review a Halloween themed game.
Story:
Wren and Reynold are twins who love Halloween and when they go out trick or treating, a monster mistakes one of them for a candy corn and gets kidnapped, so the other one must go on an adventure to save them.
Nothing much to the story. The characters aren't that memorable and while story is original enough, it's very straight forward. I would say I do like the monsters and how they're just guys doing they're job. This is very true when we get to the expansion where we get to explore the monster to overthrow a dictator.
Gameplay:
The main objective is to trick or treat at every house to open the door to the boss. Along the way you play hide and seek, bopping for apples, trading cards, collecting costumes and fighting monsters. You costumes are the most important tool as most of them have abilities to travel the area like the robot  gives you a boosts to cross ramps or the knight shield lets you get past falling debris. Unfortunately, most of them are situation and may only need to be used once outside of combat.
Being an RPG, you'll be fighting a good portion of the game and in some houses, they will ambush you. You fight using your costumes that are all cool to play, each of them having a special power that takes 3 turns to charge and these can really help if you use it at the right time. I mean, there's no point in using a health move when you have full health. Also, you can buy stamps that can either raise a stat or give you a move like throwing toilet paper to stun enemies.
However, if there's one problem with the game which could be serious is that it's repetitive. That first line in gameplay is not a few things you can do, that's every area. Even the battles can get boring after a while and you'll have to fight every one of them just to make sure you're strong enough for the boss. And there's only four enemies(melee, range, black mage and white mage), even if there's different monster types, it's still the same four guys.
Presentation:
Nothing to say about the music except I really like the battle them. I barely noticed it sometimes. Personally I really like the simple but cute art and the battle models are badass but there was a bit of lag when I played it. But I have to complain again for the expansion because the sound quality for the cut scenes sounded muffled.
Verdict:
While it is repetitive, I think it's a decent game and good to introduce children to the genre. Plus it gave us a pretty good sequel.
6/10
The treatment of the characters is what really made this game for me. It's good regardless, but the story is what pushes it over the top. Also the adorable animations.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified was not well received by mainstream reviewers, but I personally enjoyed it a lot. Overall, it feels like a stripped down version of Mass Effect, but the combat stands out above other cover shooters. The game has a lot of flaws, but I encountered no bugs in the core game. The Bureau's combat puts you in control of William Carter, a rather generic protagonist with a gravelly voice. Conversations in the game are carried out with a radial menu lifted directly from Mass Effect. The dialogue isn't terribly interesting, and some of the characters facial animations appeared to not actually be finished. Their mouths move with odd robotic motions, and their eyes look eerily dead. Carter himself, and some of the other core characters have much better, albeit repetitive animations. The story is forgettable overall, but moves the game on well enough. It doesn't come anywhere close to the likes of Mass Effect though, and the fact that the developers chose to base their game design so heavily on Mass Effect is unfortunate given the weak story. Even still, the combat made the experience worthwhile.
Combat in the Bureau is at it's core a cover shooter in the vein of Mass Effect or Gears of War. It also gives you a pair of squadmates and allows you to give direct orders to them. The rookies you start with only have one or two abilities, as well as a command to focus on a specific target, and move to a location. Choosing where to move your squadmates is where the game gets a lot of it's strategic depth. You have to take into account how long they'll be exposed for, how far the nearest ally is if they need a revive, where the enemies are, how much protection the cover offers, and how easily they can use their abilities from their location. Overall it makes for a far more interesting experience than your standard cover shooter. Abilities range from dropping mines, shield domes, artillery strikes, and others.
The combat isn't perfect though. Your squadmates seem to move into stupid locations occasionally, either exposing themselves to unnecessary fire, going down somewhere difficult to revive them, or both. It's not quite clear why this happens, but it doesn't happen very often at least. The encounters feel somewhat repetitive, but they ramp up in difficulty at a good rate. The weapons are fairly standard for a cover shooter; human and alien variations of the standard rifle, pistol, sniper and so on. Enemies on the other hand provide a bit more variety, healing their allies, granting them shields, spawning new enemies, or even mind controlling your squadmates.
The graphics generally look good, with a variety of scenes ranging from idyllic small towns to metallic alien structures. Some elements though stand out like a sore thumb. An ugly low res skybox in one of the first scenes of the game is jarringly bad to look at in stark contrast to the cutscene that precedes it. Other elements like a destroyed tank with an ugly texture and a low poly model, or the abyss below an alien tower filled with an ugly brown fog that would have been acceptable years ago, but looks disappointing today. The rest of the game, however, especially the weapon reload animations look and sound good.
The Bureau's worst offense however, is sure to be a dealbreaker for some fans of the mainstream XCOM games. The only thing The Bureau has in common with XCOM itself is the aliens and the weapon types. Unlocking new weapons is done merely by picking them up off the ground rather than researching them. Dying only puts you back to the latest checkpoint, and while you can lose squadmates permanently if they bleed out in some difficulty settings, I'm fairly sure if you die yourself they'll be back with you at the last checkpoint.
By removing research, permadeath, and forcing the player down a linear path, I'm sure some players will deem the game unworthy of the XCOM title. While these issues did grate on me at first, it was the combat that kept me playing and enjoying every minute of it. Even though the story is just average, it isn't particularly time consuming like it is in Mass Effect. While I feel the game could have played more to it's strengths, it was still well worth the time and money while on sale. I wouldn't hesitate to reccomend this game to fans of Mass Effect, though fans of the classic XCOM games or Enemy Unknown will not enjoy it unless they also enjoy a good cover shooter.

Monaco is positively hilarious. The graphics aren't much, but please don't be put off by that. It is a silly, fun, light-hearted game. Perfect to play with friends or strangers, as the community for this game is surprisingly friendly (though a bit over-focused on speed-runs).
It is an entertaining game to joke around in. The guards are hilariously incompetent (but at the same time can be very dangerous). They utter such humorous phrases as "ferk my jerkinson!" and "pepepepe!", while desperately chasing you (of course, they know that thieves never hide in ladders, vents, or stairs, so they'll break off pursuit if you duck into one of those. Bushes are an occasional - but exceptionally rare - thief hideout, so they will only chase you into a bush if they are absolutely certain they saw you go in there - no, no, I mean *certain*).
There are all sorts of fun tools you can use to creatively manuever your way through the levels (rocket launcher, machine gun, shotgun, wrench, EMP, smoke-bomb, explosives, and bandaids - those are all the ones I can remember). Use of the tools is funded by the coins you collect.
There are also a variety of characters to choose from, each with a few different key abilities.
Be prepared to die a lot (don't worry, it's infinite respawn as long as a friend is willing to come heal you. Also, they can't abandon you on a level if you die, so no worries about that).
You can make your own maps (and they run pretty smoothly overall - sometimes there are issues with bushes "not working" and coins not popping out of safes in the custom made levels). You can also access maps that were designed by others, and those are nigh infinite. It is easy to make them, and a lot of people have (and then uploaded their maps so that other players can enjoy them, too). Some maps are much better than others but it is relatively easy to identify the good ones and just grab those (free).
This is not one of those "pay to win" or "buy me and then let the producers milk money out of you for overpowered items and DLC" sorts of games.
In conclusion:
I would recommend Monaco for people who enjoy finding creative solutions to problems, being silly, and working cooperatively.
I would not recommend it for people who prefer single-solution problem-solving, prioritize aesthetics, or are looking for a competitive game. The PvP options are there, but PvP seems fairly limited in this game.
Hope that helps :)

Great game for a free weekend or hefty sale. Coop is an absolute blast, with the shenanigans and "team killing" being so much fun, its criminal. Doing convoy ambush operations is hilariously easy with two friends, a helicopter, and a couple of underbarrel grenade launchers or high power sniper rifles.
Single player/campaign quickly loses variety and interest without friends to make the missions fun. Difficulty scales oddly with enemy's aimbot, but the harder two difficulties should be the way to play the game for a good balance between fun and longevity.
ACR w/ underbarrel grenade launcher plus the HTI sniper rifle make every vehicle just moving target practice. They can be unlocked pretty early/quickly into the game. As you improve skills, your weapon capabilities become dramatically more powerful. To help keep some missions from becoming impossible, Ubi put weak alternative weapons for you to use/start with so you don't accidentally destroy a truck you're supposed to steal with a bullet through a tire or the windshield between you and the driver. Worst case scenario, you always have the EMP drone.
The latest update seemed to cause some issues with performance, as now my game has short 5-second graphical freezes quite frequently, while the action continues to play out (getting shot, flying/falling, etc). This was the final issue that caused me to uninstall the game without ever finishing the last quarter of the campaign.
TL;DR: get on a 50%+ sale or just play it til its boring over a free weekend.

I think 50 hours enough time to put into a game to get a proper feel for its mechanics and gameplay, haha.
The game is visually stunning. Bolivia is a beautiful yet terrifying environment to play in. The developers did a great job of incorporating the culture and lore of the country.
The charcter customaization options feel nearly unlimited. Personalizing a soldier that you're about to spend hours playing as is essential for me in a video game. Weapon customization in terms of parts and camo is phenomnal and all the unique weapons are interesting. Wildlands nails this.
3rd person and over the shoulder shooting takes a bit to get used to if you're not familiar with it, but its essential for the stealth gameplay. The driving mechanics are a bit annoying and clumsy, especially when flying planes.
If it weren't for the captivating storyline and weapon customization, the repetitiveness of the missions and side missions is absolutely mind numbing. It's unbearable. The single player campaign drags on and on if you don't have a group of friends to be Ghost buddies with. It almost makes you want to quit playing the main story and just play online PvP or screw around with friends.
The 4v4 PvP multiplayer is an enjoyable and unique experience most shooters don't have. If you were going to get the game for any reason, it would be for this. It's highly addictive, even if you don't have a group of friends to play with. Each class is customizable in its appearance and each class has a unique ability. A lot of fun.
That being said, I did find the game enjoyable overall and I would recommend it.

Overall: Costume Quest is a cute and adorable game about the complicated relationship siblings have with each other, set against the backdrop of one of my favorite holidays: Halloween. While the battles in the game tend to become tiresome at some point, the game is short enough (both stories) to not become overbearing. The game doesn't try to be more than it is, and is definitely worth the playthrough. Recommendation is to get it on sale as it's been bundled several times. However, if you're in a position to pay full price, please do as the devs deserve it.
Rating: 9/10 - Details below
Story: In my opinion the story was absolutely fantastic. Humor was there and though I'm not a twin, I do have a younger sister and I appreciated the sibling rivalry though I'm ancient these days. Though the main idea is to rescue someone, and though that's not very original in stories these days, it was a well told story that kept me very entertained. Further, it allowed me to revisit the child inside me and remember that power of imagination and what can be accomplished and believed in.
Graphics: Though I'm not a huge fan of cel style animation, I was extremely pleased with this medium with this game. Too many details would have ruined the power of the children's imagination and the softer non-detailed aspect of cel animation felt like it lent power to the story rather than taking away from it.
Controls: Simple and easy. No issues there. - NOTE: I used an Xbox One controller.
Sounds & Music: All basically well done. I didn't play with other music and felt like it complimented the game rather well.
Gameplay: One tiny issue was that the battles started to feel like they were more of jumping through hoops than accomplishing anything worthwhile. However, this probably has more to do with my lack of patience for grinding/leveling in games in general as I get older. Honestly, the game didn't drag at all really, and without the unknown of what knocking on the door would do, the game would lose part of the "Trick" aspect so essential to Halloween. Only real complaint is that I couldn't advance the text faster during dialogue and was forced to sit and wait though I'd completed reading the sentence. Nor could I pause the dialogue if something came up.
Final Notes: Forcing me to read at one speed as I read fast, is something that definitely will annoy me. That being said, it's a very solid game that is worth the time and energy if you enjoy Halloween, sibling rivalry and the imagination of children. If you can afford to pay full price and want to support a good game, do so.

I feel like I should be writing a review for Xcom: enemy unknown.  That game was excellent,  I was pleasantly surprised when I got it bundled with Xcom declassified.  Xcom declassified takes everything that made xcom and enemy unknown interesting, and strips it out, leaving you with a very boring, very linear game that completely disrupts the game universe' narrative.

The Bureau is a very strangely cobbled together game. During the course of its ~ 20 hour campaign, and especially in the beginning, you get the idea that several plot points were half-dismissed, or the missions in which you uncover the existence of certain things were never implemented, leading to weird, disjointed jumps in the narrative that completely squander whatever worth it might have had.
The narrative also isn't helped by the game forcing you to return to Xcom HQ between missions, where you can talk to a variety of personnel as well as view pictures and read small snippets of info. However, few of these discussions really pertain to anything of any use, and most of them are just plain boring. The base is also quite large, and you have to continuously run around just to get to all these conversations, (it even comes with the now apparently obligatory 'airlock' where you have to wait 10 seconds every time through before you can go on), and it all leads to you quickly just giving up on all this stuff.
The main quest dialogues are further hampered by a Skip button that doesn't skip just the line you were reading on the screen, but instead entire chunks of dialogue, forcing you (if you want to hear all of it) to listen to the terminally slow voice actors grind out their lines with about as much passion as your old 10th grade math teacher.
The other part of the bureau, the combat, however, is a lot of fun, but it does require you to slog through several early missions where you have♥♥♥♥♥♥weapons and absolutely USELESS team mates. The AI in the Bureau may genuinely be the worst friendly AI you've ever seen. However, once these agents gain a few levels they become less helpless, and they gain some genuinely good powers which turn the combat into an enjoyable tactical challenge, especially on higher difficulty levels.
Graphically the game is very nice, conveying its 60s theme well, and some of the levels have some pretty awesome visuals, especially in the eight main story missions. Beside these eight main missions, there are about a dozen minor operations, which each take about 20 mins or so, while the main missions take roughly an hour to complete.
And for all how terrible the story and narrative are, it does have an excellent plot twist at the end that was (to me at least) quite surprising and made for some interesting choices.
All in all, it's a shame that the many devs which worked on this game didn't get this particular vision of it hammered down earlier, because it could have been a genuinely good, perhaps even great game. (especially if there had been more open missions and XCom style research). As it is, with the HQ stuff just dragging everything down into a boring grind, it's hard to get to the fun combat at times, and the game suffers for it. I wish 2K would release a patch that would just dismiss all the HQ stuff, and just let me do all the combat missions one after another.
I'd say it's definitely worth about 10 bucks if you like third person shooters with some cool abilities and tactics to them. Just skip through all the story stuff as much as possible.

Rift is one of those games I'll keep coming back to. The concept is neat and the art is very nice, but the customization is what gets my attention.
There are 'four' character classes. Rogue, Mage, Cleric, and Warrior... but each class has about a dozen talent trees or 'souls' that you can swap out as you like. Pick a premade build or just pick whichever ones suit your fancy and use as needed.
Pros:
- Very colorful and interesting art style.
- Character customization with talent trees lets you make whatever build you want.
- You can customize your character's outfit at any time and even dye it different colors (none of the 'Hellfire Clown Suit' issues that other MMOs can have).
- Decent gameplay (classic MMO fetchquest style) with an enjoyable crafting style (why hasn't any other MMO let you process materials in groups of twenty yet?)
Cons:
- Six playable races, but it's really kinda just four. Two flavors of human, two flavors of elf, big guys, and little guys.
- Endgame is a bit of a grindfest with getting attuned and such.
- Freemium stuff is all over the place, but in their defense a lot of it is cosmetic or mounts.
Also, the PvP is apparently unbalanced. However...

My frustrations were furthered by the fact that there were seperate puzzles focused around collectible but these were hard to distinguish from the main puzzles which resulted in me spending excessive amounts of time on a puzzle to only recieve a blue orb (Collectible) at the end of it.

Considering what appears to have been a fairly lightweight budget and team, the game is surprisingly polished. The game is a good length, which is usually by biggest complaint of these kinds of games. Sometimes they can seem to overstay their welcome, but this game did not. It's also pretty bug-free.
I didn't need a guide for the puzzles, as while not necessarily intuitive, the more difficult ones tend to be sufficiently explained or hinted at in hidden documents. Although I do sort of wish there was some kind of system to catalogue all the documents you find, so you can reference them later when you need them, as I was pretty well forced to take screenshots of everything I found and awkwardly sort through them later.
The real test of my patience was with the collectables though. I did end up resorting to a guide for some of those.  Finding all of them can be a real pain in the sense that you'll be spending a lot of time "pixel hunting", or scanning every nook and cranny in every room trying to find very subtly hidden items.
My last nitpick is with the choice of engine-- Unity. I've never bought a unity game that supports exclusive fullscreen mode, only a borderless windowed fullscreen. This game is no exception, so that means no FreeSync support, nor VSR. But the game is lightweight enough that I was fine with just regular old vsync. The game rarely dipped below my screen's refresh rate of 144Hz, especially after I turned off DoF and AA.
I found the story interesting, plus the history of the characters was nicely layered. Although, it's all told through journals haphazardly laying about, so be prepared to read everything. There isn't really any narrative driven cutscenes or voice-overs. I was okay with that though.
Overall, a nice little gem of a game. It's definitely priced right, IMO.

I haven't finished this game yet, but so far I am finding it very enjoyable. I have been disappointed by recent games of a similar vein, but The Eyes Of Ara delivers on several of the fronts on which those fell flat.
For example, in multiple-step puzzles there is no obvious locking-in of each step, it all locks in at the end, so you can't just fiddle around until the puzzle solves itself. Although this makes it trickier, I find it much more gratifying.
Another big problem in point-and-click adventures is that when you get stuck you can end up retracing your steps and clicking on every inch of screen space, hoping to interact with someting. TEoA zooms in on important areas when you click them, but not once you have already exhausted that area. This takes a lot of the frustration out of searching for bits you may have missed.
These seem like finickity points, but it's the little details that make for an engaging experience which has managed to cut some of the irritation from the point-and-click genre without feeling like the player is being coddled.

Worst case scenario, you always have the EMP drone.

TL;DR: get on a 50%+ sale or just play it til its boring over a free weekend.

I think 50 hours enough time to put into a game to get a proper feel for its mechanics and gameplay, haha.
The game is visually stunning. Bolivia is a beautiful yet terrifying environment to play in. The developers did a great job of incorporating the culture and lore of the country.
The charcter customaization options feel nearly unlimited. Personalizing a soldier that you're about to spend hours playing as is essential for me in a video game. Weapon customization in terms of parts and camo is phenomnal and all the unique weapons are interesting. Wildlands nails this.
3rd person and over the shoulder shooting takes a bit to get used to if you're not familiar with it, but its essential for the stealth gameplay. The driving mechanics are a bit annoying and clumsy, especially when flying planes.
If it weren't for the captivating storyline and weapon customization, the repetitiveness of the missions and side missions is absolutely mind numbing. It's unbearable. The single player campaign drags on and on if you don't have a group of friends to be Ghost buddies with. It almost makes you want to quit playing the main story and just play online PvP or screw around with friends.
The 4v4 PvP multiplayer is an enjoyable and unique experience most shooters don't have. If you were going to get the game for any reason, it would be for this. It's highly addictive, even if you don't have a group of friends to play with. Each class is customizable in its appearance and each class has a unique ability. A lot of fun.
That being said, I did find the game enjoyable overall and I would recommend it.

Costume Quest is another great game made by Double Fine Productions. Set in a Halloween setting, this game brings forth both RPG elements and strategy, while not making the game too hard. This game isn't too long, but it isn't too short either, with the game duration being around 5-6 hours for the main story. The goal of the game is to rescue your sister from the clutches of an evil witch, and stop monsters from taking all the town's candy by trick-or-treating door to door. Along your way, you'll pick up allies and use many costumes with different abilities in and out of battle to progress through your journey. Completing side quests not only help you, but everyone else as well as you strive to finish your journey. Watch as your Halloween costumes come to life in Costume Quest.

Dishonored by Arkane Studios is one of the many games that tries to chase after what made Deus Ex special and ultimately misses the mark. Dishonored is an action game first and foremost with a frustratingly difficult non-lethal option. The game has an impressive setting but doesn’t do much with it because of a stereotypical revenge tale.
The game commits its’ first mistake early in the tutorial by informing the player that killing too many people will result in the bad ending. While I appreciate that the game’s transparency, it influences players from the get go to play stealthily in a non-lethal manner to see the good ending. The problem is there are ONLY two non-lethal options in Corvo’s repertoire, choking targets (which is only effective in 1 on 1 scenarios) and using sleep darts. The imbalance between lethal and non-lethal options are so skewed to the lethal side that if you play non-lethal you are limiting yourself from about 80% of all combat options.
The second mistake the game makes is that it shows a summary after each mission listing number of enemies killed, coins collected and so forth. The summary also lists two checkboxes indicating whether any persons (including civilians) were killed and whether Corvo was a “ghost” (indicating that no enemies were alerted). The explanation of how to get the good ending is never clear and I thought that I had to get both checkboxes to get the good ending. Getting the “ghost” achievement in a mission is frustrating because you’re never informed of whether you failed it midway in a mission. After checking online forums, I learned that in order to get the good ending you only need to have “Low Chaos” in each mission but even that aspect is not clearly defined. The “ghost” achievement isn’t necessary but prepare to save-scum A LOT playing non-lethal.
Playing the game lethal on the other hand is an absolute blast. You immediately feel like an unstoppable force, backstabbing foes, hacking electrical towers to zap enemies and summoning an army of rats to do your bidding. Depending on your skill, Corvo can pull off some really amazing feats and makes even the hardest difficulty feel like a cakewalk.
The setting of Dishonored is intriguing and promising. It takes place in an industrial revolution era where machinery runs on whale oil instead of coal. The plague is present and the poor are most vulnerable to it while the rich are enjoy lavish costume parties and visit luxurious harems. It's a shame that the game never fully takes advantage of the setting. The story is a by the books revenge tale. You can see the plot twists a mile away. The characters except for Emily are all one-dimensional and deliver cardboard performances. And there are a ton of books strewn about the world to give it flavor but I didn’t bother reading most of them because they broke the flow of the game. If you want a more engaging story experience I recommend playing both DLCs, The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches.
Ultimately I can still recommend Dishonored if you enjoy a fast paced combat game and aren’t especially interested in a deep story. The problems with the non-lethal option as well the throwaway story make this game average in my eyes and not a must play game.

As a free to play game, this game, is hands-down, a definite try.
To start with some major points, the game is all about four hunters hunting a giant beasty, which is already pretty cool. Granted, some characters are way cooler (and better than others), but really all comes down to situational awareness, skill, and team coordination (or spreading the team out, if you are the beast). Some characters and monsters have a definitive play style to them, and you can earn everything in the game for free. The game also features a progression system that lets you use perks you attain on any hunter or monster (Dab: Only if the perks are eligible for them).
The game features a huge selection of hunters for each role: Assault, Trapper, Support, and Medic, which is good news because you may very well play this game for a long while. My only gripe is that silver keys may be slow to get without any challenges active, which can be a problem if you are a new player and mis-spend them (which, my suggestion from experience is to not buy anything until you know you'll enjoy playing that specific character, or enjoy that specific perk).
Another slight issue is that the current tutorials only feature the Assault Class Makorov, and the Monster Goliath. Obviously, these are the bare-bones picks as they are fairly straight-forward. The monster tutorial also feels slightly lacking, as it doesn't offer much information about the trapper class and how that class "Fights" you as the monster in a meaningful or helpful way. I have played a few games, in which a low rank new-comer easily wiped the floor with high level hunters, and I have played many more games feature an Rage-Quit monster or an AFK monster (which is no fun), which I can mostly assume from the low-rank, is due to the lack of help from the tutorial.
That said though, there is definitely a learning curve with this game; Knowing when to hunt prey/predators, knowing when to take buffs, jetpack resource management... They all come into play in this game, and managing these objectives and resources is vital to winning the match. All of these things are in play all the time, and can mean the difference between a slow defeat, a painful steam roll, or a challenging match tie breaker to see which is better, the hunter or the monster.
Moving on to something also related, the matchmaking in this game can be really wonky at times, pairing one rank 3 player with rank 25's full house. In some cases, I could understand this as to "challenge the newcomer", but 20 ranks + over one person is ridiculous, especially when you factor perks in, as well as people who "main" a certain class/character. However, this has happened only a few times that I have seen since I started playing.
The games graphics are really beautiful, surprisingly, and all the models look amazing. However, I will mention that the Physics can really bog computers down, even the most current and up-to-date rig may experience a bit of a 10 second hiccup at times.  Despite the beautiful graphics, you may have to play on medium-high, or low settings for graphics.
The volume in the game is naturally loud, which is good for a game of this type, because it's all about hearing and listening to sounds in the area to find the monster. This is super important, because if your trapper dies, you will only have the planet scanner to give you a vague idea of where the monster is. However, the volumes for some may be too loud, especially if you are in Comms via steam chat with a group of friends.
I can't say much about the community, as I haven't seen any hunters talk in game, so that may be something you want to explore before investing a lot of time into this game ; Playing by yourself in PUGs can be fun, but only for a short time killer.
Over all, despite the mixed reviews, I would recommend this game, but only if you have a friend or two willing to play with. Definitely check out video tips and tricks to help you out as you start to supplement the bad tutorial.

X-COM: Enemy Unknown (240 hours) is one of my favorite games to this date. It is one of the best turn based strategy games I have ever played. As XCOM EU is still a hit game, many will pan The Bureau: XCOM Declassified for not being on par with XCOM EU. I on the other hand believe that The Bureau is a fantastic game especially with that 75% deal from the Summer Sale (2014).
Here is what the Bureau does good and bad in my opinion
Pros:
-Fun gameplay that is reminescent of the combat of Mass Effect 2/3.
-Fair amount of time to complete everything (I played the game for a total of 23 hours when I wrote this review)
-Characters are slightly better, there are only a few likeable characters.
-The feel of the game is like Mass Effect but more realistic especially the movement during combat.
Cons:
-Story is great in the beginning but begins to suck by the end.
-(Understand that the XCOM stories usually suck so cut 2K some slack)
-The game could feel repetitive to some people. I never felt that it was repetitive.
-24 hours of gameplay could be too short for some people.
This game is $20 when not in sale and I believe that it could be a good buy to some but those tight on cash should wait till it's on sale for at least 50% off.
VERDICT
YES- You should get this game

Dishonored by Arkane Studios is one of the many games that tries to chase after what made Deus Ex special and ultimately misses the mark. Dishonored is an action game first and foremost with a frustratingly difficult non-lethal option. The game has an impressive setting but doesn’t do much with it because of a stereotypical revenge tale.
The game commits its’ first mistake early in the tutorial by informing the player that killing too many people will result in the bad ending. While I appreciate that the game’s transparency, it influences players from the get go to play stealthily in a non-lethal manner to see the good ending. The problem is there are ONLY two non-lethal options in Corvo’s repertoire, choking targets (which is only effective in 1 on 1 scenarios) and using sleep darts. The imbalance between lethal and non-lethal options are so skewed to the lethal side that if you play non-lethal you are limiting yourself from about 80% of all combat options.
The second mistake the game makes is that it shows a summary after each mission listing number of enemies killed, coins collected and so forth. The summary also lists two checkboxes indicating whether any persons (including civilians) were killed and whether Corvo was a “ghost” (indicating that no enemies were alerted). The explanation of how to get the good ending is never clear and I thought that I had to get both checkboxes to get the good ending. Getting the “ghost” achievement in a mission is frustrating because you’re never informed of whether you failed it midway in a mission. After checking online forums, I learned that in order to get the good ending you only need to have “Low Chaos” in each mission but even that aspect is not clearly defined. The “ghost” achievement isn’t necessary but prepare to save-scum A LOT playing non-lethal.
Playing the game lethal on the other hand is an absolute blast. You immediately feel like an unstoppable force, backstabbing foes, hacking electrical towers to zap enemies and summoning an army of rats to do your bidding. Depending on your skill, Corvo can pull off some really amazing feats and makes even the hardest difficulty feel like a cakewalk.
The setting of Dishonored is intriguing and promising. It takes place in an industrial revolution era where machinery runs on whale oil instead of coal. The plague is present and the poor are most vulnerable to it while the rich are enjoy lavish costume parties and visit luxurious harems. It's a shame that the game never fully takes advantage of the setting. The story is a by the books revenge tale. You can see the plot twists a mile away. The characters except for Emily are all one-dimensional and deliver cardboard performances. And there are a ton of books strewn about the world to give it flavor but I didn’t bother reading most of them because they broke the flow of the game. If you want a more engaging story experience I recommend playing both DLCs, The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches.
Ultimately I can still recommend Dishonored if you enjoy a fast paced combat game and aren’t especially interested in a deep story. The problems with the non-lethal option as well the throwaway story make this game average in my eyes and not a must play game.

As a free to play game, this game, is hands-down, a definite try.
To start with some major points, the game is all about four hunters hunting a giant beasty, which is already pretty cool. Granted, some characters are way cooler (and better than others), but really all comes down to situational awareness, skill, and team coordination (or spreading the team out, if you are the beast). Some characters and monsters have a definitive play style to them, and you can earn everything in the game for free. The game also features a progression system that lets you use perks you attain on any hunter or monster (Dab: Only if the perks are eligible for them).
The game features a huge selection of hunters for each role: Assault, Trapper, Support, and Medic, which is good news because you may very well play this game for a long while. My only gripe is that silver keys may be slow to get without any challenges active, which can be a problem if you are a new player and mis-spend them (which, my suggestion from experience is to not buy anything until you know you'll enjoy playing that specific character, or enjoy that specific perk).
Another slight issue is that the current tutorials only feature the Assault Class Makorov, and the Monster Goliath. Obviously, these are the bare-bones picks as they are fairly straight-forward. The monster tutorial also feels slightly lacking, as it doesn't offer much information about the trapper class and how that class "Fights" you as the monster in a meaningful or helpful way. I have played a few games, in which a low rank new-comer easily wiped the floor with high level hunters, and I have played many more games feature an Rage-Quit monster or an AFK monster (which is no fun), which I can mostly assume from the low-rank, is due to the lack of help from the tutorial.
That said though, there is definitely a learning curve with this game; Knowing when to hunt prey/predators, knowing when to take buffs, jetpack resource management... They all come into play in this game, and managing these objectives and resources is vital to winning the match. All of these things are in play all the time, and can mean the difference between a slow defeat, a painful steam roll, or a challenging match tie breaker to see which is better, the hunter or the monster.
Moving on to something also related, the matchmaking in this game can be really wonky at times, pairing one rank 3 player with rank 25's full house. In some cases, I could understand this as to "challenge the newcomer", but 20 ranks + over one person is ridiculous, especially when you factor perks in, as well as people who "main" a certain class/character. However, this has happened only a few times that I have seen since I started playing.
The games graphics are really beautiful, surprisingly, and all the models look amazing. However, I will mention that the Physics can really bog computers down, even the most current and up-to-date rig may experience a bit of a 10 second hiccup at times.  Despite the beautiful graphics, you may have to play on medium-high, or low settings for graphics.
The volume in the game is naturally loud, which is good for a game of this type, because it's all about hearing and listening to sounds in the area to find the monster. This is super important, because if your trapper dies, you will only have the planet scanner to give you a vague idea of where the monster is. However, the volumes for some may be too loud, especially if you are in Comms via steam chat with a group of friends.
I can't say much about the community, as I haven't seen any hunters talk in game, so that may be something you want to explore before investing a lot of time into this game ; Playing by yourself in PUGs can be fun, but only for a short time killer.
Over all, despite the mixed reviews, I would recommend this game, but only if you have a friend or two willing to play with. Definitely check out video tips and tricks to help you out as you start to supplement the bad tutorial.

I really like this game and knew what to expect having played Hearts of Iron 3. At first look it can appear impossibly complicated. In fact at first I found myself losing interest fast due to the complexity of playing god over a large and detailed nation such as Germany.
However, I found a gentle introduction to the game was attainable by playing smaller nations where I only have 2 main army groups (east and west) and one reserve guarding the big towns and cities.
The most fun part is trying to change history, all the what ifs(?) that people still ask today.
World War 2 was a terrible waste of life and it would have been better it never occured. However for me it is one of the juisiest and politically complex wars of all time. From a gaming perspective it is the perfect time period. Not too archaic but not too modern either. In the case of the latter you have all kinds of heat-seeking, drone flying crazy technology that I find dull and predictable.
World War 2 was on the cusp of modern warfare and hence we see classic weapons such as the Mg44 and the m1 Carbine. Many of these weapons are still used in the middle east today and are still very effective.
The real downer for me however is the portraits. HOI3 was much better for having real generals and politicians who are represented by historical images. There is a very good mod by Mauro that restores the black and white portraits, however it annoyingly disables achivements. This is bad because I often play games on Steam using achivements as a motivation and lifespan booster when games start to get stale.
I suspect other details have been taken out since the research tech tree is now somewhat sparse.
One good thing is the GUI, it is very intuitive and makes a complex game very accessible. This is a genius stroke in that the game is easy to play but hard to master. Seasoned players can up the difficulty and take advantage of the more obscure details that can be the difference from winning and losing.
A great game, now more accessible although I believe some of the purists will rather play HOI3. Still, a great thinking man's game which is what Paradox specialise in!

I have been a MYST fan ever since I got the disc (only the disc w/o any info on what to expect) with my first TV bought PC. It was intriguing, challenging, and presented original puzzles that were not only logical but led you on thru the game the same way. A good amount of sound thought proceses had to be employed to them.
I respectfully disagree with those who compare EoA with MYST in any but the most superficial ways.
Where MYST had you "playing detective" (so to speak), You have to go around gathering info; then piece it all together; then see if your conclusion was right. EoA is a glorified game of Hide and Seek. Many of the "puzzles" are stupidly simple requiring little thought. Those that do require some "brain-work" rely mainly on going thru the different permutations. But what is most frustrating is running around and around looking for your last "Hide and Seek" piece with no hints or clues to guide you. For example: the stone faces around the what looks to be some kind of "secret" door.
But what's got me really ticked is light bulbs. Have you counted the number of crates and boxes there are? 75 give or take at this point. Did you notice how many of those are labled with their contents? Exactly ONE! "BULBS", in big bold letters in the downstairs closet where you find a star.
Question: When trying to turn on the light in the attic above the bathroom is it inevitable that you drop the bulb? The makers HAD to have known that could happen. Which is why they labled that ONE BOX SO BOLDLY so you'd remember. Right? WRONG! Scurry back down to get your bulb; click on the box and NOTHING HAPPENS! ARE YOU F@&KING KIDDING ME? What was the point of labling that one box with the ONE ITEM you would soon need? Or maybe the makers are just a bunch of sadistic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s?
And is there a point of gathering all those coins, photos, dolls, etc.? If not then my point of this being a "Hide & Seek" game is proven.

Picked this up in he summer sale and wasn't completely sure what to expect considering the troubled development and a lot of the fan backlash and n the end  learned a couple lessons. The first lesson wa that a name, especially a franchise name is a powerful thing, the XCOM series possessing a a very loyal fandom of strategy gamers, and that messing with how a franchise is supposed to usually work is likely to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off and makes them more likely to dislike the end product. So for starters Id like to say that The Bureau would have been more well recieved if the XCOM name weren't attached.
The next lesson for me was that the game is actually fun, by no means perfect, but fun. It's somewhere between Mass Effect and Enemy Unknown a far as the combat goes, with the player taking on the role of Agent Carter as the squad leader rather than being a disembodied commander, which I admittedly liked. The combat is real time rather than turn based with you directly fighting the enemies alongside two AI allies, which to get the most out of you will need to command them, and command them often. Aside from that you can actually explore the XCOM base which was another nice touch.
The story itself is a typical alien invasion plot, which we have likely seen many times before. Is this inherently bad? Not in my opinion after all we like XCOM because we like alien invasion stories. Thematically there is plenty in common with Enemy Unknown as there is still the idea of securing and reverse engineering alien tech for your agents, making decisions about what missions your squad will take.
My final thoughts are this, it's a fun game that makes me remember old alien invasion movies (which I loved) with a 1950s/1960s aesthetic that is got a bit of Men in Black flair to it with gameplay the works, even if you do have to keep an eye on your AIs and order them often to make the best of. I would't hve got it when it was new and full price but at the current price it's well worth it, and during a sale grab it, you'll be in for a good time, if a little cliched and frustrated at times. It's not perfect, but it is enjoyable.
