Roughly 45 mins into this game. Some basic feature requirements:
1) Smart inventory stacking. This is basic inventory management. If I have 30 iron in my backpack and 20 in my storage it becomes a stack of 50, not two stacks (30 and 20, respectively). This is absolutely required for any game with inventory management.
2) There is way too much weather changes without enough information being given to the player.
3) Running out of oxygen should just instantly kill you. Forcing you to walk and heal uup with bandages instead of outright killing the player is basically torture. Make the Oxygen bar more noticable. It's way too easy to go from 100 oxygen to 10.
4) Where are all the creatures coming from? Nothing as far as the eye can see then suddenly dozens of creatures show up.
5) Having the MP servers off for over 2 days is not acceptable for a MP game, especially over a sale weekend when you are going to get new players. I don't see a reason why this game has an official MP server especially when in early access. Just leave it at friend hosting and call it a day.

Ok, this game is amazing. I've played through the game three times. Once on Xbox (low chaos) Twice on pc (low chaos and high-ish chaos). To avoid spoliers, I got the best and second worest ending. (worst ending is barely differnet from second worst btw). So in this game you play as Corvo Attono, a man blamed for the murder of the empress. You have to attempt to take down the lord regient to get Emily, the daughter of the empress, back onto the the throne with the help of the loyalist the group that broke you out of prison. The outsider gives you powers where you first get blink, (a power that gives you a short range teleport) then if you find runes around the map you can uprgade powers and/or get new powers that range from stopping time to summoning swarms of rats that destroy anything in their path. Speaking of rats, all of Dunwall is overtaken by the plague which turns the citizens into weepers (slightly smarter and more agile zombies) that are taking over Dunwall) Avoiding spoilers, how you play affects how the city is affected by the plague. You need to sneak around to get to your main targets to where you can murder them or find a way to neutralize them. Sneaking is better for your chaos level to stay low, but go crazy and kill tons of people, your chaos will go up.The grapphics are nice, if a bit outdated even on high settings. But it still looks nice. I have noticed that the pc version is much buggier then console. It's not extremely buggy, but it is noticible. Loading screens are quick, you can plug in any type of controller (besides steam controler) or use the keyboard. Quicksaving and quickloading are here, its overall a great game. Which version should you play? Despite the bugs I would say PC because it looks better and load times are much quicker. 9/10

This is a short and sweet game that I'm glad I played. Through a Visual Novel format, you are tasked with guiding a young lady with social anxiety (or horrific shyness as it was known in the past) to make porridge. The problem is that she has to use the communal kitchen to do it, which is where her anxiety almost fells her attempts to make "dinner".
There's only one small mar, in my opinion, which is the snarky comment she gives to the girls upon leaving the kitchen. 'You can have your precious kitchen back.' They weren't waiting to use it, they hadn't said anything. If the main character is unpleasant to others, she's hardly going to endear herself to her compatriots. A nice option would have been 'nod and smile' because sometimes you don't need to talk to communicate.
Also, it highlights how some young adults are thrust into solo living without being prepared for it. Also, would any of her neighbours help her if they knew she was struggling? A simple game about making porridge, less than an hour long, made me think about all these facets, and I really like that.
There are a good few endings here, and they show you how one little missed detail can ruin someone's evening.
But I think this is a brilliant start for the developer, and it takes the Visual Novel game style in a novel (forgive the pun) direction. I'd really like more of these sorts of games.

One of the best MMORPGs hands-down.
I've mainly played this outside of Steam (hence the low playtime), but the depth and level of customization that RIFT gives you for your class is incredible, and blows WoW out of the water. Sure, other things (like the dungeon experience imo) are better in WoW, but RIFT compensates with lots of really cool smaller features that add up quickly. For example, if you outlevel a dungeon/zone, but want to go back and grab the quests, you can set your 'mentored level' down, which essentially allows you to temporarily lower your character's level at will. Player housing is also present, and you can view other player's intricate designs on persistent leaderboards based on user votes.
Combat is similar to other ability based RPGs, such as WoW, with the exception on the level of freedom that you get to design your own class. You can manually choose all your abilities from a set of about 10 talent trees (called 'souls') for each class, of which you can have 3 active at once. This means that almost every class can fill almost every role (DPS, tank, support, healer), and you can save your ability sets to allow you to change between roles on the fly (eg DPS → healer), giving each character a lot of versatility. Note that as this game is now free-to-play, some souls are locked behind a paywall, although at £15 if you shop around, it isn't too bad.
Moving onto the game's implementation of free-to-play, you can easily complete the game (and the expansions – which are free to access) without paying anything, with all the in-game shop stuff being optional. If you do subscribe (£8.99/month last time I looked), you get the usual XP boosts etc that you would expect from a sub to a free MMO. A nice change however is the fact that the game was originally designed to b pay-to-play, so all the quests and story etc is scaled to those at 100% XP rate – subscribing just allows you to skip out parts as you see fit (and the XP boost can be toggled off). This is a nice change from other games like SWTOR, which feels like it's the subscribers that are getting the 100%, with the free players left at about 75%.
Overall, it's a solid offering from Trion, which I feel is equal to, and better than is some cases, WoW.

Puzzles are sensibly arranged: i.e. if you need to find x objects to complete a puzzle they will be in the same area so you don’t have to spend hours traipsing around wondering if you missed something.

Some pretty animations for things like book opening (which if you freeze-frame you can see is Lorem Ipsum but still pretty).

It’s very engrossing, I was about an hour in when I first thought “hang on, I only came here to fix the wiring”. By that point I was unlocking some kind of electronic safe-door in a collapsing Scottish castle with two hovering aliens watching me. So that’s well done.  Apologies if it turns out they actually are aliens and that should have been spoiler tagged.

It great to see a KickStarter game deliver a finished game, rather than perpetual pre-alpha, alpha, beta, etc.

The bad:

I’m about an hour in but so far I’m yet to find any problem which couldn’t more easily be solved with a hammer and chisel.

Suffers from the point-and-click problem that it’s very hard to know what is background and what is important. For example a chisel might well seem like a jolly useful thing to have with you but in fact what it wants you to pick up is a strangely shaped bit of bend metal next to it. No not that bit of metal, THIS one. There is no cursor change when you hover over useful stuff versus scenery so that’s bad.

It seems to want you to collect photograph and Roman coins but it doesn’t explain why or allow you to look at them. I don’t approve of this. Unless we are going to find a slot machine at the end.

Clichés: If you don’t want someone to get into your work, password-protect it, or get a decent lock. Don’t leave a series of quite difficult puzzles set out like a series of escape room games. And why would you rip pages out of your diary and spread them around the castle like confetti? I know these are mystery game staples but still a bit tedious.

Some puzzles make it easier to guess than solve. For example I had to place these four computer tablets on things that looked like an ipod shuffle base. The tablets could be in one of about seven settings but you had to place one at a time and it would not let you place them if they were in the wrong position. I’m sure there was a solution, but it was way more efficient to just brute force it than to go looking for the proper way to do it.

The ugly:

The interface moves from free camera rotation to fixed camera when you click on certain objects and you have to double click somewhere near the bottom to get back to free camera mode. However there is no indication that this has happened, leading to anger and rage.

Transition from fixed camera point A to fixed camera point B is slow and annoying. I guess there is some programming or development reason for this but it would be much better if we could move freely at least within a single room.

OMG the rotation. It’s hard to know if the thing you are trying to unlock is stopping at a given point because you’ve not correctly completed the puzzle or if the mouse is just stuck in the rotation animation. I think this could be because it was designed with tablets in mind, but this needs fixing. There is one bit with a clock with a rotating face where I wasted ages not realising that I had solved the puzzle but the mouse control was so inexact that I failed at rotating the face.  Another time I spent ages trying to get a handle to move, gave up and had to find a walkthrough to discover it was meant to move, I just hadn’t got the exact correct turney motion angle. There was one bit where you have to use a record-player turntable to open a drawer, each rotation of the LP took about 1 minute and opened the drawer an eighth of an inch. For a game which relies so much on turney-turney it should sort that♥♥♥♥♥♥out.

Finally, when I click on a door, it opens the door ajar, but doesn’t move me through it. I have to click again to move through it. Why would you do this?

Conclusion:

Glad I backed it. Fun, creative but low-budget puzzle game. Sort of what I expected.

Underrated squad-based third-person shooter with light tactical strategy elements set in the XCOM Universe. Most similar to Mass Effect 2/3 in how the combat plays and feels, though it is not quite as smooth, you and your teammates are not as resilent, and there is a much greater emphasis on flanking.
Although the product as a whole feels a little incomplete  (The game is short for a strategy title, clocking in at about 15-20 hours), there are enough interesting elements here to give it a look. On most difficulty levels, Squad members have permadeath, which means you must be careful - if they bleed out,  they are gone for good. "Dispatch" missions also exist whe you can send inactive squad members out or eliminate the need for grinding up your reserves, and tinkering is usually kept pretty light. The game is challenging, but fair for the most part, with only a few chokepoints of  design stupidity.
Plot is decent-to-good, gaining momentum towards the final 4-5 hours of the game.
Drawbacks are that grenade spam can occasionally reach absurd levels, the characters are somewhat flat, and the game simply does not have the same level of polish that Unknown/Within have.
It is not as compelling as Enemy Unknown/Within, but people looking for a squad-based tps with a science fiction flavor, or simply looking for a game with combat similar to Mass Effect with a slightly more strategic bent, will enjoy this.
Worth picking up on a deal or a sale.

This game takes the crafting to the next level. Your camp level affects everything you do, as you can only level your character to your camp level. Item recipes are locked behind levels of buildings, which you will need to gather many supplies to upgrade, to finally build yourself some decent gear.

I enjoy the little humour the game has and some of the quests are just the right amount of silly. It's one of the things that really charmed me in the first game and I'm glad they kept to it. There are enough "try hard serious" zombie games out there, this one is just good fun.

I can't recommend this game in its current state. Its playable of course, but its horribly unbalanced. I've put in 25+ hours into TAB, the majority of the 7 or so games I've played were at 75% score factor (less than "normal" difficulty, I presume), and I've lost every single time. Note that I'm relatively good at games like Age of Empires, so stow the "you suck lol" or "this game just isn't for you" arguments, please. Those arguments simply make you look silly.
I have a list of the games faults below, in no particular order of importance. I'll go through them in detail. If the game changes and these problems are fixed, I'll happily amend my review.
- "You can't build that here". Massive amounts of building restrictions. Extremely aggravating, and hugely complicates space conservation which is vital to winning. TAB is unnecessarily anal about spacing when it absolutely shouldn't be. Units wont walk through buildings when they absolutely should (units have bad pathfinding in general). Randomly generated terrain affects the spacing problem as well, like odd cracks in the ground and ore deposits that prevent a proper line of walls from being built. Also, some buildings, like the Warehouse and research buildings, are far too large (nothing aside from endgame buildings should be larger than 3x3). Overall, the space the game gives you in the Dark Moorlands is a chore to deal with, and this could very likely be the case with other map types. And to top things off, most buildings have an additional spacing limit ("free access") that effectively makes a 2x2 building act like a 3x3, 3x3 act like a 4x4, etc., which makes the spacing problems even worse.
- Buildings essentially have half health vs zombies. At 50% health, the building shuts down and creates more zombies to attack more buildings, rinse and repeat until you lose. One zombie can (and will) snowball into an unfair loss when the game is already a chore micromanaging each defense line. Additionally, the Command Center has effectively 2,500 HP rather than 5,000 since you lose once it becomes "infected". Why list buildings with "HP" when their yellow health portion is the only part that matters? The yellow health should either be extended or removed entirely, because regular green health serves no practical purpose unless its a wall.
- Gold generation is unbalanced, and you need gold to build anything substantial. Unless you're supposed to know some MLG secret, there's something very wrong with gold generation, even if you create massive amounts of houses (which generate your gold). The gold price of some buildings and units could also be the problem. 330 for a tower, 240 gold for a soldier, and 200 for a stone gate seem particularly unbalanced for early game. This might be solved by reducing (or eliminating) building "Upkeep" costs (not even sure why Upkeep costs even exist).
- Alerts on where undead are attacking aren't reliable enough. I lost when a late-game horde split into two groups under my nose - I focused on one as the other broke into my colony. As previously mentioned, there are also too many perimeters to check and maintain during mid/late game, and the alerts and mini-map don't do their job well enough.
- The horde can come from any direction, and when it does, you only have minutes to prepare and direct troop movement. Having to unload all units from every perimeter tower and bring them to one location is a hassle and wastes time. You also have to partially guess where the horde will end up, as a yellow skull on the mini map doesn't provide enough information, and if your prediction fails, you take heavy losses, if not outright lose, because you sent your troops to the wrong spot. A pathway on the minimap showing the horde's movement might fix this.
- There are only 6 offensive units in the game (three of them are late-game units), meaning its a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor selection of player options.
- Too many infected "types". Infected Aged, Decrepit, and Young have the same stats and are the same unit, and Fresh Infected and Infected Colonist are (basically) the same unit. They can keep the different art, but should all have the same name to avoid confusion.
- Villages of Doom (structures that spawn hordes of zombies) should never spawn near the player's starting point. Ever.
- There should be a button to retry or reroll a map. Currently you have to start a new game with a new name to "reroll".
Overall, for me, the beginning of the game is fun and tense, but mid-to-late game becomes a cluster♥♥♥♥ due to lack of defenses, which in turn was mostly caused by a lack of gold, despite having a huge amount of houses plus a bank. There are more gripes I have with TAB, but these are the most noteworthy. Really hope to see these rebalanced. My batch of losses honestly feel like they belong to a 150% score factor game, not a 75% one. Something isn't adding up here.

The setup is way too difficult even on all easiest settings (and I'm not new by any means to RTS games).   It really doesn't take much for one infected to break a wall in a few seconds (which is just not right - ever watch the walking dead? Ever see one break down a huge wooden wall in seconds? nope.), infect one other person, then a tent (which converts in seconds also – I guess the workers are sleeping during the day and not working), and even if it was a slow walking dead that snuck in somehow, suddenly the converts are raving lunatics running around infecting others so fast it's like the colonists have no sense of self preservation at all (I'm pretty sure some would protect themselves). There's no possible way to contain it, especially when starting out. Even with a very large colony and dozens of fighters, your hours of building is doomed (It’s so set in stone that I think right now an “abandon mission” type button would be handy to just delete the whole thing and start over on one click, since recovery is pointless). I'm almost certain the AI "cheats" as well, changing the horde's attack point on the fly as you move to protect one part of the base (that is, long before they arrive). The developer did mention, there is no save and reload for where you were, so keep this in mind.  Once you die, your dead, no going back.  For me, this limits the replayability to try "what if I did this instead" scenarios. Since every map is different, it will be hard to learn better ways based on map situations. There is a save game folder however, so I may be able to backup my saves manually.
On another note, it seems I'm always fighting with the system at every turn and it is sucking all the fun out of it (especially loosing everything after spending hours on an awesome colony [I tried the default settings first], only to have to start from scratch).  Need workers? Build tents.  Want fighters? Convert workers into fighters. Need more workers? Too bad, they are all fighters, build more tents to get workers.  Oops, need more food, but wait, can't, because I can only have one fishing spot and hunter shed next to the only one water hole and forest next to the colony (they must be far apart). Since the only few fighters I have are protecting the colony (usually in quite an open area) I cannot thin the ranks to turn them back into workers, (especially with so little fighters able to protect the base as is already), so then I’m forced to expand the colony to find more food areas - but guess what? I need 1 worker for every Tesla Tower expansion point (that makes no sense at all to me – I can understand a worker needed to *build* a power point, but it is NOT a power STATION, so what gives?), so that also sucks what little workers I might have remaining. The food shortages are the worst since, again, the buildings must be extremely far apart, and many times the forest or water is not large enough in the starting area. Yes, there are farms, but only if your lucky enough to have lots of grass near by, and you also have to get to the point of researching it first (good luck on anything other than easy). Then the first wave comes and, well, if you didn’t get your walls up (spikes really help here also), you’re doomed. Things just don’t seem well balanced to me.  Even for a hard-core game, things should make sense, otherwise it just seems like unrealistic difficulties for no good reason.  If the developers change it so the colonists fight back also (if even with rocks and sticks, at least to cause some damage before getting turned), give more defence to the walls and buildings, and not have the Tesla Towers need a worker, then it would feel more realistic – then I can actually enjoy my creation and live in the game … sort of. ;) And I can imagine, even with those changes, the game will still be hard-core for sure.

They really need a mode like that in this game for people like me I guess. ;)

Long Review - Scroll to bottom for TLDR;
First of all I want to mention that several of these other reviews are based of what the game is in its current states and not considering it is in early access and has wonderful potential.
'They Are Billions' is a beautifully crafted game in a genre lacking in today's market. It cuts out the bells and whistles other  titles have such as CIV or AOE and brings you back to core roots of a simple RTS similar to the Command & Conquer series. The visuals are very nice and the steampunk style looks great. It really is gorgeous.
The game currently has no multiplayer but IF and WHEN (Lord I hope so!) they decide to implement multiplayer and tweak the game balance issues this game will be a solid winner hands down.
Currently the game only has a survival challenge mode which is very fun and introduces you to the game although it can be challenging. From my knowledge of reading on the forums, and following Dev releases, they are working on a campaign mode.
My personal ratings of features of the game with a brief explanation keeping in mind the game is a work in progress.
9/10 Combat: Although pathing is somewhat clunky at times the combat is spot on. kiting is viable and multitasking and macro help further your strategy.
7/10 Units: All in all I am thoroughly pleased with the design of the units and sizes. There are definitely several balance changes that need to be made but I am hopeful they will work it out in the end.
9/10 Graphics: The steampunk style looks great and the animation and colors fit perfectly.
9/10 AI: AI targeting and pathing works fairly well. I have yet to experience any issues or bugs with enemy AI.
7/10 Mayor System: This is a wonderful idea but it definitely needs tweaks and balance checks. A skill tree you could select prior to game or having more options to choose from would really broaden this. I the current state it is hit or miss on how useful they can be.
8/10 Building: The building is wonderful in this game but it MOST definitely needs to be tweaked. The numbers at time feel insane and leave you exasperated struggling to find options to make your colony efficient yet defensive. This is something that can easily be manipulated and I have faith that with time and patience this will be polished.
7/10 Upgrades: In dire need of work. It is currently very easy to manage the upgrade system but it definitely flawed. Building space is the most important resource and the workshop buildings are not able to be upgraded themselves and take up 3 huge areas in realty.
9/10 RTS Style: This game truly fits the genre. Other titles on steam may be listed as RTS but they are a far cry from what many of us know and love from a true RTS game.
Features I would like to see implemented -
- Skill Tree's or some other type of customization feature for mayors and units.
- Ability to hide or make transparent a building so that you may select buildings behind it.
- Unit stroke outlines as they pass through buildings and terrain.
- Have housing utilize one square as opposed to four.
- Upgradeable workshops (ie - upgrading to the next tier will allow research from the past and current tiers)
- Multiplayer. MULTIplayer. MULTIPLAYER. ONLINE MULTIPLAYER :)
Overall 8/10
TLDR; If you are looking are looking for a nostalgic C&C style game this is for you. Although it is currently only single player it is fun enough to shell out $25 if you are an old RTS addict and looking for your fix, otherwise wait for multiplayer to be released or for a price drop. If you are not big on RTS games but interested in giving it a try I probably would wait till the price drops to the $15ish range. If anyone has read my reviews before, you know I will play for some time before posting so be ready for a balanced (as much as possible anyways) and fair OPINION of why you should get this game. I will keep it detailed but not a novel so here we go.
WHAT I LOVE ABOUT TAB/BASIC GAMEPLAY
They Are Billions (TAB) is a colony-management game set in a dark and foreboding steampunk setting where the entire world is overrun with walking dead and you must help manage your colony lest it become another breeding pit for the damned. You must maintain an army, build fortifications, research new technologies and otherwise build a new life potentially surrounded by shambling undead ready to eat your face off at any given mistake. The thing I love most about it? Honestly? How much it forces you to think three steps ahead in your placement of your buildings as some give bonuses for being around production buildings and others around houses, etc. It really makes you think... Hmm... Is my walls better here where its aethetically pleasing or strategically sound where if they break through here I have a second line of defense? Choices and RNG at times can really, REALLY punish you but in the end once you figure out how the game operates and such you kind of feel rewarded.
WHAT DON'T I LIKE/ENJOY ABOUT TAB?
Difficulty scaling is a bit of a major stretch. The game really is not easy and with no tutorial (at the time of writing this in Early Access open beta mode) you have to learn through trial and error what to do and what not to do. The maps are locked behind difficulty which I actually do not mind but sometimes you will die to the simplest mistakes and you won't know whether it was your fault or the game's kinda wonky pathing. The game works flawlessly, even with potentially thousands of units on screen (not joking, sometimes the hordes get very, VERY dense) but you are pressed to figure out how to KILL said dense hordes.
TL;DR the game is very enjoyable, and actually feels like an early access title should at this stage. Sure they still need some polish and tweaks but all in all I am very pleased to finally get my hands on it after watching patiently for it to be released for so long. Hopefully we will see a randomizer for the missions or something more akin to a random scenario on a random tileset or something in the future but for now, They Are Billions is worthy of a time killer in your collection and I will definitely be playing and streaming it more on Twitch.tv . Thank you for reading everyone. Kerrigan Out.

After the tons of fun that was Test Drive Unlimited, I bought the sequel, expecting more of the same good stuff. Boy, was I wrong...
After the free-roaming driving game with many fun cars (and some nice bikes), plenty of different races/missions to do and a near complete lack of nonsense that was the first TDU, we get a sequel that has almost nothing of that.
I'm completely uninterested in the online component, as I would rather play single player than be run into by various morons, strangers and griefers (no offense to you strangers who happen to be nice), which is the same way I felt about TDU1 (which I played 99+% offline), so I won't be commenting on any differences in that aspect. A simple LAN mode, with or without the possibility of setting up a dedicated server, would have made it a better game to play with friends and people one can tolerate.
Anyway, in comparison with TDU1, TDU2 has some of the following differences:
+ Slightly nicer graphics
+ More than one island to drive around on
+ Some weather
- No Lamborghini cars (probably not the devs' fault, but they were some of the most fun ones in TDU1)
- Really bad physics and car handling
- A lot of dead weight in the form of bad narrative, boring cutscenes and other "cinematic" nonsense
- A very linear progression, with missions locked until you complete the previous bunch.
- Mandatory driving schools (several "tiers" of them for each of the three car types, too) before you can access a huge amount of the content. Also, they are harder to get through than most of the game, for no good reason. I hate them.
To sum it all up...
If you liked the first Test Drive Unlimited, you should avoid this.
If you just want a fun driving/racing game (other than just cruising around), you should avoid this.
If you like player freedom, you should avoid this.
If you want a game free of "cinematic" garbage and general fluff, you should avoid this.
If, on the other hand, you like being forced through bad narrative, watching cutscenes, playing frustrating mandatory tutorials and being rail-roaded through a really linear waste of time? Well, feel free to knock yourself out and play this. I know I won't touch it anymore. I'm just gonna go back and play TDU1 and  Need for Speed 3. At least, those games did racing and driving fun.

The player will just do what the Loyalist tell him to and then follow the little arrow on the screen. They are rewarded merely with some coins and bullets for going off-track. The player is so powerful he has no need to stop for a second and analyze the environment, you only stop to think of a funny way to kill those 3 Watch Officers at the distance.
This is a fun and relatively well designed game that can be replayed a bunch by more completionist minded people, but if you're looking for a unique work of art, you're looking in the wrong place.

For The Cake:
1 2/3 cups all-purpose flour
1 1/2 cups granulated sugar
2/3 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1 1/2 teaspoons baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1 1/2 cups buttermilk
1/2 cup vegetable shortening
2 eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 cup Kirsch (cherry liqueur)
For the filling:
¼ cup Kirsch
2 cans sour cherries
3 cups heavy whipping cream
¼ cup confectioners' sugar
3 tablespoons cocoa
For the Garnish:
1 semisweet chocolate bar, frozen
At least 8 maraschino cherries (no stems)
One white candle
Directions
1) Preheat your oven to 350°F.
2) Grease and flour two 8 inch cakepans, or line with parchment paper.
3) Sift together the flour, the cocoa, the baking soda and the salt. Set this aside.
4) Beat the shortening and sugar together until they are fluffy. Add the eggs an vanilla and beat thoroughly.
5) Slowly beat in the flour mixture, occasionally alternating with the buttermilk. Beat until combined.
6) Pour the batter into the cakepans.
7) Bake for about 35 or 40 minutes (or until a a fork or a wooden pick comes out clean when inserted into the cake. Let the cake cool completely. The cake will be easier to cut if you keep it in the fridge for a few hours before cutting.
8) After the cake has cooled, cut each layer in half (horizontally) to make four total layers. Sprinkle the layers with the 1/2 cup of Kirsch.
9) Drain the canned cherries in a colander to remove most of the juice.
10) Beat the whipping cream with confectioners' sugar until it thickens to desired texture.
11) Put a small amount of the cream/sugar mixture aside for garnish. Mix the cocoa powder into the remaining majority of the whipped cream frosting.
12) Place one cake layer on the serving dish you wish to use. Spread about one 6th of the whipped cream on the layer, and strew a third of the cherries on top of the whipped cream.
13) Add the second cake layer on top of the first. Spread one 6th of the whipped cream on the second layer and 1/3 of the cherries on top.
14) Add the third cake layer. Spread 1/6 of the whipped cream on that and add the remaining cherries.
15) Top with the last cake layer. Frost the top and sides of the cake with remaining frosting.
16) Use a potato peeler on the chocolate to create thin shaves. Gently pat the chocolate shaves on to the sides and top of the cake, completely coating it.
17) Use the whipped cream you set aside earlier to place eight small circles around the top of the cake. Place your non-stemmed maraschino cherries on each one.
18) Place white candle in the center and light. Congratulations, you have made the cake a reality!

I don't like bashing things repeatedly, nor do I like inexperience and brashness forming my decisions. So, here goes...
Osiris: New Dawn
The majority of my experience in Osiris: New Dawn comes from solo play, though about 4 to 5 hours worth of it was co-op.
Before even jumping into a game  I noticed the settings had player progress rather slow, and the amount of aliens faced looked rather challenging(their wordage was "Infested" ). So, to counter the default higher rates of aliens, I upped the amount of points I got per level up. My thought behind this was, if I'm going to be in combat a lot I want it to be worth it. After playing ARK: Survival Evolved for so long and seeing the similarities between Osiris and Ark already apparent I found this to be a good move once in game.
Pros:
-> Graphics are beautiful
-> Sound is excellent and adds to the survival horror aspect quite nicely.
-> Gun-combat...decent but needs work, I play mostly in third-person view and DooM style with high movement and utilizing range--the pistol with its unlimited ammo are your best friend starting out and animations when third-person mode need tweaking. My cursor would be on the target and my character is shooting behind him at whatever is back there while Im aiming and trying to hit the target on my screen.
-> Vehicle Controls are brilliant and worked very well but the vehicle movement and collision can sometimes be lacking. The hover bike likes to nose plant into the ground, while the Spaceship flies brilliantly though sometimes will land but not-land where the gear is out and you're on the ground but the controls are still as if youre flying(only the hover and throttle controls are workable, currently taking off again and landing elsewhere can fix this otherwise there is no notification that something is off).
-> The building process of a base or weapon is very unique and a nice touch. Though vehicles I found were very easy to obtain once one built the laboratory.
Cons
-> Melee combat needs some major love. The machete you can make in your inventory is just plain meh, in fact I've yet to understand what any of those tools are good for and even some resources. However, I believe these may become relevant down the road. The only melee tool that really found success was the "Dragon's Tooth" and even then it was iffy. Crab legs could be chopped or other things insta-killed with it. Melee combat was really utilized by my friend during the time we co-oped together and that was because we had gotten jumped on trek out to get lithium and his body has disappeared(decay rates should be tweakable for private servers and singleplayer). I distracted most mobs by engaging them first with the pistol and then he would flank them from behind with the Dragon's Tooth and either wound them or finish them off.
-> Alien attacks are relentless and can easily overwhelm solo players by their 2nd day on "Infested" levels. During the day I'd mine resources and try to work as much as I could towards getting more rifle ammo because I knew when the night came nothing but trying to kill the overly aggressive aliens would be all I could do and not surprisingly I'd die a lot by being overwhelmed with 5 aliens at once. I don't mind a challenge but theres a certain point where you just cant do anything to even stop yourself from getting hosed. Not even wait the aliens out from a distance to recover your stuff when theyve scattered. Why? Because theres a ten minute timer on every body you die in.
-> Base building can often be confusing but like all things can be figured out with help from the internet. The same goes for where to find critical resources like lithium, diamond, etc. Though I've found that instinct, and a natural wanderlust can be just as helpful.
-> The meotors are highly annoying after so long and do not make much sense as they always seem to target the player and are never just striking at random.
-> Satellites show up randomly downed on the map but theres no animation or anything visible as to how they got downed.
-> Someone dies but you're near and still alive, can you retrieve their stuff...no. Maybe this is just because we did PvE. But either way when we got jumped both of us died and ran back to retrieve our stuff and die again while fighting off the aliens that would not leave us alone(we did not instigate the fight). When I arrived the third time, my friend was still alive and we managed to kill off the last of them together but he died his second time from a lack of oxygen. I'm standing right next to where he died but I don't see any body nor bag or anything. The timer runs out on his body and thus we encouter a semi-huge setback as his assault rifle(with 3 mags) and pistol are now gone. I have encoutered this situation is singleplayer as well and it is practically impossible to recover from on "Infested" levels. Especially when I have a dragons tooth and a gnat or arachnoid can just one shot me from full health at a distance. What is eliminated here is not a concept of "fairness" but rather a chance to overcome.
Overall: I reccommend this game, the price point is a little high for what all is there right now. So, grab it when its on sale and passively enjoy it. This game is about patience and has a tedious aura to it. In the moment you could horrified, angered, overjoyed, or completely reactionary. But planning and constant level-headed thinking can overcome most anything. During the co-op session my friend lost his guns and some much needed resources but I loaned him my pistol and made us melee weapons should the worst come while I used the assault rifle. Continuing on we have bounced back and have even explored space quite a bit. Natural curiosity has found almost all the resources we needed were actually quite close to us and all we had to do was look and find them. Personally, I still play Osiris because I simply enjoy the environment and exploring it now. Though the only real area for exploration is the surface of the planet, space has very little at the moment.
This something I highly encourage people to pick up if they like survival games when its on sale but its also something I would say,"Wait and see" to those that are on the fence. The more the mobs are turned up, or left at the default setting of maximum amount the more it is reccommend to play with friends or at least work with someone to watch each others backs.

As fancy and flashy the game may look, it does little to keep it interesting. With a total of 2 attacks, 1 aerial attack, and 2 power attacks, you find yourself mashing X and Y in random order hoping to dish out some damage. There are only 3 types of enemies, and one boss. The first enemy introduced are slow shadow guys, that have one attack. They are the obvious grunts of the game, and provide no challenge unless they group up on you in a party of over 10 at once. Even then it just takes a simple dash away, and half of them forget you ever existed.
The next enemy looks much like the first, only with a gun and no brain. For being the long distance foe, they seem to have very short-sighted vision, as they don't seem to notice you until you are brushing arms together. Their run is exactly as fast as yours, and when they see you, that is exactly what they do. Your only option is to dash after them, which usually puts you ahead of them, and they run the other way.   Oh, did I mention they only fire about once every 5 minutes? Yea, so there is that. You corner the non-hostile snipers against a wall, mash your two buttons, until they die and fall through the wall, with their feet sticking out.
The third enemy is introduced like the others were, randomly. They are (pretty cool looking) giants with a cannon that shoots exploding projectiles. Normally by the third enemy type in a game, they introduce an enemy that requires thinking and logic to overcome. Not this guy. You dash through his chest (apparently you are ethereal) and wack a few times. Repeat until dead.
The boss comes after a room so full of enemies you think "I could use a health pot" but the pot does not come until the boss room, and they spawn behind the titan. This large guy appears to have fewer attacks than you, which is to say less than 4. You wack at his feet, and slowly chip away at his ridiculous health bar. You defeat him the same way you do the last guys; dash, wack, dash, wack...
You ever play a Zelda game, and destroy pots for the rupies? Well apperntly in this universe they store green healing magic in their pots rather than money. No big deal.
The game simply looks amazing, and is probably what drags most people into it. However, after just a few minutes you notice how blocky the animations are, lacking any fluidity. The second enemy obviously takes assets from the first, and the boss obviously takes assets from the third enemy.
Controls are simple, but use of power attacks took a little experimenting (due to there being no tutorial). The camera acts like a strung out toddler swatting flies. The left stick (which moves you) also moves your camera, rather harshly. While the right stick has little control at all. You find yourself letting the camera do its own thing, and using the right stick to correct its errors.
The lack of any tutorial or the effort to copy and past into Google Translate not only seems lazy, but drags down the 20 minute game. You are thrown into a ♥♥♥♥♥torm of flailing husks with arms, and asked to mash two buttons in an attempt to knock the husks through the walls.
I suggest trying the game for yourself, laugh at how easy it is, then die to the overpowered boss.
Failing that, at least you get to see some♥♥♥♥♥♥

A charming and cartoony JRPG about kids saving Halloween, bogged down by a a battle system where the best three costumes are the first three you get, and where combat boils down to everyone attacking normally for two rounds, suing their special ability on the third, and repeating until the fight's over. There's no real reason to use any of the other costumes because none of them have as good stats or as good special ability as an all area hitting massive nuke with follow up DoT damage, a powerful shield capable of turning hits into 1 or 2 damage, or the only heal in the game that doesn't require the target to be dead first to revive them. The combat system is incredibly repetitive, although active due to needing to do timed button presses. Ultimately, though, literally every fight becomes attack -> attack -> special -> repeat. Battle Stamps, the game's only equipment, don't alleviate this issue at all - some of the stamps offer side abilities that Stun or Slow enemies, but you're still doing the same attack/attack/spell trio the entire game.
I'm giving the game a positive recommendation because the repetitive and dull combat system ultimately wasn't enough to dissuade me from completing the (relatively short: 4-6 hours) game. It's still fun running around, collecting candy, and trick or treating, and seeing what the costumes look like in fights. If the game was any longer, the combat system would start to do real damage, but thanks to how short it is, it's not that big a deal.

+More than 50 different "mods", each with unique strategy. I personally dislike some of the more common ones, because it's too common to win after the first turn, but that's fine because mods like Tilt_Fix (where you joust on a horse) and Lenshu (where you need to be on the ground for a second straight to lose) play completely differently from them!
+The 1v1 nature of the game makes it very fun with friends. And even if your friend has never played the game before, you can "go easy on him" and still have lots of fun by trying crazy moves that you don't think you can pull off right.
+Simultaneous turns mean that the game happens pretty quickly, even though it is technically turn-based.
-Controls are difficult. I would prefer to have each joint bound to a different key.
-No "Quick Match" feature, so you often get stuck waiting for the other people on the server to finish...
-First 5-10 hours are TERRIBLE. I rage-quit multiple times. But honestly, it's not as bad as learning LoL or DotA.
"But it's too hard" - IGN 4/10 (no srsly that actually happened)

I was brought up in American suburbia, and Halloween was always my favorite holiday growing up, probably because I was kind of a dork. I just loved the idea of one night where all kids, regardless of their popularity or class, got to assume fun new identities, put on cool costumes, go to their neighbors, and ask for candy. It was magical. I never liked the scarier parts of the holiday because I was always kind of a timid kid, but the dressing-up, the friendship that you could feel on Halloween night, was very special.
With that said, this game is great. It's a love letter to suburban Halloween, with none of the scares and all of the fun and fantasy. I was a little skeptical of it before playing it as I had heard somewhat middling reviews upon its initial release, but after grabbing it in a Steam sale, I could not be happier with my purchase. Double Fine's characteristically thoughtful and funny writing is here in spades, and the characters you interact with are just delightful. That's a word I could apply to a lot of things in this game, actually—delightful.

This game is far too difficult for me to enjoy yet. As an ethusiast of many difficult games, including Factorio and FTL, I'm not able to enjoy this one yet.
The problem comes from the way in which zombie attack waves are implemented. You're building your own, and everything is fine, and then all of the sudden a MASSIVE horde shows up that's far larger than anything your defenses can handle. When this happens and you die, there's no real way to learn from it. What should I have done differently?
Other games give you tips like "Use this unit to counter that type of unit", or , "Have at least one X for every Y". Nope, withi this game you just get crushed over and over. The game has no way to educate me on how to improve, and I'm not willing to look outside the game for guides that simply tell me what to do, since that spoils the fun that I normally get from other games.
Sure, people could turn the difficulty down, but that's not something I'm looking to do in games that I play. I don't want the "easy mode". I want a mode that's difficult and punishing, and that teaches you what you did wrong so that you can improve along the way.
So far, They Are Billions is all grinding with no improvement. I doin't recommend it in its current state, since it's liable to be frustrating more than fun. The core mechanics are interesting, but the feedback loop is too long and indirect. The game needs to help teach players what they learn to improve. I'm left wondering that myself. Do I need to make more troops? More defenses? Make different types of troops? Better quality? There's no information in the game to help me understand what I need to do different the next time around.
After several playthroughs, I'm about to give up, For an example of games that do help educate the player on how to counter threats within the game, see Empires of the Undergrowth.
I think the game has a lot of potential and will be amazing once players are given information and options they need to react tacticall and improve. However, in its current early-access state, there isn't a lot of content in the game with which a player can react. I will update my review as the product changes over time.

(There are mild spoilers in this.)
You play as an ultra-anxious future cat-lady who hates all interaction with all people.
Not being such a person, I can't determine whether or not this is an accurate portrayal of such people. However, I can say that this is not fun; the writing completely fails to make you care about the main character. This was a short game: it should've been very easy to polish the writing enough to make you care about your character, at least a little bit! Instead, we're just told to "go fetch the oatmeal." A key example: one of your choices is "WHAT ABOUT THE THINGS?". This actually influences the game, but it's so silly that anyone who is not an ultra-anxious future cat-lady would just sort of roll their eyes at this. Moreover, the outcomes just seemed lazily done; you have a chance to drop your oatmeal (which happens if you undercook it), and when this happens, LITERALLY EVERYONE comes out to laugh at you. It's unrealistic (*one* person doing this, asking if you're OK, and then you freaking out would've been more realistic).
The music rather annoyed me. This is mostly a personal taste thing, I think there are people who would like it; I'll assume that I'm not in the target audience.
For all of the negatives, the art style struck me as cute. I liked it, and it probably hits the target audience well.
The key driving factor of a Visual Novel is the "Novel" part, and I have read better written fanfics. This is not worth even the 10 or so minutes I spent on it. If this had been worked on for far longer, it would have had potential.
It is, however, better than Depression Quest.

A really bad visual novel (and that's even stretching the term visual novel because this has less content than most) where a mentally handicapped person shows us just how mentally handicapped they are and are unable to perform basic human tasks. How they even got into a university in the first place is a good question to ask considering they would have had to talk to many different people to even get into a school. So the entire premise of this "visual novel" isn't even believable.
Your choices barely matter because most of the time you end up forced doing something according to the story narrative, which means this isn't much of a visual novel to begin with since the point of visual novels is to let players decide how the narrative goes, not how the narrative tells what the player to do.
Also the game is 115 MBs. Why? Surely file compression isn't that unheard of for these people, and they surely at least tried to compress the images and audio in the game, right? Nope. The images folder takes up around 56 MBs, and the audio 86 MBs. There are ways to compress these things without loss and they simply didn't even try. Sure, this seems like a weird thing to complain about, but optimization and efficiency should be a number one priority for developers of all kinds. This shows sloppiness and lack of dedication to the art of programming.
And speaking of art the art is the blandest and most uninspired stuff I've ever seen. The art style is something nearly everybody has probably seen if you even glance at one of those advice books for teenage girls, or spend a few minutes on tumblr.
To be honest, as someone with anxiety disorder myself, this thing paints people like me in a terrible light, as if we're unable to even perform basic tasks like getting food without anguish. The entirety of this thing screams "first world problems", which is pretty pretentious and shallow.
All in all you're better off making your own oatmeal in real life. Put some extra cinnamon and sugar on it, it'll help wash way the bad taste of this "interactive story".

For The Cake:
1 2/3 cups all-purpose flour
1 1/2 cups granulated sugar
2/3 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1 1/2 teaspoons baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1 1/2 cups buttermilk
1/2 cup vegetable shortening
2 eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 cup Kirsch (cherry liqueur)
For the filling:
¼ cup Kirsch
2 cans sour cherries
3 cups heavy whipping cream
¼ cup confectioners' sugar
3 tablespoons cocoa
For the Garnish:
1 semisweet chocolate bar, frozen
At least 8 maraschino cherries (no stems)
One white candle
Directions
1) Preheat your oven to 350°F.
2) Grease and flour two 8 inch cakepans, or line with parchment paper.
3) Sift together the flour, the cocoa, the baking soda and the salt. Set this aside.
4) Beat the shortening and sugar together until they are fluffy. Add the eggs an vanilla and beat thoroughly.
5) Slowly beat in the flour mixture, occasionally alternating with the buttermilk. Beat until combined.
6) Pour the batter into the cakepans.
7) Bake for about 35 or 40 minutes (or until a a fork or a wooden pick comes out clean when inserted into the cake. Let the cake cool completely. The cake will be easier to cut if you keep it in the fridge for a few hours before cutting.
8) After the cake has cooled, cut each layer in half (horizontally) to make four total layers. Sprinkle the layers with the 1/2 cup of Kirsch.
9) Drain the canned cherries in a colander to remove most of the juice.
10) Beat the whipping cream with confectioners' sugar until it thickens to desired texture.
11) Put a small amount of the cream/sugar mixture aside for garnish. Mix the cocoa powder into the remaining majority of the whipped cream frosting.
12) Place one cake layer on the serving dish you wish to use. Spread about one 6th of the whipped cream on the layer, and strew a third of the cherries on top of the whipped cream.
13) Add the second cake layer on top of the first. Spread one 6th of the whipped cream on the second layer and 1/3 of the cherries on top.
14) Add the third cake layer. Spread 1/6 of the whipped cream on that and add the remaining cherries.
15) Top with the last cake layer. Frost the top and sides of the cake with remaining frosting.
16) Use a potato peeler on the chocolate to create thin shaves. Gently pat the chocolate shaves on to the sides and top of the cake, completely coating it.
17) Use the whipped cream you set aside earlier to place eight small circles around the top of the cake. Place your non-stemmed maraschino cherries on each one.
18) Place white candle in the center and light. Congratulations, you have made the cake a reality!

He drove past us just before we decided to stop, though I didn't know it was him. We found a great base location and set up there, placing a lot of structures off the bat as Ethan had a lot of resources. Another guy, named Royal, joined our Colony. Royal eventually went off and I gathered supplies for Ethan.
Day 2:
In a very short space of time, Ethan had managed to build a host of vehicles, two mechs and a bike, as well as a GAV (a sort of armoured truck with a gun mounted on top). The bike made things much easier, and before I knew it Ethan had built TWO ships. We flew into space, messed around for a bit and built a small base on Aziel, the other planet, though eventually we retired back to Proteus 2, the starting planet.
Day 3:
I flew around on Proteus 2 in my ship, stopping to greet some people and give them supplies. A guy with no name was scaring people, making creepy comments, etc. He told me he would find me. Later I found a pretty cool base while flying around and noticed a guy there, so I came in for a landing, all of a sudden I was shot down and running on foot, and was finished off. Turns out it was the no name guy, and when I got back I realised he had the ranger class, and he gave me some vague answers about the TCP connections not being encrypted and that's how he got it.
Days 4-6:
I took a while trying to build a new ship and eventually manged it. Nothing much else happened.
Day 7: Using my new ship, I went to space and tried to go to Aziel, upon which I was disconnected 'by ServerLogic'. The ship was stuck in orbit while I was stuck on the ground.
Day 8:
Base was destroyed by the no name guy because our automated turrets shot him. We only had our domes left, and a bike that I left in the desert.
Days 8-10:
Re-built base, met two guys named Zergpooh and Hunterrosir. They helped, as well as Royal.
Day 11:
Made a new ship and flew into space. Base was attacked by a mech, which are not able to take damage. Base was completely destroyed and we were forced to make a new one, Zergpooh and Royal died in the attack when no name turned up. Hunterrosir had his internet go down about 15 minutes before. No name gave me a sniper rifle, a weapon not even implemented yet.
Day 12:
With the ship, Royal and I scouted for a new base location, and eventually found one and set up, then after a 50 meter travel I saw a mech, so I sneaked towards it to see who owned it. The Colony number looked awfully familiar so I checked  it against our number. It was our mech. We had base 50 meters away from the old base.
Day 13:
With just Royal and I, we decided to look for diamonds in the large caves. I planned to go into space and then find the caves from there (they were that big) and then place a beacon there so Royal could come. I went there, but it was impossibly far for Royal to traverse. I decided to wait it out in space after Royal discovered different diamond caves right near our base. I got disconnected again by ServerLogic, and lost my ship. Again. I had to walk all that distance back to base, but had to divert when Royal was attacked at the caves. He had died from starvation, and some of his loot was missing, including an expensive pistol, so we thought a guy there had stolen it. We didn't get it back, and returned to base.
Day 14:
I logged in to find the new base gone, and just the mechs left (because they're invincible). I went to Steam and tried to message Royal telling him to join, but he had removed me from Steam for some reason. I tried to add him again, yet he declined the invite. To this day, I am awaiting a response from him and have asked Zergpooh and Hunterrosir to add him in order to ask why he deleted me.

This game was an excercise in frustration. Despite there being a hint of a good game in there somewhere, the gameplay mechanics all come together to make playing it as frustrating as possible. Horrible UI, bad performance for how it looks, enemies are simply either a pushover or impossible to fight, your assistant ai robot is as dumb as a rock (and sometimes as useful as one), and actually progressing is more about trudging from one predetermined spawn location for resources you need to the next.
That doesn't even count the quality of life issues this game has. There are numerous little niggling things which are standard in most any game of quality these days, and they are all lacking in Osiris. Examples of QOL issues being inventory management being horribly cumbersome, plotting and building things being an excercise in frustration due to the grid/snaplock system they use and last but not least this game doesn't even let you change the mouse sensitivity from what I can tell (and also appears to use mouse accelleration) which makes aiming at enemies frustrating as hell.
TL/DR: Not worth the money for the quality of game you get. May have a good game in there somewhere if you can stomach the monotony and frustration it will bring you.

This game is an operator wannabe's wet dream. You got gun customization, character customization, and a third world country conflict setting. But Ubisoft is up to their old tricks again.
Let's start with my gripes with this game:
The optimization is abysmal.
Open world has it's limits. What Ubisoft did here is they made a massive map with provinces of different shapes and sizes, but they're all in a square. This has of course beautiful landscapes, foliage, villages, army bases, checkpoints, all you could dream of. But there's just so goddamn many of them that you forget what they're even called. All the content would be good if it didn't make the average PC run and stutter like an autistic kid on his first date with a cheerleader. They take two steps forward and take huge leaps back. The menus and all are okay, the content is okay, but they overdid it and I wonder in a few years if we'll be able to dust off some old hardware and play it again as intended.
Story sets a good premise but I guess it's differences in culture which doesn't get me interested. Or maybe the characters I'm supposed to be taking down are one-dimensional and don't have any meaningful introduction or conclusion.
The gameplay is alright. Best enjoyed with friends but I'm really not a fan of respawning enemies which are harder to fight due to the game engine chugging down a huge bottle of whiskey and falling down stairs.
If you have a good enough computer or found a community patch which fixes all the issues, purchase this only if you're a serious operator enthusiast and at a discounted price. 60 bucks is just not worth it.

Long ago, there was a great battle between the Golem Master and the Seal God (Seal as in lock, not the animal). The 2 factions were about to destroy the world with their conflict. In order to win and prevent the end of civilization, the Master of the Skies unlocks the Five-Coloured Seal. Unfortunately, by doing so, he incurrs Heaven's Punishment. After the war, the Five Coloured Seal is presumably sealed. A thousand years later, the forbidden seal is once again broken and the demi-goddess, He Yin, awakens and is called upon to save the world. You awake in the temple and you are surprised to find that there are puppets/golems running amok and theorize that the temple is under attack.
You use the WASD keys for movement, Shift to run and target your nearest enemy, F for dash dodge, LMB for light attacks, RMB for Heavy attacks, 123 for energy blade, spin attack and qi bomb.
To kill the last boss, slash 3 times and dodge behind him. Rinse, repeat.
PROS
1. The Opening
Very nice. The robot awakening.
2. Free
You don't have to pay a single cent. That's the best part.
3. F Dash
Very nice. Dodges all attacks.
CONS
1. Checkpoints
You tend to start from the very beginning if you fall off a cliff. Most annoying.
2. Clunky movement
I don't know how to describe it but the way the heroine moves is very plastic. Compare this to games like Darksiders to get an understanding of the clunky movement.
3. Strange Enemy Attacks
You just see a claw symbol on the heroine. You have no idea where the attacks come from
4. Aggro Zone
You have to be within the Aggro Zone to get the enemies to attack you.
5. Riflemen Enemies
They always have their backs turned to you. Why? Somehow you know they will move backwards without turning to look at you.
6. Jump Pads
You can actually fall off mid jump. It's very bad. The way she moves when she jumps from 1 jump pad to another is similar to wall hacking.
NEUTRAL
1. Hitting Jars
To get healing from random jars is a standard fare but it's getting kind of old.
2. The Robot
It looks like the Gorilla Mecha from Dark Sector or the M05 Silverback from Section 8.
Well, looks like I have a new favourite game.

The world has died, everyone you've ever known and loved has succumb to the infection and tried to feast on your flesh. When all hope seemed lost, you see a light in the distance. Pulling yourself up and over this final hill reveals, civilization.
It's haphazard walls and somewhat steam punk exterior are unmistakable, and on the wind you hear the hustle and bustle of life with a gunshot or two drifting in from the distance.
Making your way forward you approach a large wooden gate and suddenly feel the whiz of a bullet as it fly's inches from your face. You quickly raise your hands and shout at the defenders to prove you're not infected. After a few minutes of silence the gate slowly begins to creak open and reveal, humanity; or what's left of it anyway.
Stepping into the city you see tents of survivors and industry lining the thin walk-ways, as well as small farms and fishing posts. You approach the command center, and standing in-front of it all is the man who you know is going to save, not just you, but humanity. However, that man, is not me.
Suddenly you hear blood-curdling screams echoing from the far end of the encampment, and as you turn to see what's happening, it's nearly unbelievable. You could have sworn a massive impenetrable wall stood where you are looking only moments ago, but instead you watch as thousands of the undead flood into the streets, killing and infecting hundreds of people as they quickly advance towards the command center.
You stop and think about you're long journey, from the start of the pandemic to now and realize that this was always the way it would end. As you stand there contemplating your existence, an infected bares down upon you and then, nothing.
Suddenly you're jolted awake, feeling not quite like yourself; but one thing is for sure, you need to eat.

Pros

- Very polished finished product
- Enjoyable timing-based combat (think Paper Mario)

- Funny at times

Cons

I actually really enjoyed this game.  It’s a very simple and short turn-based RPG that hit a lot of the right notes.  It just has a certain charm to it that is hard to describe. The combat contains a timing-based component where if you perform the correct action at the right time, your attacks will do more damage or you will take less damage on defense.  This helps keep you engaged in all of the battles.  Thankfully this component was included, because otherwise you have very few options in combat (attack, use a special if it is charged, or use a battle stamp which gives a combat ability).  In terms of battle stamps, these are reusable and basically replace items in the game, and can either confer an ability in combat (e.g. stun a single enemy) or a passive ability (e.g. more health).  The other source of variety in combat is the inclusion of 13 different combat costumes, each of which have their own abilities and play style (single target DPS, AoE, defense, healer, etc.).  That being said, even with these additions the combat can still drag at times.  Fighting a limited variety of enemies in the same environment over and over can become tedious.  Overall most battles are quite easy, but a few boss battles require strategy when selecting which battle stamps and costumes to use.  The story doesn’t contribute much, but the writing is good and there are some funny moments.  If you enjoy RPGs that don’t take themselves too seriously, this is a good game.  In addition, the simplified and streamlined nature of the game would make it a good option for someone who is new to RPGs or a younger gamer.

Cutting to the chase: this is a 15-20 minute game about a college girl making oatmeal. And I enjoyed this game. It's really visually cute, short, and sweet. I'm disappointed in the negative reviews it's getting. People seem to be missing the mark on what this game is about. It's not about Samantha being "pretentious" or "quirky and awkward", it's about her having social anxiety, especially within communal living. I, for one, like how it doesn't blow this fact out of proportion and shove it down your throat. If you know what to look for, the game's theme is pretty clear and I think elegantly displayed by the devs. Having social anxiety, yes, every average day is an adventure, because the outcomes are never clear to the person experiencing it, while others can simply stroll through the average day without much fuss or insecurity.
I would recommend a play, even just for the experience of something not everyone experiences. And really, taking a risk on a game that's less than 30 minutes long and is also free is really not too much too ask for, is it?

First off, if you're buying this thinking it is like Space Engineers or Empyrion Galactic Survival, I am going to put that opinion to rest now, it isn't either of those games and it is definitely in a class of its own in my eyes.
The game looks great, the concept is great, and even on minimum settings it feels pretty good, but there are a few issues which are expected since this is a DEVELOPING game.
The major issues are actually fairly minor bugs that the developer is working on to the best of my knowledge, however I won't argue that the meteors that target your character are a bit annoying, aliens that can pop up out of nowhere are also annoying.  Those issues are balanced out with the ability to change how many aliens there are and how often they appear, as well as the amount of damage they can dish out and take in turn meaning you can have metaphorical glass cannons for aliens to battle in hordes, or maybe on occasion just find a single alien that is exceptionally tough but has very little bite to them.
The Building and Repair system is the only real deal breaker I will admit, since every building with the exception of the Bio-dome is made up of individual parts that need to be assembled (on top of the building's base cost) and repaired individually by hand, however it isn't necessarily a bad thing since if you are a hardcore survival fan that enjoys the feeling of living on an alien world it makes a lot of sense since things happen.  An alien can rip a hole in a hallway causing air to leak from your base (once it is properly implemented), or the weather eats away at your base's hitpoints like you would expect from a real storm.
All in all I would easily say that this is my go to game for a challenging survival game since you don't know where anything actually is when you spawn, and you have to discover ways to survive and where resources are.
In my opinion, game score on a 1-10 rating scale, I'd give it a solid 5 or 6, I may change my review in the future as updates roll in, but I can safely say that this is going to be something to keep an eye on for a long time since I feel good about this game.

It's also difficult to plan and give orders with much precision during the heat of battle, as "Battle Focus Mode" doesn't pause battle but instead slows it down. It's sad to think that this one change to Battle Focus Mode may have made the bad AI much more palatable.
As for this game's addition to the XCOM canon, that's really up in the air. It's nifty to see the 60's style XCOM take shape, but that's not really the main draw of the game for me in the end.
All in all, tactical FPSes have seen better renditions. Mass Effect 2's battle system felt much more fluid, and even the venerable Freedom Fighters does it better.

This game combines good third-person shooter with the field strategy elements in the original xcom games. It has a really nice combat system making you think each of your moves before excuting them. While fun for the first half of the game, I quickly got bored because of the repetitive gameplay. It is basically moving to an area, killing a bunch of ailens, and then move to another area, kill more ailens, etc. and finally get the objective. It gets really boring espicially witout the base-management system in the traditional xcom game.
The enemy AI is really good espically if you play on the harder difficulties; however, the friendly AI are really bad. In my play through, my agents got stuck in corners and wouldn't move when I tell them to regroup; they constantly ran into gernades; sometimes stand still for minutes before moving to their assigned location. My most memerable experience was when I got shot down right beside one of my agents. I ordered him to revive me, while the other agent taunts the enemy. But the agent kept on shooting, even after I commanded him several more times to revive me, leading me to die and reload the last checkpoint.
As for the story and the interactions between you and the other characters, it is well made and indepth. The characters are intresting and you can read their files to find out more about them. Each characters have different personalities making it very intresting to talk with them.
In conclusion, the game is repetitive and sometimes frustrating witht he glitchy friendly AI, however the challenging enemy AI and the intresting story made up for it. I would give it a 5/10 if there was a rating system.

I've not even played half an hour of this game but I'm afraid I can already tell you that I can't recommend it. That's not me being spiteful or anything either, because I loved TDU1 on PSP and PS2.

F11 and the maximise button did not fix this, and although there was an option to change the resolution in the settings, there was no fullscreen option. I'm not sure if it's me being mad, but full games running in windowed mode tend to result in choppier framerates, and that was certainly the case here.
Then we have the car handling itself. The tiniest of braking will send you spinning out of control for no reason whatsoever. It makes the game unplayable. It was the same in both the high-end Ferrari care the game teases you with in the beginning (which was really just slow and spinny), and with the starter car you buy.
Furthermore, when in first person mode the mouse sensitivity is extremely slow, even when set to the highest possibility in the settings.
I would advise against buying.

i really wanted to write a review about this much earlier... but i got so hooked on this game that i have to do that now.
first of all, i read many of the reviews before i finally bought this game, many people complained about that its too unrealistic.
well, its in fact not a racing simulator, nor a driving simulator, and its hard for me to find a correct description for it.
the car handling is a bit like at "grand theft auto", or the older "need for speed" games.
just imagine two giant gaming worlds, filled with streets, offroad tracks and a beautiful landscape, detailed cities and viliages, where you can drive 100% freely, without any pressure.
all original licensed cars and motorbikes, , no fantasy vehicles!
you can go to different driving schools,  learn to handle normal street cars, supersport cars, offroad cars or oldtimers, step by step, afterwards you can participate in races in those vehicle classes.
you can provoke the police for car chases.
if youre not a fan of this, doesnt matter, you can also just buy vehicles, drive around, for HOURS over hours, discover many awesome places.
you can discover hidden treasures, in form of special cars, you can buy houses and decorate them, buy clothes for your avatar, change it's hair and body,  you can paint, wash, tune your cars and bikes... you can crash into other cars, see them lose control :D

you can drive online together with friends or many other people, invite them to cruise around, to races, or create car clubs with them, or just goof along with your cars.
as additional feature there is also a casino where you can play poker or roulette against other human players, or alone at the slotmachine.
what did i forget? probably a lot, since the game offers such an incredible range of features...

some other things that might be good to know:
the graphics look fine, the sounds are good, the voiceacting is moderate, there is not much of a story, there are two in car radiostations 1.rock and 2. a mixxed playist of hiphop/trance/house/pop/rock, you can chat with other people easily.
bad things:

last but not least: ITS IMPORTANT TO GET A GAMEPAD/CONTROLLER FOR THIS! keyboard is possible, but not really fun, in my eyes.

Let preface my review by saying that I don't really hate this game, and I'm not even saying no one should play this. I knew what to expect from it, and I wasn't "disappointed". However, I want to review this game objectively as possible (which I understand is near impossible to "objectively" review a game, seeing as one person's experience with something is their subjective feelings). This game is clearly unfinished, and considering that its free, I can overlook that to an extent. I'm no stranger to action games, nor am I an expert.However I've played quite a bit of Metal Gear Rising and Devil May Cry. This game is nowhere near as good as those games. The controls are very simple, X and Y are attack buttons, RB is dodge, LT is target, A is jump. Then obviously the analog sticks are for camara and movement. But that's it. There's no block, no other attacks besides the basics, and as far as I could tell, no real combos. Again, this game is not a big budget release, so I wasn't expecting all that much from it. The combat is fuctional, but really not that fun. With little actions you have, and no real combos to perform, you can largely get away with mashing X until you start seeing tougher enemies. And that isn't fun. Once you start seeing tougher and more enemies at once, you end up taking a lot of damage unless you're dodging a lot, but you have to dodge so often you can barely keep any semblance of a combo going. Actual hits don't even feel that good. Hitting an enemy should feel satisfying, but here it just feels lame. But let me be clear, it doesn't feel terrible. This really feels like a prototype for a much bigger game. More than anything, this is proof of concept. I felt so bored from the gameplay that I couldn't even finish it. The graphics are decent, but that really isn't the most important thing. The developers show that they can make a decent game here, if they had a proper budget and enough time. This has the potenetial to be better, maybe not as good as DMC or MGR, but it could still be a solid game. They just need to tweak the combat to feel more satisfying. I would gladly like to see this game given better treatment and the gameplay fine tuned to feel faster, more fun, and overall more satisfying. Let me reiterate, even though I'm giving this game a thumbs down, I'm not saying not to play this game. I actually think people should check this out and see for yourself what this game is like. However, I needed to state my criticisms in hope that the devs would read this and hopefully work on it and make it better.

Hatoful Boyfriend is an interesting experience.  I think a lot of people go in not really knowing just what to expect.  I mean, on the surface all you see is a Visual Novel and Dating Sim where almost all the characters are birds.  The normal reaction to that is to say "...uh, wait.  What?"  But after you spend some time in the game, getting to know the characters and the world the whole bird thing just kind of shifts off to the side.  Your brain starts to think of it as normal.  I'm not really sure why, if it is because of the clever writing, the wonderfully crafted characters, or if I'm  just weird.  The most interesting thing about Hatoful Boyfriend however is that it manages to scratch every single itch a player would have when it comes to a Visual Novel type experience.  Did you want something light hearted and funny?  There is a path for that.  Did you want something super creepy?  Hey, we got a path for that too.  How about something epic and grand complete with a throw back reference to old school JRPGs and some rocking tunes?  You know what?  It actually has that too.  That just scratches the surface.
But most importantly, after you go through and finish each of the characters endings something magical happens: You get to fulfill a promise from long ago.  Not only do you have a shift in the game once more but you actually get the real meat of the experience and all the details that make up the world the game is set in.  And it is glorious.  Absolutely glorious.
