I'm disappointed with this one because of a few points.
The game feels like a tactical mashup of Far cry and GTA. Taking what was bad about those games and chucking them together. Long drives to soak up time, idiot ai and random encounter Intel missions.
When you load up the game for the first timex the aiming setup is set for third person character controls and aim down sights (ADS). The switch from third person to ADS feels clunky and disorienting

This is a simple strategy boardgame, but that simplicity allows for a lot of interesting strategic game play.  The combat system resembled the classic Axis And Allies board game rules, but with only two unit types -- attack (armor, knight), and defense (infantry).  Like that game, you can only build new units in your factory (or castle or city or whatever it gets called).
Unlike most board games  (but like Diplomacy), all moves are simlutaneous.  Every player issues orders to all units, then when all are complete they all execute at once.  This makes attacking a risk, as you must move defending units off a territory in order to attack.  Your opponent and you can actually exchange territories.
The border system is like Risk (or Lux Delux, based on Risk), or Diplomacy, but there are some interesting quirks used on some maps.  One-way borders and impassable terrain can complicate attack and defense plans.
The Alliance part of the name comes in how the sides in a map/scenario are laid out.  Some sides -- like in classic Axis And Allies -- will be allied, and work together.
While the game offers online play, I found it hard to get a quick game together.  A slower, play by email pace is easier to find.  I think that with friends you could get a quick game together.  The AI has several "personalities" to choose from, which range of easy (not so smart) to hard (usually competent), which makes the opponents challenging.
The economy of the game is sort of a mix of Axis And Allies and Risk in concept.  Each territory/province has a production value, while groups of territories make continents/regions/nations, and give a bonus if an alliance owns all of them.  The critical factory/castle/city production locations are usually in higher production spaces, but in some maps they can be extremely high.  Some maps give one side ONLY that single, high value location at the start.
The simple rules I believe let the AI adapt to just about any map and do OK.  Even some of the odd ones.  For example. there is a War In The Congo map where the key high value locations are effectively "off the map" with one way connections to them.  There are three locations which let you attack them, but any forces you send there are stuck, unable to return.  The AI did a decent job of both attacking the key connecting locations and sending forces to attack and defend those production sources, even though they aren't on the direct path to the enemy's home territory.
Add in the choice of sides and alliances and the many, many maps, and you can always find a challenge when playing this game.
Big plus:  You can play a game in under an hour.  The combat resolution is fast, no dice rolling simulations or (as in Axis And Allies) tactical choices within combat.  The simultaneous turns mean no waiting, just set your orders and see how they play out.
This isn't an amazingly polished game.  Note -- turn off Steam Overlay when playing this, it is broken in game.  But it makes up for it in game play.

I played this game a few years ago under its previous name, Castle Vox. It is OK playing against the AI, but against capable human players it really shines like a tactical gem. Not a complex tactical game, but for what it is (Axis & Allies meets Risk) it is very cool. The simultaneous turns mean that you have to weigh everything your opponent can do, then decide what the best move he/she would make, and then consider something else (because the best move will be one that surprises you). There is a surprising amount of tactical depth in this otherwise simple game. The multiplayer world of players was severely limited when I played years ago, so if being on Steam improves this the game could really shine.

I have never seen a game that wants to milk my wallet dry this much before. Not only is the game itself quite expensive, but then if I want a DLC for it I basically have to pay for the entire game again to get the DLC (the DLCs cost about the same as the game itself).
And also, the major powers such as German Reich, France, Britain, etc. Are really the only WWII countries who get portrayed what so ever. Countries such as Norway and Denmark (for example) have just been given a default set of options (National Focus Tree) such as countries who weren't involved in any wars.

As of today, there is only a survival mode implemented, which is so good, it deserves a recommendation of it's own.
They are billions is a very satisfying mix of RTS and Horde Survival.
It is VERY difficult, but in a very fair way.
Periodically you will get notified of hordes of zombies that will attack from a specific direction, and you'll be given a little time to prepare for it.
Hordes attack fronts that are underdeveloped and ramp up in number of zombies and get different types of zombies the longer you'll last.
You got a variety of tech and units at your disposal, ranging from simple archers to massive Minigun Towers of doom, Combat Mechs and Rocket Troopers.
You build, expand and defend your colony, until you most likely get overrun and eaten.
But every time you get wiped you'll see, probably when it's too late already, WHY your base collapsed.
You dismissed one front? Wipe
You didn't expand? Wipe
You expanded too fast? Wipe
You tech wasn't up to snuff? Wipe
You get the concept. It's probably your fault that you ended up as dinner.
Every time you fail you develop your strategies further, until you'll hopefully win.
Then it's off to the next map, which raises the bar even higher.
Honestly, it's a fantastic game already, completely surprising me this late in a year of great games.
Even this early in development (V0.4), you'll have a great time with it.

Hatoful Boyfriend is probably my favourite visual novel of all time. But I'm going to have to give this version an 8/10.
It's a very well written game. I'd recommend it to anyone that wants to romance birds, likes parodies or likes birds. Or even big convoluted plots that all seem to be intertwined with eachother leading to a larger plot that's quite unexpected on a game for wooing birds.
I've also 100%-ed the original version, Holiday Star and this HD version. Basically I've spent a lot of time on it, ok?
That being said, while I do love this new version, I do have a few complaints as a person that played the original hatoful. All of them being about the last, unlockeable route. It's mostly about technicalities but yeah.
[Possible Spoilers Ahead, Be Warned]
While I don't mind the less-than-perfect saving system, most of my sort of distate came from the new changes (or lack thereof) in the bad boys love route, 'hurtful boyfriend'.
I noticed that you can actually save whenever you want to which takes off the thrill of not being able to save and not knowing when youll have the chance or the choices youre gonna make, thus making it super important to just remember all the important details.
The other thing I noticed is that there is no colored text. I think it was made as a reference joke to the Higurashi games, but even then it was still visual cues as to what happened and was going to happen, and I was kind of disappointed for the lack of colored text. It worked very well for the murder-mystery going on.
On a minor note, I don't remember there being a skip button on the bbl route, thus having to read the story again if you'd missed your chance. Basically having it there changes the pace. It feels like there would be less trouble as a reader but it also feels as if the buildup can be skipped even if by accident.
[End of Warning]
Anyhow, If you get the collectors edition, you also get a copy of the original game, which I'd bother everyone to try out even after playing the regular game. Just to see how much it's changed. I'm so happy that I got to play this game again and I will forever recommend anyone to play it.

I got this game because I thought it would be light-hearted, fun otome game that replaced all of the typical husbando stereotypes with pigeons. It started out that way. Then sh*t got real. It was not fun. It was not light-hearted. Your boyfriends turn out to be dead, or pudding-deities, or too old, or mad scientists. A lot of them leave you in the end, or decide to keep your brain in a jar. Yet I still found it oddly intriguing, and found dating fictional pigeons to be much more enjoyable than dating fictional humans.
My only real problem with the game is that they never tell you if the pigeons you're dating are normal sized pigeons, or giant human sized pigeons. That mystery really hindered my ability to properly visualize many parts of the story.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a pretty simple game, in terms of gameplay; you read through story bits, every now and then you make a choice. Depending on your choices, you ultimately get to an ending; getting certain endings unlocks other options for other stories. Simple. The real attraction, therefore, is in the story. The premise is frankly insane; you are the only human attending a school for intelligent birds. And yet...And yet the premise is developed in a consistent and plausible way. All the characters are fully realized, and it's easy to get emotionally invested. If you go through every storyline, little bits that seemed filler will suddenly take on a larger context, and you'll realize that a *lot* of work went into the story. But even in the most emotional storylines, there are bits that will come out of nowhere and make you go "WTF!". That's the thing that really impresses me, that the game is consistently surprising. At turns cheery, tragic, silly, absurd, gruesome, parodic, heartwrenching and insane, it's an experience I can't help but recommend.

Wildlands attempts to create a world where you can seemlessly enter into the story-based missions in any way you please.
Its closest comparison is MetalGearSolid V in my opinion. Its a worthy attempt but it is completely destroyed by all things Ubisoft.
Firstly Bolivia is a terrible choice for an open world game. Because traversing any south american country is just not fun to do. 5km of winding roads to get to a place uphil about 500m away as the crow flies, is a pain. Add Ubisofts driving mechanics and you have a terrible experience.
Walking, jumping, climbing, etc,... those mechanics are very poor aswell. I had a feeling I was playing a game in Alpha mode like Dayz or Rust at times. Theres bugs like falling through the floor. Not being able to scale a half foot ledge... etc.
The endless animations of getting into a car,... grabbing someone... taking out your sidearm.... switching seats... with the endless holding down of the action button gets really annoying fast in a firefight.
The day and nightcycle are unchangable... meaning that you will be forced to play a mission at night... if that happens to be the time you showed up at the location it is at. And that will be about half of the time.
The missions are really terrible at most. They are copy paste from an Assassins creed game. Protect this guy, steal that document whilst remaining undetected. Abduct that guy.... all insta-fail missions. Terrible to play in an open world context because it really narrows down what you can do and get away with... Expect 20 hours of: "youre to far from your target" or "Your target has died"
Following the failure of a mission you will be dropped 500 random meters from your mission area. Randomly! meaning that your previous vantage point in the mountains from where you wanted to snipe people is completely gone... and now you are on the opposite side of the base.
Your Squadmates in singleplayer are useless. They dont take initiative to fire at anyone. They lag behind like crazy. And im not even speaking of the random♥♥♥♥♥♥they keep saying that makes you want to leave them behind every single mission.
The general storyline and mood towards south america, its culture and people is pretty degrading in my opinion. But thats a whole different subject.
Being locked in an interrogation scene when some guy is talking about his dog.... and the bullets are flying around your head is one of the worst elements of the game... 66 procent of the missions will have an interrogation of someone. And all of them test your patience and make you wonder why Ubisoft thought this would be fun or effectual at all.
Missions will also give you random objectives that you cannot reasonably have forseen. Meaning some guy will take off at 100km/h all of a sudden and you are left without a vehicle causing a fail.
Some missions will overlap, because for example a convoi mission passes by a mission where you are busy clearing a base... all of a sudden you fail the convoi mission, that you werent even engaged in... and now your progress on the base clearing mission is also gone and your 3km away. In general any planning into missions is destroyed by stuff that you dont expect....
Kill this convoi was a mission that I planned to take on by placing mines on the road.... except the fact that the convoi never left the base.
Kill the chopper as it arrives at the airport had me placing c4 on the runway.... only the chopper never intended to land.
Say goodbye to any tactical ideas you have to clear missions.... Cuz ubisoft want to keep giving you their take on events... mostly... Tail, Interrogate, protect, Chase....
I could go on about all of these little grievences... lets just say. save yourself the trouble and the agony... MGSV is a great tactical game. JustCause3 is a great open world base destroying game... have fun with those...

The tactical shooter within Ghost Recon Wildlands, at times, can be very good and make you feel like a military badass. Heloing in to a zone, sneaking around and systematically eliminating sicario after sicario, completing your objective, and then getting out without anyone knowing you were there. Sadly those moments are few and far between. There are several issues that hurt enjoyment of the game and bog it down in the mud.
Firstly is the horrible AI on both sides of the coin. Enemies will stand out in the open waiting for you to pop one in their skull, but the most infuriating detail are the friendly AI "teammates". People will say that it's a co-op game and to play with others but it doesn't excuse the problem in any way, shape, or form. During my time playing the game I had multiple instances of AI teammates standing on railway tracks getting run over by a train causing me to fail a mission. I continually had issues getting the sync shot to work if an enemy was tagged inside of something like a pillbox where there would be a split second to execute or the teammate would lose the target and not get them bad despite the fact the enemy wasn't impeded by any obstacle (Future Soldier at least had the sync shot work properly and teammates would intelligently move to the best sightline for a shot). Multiple times I would go into a cave network, bunker, or even just a simple building (the buildings would be tied to the Diversion Rebel Support ability) and would have to clear it out solo because my "teammates" wouldn't follow me in. During one mission I triggered an alarm and get downed within a fairly large cave complex while taking on one of the bosses. All I could do is sit helplessly watching the bleedout timer expire because no "teammate" was around to revive me thus causing me to fail the mission.
Second main issue I had with the game was the driving mechanics of virtually all the vehicles. Again multiple instances I would be going along on something like a dirtbike and would slightly turn left but the physics system would go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I would do an instant 180 degree turn heading the opposite direction. The APC in the game feels like it's wheels are made out of butter and it slides around endlessly. The only viable mode of getting around are helicopters which again can be an issue because of SAM launchers on the ground and an insanely slow turning radius in addition to zero counter-measures. The planes as a whole are useless, slow, and again zero counter-measures to SAM launchers which can be an issue when doing some of the supply run missions in the north section of the map as one zone (Media Luna) has them spread all over the place.
Third main issue I had with the game was the repetitive grind. The main missions themselves felt varied enough but the in between parts were the problem. When I personally entered a new zone of the map I would immediately find the Intel Caches or Cartel Lieutenants, who basically act like this games viewpoints in typical Ubisoft tripe fashion, to get the location of Skill Points, Weapons and Weapon Attachments, Bonus Medels (which apply buffs based on the skill system), and then move on. I would go either left to right or top to bottom clearing out sections while doing the Rebel Missions (of which there are only 5 variations), Supply Missions (of which there are only 3 variations with ones involving convoys being random), getting the Kingslayer details of that particular Cartel Boss tied to the province, finish up, and then move on. This could have been me "playing wrong" but there just isn't enough variety for such a massive open world. It all feels paint by numbers.
That brings me to my biggest issue is it's open world. You can spend minutes flying to one location only to fly minutes to another location. And this is where I'm going to say something that might not make much sense since I complained about mission variety, but the game might have been better off as a scripted focused game based on levels instead of the open world. The open world is the main crux of all the problems. It's the reason why the AI teammates feel dumb since the AI has to script itself to move around in literally half of Bolivia. It's the reason why the driving mechanics feel so bad because it's a chore to get around in the first place. It's the reason why the game feels like a grind because of the vast expanses of nothingness. It's both one gigantic open world while at the same time being 21 huge open worlds as each province is basically it's own open world. There's just too much and it feels disjointed most of the time.
Should you buy it? Get it when it's on a deep sale for no more than 15 dollars. It isn't awful but it could be so much more just by being... less.

text:
This game is one of those rare few that seems like its one thing, and then it ends up being something much, MUCH, greater than expected. Going into it you might think its just a weird Japanese visual novel about dating birds. And, well, it sort of is. But what you wouldn't know without playing it is just how much more there is to this game.
The vast amount of diversity speaks volumes of the effort put into making this game the experience that it is. Although it is classed as a dating sim, this is one of the few games that tackles many other genres, and actually does it well. Basically, each of the different characters' story lines you can follow are unique to one another. Each character has a very different personality and backstory, as well as their routes have their own uniqe themes and plots that other characters routes don't necessarily have a focus on. This is what makes this such a great game, because it makes you WANT to complete every route so you can learn the whole story, rather than making you feel like you have to suffer through several playthroughs of the same thing to get the end result. Each of the different characters stories are enjoyable and entertaing in their own unique way, be it a sweet romance, or a bone-chilling mystery, they are all very different.
Then of course, there is the secret "true ending" story route, wheather it can be called that or not, it is one of the most fantastic works of story telling I have ever experienced in a visual novel. I'm not going to spoil anything, as it really should be played without any prior knowledge or spoilers, but I strongly encourage players to play through every possible story route even if some may be silly at times, as that's what gives this game its charm. Each one of the stories you can play through will entertain you with silly jokes, emotion evoking plots, or even suspensful and horrorific secrets. Then after all those memorable events, you will be able to enjoy yet another very unique, very interesting, and very well written and played out "true ending" scenario. I could talk for hours about how great all the individual routes and the overarching plots are, but it is truely something that is best left for you, the player, to discover by playing the game for yourselves.
If you havn't yet bought Hatoful Boyfriend, or are maybe considering the purchase but are unsure if you will enjoy it, then you have my reccomendation to buy and play this game, and  that it will be something that you'll be able to enjoy playing, and re-playing, for a very long time to come. For the amount of content this game has, it is definately worth buying. Through all of its silly laughs, its shocking secrets, and its heartbreaking emotional moments, Hatoful Boyfriend has become a personal favourite, and hopefully you will enjoy it too.

As someone who normally doesn't like dating sims, I only played this game because it looked funny and a bit unique. "A dating sim, but all the boys are pigeons?" I thought, "Sounds incredible, I have to play." And sure enough, it was incredible. Just not in the way I expected.
Hatoful Boyfriend is funny, it's true, it has a very funny and quirky sense of humor that will be incredibly enjoyable for anyone who enjoys puns or jokes that almost slip under your radar, but when you catch them make you snort with amusment. Oh, and the fact that your character, as the only human in a school full of pigeons, is treated in the same stereotypical way that a singular intellegent bird would probably be treated if the situation was reversed ("stereotypical" human/primate behavior, constant references to her species in both jokes and regular conversation, she literally lives in a cave), is very funny as well. However, the real charm of Hatoful Boyfriend is when it is not being funny. This game, at times, is much more serious than you would think possible, even heartwrenching and disturbing. This game will make you laugh, it will make you cry, and it will constantly shock you (assuming you manage to avoid spoilers before playing, which is very recommended as the shock is part of the game's charm) and keep you interested and wanting to play all the way to the end.
I pirated this game years ago expecting a joke game and now I've bought the $15 special edition on steam because I believe that this game absolutely deserves every penny. This game has made such a big impact on me, it is easily one of the best visual novel-type games that I have ever played and I would absolutely reccommend it to anyone and everyone with the attention span for visual novels. Even if you don't think you have the attention span, watch a playthrough or try it out somehow because this is one game that really should not be missed. Also I just want to mention that the music is incredible.
tl;dr
Come for the pigeons, stay for the amazing story and shocking turns (and the great bgm).

Cute and charming. It seems geared toward younger folk and casual players. There's strategy but it's still easy for RPG pros. It's on the same level as Super Mario RPG, with some light timing action for attack and defend. The class/attribute/skill system based on costumes and collectable badges works very well and integrates into the story nearly transparently. The trick-or-treating mechanism for battles is clever. You don't feel like you're grinding more than you have to.
There are a few light puzzles, the models and environments are great, the music fits in just right. The game is intended to be beaten, but winning the game isn't the goal, it's experiencing it. It's very forgiving, allowing you to replay a lost battle as long as you want. It's somewhat short, well under 10 hours of playtime. The achivements are reachable by most people but provide just enough challenge to create satisfaction. The story is light in nature, with just enough spookiness for kids. It's very well-made.
I recommend using a controller. With a keyboard you'll be hunting fast for awkwardly placed keys. It worked with my Xbox360 controller out of the box, just make sure the first input comes from it.
Thoroughly recommended for kids and casual RPG players.

i really want to like this game more than i do, and i realize that it is still very much in an early stage of developement, but there are a couple things that just arent sitting right and making the experience unenjoyable to the point of stressfulness for me, and i wish i could give this a neutral review. this is my first real review so bear with me.
as things are right now;
1: the fact that this game is incredibly difficult for the average player even when the difficulty slider is brought down is extremely frustrating considering the fact that without having the difficulty multiplier at 100%, you will be unable to unlock the next map if you manage to win somehow. I got to the final wave at 75% difficulty with just the zombie population down to accessible and was completely annihilated by the final wave which was exponentially stronger than anything i had seen until then. i'm definately not a pro at RTS and i can already tell that i will never see the other maps this game has to offer without watching some masochist on youtube play, which is also frustrating because i will never see content i payed for myself. considering this is a singleplayer game, having a difficulty lock on the other levels is absolutley ridiculous when the difficulty is so, well, dificult.
2: i dont understand why i cant build quarries on top of the resource patches they farm, and why gates are only able to be built at such strange angles. I have constantly run into the problem of having large amounts of resource patches near my HQ and having to decide if its worth the resource drain to have two quarries trying to make the most of a 6 stone patch, or to just build the one quarry for 4 or 5 stone so i dont have to sacrafice the manpower. wouldn't it make sense to just have it in the middle of the patch so i can save room, manpower, and have maximum efficiency? it stresses my economy in a game where resource management can make or break you, and makes it more difficult to expand in a way that lets you have the resources to deal with the crazy hordes you'll see. now as far as gates go, i can live with them how they are, but they make for some odd building patterns and sometimes make defending them a rather arduous task the way you are forced to place them, but maybe thats just me.
3: i dont like the fact that there are no "controls" for the map generation. I cant tell you how many times i've just re-rolled the map because there was a doomed village mere feet from my colony, or the map was wide open and resourceless in most directions, and again, this wouldn't be a huge issue if i knew the game wasn't so damned difficult, especially the end-game. if you dont expand quickly, but cautiously, you will be overrun by one of the coming waves, and your ability to expand is directly impacted by what the map generation gives you. im sure if i was one of the elitists that plays this i wouldn't have an issue with most of the maps i'm given but i'm definately struggling with maps that are GOOD, so i dont know if it's just me or this is a valid issue.
It's not all doom and gloom however, this game is fantastic as far as hardcore RTS goes and it is very well done in most regards. having a zombie break in and attack your housing gives you an anxious and exciting feeling as you rush your troops to try and stem the flow before they take over everything. watching hordes of zombies break like waves over your defenses is also adrenaline pumping as you pray your walls hold long enough for your ballistas to blast the remaining foes. graphics wise this game looks fantastic and is really true to the steampunk theme with most units and buildings which makes battles aesthetically pleasing. THE HORDES!: once you get into late game (or a reasonably placed doomed village) the hordes you can have on screen at times is absolutely ridiculous and amazing to see, i have a GTX1070 and the final wave made my frames stutter and rubber-band as i stared in awe at the sea of corpses flowing into my base, absolutely fantastic. overall i would recommend the game, just dont expect to be able to beat anything without REALLY investing time and effort into it, or settling for beating the lower difficulties and never seeing another map type.
i really like that the game can be as difficult as it can for the people who like or want that challenge, but for the rest of us that aren't some korean super-computer of a human, it'd be nice to be able to progress at a pace suitable for our skill level, that doesn't lock away maps because im not as good as the devs want me to or think i can be.
TL;DR:  fun as far as hardcore RTS goes but the difficulty really needs some adjusting as well as a few gameplay aspects to be truly good to the average joe. would recommend if you enjoyed dark souls and never being good enough to win.

In the glorious words of the immortal Ernest P. Worrell I bring you these words of advice.. "Pretty soon the kids won't have to worry about eating their Brussel sprouts because the Brussel sprouts will be eating them."
Exchange the word Brussel sprouts with candy corn and you'll understand the game of Costume quest, a cute Halloween themed adventure game from the wonderful team at Double Fine entertainment.  The same group responsible for such classics as Psychonauts and Brutal Legend
In this game you play as Reynold and Wren a pair of twins who have recently moved to a new neighborhood, it's Halloween night and they are planning on going trick or treating.   After selecting which sibling you want to control, either Wren, the 10 minute older sister or Reynold the 10 pound heavier member of the dynamite duo, you are shipped off into the world.  The selected sibling gets a Robot custom, the other gets dressed as a piece of Candy Corn..  Social norms be damned if you pick the female character..  who says females aren't into Robots :-D  certainly not me.
After trick or treating at the first house, the pair try a second, only this time the candy corn gets abducted by a candy stealing grubbin monster...  OH MY!!!..   So off we go on an adventure to rescue our sister/brother from the clutches of a nasty candy stealing evil corporation, I'm talking a really dirty nasty organization we haven't seen in video games since Umbrella corporation..   Along the way to rescue your sibling you meet new friends, discover a sinister plot to steal candy, and defeat some monsters making for an amazing Halloween adventure which can be enjoyed at any time of year.
I pretty much described the story above, siblings, candy, stealing, adventure.  The story takes place in three locations, Auburn Pines, which is the starting neighborhood, Autumn Haven Mall (easy enough it's a Mall), and Fall Valley carnival, each area offers up the chance to explore, trick or treat, bob for candy apples, defeat monsters and oh yeah... get that sweet, sweet candy baby.. nuff said!!!
The first aspect the gamer is introduced to is trick or treating, which is just as it sounds, you go up to a house, knock on the door and wait for a trick (battle) or a trick (candy)  It's as simplistic as that.  Knocking on doors isn't the only way to collect candy, numerous interactive objects in the environment such as mailboxes, trashcans, shrubs, etc etc etc, can be pounded on by your candy pail in an attempt to wriggle loose a few extra pieces of candy, also numerous areas have candy thrown about on the ground...
.  The game features three types of collectibles, the first is Costumes, you start with the Robot costume, and soon after acquire a knight outfit, others you can collect are the statue of liberty, a unicorn, french fries and many more.  Many of the costumes have two special benefits, the first being an extra ability you can use while out of combat, like the Robot which can travel faster, or the Knight, that can shield from falling items.  The second ability is a special battle ability, whether it's rockets, a shield of protection or a powerful group heal.
The second type of collectible in the game are battle cards, these cards can be used to further enhance your character, give them additional HP, defense, a stun, etc etc etc, you can buy the cards from Sadie using the candy you collect during your adventure.  With each new area, additional cards are added for you to buy, the new cards offer upgrades over the older cards.  These are very useful in helping to gain the advantage in your battles to come.  The final collectibles are called treat cards, these resemble trading cards, they really serve no purpose, outside of being necessary to complete a few quest and unlocking a costume for collecting all of them.   You gain treat cards by defeating enemies and completing quest.
The combat in Costume Quest is rather unique, upon starting the battle your given one option to select basic attack
after selecting that option you're taken into a quick time event.  If you succeed in the quicktime event your character does extra damage, if you fail, your character does quite a bit less damage.  During the enemy phase of combat, when an enemy attacks one of your characters, you're given another quick time event, if you are successful you defend some of the damage and minimize the damage you receive, if you fail the quick time event the enemy a significant amount of extra damage.
Special ability's   -  those special abilities each costume has I mentioned above are useful here, after three combat turns each of your character unlocks their costumes special ability, this can be anything from from protection, heals, massive damage to a single or all enemies.  It's a good idea to mix and match your party to ensure you have all your bases covered in terms of combat, defense and healing.  A good defense is a good offense makes sense in this case.  It's especially important to include some type of healing for your party, as no healing exist outside of special ability or battle cards.
The combat sounds simplistic and it is, but the quick time events keep the gamer engaged and on their seat with each successive battle, letting your guard down can and probably will result in you suffering a defeat.
Good story,
interesting characters
unique combat system
very fun to play
easy to 100% if you're into achievements
controller support
Can be a bit too easy with the right combination of costumes/battle cards
Slightly repetitive enemies
occasionally controls can glitch out
I'd highly recommend this game, on paper it looks rather simplistic, it seems to have many strikes against it from a gamer's perspective prior to even installing it, but trust me on this one, once you start playing and get into the story you'll be thoroughly entertained as I was.  A fun game to play and enjoy, once you start to play you'll want to keep playing until you finish the the story.  It can be a bit difficult to get into, especially when you realize you'll be playing with children as characters, but that's part of the charm, a person of any age can kick back and enjoy the thrills and exciting of going trick or treating once again..
I'd really suggest taking the plunge, buying the game, collecting the candy and saving Halloween for children and adults all across the world..

I have to say when I purchased Osiris: New Dawn, even though it had good reviews and ws on sale I wasn't expecting much.  The game is still in Early Access it is not by any means a finished product, and literally everything is still a work in progress.
BUT
And yes there is a but, the game is actually good and enjoyable.  You play as a survivor/expeditionary from one of two factions on this alien world.  It seems once the game is done you will have a choicwe of one of four classes, however in the Alpha release there is only one Scientist (supposedly good at crafting starships) and you are male (hopefully the final game WILL have female avatars), you have a limited amount of color customisation to your space suit but no actual means to customise anything else about your avatar other than his name.
When you enter the game you start with a few basics, some weapons, limited ammo, some food and tools, an inflatable tent (basic habitat in which you can save) and a single incredly dense robot companion who can supposedly, mine for you or repair for you but unless he's actually following you and being used as a pack mule is pretty much useless in every other regard as using the other commands it gets stuck on terrain due to poor pathing and will literally spend the entire game driving into a wall, or unable to cross a crater, or stuck between a building unless you hunt it out and tell it to follow every five minutes.  And occasionally it will even disappear entirely seemingly somewhere UNDER the map? only to re-appear once you exit and reload the game.  Robot issues aside though once the planet you are placed with your supplies at a seemingly random spot on the planets surface your survival has begun.
What happens next is the mainstay of most survival open world games, seeking resources, cultivating them, improving your gear, building more useful structures, attaining some means of self sustainability etc..
You have a number of things to worry about food and water (these deplete pretty slowly which works fine for this game), Health yours and your suits (very important), you have the means to patch your suit which is good because if it is breached you will slowly loose health until dead.  And if you die you have limited time to get back to your body to retrieve ALL of your equipment.  Not so much an issue in single player PVE.. but in multiplayer or multiplayer PVP..a single death can make your existence SUBSTANTIALLY more difficult unless you have a well developed stash to fall back on.
Osiris however is no simple man vs environment game though and the environment is an issue, not just a night/day cycle but all manner of space weather from mists, to dust storms to meteor showers that seems to aim specifically AT you to certain vegetation that must be circumvented as it cannot be passed through.. no Osiris is a space HORROR Survival game.
So what is the horror you ask?  Well the planet is notunihabited you see it has some pretty unpeasant fauna living it that objects to some fleshy pink bag of water interfering with it.  Big Crab like creatures, small really fast parasytes, to space mnkeys that leap at you, to small four legged gants to things that swim under and on the sand right up to a gigantic and I do mean gigantic Shai'Hulud like sand worm that the first time you see, you will literally need a change of underwear for (if you come across this at night, turn your light off, torun 90 degrees left or right and run and jump for all you can otherwise your toast), but literally any of these can kill you fast.  Plus if your PVP you also have the other faction players to contend with all of whom are armed and building just like you.
There are some dociale alien wildlife too, but typically although many of these aliens spawn on the planets at certain locations fairly regularly they are also attracted to your mining and movments.  Come to close or mine too long and something comes..garunteed, you ge t a slight warning from the change of music but as to where and from what direction you have to look and fast as they come in quick and hit hard.
Aliens aside as I say you spend the majority of your time collecting resources, refinign them into parts, using the parts to build things from better weapons, to facilities, to vehicles, to robots to turrets, to lights and flags...there isn't a HUGE amount on the build list atm but again early access.
The game also have an RPG element to it in so much as your activities gain you XP, with xp you can level up, each level up you can spend point to improve your stats making you stronger, faster, more durable etc.. and you also gain points in either combat, science or engineering based on your activities which can be spent on a tech tree, which enables you to build certain things or upgrade certain things... none of which you can get by standing around you literally have to play to survive :)
Another thing to note is everything built in game has a durability and also decays slowly over time, so although things can get damaged by enemies or aliens or even you if your a bad shot or driver over time things break down and need repairing anyway.  repairing is fairly simple but is also constant when it comes to your structures.  So if you have a loarge base and walls and turrets and lights and flags, and storage bins and vehicles, and robots and solar panels it all needs constantly fixing.  It uses no resources but you have to run around with a multi tool and fix everything (or the robots would if they worked well)  in multiplayer this is fine but in single player the natural decay is a massive time sink and pain in the behind.  it would be nice to have the option to turn decay off, or make decay limited to attack/aliens only just removing the natural decay in single player.
To sum up Osiris is a work in progres, but it is beautiful, atmospheric and a great start and what will hopefuly once done be a fare more expansive game (with some story i hope).  It has issues a plenty as any work in progress would from disappearing, dumb as mud robots to moving around your base to suddenly find yourself catapulted far away due to some glitch, round to interiors with no lighting once built even though they should.. some of them can be frustrating but none of them detract from the promise this game shows.

-Character skills upgrade system
-Story is better than average
-Tom Clancy's: The Division style third person mechanics, but with the option of first person while aiming down sights
-Fallen Ghost DLC is good
-Great value when on sale
Cons:
-Mission mechanics are repetative.  Go here, stop convoy, interrigate person of interest, kill target, blow up target.
-Playing co-op with less than four players limits your squad to the number of co-op players playing.   Game should fillout squad with those personal bots and a squad leader destinated and have control of them.

-EVGA's PrecisionX OC software on screen display feature is blocked by the game (probably for a good reason though, such as anti-cheating code written into the game)

, then look no futher than the above header. This game contains all the elements of several past games and manages to go a bit further too in some regards. Mixing them all
... Yes I'll say that again,
, together. It's without a shadow of a doubt that
is one heck of a wonderfully fun shooter. One that manages to work just as effective in Solo play as it does in Co-Op.
You'll already know what to expect from the premise, what with having
s name attached to it. More international intrigue caused by one backward bunch of foreigners or another, that only the good ol' Western Military Industrial Complex can put right.  In this instance, the bad guys aren't just evil
but more evil(er)
-terrorists ! And it is up to
and your fellow team of ghost operatives to put a stop to their nefarious dealings, ruin their cocaine industry and restore Bolivia back to its rightful people. I guess the irony of how both the US and UK have helped guard and increase drug production in certain parts of the planet, has escaped Mr. Clancy somewhere along the way. Though banter between your NPC squad buddies in Solo. Do question their part in this little war from time to time, so it's not all Gung ho America f**K Yeah ! Which is nice.
However I've never really been one for the real world approach as it is and is why I have always respected the likes of
and
for their approach to story done in alternate Earth-like worlds. Where you can have the familiarity of the world around you, but you're not bogged down in real world issues or points of view. Some of which, when it comes to these types of games could easily be considered as being dangerously propagandist. We as gamers should always be appreciative of that extra special level of escapism. And it must've been serious enough this time around as there has been reports that the Bolivian Government aren't that happy with their countries portrayal here. And UbiSoft have even put a disclaimer on the loading screen about how it is not a representation of the REALITY of Bolivia and all that. So it all seems like it's defeating its own purpose from the get-go, having the game set in an actual country (Just as a side note, it's going to be interesting to see if the Christians of Montana will be shown a similar courtesy when FarCry 5 arrives in February. Will just have to wait and see on that one. Though my cynical side is saying that they probably won't).
Anyway, despite all this GRW is fantatstic. As simple as it is complex, very accessible and easy to pick up and has one of the most beautiful sandboxes I have ever had the pleasure to game in. Easily the best environment I have played in since Skyrim, it is just shocking how beautiful it is. As well as being a massive play area and contains a huge amount of variety in environment, ranging from grasslands to desert to high snow covered mountainous terrain. GRWs Bolivia boasts a huge, HUGE playground of destruction and guerilla warfare for you to get stuck into.
The environmental effects are nothing short of stunning too. Creating a wide variety of weather patterns that constantly change the look of your surroundings with stunning results. No more is this so keenly represented as after a good nights rainfall. When the sun is rising and you can see the morning sky reflected in puddles and tire tracks. Or the blinding shine of the sun on a wet road surface. It's absolutely incredible to see. And much to the credit of the talent of the devs.
Somewhere along the line it feels like the devs have been to the
school of game creation. What with GWR being essentially a massive sandbox filled with quests, collectibles and side mission galore. Except they have also learned enough to realise how bloated and boring your average WB game can get. So they've made it that even getting the most basic of collectable, requires planning and tight execution in order to get into the area and get out with your desired object. This, for me raises the bar slightly beyond the likes of your average Mad Max or Arkham Knight. As all your objectives (big and small) are so very interesting and challenging to achieve. And even with that said the challenge is as difficult as you like. Not content with just having
difficulty settings. GRW also has a huge host of other options to offer that can tailor a very personalised experience for the player.
Also when it comes to personalisation, the customisation of your character and weapons are extensive and offers a huge array of options (just as long as you have collected the part that you need). But be prepared for a lot of the cool vanity items to be locked away behind DLC and other various paywalls. Some feeling like they are present just to give Ubisofts useless and unnecassary DRM browser,
something to do. In another vain attempt to give it some sort of credibility. But as reality dictates, it is just a bloody nuisance.
But unlike weapon parts, appearences are just that. The various items of clothing won't give you any kind of bonus, so you're not missing out on anything if you refuse to spend your Ubi Points (the ones you get for achievements that is) on stuff in game. And other stuff that can be bought with Ubi Points (the ones you actually pay real money for). Are so ludicrously over priced I wouldn't blame you for vomiting for just thinking about it. I'm not sure if these items are anymore accessible through getting the Season Pass. But the general internet chatter is casting quite a dim light on GRWs SP and on the extra DLC in general. Stating that out of the just
expansions. Only one is kind of OK. And the other one is a pointless racing game add on. It doesn't look like something I'm willing to shed cash on. Not without at least a good 75 - 80% discount anyway. As that all it seems to be worth for all that it offers..
Character customisation also comes with an (A)RPG style levelling up system and you have a range of upgradable skillsets to fill up. And once you have maxed your level out. This then carries on further with a clever little "Tier" system that allows extra bonuses to be earned as you play.
Before I wrap up, I must make special mention of the Co-Op as it is one of the best and accessible I have ever encountered. And it is all down to how the game itself has been so brilliantly constructed. Even when you start the game. I don't think that there is a single area on the entire map that isn't accessible. You are fed intel when entering regions and it is up to you whether you want to chase various missions or not. Which not only gives you a great sense of freedom. But also makes it so easy to get into Co-Op with fellow players no matter what their skill or progress.
GRW is a treat and a total joy to have a blast around on. Allowing you to play as sneaky or as Rambo-like as you want. A fully enjoyable game in a stunning setting. Not as complex as your games like Arma but not as basic as your CoDs either. Just a real nicely balanced, accessible fun game with very few downsides and there are some, it would be unrealistic not to expect them. I'm going to single out the radio for particular criticism here. Fair enough, nefarious drug traffickers have taken over a country and they are really bad guys. And you can tell they have gone for a surreal / comical GTA style approach when doing their representation of Bolivian radio. But I have to say it just did not work for me. Some of the music was just awful and the DJ commentary was nothing short of vulgar. It won't be winning any OST awards from me anytime soon, I can tell you.
but other than that, I can't recommend this enough.

Hey Folks!  I thought I would pop on here and leave a review for this How to Survive 2.  I had this title given to me by a friend who thought given my love of Zombie titles that I would like it.  Even though I have owned the original for awhile I never actually got around to playing it.  As a result I was not exactly sure what to expect when I started playing it.
I wrote up an impressions piece on
but I have to say I was pleasantly surprised.  That said the game is very much not finished, but because of that I can't really judge it any more harshly than any other Early Access title.  The price-tag of $20 seems extremely reasonable for the experience, and I have been using this as a game when I don't really have much time to play something deeper.  It allows me to get in, run a few missions... and feel like I have made some progress.
There is a nostalgic characteristic to the game that reminds me of the way it used to feel to explore maps in the original two fallout games.  For being a top down isometric game... it is strangely suspenseful anytime you explore an area with only the cone of your flashlight to see by.  There were several times I was surprised as zombies lumbered in from directions I was not quite expecting them.  At first the zombies are pretty brain dead, but as you level both your camp and your character... they start mixing in some of the modern track star zombies, and other types like boomers.
My biggest complaint right now is that there isn't much of a tutorial and I had to rely largely on copious amounts of googling to sort out how various aspects of the game actually work.  The game loaded fast enough that the keyboard screen was not up for long enough for me to memorize the various hotkeys...  and it was only by accident that I realized how to bring that menu back up.  That said... at this stage of the game no game really has a functional tutorial.  It is a game in progress, and so long as you are willing to play a beta product you should enjoy yourself. I’m playing the game since the beginning of the early access and it has come a long way since so it’s time to do a check-up.
Pros :
- Play local solo or coop. Play online or even local coop online!
- Build your own place to survive. You will spend some time before getting a good camp. With the most recent update, you can set a camp attack and defend it from zombies waves!
- Kovac. This character is hilarious!
- Various recipes for crafting. Literally everything is used for crafting, even junk you can melt in a foundry. No leftover.
- Missions : you will go on several missions to gain xp and loot. You can increase the level of the mission for a “high risk, high reward” gameplay but you can also decrease it if you want to go on an easy way.
- Battle gameplay. Use melee weapons or guns but don’t get outrun nor outnumbered otherwise you will have a bad time. You need to aim your enemy and keep it in sight for a critical shot. The faster you can get it, the better.
- Post-apo weapons : you see that they are really made of what you used to craft them!
- Finishing moves. It feels so good !
- Flying pets!
- Season events: we got thanksgiving or christmas missions and specific loots!
- You can customize your character from the inventory at any time. (Topless character against zombies ftw!)
Cons :
- It’s still early access. Some things are unfinished but as the time goes, we have less and less missing features.
- Environnement is repetitive. It’s either swamps or city with the same look.
- Some resources are hard to find, even quest related ones.
- In order to craft/upgrade specific weapons or buildings, you will need to grind levels or farm resources.
- The hunger and thirst does not penalize you enough. Having 0% hunger/thirst penalize you in combat (You will hit like a fly and your aim will be awfully slow) but your health will remain unchanged so it cuts the “survival” a half.
- If you play in public, be prepared : you obviously have player killers, robbers and griefers. So I recommend playing with friends only for the best coop experience. (On the contrary, if you search for a “pvp” like gameplay style, go for it!)
The game is on the right path and has improved a lot since its launch so if you like zombies, crafting and survival in hostile and desolate territory, buy it, you’ll enjoy the journey. And of course, with friends. The more, the merrier! (With the notable exception of your resources.)

Quick Summary: Costume Quest is a “children’s” RPG focused more on story than on graphics or complexity. The actual gameplay reminds me of a simplified Chrono Trigger or similar Japanese RPG where you travel the map with semi random encounters and fight by taking turns exchanging attacks with the enemy.
I called it a children’s RPG, by which I mean not only is the story about a group of kids (even the main bad guy is a child) but the story would be considered PG if it were a movie. You control a group of kids teamed up on Halloween to stop monsters from stealing all the candy, using the power of your Halloween costumes. In the main world you look like a bunch of kids in homemade costumes, but when you encounter enemies and enter battle, you become whatever you’re dressed as. For example some of the costumes are robot, jack o’ lantern, or unicorn. Outside of battle you’re free to change your team’s costumes to whatever you have unlocked, and some costumes have some sort of real world effect (for example the robot allows you to run fast).
When your team is in battle, the options are extremely limited. You can either run away, attack, or use a special move. The special move is unlocked every few combat rounds and usually it’s something like a big attack or a healing spell for your team. An added combat mechanic is the ability to boost your attack or weaken the enemy attack by doing an easy quicktime event. For example every time you attack you press the correct button in time and your attack does 10% more damage, or you press it at the right time during the enemy attack and only take 90% normal damage.
Pros:
+Decent cutesy, fun story for kids. Nothing a parent would have to worry about.
+Very simplified gameplay, with some element of skill in boosting attacks or finding hidden items in the world.
+The DLC Grubbins on Ice is included and adds a few hours more gameplay.
Cons:
-Kind of a childish game, but you knew what you were getting into.
Overall the game is a nice diversion that you can finish in a few days. I only played it at first because when Steam was releasing their trading cards, this was the one of the first games I owned with cards and I figured I’d give it a try while waiting for cards to drop. It was not disappointing.

It's Halloween.  You're out trick or treating, and your brother/sister gets kidnapped!  It turns out that there is a plot by real monsters to steal all the candy in the world, and only you and your friends can stop them.
Your costumes have different abilities to use while you're walking around town.  One has a flashlight so you can cross dark areas.  One has a helmet so you can cross areas with dripping water or debris.  One lets you roller skate and jump off ramps.  Another lets you into a secret club in your neighborhood.
The costumes become REAL during combat, and each has a different fighting style.  So if you're dressed as the Statue of Liberty, you can use a healing spell to restore HP to the whole group, or you can hit the enemy with your torch to set them on fire.  If you are the robot, you can rocket-punch a single enemy or use your missiles to attack all the enemies.  And the other costumes have additional things going for them.  As you play more of the game, you will find parts of new costumes.  Only if you find all the parts can you make the costume.
In addition to changing costumes, you can also buy badges that give additional abilities.  One lets you add a little poison to your attacks.  Another adds a bigger poison with splash damage to nearby enemies.  Another boosts your HP so you live longer.  Another boosts your damage, but only if you make a critical hit.  You make a critical hit by getting good timing when you push the button displayed on screen.  Critical hits are very easy, I think I only ever missed two.  The first was because I didn't know how to do it yet, the second was because I sneezed and it messed up my timing.
This game is not particularly difficult.  It is also not very big or long.  Still, it is fun for a little while.  It also has an expansion pack (standalone) where the kids visit the monster world at Christmas time and help the monsters overthrow a dictator.  New costumes are available in the expansion.  You can load your end-game save from the original game and start with the same characters, badges, and costumes when you boot up the expansion.
Bottom line:  it's cute and fun, but don't expect too much from this one.

SLI is supported, there's a graphical benchmark tool, VRAM usage visualiser, example pictures and explanations of graphical setting options.  When you spend your hard earned money to build a highend PC with two highend video cards, you expect PC games to support SLI and impress you.  In my opinion, TC GRW does a great job.
Pros:
-Graphics, SLI supported, vast graphical options, and Nvidia Ansel feature
-Co-op campaign up to four players
-Personable bot squad members with their hilarious conversations and banter
-Gigantic vast open world & open story progression & open world exploration
-Character skills upgrade system
-Story is better than average
-Tom Clancy's: The Division style third person mechanics, but with the option of first person while aiming down sights
-Fallen Ghost DLC is good
-Great value when on sale
Cons:
-Mission mechanics are repetative.  Go here, stop convoy, interrigate person of interest, kill target, blow up target.
-Playing co-op with less than four players limits your squad to the number of co-op players playing.   Game should fillout squad with those personal bots and a squad leader destinated and have control of them.
-Narco Road DLC is not good
-EVGA's PrecisionX OC software on screen display feature is blocked by the game (probably for a good reason though, such as anti-cheating code written into the game)

If you want an immediate "
" SMASH style description of
, then look no futher than the above header. This game contains all the elements of several past games and manages to go a bit further too in some regards. Mixing them all
... Yes I'll say that again,
, together. It's without a shadow of a doubt that
is one heck of a wonderfully fun shooter. One that manages to work just as effective in Solo play as it does in Co-Op.
You'll already know what to expect from the premise, what with having
s name attached to it. More international intrigue caused by one backward bunch of foreigners or another, that only the good ol' Western Military Industrial Complex can put right.  In this instance, the bad guys aren't just evil
but more evil(er)
-terrorists ! And it is up to
and your fellow team of ghost operatives to put a stop to their nefarious dealings, ruin their cocaine industry and restore Bolivia back to its rightful people. I guess the irony of how both the US and UK have helped guard and increase drug production in certain parts of the planet, has escaped Mr. Clancy somewhere along the way. Though banter between your NPC squad buddies in Solo. Do question their part in this little war from time to time, so it's not all Gung ho America f**K Yeah ! Which is nice.
However I've never really been one for the real world approach as it is and is why I have always respected the likes of
and
for their approach to story done in alternate Earth-like worlds. Where you can have the familiarity of the world around you, but you're not bogged down in real world issues or points of view. Some of which, when it comes to these types of games could easily be considered as being dangerously propagandist. We as gamers should always be appreciative of that extra special level of escapism. And it must've been serious enough this time around as there has been reports that the Bolivian Government aren't that happy with their countries portrayal here. And UbiSoft have even put a disclaimer on the loading screen about how it is not a representation of the REALITY of Bolivia and all that. So it all seems like it's defeating its own purpose from the get-go, having the game set in an actual country (Just as a side note, it's going to be interesting to see if the Christians of Montana will be shown a similar courtesy when FarCry 5 arrives in February. Will just have to wait and see on that one. Though my cynical side is saying that they probably won't).
Anyway, despite all this GRW is fantatstic. As simple as it is complex, very accessible and easy to pick up and has one of the most beautiful sandboxes I have ever had the pleasure to game in. Easily the best environment I have played in since Skyrim, it is just shocking how beautiful it is. As well as being a massive play area and contains a huge amount of variety in environment, ranging from grasslands to desert to high snow covered mountainous terrain. GRWs Bolivia boasts a huge, HUGE playground of destruction and guerilla warfare for you to get stuck into.
The environmental effects are nothing short of stunning too. Creating a wide variety of weather patterns that constantly change the look of your surroundings with stunning results. No more is this so keenly represented as after a good nights rainfall. When the sun is rising and you can see the morning sky reflected in puddles and tire tracks. Or the blinding shine of the sun on a wet road surface. It's absolutely incredible to see. And much to the credit of the talent of the devs.
Somewhere along the line it feels like the devs have been to the
school of game creation. What with GWR being essentially a massive sandbox filled with quests, collectibles and side mission galore. Except they have also learned enough to realise how bloated and boring your average WB game can get. So they've made it that even getting the most basic of collectable, requires planning and tight execution in order to get into the area and get out with your desired object. This, for me raises the bar slightly beyond the likes of your average Mad Max or Arkham Knight. As all your objectives (big and small) are so very interesting and challenging to achieve. And even with that said the challenge is as difficult as you like. Not content with just having
difficulty settings. GRW also has a huge host of other options to offer that can tailor a very personalised experience for the player.
Also when it comes to personalisation, the customisation of your character and weapons are extensive and offers a huge array of options (just as long as you have collected the part that you need). But be prepared for a lot of the cool vanity items to be locked away behind DLC and other various paywalls. Some feeling like they are present just to give Ubisofts useless and unnecassary DRM browser,
something to do. In another vain attempt to give it some sort of credibility. But as reality dictates, it is just a bloody nuisance.
But unlike weapon parts, appearences are just that. The various items of clothing won't give you any kind of bonus, so you're not missing out on anything if you refuse to spend your Ubi Points (the ones you get for achievements that is) on stuff in game. And other stuff that can be bought with Ubi Points (the ones you actually pay real money for). Are so ludicrously over priced I wouldn't blame you for vomiting for just thinking about it. I'm not sure if these items are anymore accessible through getting the Season Pass. But the general internet chatter is casting quite a dim light on GRWs SP and on the extra DLC in general. Stating that out of the just
expansions. Only one is kind of OK. And the other one is a pointless racing game add on. It doesn't look like something I'm willing to shed cash on. Not without at least a good 75 - 80% discount anyway. As that all it seems to be worth for all that it offers..
Character customisation also comes with an (A)RPG style levelling up system and you have a range of upgradable skillsets to fill up. And once you have maxed your level out. This then carries on further with a clever little "Tier" system that allows extra bonuses to be earned as you play.
Before I wrap up, I must make special mention of the Co-Op as it is one of the best and accessible I have ever encountered. And it is all down to how the game itself has been so brilliantly constructed. Even when you start the game. I don't think that there is a single area on the entire map that isn't accessible. You are fed intel when entering regions and it is up to you whether you want to chase various missions or not. Which not only gives you a great sense of freedom. But also makes it so easy to get into Co-Op with fellow players no matter what their skill or progress.
GRW is a treat and a total joy to have a blast around on. Allowing you to play as sneaky or as Rambo-like as you want. A fully enjoyable game in a stunning setting. Not as complex as your games like Arma but not as basic as your CoDs either. Just a real nicely balanced, accessible fun game with very few downsides and there are some, it would be unrealistic not to expect them. I'm going to single out the radio for particular criticism here. Fair enough, nefarious drug traffickers have taken over a country and they are really bad guys. And you can tell they have gone for a surreal / comical GTA style approach when doing their representation of Bolivian radio. But I have to say it just did not work for me. Some of the music was just awful and the DJ commentary was nothing short of vulgar. It won't be winning any OST awards from me anytime soon, I can tell you.
but other than that, I can't recommend this enough.

Fun little puzzler, only a few hours long, but a good logic workout. If you ever have to guess you've missed something. As is the fashion, concepts are introduced wordlessly with a few simple training puzzles, then you're in for the real ones in each section.  If you've learned the correct rules from the training puzzles (pay careful attention to these), then it's just a matter of deduction to solve that section. Any confusion will probably stem from having "learned" a slightly incorrect version of the rule, and in this way it reminds me a lot of The Witness, though the games are not otherwise similar.

It always feels really good when you hit that moment when playing a puzzle game where you've got it, you've figured it out, and everything falls into place one after another. this game has the opposite feeling; I solve a puzzle, but mostly feel frustrated because I'm not really sure why that's the solution.
At first, when the game is introducing just the basic rules, it does a good enough job at teaching-by-doing. but as the rules get more complicated. it starts to do a worse job of it. I have completed the "white circle" themed area but have no idea what those circles mean - it was all just brute force and guesswork on my part. and even in areas with rules I understand I feel like the game's just not giving me enough specific information to solve the puzzles. The Witness tried a similar thing, and failed for a similar reason - it's very easy to either not understand what the game is trying to teach you, or to get the wrong lesson from the tutorials only to suddenly be confronted with that lesson not applying in the actual game.
I feel like the game would have benefited from sacrificing the aesthetic for a more specific tutorial. perhaps give the player the option to turn it off and figure out the rules on their own. as it is, it's too easy to just not figure out what the game wants you to do, and from there there's nothing stopping you from giving up and brute forcing the answer - maybe let the player make incorrect inputs. colour a block blue that's supposed to be green, and when you get to the end of the puzzle just don't progress the game until the player figures out where he went wrong? I dunno, just shooting in the dark here.
I really do wanna like this game. it's got a good aesthetic and it's a good game to play in the background while doing other things. but it just ultimately fails as a puzzle game. it's close, but not quite there. The logic is unclear and poorly communicated compared to other puzzle games on steam. I'll just go back to playing that one picross game i bought for basically the same purpose that does a much better job of fulfiling that purpose.

My first impressions are very good; though the controls tutorial seems a little incomplete, that's only to be expected in early access. I'm especially pleased with the camera--though I was worried a bit when I didn't have a lot of camera control and we're in a forest... those trees open up in a "viewport" that reminds me of Katamari Damacy when something's blocking the view.
The crafting and leveling system seems simple enough to not detract from the main action of the game, while having deep enough customization to make things interesting.
There's not a lot of appearance customization, but that's fine in a game with this angle--many other games with a similar look and feel, like Diablo 3, don't allow customization at all, and you're not going to be focusing on the nuances of your characters face when fighting zombies.
In fact, I'd be willing to trade away all the facial customization, in favor of more body shape customization. Different body shapes will help in distinguishing teammates in multiplayer games. It's important in first-person team based games like L4D2 and TF2, but it's especially important in a game like this where you need to identify your own character if you lose sight of them in a big zombie pileup.
I haven't had a chance to play multiplayer yet, but I find myself looking forward to it. Definitely a game to keep watch on, even if you don't care for the early access model. Heartily recommend it.

Disclaimer: The review is based on what currently is in the game. (v1.089)
In summary, I only can say that this game at the beginning is very hostile and tries to kill you all the time and it tries to do that so hard, it at some point turned me away from actually continuing to grind through the game.
The trailer looks cool and all, but the game is pretty dry to the taste and that comes from a player, that has played a lot of open world sandbox games, where you grind and build your way up.
Pros:
+ Premise of the game
+ Has decent crafting
+ Has vehicles
+ Vehicles have modular damage model
+ Has multiple planets, that you can travel to
+ Interesting creature designs
Cons:
- Terrain graphics are mediocre (In caves it's alright)
- Poor AI both for the companion drones and wildlife mobs
- Very limited base building and amount of vehicles you can own
- Tedious base maintenance
- Resource gathering is repetitive and boring, most resource nodes look the same, just retextured
- User interface is cluttered with tons of information and clunky
- Poor character responsivnes
- Third person camera for the most part is unplayable and even less responsive than in first person view, it's good only for taking screenshots I guess
The combat is dull. Not to mention, that you can climb on a storage crate or a forge and enemies can't get to you and you shoot them from the comfort of higher ground. But if you get to go hand to hand with a creature of some sort, you are gonna struggle with controlling the character more than you actually try to aim and hit enemies. The camera has a mind of its own when you are getting damage and disorients you a lot.
Game has some nice sand storms, though they are too frequent, too long and are annoying to say the least after a while and limits the exploration of the planet and you are forced to sit in your base whenever a sandstorm is outside or it's dark.
The meteorite showers are cool and all, but when you start to experience them over and over and over again, they are very annoying.
The jetpack is horrible and whenever you use it and land, you are sometimes immobilized for a second or so. The range of the jetpack and height isn't that great either.
The movement of the character feels very clunky (including the jetpack mechanic) and you constantly get tired and overheated. Why future sci-fi space suit didn't include air conditioning and smart fabric? We already have thermo clothing available in real life, but no, in this game you overheat after 50 or so meters sprint.
The droid helper, that spawns right next to you is so stupid, the AI is bare bones and it just follows a straight path and doesn't give crap if there are structures or anything else blocking his way, he never goes around something bigger than himself and sometimes he can't even accomplish that. Not to mention that when you are sprinting, he is falls behind and gets lost and never catches up because he gets stuck at some point. And whenever you save the game, load it back up, the droid will magically appear next to your base, no matter where he was previously located.
The majority of the starting gameplay is grinding, grinding and more grinding and trying to battle against mobs, that troll you all the time and magically spawn from the ground.
The gameplay is for the most part related on gathering resources (grinding) and it itself is quite boring and repetitive. The gathering sequence is clunky (No Mans Sky resource gathering feels several times better than this and that game isn't great) Not to mention, that whenever you hit a resource node for a few times, almost 95% the time some random mob will spawn and try to nibble your feet off or kill you.
Once you get your first vehicle (hoverbike), you can shoot the nodes and the enemies that spawn and then collect the resources somewhat safely.
On top of the usual resource nodes you have geizers that shoot gases in the air (Oxygen, Hydrogen and others) and you collect those in sealed gas tanks that are reusable.
It's about 1/3 of the gameplay and it's very bleh as well. You can split stacks of certain things, but you can split stacks only in half and can't input specific amounts you want the stack to be split.
You have your own inventory and crafting stations inventories and whenever you try to craft something, the result material is stored in the crafting inventory that is hidden on the second tab of the crafting station, where the first tab has the blueprints, so you constantly have to switch tabs to see what's going on with the inventory. Better design would be to simply output the result in your own inventory instead of the stations one.
You will have to constantly battle against your carry capacity, which gets overburden pretty fast, even with 50% more carry weight from stats.
I think the interface has too much things going on at the same time and tries to give the player as much information as it can, thus making it very cluttered.
Minimap is horrible in this game. You access it through using a tool in your hand. You can cycle through waypoints only in one direction with your mouse click and can't go back to previous ones unless you go full circle. The Beacons and anything you mark in the world don't show up in the actual map as waypoints, but instead an arrow pointer on the top left hud is shown where you need to go and distance till the destination.
Terrain is indestructible. Building something in this game is usually gated by several middle components, that require resources from all over the map, and if your initial spawn point was very far from any interesting resource nodes, well... good luck sprinting all that distance, because you won't be able to build a vehicle any time soon, because the hangar, that you use to build vehicles requires a crap ton of various resources, components and sub components to be built. Also you have to figure out where resources are scattered about, because there is no clear indication where you could find rare elements such as Lead, Lithium, Diamonds (Wiki can help).
Building in this game is very limiting, because your habitat dome and your survival dome have a spherical range, that you can't build next to the same building type and thus resulting with the inability to expand large bases.
You have limited amount of buildings, that you can create even in single player. Players are restricted to 20 large buildings to be built per whole game and that is even worse than No Mans Sky limitations and I thought, that it was bad in NMS, this is worse.
Now I understand multiplayer servers can't have unlimited real estate for buildings, but in single player such limits shouldn't be present. Small placeable objects don't take up building space, but the large ones do (Habitat, Barracks, Dome etc).
