While I enjoy this game quiet a bit, it's got a tremendous number of critical problems.
During the Free-Weekend event prior to its sale in celebration of their new tacked-on, last minute PvP add-on, they promised any and all progress made would be saved so you could continue where you left off. As it turns out, many players purchased the game, myself included, to find all of our data deleted. When I confronted Support with my problem, they closed my ticket immediately without any explanation given. As I enjoyed the game, I was actually happy to start fresh and get more playtime in as my save within the 3 days of free-play was more than 75% complete the game.
Universal Handling
Many games, like GTA V for example, cause your vehicle to respond instantly to your input. As such, pushing A or D to turn left or right immediately snaps your wheels in the corresponding direction. To change the turn radius of a vehicle or vehicle class, these games usually set a forced limit to the angle the wheels can reach and change the center of gravity, traction, and sometimes even more complex systems like downward force. Wildlands does not perform as such.
Much like the recent Mad Max game, but far worse so, your vehicles do not respond instantly to your input. This means that pushing A or D to turn left or right respectively causes your wheels to turn at a specific rate. If you extend your wheels entirely to the left for a left turn, then attempt to turn right, it will take twice as long to reset the tires to default and then turn right. To account for turn radius, Wildlands changes all of the above features, but also tweaks the rate that wheels turn.
This makes driving feel clunky, though some may in fact prefer it.
Bikes
They hardly drive, anywhere. Difficult to control, easy to fall off of due to the terrain. Best suited for steady roads and paved streets. Odd for a dirtbike in a game.
Cars, Trucks and SUVs
Squishy as hell, odd to control. Similar problems to the bikes, hard to take off-road. Makes sense to be fair.
Helicopters
They released an update at some point that makes helicopters more usable in a combat scenario, thanks to new controls that offer you more control of your helicopter, but they still feel slow and clunky. Due to enforced aim acceleration for the helicopter, it can be difficult to use your wingmounted weapons to land any killshots, homing missiles included.
Airplanes
Eh, I wouldn't say they fly well at all, but they don't ever get used in combat scenarios. It's a vehicle you use only because a mission will ask you to, such as Supply Raids where the Supply Vessel
an airplane.
Enemy Resilience
A classic problem for increasing difficulty. As you increase the difficulty, enemies become more alert, can survive what seems to be up to more than 300% more damage in all scenarios. This wouldn't be much of a problem, however increasing difficulty reduces your bullet resistance.
Player Resilience
Where in Normal or Easy you can survive entire magazines of bullets from untrained, spraying, panicking sicarios, on Extreme, you can survive roughly 3 bullets without any skillpoints invested in survivability. With full bullet resistance invested, including the Medal you find in the world that adds to your skill, I've survived up to 4 bullets, 5 after regeneration started to kick in. To help drive home why this is a problem I should include the weapons you're up against. M134's, LMGs with up to 175 bullets in its box magazine, dual Mac-11's and Skorpions, assault rifles, sniper rifles and of course helicopters with missile pods, homing missile pods, SAMs, ground vehicles like trucks or SUVs with mounted M134's, APC's with HE cannons, etc. All of these become laser accurate on the highest difficulty.
Tier One
Once you've activated Tier One mode, the end-game levelling system available after you've maxxed your level, you become locked to a Difficulty level. The higher level Tier you level up to, the higher level you're locked to until you're locked to Max Difficulty.
Stealth and Guerilla warfare
Another classic in stealth oriented games for Difficulty-Ups. I normally would actually applaud this added difficulty, however it can be rather buggy and has led to many failed stealth missions, and even more failed Loud missions. Adding to the laser accurate dual wielded SMGs at mid-to-long range capable of dropping you in 5 bullets or less, on Extreme enemy detection markers indicating how aware of you they are become very spotty. Often times my detection meter will fill slowly but before it's even halfway filled, the enemy detecting me is already shooting at me fully aware of my position. This makes using cover to get surprise guerilla attacks very risky, and very unreliable. It's more luck based than skill based, regardless of range in many cases.
Overcast
On Advanced and below difficulties, enemies are shown on your minimap as vague red clouds. You can mark them with your drone, or Rebel Spotter Support Skill to remove the cloud and add certainty to enemy positions. This I find is a crutch and can be disabled in the HUD options, +1 points. My friend who had never played Wildlands found that the Detection Clouds were enabled by default. This could be a -10 for a player that gets suddenly floored by Tier One mode disabling their Detection Clouds.
Much of this game is simply repetitive busywork, it's a typical checkbox an openworld game would have to tick to offer a low cost, high yield turnout of gameplay for the players to tackle. You'll find yourself stopping convoys all across the country from province to province, hijacking helicopters for supplies, blowing up airplanes 'cause you'd rather not do that Supply Mission and instead see the plane explode.
You'll be collecting your typical collectibles like story tidbits, music, pictures and items.
Collecting intel to mark important intel such as additional Skill Points and Supplies used to invest in skills such as weapon stability, inventory upgrades such as C4 and capacity, flashbangs, drone upgrades, etc.
I found that the team hiding skillpoints, weapons, weapon parts, skill medals, Rebel Ops, Supply Raids, and so on, did a
good job building encounters in spite of many of them being random encounters. For many, this can actually be a plus, but a lot of it was added solely as a low-cost means of extending gameplay.
You can refer to the massive list of complaints against Uplay that everyone everywhere lists about this wannabe Steam clone. It has launch errors and bugs, often becomes unresponsive and the achievement systems that reward points to allow you to unlock items in-game(as a sneaky way to introduce you to the microtransaction items available for purchase) often don't reward you the item you bought for weeks on end using achievement points. Does not bode well for items you would purchase with cash.
Tying into the Uplay problems, many programs cause launch errors with Uplay games and many can be hard to identify. I haven't discovered a fail-safe method of detecting programs that prevent Uplay titles from launching, but after buying this game it took me well over 3 hours to figure out how to launch the game. As it turns out recording software, in my case Plays.tv, can prevent the game from launching.
I have still have many more complaints but Steam won't let me extend this review further.

Enjoyed the game a lot and would definitely recommend it - especially given the low price.
I really liked the aesthetics and the elegance of the game: step by step increasing difficulty and implementing new mechanics without the need to give written instructions. Thought process wise, it feels like an elaborate version of a mixture of Sudoku and Minesweeper. So if you enjoy these games or enjoy puzzles in general, you should get the game.
I also really liked that there was no timer or score involved. It was only about the intriguing puzzles.
It took me 3-4 hours to complete the entire game and while it is not the longest game, it is still well worth the price.
Small comment: A puzzle resets if you make 3 mistakes; so in theory, you could simply brute force the solution by trying all possible answers. Make sure to not go for that route because it will simply ruin the fun. Try to always think until you are sure you are making the correct move, since the game has no mechanic to punish this trial and error behavior.
So once again: I had a lot of fun playing this.
Thanks!
PS: Also check out the YouTube Channel "FLEB" where the developer of this game showcases different puzzles.

As many have stated before, HOI4 is a fun game to play if you are relatively new to the series and just want to mess around. However, when you really look at the gmae closely, you tend to notice a lot of issues that have yet to be fixed or even added to the game a year after its release.
Cons
-The AI is laughable. So bad that CIV VI AI looks good. Grand battle plan just doesn't work. The units that you have carefully placed along the French border? All decided to come together at one district, or just hopscotch between districts because AI doesn't know what "forward advance" means, thus leaving an entire front wide open for flanking. Or better yet, the AI will reorganize its army to have reinforcements go to a part of the front that does not require any reinforncements, thus leaving the crucial part of the front that actually needs reinforcement, wide open for being overrun.
-Bordergore. If you want to see some art..er I mean...unfathomable and illogical map carving, I encoruage you to check it on Reddit or simply Google it.
-Lots of minor nations are just meh, and not entirely enjoyable to play. It'd help if they had some interesting focus trees that does not require me to shell out $10-$15 just to "enhance" my gameplay
-Some of the major powers don't feel exciting to play, especiialy when you comapre the focus trees to what the Community offers (Look at Vanilla Gemrany focus tree and then look at Edelweiß's "Germany Techtree overhaul. It offers way more focuses that are logically and fun to use, rather than some lackuluster focuses.)
-DLCs are overpriced for what they barely offer. I don't understand why I should pay $10-$15 for game features that should have been in the game Day 1, as well as play nations that should have had their focus tree fleshed out from the start. Seriously, just to play any other Commenwealth nation (Australia, New Zealand, Canada, South Africa, and India), have the concept of Autonomy (become an independant nation) in play, as well as Battle Combat Logs, One new tactical attack option, and Tech sharing, you need to cough up $15. Paradox...dude, you're like EA now.
Pros:

Maybe the workshop and the mods that are offered? Yeah that's the actual good thing about this game. The modding cumminuty that actually fixes the game and makes it interesting.
TL:DR
-Game is fun if you never played HOI before, and do not give a crap about some missing features. However, if you want said features (that should've been present since Day 1), expect to pay up half the price of a AAA title just for some few lines of codes to work in your game, and maybe some interesting/lackluster nations to play.
EDIT: Oh and they also jacked the price up in some regions, thus nullifying the benefit of a Summer Sale. Expect Jim F-ing Sterling-son to make a video about this.

After having played Train Town I had serious doubts about developer N3V’s next game, Trainz Trouble, but it turns out I had nothing to worry about. In fact, it’s one of the most fun and challenging (and also casual) puzzle games I’ve played to this date.
Trainz Trouble is a puzzle game at heart, aimed at the casual audience. Meaning anyone can pick up and play this without having to worry about difficult controls or deep mechanics. And even if it doesn’t have very deep mechanics the puzzles it throws at you are at times quite challenging. You have to be stress resistant and be able to micromanage several trains at the same time.
It is possible to slow down time, or even speed it up if you know exactly what you’re doing, but you’ll usually have to think things through before you even start.
There are 4 settings; USA, UK, Germany and Australia and each country has their own set of rules.
USA wants you to ride around and micromanage several trains at the same time while collecting money from the banks and blowing up rocks. UK wants you to manage the traffic while riding around. Germany wants you to avoid collisions with high speed trains and in Australia you have to pay attention to (and redirect/outrun) a faster black train.
The real goal is to get to the end of the station without crashing into something. You can switch railroad track directions with the press of a mouse button and if you time it right and do this correctly you won’t lose any stars at the end of the level, when you’re being rated for all of your efforts. But things aren’t really that easy. You sometimes have to time things and let trains wait before they should ride. You’re usually dealing with multiple trains. So that makes this a game that requires both reflexes and brains.
Each of the countries has 15 levels but USA has 24 in total. But these extra levels are mostly for tutorial purposes. So in total there are 69 levels, which should be more than enough to keep you occupied for at least a couple of hours.
There’s also an in-game store that I wasn’t able to access. The button never lit up for me so I was never able to take a look at it. But there should be items in there to make things easier for you. As you can imagine I’m afraid that I can’t give you any examples here.
The game also has the tendency to lose focus. I’ve had several times that I could click the mouse anywhere I want and the game would not respond to it. Alt+Tab didn’t work, but restarting the game completely seemingly fixed the problem. It’s a random, but frustrating problem and I recommend that you at least do not Alt+Tab while playing because that’s one of the things that seems to break the game.
Graphically Trainz Trouble still isn’t the most beautiful game out there and its graphics and style are reminiscent to the ones used in Train Town. It all looks sharp and since the game is viewed from an isometric viewpoint there’s no real need to zoom in anyway.
It really is a very colorful game that mixes both exaggerated and realistic models and that’s what gives it a unique look. I like it.
If you’ve ever been to the Big Thunder Mountain attraction in Disney Land you pretty much have an idea what the music sounds like. It sounds like hillbilly kind of music.
The sounds that the trains make sound realistic but not overly so and same goes for the explosions (which are fun to look at it, by the way !).
Trainz Trouble is a much, much better game than Train Town and I wish I had played this one first. It’s definitely the better game between the two, even if they’re both focused on entirely different audiences. If you like casual puzzle games, or if you just like trains in general, then you can’t really pass up on Trainz Trouble. Choo choo !

The Bureau is an odd game.  It has many great ideas, but ultimately it doesn't live up to them.
The tactical combat is nice, but the interface is clearly simplified for controllers, and very gimmicky to use.  The weapon progression is interesting, but there are huge gaps at certain points in time, most notibly for the snipers, which mean that they're almost never worth taking.  The plot is interesting, and the ending I really enjoyed, but it feels like horribly cut and recut so many times that I'm certain that some things were never properly explained or even made sense.  There was one instance, fairly early on, where I was sure that one thing had happened to a minor character, but everyone in the game said something else was happened.  It was as if the cutscene and the dialoge options were from different scripts.
There were two main things that stuck out to me as really well done:  The graphics and the ending.
The graphics were an absolute fantastic instance of good design.  All the alien tech had advanced particle physics, complex animation and was brightly coloured, and all the human 1950s tech was sepia toned, washed out and mechanical.  They really felt worlds apart and made you feel as if you were fighting a technologically superior foe.
The ending I will not spoil, but I shall say that while I wasn't particularly interested in the game until the last series of missions, those last few really hooked me in and made me want to power through to the end.  Unfortunately the end was very close to that point, and the game was over less than an hour later.
The very worst part of the game was the difficulty.  I started on the standard 'I've played a few video games in my day' setting.  My agents were dying, and I was having a challenging time, but it just wasn't fun.  The main reason was that my primary difficulties on this setting were a lack of ammunition.  The enemies were literal walking bullet sponges.  Sadly, there is only one difficulty slider, so when I reduced it to an easier setting the game not only reduces enemy health, but also changes things like agent bleedout time and resupply frequency.  I would much rather have been able to set the mechanics to hard with low enemy health.
Overall, would I recommend this game?  I don't think that I would.  There are better, more realised games that you could buy with your money that I think you would enjoy more.  However, if you are a fan of 3rd person shooters, then it's not a bad choice to pick up.
However as a final word I shall say that I am very glad that it exists.  It stands as a great example of what a game can aspire to be, and the sorts of things that make you fail to get there.

This is a third person gears of war style cover shooter mixed with a hipsterific alternate sixties setting and topped off with strategy elements on cooldown. Basically Mass Effect meets Mad Men meets Men in Black. If you play this game on the veteran setting and spend most of your time in battle focus mode, it makes for a decently entertaining challenge. The combat is solid, the strategy elements make it fun as long as you baby sit your teammates. Throw down turrets, lift enemies out of cover, sniper shots, stim buffs, it's got a nice variety of classes and skills, making most builds useful.
The graphics are top notch, with support for DX11 and very cool eerie atmospheric environments and events. This game could have easily been a triple A epic, but in the end falls short of the hype to forever be destined to only be decently average experience.
The story, unfortunately is all over the place, the game can't decide if it's a linear action heavy popcorn flick, a deep choice driven narrative, or a half-baked open sandbox rpg and just ends up with a sort of muddled, forgettable plot with everything thrown in. I have a feeling many cutscenes were endlessly revised by the devs.
If you love the xcom games, then you'll probably hate this game, but if you like Mass Effect, then pick this up and you'll have a weekend rental ... errr whatever steam's equivalent is, sale price, yea ... thats it.

A cover-based shooter trying to blend itself with the tactical features of its strategy forefathers. Despite its messy development history it's now a decent game for a decent price. As long as you remember that The Bureau is an action spinoff you will have your fun.
Pros
* Managing your agents is cool and their capacities will make a difference considering you are not given enough ammo to work alone
* The story lay down the foundations for the modern XCOM organization with a nice '60s twist
* The underground base is quite alive (as long as you visit it once per main mission) with plenty of dialogs and little animations
Cons
* The gameplay is not varied and you will often yawn at seeing predictable chest-high walls and meeting the same enemies just with more and more health points
* The IA of your teammates is pretty bad and will require you to micromanage them, but is overall tolerable if you stick to the Squaddie difficulty
* The RPG elements are light with the game itself being rather linear
Some polish would have been a welcome improvement but you can still see in the details that much love was poured into the game. It is also pretty easy to get most, if not all of the achievements!

Do you want a fighting game where you can screw around with your drunk friends on the weekends laughing at how dumb you guys look trying to fight each other, a la Sumotori Dreams? Then download this game.
Do you want a fighting simulator that you can get into immediately? Do you expect to look like the guys in that video up there right away? If you do, then don't download this game.
You'll get discouraged VERY quickly.
When they say you have total control, they mean it. You control every single muscle in your fighter's body. Are you expecting to know how to do a jump kick right away? Throw a punch? Expect to educate yourself on muscle movements instead, because trust me, you have no idea how complex even throwing a simple punch is.
I'm not kidding about learning muscle movements. You basically have to take an anatomy and physiology course before you can make your fighter even look human.
Go through the tutorial. It'll teach you some basics, but expect your fighter to look like a robot while fighting, and expect to get beat. A lot.
Then, watch some more advanced tutorials on Youtube. There are a surprising number of these, but for a game as complex as this, I'm not really that shocked. Even after practicing and watching Youtube videos, you'll still get beat, but don't get discouraged. There is a very high learning curve, but this is part of what makes this game exciting! I've played this game on and off for 7 years, and I'm still nowhere near as good as the higher ranked guys.
Playing this game takes commitment. It'll take a LONG time before your character will even make fluid movements. Don't expect to look like the guys in that video up there without years of practice. It'll take a long time, but is it worth it? You bet.
P.S. If you want to get serious and actually make your fighter look cool, be willing to spend a fortune because the shop is stupidly overpriced.

To clarify, people saying that the monsters are too strong are in unranked play. When I played unranked as monster, I beat everyone silly. But now that I am in ranked, it looks like the hunters havve the upperhand, esspecially when you consider the monster can't sneak around and is always having to run.
Evolve is a fun game where you play as the monster or the hunter, and the hunters have to fight the monster before he gets to stage three. When the monster hits stage 3 he can destory the power relay, and the monster will win if so. There are 3 stages, where the monster gets stronger with each one.

The monster does not regen health, but he can get armor by eating dead animals/hunters. When you eat things you also get "evolve points", represented with a circular blue bar. When it is filled up, the monster can evolve to the next stage.
The monster has four abilites and four abilities points at the beggining, so the monster can have all of his perks in the beggining. All the perks can be upgraded three times, so its possible to have all the abilities, but not maxed out ones. This allows for some diversity on the way you play a monster. When you reach stage two, you get 3 more abilitiy points, and at stage 3 you get 2 more.
My issue with this game is how a full cycle of abilities sometimes wont kill a hunter. Also, the trapper makes it uselss to sneak around since can use his Plant Scanner to find you for him and his teammates.
I'm sure that most of the balance issues will be fixed or nerfed later.
I would play this game, but know what you are getting in to.

Just don't poke it.
I made that mistake.
I died.
The Bad:
So I get it, apocalypse game is suppose to feel lonely and despondent. But this game felt a bit too lonely.
If you're big on ambience, and it affects your mood significantly then this game has enough of it. You're met with a near constant whistling of the wind, and an occasional guitar string pluck. Great, emotional visual novel/ dating simulator full of giggles and tears, would recommend.

Costume Quest is a really fun to play Halloween themed, turn based RPG.
I recently have been getting into playing alot of smaller indie type games as opposed to the larger AAA games because im finding those bigger developers nowadays are just money grabbing Ctrl + C, Ctrl + V all their games and sequels. Small games like this for me are far more exciting and interesting to play because they can be so random.
Costume Quest is clearly a Halloween themed game where you play as a child whose brother/sister has been taken captive by monsters (Grubbins) that think he/she is a giant piece of candy. Progressing through the game, there are 3 or 4 main quest areas/neighborhoods that you 'Trick or Treat' for candy and do various quests such as trading collectible Creepy Treat Cards with other kids, bobbing for apples and finding 6 children that are hiding to get a reward.
There are of course Costumes that you find materials for and use to fight your enemies, you can buy Battle Stamps or receive them after winning a fight which improve your damage, hp, attack power or chance to dodge etc. Each costume has its own unique ability and attack moves which really adds a little strategy as to which costumes your characters wear to a fight.
All in all, i really have enjoyed playing through this game! It has a very South Park: Stick of Truth feel to it, in the sense that you are playing as children, exploring the neighborhood, fighting other children in turn based fights, finding collectibles, doing certain quests to unlock access to new areas, having boss fights and so on. The only difference here is that Costume Quest is a fraction of the price and isnt quite as content filled as South Park: Stick of Truth, but it is worth the price by far in my opinion.
I have been uploading all of my gameplay to Youtube if you would like to see some gameplay but there are of course spoilers if you do watch them :steamhappy:
new addiction!

Costume Quest is a really wonderful and fun adventure for kids and adults, who still remember how it's - be a kid. It's simple, funny, touching, it's make you laugh a little and smile a lot and there aren't many things, that can do so, so I appreceate the experience. You should know though that the game is very repetitive: rob some shop, fight with monsters, do it again and again. Still, it doesn't mean that Costume Quest aren't enjoyable - quite the opposite actually, but I just give you warning.
Now for the main part: it's a Halloween adventure and we have two siblings, who want to celebrate and take all sweets for themselves. They are boy and girl, it's your choice who you want to play with (hint: the choice happens, when your mother decide who will be in charge). But quite quickly events become much more difficult - the big green monster steals your sibling and now you HAVE to find him\her. Or take the wrath of your mother. Monsters just don't look so scary now, come to think of it...
Gameplay is very simple: you must take sweets from shops and homes, you must fight monsters that come your way and take some side quests and exploration if you like. It may sounds boring, but actually it's pretty fun because of battle system, story and dialogs. Battle system looks like a Dream world, where your nice costume (i didn't mention this? Come on, the game has a "costume" in title!) becomes a powerful weapon. Like, robot costume transforms into actual fabulous robot. There are also ninja, Statue of Liberty, Space warrior, magic unicorn... and french fries. Where else you can fight with your enemies, using your french fries powers?! Okay, to actual battles. Little warning: you need some reaction for this, because you will need to quickly press some buttons while you attacking or defending to make better results. And yeah, each costume have it's own special powers for battle. Like, healing allies or making a powerful attack, or shielding the ally or yourself. It's your choice what combination to prefer (hint: you aren't all alone, there will be friends, some from the very beginning, some later).
As for the story, I just don't want to spoil it for you, but it's wery fun and enjoyable with all jokes, references for popular culture, dantists's twist plots... You'll see many absurd situations and many exapmles of wonderful wrinting. Seroiusly, it's good and not only for child's taste. I highly recommend to complete every quest and talk with everyone - dialogs are pretty hilarious here, really, you will have a good time.
So, if you are kid in your heart or at least can be, try the Costume Quest. Despite all its humorous self, it tells a story about siblings, about people, who may fight and tell a pretty bad things, but they're still family. They still love each other, even if it take a monster invasion to understand such a simple fact.
And if you still wondering: of course adults don't help children to fight monsters. When they ever did? *sigh* Adults.
P. S. If you encounter sudden perfomance problems (characters move very-very slow), try to reboot your computer. Strange advice, but it helps me.

Costume Quest is an adventure game developed by the wonderful people behind Stacking, Brutal Legend and Grim Fandango: Remastered. Double Fine Producitons once again hits the nail again with their cleverly designed and well thought out game
Costume Quest is an adventure game where you play a brother and sister who go out during Halloween to do trick or treating but they find out that there are monsters known as Grubbins who are stealing all the candy, you have to stop them!
Across the game's worlds you have to go and knock doors to ask for candy. Sometimes you will get regular human beings who give you candy, sometimes its the nasty Grubbins which it will send you into an RPG button prompt combat system. The combat system is sort of fun but can get very repetitive and boring
This game, the same with Stacking, is meant for people unlike me who are known as completionists. Completionists will have a ball playing Costume Quest and leveling up. The game's graphics are really cute and well designed, the music is nothing special but it is good nevertheless
Costume Quest is very repetitive. Expect to enter the boring combat system multiple times and doing the same thing which is trick or treating can get boring and repetitive too. The game's difficulty is good but the game experiences a huge difficulty spike at the end, so much so, that many people I know who have played the game cannot beat the boss battle. I had a hell of a job trying to defeat the boss battle, but the game forces you to level up by completing other side missions and entering more of the boring combat system, which for me, I don't like... the game is okay at first but it can be impossible to finish if you are not leveled up properly
Costume Quest also offers an additional story through a free DLC known as Grubbins on Ice, I tried playing the DLC story, but sadly, I just gave up when the offered the same things as the original game...
Don't get me wrong, Costume Quest is a wonderful game to play, however, with the game's repetitiveness, boring combat system and huge difficulty spike can put some people off, but overall it is a nice RPG adventure game to play

Basic. That's the best way I can really sum up this game. Actually, this is less a game and more a very, VERY early tech demo. Don't expect to jump in and start wailing enemies all stylish and cool, like Dante or Bayonetta. All you're really given are 3 types of attacks. One button for sword swinging, one button for kicking, and holding down the Right Trigger and pressing any of the other 2 previous attack buttons will activate a special type of attack. Even with mixing up all 3 of these attacks, there's very little combo you can do in this game, and with the animation of the game being pretty stilted, even trying to exploit something here is out of the question. You also have a dash which lets you shoot straight across for a sudden burst of speed. This is only really helpful for getting out of enemy attacks but it also serves to let you cancel any attack you're doing (Dash cancelling basically).
Enemies are as typical as it gets. Ninja mooks, gorilla-like mooks, a big dude that shoots rocket, and one big boss that's a combination of all other enemies you've encountered. Enemies don't seem to flinch when you attack them, so the entire combat experience just gets really dull, especially with how huge the environment is and how slow you run. On the plus side, I can say that the game does look really wonderful. The obvious Chinese inspired locations and theme while under the night sky looks very beautiful, which is saying something for what is pretty much a tech demo.
The only real reason I'm giving this a pass is because it's a free game, so I really can't complain. As a dude who loves action beat-em-ups like Wonderful 101 and Bayonetta, I want to look at the plus side of things, and there's definitely a lot of room for improvements with this game. I envision a lot of cool things that this game can be capable of pulling off, but that's up to the developers themselves to work on.
Give this demo a shot if you truly have nothing better to do though.

I got this because I enjoyed the first game but the gameplay and controls feel nothing like its predecessor. This review is of early access and I would not recommend getting this game yet as it is still not at a stage where it is an enjoyable experience.
Edit: I originally put this review up just for any friends that would stumble upon it, but I was requested to provide more detailed feedback.
As I mentioned the controls feel nothing like the previous game, notably when you charge up a melee attack you are stuck in one spot and you are no longer able to hold the attack longer nor release early.
In the previous game all the areas were interconnected which was more satisfying when exploring and revisiting the area again later would have map revealed. In this game the areas are temporary instances which can be replayed with random changes, which maybe be good for replay but they aren't connected to anything and there is really no reason to bother replaying.
The difficulty in this game scales up as you increase in level, unlike in the previous game where your  improvements help to make enemies easier, the increasing difficulty completely negates any advantages being of higher level if not making enemies more difficult to deal with.
It might be fun to play this game multiplayer, but this area is lacking. Multiplayer menus and searching are not intuitive and/or not existant, I am not really sure as I haven't worked it out.
Character creation or selection should be the first thing you do in the game. Starting with a generic character and having to find the customisation menu hidden away somewhere, I found that there wasn't any particular attachment to the character. In the previous game even with only 3 character to choose from, I seemed more invested in the character.

This was a triumph of a game!!! My friend gave this game to me as a gift to introduce me to video games. I recommend it to any such person.
In the most basic sense, Portal is a puzzle game. You are presented with a task and have to find a way to excute it as you develop new ways of thinking (Think with Portals!) The tasks become increasingly complicated and  the environments become increasingly harder to navigate. Don't let that discourage you though, there's no sense in crying over every mistake. You just keep on trying!! If my clueless butt could do it, you can too!!
Throughout the game you are kept company by GLaDOS, the Aperture Science AI sweetheart (She offers you a great cake that is so delicious and moist!) GLaDOS will also give you words of encouragement, advice, warnings, and praise! There will be consequences for failure. Usually failure will just result in an 'unsatisfactory' mark on your official testing record followed by death. No biggie. You will soon come to find her voice comforting and welcoming.
The game is relatively short, but very fun and fast paced, so it never gets tedious. If you wanna play longer, simply do the advanced maps. As much as I enjoy this game, there is nothing that can stop me from recognising how utterly♥♥♥♥♥♥it is. At every available opportunity, the developers will attempt to screw you over for a little extra money to fill their pockets.
You can expect from this game:
--- A stunning, and aggressive lack of content. With the exception of a couple of favourites, nearly every country is lacking flavour text to make it at all interesting or different in experience.
--- Unrealistic gameplay. Due to balancing, an awful tech tree, and typically overpowered and samey national focus trees, the game does not play like a historical simulation to any concievable degree, despite what it claims to be. As opposed to a grand strategy game, it feels more like a "WWII themed sandbox."
--- Boring gameplay. For years of the game, there will be nothing to do except hit alt+tab and have fun while you wait for the game to become fun. If you're not at war, it is boring, and even when at war, it feels boring and tedious after you figure out the God-awful AI's favourite strategies and how to easily counter them. At the hardest difficulty, which actively boosts AI performance and degrades your own through modifiers on production, research, and army organisation, the AI still makes decisions that rookie players could find fault with.
--- Simple mechanics. There is not in-depth and hardcore design to the game found in other, older Paradox titles such as Victoria II, or even the constantly updated EUIV. These games require experience to play, and have a learning curve that allows the player to start every new game with more and more skill. HOI4 does not. It is simple, easy to figure out and does not change.
--- An active modding community. One of the only good things about this game is its modding community, which has made many features and developments that make the game, which has been developed by a studio specifically catred to grand strategy games, look in comparison bland and boring. Look at Kaiserreich for example, whose gameplay FAR outmatches the base game.
--- DLC whoring. Expect the game to feel absolutely garbage for years to come. While Stellaris has far superceded this game in terms of content and playability, HOI4 still drags its feet through the special kid's special sandbox. It's actually awfully unfun.

Before I start let me say that I love the survival genre. Even though I feel like there are a lot of games that miss the mark. It's one of my favorite types of games on PC. That being said. This game fits in the genre perfectly to me. I will Rank the parts and explain as I go.
1. Story - 5/10 They are trying. It definitely throws Ideas out there of how it all began atleast. It is severely underdeveloped. That is the case for a lot of survival games though.
2. Gameplay - 9/10 They are still working on it. There is still quite a bit here however. Action packed encounters with Aliens and Players alike. You can colonize with others, explore caves, build a small base, vehicles, and even explore some parts of space as well as another planet/moon. The combat system is fluid and your survivability is determined on what you have on your hotbar as well as how you manage your oxygen for maneuvering and gathering resources.
3. Content - 5/10 This is where the game is lacking. The Dev Team is very very very small. I bought it when it first came out. Joined up with one other person and we accomplished everything within a few days. Now that they are adding more content. I have to say I am anxious to revisit the game. There are still a lot and I mean  a lot of features and things that are not in the game yet though.
This game is very much Early Access, and is very much under development. I believe this game is going in the right direction. I just think it will take them forever to finish it. For what it's worth. Buy the game when its on sale and try it out. As long as they do finish the game. It will be well worth it in the long run.

Architect Update:
When I initially bought Osiris, I gave it a positive rating because it was a great game. Like with all survival games though, Osiris has a cult following of diehard survivalists who enjoy difficulty and grinding. These players were very passionate, so we had a vocal minority who kept steering the direction of Osiris towards more grinding -- this reflected in Osiris's ratings, which dropped by 25% from what they once were. I swapped my rating to negative after this.
I am now reversing my rating again to positive. Fenix Fire Entertainment noticed that this was problematic, and swiftly and thoroughly resolved the problem. They recognized that by pushing too far in one direction, it detracted from the experience of other groups -- moving to some awkward compromise in the middle was no option either, as it was no good to sit in mediocrity. Thus came the ability to tailor gameplay to our preferences, and even more amazing updates at the same time.
The settings:
Offering a setting for everything is a bandwagon anti-pattern -- games that fall victim to this offer large amounts of trivial customization that looks good on paper (large quantity of options), but have little effect. Osiris did not make this mistake, and the available options are concerning the most important features for determining user experience for certain play styles. Not only does this allow players to tailor their own experiences to what they'd prefer most, but Fenix Fire can develop individual play styles far more than had they just settled at a happy medium.
The updates:
Even if Osiris didn't have a grinding problem and the options weren't part of this update, it's still a great update. Building hadn't been touched very much since I purchased the game, and we were pretty limited in what we could do. I always ended up building the same structure more or less, because there wasn't much we could do with linear buildings. Being able to connect habitats and stack them vertically alone allows us to wind and twist our bases for much more customization, but Fenix Fire didn't stop there. They also added freeform building, which is amazing. Osiris has always been one of my favorite games due to base building, and it just got so much better.
In addition to the base building, there were some more defenses added, more items, and general rebalances. It's amazing how Fenix Fire didn't just resolve the grind creep with this update, but went far, far beyond the status quo. Given how much I liked Osiris, I was severely put off by the grind creep and couldn't put into words how bad I felt that such a good game had gone downhill, but my trust in Fenix Fire is entirely restored, and I have newfound respect for them, as I've seen few games make this substantial of a turnaround.

I downloaded Rift two weeks ago, due to curiosity. After being an avid WoW player for the past 8 years, and having the game decline as it did, I began to look for a new MMO. And let me tell you I found it here. Rift is a beautiful game, with great mechanics. There's so many great aspects to the game, such as zone events that bring players together, that don't feel forced in the least, and are just downright fun. PvP is awesome too for as much as I've done of it, WoW's pvp seems rather lackluster, and much more infuriating than Rifts. The community is amazing as well, I was surprised at how helpful a majority of the people come across. Almost always willing to answer questions and aid as best they can. It's a wonderful game, and atmosphere that I've really come to adore in the short time, and would absolutely recommend it for anyone, if you're new to MMO's, an ex-WoW player, someone looking for something casual. It's really suitable for all.
A second aspect is that it's free, and the amount of content you get for it being FREE for the first 50 levels is outstanding. I was a little taken aback at the $5  you need to spend to access the AH, but when you think about it, the one time $5 is much less than a monthly subscription.
All in all it's great fun, great value, and just a great game.

I'm not very far into this yet and already I have tons of problems with it--problems that have nothing to do with X-Com loyalty. I'm not even that experienced with traditional X-Com. My problems stem from this being a very problematically designed tactical shooter with a story and writing that just doesn't add up...or make sense...or make me feel anything.
First off lets talk mechanics. As a tactical shooter, this game does at least try to bring more complexity to the genre, but that complexity is undermined by a control system that feels very loose and innacurate (I'm talking about aiming and shooting here). In addition to that, the AI of your companions leaves much to be desired.  Even when you are giving them orders regularly and changing their positions often, you will find that they are generally inneffective and frustrating to work with. I'm sure that they improve some as they level, but I doubt even then that it will totally solve how chaotically and unpredictably they behave.
As for the story, it is about as mediocre as they come. Neither the writing nor the cinematic presentation are very good at all. Often the cinematography and dialog are so bad that I have no idea what is happening. The result is a game that feels like it is coming apart at the seems. The presentation is so sloppy and disjointed that the only way anyone could possibly enjoy it is by not paying attention to it and filling in the blanks with their own imagination.
This game should have had it all for me. I am huge fan of retro science fiction worlds and X-Files-esque conspiracy laden story telling. Despite that, I can only express dissatisfaction with this game as a product. It is simply a broken, unpolished, cash-in by a company that should know better at this point. For shame 2K. For shame.
If you're just looking for a tactical shooter with a decent story, try Spec Ops: The Line instead. That game has an incredibly satisfying cinematic atmosphere, despite its tactical mechanics being simpler and more familiar. If you're looking for a good retro sci-fi game with aliens and government agents and all that stuff...well, tell me when you find one because I'd love to play it.
Who I'd recommend this for:
Virtually no one. This is one of those games that is only for people who have decided to like it before they ever even played it. If you're into the surfaces of the game world and have a lot of patience for poor mechanics, you might have a good time. If you're someone who is simply interested in playing bad games (and I say that earnestly because I do think there is nobility in that, especially for designers) you might want to give it a try as well, but I wouldn't pay full price if that's the case. Hell, I wouldn't even pay half price. I bought this game on sale for $15, and I wish I had waited until they were chuckin' it away for $5.

After reading some of these comments of people who don't like the game because it is not what they know - they know so little - I decided to create a review where I tell you:
Buy this game!
My reasons:
- The story is good
- It is the real beginning of XCOM and told in a way I can believe
- It is not like a DLC to XCOM, Enemey Unknown, but instead a game of its own
- The graphics are great
- I like the sound
- The gameplay is fun
- The characters are real characters - at least some of them. Not just soldier xy.
- soldiers who are not in your team can be on their own missions and level in these missions
- all soldiers have ... "magic" :)
What you have to understand is, that this is not a game where you run around with guns blazing.
You have to move from cover to cover, give your two teammates commands and use the special commands ("magic", whatever) as often as possible.
You have to manage your two team mages, THAT is your job.
NOT killing as many enemies as possible yourself.
If you are one of these idiots who writes in Killing Floor or other Coop games things like "don't steal my kills", then you will hate this game because you are an idiot and idiots can't like this game.
I do not say, that everyone who hates the game is an idiot, or that all idiots will hate this game, I just wanted to mention the possibility :)
If you did not understand the above sentence, don't bother to play the game. It is not for you.
A little bit about the game and not about the mindless haters:
It is real time when you explore the level or do combat.
But all the time you have the option to pause the game and queue commands for yourself and your mates.
Because the game is not really paused but instead is running very slow, you still have to act quickly.
Sometimes one of your mates will attack the enemy in a mindless way, he will leave his cover and storm toward the enemy.
Without any valid reason.
YOU have to manage them and bring them back to cover.
You have to use your men and their abilities, like decoys, to either just bring the enemy down with force or get your men in superior positions, for example you can flank the enemy.
All levels are in a way, that you CAN do it in different ways.
And depending on your choice of mates and your own weapons you have totally different "magic" abilities and ranges of weapons.
Depending on your weapon/ability choice you have to stay away from the enemy or you HAVE to close in.
Do you want to use shields and shotguns? Or do you want to use sniper rifles and rocket turrets? Your choice.
The game is fun. From the beginning to the end.
The end is not drawing on and on and one like in other games.
There is a story and they did not kill the story to make the game longer.
There ARE moments when you want to eat your keyboard, because you did something wrong.
Mostly it is not the game but you, who is doing it wrong.
There are shortcuts to move from cover to cover, or to to jump over cover to be able to run towards the enemy or even to jump over the cover to use the cover from the other side which is VERY interesting in boss fights.
But if you are under stress, you make errors and use the wrong combination.
Then you die and you hate the game.
But the game is really good, it is fun and it is not too long.
It took me over 20 hours to finish it, that is more than ok.
I tried to do every mission and talk to everyone who wanted to talk to me.
I checked the maps for schemata for better equipment and did not rush the game.
I like the game.
It is NOT like XCom-Enemy Unkown, it IS a game of its own and if you can't understand that, then you will not like the game.
It has not the replayability like XCOM Enemy Unkown, because there are not so many choices where you would want to try the different approach. If you once decide to sacrifice someone, why would you save him the next time? The cirumstances are the same. I saved him! :) And the weapon choices are only choices for yourself. For you men it is more like, new weapon? Ok, use it.
It is not a sandbox game. It is not a openworld game. It is not multiplayer.
If you need these to be happy, stay away.
If you are a gamer and like good games with stories, get it and have a blast for 3 days.
Then back to your long term games :)

I've decided to leave a proper review because I truly believe this game HAD a lot of potential and could have been done so much better. XCOM is a gold mine but after this game, you'll need a form of redemption to regain the reputation XCOM earnt after Enemy Unknown.
**SPOILER WARNING**
I DISCUSS THE STORY OF THE BUREAU AND XCOM ENEMY WITHIN INCLUDING ENDINGS
Context:
I have recently finished XCOM Enemy Unknown (complete) and will be combining the two stories together, as they should be.
Difficulty:
Squaddie
Beginning mission
- Gameplay
The gameplay was average but still felt almost *good*. I really enjoyed the semi-pressured tutorials but the encounters were so breif leaving my with little opportunities to experiment with this unique and totally alien combat system. Personally, I love using the commands and try to play it as much like XCOM Enemy Unknown as possible but the simple truth is that it's completely unnessacary. You can just sit behind cover and gun down all of the enemies with ease. I considered the argument that successfully using skills could dispatch units faster but I'm certain that's only possible with the first snipers ability that orders an area to be bombed (wat?). I really enjoyed the way the engineer, sniper and commander gameplay complimented each other though. Another issue was with extremely important dialogue that I missed because I felt like I had to run from the detonating nukes and collapsing ellirium facility. Next time, if that's the case, fuse the drama with the gameplay and have them talk about (mostly) irrelevant stuff at a more slow paced time and keep the dialogue breif and paniced. The final comment I'd like to make on the gameplay was the seriously awkward animations that made me feel like I needed to avoid looking at them to "stay in the mood". In combination with the conversation "wheel" that gives us as players a choice to listen to extra dialogue (which unfortunately has no benefit at all throughout the entire game) it leaves the player desperate to avoid the narratives of which is foundational to the success of XCOM. Remember the final mission in Enemy Unknown? Do you remember how incredibly insightful the narrative was? Imagine if each player got to that point and just wanted to skip through it. Just something to think about.
- Storyline
Well, I'm taking plasma bullets to the face and dropping alien commanders decked out with impressive armor with ease, with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rifle I picked up off the ground. Instantly, horrible way to begin. XCOM Enemy Unknown built up the suspense, the story and the difficulty by having progressively difficulty mobs that gave its storyline an edge and a great feeling. If I were running around exploding sectoid heads with my rifle I would have no issue but shooting through the armor of high ranked aliens with low powered and poorly designed bullets is a no go. Do NOT make this mistake next time. I also believe a character like William Carter was a miserable option. XCOM Enemy Unknown was impersonal; this was an excellent choice. It focused the players attention on the aliens, THE most interesting factor of the story, not a sad and sour man. One man. The planet is being invaded, blown up, sleeper agent virus freaking technology morphing mountains, dirt and buildings into alien fortifications freaking collective of alien species that have been enslaved and adapted to suit the purpose of god knows what ... oh and your character has a drinking problem due to an accident that caused the death of his loved ones. Uuuhhhhhh.... COME ON. It just makes for extremely awkward cut scenes and gives him no actual reason to fight against the aliens. I understand that he feels like he has to do something because of his trauma but it just doesn't have a place in the bigger picture. Why couldn't he be a scientist? Or a guy serving as an agent that is a quiet genius? Someone who actually understands what the F**K is going on in a deeper way then "I have to do something". Terrible, terrible choice on this one. Doctor Shen from Enemy Unknown was the leader of engineering and STILL had so much deeper of an impact then you, as the "commander", story wise. This was a GREAT decision because it still placed complete focus on the ALIENS. Freaking ALIENS!!! What are you people doing to this franchise?? I'm glad the story picks up but I'm disappointed that I have to share it with an ignorant and sour brute like Carter. I wish the Ethereal controlling him had some taste in his hosts.
Unfortunately I missed about 60%+ of the dialogue I was desperate to hear because I was immersed by the setting you put me in. Apparently sprinting through an area that's being bombed, invaded and morphed wasn't what the developers had intended you do, but instead to stand in small rooms in which the dialogue initiates, listening to semi-irrelevant comments before the main points were finally brought up. At one point running through the map, I had lost all immersion and my mind exploded with "holy f**k did they PLAY this game before they released it?". Also, the story line in XCOM The Bureau conflicts deeply with the story in XCOM Enemy Within. The aliens of the past (The Bureau's setting) are far more advanced, organized, planned and structured then those set in the modern word (Enemy Within). Not only in the general sense but in their motives.
It gives me great insight, nevertheless; the Ethereals controlling the aliens in Enemy Unknown seem to be outside of the collective that's controlling the enormous amounts of aliens in The Burea. It makes my wonder why one collective group of Ethereal's controlled and bred aliens to assist their search for strong willed species that could use "the gift" while retaining positive traits (instead of cowardice and frality that the Ethereals claim they have as traits) and others have seemingly become enslaved by an enormous collection of aliens species that have discovered their existance. The first bit of context in The Bureau was crucial and the developers missed the mark completely, even just in the gameplay sense. I can understand a full scale invasion at the beginning of the game but there would have been much better ways to introduce storyline-to-gameplay synchronicity, such as having soft squishies grunts (like Sectoids) being the only alien you could easily kill. I mean the very first time you KILL an alien ... you easily drop up to 12 more within seconds ... completely killing the suspense for the rest of the game onwards. That being said, I have finished this game before and I know there are some enemies ahead that shake your confidence and have the suspense reborn, although, the developers should have followed the same method the developers of XCOM Enemy Unknown used as it created excellent story and gameplay as a result.
Impression of XCOM base:
The idea of The Bureau is incredibly well thought, well done to those who cemented this idea as a plot. However, the resulting story line is completely bizarree. I won't be going into long details in this section, rather, I'll give breif opinions. We get the first taste of the totally redundant back story to Carter that makes for awkward cut scenes and conversations that have nothing to do with your recent encounter with ALIENS(!!!!!!!!!!!) and instead narcassistic rambling. After this, you're expected to gain your footing and settle in by staying strictly designating areas because other areas aren't unlocked yet; despite the fact that only 2 of the areas have any value to the story while the others are as redundant as Carter's backstory. Almost immediately you're given a "side quest"/"side mission" which involves you paroting the radio that's right next to the operator (why??? CAN'T SHE HEAR IT???). That's it. No reward. No back story. A short explaination on how she (the operator) will send help and stop them from broadcasting. That's it. Honestly, this game isn't worth the money and the devs don't deserve it.

First off let me say this game is still in early access so yeah it's going to have it's kinks and glitches. With that said even at this stage, this is one incredible and fun game. So far I have a little ove 40 hours on this and I have loved every minute of it.   The devs are responsive and darqflame is an outstanding community leader for this game.
Pros:
User selected levels for each challenge - you can up the level for each map for a better challenge or decrease the level if you're just in it to grind mats.
Crafting system - The crafting system in htis game is incredible. It keeps you grinding for certain mats and gives the game that "one more turn" feel.
Stats - Each crafted item has a large set of stats and allows you to create a weapon and armor set to fit your gameplay style.
Cons:
- Some of the collisions in the game are a bit bad. For instance, zombies seem to get hung up on a curb on a street a little too easily and zombies tend to twitch when killed.
- There is no pause on this game. If you leave your character in game and move away from the game, when you return it is very likely he will be dead or at least thirsty.
- If you Alt-Tab out of game, your character can get stuck in an attacking pose and will continue to attack until you return.
With this being early access, I feel most of these "cons" will be corrected by the time the games goes into full production. Either way I have enjoyed every hour I have put into this and will be putting many, many more into it before it's done.
All in all, I would recommend this game to all. Get in now and watch the polish happen.

How to Survive 2!  I was really looking forward to this game.  I'm a big fan of the first one mainly because it was so much fun playing coop.   So I was excited to hear HtS2 supported four players!  I have not been dissapointed.   How to Survive 2 offers up a solid coop experience where you get to explore, craft, and kill zombies... again.   Keep in mind the game is in early release so I expect there to be a lot of positive changes.
The positives:
-An open world to explore
- A camp building feature that allows you to build multiple camps any where on the map
- Lots of new weapons and upgrades: melee, bows, crossbows, pistols, rifles, SMGs etc.
- Multiple attack types with melee weapons
- Quests with a good variety of map types
- Peircing damage!  I love lining up zombies and taking them out with one shot
- Scaling difficulty based on the level of your camp and player
Negatives
- Invisible zombies.  Yes, it's a bug and I would bet it's on the top of their bug list.  Luckly others in your party can warn you of the impending attack so you can melee or run
- No melee finishing moves.   I hope they put these back in from H2S.  It was very satisfying
- The game is a bit unbalanced right now.  You get way more food then you need and a chem lab where you can make buffs you don't need.  I'd like to see them become usefull.
- A couple of bugged quests.  Again, it's early release.  There are work arounds.
Overall it's totatly worth playing, especially for the cost.

Fantastic real-time strategy / city builder game. When a lot of RTS games are moving away from base building to try and increase action this game brings it back in style and it feels fanastic to build and maintain a massive base and to try and defend it against the zombie horde. Tthe thousands of units on screen at once is easily this game's best feature.
What I think a few people are struggling with in this game is the roguelike nature of the current survival mode. A full run usually only takes about 3-6 hours (based on how often you pause) so losing and having to start over isn't the end of the world, and usually when you lose it's way quicker than that. In the beginning you will die fast and often and then you'll gradually last longer and longer as you learn what works and what doesn't. And it's really fun to explore the randomly generated maps and to try and make it if you're given a bad
or interesting starting location.
I don't think the developer expected the surivial mode to be this popular, and If it was up to me I would scrap the planned campaign mode and focus entirely on the current survival mode because that's what makes this game unique, and there's no way the campaign mode will surpass this in my opinion. I'm thinking it will end up feeling fairly generic, but the developer may have an ace up their sleeve for all I know.
The game is still a bit rough around the edges, it's lacking a bit of depth and the replayability isn't great once you figure out how you need to play to win, but I've already had a blast with this game and whatever happens next is just a bonus.
PS: I've played the game for at least twice as long as what's listed here. My beta hours are missing for some reason.

Original Review:
Bought a steam key for the original for $5 right when it flipped to F2P, got 80% of the characters unlocked for free day 1 as a result. The people who spent $120+ on the original's godawful business model can stay mad, especially when their complaints are "waaaaaaah, I get to keep all the characters and skins I paid for back in the old version, -and- get a heapload of game cash, but I want moaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaarrrrrr!" Your game barely had 100 people left concurrently playing it, losing your profile's experience points (and associated -cosmetic- unlocks, which you can -earn back-) and a few gamemodes nobody touched is beyond fair compensation for finally having a playerbase again. This isn't even bearing mention to the fact that the Legacy version can still be installed by anyone who owned it.
As far as actual reviewing goes, this is an incredibly solid asymmetrical multiplayer game. There's a bit of balancing work to be done due to Stage 2 changing up the flow of a game a good bit, but so far I've still had my matches end roughly 50/50 for either the hunters or monster.
Playing as the monster is a ton of fun whether you're evading the hunters and bulking up, or duking it out with them inside of the dome, and there's monsters for a nice variety of playstyles.
Likewise, while the f2p switch can lead to you ending up with a lot of inexperienced hunters, if you have friends/end up with a team who know how to play their roles, it's a blast working together to track down and take out the monster, and with 6+ characters per class you've got a crapton of different team setups.
Also, despite being f2p the game still has fully offline botmode support. You earn basically no cash/exp from it, but it's still nice that you can play even if your internet's out, and if you're a founder who stuck to fighting bots in the original you'll still have nearly if not everyone available from the get-go, so you can keep playing on your own if that's your style.
Finally, the gamecash is earned at a decent rate. After my free 30k coins and unlocks from being founder I was left with 4 (maybe 5?) locked characters, and in about 10-15 matches and 5 or so days of login bonuses, I've already unlocked 2 (maybe 3?) of them.
I'd recommend free players check the wiki or youtube to take a look at the various hunters/monsters, as so far I've had fun playing everyone aside from Torvald (having at least once played all of assault, support, and monster, and about half of medic and trapper), so if you see someone whose moveset looks cool, you can prioritize them as one of your first unlocks, and having someone you like playing beyond the free weekly rotation will be a big help in motivating you to earn the coins for the rest of the cast.

As many have stated before, HOI4 is a fun game to play if you are relatively new to the series and just want to mess around. However, when you really look at the gmae closely, you tend to notice a lot of issues that have yet to be fixed or even added to the game a year after its release.
Cons
-The AI is laughable. So bad that CIV VI AI looks good. Grand battle plan just doesn't work. The units that you have carefully placed along the French border? All decided to come together at one district, or just hopscotch between districts because AI doesn't know what "forward advance" means, thus leaving an entire front wide open for flanking. Or better yet, the AI will reorganize its army to have reinforcements go to a part of the front that does not require any reinforncements, thus leaving the crucial part of the front that actually needs reinforcement, wide open for being overrun.
-Bordergore. If you want to see some art..er I mean...unfathomable and illogical map carving, I encoruage you to check it on Reddit or simply Google it.
-Lots of minor nations are just meh, and not entirely enjoyable to play. It'd help if they had some interesting focus trees that does not require me to shell out $10-$15 just to "enhance" my gameplay
-Some of the major powers don't feel exciting to play, especiialy when you comapre the focus trees to what the Community offers (Look at Vanilla Gemrany focus tree and then look at Edelweiß's "Germany Techtree overhaul. It offers way more focuses that are logically and fun to use, rather than some lackuluster focuses.)
-DLCs are overpriced for what they barely offer. I don't understand why I should pay $10-$15 for game features that should have been in the game Day 1, as well as play nations that should have had their focus tree fleshed out from the start. Seriously, just to play any other Commenwealth nation (Australia, New Zealand, Canada, South Africa, and India), have the concept of Autonomy (become an independant nation) in play, as well as Battle Combat Logs, One new tactical attack option, and Tech sharing, you need to cough up $15. Paradox...dude, you're like EA now.
Pros:
-I honestly can't think of a postitive thing since the things that I like about this game, is greatly overshadowed by the amount of trouble and bugs that this game has. Maybe the workshop and the mods that are offered? Yeah that's the actual good thing about this game. The modding cumminuty that actually fixes the game and makes it interesting.
TL:DR
-Game is fun if you never played HOI before, and do not give a crap about some missing features. However, if you want said features (that should've been present since Day 1), expect to pay up half the price of a AAA title just for some few lines of codes to work in your game, and maybe some interesting/lackluster nations to play.
EDIT: Oh and they also jacked the price up in some regions, thus nullifying the benefit of a Summer Sale. Expect Jim F-ing Sterling-son to make a video about this.

Hatoful Boyfriend appears on the surface to be some sort of joke, but it's actually a lot, and I mean *a lot* better than it has any right to be. It starts off as an otome-style dating sim/visual novel with cutout photographs of birds, primarily pigeons. It sounds like the most bizarre premise for a game ever, and for the first couple of playthroughs, it is. You'll laugh at the madness, the implausible scenarios (just how do pigeons use those desks from the classroom background, anyway?) and the goofy dialogue. You'll probably get Okosan's ending first, because it's just too absurd to resist. You'll treat the game as if the whole thing were some sort of silly parody.
But then ... something happens, and you acclimate yourself to the weird world of pigeon dating, and all the sudden the cast reveals itself as the well-developed, sympathetic, and strong characters they all actually secretly are. Certain paths start to break your heart instead of your brain. (I'm looking at you, Nageki and Ryouta.) Then, if you get all the standard endings, it unlocks a final route with a sudden turn into a dark, deeply emotional horror/mystery that completely defies description.
In short, you laugh at the very premise of this game, and you are right to do so. However, like some sort of Trojan Pigeon, that goofy exterior is used to deliver one of the greatest visual novels, if not one of the greatest games of any genre ever made. I'm serious. So is the game, eventually.
(I do have to dock a point or two for the combined total of some minor text errors and gameplay bugs in the current version.  However, please do not let this dissuade you.  Still HIGHLY recommended.)

Full Review:

I wanted to like this game! It pushes several of my happy buttons, from the XCOM branding, to the Cold War paranoia, to the retrofuturistic aesthetic. This could have been the ambitious first entry in a new spin-off franchise... but unfortunately, nearly everything in the game is marred by a clear lack of polish.
I could write about the outdated interface (no mission objectives onscreen or all the other nice little UI touches we've come to expect over the last 20 years), the poor level design (lots of railroading and impassable waist-high obstacles), or several other issues, but by far the worst offender is the combat system. Instead of a fluid, enjoyable experience like Mass Effect 2 or 3, the tactical squad combat is clunky, poorly explained, and extremely unforgiving. It's the heart of the game, and it simply isn't
Overall,
isn't a bad game... just a mediocre one. It does nothing terribly, but nothing particularly well, either. I found myself simply grinding through each little combat set-piece in the hopes that I could reach a more rewarding part of the game, but eventually I just gave up -- my leisure hours are limited, and there are simply more entertaining ways to spend them.

"Oh, it's a... third-person shooter."  I was a bit surprised, expecting something a little more like the previous XCOM game, Enemy Unknown.  The setting looked quite promising, at first.  I even snickered a little bit in the first mission, when I picked up an 1962-vintage M14 battle rifle to shoot aliens with.
Of course, it has the obligatory cover system which seems to be required of any run n' gun game of this sort, but only some manage to execute effectively.  Does this game?  Well... sort of: considering the fact that some other games' cover systems can manage any maneuver with nothing more than WASD, the direction you're looking, and the Spacebar, The Bureau seems to go more for a style where each little variation on "jumping from cover to cover" needs its own key.  Good, I suppose, if you've had trouble getting the more "intuitive" cover systems to do what you want, but for me it breaks up the action a little too much.  "Okay, I need to get to that desk which is a bit ahead of me and to my left.  So, I hold Left, and press... V, I think, and then..."
A bit of a learning curve on the cover controls, though, is not a game-breaker.  It did, however, all fall apart for me eventually.
Pretty soon after you've gotten a taste of "how to shoot" and "how to not get shot," you're presented with a big, steaming pile of a squad command system.  The Bureau has you giving commands to your agents, not too unlike Enemy Unknown did - apart from the fact that you *are* also one of the agents.  What you end up with, then, is a game where you play a real-time, but dumbed-down version of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, in between bouts of playing an okay-but-not-amazing third-person shooter game, using a clumsier version of the dynamic pause squad-command system from the Mass Effect trilogy.
So, if you *liked* XCOM: Enemy Unknown, or the Mass Effect trilogy... don't play this.  If you like the XCOM series enough that you simply must at least *try* The Bureau, do yourself a favour and at least wait for a sale, which will reduce the sting if you end up being as disappointed as I was.
