I wish there was a neutral option or check again after the next update.  I love the idea, the gameplay is fun, if you're an RTS fan I would imagine it could get addicting.  There are just too many annoying things that I wish I could tweak through options, surprise there are basically none, and the gameplay after you've gotten through the new-ness was infuriating to me.  It is an Early Access game, but some of this stuff is just seems like Day 1 stuff.
My frustration in a nut-shell.  I spend multiple hours on the map, spawning near mid-bottom left side of the map.  I naturally expand outward, identify the natural choke points, start building up defenses at the choke points.  Great.  I am systematically clearing any of the infected that are still scattered between my choke points and the map edges.  During this time I deal with multiple outbreaks of infected randomly spawning (no idea where they come from, they apparently just walk by towers) and training into my housing areas, cascading into annoying waves that just constantly eat up time, soldiers and resources.
It is at this time I realize that there is an area of infected in the southwest corner of the map that I can't actually move my camera to.  I can apparently see them on the mini map, direct soldiers to attack the mini map area, but I can't actually see it because interface is in the way.  I clear the area, thinking as long as they are cleared no problem.  Oh no, they randomly spawn back at least twice more and proceed to train towards my housing.  Delightful.  I can't actually build anything down there, and the area itself is so ridiculously large and lacking of any real chokepoint that it will require me to build the great wall of China to secure that edge of the map.  Don't forget that this is the only RTS game I've ever played that also prevents you from building near the "edge of the map".  I guess my definition of the edge of the map varies from the developers, as 10 blocks away really isn't an edge.
As I begin my endeavor to make the 8th wonder of the world, a wave of infected spawns and proceeds to crash through three choke points.  Each choke point features at least 20 soliders, 2-3 ballistas and pit traps that would have required stripping every tree from the Continental Divide to the Pacific to fill.  There was an odd sense of amusement as I watched my soldiers fail to path around things and get caught long enough on a pixel for a wave of infected to rip them apart.   At this point I alt+f4ed.
The game has a great idea, but just has some headshaking crap that makes me wonder at what point you don't realize that you can't actually pan to the bottom of the screen because the interface blocks it.
PS:  The grid system drove me absolutely insane,  The 45* rotation on the grid from a normal cartesian plane made for some of the stupidest building angles for gates.

Costume Quest is a lovable adventure you will never forget and if you do forget it, you are dead to me. This game is a superb JRPG with great level designs which sometimes want you to get a walkthrough (I had to use a walkthrough about 3-4 times). The story is a bit short but if you did all side quests (like me), you would at least have about 6-7 hours put in this. If you didnt do all side quests, you would have approximately 2-4 hours put in this.
The game is beautiful for a halloween-themed game. Coffins are chests, you can trick-or-treat houses for candy or enemy encounters, battle stamps which improve your character in fights and several comedic speeches for all ages. I absolutely adore this game.
Just like in every RPG game, there is a leveling up system. In order to level up, you defeat enemies (just like every RPG). It does take quite a while to level up in this game but that made me want to farm enemies and destroy bosses.
Every game (excluding racing games) contain bosses (I think). These bosses were rather time consuming but if you had the right costumes for your team, it would be a piece of cake. I did find one boss in the game rather annoying but dont want to spoil it. I would say something about the boss, but just wait till you fight her.
There are costumes you find from side quests or just main quests. These costumes play a big part of the game not just because its the games title, but you actually get different move sets aswell. The costumes I found made the final boss a 1 try victory for me. The game can be a bit easy if you get guides on where the costumes are located and its pieces.
There is another playable DLC you get automatically if you purchase this game on steam, called Grubbins on Ice. It's not extremely long, its about 1/3 of the games length. I did enjoy it though because it gave me three costumes, several battle stamps and a nice adventure. I would prefer playing this after the base game because everthing from your first save in Costume Quest, gets sent over into the DLC. It's pretty helpful. It is recommended to do that because enemies are about lvl 13 and your cap is lvl 10 (in the base game).

I am borderline between recommending this or not.  The concept of the game is great and unique.  You run into enemy blocks, and if you are successful, you add them to your ship along with their firepower.  The shooting is passive and totally dependent on the blocks you collect: if you collect a block that shoots one shot a second, your ship will now shoot one extra shot a second from that block.  You can then destroy blocks with your uncontrollable firepower (including the blocks you are trying to add to your ship).  When you die, you can instantly restart which is great, and the game can be really addicting.
Where it falls apart for me is the areas between boss fights.  You have about 90 seconds of various blocks coming into the screen and firing on you until you get to a boss fight.  I wish that could be cut down to 45 seconds instead to focus more on the boss fights.  It is very difficult, and your 60 block ship can fall apart in an instant if unlucky.  It does not help that the screen can be covered in bullets while the ship feels relatively slow.  However, the most enjoyable part of the game is fighting the bosses.  I just wish I could fight all the bosses in the colosseum (where you can time trial fight a boss) from the very beginning, but you cannot until you come across each boss individually in the game and beat it.  The bosses are tied to the difficulty setting, which means you cannot just grind away on easy to unlock them.  So the higher I get in difficulty, the less time I get to spend with the bosses, and it just burned me out.

There are great EA games, mediocre EA games, bad EA games and EA with plenty potential. I would rate Osiris in the last category, but it comes with a huge disclaimer. Osiris does a few things pretty well. but it's not so much the missing content missing, or the quality of the assets in te game, but mere the horribly bad design decision that are all over the place.
They can continue to add tons of content, polish graphics and sounds, balance difficulty and so on, but only with some drastic changes in it's core design it will become an interesting game.
Allow me to mention a few:
- each and every object you build consists of several parts. A habitat is a frame and it takes another 12 or more panels to finish it. That is a fun way of building alright and gives the player the feeling that there is plenty content. The problem though is that whatever you build gets a green outline in the HUD. The not so well designed HUD gets even more cluttered with all these annoying green outlines, damage indicators, name of the object etc. When you have a base, there will be > 100 of these object within your visual range and whatever is if you look at, you will get these changes on the screen, in the HUD etc. Very annoying. In fact they should only show these when you have your welding tool equipped.
- combat is plain bad. Someone who calls himself a game designer thought it would be great to  change your camera if you get hit by a monster / alien. So, whenever you get hit you have to adjust your camera and try to understand where you are, where the creature is that you are fighting. In the meantime you have to equip your sticky tape to repair your suit and if you are hit, you have to somehow heal yourself too. There is a big chance that once you get ready to fight again, you are hit once more and you can start over. On paper this is a nice idea maybe, adding realism and so. But it sucks big time and one of many exampes that adding realism is more often than not a bad choice.
- you have a droid. It is suppossed to do stuff. Like repair or defend or just follow you. But it will almost never do any of these, because it will get stuck no matter where you go or what you do or you ask it to do. It's a pain and it adds nothing but headaches.
- skill tree. A skill tree can be an interesting part of a game when it forces the player to make decisions. This skill tree is not interesting, not adding anything, not even balance to the game. It has poor design written all over it.
- inventory management is about 30% of all gameplay. You pick something up and you have a big chance that your are overburden. Even at 100,0% you are unable to run. Also the who UI/UX design of inventory management is not even Pre-Alpha. Each and every machine / cabinet / etc. has its own inventory. So you keep running around to see if you have any resources left in any of your inventories, which will add up to around 10 before you are even half way through what you can build.
There is a lot more to nag about, but I will stop here. I think this can still be a good game at some point. I am also pretty confident that it will have enough content. My biggest worry is that the design decisions that were made up to this point show a lack of skill by those who make these. Hire a decent and experienced game designer before it is too late and all this ppor choices will ruin your game forever. Then I will come back, enjoy your game and write something nice about it instead.
For all players: there is plenty more out there for you to enjoy. Don't buy this until they prove that they can do it.

The hand drawn artwork is lovely throughout.  It looks like a lot of time and love has been spent on all the backgrounds and characters.  The voice acting is generally of a high standard, and most importantly Nelly herself has great humour and charm with which she delivers her lines.
The puzzles are sometimes easy, sometimes tricky, and I haven't yet been stuck frustratingly on anything for too long.  Most importantly the game has oodles of humour, and the next laugh, chuckle or guffaw is never far away.

Overall, a pretty good game. I'll start with a few criticisms.
The first one is that the early segments are badly designed. The first time I participated in the sports festival, it was a fun event, but by the fifth time I was skipping through the text as fast as possible. Forcing the player to read through the exact same scenarios in the exact same order is a terrible idea, and I can see some people being turned off by the amount of repetitive scenes. (Plus, the three extra epilogues count as separate endings? Seriously?) This is exacerbated by the fact that the true ending is so well hidden that I've already seen a couple of people who seem to have missed it entirely, amidst all the reloading (for those curious, you need to start a new game after getting a certain number of endings).
The second flaw is more of a personal thing that plenty of people will probably disagree with: the quality of the writing is uneven. For every character that knocks the drama and/or comedy out of the park, there's another that is totally uninspired. There's also plenty of cliches; expect your fill of childhood promises and dying wishes.
That being said, there's enough high points to explain why this thing is a cult hit. There's some brilliantly written jokes, characters and plot twists, and that's all you really need to know. Make sure you get the BBL ending! Whether this version is worth double the original price is up to you to decide: what you get is great new art, Steam integration, a short and rather underwhelming extra ending, and font that isn't hideous.

But what this game really did was teach me that you can't judge a book (or a game) by its cover, that being open-minded and looking past your preconceptions is important, and that it's nice to try new things once in a while. You might be surprised by what you find.
If you think the very concept of this game isn't reason enough to give it a try, I'm not sure what to say. Come back and try again later?
This less-than-ten-bucks game that looked like nothing but a silly joke, with only one picture for every character, that used mostly free resources and stock images, managed to be so much more immersive and interesting than any other high-budget visual novel I've played.
The game does play like a parody of dating sims for at least half of the game, but even then, the characters are very fleshed out and well written, so if you're looking for something nice to break away from the generic high school girls with the same old no-plot dating experience, this is it.
If you're familiar with dating sims (or harem anime) you'll recognize the character types right away: you have the childhood friend, the teacher, the quiet one you're not sure how to approach, the ladies man, the spoiled one, and the list goes on. But there's a lot more to these characters than what you can see at first glance, and figuring out their stories and why's and how's is half the fun.
There are many funny moments, yes, oh so many. Hatoful Boyfriend fully embraces its weird concept, which makes it very enjoyable and fun to play. It's not just the birds - the player character is also a very funny character with quite a few gems in her dialogue.
But as you play you can easily notice there's so much more going on; there's always that hint of something deeper and darker on the back of every route. The game doesn't just take things for granted - most questions raised during the game will be answered. For example, why you're the only human in a school for birds. Yes, this is addressed in the game, and you might be quite surprised by the explanation.
The storytelling in this game is incredibly well done. It's not just what's expected of a visual novel, but a step above.
There's not much more I can say about it without getting into spoiler territory, so you'll just have to see for yourself.
TL;DR: There's something for everyone in this game. If you're not afraid of new experiences, give it a try - you may be surprised by how easy it is to get absorbed into this game's odd, comical atmosphere. Once you're into it, you may want to go all the way in. The routes are short enough that you'll find the time to play more of them. If you don't like it, well, at least you can say you tried - brag to your friends about how you didn't survive the pigeon dating sim!

Summary of Pros & Cons first, review later.
Pros:
1) Well-Designed Tier System/Research System
2) Amazing art style and theme.
3) Coherent UI with options for arrow keys & WASD (so many games lack WASD default options)
4) Excelent gameplay.
5) Still In Progress as a game.
Cons:
1) Unstable Income/Expenses Over Time
2) No Freebuild Option
3) Easiest Setting is still pretty difficult.
4) No tutorial - must learn as you play.
5) All but 1 map is locked until you defeat the first map.
So, on the Tier System. Most of the game buildings have multiple 'teirs' as it were. With the exception of a handful of beginner buildings (Sawmill, Tent, Fishing Hut, Barracks, the like) all buildings have different tiers. Some of them can be upgraded (Tent, Farm, Windmill, ex) while others are merely advanced buildings you need to unlock. The Tier Sytem this game uses is easily my favorite aspect of the game - it's balanced (mostly), straightforward, and both linear AND choose-your-own at the same time. The biggest flaw, however, is that High Tier buildings cost expotentially more to maintain while High Tier housing does not produce expotentially increased income. This makes it difficult to maintain a high level Colony over time due to the expenses of maintaining defenses and production facilities. In short, there is a dminishing returns as expansion increases, and this hurts the game overall by making it that much more difficult to survive the Zombies.
The Art Style is glorious, like, truly glorious. I wanted the game based on the appearance alone when I first saw it, and the game does NOT dissapoint. What is a bit sad is that there isn't a "chill" mode, so to speak. There is no mode without swarms of zombies, or where the goal is to reach a certain size rather than survive the swarms that arrive periodically to wreck everything. That said, it is a minor complaint.
The UI is very well designed as it currently is. The only fault is the lack of a tutorial, but thanks to the UI it's pretty easy to figure the game out on one's own. The Infotips are also helpful in that regard, though they could add a few details (like that "Advanced Mills" are not in fact advanced Lumber Mills, but rather the next tier of Windmill). Overall, can't complain about the UI, Gameplay, or Infotips.
What I can complain about is the overall difficulty. See, the only things that a player can change are the length of the game and the number of zombies that spawn with the initial map. The Swarms, which are steadily increasing numbers of zombies that charge at your colony Admistration Building, do not increase or decrease in overall strength regardless of what rating the game is on. The only thing that changes is the time between each Swarm - the longer the game lasts, the longer one has to rebuild between swarms. This makes the game decidedly difficult regardless of what difficulty setting it's played on... which in turn makes it harder to unlock the other 3 maps, which can only be unlocked by surviving the previous map at a certain level of difficulty.
All things said and done, however, this game is effectively complete upon Early Access, so I can only hope that it's going to go great places given the time to be finished. I'm fairly certain there's a campaign coming which will hopefully have a tutorial built into it or added to the game. Hopefully they'll fix the income/expenses disbalance as well. But with an Early Access game, we can indeed hope :D
Giving this is 8/10: Fun, Replayable, Great Art, Good Tier System, just needs work on difficulty settings and minor balancing.

Overall, an enjoyable little game with a decent amount of flaws. Definitely a Diamond in the Rough.
The concept in and of itself is very enjoyable and I feel that people who enjoy base builders like Age of Empires and the like will enjoy this game. The graphics are stylistic and simple, but it works for this games  cartoonish, steampunk aesthetic.
An issue for some though is the difficulty. This game is very difficult. I have been playing for about 12 hours as I am writing this review and I have yet to survive the first map. I have started five games, got killed off by the horde in three of them after 100 turns and, unfortunately, my last two playthroughs ended up with the game crashing and corrupting my saves. This is a big issue as the other maps are locked off unless you complete the preceding map. This is a questionable design choice as you must beat the map at a certain difficulty level.
As the title of the game suggests, "They are Billions", it's very literal. You will fight off many waves of thousands upon hundreds of thousands of zombies. However, this game, in its focus on the quantity, seemed to forget about the quality of the content.
- Lack of variety in both enemy type and controllable units
--Enemy units consist of low health and damage fodder units (of which there are many variations), a Harpy (Fast unit that can jump over defenses), a Venom (Ranged Spitter), and finally Chubby (Fat, hard hitting, bullet sponge).
--Controllable Units consist of the Ranger (Fast scout wielding a Silent Bow), The Soldier (Armored frontline infantry), and the Sniper (He snipes at long range). As you research technology, if you survive long enough you will eventually be able to recruit another three units who are based on the Oil resource, Lucifer (Big Daddy from Bioshock who wields a flamethrower), Thanatos (Muscle man with rocket launcher), and the Titan (Pompous dude piloting a badass zombie killing machine).
-- Defenses are much worse in terms of variety. You get wood towers, walls, and gates which upgrade to stone towers, walls, and gates. You would think that there would be a third tier, relating to the different tiers of resources you acquire, (Wood, Stone, Iron, Oil). There is not though. Concrete or Iron walls would be nice. There are also three different towers you can build, a ballista tower, a tesla shock tower, and a tower with a giant minigun on it.  In addition to that there is one additional fortification wooden stakes which upgrade to metal barbed wire.
Of all these units, and the largest issue I ran into, was that only the Thanatos had access to an Area of Effect weapon. You get no bombs, no rockets, and no mines, other than what a roided up dude can shoot every few seconds. This is an even greater insult when The Titan unit only has a range which is one unit shorter than the Thanatos.
Another qualm I had was the poor pathfinding as well as the lack of creating formations for larger groups of units. If you build your base relatively tight and close together, odds are that your units will get stuck along corners especially larger units like the Titan. Hell, they even got stuck along cliff sides and trees when there was ample room to manuever.
The lack of formations also impacts the  pathfinding as units often blob up worse than the damn zombie hordes they are trying to fight. Units act as individuals, which is good toward the beginning, but when dealing with late game hordes this can severely hinder players as units will haphazardly split up in forks in the colony and landscape, or place your long range snipers in the front of your army with your short range flamethrower troops in the rear.
As it is I do enjoy this game, but I hope that the developers continue to add new features and create more variation in the unit types and defenses, as well as fixing its obvious flaws.
For now I will be giving this game a thumbs up, but I urge you not to buy it yet. I would say wait a month or two and read the inevitable updates for this game and if they do indeed listen to player feedback and don't just drop the game like a child at the orphanage, then do buy it. It is well worth the price in that case.

This game does a lot of things well and a few things not so well.
- I love the sheer idea of this game. A group of kids must use their costumes that ACTUALLY TRANSFORM THE WEARERS to fight monsters, save a sibling, and collect tons of candy along the way. It sounds like all of my childhood halloween fantasies at once.
- Less predicatable than one might image. It has just enough twists to keep it interesting, but manages to keep it simple enough for a younger person to enjoy it.
- Likeable child characters are comparable to black republicans nowadays: maybe there's one or two here and there, but overall they're pretty rare. The children in this game are highly likeable and funny, which is a metaphorical breath of fresh air.
- My inner 10 year old got a real kick out of this game. The jokes are silly and childish, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't laugh quite a bit during my playthrough. I wish more games could imbue such a good sense of humour into their games.
- It wasn't exactly a synphonic masterpiece, but it does add to the immersion. My only qualm is that the battle music can get a bit repettitive.
- Again, it wasn't mind blowing or pioneering or anything like that. Each area is pretty different, which does well to break up any monotony. Some environmental objects (specifically, ramps) can feel really clunky, but all-in-all it doesn't affect the enjoyment of the game.
- I believe that the Devs wanted to create a simple RPG that was less about combat and leveling up and more about the story. They absolutely succeeded, so props to them. I do wish that there would have been a slightly more in-depth character upgrade system, but that's just me.
- Like I said above, the game isn't really combat or skill focused. The combat is simple and easy to learn, which is good. The problem with simple combat is that it can get very, very repetitive. I was actually somewhat sad when the thought "ugh, do I really have to fight these guys?" came to mind, because to me it meant that the combat had gotten boring. It's worth noting that I was admittedly about 3/4 of the way through before that happened.
- My last minor complaint is the lighting in the game. For the majority of the game, the Devs did a great job of keeping the overall lighting pretty low, but bright enough to see where you were going and to find the things you needed to find. However, the
are just too dark. There is a brightness option in the menu, but amping up the brightness seems almost to be cheating, since part of the game's charm is the comic-spookiness of low lighting. That's really my only complaint on the world design.

Welcome to Dunwall, a industrial city where technology and otherworldly force coexist. Takes places between 1800s until early 1900s, The city was stricken with a plague spread by rats (known as Black Death pandemic) which is killing the poor and isolating the rich. The infected, known as "weepers", cry blood and can become violent. The government uses the plague as an excuse to take or purge citizens as they wish while the city was ruled by oppressive regime that come to power following the assassination of the Empress and the kidnapping of her daughter.
You will play as Corvo Attano, the former bodyguard to Dunwall's Empress Jessamine Kaldwin. Was farmed for for the Empress' murder and kidnapping, Corvo was due to be executed. In his cell, a letter from Empire Loyalists is smuggled to Corvo, and he is given the means to escape. After escaping, Samuel ferries Corvo to the Hound Pits pub to meet the Loyalists, led by Admiral Havelock.
While resting at the pub, Corvo is taken to a dream world where he meets the Outsider, who brands Corvo with his mark. The Outsider offers to help Corvo in his quest. Described as a mixture of God and the Devil, The Outsider imprints his mark on Corvo, imbuing him with magical abilities, and provides him with a mechanically altered human heart that tells Corvo secrets.

Low Chaos otherwise, keep your hand clean as possible ( might be difficult on some mission, but worth it ) avoid any guards and use nonlethal approach to eliminate your key targets.

Imagine you are but a pixel, and it is through combining forces with other like-minded pixels that you will be able to take on anything that stands in your way. Well that's basically what Pixel Galaxy is with bright colors, a strong soundtrack, and lots of challenging fun.
You see in this pixelated space world, you start off as a single pixel, and if you get hit, well that single pixel gets hit, its game over, lights out, please try again. Here's the interesting thing though, its not all about dodging all that could destroy that single pixel. You see if you time it right the other pixels that might have appeared as foes can become part of you.
That's right, as you play through the levels you will have the chance to touch pixels that are moving, or perhaps are stationary on the screen, and in this action you can add them to you. Doing this will, hopefully, build a barrier of expendable pixels between damage and your starting, single pixel.
You will be faced with varying levels of difficulty, and of course which each higher difficulty new things will open up for you to play against. New bosses will test your skill, and you will definitely need to be fast at dodging while hopefully holding on to pixels that can shoot so that you can return fire.
I highly recommend that you play this game with a gamepad, there's something about controlling the pixel, or the collection of pixels with the left analog that just feels so natural. There's also the ability to rotate with the triggers, something that you are going to want to master so that you can evenly disperse your collection of pixels, be able to aim a bit better, and of course protect the starting pixel from damage.
This is the type of game that I never had an issue with coming back and playing some more. There's always that chance that I will man up and try to take on the next level of difficulty, and of course after getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked I'll jump into a lower difficulty, kick some♥♥♥♥♥ and once again feel really good about myself.
This is a challenging game that has quite a few layers to it, and unique experiences each time as how the pixels come out each time are random, which I have to say I both love and hate. I love because that means no two games are alike, but I hate because I can't learn through repetition to find the best solution. In the end though I think I'd much rather have the unique gameplay than the repetition which I could possibly burn out on.
If you are looking for something a little different, spacey, and pretty easy to pick up, you're going to want to add this game to your collection, there's no question that this should be a game that everyone should take for a spin. This game gets a 9.2 out of 10.

Great MMO if you're looking for something a little different from the usual rhetoric out there.
Positives:
Customisation of classes - With four overarching class types to choose from, each class has several sub-domains that a player can choose, either utilising premade setups, or by creating their own out of three.
Customisation of roles - Tank, Damage, Healer and Support roles are all available to any of the four main classes, depending on the arrangement of subdomains, providing more creativity and player customisation to individual play styles.
World Events - They're per zone, daily and fun. They can also be challenging and often attract up to 25+ players into one area. Additionally, public grouping is an available (and useful) option.
It's isn't pay to win! Yaaay! - Additionally, mounts and pets are lootable, events offer limited items and hard work will pay off if you're looking to purchase real currency items, given the game's tradeable REX.
And there's more, but I don't really have time to get more detailed right now.
Negatives:
I would love to see more players and more development. Other than that, none really come to mind as of yet.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. I'm an old WoW/EQ player and have had plenty of experience with other MMOs offered, both F2P and P2P.

I’ve
, Kickstarted the sequel, and was rather looking forward to this. Let’s break down my impressions, from least important to the most:
Graphics: I kinda miss the original hand-drawn look. It had a unique charm to it that the smoother and less unique 3d models lack.
Voicework: Quite good all around. Except from some British TV guy – apparently everyone were so excited to have him on that they forgot to check whether his voice fits the character.
Controls: Remarkably bad, by adventure game standards. Everything feels a bit sluggish and slow to react to commands. Whenever you try to click two items in quick succession (quick = within a second or two) the game is sure to get confused and randomly misapply your clicks.
Puzzle quality: Generally decent – moderately challenging at times, but logical and sensible. You never have to resort to random item combinations, your inventory is emptied of formerly useful items in regular intervals, and the big puzzle sets require just the right amount of thought. I got stuck on two separate occasions – one is a bit of accidental misinformation the developer promised to remove, while the other was a random piece of the puzzle stuck in a cluttered screen where it had no reason to be.
HOWEVER. There are mini-games scattered at regular intervals, and they are terrible at conveying their control schemes and victory conditions.
Writing quality: Maintains the quirky charm of the original, has a few laugh out loud moments every so often (helped by the voice work and decent comic timing). However, every so often you’ll get a random meme shoved in, not at all meshing with the overall writing style. The game has an “arrow to the knee” joke. In 2016(!)
Also, I think the ending and the airship section were severely cut during the production stage, and it SHOWS. Just a bit of a mess from the writing perspective.
Overall: 7/10. Cute and charming, if not a particularly innovative. It’s probably a bit too late to actually fix the ending into something coherent, but improving the controls, mini-game instructions and dumping the memes would bump the rating up to 8/10.

First things first, I should mention that one of my friends was involved in the production of this game -- and voices a pompous sea bird -- and I've spent an afternoon playing
with both the creator of the game and Nelly Cootalot herself, or at least her inspiration and voice actor.
is a comedic point and click adventure game about pirates. If you are now thinking "Gosh, that's a bit like deciding to be a sprinter and challenging Usain Bolt to a race your first time out" then that's a bit weird that we both thought of that, but you'd be correct. The shadow of
looms large over this game -- now I'm imagining a Lovecraft pastiche;
-- but not only does the script acknowledge the influence, Nelly Cootalot is strong enough to stand up to and apart from its illustrious predecessor.
The writing for the most part is strong, and the characters' personalties come across well, helped in no small part by good voice acting throughout. Nelly herself is a charming protagonist; everyone seems to like her, and her cheerful approach to adventure is infectious. The main villains are a bit sketchy, and not in the appropriate sense of the word; I think they return from the original game in the series, but as I've not played that, their motivations and personalities seem a bit vague in this instalment. A new villain introduced in the middle section of the game comes across far better, although again his motivations and connection to the main plot are somewhat unclear. Still, it's Nelly and her friends who are most important and they are well-written and acted; aside from Nelly herself, I was most impressed by her sidekick Sebastian, voiced by Tom "
" Baker. To be honest, I was expecting someone of Sir Tom's prestige to sleepwalk through his role but he brings a lot of personality to Sebastian, even though he has one of those voices that means you can never quite forget that there's an actor behind the character.
The game is funny, and there's a varied approach to the jokes, with plenty of references to films and games, a bit of witty wordplay, a dash of satire here and there, and at least one bit of smutty innuendo, although that last one doesn't land as well as it could have due to some clumsy back-pedalling. Some comments and reviews have claimed that the game is for children -- perhaps because of the art style -- but the latter joke suggests not, and some of the references are going to go right over the heads of most kids, unless they are showing Jack Nicholson films in primary schools these days.
The game looks good too. The trailers did look a bit ropey, with a flat animation style reminiscent of Flash or a cheap CBeebies programme, but the game itself looks much better. The character models look to be cel-shaded and that gives them a bit more weight, and they are for the most part well-animated; it is a bit of a shame that they don't tend to do anything when Nelly isn't interacting with them, but one has to remember that this isn't a multi-million pound game with a hundred-strong creative team behind it. That said, it's a pleasant surprise when you spot a character making a small movement or gesture that must have added time to the production schedule and is irrelevant to wider game, but helps to bring the character to life. It shows a dedication and craftsmanship that you don't often see in the aforementioned larger productions.
I did encounter a couple of graphical glitches; during one part of the Guttering Howls section Nelly walks in front of and through something she should be behind, and in the penultimate chapter the inventory panel goes a bit wonky, but is still usable. I also had a bit of trouble with the game's interface being slow to register what was under the pointer, although the mechanics worked as expected, so it wasn't a major issue. I played the game on Linux Mint 17.3 and I don't know if these glitches are in every port.
Heh, "port". Like sailors. Heh.
's puzzles are varied and often require different approaches and techniques to solve; even when they are of the give-item-A-to-person-B sort, they are at least presented in novel ways so the game never gets dull. In terms of difficulty, the puzzles are if not simple, then logical, so you are never hunting for rogue pixels or throwing every item at every character, hoping for the best.
That said if there is a flaw in
-- and to be fair, it is the only thing I would consider a proper flaw -- it's the wider game and story logic surrounding the puzzles. On a few occasions I worked out the solution to a problem, and had all the correct items in my inventory ready to go, but I couldn't apply said solution because I hadn't gone to talk to someone -- often in another location -- who was supposed to give me the idea I'd already had. This led to frustration and -- in one case near the end of the game -- a suspicion that there was a game-breaking bug. On the plus side, Sebastian is able to give hints about what to do next, and in at least one case this helped resolve the impasse, although in the latter instance I did end up roaming around clicking on everything and everyone until I spoke to the right person.
Creator Alasdair Beckett-King is a jolly nice fellow -- and is not bad at
-- but it turns out he's quite good at making computer games too. I had great fun playing
and although it is short -- it can be completed in about five hours or so, although getting the Steam achievements will take longer -- I think it is worth the £12 I paid for it. There are rough edges, and places where I feel Alasdair and his team could have done a tiny bit more, but what's here is good, and I hope the game is enough of a success that we see more from him.
If you like point and click adventure games, give this a try because you'll probably ike it. If you don't, give it a try anyway, as it's charming and funny and may change your mind.

This is a FANTASTIC looking game. The graphics are amazing, it's got a great weather system, creatures are appropriately menacing and scary looking. However, its still in Early Access, so it needs a little balancing and some additional content. Positional audio isn't there at all; by the time you hear a monster, its on top of you, and trying to track its position relative to you via sound is pointless. The inventory system is still a bit rough; items don't auto stack in boxes, and you'll have to sort things in containers manually to get the stacks right and free up space. There's not a lot of variety in weapons just yet, no armor to speak of, and getting a ground vehicle takes a long time, you'll do a lot of running up until then.
All that said, its a gorgeous game that looks like it has a lot of potential and is still fun to play despite some rough edges. Hopefully the dev team will be pretty active and update it regularly. If you at all enjoy sci-fi survival games, I'd recommend picking this up while its still inexpensive and in Early Access.

This game gets a load of stick because its different from normal xcom. But I ask you.... Whats wrong with being different?

Do not play this game in expectation of a turn based strategy game, do not even hope for a deep tactical gameplay. Instead go for it with a clear mind and let game suprise you with a whole new turn on xcom formula. My experience with Bureau is quite positive. It is  a very decent squad based cover shooter with a light tactical option and with a bit of a rpg element. Visualy I consider this game quite impressive with a great attention to detail. Nice vistas and detailed level design is a candy for eyes. Story is set in mid 60s and its add up to great atmosphere based on a conspirational theories about UFOs. The story is well written, altough with a few plot holes, but still manages you to keep on going. The XCOM legacy is nicely integrated troughout the game. The gameplay divided along missions is not that varied, but you will have sense of progress thanks to a light RPG elements probably inspired by Mass Effect trilogy, where you battle experience are transformed into character levels upon each  of the level progress you can choose from an ability tree. This goes also for you teammates, where their ability tree is defined by their class. The variablity here is in a option to combine classes and their abilities which can end up in a quite satisfying results on battlefield. So if you are looking for a solid cover based shooter with a good tactical and RPG element with a solid story backed up by a solid cast look no further and give Bureau a chance. I was nicely suprised by its outcome.

If like me you think wow, that looks cool, i bet i would have lots of fun, think again.
I know this is an EA though and as such a lot can change, and boy does it need too.
I will say though the graphics, music, and UI etc are pretty good, not many bugs, which for an EA is surprising, it's just the mechanics which are the deal breaker.
This is why i have to give it a negative at this point in time, even though i wish i didnt as the concept could be great if only done right, which so far its not.
There are so many issues with this game i don't know where to start.
But if you fancy after several hours your left feeling you wasted your time with little enjoyment and mainly frustration, then hell, buy it now !
The survival mode (only thing available atm) is just dreadful, and the main reason for this is the ridiculous random generation, why they didnt include hand made maps, easpecially for the challenges is completely beyond me, don't get me wrong, having random gen is cool, but the devs so far have done a terrible job of making the game actually balanced and playable because of this.
Even on the easy settings the challenge is a joke, some problems you will face are listed below
being spawned next to zombie villages,
Having no materials to gather close by,
Being wiped out before having a chance to build more than a few buildings
Having no scenery close by to help use as protection,
Having no room to build, meaning having to wait for resources to increase naturally as you try span power into space and near resouces that can be used, which yet again so far i have found is impossible to then protect before getting wiped out.
This is why i cannot and will not recommend this game in its current state.
I have lost count of the times before getting more than a few houses and buildings etc your wiped out 99% of the time
Your left with bad gen after bad gen which you will stand no chance what so ever of surviving.
Yes you can quit once had a scout around, but how many hours do you want to waste doing this before finding a gen that you may stand a chance of lasting a while and actualy getting to build and use most of whats included ?
Not to mention, there's only a slim chance that the hordes wont just wipe you out anyway.
After over 13 hours the highest round i have managed was 108, and this was taking it very careful, with a half decent gen, not letting the soldier shoot, doubling, tripling defences and walls and other tactics to try help.
This is not what i expected on easy, and having played a lot of C&C style of games for many years on the hardest settings, this is harder than all of them, and this is on the easy setting? omg!
A lot of issues could be solved quite easily to give you at least a fighting chance of getting established,
higher resouce limit and more resources to build with at the start,
better gen (in dying need of more lines of code stopping certain things happening, some of which are mentioned above)
Hand made maps for the challenges, with the option to use random gen if you so wish.
Nerfing zombies for easier setting, although i expect this would need doing on the higher settings too.
Also could do with a speed selection feature like most others of this type have, the game can feel a little boring at times.
I could go on, but i'm sure if you read other comments from non fanboys, you will get the picture.
DONT FORGET TO CHECK BACK THOUGH, this could all change in time as its EA at the moment.
I'm hoping the devs will address these and more problems, and then the game could become as epic as we all first thought it would be.
Just can't get into it.

Hi all, nukes here.
I personally loved every bit of Dishonored.
Blinking
in and out, stopping time and silently slitting a key targets throat and then vanishing, before the guards know what happened, well after a bit of practice I sure as hell set off alarms.
Anyway... You play first person as a supernatural assassin named Corvo, set in a steam punk world that runs on whale oil and with a city that is stricken with by plague.
Out for revenge the story captured me from the get go. Keeping me immersed the whole way through. The many different choices that the game presents you, giving this game an untold value. This is not to mention the abilities you acquire as my friend said.
You are able to play this game however you feel, this could be non killing, stealthily or making lots of noise killing everyone you see, or a large mixture of both.
This is entirely up to you, this being said each mission can be played and completed in a variety of ways.
I like to play games for the difficulty and challenge this game is just that on its hardest mode I felt challenge but not near breaking point.
With the hardest difficulty it feels more realistic than normal, in combat if you make a mistake it can kill you quite quickly.
This game supports both keyboard & mouse and controller, I preferred keyboard and mouse, hence I am a PC gamer.
I found the steam achievements challenging but not overly and enjoyed seeing them pop up.
The story is immersive and I felt it kept me wanting to finish the game, as I wanted to find out what happened.
With all the abilities and weapons, the combat system keeps you on your toes. That next guard may spot you, before your blade kills him, could even be the one that kills you.
Melee combat in this game is difficult to get the hang of, once mastered it is incredibly fun although timing can be a pain to get use to.
Stopping time to sever someone's head, that you can then pick up to throw at the next unfortunate victim is just another brilliant creative way to alert the guards.
Dishonored gives you the choice of different unique powers most of them are active with a some passive.
You are also give the chance to collect bone charms that are interchangeable supernatural perks.
Choose wisely as you can't have everything.
The music done by Daniel Licht is perfect for the game, designed to represent the 19th century London and the credits song at the end is a brilliant song. Don't spoil it for yourself, complete the game.
Dishonored was originally to be set in feudal Japan, later switching to a late 19th century London with futuristic characteristics.
I found the art styles great but would welcome a HD remaster of the game.
The cut scenes stay true to the immersion but not just the cut scenes sitting back and listening to some of the conversation between guards is just as good.
Wanted posters appear for Corvo's capture all around Dunwall through the game, if you manage to remain unnoticed throughout. The wanted posters  will only depict an unknown assailant or a masked felon.
The game offers manual saving and auto saving features which are extremely useful.
I recommend getting the full edition with all downloadable content as it offers a nice expansions and the trails of Dunwall which will test and challenge your skills.
I encountered no game breaking bugs on any my playthroughs.
Dishonored is truly all round fantastic game, which a lot of effort has gone into to producing such a unique universe. If you get the chance, I hope you will enjoy it as much as I did.
I look forward to Dishonored 2, hoping to enjoy it as much as I did this.
One last piece of advice try your first run as stealthy low chaos. Cause the second playthrough you can unleash the tides chaos from within, but up to you.
Whatever path you choose, enjoy and hope I helped.

The cake was a lie, but the hype around this game wasn't.
I'd never played this game before, so I'm untainted by nostalgia. Portal has quite the reputation as a "must-play" video game, and I wondered if it lived up to expectations and if it was still relevant today.
Frankly, the answer is yes.
Portal is an excellently designed game and is probably the best puzzle game I've played since Ocarina of Time. The levels are easy enough as to not be frustrating and still challenging enough to give the player a sense of satisfaction. They become more complex as the game goes on, but the progression feels very natural.
Story-wise, Portal is also very good. The atmosphere is always framed well, going from whimsical to foreboding in stride while maintaining a great sense of humor. The story and gameplay blended together nicely and complemented each other well. I appreciate the lack of distracting cut-scenes.
I blasted through the game in about 3 hours, and I enjoyed every minute. If you are looking for an interesting and unique game to pass the time, I highly recommend it. It's one of those "low-risk, high-reward" sort of games. It really had a bigger impact on me than expected.
One thing's for sure: that ending credits song is going to be with me for a while.

Pixel Galaxy is a new "space" shooter from indie developer Serenity Forge. At its core the game is a "bullet hell" shooter where you start out as a single pixel. From there more pixels race on to the screen, some of them shooting (lots of) bullets at you. If you can dodge the plethora of bullets and run into the pixel firing at you then that pixel is added to you. The more pixels you get the bigger you are. These new pixels may even fire bullets to take out other pixels and add protection for you, the core pixel. But this also means you are less nimble and will get hit by more bullets. Keep this up and take out one of the numerous bosses and you may unlock the next difficulty level. Since I suck I have only unlocked easiest and easier. I still have easy, normal, normaler and normalest to unlock along with boss rush where you are bombarded with the bosses you have seen. Finally, if you have a someone close by, there is local co-op for two pixels versus the world.
There are two main things that I enjoy about this game. One, it is short. I don't always have a lot of time to play my games, so something that I can play is less then 5 minutes is welcome. Although I don't think I have ever actually played a round that lasted even that long. Second is, even on the same difficulty you never play the same exact level twice. The enemy abilities change as do their attack patterns. It makes for an entertaining game. If you enjoyed games likes Galaga then this would be right up your alley.

In Hatoful Boyfriend, you play as Hiyoko Tosaka (or whatever you choose to name her), the only human in a school of pigeons. You can even get yourself a birdy boyfriend! There's Ryouta the childhood friend, Sakuya the fancypants, Yuuya the ladies man, and many more amazing avians. It plays out like a regular otome/visual novel does, read the text and make some choices. I bet you're thinking "omg so random, dating pigeons lol", and that's a natural response. But if you were to look up the definition of "don't judge a book by its cover", I'm pretty sure there would be a picture of Hatoful Boyfriend there.
You see, the pigeon dating sim premise is just a cover for the real story. After you unlock certain endings with different birds, you can start a new game and the true story will reveal itself, aka the Hurtful Boyfriend (or Bad Boys Love) route. In BBL you will learn why Hiyoko is the only human at the pigeon school, why the pigeons can talk, why she needs to form a bond with the birds, and much more. I can only say so much without spoiling it, but be prepared for a mental meltdown. It is filled with drama, tragedy and unsettling content. After seeing certain endings in the dating sim part, you'll probably be thinking "well, I've already seen some disturbing stuff... This will be a piece of cake". LOL NOPE. The dating sim endings are nothing compared to the true BBL route.
To put it simply, this game is like one of those sweet & sour candies; it looks and tastes sweet on the outside, but once you delve deeper in you'll reel back in shock and wonder wtf happened to the sugary outer shell.
Brilliant, quirky fun. Much weirder than it seems, unlikely as that sounds. I'd recommend it to everyone.

I can not explain why because of spoilers really, but i did not expect so much out of something like this.  Hatoful boyfriend is something spectacular, and much more than a pigeon dating sim, play it if you dont believe me, i guarantee you will not be dissapointed.

Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is great fun. The animation and art are wonderful and the voice acting was some of truly best I've ever heard. Having backed its Kickstarter ages ago, I was very well pleased with the money spent and I would have no qualms about backing them again.
It's only drawback for me is that it's rather short. I finished it in about 5.5 hours, and that's looking at every single thing.
I would certainly recommend it, though. It's puzzles are well plotted and are much more logical than a lot of adventure games of old, but on the easy side for anyone who's played many adventure games. I've been playing them for over 20 years and had very little trouble with any of them.
There were a couple of bugs that I noticed. The cursor doesn't always change once you take it off of an item and hover over a different one (for example, you look at Crow's Nest and then Roof, but the cursor will still say Crow's Nest, even though it gives you information on Roof if you click on it). The other bug is when Nelly is supposed to be walking up a hill behind a building. It looks as though she's walking up the front of the building instead.
The only other thing I would say is that if you want to have a go at getting all of the achievements, they aren't all working yet. The final one (the Timewaster, the one for having achieved all the others) doesn't show up, despite having all the other 19. I had enough pleasure in playing the game, though, that I will go back and play it again once that's fixed.
Beautiful artwork and puzzles are just the right side of difficultly. Even my girlfriend who doesn't like video games was hooked, which says it all.

Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is a fairly straightforward game that does not make you stop and think too long about each puzzle or force you to combine items aimlessly to figure out what to do next. Your goals are simple, and the way to accomplish them is often hinted at with just an ounce of subtlety by dialogue or object descriptions. The first minigame was the only one I didn't really grasp, and I still made it on my first try with a lucky guess. The others could have used some explanation at least for using their interfaces like Daedalic did for the Deponia series, but trial and error doesn't punish you for failure, so you can just figure it out on your own.
The main selling point of the game would be its humor, which had me not only smile at the numerous puns but genuinely laugh out loud at some of the main character's quips. Nelly herself is another high point of the game with her endearing mix of lawlessness and cluelessness. Her remarks make you want to look at every object twice to make sure you hear all the clever little things she has to say about them.
Overall the game is a bit on the short side (a little over 5 hours for me), but a fun and relaxing interactive adventure throughout. Likely an excellent choice to introduce your kids to the genre!

Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is the follow-up to the popular 2007 freeware adventure,
, which won five AGS Awards and was nominated for seven more. In this game, we're introduced to our heroine Nelly Cootalot in a tutorial set aboard the mailship Undeliverable. Here you'll learn how to interact with other characters, to examine, pick up and use items, and how to combine them in your inventory. This is also where you learn of the villanous Baron Widebeard's evil plans, which involves a fleet of hypnotised birds.
As a bird-lover and defender of adorable creatures, Nelly wants none of that, and sets off in pursuit of Widebeard to his last known location. In order to progress from there, you must figure out the Baron's next destination by correctly applying information from a log book to a wall chart of ship departures—a puzzle that is one of my favorites in the game. You also have to gain permission to leave the docks by helping the miserable Admiral Woebegone by solving a classic "three trials" style branching puzzle.
Your next leg of the journey takes you to the main area of the game, which is a large area of three connected islands. Among other things, it has two main streets, several stores, food and drink establishments and a few public service buildings. In short, most of what you'd expect of an actual town, and it reminds me of memorable areas of the classics, such as Rubacava and the towns of the Tri-Island Area. Luckily, you can double-click on exits to teleport, and there's also a map you can use for fast-travel.
This is also the most diverse area in the puzzle department, and it is where you'll spend most of your time with the game. A puzzle revolving around a pirate-ified version of the classic board game Operation offered the biggest challenge to me, but since there are several other puzzles to tackle, I never felt completely stuck. If you do though, you can always get your bird companion Sebastian to give you a recap of your current objectives, without running the risk of spoiling anything.
A location placed inside the subconsious of a shaman monkey is also worth mentioning, but unfortunately it was all over rather quickly. There's also one large Viking inspired area left after that, but I don't want to spoil more than I already have.
The game features high-quality voice acting from a large cast of talented British actors, including Tom Baker of
and
. It is also of the funnier games I have played, which should come as no surprise if you played the previous game or witnessed the Kickstarter pitch video or any of the YouTube announcements leading up to the release.
As a Kickstarter backer, I have participated in the beta since January, and I've been impressed by the developers, who have been very responsive in fixing all of the tricky Linux issues that cropped during the beta, and made me feel like a first-class customer. They have also been exceptionally friendly througout what must have been a long and stressful crunch.
My first playthrough of the beta took me 5–6 hours, according to my notes, but I've seen estimates of much longer play times, and it's of course highly dependent on your previous experience with the genre. A few of the puzzles felt a bit underwhelming, including a certain barrel puzzle and the finale. Other than that though, the game feels solid throughout, and I think it's a good all-rounder that will appeal to most players.

Well, if some day someone asks me what is the best RTS videogame addon that I know, perhaps I will mention Chaos rising. Devs managed to keep the strong sides of actual game, yet also managed to fix majority of old issues that original game used to have. So by purchasing this game you'll have story continuation with same old characters from Warhammer 40k DoW 2 plus some new ones. You'll also have way more maps and tilesets to play on. Co-op mode still works and it's still awesome! Secondary missions now actually make sense, since they affect final ending of the game. Secondary objectives in missions are also important, since they give you various bonuses.
And yeah, just in case you don't know anything about this game:
Warhammer DoW 2 - Chaos rising is a story continuation of original Warhammer 40000 DoW 2, where you play as elite imperial marines, fighting with enemies of mankind and saving the galaxy from various evils. In previous game you were fighting hordes of tyranids. Their "strenght" was constant evolution and adaptation, yet they were mindless horde of creatures, without single personality. Just weird-shaped animals pack. Well, more or less...
This time, however, you have WAY more serious enemy. And this enemy is Chaos Marines. To put it in simple words - demons from outer space. Now, I know it sounds awkward. Demons in space?! Wut did devs smoke?!?!? but as you play the game, you'll most likely find that idea to be a genius one. Anyhow, I'm not gonna spoiler you any info about who these demons actually are, or why did they even come to this world, instead I'll tell you their main strenght (and that is important!). So yeah, their main strenght is corruption. Just like any other demons in various stories, these bad guys spoil your soldiers' souls, by bringing heretic thoughts at them, making them 'dirty'. Every primary mission you complete, adds small corruption level to deployed soldiers. In order to clear them from corruption (and get some extra bonuses) you need to complete secondary missions. And honestly, this is simply genius idea! Whole campaign is based around that corruption. Either you corrupt your soldiers and get hugea$$ bonuses and new skills, or you remain pure for as long as you can. On high game difficulties it actually is a good dilemma, since game keeps somewhat same dificulty level as its predcessor.
Of course, not everything is so great. First of all they still have same old issue where you control few units, who clear whole map, making you feel somewhat miserable, rather than strong. Maybe it wouldn't be a huge issue, if during one mission you hadn't had to fight your fellow brothers. I mean I used to think marines are outnumbered and stuff, but during this one mission I saw full potential of Space Marines army. APC's tanks, artillery, hundreds of infantry units... Yet YOU still control four squads. Yeah sure, you fight with another high ranked commander, which has lots of power, but hey, was it so difficult for YOUR commander to leave at least 4-5 TANKS at your service? I personally consider that as a story flaw. Because seriously, wiping out hundreds of tanks using only infantry is fun at start, but by the end of the game you just start thinking how wrong it is. Even for such famous warriors like your heroes.
Another issue with campaign is... ironically, some new weapons. Devs rushed for bigger variety of weapons, thus, trying to give you more tactical choices, but some weapons are just way too overpowered. Me & friend managed to complete final boss with next to no problem because he had some stun gun. It's somewhat cool, but shouldn't final boss be of a more challenge?
The last issue for me is, ironically, part of the campaign plot. Did you play Warhammer 40k DoW 1? The very first one from early '00s, where you play as Gabriel Angelos? Well, if you did, you'll recognize that story, because it just borrows so many things from original DoW so that even makes me confused.

How to Survive 2 is a game where you fend off zombies while looking for supplies
In the game's current state I can not recommend it. It is far from being a bad game, it just currently lacks any depth, and needs polishing.
You start off in a hub area, where you can select your next mission by talking to a character. After doing that, you will be transported to another small area where you are given a task. This is where the problems start with the game. Each mission feels the same. You walk around picking up random scattered items, or walk somewhere and complete the mission in 5-10 minutes. They feel like cheap fetch quests, and offer little variety.
This wouldn't be too bad if the gameplay was fun, but it gets repetitive. The combat consists of mashing the same button over and over again. It doesn't feel satisfying. You can also hold the attack button to do a charged attack, or sprint and then attack a zombie but all of these don't really add much. Using a ranged weapon like a bow is a bit different. You aim the weapon at a zombie and a circle will appear on their head. A line goes back and forth which requires that you press the button at the right time for what I'm assuming is more damage. I never really noticed a difference since it seemed to do the same amount of damage whether I got the timing right or not. Perhaps it's because I played on an easier difficulty.
Before starting a mission you can increase the difficulty which will also allow you to reap a higher xp reward.
The inventory/crafting/XP system has a lot of problems. First off, you can't create your character. You hit a randomize button and keep doing it until you like the look of your character. The crafting system looks ugly, although it works. My main gripe comes with the leveling up system. If you want to get a new skill, for example, do more damage, then you'll see a 500xp price tag on it. You spend the xp, and still won't level up that skill. That's because you need to level it up in 4 different chunks before actually getting the upgrade. Why? Why not just ask for 2000xp and level up the entire thing at once. It's not a big deal, but adds clutter the leveling system doesn't need. To add to that, in order to be able to upgrade your skill, you need to first upgrade your character, and in order to upgrade your character you need to upgrade your camp. It's a needlessly complicated system.
I personally dislike the PC controls. You can't rebind them, so I was forced to use controller controls as they felt a bit better. Even if you use PC controls, the inventory system will show xbox controls and require that you press "R1" to navigate, or the yellow "Y" button. Even if you use a controller, you'll be forced to navigate the inventory slowly with your analogue stick acting as a mouse cursor. It's all over the place.
Overall, the game feels like it has potential, but it doesn't offer enough variety and needs a lot of polishing as it is. It's in early access currently, so I trust the devs will mend most of these problems, and if that's the case then I might change my review to a positive recommendation.
Consider checking out my video for a more in-depth look, and perhaps you'll think the game is worth your money.
EDIT: They're updating the game, as expected. You now have more control over how your character looks, and can change the controls. However, I still can't recommend the game due to the lack fun gameplay in my opinion.

The goal for this game seems to have been an attempt to combine the game play of Mass Effect, the setting of XCom and the aesthics of the 60s. In theory this isn't a bad idea and I think that there is the potential for a good game there but it fails on the execution.
Overall the game is just bland. The basic game play suffers from a poor control scheme (espeically with regards to cover) and boring combat. The plot is just as bad being predictable and linear without the options that you'd get in something like Mass Effect. Additionally the game adopts the XCOM tradition of making your squad mates disposable. While that is true to the source material it means that the game cannot develop them as characters which is part of the appeal of most squad based shooters.

Like others, I was initially put off by the low metacritic score, as well as the thumbs down by other players, mostly it would seem due to griping about the lack of sophisticated AI within the game. To be honest, having played XCOM Enemy Unknown extensively, I feel that XCOM Bureau has captured the spirit and essence of that game down to a T. There isn't (nor should there be) sophisticated AI, primarily because it's down to your skill as the field commander to actually govern your squad accordingly and give them the appropriate instructions to keep them alive and kill the enemy. This is no different to the way XCOM itself plays, except instead of being turn-based it's time-based, so you only have a limited amount of time to carry out your decisions. This is done by an innovative slow-time system, where time slows down so you have some extra thinking room to be able to issue orders to the squad. In some cases, I've found that certain areas require squad planning and coordination. In others, it's all about using the squad as a distraction and then barreling in yourself with a shotgun or other appropriate weapon and kicking hell out of the enemy from a flanking position. This in my opinion mixes the best of the XCOM strategy and the FPS genres, and combined with very effective voice acting (though the lip synch leaves something to be desired, but that's a minor issue), as well as a hugely compelling story, anyone who enjoys both first person shooters AND the strategic aspect of XCOM won't be disappointed. I got this game on sale at £5 but I would still have no qualms about recommending it at the full price. I love it.

Well, I know some people criticized the plot and the part of the game play. I must say I like it but not completely satisfied by the experience.
1- The Plot [ Partial spoiler alert!]
The plot in the first 80% is like is the classic good guy vs bad guy thingy just like what we always see in other games/ movies. It is classy and I don't hate it. However, everyhing happened too fast in the end and it didn't give enough explaination why the main character turned againist the agency and the disagree the idea that supported by all other agents. Anyway, the plot twist is kind of clever and I've never seen any human vs alien game/ movies that can surprise me liket that.. (perhaps I didnt watch enough si-fi movies) Anyway, the plot is good in general.. and this game got an interesting story instead of just plainly good guy vs bad guy and the good guy won and saved the day.
To be fair, there are tons of details in the map like tape recorders telling what happened to other people before they turned into sleepwalkers, what other agents say about you or other things happened around the agency. You can talk to a lot people to see what they think and experienced. It is like Mass effect that allow player go deeper into the story and feel like being involved.
The ending is ..... okay but just a little below decent. It is still better than the ending of Mass Effect 3 (because the 1st ver of Mass Effect 3 ending is bad lol and that was a shame to the entire series of Mass Effect). Generally, the ending can use more polish.... what happened to a few important characters in the end were not mentioned.... I dont know why they wanted to keep it. Perhaps they want to make a sequel... who knows.
2- Game play
Well..... if you play normal, the game play is kind of messed up by the FPS and less strategy focus because the enemy is easy to kill. However, if you play hard/ very hard ( veteran/ commander), you really need to work on the strategy aspect because it is impossible to survive without taking the right cover, running around, using perks and call your teammates to cover here and there etc. I played the vateran at first and in the first few chapters, I feel like I was playing FPS at first instead of XCOM.... then I started to feel like I am playing FPS + XCOM: enemy unkwon.
Still, it is unlike the XCOM: enemy unkwon, I can shoot people myself and I kind of like it this way.
Anyway, the AI... I mean the teamamtes AI are not very smart but the enemy AI are smarter. Sometimes the teammates AI just randomly run from the cover I've assigned them to another cover that is bad and got themselves shot down.
I must say it is a little like Mass Effect but not simply copying it.... hell, even the conversion selection is very similar to smart effect lol and I like.
Weapons.. yes.. there are a lot of weapons but they are simply like the XCOM: enemy unknown.... I know they were trying to make them connected to the "enemy unknown". However, the weapons are similar with  just some weapons you get later give higher damage and they shoot almost the same way. I prefer weapons like HL2 that each weapon is unique and nothing is going to be useless in the later part of the game. That makes the actual choice of weapon to be only 1 or 2 in each chapter because you know you don't want weak weapons and have to give up that sniper rifle even you really like it.
The backpack is a little creative idea. Still, sooner or later I found out I just stick with one or two backpacks out of 20 selections. Again, some of them are not very useful.
Level Tree: The main character can go up to LV 10 but the teammates can only go up to 5.... it is not very usful and I found out I just stick with 2 engineers and keep throwing mines and turrets.... coz they cannot really shoot anything and I have to kill almost everyone by myself. The turrets are the only things that are useful and they are better than any human teammate.
3- Game design and environment
I like the design and the classic 1960 feel of the environment. The nailed it good. Some map got alien tech like from si-fi in the 2000s so it is a bit odd to see the 2 styles mixed together. It is fresh and a bit confusing.. but not a bad combination. I mean not excellent but not bad. Still, I like the type of games like Fallout more.
After all, the game has a lot of potential in both gameplay and plot. The idea of the story and game play are excellent but the outcome is .... let's say... decent and enjoyable...but not reaching it's full potential. I hope they are going to make a sequel and make it right next time.

Not much to say other than “This game is awesomely fun!”
If you love the classic turn based RPG's and comical adventures, then you will like this game. As the name implies, the game is about costumes. You and your sibbling start out Trick or Treating when these monsters kidnap one of you mistaking you for candy. You must go on a quest to recover your sibbling before the night is over.
The game works on two levels. The first is the main view (or town) where you solve simple puzzles and go door to door Trick or Treating. When you meat a monster you go to the battle level.
In the town you are in a cheaply made costume that looks like a kid made it. The streets have other kids walking around in various costumes and adults that have quests that need completing in order to pass by. Once you have visited all the houses, you are allowed to go to the next part of town.
In the battle section, your characters transform into whatever costume you had on. Each costume has normal attacks, special attacks, stat benefits, and/or a special ability outside combat.
The graphics for this game are in no way realistic. It was designed to look cartoonish. Not saying that the graphics are bad. On the contrary, for the style they went with, they look awesome. The backgrounds are highly detailed, the characters look smooth, the costumes really look like they were pieced together with cardboard and various things around the house.
The combat is probably the only place I would have any complaints with. When you begin, you can only do a normal attack unless you have a “battle stamp” that allows a secondary attack. On your third turn you will be allowed a special move. You can use it then or save it for later. The problem is that you have to wait 3 turns to use it again. Additionally, when you go to do your normal attack you have to press the corect sequence or yo will do about 1/2 to 3/4 damage. This is also tru with defending. If you fail to hit the proper button on time you will receive full damage. “Battle Stamps” will help with the combat but are limited to 1 per character. This is all there is to the fights. Granted there is a bit of strategy involved with the combat, this is very limiting.
All in all, this was a very fun game and the DLC was also fun. Neither are super long but are very fun to play...
