Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is an amazing adventure game. Its story has surprising depth, the characters are lovable, the puzzles are great fun and it wraps it all up in a layer of fantastic humour!
You can read the full review on The Mental Attic:

There was a time when Nelly was somewhat of a great pirate. She saved the Spoonbeaks once upon a time but now she’s a lowly mail clerk on a mail ship. Her ol’ ghost pirate pal, Bloodbeard, shows up to let her know that her great enemy Widebeard is up to his old tricks again. This time he’s manipulating the Spoonbeaks and various other beards and using them to do his bidding. Now Nelly must find Widebeard and stop him before he releases his Fowl Fleet!
Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is the sequel to an Adventure Game Studio title called Nelly Cootalot: Spoonbeaks Ahoy! While that game featured a hand drawn 2D style of gameplay. The Fowl Fleet is beautifully rendered in vibrant 3D visuals. The animations for the various characters and actions are simple but sweet. Don’t expect too much wacky movement outside of a few cut scenes and you should be golden.
The world of Nelly Cootalot likes to keep it simple, but there are still plenty of kicks to get out of the characters movements. One particularly humorous example is after Nelly helps a bird move to a new home, and he thanks her by giving her a hat full of his poop before sliding away into his new nest. It’s simple and sweet and adds a different sort of hilarity to the world.
Nelly Cootalot is a comedic adventure title and it never stops reminding us. Nelly is gung-ho but completely dimwitted at the same time. She’s like a stupider version of Drax from Guardians of the Galaxy. She takes most anything people tell her literally, so she’ll end up asking ridiculous questions or won’t fully understand basic innuendo.
Luckily, a wide variety of the people she meets are quick to crack a few jokes or two. One of my favorite characters in the game is named, “Gusty Nethers.” Yeah… that’s right… Gusty Nethers. He also has a few other ridiculous names he starts to call himself over the course the game. Gusty is just one of many characters that don’t take themselves too seriously. It makes for some wonderful back and forth banter between Nelly and the various characters.
There are some downsides and most of it comes in the form of the voice acting. It’s not to say that the voice acting is bad, in fact a lot of it is great. It’s that the jokes fall flat because the timing or the emotion isn’t particularly perfect. Sometimes Nelly or another character will tell a joke and there is no oomph to it whatsoever. Other times there will be a witty back and forth and the timing of a joke is just not enough to evoke laughter. It’s the moments like these that are a bit of a drawback to The Fowl Fleet, because it’s filled with hit and miss jokes.
When it comes to the mechanics of the title. The team sought to make a game that isn’t just ham-fisted with combining items and clicking things. There are quite a few thoughtful puzzles in the game that think outside the box. Lots of the brainteasers rely on some well thought out and even nostalgic design choices. The enigma of it all functions by figuring out elements of a puzzle and piecing it altogether to create one cohesive part.
A sample of this is one of the first real puzzles, where Nelly has to figure out the route of a fleet of ships by studying a log. Using different days as a reference you have to piece together the name and location of a ship she has to board. There are a variation of moments like these that shirk the usual “Click on random things” design of most adventure titles. Nelly Cootalot gives me a Professor Layton vibe as it consistently gives us amusing and well-thought out puzzles to enjoy.
Nelly Cootalot may not be a particularly hard game, but how many Adventure games truly are? Most of them are difficult because you didn’t click the right objects, or you missed some dialogue that you can’t see again. Nelly Cootalot never leaves you lingering for too long on one of the many riddles. If you interact with the characters and observe the items, you’ll zip through the game without being tied down by boring pixel clicking.
I appreciate this, because I do enjoy the experience and the story of adventure games more than being stranded on Puzzle Island. I like to be challenged but not to the point where I’m stuck in one specific area for three hours because of something I didn’t notice. Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet is middle of the road in difficulty and I’m perfectly fine with that.
I have some early build concerns that hopefully will be addressed in the retail version. The first area of the game is ripe with UI and scrolling problems. The item slot would occasionally stay on-screen which impeded my ability to interact with anything else. Also, there were times when the screen would stop scrolling and I couldn’t walk to an area I needed to visit.  This game doesn’t realize when you’re using dual-monitors and uses the secondary screen instead. I had to switch to single-screen settings if I wanted to record video of the game.
Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet started off as something I would have dismissed because it was trying too hard to be funny. It’s not until I ran into the first real puzzle before I said, “Hey, this is actually different for an adventure game.” Suddenly, I was hankering for the next new puzzle and engaged in solving any riddle that came my way.
I began to appreciate the simplistic animations and suddenly fell in love with the world of Nelly Cootalot. If you’re looking for an entertaining and different Adventure title, Nelly Cootalot might be the game with just enough charm to draw you in. Nelly is no Guybrush Threepwood, but she is certainly in a position to take over where he left off.

This game is like a cute younger sibling to Monkey Island.
I backed Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet on Kickstarter, because I was a fan of the previous Nelly Cootalot game. I loved the background art, but was skeptical on how well the new character designs were going to work. Playing the game, the character designs did really grow on me, so I'd say don't write it off if you have the same initial issue. The puzzles are typical for a point-and-click adventure, with nothing too challenging. Really, this game is about its great sense of humor. If you like your games to be a bit clever and adorable, this one is on point. It certainly is one of the punnier games I've played.
Also, Tom Baker as Sebastian is too charming. Such a great companion to have through the game.

Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet surprised me. The game's story/setting is charming/quirky and I enjoyed it a lot more than I was expecting. There are quite a few funny moments in the game as well.  The story might not appeal to everyone but I enjoyed it quite a bit.
The puzzles are pretty clever and well designed. Unlike some point and click adventure games the puzzles aren't obtuse where you have to guess your ways to the correct answer. The game is just really well made.
I really only had two complaints with Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet. First the game is kind of on the shorter side. The game lasts around five to six hours. Since I was really enjoying the game I wish it was a little longer. The other problem is that for the most part I found the game to be kind of easy. You probably aren't going to be really challenged by the game.
Although not totally necessary, I would recommend playing the original game first. You won't be lost if you don't play the first game but the game does sometimes address things that happen in the first game so you might be slightly confused a couple times in the game. The original game can be found online for free.
If you like point and click adventure games I think you will enjoy Nelly Cootalot: The Fowl Fleet.

Pros:
+ Graphics are beautiful looking
+ Sounds are amazing from walking to firing off different weapons
+ Guns and using the Gunsmith
+ Open world and you can do any mission is any order you want to
+ A good story, but based more on investigations and missions rather than just pure dialogue (e.g. RP games).
+ Background information about Bolivia and that a lot of it is based on actual facts
+ Customizations
Neutral:
*/- Stealth
*/- Camouflage
Cons:
- AI at times makes you question their intelligence
- Driving a car can feel like you’re constantly playing a drifting simulator
- Crashes that happen once in a while when playing co-op
The story really isn’t a story, but about missions with slight background knowledge about who you need to take out. You hardly know anything about who you are, who your operatives that you work with are, or who your boss is and know very little about even the organization you work for. They made the story more or less to investigation and/or criminal solving shows (Law and Order, Criminal Minds, etc.) in sense where you finish a case and move onto the next case. In the end, you know more about the enemy than you do about yourself and/or your own operatives. They did an excellent job at executing the story in this regard, but don’t expect a big time story from games that relate more around Roleplaying titles.
The game looks amazing. All my settings are on max and never seen any AA issues; as well never seen any stuttering or FPS drops. The grass and bushes will move or get flatten when moving over them or when in prone position so you can flatten the grass, move back slightly, and snipe people from afar. The different biomes and the weather effects with a day and night cycle makes the game feel realistic and does an accurate job (more or less based on the given Kilometers within the game) of showing off Bolivia’s landscape.
The sounds whether walking on snow, dirt, mud, or diving into the water is very noticeable. It adds to that realism compared to other games where a lot of the footing is the same regardless what biome you’re in. The voice actors do a good job at commenting about missions, syncing shots, cinematics that occur, and just bluntly describing how they’d love to ‘stick it to them’. At times they’ll throw in a joke or give some insight about where they came from and/or who they (not a lot, but at least it’s something). Vehicles in general sound different from one another; whether it’s a four door coup, to a lambo, to a pick-up truck, they all have their distinctive sounds. Both helicopters sound different from one another and the bush plane sounds like a bush plane.
From firing off a MP5 to a M4A1 to a G28 all sound genuine to their counterparts. Adding a compressor only makes it feel more genuine when doing stealth combat. You have an ample amount of customization for your weapons: scopes, barrels, grips, muzzles, triggers, stocks, and few other options. Each option as dozen or more items that help with accuracy, handling, rate of fire, damage, etc.; you customize your weapon based on your playstyle or how you want the weapon to feel in terms of gun n’ gun, aiming, or hip fire. Depending on how customize your weapons they’ll lean toward one direction or have a recoil higher than other weapons and they feel all very accurate based on how you fit your weapon. Also, you have multiple options to paint your weapons.
This game has kept its word about doing any province in any order you want to. I felt like this was a great aspect of the game and a feature that wasn’t a lie or falsely advertised. I went from one area to another based on certain weapons and gadgets for said weapons early on and finished other zones for pure enjoyment. You have multiple ways of transportation: cars, trucks, diesel trucks; planes, helicopters, boats, motorcycles, and parachutes. You do have to get used to flying, but once you have that in place flying becomes easier that other modern warfare titles. Some of the vehicles are horrendous when driving regardless of how fast or slow one would takes around a curve or eases on the brakes. Some of the vehicles feel like they were imported from an actual drifting game and with a lot of roads being on hills and/or trying to pursuit someone can become an absolute headache at times.
Customization in general of your character is appealing compared to other titles that fit within this genre. You can wear sunglasses, hat, different vest types, you can wear civilian clothing and/or military clothing; you can mismatch items and numerous color variations regardless how you pick your items. When it comes to using camouflage to hide yourself from enemies, this concept goes entirely out of the window. You could be engulfed in a full ghillie suit and the enemy will still see you a few hundred meters away. This is applied if you’re in full black camouflage and in pitch darkness where they don’t have any Night Vision on and still can see you through the brush when using a compressor. I would like to see some rework on how camouflage works as this is a major factor at times when using stealth against the enemy.
Most of the times stealth works to a degree; one can sneak up behind an enemy and eliminate them in melee or sniping them well over five hundred meters away. Factors that can hurt your stealth is noise (gunfire, running, explosions, etc.), another guard seeing the corpse of a fallen member, or being noticed because camouflage didn’t do its job. There are traits to help prevent from being detected, which at times makes it too easy (e.g. If you’re about to be spotted and you’re hundred and twenty meters away, just prone and they’ll stop noticing you). There are devices to help distract guards to your location so you can pick them off without someone else spotting their body. I would’ve liked to see an option about picking up the corpse and moving it instead of waiting a few seconds and having it magically disappear. Also, regardless of what weapon you use, you can one shot anyone as long as you’re in stealth mode. I understand this helps in co-op to do sync shots, but I feel like that this method is way too easy. If you’re not in co-op mode, sync shots with your AI counterparts are an amazing feature and it helps clear out majority of the operations you take.
The AI at times can be the best help or the worst help. They will NOT engage unless you command them to do so or if you are under heavy amounts of fire where you will automatically command your operatives to attack. They will remain in stealth mode for majority of the time and the more you upgrade your sync shots the more use you can get out from your operatives. When they do open fire, they just seem at times not knowing how to eliminate an enemy when it really matters. There really isn’t a middle ground with your AI operatives. I’ve seen them meters away from an enemy and just eating all their bullets instead of turning around and shooting them instead. The AI does need work, but you can finish the game on a higher difficulty – just expect a headache at times dealing with them.
I did experience some crashes when playing in co-op mode and when I finished the game (both endings). In co-op mode, if one person joins the game, then it’s you two vs Bolivia instead of two people and two AI, or three players and one AI. The AI will still talk even though they aren’t in your squad and it’s to keep the immersion within the game. I never experienced any lag or disconnects when playing with my friends, but the crashes would happen randomly. Co-op needs work, but when it does work it is an amazing experience with friends.
I recommend buying this title to play with your friends. Unfortunately, I can't add any more information - I exceeded the amount.

I saw one or two videos about this game, and when the free weekend came, I was more than eager to try it out. Here's my review, and excuse my unprofessional language, I'm just some dude. :p
First off, this game looks amazing, even on an older machine. I ran it on just a 1 GB graphics card, and even on the lowest settings the options told me I'd need at least around 1,7 GB, but apart from some tearing in the facial animations of minor characters in cutscenes, it ran smoothly and I could enjoy the beautiful environments as well as even the toughest fights with dozens of actors involved.
Gameplay-wise, this was right up my alley, and reminded me of the many fun hours I spent playing Far Cry 3 and Just Cause 2. Sure, it uses the proven "Ubisoft formula" of having stealthy and not-so-stealthy ways of playing a mission, infiltrating a base, getting supplies etc., but the versatile drone, the wide arsenal of weapons and upgrades, your teammates and the fire support you can call in provide you with enough diversity that no two camps and settlements feel the same (even more so due to the level design and enemy placement/habits).
I definitely recommend this game for people who liked games like the aforementioned Far Cry and Just Cause series. The only minor negative point I found was the land and air vehicle handling, which takes some time getting used to (again, comparing it in my head with Just Cause 2), but by the end of weekend, it was no problem anymore.
So yeah, Ghost Recon Wildlands is top priority on my wishlist right now, and I'm gonna get it as soon as I'm done with the Witcher 3 GotY, because I am that sure Wildlands would make me stop playing the best game of 2015.

A simple and fun game, that's rather difficult to master.
As a vulnerable you need to hit and attach other pixels, especially shooting ones to do your fighting for you. This becomes rather difficult as if they easily kill you as one hit and you're done for.
Due to this you really need to acquire as many pixels as possible as they need to be your shields, and get destroyed. You can also rotate yourself so you're able to try and balance out the pixel build up. It's gets very awkward if you have a mass of them on one side, and nothing else where.
Boss battles are intense, as they're packed heavily and have a massive arsenal. In order to advance each difficulty you must destroy them, which is no easy task.
I strongly recommend using a controller for this one, I found it much easier with an analog stick.
The game may be very plain looking, but the music is great and certainly adds more to the game. I honestly think it would be rather boring without it.
If you're sensitive to any lights I would advise avoiding the game though. There's a lot of different colours on some levels and quite a bit of flashing.
PC Gameplay

Pixel Galaxy is a game about survival, growing and adapting. You play as a lone pixel that has to make friends and recruit others to build up a bigger pixel that is capable of defending you against and shooting other enemies. It sounds simple but as you progress into the game it ramps up the challenge, the game has 6 difficulty modes as well as the option to replay invidiual bosses or a chance to fight them all in Boss Rush.
Gameplay is pretty simple here, you move around the screen and collect other pixels that attach to you and upgrade your size/abilities. Though the bigger your ship is the more danger you're likely to be in as dodging things can be a bit tough (especially on the harder difficulties). It's a bit like Tetris mixed with something like Geometry Wars, gameplay can be fast paced and satisfying. You also have a Local Co-op mode that lets you and a friend make your own pixels to battle stages and fight bosses together.
Plenty of different types of enemies in each stage, you also have a visual theme to each level that brings a treat as you progress to another one. Graphically the game is quite simple but it's surprisingly effective at delivering a great experience.
The soundtrack is quite a treat, I did enjoy the music in the game and often felt myself lost in the music that even cost me a couple of deaths! Might even be something you'd enjoy listening to on your phone/outside the game.
It's a refreshing experience to the bullet hell genre and something I'd be happy to recommend, there is plenty here to do and the game has around 129 achievements for the completionists out there. If you're a fan of games like Geometry Wars then you'll enjoy this.

Draw Rider is a game for extreme sports fans who dont mind getting their hands and legs dirty on a computer screen playing an indie game,every now and than.The game is for those who have a few hours of spare time.But before you read this review be advised  PG(parental guidance) needed while playing this fun game.
The game itself is a lead based game as in you play on a terrain which looks simmilar to a hand crafted pencil lead drawn background.Also the game leads you to various types of situatuions and even though the application of physics is minimal. The game has seven levels and 175 chapters, each adding its own distinctness to the game.Every level leads you to a new circumstance.In some there is high gravity,some has Earth like systems,while some are designed for the hardcore extreme sports fans amongst you.So much is the vastness of the game that it allows you to edit your own custom maps for you and your friends in the editor mode.
There are typically 25 chapters in each level on an average,with the Earth level having a minimum of 6 chapters and the bonus level having a maximum of 41 chapters.Be warned though as you finish each chapter you face an even harder chapter.In Earth based system you play in a situation simmilar to that of what you face on  Earth.In hardcore you get to do extreme stunts based on the limitations of physics applied to the game.In gravity you face extreme gravity,while black and white is for fun,Beginning is for the absoulte starters.(Had some nice time in it).Challenge is a bit more punishing than the beginners and lastly the bonus is for  the kid amongst you.As mentioned they make up together a complete game.
Its not just one vehicle you can have fun on but there are bikes,sleds,unicycles,you can even walk,apart from cycling.You die a plenty of times during the game play or your vehicle breaks ,so advised dont try this anywhere.The game itself is fun and is sure to entertain you for hours if not days being a 2d game its a refreshing change from all the other 3d games or even from the ones in its class.
PROS
+The levels themselves are exciting and varied
+Good music,simple yet enticing
+So many levels to choose from
+Various kinds of vehicles to chose from,from cycles to bikes.from sleds to unicycles
+Its pocket friendly
+you can edit your own levels
CONS
There are no noticable cons to this good game but if i have to mention
-each chapter is locked and you cannot step jump
-Its a bit unpolished and the game can do with a bit more polishing (coloring)
Apart from that its an extreme sports fans dream come true And as I mentioned in the beginning PG is advised for if you try out this stunts even in this game you die a gory death some times.(Trust me  I have died plenty of times and would die again !) All in all A solid 6.5/10 for presentation. Definitely a go getter for an extreme sports fan.

I will make this quick.. ish. I went into They Are Billions with a slightly negative attitude. Based on what I had seen, the game seemed a bit too simple to justify how long games lasted. After actually playing my first game, however, I realized that They Are Billions delivers in the 1-player RTS and resource management genre shockingly well. The progression is also surprisingly well-paced for being about 3 hour long games, if you win.
Also, I still have not actually won a match yet. For those who might claim I think the game is good because I am good at it, or something. My last game I had lost last night 80ish days, out of 100, into it because I anticipated the attack in the wrong spot, well it split in half actually. I appreciate a game that really shows a no-mercy zombie infection spread.
Those who are on the fence warnings:
Successful games take a long time (roughly 3 hours it would apear).
This game IS challenging so either start with very easy settings, or be prepared to suffer many defeats.
This game punishes certain small mistakes HARD. Ex: In the early game, if you don't notice 1 zombie walk to a house, it is essentially over.
You can NOT do manual saves to reload after you make mistakes; however, if you want to exploit the system, I have not because I think it ruins the whole point of the game, you can end the task from the task manager and it should force it to close without overwriting the last back up save allowing you to correct a mistake.
Learning is part of the fun and a non humble player may hate a game like this.
Lastly, there is some kind of bug with mouse clicks, at least for me. Sometimes they do not register and you have to redo a click. It is a tiny bit annoying.

I find it funny how out of order I played these games. I went Retribution to original and then to Chaos Rising. Regardless of the order, the stories can all be enjoy separately, and they were designed like that to begin with.
Chaos Rising doesn’t change too much to the formula, more like it just adds content. It’s an expansion pack through and through, maybe not as big as older titles but still very worthwhile. I’ll bypass sections here and just mention the highlights of it.

*Game mechanic spoilers, no story spoilers*

In the campaign, business is still the same, minus the Tyranid invasion mechanic. In lieu of that, you’re granted several new options to play with. There’s new types of wargear available, a new hero to use, more dialogue in between missions – some of which is optional and discoverable based and finally there’s the Corruption system.
The corruption system enables you to bow down to Chaos and obtain dark powers during your missions. You’re presented with the chances to descend deeper into Chaos by performing certain actions in missions, such as deliberately destroying Angel Forge’s gate – which lets you get in fast, but permanently disables Meridian (story context only) by doing this. There are almost always conditions to become more corrupted throughout the game, whilst also having the option of being Redeemed. These are more stressful objectives that allow you to head back to the light of sanity and order, such as making sure an entire friendly army survives an encounter.
Becoming corrupted gives you new powers and abilities, and the price to pay is the allegience of your non-corrupted members as well as negative stats (less energy regen mostly). Being pure on the other hand gives you fewer cool powers, but more stoic advantages that you don’t have to work for, you just have to keep them. First the actions you can take to become more corrupted aren’t so big, they don’t seem so bad but by the end of the game, you’ll really start to question what it is exactly that you’re doing. I don’t often feel so impacted by choices in games, especially when they’re not so story focused, but this made me think.
There’s a new enemy through the campaign which is now the Chaos Marines. Suddenly poof there’s Aurelia, former world of the Blood Ravens, and now they’re up to no good. You shift attention away from the Orks and Eldar and go out to kill these ♥♥♥♥ers instead. The story is actually more in depth this time than the first game’s, being that you can have several dialogue pieces with your comrades and others in between missions, your actions have more lasting effects on their opinions and just a general sense of things either going good or bad arise. Also, ♥♥♥♥ yeah the Space Hulk.
The difficulty I found was actually much tougher than the original’s, part in due that all enemies scale to you and eventually have literally x40 (heh) your health in fights so, it can take some time to kill, but just that action is tougher and requires more control and response. In multiplayer you have access to the Chaos Marines both in versus and Last Stand, so go nuts.

Other than these remarks there’s not a ton to touch on, this was a good release through and through, though Retribution obviously improves even further on it as far as multiplayer goes.
It’s some good♥♥♥♥♥♥ If there’s something to be taken from game design, this is how you can slowly add onto a game with new mechanics and options. They did it right here with it’s integration, it wasn’t overwriting stuff – it was adding it.

Bought this as part of a daily deal and afraid I got the worse end of it.
The Bureau attempts to take the XCOM series and translate it into a cover shooter.  It makes some token nods towards the turn-based tactical history of the series by offering a tactical planning mode where you can manage your squadmates but doesn't fundamentally change it from the game pattern you figure out after about 5 minutes:   Spend some time walking through a 3d maze and getting a little backstory, to arrive at a location where you will spend the next few minutes toggling the cover button to shoot at aliens.
To top it off, this game was obviously designed for a console and something did not go well in its translation to the PC.  Moving in and out of cover requires specific key-sequences, without which your character gets stuck hugging a wall or desk.  The instructions give two keys to press simultaneously but in practice only seems to work if one is pressed before the other.  All of this convinces you to basically stay in one place rather than fight the controls.
I've been a big fan of the XCOM franchise.  I just wish this game wasn't in it.

The best MMO I've played. Really.
Only thing I can compare it to is WoW. But there the world is pretty static (or at least was, since I've only played it till WotLK and got bored, so no idea how the things look after the Cataclysm). Here you can get a rift open right above your head if you are (un)lucky enough. There's hardly a way to have nothing to do in this game, since the world changes every minute, bringing forth new challenges.
Of things that I like (concerning gameplay):
- tons of quests, including daily crafting ones (helps improving crafting skills a lot)
- public group option: now you don't have to put the group up yourself, invite each player separately etc; just one click and you're in with all the group bonuses
- invasions!!! Those really bring players together (since it takes quite a lot of running around to fend off all the atacking mobs, seal rifts and defend ward stones in different points of the map at the same time)
- fishing (holy cow, I love fishing in this game!)
- tons of things-to-do-except-for-standard-MMO-stuff: artifacts hunting, minions quests etc.
- it's free; like really - everything u can get with real money, you can get with the in-game currency, it just takes time to gather some coin, but it's doable
Only-one-thing-I-don't-like:
- Auction House is not available untill you get Loyalty points - and you can get them only by paying real money or buying one terribly expensive stuff in game (called Rift EXchange); but well, I guess that can be forgiven - that's the only inconvenience I met and it's not really a problem - if the AH was available, REX would be even more expensive since the in-game currency would be easier to get or, in worse case, they would make something else not available to provoke ppl to pay; and one can live without AH, especially if u get into some guild where u can trade with your guildmates (or more like ppl just leave stuff they don't need in guild vault and you just come and get what you need, leaving your thing for others).
Of non-gameplay matters:
- graphic is really great (see screenshots); remember it's an MMO (so u tend to have XX players and mobs on the screen running around, casting spells etc.), and it all runs smoothly even though you can find worse models/animations in single-player games; guys who did the optimization for this game did their job really well
- also graphics stuff - landscapes are beautiful and vast; sure the map is divided into zones, but it's done neatly and not hurting ones eyes (like suddenly coming out of dense forest into almost-desert plains)
- I like how female models are done; I'm always irritaded when I see the "very-fantasy" heroines on high heels, with almost no armor and their boobs bigger than their heads; here the female heroes have quite realistic bodies (like one guy said "hey, I noticed my XXX doesn't wear a bra!") and if they're supposed to be warriors, they wear a full plate (even my rogue wears a full leather)
So if you like MMOs, this one is definitely worth a shot. It has everything a "standard" one should have + some things from itself - and everything done really well.

Let's be honest: we all buy Hatoful Boyfriend for the sheer absurdity of what is, at its core, a visual novel pigeon dating game. And, on its surface at least, Hatoful Boyfriend is a shallow dating sim where the human main character is enrolled at St. PigeoNation's, a school for pigeons. She takes classes, she goes to festivals, and she romances and falls in love with various species of birds. However, Hatoful Boyfriend's stereotypical high school romance exterior is only an entertaining and light-hearted charade that covers up a plot full of politics, intrigue, mystery, and sorrow.
The first half of Hatoful Boyfriend is quirky and humorous, filled with various pop culture jokes and absurd situations. Players find themselves romancing one of several standard character archetypes: the childhood best friend, the lazy professor, the haughty aristocrat, the womanizing jock, the bullied library nerd, and so on. The scenarios are cute and heart-warming, with each character having their own separate little storyline. Every short playthrough of the game—which frequently take under an hour even if you read all of the text—ends with a primarily sappy romantic ending.
As players go through multiple playthroughs of Hatoful Boyfriend, however, a more insidious underlying plot is slowly revealed. Every romantic plot line will unveil more pieces of St. PigeoNation's dark history and the tragic cast of characters that attend classes there. These pieces on their own add spice to an otherwise bland dating sim that seems to cash in on its unique and somewhat ridiculous premise of a human girl dating pigeons. And, if one were to stop playing Hatoful Boyfriend after only a couple of playthroughs, that would be the feeling that one would be left with: Hatoful Boyfriend is an amusing dating game to spend an afternoon on, but nothing remarkable.
However, players that choose to stop playing Hatoful Boyfriend after only a few short playthroughs are missing out on the part of Hatoful Boyfriend that makes it an excellent game. If the first thirteen playthroughs of Hatoful Boyfriend are an amusing way to pass an afternoon, then the last playthrough is a gut-wrenching ride through a twisting plot that ties together everything the player has done up to that point. The short of it is this: this isn't just a game that you should play, it's a game that you should strive to complete 100% of the way.

They are Billions is a nice game where your goal is to survive hordes of zombies periodically spawning at the edge of the map. But they aren't the only zombies! The whole map is covered with them! They're everywhere! They are Billions!
You begin by setting up first buildings like tents, fisherman cottages and sawmills anno-style. Those have to be of course protected. Build walls and train a variety of units like rangers (women with bows) or soldiers (dudes with guns). As your colony grows you will have to carefully plan ahead where you go and what you attack.
Why? Because noise is a part of the mechanics. The louder you are, the more zombies will come towards you. Furthermore one can pause the game whenever he wants by pressing space. This allows for less hectic gameplay and more thought through decisions.
On round takes about 4h +-1h to complete and has different stages.
As mentioned before, every now and then smaller packs of zombies will arrive and try to chomp through your walls. In the End although, there is a HUGE wave of zombies coming in from all directions and you are basically only preparing for that specific wave.
Warning: This game is hard. There is permadeth, no save-scamming and no tutorial (yet). You will probably fail a lot (like me).
Pros:
+ much content for EA
+ nice graphics
+ next to no bugs (haven't experiencend anything tremendous until now)
+ fluent gameplay
+ thriving community
+ long playtime (I didn't even make it past the first of four maps)
+ possibility of pausing the game
Cons:
- only survival Mode playable yet
- no keybord layout customization (yet probably)
- bugs, but only smaller ones
- no tutorial. Learn by watching other people
- frustration factor when you play for 4 hours just to get crushed in the last ten minutes
TL;DR
- It's hard
- It's fun
- You get more than what you pay if you like the genre
One of those games I will have to restrain my self from playing until the final release. It's to much fun and I don't want to get tired of playing it before everything is implemented.

Pros:
+ Graphics are beautiful looking
+ Sounds are amazing from walking to firing off different weapons
+ Guns and using the Gunsmith
+ Open world and you can do any mission is any order you want to
+ A good story, but based more on investigations and missions rather than just pure dialogue (e.g. RP games).
+ Background information about Bolivia and that a lot of it is based on actual facts
+ Customizations
Neutral:
*/- Stealth
*/- Camouflage
Cons:
- AI at times makes you question their intelligence
- Driving a car can feel like you’re constantly playing a drifting simulator
- Crashes that happen once in a while when playing co-op
The story really isn’t a story, but about missions with slight background knowledge about who you need to take out. You hardly know anything about who you are, who your operatives that you work with are, or who your boss is and know very little about even the organization you work for. They made the story more or less to investigation and/or criminal solving shows (Law and Order, Criminal Minds, etc.) in sense where you finish a case and move onto the next case. In the end, you know more about the enemy than you do about yourself and/or your own operatives. They did an excellent job at executing the story in this regard, but don’t expect a big time story from games that relate more around Roleplaying titles.
The game looks amazing. All my settings are on max and never seen any AA issues; as well never seen any stuttering or FPS drops. The grass and bushes will move or get flatten when moving over them or when in prone position so you can flatten the grass, move back slightly, and snipe people from afar. The different biomes and the weather effects with a day and night cycle makes the game feel realistic and does an accurate job (more or less based on the given Kilometers within the game) of showing off Bolivia’s landscape.
The sounds whether walking on snow, dirt, mud, or diving into the water is very noticeable. It adds to that realism compared to other games where a lot of the footing is the same regardless what biome you’re in. The voice actors do a good job at commenting about missions, syncing shots, cinematics that occur, and just bluntly describing how they’d love to ‘stick it to them’. At times they’ll throw in a joke or give some insight about where they came from and/or who they (not a lot, but at least it’s something). Vehicles in general sound different from one another; whether it’s a four door coup, to a lambo, to a pick-up truck, they all have their distinctive sounds. Both helicopters sound different from one another and the bush plane sounds like a bush plane.
From firing off a MP5 to a M4A1 to a G28 all sound genuine to their counterparts. Adding a compressor only makes it feel more genuine when doing stealth combat. You have an ample amount of customization for your weapons: scopes, barrels, grips, muzzles, triggers, stocks, and few other options. Each option as dozen or more items that help with accuracy, handling, rate of fire, damage, etc.; you customize your weapon based on your playstyle or how you want the weapon to feel in terms of gun n’ gun, aiming, or hip fire. Depending on how customize your weapons they’ll lean toward one direction or have a recoil higher than other weapons and they feel all very accurate based on how you fit your weapon. Also, you have multiple options to paint your weapons.
This game has kept its word about doing any province in any order you want to. I felt like this was a great aspect of the game and a feature that wasn’t a lie or falsely advertised. I went from one area to another based on certain weapons and gadgets for said weapons early on and finished other zones for pure enjoyment. You have multiple ways of transportation: cars, trucks, diesel trucks; planes, helicopters, boats, motorcycles, and parachutes. You do have to get used to flying, but once you have that in place flying becomes easier that other modern warfare titles. Some of the vehicles are horrendous when driving regardless of how fast or slow one would takes around a curve or eases on the brakes. Some of the vehicles feel like they were imported from an actual drifting game and with a lot of roads being on hills and/or trying to pursuit someone can become an absolute headache at times.
Customization in general of your character is appealing compared to other titles that fit within this genre. You can wear sunglasses, hat, different vest types, you can wear civilian clothing and/or military clothing; you can mismatch items and numerous color variations regardless how you pick your items. When it comes to using camouflage to hide yourself from enemies, this concept goes entirely out of the window. You could be engulfed in a full ghillie suit and the enemy will still see you a few hundred meters away. This is applied if you’re in full black camouflage and in pitch darkness where they don’t have any Night Vision on and still can see you through the brush when using a compressor. I would like to see some rework on how camouflage works as this is a major factor at times when using stealth against the enemy.
Most of the times stealth works to a degree; one can sneak up behind an enemy and eliminate them in melee or sniping them well over five hundred meters away. Factors that can hurt your stealth is noise (gunfire, running, explosions, etc.), another guard seeing the corpse of a fallen member, or being noticed because camouflage didn’t do its job. There are traits to help prevent from being detected, which at times makes it too easy (e.g. If you’re about to be spotted and you’re hundred and twenty meters away, just prone and they’ll stop noticing you). There are devices to help distract guards to your location so you can pick them off without someone else spotting their body. I would’ve liked to see an option about picking up the corpse and moving it instead of waiting a few seconds and having it magically disappear. Also, regardless of what weapon you use, you can one shot anyone as long as you’re in stealth mode. I understand this helps in co-op to do sync shots, but I feel like that this method is way too easy. If you’re not in co-op mode, sync shots with your AI counterparts are an amazing feature and it helps clear out majority of the operations you take.
The AI at times can be the best help or the worst help. They will NOT engage unless you command them to do so or if you are under heavy amounts of fire where you will automatically command your operatives to attack. They will remain in stealth mode for majority of the time and the more you upgrade your sync shots the more use you can get out from your operatives. When they do open fire, they just seem at times not knowing how to eliminate an enemy when it really matters. There really isn’t a middle ground with your AI operatives. I’ve seen them meters away from an enemy and just eating all their bullets instead of turning around and shooting them instead. The AI does need work, but you can finish the game on a higher difficulty – just expect a headache at times dealing with them.
I did experience some crashes when playing in co-op mode and when I finished the game (both endings). In co-op mode, if one person joins the game, then it’s you two vs Bolivia instead of two people and two AI, or three players and one AI. The AI will still talk even though they aren’t in your squad and it’s to keep the immersion within the game. I never experienced any lag or disconnects when playing with my friends, but the crashes would happen randomly. Co-op needs work, but when it does work it is an amazing experience with friends.
I recommend buying this title to play with your friends. Unfortunately, I can't add any more information - I exceeded the amount.

I saw one or two videos about this game, and when the free weekend came, I was more than eager to try it out. Here's my review, and excuse my unprofessional language, I'm just some dude. :p
First off, this game looks amazing, even on an older machine. I ran it on just a 1 GB graphics card, and even on the lowest settings the options told me I'd need at least around 1,7 GB, but apart from some tearing in the facial animations of minor characters in cutscenes, it ran smoothly and I could enjoy the beautiful environments as well as even the toughest fights with dozens of actors involved.
Gameplay-wise, this was right up my alley, and reminded me of the many fun hours I spent playing Far Cry 3 and Just Cause 2. Sure, it uses the proven "Ubisoft formula" of having stealthy and not-so-stealthy ways of playing a mission, infiltrating a base, getting supplies etc., but the versatile drone, the wide arsenal of weapons and upgrades, your teammates and the fire support you can call in provide you with enough diversity that no two camps and settlements feel the same (even more so due to the level design and enemy placement/habits).
I definitely recommend this game for people who liked games like the aforementioned Far Cry and Just Cause series. The only minor negative point I found was the land and air vehicle handling, which takes some time getting used to (again, comparing it in my head with Just Cause 2), but by the end of weekend, it was no problem anymore.
So yeah, Ghost Recon Wildlands is top priority on my wishlist right now, and I'm gonna get it as soon as I'm done with the Witcher 3 GotY, because I am that sure Wildlands would make me stop playing the best game of 2015.

Gameplay:
4 people track a solo player (the monster) down and desperately try to exterminate the threat before it grows into it's next stage were it's talents become more vicious and un-forgiving. The monster must hide it's tracks from the bloodthirsty hunters and eat the surrounding wildlife to gain energy for evolution so it may fight back bigger and harder. Note: the role of monster takes a lot of skill if you are opposed by skilled hunters. But you must stay determined! (some will get that)
An honest opinion of the game and it's current state:
This game is astonishing for a free to play. The characters have a story behind them all so you aren't just playing as a cardboard cut-out with guns. The monsters are all unique and do NOT share any skills other than smelling their environment for prey to devour. All their other skills range from terrain altering to fire spitting to trap laying to even self-destructing!
Again, be aware that this game is in the development stage so please for the love of God don't post a negative review saying that this game has bugs. The fact that 'beta' is all over the game literally screams to the player/s that it has issues that may be removed/tested/altered. I've seen reviews claiming that the player couldn't find the monster and that meant it was a boring and unfair game. It's hard to believe that someone would not realise that the player they were against was of a higher skill group but what's worse is that this particular player has spent 1.3hrs on record!!!
Bugs are common, especially for a game that has been comepletely re-worked to support fair games on a free to play level and also allow people of many skill groups to partake in the loveable game that is now Evolve Stage 2. People suggested that they add cars to the game so it's easier for hunters. Just let that one sink in. Cars... against a monster who tears through flesh and metal for surviaval. They also asked for the maps to be cut down. I can see why they want that but to be honest, the map size isn't just for a good gameplay area, it's also for immersive games. Where you feel like you are actually on a different planet entirely that has a HUGE surface area.
Another great thing is that there are NO MICRO-TRANSACTIONS! That's right, folks! Now you can play a AAA game for FREE with absoloutely 0 corner cutting rich kids who buy their way to victory.

When Evolve first released, it was this wonderful game that required teamwork and strategy on the part of the hunters, while the monster required cunning and skill to dodge the hunters long enough to become strong enough to fight them. Every hunter had a role to play, and if they didn't do it right, the monster was going to cause some damage or get away.
Now, however, that complexity has been traded in for a watered down version of 'run away simulator'. The trapper lost the one job that made it so vital to the team, and rather traded in for a scanner that will tell them where the monster is no matter the distance between the hunters and the monster. They might as well have just made that an ability all the hunters can use, and gotten rid of the Trapper class altogether so the hunters can take two assaults instead.
Speaking of abilities all the hunters can use, everyone can use the dome now, so there's no real point to staying as a cohesive unit since the wildlife is killed so easily or is easy to dodge. You lose the feeling of being a team player and rather feel like you're playing 'separately together'. In the same game with the same goal, but not really coordinating, just doing what the game wants you to do.
As for the monster, cunning has been traded in with how quickly you can use your leaping/flying/charge to get away from the hunters while also trying desperately to evolve. The Hunters know where you are about every 30 seconds thanks to the scanner, and since they don't need to stick together, they can easily cut you off and any one of them can dome you in. At the same time, however, the monster is ridiculously strong even at stage one. In the original Evolve, if you got caught at Stage one, you had no chance of winning unless the hunters were EXTREMELY BAD. At Stage 2 you could do some damage but you were likely going to lose. At Stage 3, the hunters had their work cut out for them.
I believe now the majority of games end with the Monster at Stage 2, either by killing the Hunters or being killed. About 50-50 either way. But the matches are too short and very few monsters ever make it to stage 3 before time runs out. And Stage 3 is where it used to be the most fun as the monster became a true challenge. So many monsters were sure of themselves even in Stage 1 that they would attack as soon as the match started, just because they were that powerful. Turtle Rock didn't take a hint that the monsters at Stage 1 were too strong and rather just gave a boost to the defense of the Hunters when coming off the dropship.
Turtle Rock has made a grave error. Instead of keeping the complexity that made the paid for game great, they dumbed it down so seven year olds could be able to play it without any issue.  If they had kept the game as it was when they went free to play, I would absolutely recommend this game. But I can't and will not recommend this game as it is now. It's too simple to keep you entertained.

Costume quest is a small, but fun game about saving your sibling after he/she is kidnapped by monsters who are trying to steal all of the candy. The objective of the game is to go to each area, collect candy as well as costumes (hence the name costume quest) and fight any monsters that cross your path.
The game style is turn based combat with each costume giving you a different ability, and different quicktime event-like buttons to press to do more damage. The one little problem I have with the game is the fact that the (spoiler alert) French Fry and Vampire costume quicktime event/button press can prompt you to mash the shift key. On Windows, this is a little bit of a nuisance, as the game will minimize and ask if you want to turn sticky keys on. It isn't that big of a deal however, due to the fact that it's a turn based game.
The game is not too much of a challenge if you can find the right combinations of costumes and battle stamps with which to fight the enemies. One can easily finish all of the quests simply by playing the game and not going too far out of the way to complete objectives.
The characters are lovable (even the grubbins), the style is pretty cool, and the story, while not too exciting, is fun.
I would reccomend trying it out.

Alright so let's talk about dishonored:
Dishonored is a Singleplayer-only game.
The graphics are nothing ground breaking, but that doesn't mean they are bad. It just means there aren't going to be Crysis level water-shaders, etc. Which means the game should run smoothly even on not so powerfull systems.
Personally I really like the art style of Dishonored. It's heavily inspired by victorian england, but does also include some fictional elements, which are commonly referred to as Steampunk. So overall I think the graphics are very good, primarily because of the amazing art style and not so much because of the technical side of things.
The story is pretty good in my opinion, it's well narrated, either directly through dialogue and cutscenes or through enviromental story telling (I could try and explain the term, but it's easier if you just google it, if you dont know what I mean by that).
The gameplay mechanics work really well. You have a set of a bunch of supernatural abilities along side your weapons such as sword, and crossbow.
You can complete the game by playing stealth and not beeing seen the entire time, or going on a killing spree and murdering everybody who stands in you way (or any middleway in between)
I can't really think of anything I dislike about this game, so it gets a definite recommendation from me.

Visually it's very stunning. The plot is great, and I love how choices affect the ending of the game. This way you can keep replaying the game to get different outcomes, without it getting boring. Highly recommend this game!

In Dunwall, a city marred by corruption, political machinations, and a devastating rat plague, you play as Corvo Attano, protector to the Empress. After a long voyage to seek aid from other nations, you are finally back at home. Something has changed, however. From the dark alleys where gangs reign supreme to the brothels where the rich seek an ephemeral escape, an atmosphere of fear and suspicion has settled in.
As you deliver the correspondence from the other nations to the Empress, your world shatters in a brief moment. With the blood of a nation staining your hands, only you can decide how you will seek your vengeance.
took me a bit by surprise, in ways both good and bad. It’s built on strong foundations--it’s set in a beautiful dystopian, steampunk world with a rich backstory, yet fails to execute in several areas. Ultimately, an unsatisfactory storyline, stifling gameplay, and a lack of direct interaction with the world renders what could have been a masterpiece into “just” a great game.
The world
has created is a breath of fresh air and it’s quite frankly the main reason the game was able to hold my attention. Much of the story is revealed not through exposition, but through exploration of the world itself (books scattered across levels, guard conversations, letters, locations). But sadly, this is going to be missed by a lot of players.
With sneaky side routes for stealth players and sprawling hubs for the more aggressive players,
provides the means for a wide range of gameplay styles. Aesthetically, the level design coincides perfectly with the world’s grim setting; ostentatiously adorned mansions provide a stark contrast to the muddied slums in which survivors and weepers reside, and the architecture blends traditional British housing and steampunk elements beautifully.
Although the characters of
have been written and voice acted quite well, they lack in depth and development, ultimately rendering most of them forgettable; the admiral is predictably self-righteous and evidently power hungry; Martin, who I thought would get more development after his rescue, is static and in fact, gets practically no screen time; Emily is a bit more fleshed out, but again, there are very few interactions with her; Lord Pendleton is actually quite funny and realistic in his morality; Sam, the boatman, was surprisingly the character I felt most attached to. The cast isn’t bad, but it’s nothing deserving of high praise.
At first, I was delighted when I saw the vast arsenal of weapons and powers presented to me. However, when I learned that killing enemies contributes to a high chaos level, an integrated mechanic of the game, and that a high chaos levels equates to a bad ending, I was disappointed to find myself being practically forced to stealth through the game. While some would argue that it is your choice to fight or stealth, I am willing to bet most players will want a happy (or at least happier) ending.
For having such a beautifully crafted world, I expected an equally tantalizing story. Unfortunately, the story has been wholly predictable thus far--I am still playing through the game--and rather generic. It’s nothing revolutionary, but what it does, it does fairly well.
Now the bad. The AI in this game are so incredibly blind and deaf that I laughed on many occasions. I’ve walked into wide open spaces in daylight and gone completely unseen by four or five guards many times. Just because I’m crouched shouldn’t mean that I’m practically invisible. Additionally, if an enemy sees you, and you manage to hide behind something, he’ll just stumble about for a few seconds and give up his pursuit. But if, god forbid, you hit an enemy in any way, he’ll call every single guard in the vicinity over to your position. So yeah, bad AI.
For a game that pushes you to be stealthy, you’d figure the sound would be good. It’s decent at best in this game and at times, horrid. Sometimes, I’d find myself hearing the footsteps of guards in other rooms. Also, conversations don’t fade out realistically, instead, they just halt abruptly as you walk away.
In some of the levels, you do interact with the world (and it’s usually done very well), but for the most part, it feels as though you’re playing in an empty world. Of course,  there is a rat plague beating away at the city’s population, but I’d imagine there would be more survivors, gang members, weepers, and guards. Also, where are the engineers fixing and maintaining the city’s circuits? Where are the fishermen who provide the city with its whale oil? It feels as though the game is trying to convince you that the world is alive and breathing, but with such weak interaction with npcs, I wasn’t convinced.
is a great game that provides players with a beautiful world to explore and a rich backstory. Unfortunately, the story and cast are unable to take advantage of this brilliance. Poor AI coupled with the game’s aggressive push towards the player using stealth and a general lack of interaction with the world lead to the game falling short of being a masterpiece.

I bought this game for £15, I have 300+ hours in this game. That means for every pound i spent on this game i got atleast  20 hours of game time. That being said, I think this is a great game for people who enjoy strategy games, or enjoy things like World War 2 (or even conflicts that happened before/after with mods, some even let you play in 2017, and even further)!
The problem many people have had with this game is the DLCs. Together for Victory implemented a feature that many people have said should be in the base game. I think that is a valid argument - especially some features like the request a land lease from a country. I mainly bought the DLC for the main purpose of it being sold, which is the autonomy system and the added focus trees for the commonwealth nations. They're solid trees, allowing you to break free from the British or sticking by their side in the time of war. I also like the spearhead command, letting you encircle your enemies army easier. This also lets you make more precise, and complex, blitzkreig tactics the German's used in WW2.
One problem I faced in Hearts of Iron 4 was the AI; they didn't utilise their army. In every game I've played (except for multiplayer) I have not had to worry about garrisoning my mainland, just the coast to defend from naval invasions. This esentially made me able to put every single unit on the border and push, while the AI put most of their divisions garrisoning their capital and VPs, incase of my paratroopers.
Multiplayer is great fun in this game, if you can find a good group of people to play it with. I joined the Bokoen1 discord and have had many great laughs with the many people in it. Alot of the games weren't serious and were meant to provide fun, which most of them did. The biggest problem i faced in MP was the small chat box, almost everyone who used a mic didn't pay attention to it. I liked the way the chat worked in EU4, you would see what someone wrote without even opening the chat, it would usually be in the top left/right corners. I think that this would be great implemented into HOI4.

Ghost Recon: Wildlands is a co-op open world game where you and up to three buddies can take on the Santa Blanca Cartel, across a fictionalized version of Bolivia where this massive organization has essentially taken over the country. You and your team of Ghosts can systematically take down piece by piece. All at your own pace, the game doesn't guide you by the hand past the first zone. Recently, the game also includes a PvP component. Ghost War, a 4v4 class based tactical elimination gamemode. Is it worth your time? Well read on to find out.
Pros
-Immersion. Top notch if you let it. Or not, you can ignore the story and just kill these bad dudes.
-You can do this, by blowing up, knocking out, shooting, or stealthily taking down the cartel.
-Some members of the Cartel are actual characters and you can change the outcome of the story based on how you take down the Cartel.
-Loads of firearms and gunsmith to customize your guns. You can carry two large guns, and a pistol on you at all times.
_> Gunsmith: You can make any gun better suit your playstyle with a large amount of attachments.
-Lots of objectives and things to collect. The world is actually very much realized for what it is. Easily 50 hours of content.
-Gunplay is chunky and feels good in both PvE and PvP.
_> Why? Ballistics. The game utilizes an exaggerated bullet drop system where bullets fly 3x slower than in real-life. This makes bullets feel weighty and makes the gunplay more skillful.
-The game looks amazing in some spots, and can feel like you are going on a vacation in Bolivia sometimes.
-Both stealth, and brute force are valid tactics.
-Loads of vehicles, super cars, helicopters, planes, jeeps, armored personnel carriers, and trucks with miniguns on them.
-PvP has a role for many play styles. Teamplay can really make or break a team composition.
Neutrals
-Average character creator, it's passable. You can operate in proper tactical gear, or you can walk around in a t-shirt and jeans.
-Game is HUGE, both in map size, and in real estate on your hard drive. This is a double edged sword.
_>Map has 21 regions, and 11 different biomes from the desert, to swamps, forests and even snowy mountain tops.
_>Game is about 50 gigabytes big.
-Co-op can get slightly monotonous for some people. As there are a set amount of objectives.
-PvP is currently only elimination. Across 8 distinct maps. There are 12 classes, that keep the game fresh.
-Some missions autofail, if a player is seen. These can be annoying if you aren't good at hiding.
Cons
-Game needs a bit of optimization. And by a bit I mean quite a bit. Most PCs, cannot sustain a solid 60 fps.
-Crashes tend to occur if you have an antivirus that the game doesn't like.
-Has a few odd bugs, physics based usually. Falling through the world sometimes, etc.
-Sometimes hangups occur, and the game may not register certain things like launched grenades.
-Very odd bug, where your teammates aren't shown where they actually actually are. I've had this happen in both PvP and PvE.
-PvP can be a tad bit imbalanced toward higher leveled players, because they have access to more classes. For example, the Medic character is unavailable from the beginning and has a very powerful abilty to revive a player from a distance.
Feel free to ask questions in the comments. Overall I give the game a solid 8/10 it has it's problems, but what game doesn't? I'd say that you should definitely pick this game up, and on sale this game is an absolute steal. There's a lot of fun to be had in the Wildlands. Good luck out there, Ghosts.

A lot of negative critique of this game seems to be based on the poor rewards given to players who bought the game while it was a exclusively a paid product. While that is a fair point and something noteworthy to returning players, basing entire reviews on this point alone is mostly irrelevant to new players. And, really, the game was on its last legs. The product you paid for is getting a breath of new life that has real effort behind it, and a real chance to stick around. That's something most games don't get. But, yes, owners of various editions of the original game should be compensated far better, that's a given.
Now, the game itself? I'll admit, I've run out of steam and mostly wrote this review as a result of seeing so much discussion based purely on how owners of the paid game got ripped off. Evolve plays a bit like competitive Left 4 Dead, with the monster in the survivors' shoes and the hunters in the zombies'. The game seems to favour the monster right now, but I hear that that will change after the initial free to play release. The progression model seems reasonable so far, and as of the time of this review no payment model exists. A promising (re-)release, if a mixed bag.

One of the greatest driving games, that sadly you may never play. I have owned this game a little over 3 weeks and have made/met 18 of the coolest friends in that short time plus an absolute bucket load of friends using the retail version.
I'll cut to the bad news first. Firstly you have to make an account at
to be able to play this game and to buy DLC. Secondly, Eden games made this and unfortunately for what ever reson went belly-up. Atari luckily stepped in and took the game over but clearly they haven't got the server side stuff in control.
This means you get things like:
- Losing friends out of your profile and then sometimes they re-appear.
- You can buy DLC and then have them turn into mardi gras pink mustangs ( no joke they are vehicles won through a one on one duel with a campaign progress character).

- If you want to get the casino and or drive a range of cars and bikes you have to buy Atari points at the TDU2 website which is a turn off for many people to say the least because it can be tedious although myself, I never had any issues with it.
The Casino DLC is $10AUD and cars work out to be $1AUD each @ $5AUD for 400 Atari points (Pay by Paypal for less hassle).
These things are the worst parts of the game and some come and go as mentioned.
Great things about the game:
- You drive in an open world and work your way through getting licenses for different classes of vehicles and events on the islands of Ibiza and Hawaii.
- Meet a lot of great people and make friends with people all over the world (personally I dont even have a problem with non english players) I just ask them, 'you use Steam? Add me as friend :)' even if they don't use the Steam version some make Steam accounts and add the game to non-Steam shortcuts. Then its easy, the add me and I have Google Translate open in the Steam in game browser so they can talk to me in their own language outside of in game chat, problem solved! :)
- Did I mention Bikes? :D
- Huge amount of Cars (some are DLC), unfortunately only 3 Bikes (DLC), huge array of clothing and customisations to your character by the use of plastic surgeon and to your cars by paintshops and tuning upgrades, a Casino and many properties that you can buy to house your vehicles. I dedicate this review to all the great people I have met in the game, they 'make' the game in my opinion. Also I'm going to put up some of the screenshots I have and will hopefully get the time to make a Youtube tribute to the game if not also my friends. In Dunwall, a city marred by corruption, political machinations, and a devastating rat plague, you play as Corvo Attano, protector to the Empress. After a long voyage to seek aid from other nations, you are finally back at home. Something has changed, however. From the dark alleys where gangs reign supreme to the brothels where the rich seek an ephemeral escape, an atmosphere of fear and suspicion has settled in.
As you deliver the correspondence from the other nations to the Empress, your world shatters in a brief moment. With the blood of a nation staining your hands, only you can decide how you will seek your vengeance.
took me a bit by surprise, in ways both good and bad. It’s built on strong foundations--it’s set in a beautiful dystopian, steampunk world with a rich backstory, yet fails to execute in several areas. Ultimately, an unsatisfactory storyline, stifling gameplay, and a lack of direct interaction with the world renders what could have been a masterpiece into “just” a great game.
The world
has created is a breath of fresh air and it’s quite frankly the main reason the game was able to hold my attention. Much of the story is revealed not through exposition, but through exploration of the world itself (books scattered across levels, guard conversations, letters, locations). But sadly, this is going to be missed by a lot of players.
With sneaky side routes for stealth players and sprawling hubs for the more aggressive players,
provides the means for a wide range of gameplay styles. Aesthetically, the level design coincides perfectly with the world’s grim setting; ostentatiously adorned mansions provide a stark contrast to the muddied slums in which survivors and weepers reside, and the architecture blends traditional British housing and steampunk elements beautifully.
Although the characters of
have been written and voice acted quite well, they lack in depth and development, ultimately rendering most of them forgettable; the admiral is predictably self-righteous and evidently power hungry; Martin, who I thought would get more development after his rescue, is static and in fact, gets practically no screen time; Emily is a bit more fleshed out, but again, there are very few interactions with her; Lord Pendleton is actually quite funny and realistic in his morality; Sam, the boatman, was surprisingly the character I felt most attached to. The cast isn’t bad, but it’s nothing deserving of high praise.
At first, I was delighted when I saw the vast arsenal of weapons and powers presented to me. However, when I learned that killing enemies contributes to a high chaos level, an integrated mechanic of the game, and that a high chaos levels equates to a bad ending, I was disappointed to find myself being practically forced to stealth through the game. While some would argue that it is your choice to fight or stealth, I am willing to bet most players will want a happy (or at least happier) ending.
For having such a beautifully crafted world, I expected an equally tantalizing story. Unfortunately, the story has been wholly predictable thus far--I am still playing through the game--and rather generic. It’s nothing revolutionary, but what it does, it does fairly well.
Now the bad. The AI in this game are so incredibly blind and deaf that I laughed on many occasions. I’ve walked into wide open spaces in daylight and gone completely unseen by four or five guards many times. Just because I’m crouched shouldn’t mean that I’m practically invisible. Additionally, if an enemy sees you, and you manage to hide behind something, he’ll just stumble about for a few seconds and give up his pursuit. But if, god forbid, you hit an enemy in any way, he’ll call every single guard in the vicinity over to your position. So yeah, bad AI.
For a game that pushes you to be stealthy, you’d figure the sound would be good. It’s decent at best in this game and at times, horrid. Sometimes, I’d find myself hearing the footsteps of guards in other rooms. Also, conversations don’t fade out realistically, instead, they just halt abruptly as you walk away.
In some of the levels, you do interact with the world (and it’s usually done very well), but for the most part, it feels as though you’re playing in an empty world. Of course,  there is a rat plague beating away at the city’s population, but I’d imagine there would be more survivors, gang members, weepers, and guards. Also, where are the engineers fixing and maintaining the city’s circuits? Where are the fishermen who provide the city with its whale oil? It feels as though the game is trying to convince you that the world is alive and breathing, but with such weak interaction with npcs, I wasn’t convinced.
is a great game that provides players with a beautiful world to explore and a rich backstory. Unfortunately, the story and cast are unable to take advantage of this brilliance. Poor AI coupled with the game’s aggressive push towards the player using stealth and a general lack of interaction with the world lead to the game falling short of being a masterpiece.

Every once in a while, you run into something that challenges your expectations in ways you couldn’t have possibly expected. It wears the surface layer like a wolf in pigeon’s clothing, promising a few quick laughs through the trappings of a dolled up Visual Novel featuring an all-bird cast. And if you were to think of it as nothing more, what with all of the pink upholstery and hearts surrounding every element of the game’s outward presentation, then no one could blame you. But it also counts on this charade to drag the player into something beneath its skin. Hatoful Boyfriend is indeed a game about attending an all-bird high school as the only human in the academy. Yet, if one cares to look above, they’ll see a murder of crows circling overhead.
Hatoful Boyfriend will appear familiar to anyone who has played a Visual Novel or two. Once you’ve started a new game, it will ask for your name, introduce you to the majority of characters in a warm and friendly environment, and generally settle you into daily life at St. PigeoNation. Navigation works similarly to the thousands which have come before it. You progress forward by clicking or hitting enter as a dialog box completes to display the next one and advance the story, occasionally make a selection to build your stats or guide which bird you will chase for their affection. There’s also the option to save and load, as well as alter some basic settings, and a convenient fast-forward button in the upper corner, should you wish to skip over dialog you’ve already seen. And of course, branching paths which all lead to their own endings, all depending on choices you make.
The first trick Hatoful Boyfriend pulls out of its hat is how short a single run can last. The very first run I completed took me about an hour in total, which draws the player in, promising quick trips down alternative paths to collect all of the pigeon husbando~ hearts. This is exactly what it wants you to do. Only going through the game once wouldn’t allow for the seams in the feathered costume begin to show, so it pushes you towards seeking every han- er, wing, you possibly can. With every successful unique ending, you’re rewarded with curious snippets in the “archive” section in the main menu. Between the diary entries and newspaper clippings, it’s trying to warn you. Only, we’re too occupied as players staring at the plumes of tail feathers to see the forest for the trees.
And it’s hard not to. The game’s use of standard visual novel/anime characterizations intelligently manipulates the player into wanting to chase down the Tsundere French transfer student, the plucky best friend you’ve known since you were both younger, the goth kid who speaks a language all his own, and even the creepy one who mutters statements under his breath that would be admissible evidence in court. Down each path, there’s plenty of humorous dialog and heart-tugging character development. The fact that they are all birds instead of humans or anime portraits just pulls the covers over your eyes when the real drama finally hits. They’re all entertainingly written, even if they stay extremely close to the tropes that birthed them. Let’s not allow the down comforter to be pulled over our eyes though. Several of the paths lean heavily into exposing Hatoful Boyfriend’s big secret, which is given to the player after certain endings have been cleared.
BBL mode, known as “Bad Boys Love”, is what Hatoful Boyfriend is really building towards. All of the characters you meet, all of the interactions you have, they all lead down the path towards BBL mode’s story. To explain what exactly BBL is would be to spoil the true meat and potatoes of the game, and thus I can’t in good conscience actually explain it to you. Even if I did tell you, in great detail, what it is and what happens during it, there’s no way you’d actually believe me. It is a much bigger bird than the others, with secrets tucked between every feather. I’ve seen many reviews not even mention it in fear of spoiling it but I feel as though that isn’t enough to truly entice someone into playing the game. Much like Hatoful Boyfriend’s tricks, I have spent most of this review building up to BBL mode simply to get you interested in what lies beyond that cage door. In order for you to discover the truth, however, you’ll have to spread your wings on your own.
It might just be because I let my guard down from the pigeon-centric cast but Hatoful Boyfriend left me feeling shaken. What I’d gone through was both hilarious and frightening at the same time. Just keep your wits about you, reinforce your constitution, and carve it into your soul. Hatoful Boyfriend is not just a dating sim where your boyfriends all have winged limbs and beaks. It’s an example of playing to the strengths and comforts of a genre while turning convention on its head to have the stork deliver a story so full of twists that it took me 3 sheets of paper and small handwriting to keep track of it all.
