Rift hit the massively multiplayer online scene a few years ago and since it has become one of the largest and most popular games of the genre. Rift is a free, micro-transaction based game set in a high fantasy world. Rift established a few boundaries that other massively multiplayer online games have done well to copy. Some of the most fundamental things that Rift did different – and did right include a free to play structure, the limiting of abilities to a more refined, limited selection and also the addition of an interactive and evolving game-world. These things have established Rift as a pathfinder in the market and make it a sturdy title to contend with.
Though originally for a foreign audience, Rift was repackaged for westerners due to demand. The game allows for extensive customization of your avatar as well as plenty of micro-transactions which are purely for aesthetic appeal. This becomes one of the biggest gripes most gamers tend to have, that distinction must be “bought.” Even though by no means does the game require you to purchase anything to play, the cash store and micro-transactions are present to make the game profitable. People complain that micro-transactions destroy the game and make you spend excessive amounts of money on the game – but let's take a step back and examine the situation. Micro-transactions ensure that you only pay for content you're going to use, or at least want and generally a few little purchases dwarfs in comparison to shelling out the full retail price for the game package and a monthly subscription cost. Micro-transactions are good for players and game producers alike.
Another are that Rift excels in is the open world environment which invites you to explore and experiment. As the name of the game implies, rifts to other dimensions can be opened in the world – sometimes willingly sometimes spontaneously. Generally rifts are conquered by players to gain rewards, but sometimes if left to its own devices a rift might grow and begin to call in reinforcement troops which will assault towns, players and other rifts. This dynamic creates a totally different feel to the game, because normally titles in this genre have a rule of thumb that the world itself is pretty unchangeable by the players. Though you're not exactly reshaping the world with developer's tools, being able to open and close rifts gives you a sense of mastery of environment not seen elsewhere.
Another concept adopted and brought forward by Rift is the reduction of abilities and the simplification of controls. Recently, even big names such as World of Warcraft have taken steps to remove abilities and simplify gameplay. If anyone has ever compared the difference between abilities in older massively multiplayer online games and newer titles, one notices that newer titles only offer a limited selection of active abilities which can be changed but never giving the player an excess of options. For the casual player your head literally could spin trying to remember all of the abilities, commands, keybinds and micros found in more classic massively multiplayer online titles. Streamlined abilities are what make this game great and easy to pick up and play by even casual gamers.
The graphics are crisp and inspiring, definitely with the quality level expected for a game of modern times. Of course being on a personal computer engine, largely the graphics will depend on your settings but with maxed out specifications the game itself is stunning. Even on lower settings, the quality and attention to detail brought to the plate are sure to impress. Textures aren't everything though, animations are smooth, monsters are imaginative yet still fitting and the scenery and terrain are world class. Similar detail is also seen in the audio of the game, going into great detail to make sure ever effect has the right sound and that the melodies are peppered with dramatic but suitable overtures serving to further immerse one into the also visually stunning environment.
Sometimes the worlds of online multiplayer gaming can be threatening or maybe just a little intimidating. For the casual console gamer of the past, when looking at a massively multiplayer online game one is probably reminded of a dungeons and dragons setup. Without sacrificing depth and the details many online gamers do like, Rift gives casual players an opportunity to enjoy the genre as well. Because it does not require any purchases, its easy for anyone to gain access to the game and try it out. Newer players will be drawn in by the content and ease of play the streamlined abilities offer. Though it is a step into definite nerddom I definitely recommend Rift to anyone interested. It's free after all, give it a try! If you would like a chance to play for free, be sure to check it out!

I bought this game for a friend for christmas. To start with we were wowed by the graphics. But it didnt take long for the initial glossy veneer to fade. Let me first say i like survival games of this ilk like Ark that have steep learning curves. But this game takes a starting grind and turns it into a horrible hateful unnecessarily grindy direction.
You initially spawn into a random area in the gameworld and then proceed to collect planetary resources that are needed to improve your basecamp. But while you are collecting the required items you are constantly being plagued by aliens who are ludicrously hard to hit because of terrible hitboxes surrounding them.  This would be fine if you could outwit the enemy AI or use different tactics or manouvers to kill the enemy or covertly hide in your starter dome from them. But when three or 4 mobs randomly spawn next to you even if you manage to hide in your starter dome the creatures seem to be able to clip into your small dome and hit you even when the door is closed, after trying a few tactics the best you can hope for is to just die and hope the alien moves on or despawns so you can loot your body. If you manage to venture out too far and lose your body completely whilst out foraging you lose your guns and any items you were carrying. This makes the game even harder and frustrating when starting out after you respawn. Should you be unfortunate enough to lose your starter guns its a super long grind to get enough supplies to build the crafting station equipment needed to replace even the lowliest starter pistol gun......
Add to this a AI droid companion that is buggy / gets stuck or  disappears completely in the gameworld from time to time for no reason and you have a game that is just way too frustrating to put your time into. If the devs are reading this please please allow noobs to at least respawn with the pistol when they die when initially starting out.  Also try to make the starting out grind just that little bit easier. Its one thing for a game to be challenging because it requires skill but this games failings just made me want to uninstall rather than spend my time grinding for the sake of grinding.
TLDR : it looks great but has a lot of bugs and is frustratingly hard for all the wrong reasons

If you are a big Xcom fan like I am, you will consider this a more than fine addition to the Xcom Franchise -- although it is a significant departure from the "canon" of the other games. Set in the 50s, It pits the protagonist and two squad-mates against an alien invasion with WW2 weaponry until you can capture the weapons of your foes. Your squad mates can be different classes, and develop cool powers over time, which should allow for different play styles, but sadly there is little motivation to swap between your favorite (and most experienced) soldiers most of the time. Graphics are cool, power implementation is cool, and you can "bullet time" at any point in combat to decide exactly what your squad does (and positioning as well as skill management MATTERS) but the time does not go SO slowly that you don't have to think fast to avoid trouble (cooking grenades, sudden flanking) -- combat is fun and really makes you think... I drew satisfaction both from pitched battles and finding clever solutions to situations. The story is engaging, in a genre where there's been enough retread over the same types of mysterious baddies this game has a novel take on the enemy -- they are both worthy of wanting to understand, contempt, and fear. Types of enemies are QUITE varied, too.
The Bad?: Game is pretty linear, though tries not to be. Squad size a step back from every other Xcom game. No research or Alien Autopsy (which is arguably one of the cooler elements of Xcom) though there IS some alien interrogation.
Overall, a pretty spiffy game that is fun to play and has a cool story and it's own flavor. Both different enough to be novel, and familiar enough to please the Xcom fan. No regrets here, great squad-based 3rd-person tactical.

Hatoful Boyfriend is a game where you go to bird school, which is for birds (and you, a human), and you date a bunch of different pigeons (or quails, or even a java sparrow) over a series of eight different routes. The game is relatively short in this aspect! I was surprised by how quickly I was getting through each route--even with fourteen endings to get (some sweet, some sad, some downright horrifying), the game itself feels surprisingly short.
However, this is likely because completing specific routes unlocks the other "half" of the game, as such--a more straight-up visual novel that reveals the secrets behind St. PigeoNation's (the school that you attend) and exemplifies some pretty excellent worldbuilding for what, on the surface, appears to be a game about dating birds. It also delves further into the backgrounds of each of the main characters and will emotionally destroy you.
The game has a few typos and questionably built sentences, but it's overall an enjoyable playing experience. The background art is pretty nice to look at and some of the music is so great I sort of regret not buying the collector's edition to get the soundtrack.
10/10, would let pigeons emotionally destroy me again.

Costume Quest with its add-on Grubbins on Ice is a nice Halloween-themed almost-RPG. It's, in one word, candy. I like candy.
I highly recommend using a controller with this game. Keyboard controls felt pretty odd.
Achievement Hint:
+ Creepy Treats (collectibles) design
+ Non-irritating but forgettable music
+ Back To The Future discovery sound
+ Costumes with exploration effects in addition to battle effects
+ Costume battle action design
0 no map
0 Mostly inconsequential Battle Stamps (buffs)
0 Level caps
- Incorrect Battle Stamp descriptions
- Pretty linear
- Almost consistently no challenge
- No description on save slots when loading
- After the main game we see the credits headlined "Grubbins on Ice"
Technically the game is about quasi-isometric exploration with battle intermezzi.
The battles are similar to those associated with RPG-Maker games or for example Final Fantasy 7 but instead of action meters there is simply a battle order. Without fail, first your up to three character attack, then the up to three enemies - repeat until defeat.
Although this may sound dry, the game is surprisingly fun. I played the game for maybe 11 hours, got stuck twice for a total of about 90 Minutes (misunderstood game mechanics in the beginning + final boss in the add-on) and it was entertaining enough to feel like around 4 hours.
This is mostly due to a number of good design decision. For me, the game wasn't so much about the main storyline but more about your party of characters speaking with each other, other inhabitants of the area and enemies, and it was about the battles. For some reason those things made me think, I'd like to play this in a Spongebob Squarepants world, at one point.
In order of relevance the advancements in the game are: gaining companions, completing new costumes and getting Battle Stamps. Ultimately progress in the game requires the player to win fights (actually you go trick-or-treating but half the time that results in fights) but there are a number of obstacles that require you to explore beforehand.
*Companions*
Companions come with a new costume and provide an extra action per round in battle.
*Costumes*
You get costumes with characters or you are given a blueprint which sort of tells you, by way of a somewhat indiscriminate outline, which three components/materials you need to complete the costume. Components are unique and can be found in more or less hidden treasure chests, given to you by inhabitants of the world, and maybe, I don't quite remember, be part of battle spoils. Once a costume is complete, it can be assigned to any of your characters.
Half of the costumes come with an Exploration Ability, i.e. an ability that can and (with the exception of one  costume in the add-on) must be used in the exploration part of the game. The most important ability is the Boost that you get with your very first costume. The Boost allows your party to speed across the area and is essential to the pacing of the game. At one point or another, the player is likely to miss something plus there is a little back and forth in the game anyway. Without the Boost ability that could have easily turned into a chore - very good design decision.
All of the costumes but one have a Combat Ability, i.e. a special that needs two battle rounds to load and can be executed instead of a normal attack.
Apart from having an effect on game-play the costumes just look cool. Even if there wasn't an achievement connected to that I'd still recommend to take every costume into battle at least once. I simply like the progression of the costumes from the materials you have to collect over the (not really) crappy "not quite there" or "Dad did the best he could" design of the costume as the characters are wearing it in exploration mode to the awesome "this is how the kids see it" (or maybe "this is what adult think how the kids see it") design in battle, character design and attacks.
*Buffs*
Battle Stamps are buffs that can be assigned to your party's characters, one each. Buffs include boosts to health, defence, dodging, counter-attacks, the over-powerful stun and the underwhelming auto-revive - usually buffs are passive. I basically stuck to the same buffs throughout the game, occasionally upgrading when a better version of the buff turned up.
Unfortunately, some of the buffs have misleading descriptions, most irritatingly the auto-revive is supposed to revive a character after one round. While this is technically correct a more apt description would explain, the character is revived after two rounds (one round after one round, see?). I only ever tried the buff when I had trouble with the final boss in the add-on and having a character inactive for two rounds is just unacceptable in that fight.
*Collectibles*
The Creepy Treats are mostly just nice-to-have. You collect them mainly as battle spoils and sometimes trade them with inhabitants. I guess they are mostly original ideas, e.g. Licorice Cables, Chocolate Hamburgers, Coconuts & Bolts, Misfortune Cookies.
*Battles*
As said before, each round in battle has your character(s) act first, then the up to three enemies. Usually, rounds go on until one side is defeated. In theory, there is an option to run away but I haven't tried it yet.
Each round each character chooses one of standard attack, the costume's Combat Ability (if ready) or the Battle Stamp buff (if active). Standard attacks have QTEs connected to them. There is a number of different QTEs, i.e. hitting a specific, dynamic button in time, hitting a specific, dynamic button on time, moving the left analogue stick around, and repeatedly pressing a specific, dynamic button. The type of QTE is dependent on the costume. If you pass the QTE, the character deals 50% more damage.
Combat Abilities need two rounds to load so they can be used every third round. They are usually a tactical option and it's not always useful to use them right away. For some reason, attack buffs do not affect Combat Abilities. This may even make the standard attack a preferable option overall.
Some Battle Stamp active buffs can be executed instead of a standard attack. Of those the most powerful are likely the different stun abilities which can take a single enemy out of the fight for up to two rounds. Except for bosses, the later game can be played without ever getting hit by an enemy. This is very powerful since even a "failed" enemy attack can take as much as 25% of a characters live away.
Some Combat Abilities can prevent almost all damage to characters.
Enemies mostly do standard attacks which lead to a defensive QTE which, on success, prevents half of the damage to the character. Magically inclined enemies can heal, buff attack or defence of one of the enemies.
Battles are pretty short and easy but fun, largely because of the costumes.
*Game Experience*
A few more words on the game. One of the rather negative aspects about the game is its linearity. Bring me this and that or you cannot go on, fight those guys or you cannot go on, complete a costume or you cannot go on. But this is well compensated by the entertainment factor.
Even though of limited use, I'd have liked a map to come with each area. This was sort of addressed in the add-on where you gain the ability to zoom out a bit with a costume.
The game was a bit on the easy side.
When loading/continuing a previous savestate the game doesn't tell you anything about the progress made. The game simply lists "Slot 1", "Slot 2" and "Slot 3". There isn't even an indication whether the slot actually contains any saved progress. This is a minor ugliness.
I had a lot of fun with Costume Quest and Grubbins on Ice and highly recommend the game. I'm looking forward to playing the sequel.

This is essentially a casual RPG for kids, but I'm reviewing it anyway as an adult.
Costume Quest is a very short turn-based RPG, but the highlight of its features are what it doesn't have. It's devoid of pretty much any interesting game system. The slim turn-based combat system present is similar to the Final Fantasy games, but you'll get more depth out of Final Fantasy games or 99% of their copycats. All of the combat uses Quick Time Events as well, which gets old after the second or third combat encounter. Game balance is simple and a little skewed. The game can be difficult (but hardly) when you only have two party members, and its trivially easy once you have three.
The overworld is linear. There's a tiny bit of exploration to be had, but not much. There are roughly four quests in the entire game, each repeated several times for each phase of the game: find a card off a monster (combat encounters), bob for apples (simple mini-game), trick or treat houses (random combat encounters), and find six hiding kids (semi-hidden on overworld).
The game crashed a few times, and since there is no manual save feature at any time, I lost 15-20 minutes of progress each time. The game plays the same every time.
There are costumes to get, which are your battle suits or "classes". Variation here is only relevant in the costume's "special ability" but the game is so easy that once you have three party members, battle strategy matters little.
Graphics meh, sound meh, witty dialogue is OK but not astounding. No voice acting.
I don't recommend this game. You can find much better games in all of its genres for cheaper.  If you insist on wanting it, it's worth $2-3 on a sale perhaps. My playtime says 16 hours but that included a long idling session by accident. It's a 5-7 hour game.

The game has unfortunately been a major flop.
I have been been a long-time Paradox fan and follower of the HOI franchise, however it seems that Paradox is beginning to abandon the initial principles which built the grand strategy franchise for which it is renown.
While previous Paradox games have received major expansions and updates which genuinely improved the quality of gameplay, AI and historical immersion; notable examples being the likes of Art of War and the Old Gods from previous games, Paradox's newer games have shown a very evident decline in quality. It seems that Hearts of Iron 4 is the most recent example of this, coupled with the recent abysmal quality DLC for EU4 that added no real content and ultimately further damaged and unbalanced the overall gameplay. Rather than genuinely improving the game, Paradox instead shows a very blatant half-arsed effort in which most of the world's leaders don't even have actual portraits, many nations don't even have named parties (such as Czechoslovakia, who despite just getting a DLC, still has a fascist party called "Fascist" with an ahistorical leader). In addition, Paradox's most recent patch completely ruined the game as it broke the generic focus trees, thus causing all non-custom focus trees to "retire" the country's leader (which is the VAST majority of countries by the way). The game has very few events and different paths to take, with little to no flavour (bar about three news events in the first four years of the game) - all references to Nazi plans are completely omited along with the Swastika, which could have easily been added along with the DLC which added a Hitler portrait for non-German players - instead, Paradox actively bans people who dare to criticse this on their forums, going so far as to ban mod authors who post Swastikas on the forums from their mods. Even the likes of Wolfenstein and Call of Duty has not stooped to these levels in the past, yet a company prided on its accurate representation of history outright refuses to depict history? They even got the flags for countries such as Japan, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Hungary wrong...
This doesn't even mention the abysmal gameplay, which is simply FAR TOO EASY. I cannot emphasise just how simplistic and easy this game is - it is quite literally possible to turn the likes of Albania into a global superpower through very simple methods. There is no diversity of gameplay at all, and it has taken them a whole year to fix the air interface which was equally terrible, as it still poses no real difference - I can play many-a-game forgetting to even touch my airforce with very little difference. The political management of countries is far too easy as well, as the "boost party" system is completely unbalanced, as the AI will never use it or attempt to start coups, while simultaneously not even bothering to in anyway oppose any attempts by the player to boost. A German player can simply flip the USA to fascism if they begin boosting from the start - it's shocking. The mod Kasierreich seemingly combats the easiness of the game by adding many events and playing with the game mechanics quite successfully - yet apparently Paradox is unable to do the same to their own game.
In conclusion, it seems evident that Paradox is growing increasingly greedy, lazy and EA-esque as time goes on. Instead of producing high quality, large encompassing DLCs, they instead pump out tiny little sub-standard focus tree packs that lock little game mechanics behind pay walls that should've been in the game initially. It seems that they have become reliant on modders to fix their own game and add new content rather than actually doing it themselves.

While parts of this game are enjoyable, the lack of a functional AI means that even basic strategies make you seem like Rommel due to the ineptness of your enemies. If by some miracle the enemy decides toa ctually man the front against you, they will inevitabely ignore any opportunities coming their way, instead choosing to send the bulk of their forces by sea towards the nearest hostile fleet.
This game has so much potential, but until they fix the AI (already a year in development with no progress), this game is not worth buying.

This game is more of a Walking Simulator than anything, with its gameplay being very limited as you slowly plod along throughout creepy environments, with minimal stealth elements requiring you hide from cult members in a variety of locales, ranging from dank, dreary dungeon areas to creepy cabins on hillsides, the locales in the game vary often which make it feel like you are progressing through a storyline rather than just sitting around one place for too long.
The heavy camera effects (similar to a VHS tape thats lost its tracking) as well as the constant white noise, and beeping, clicking sounds (also trying to reflect a tape, hence the game's title... ) can be very jarring and off-putting at first, however, I have gotten used to them and think they add to the game's overall intentionally (??) cheap, tongue-in-cheek, Nosferatu / silent film esque quality. That being said, many people may find the game's overall slow pace combined with the very grating effects as too much to handle and not enjoy the experience at all.
What audio is present in the game is very well done and immersive with eerie, subtle sounds from your surroundings emanating as you slowly creep through the environments. Though a personal preference, I'm glad the player character remains silent, with no repetitive "breathing / startled" sound effects or narration affecting how immersed you become. There is very little voice acting in the game aside from the occasional scream, lurch, or moan from NPCs during the gameplay or cutscenes, leaving much of the cutscenes and characters up to the player's interpretation, for better or for worse.
The game often presents macabre, surreal situations to the player including torsos popping out of bloody beds or cult members shuffling along distant bridges while carrying torches. The game does a good job of making you dread what you will see or run into around corners, but is less reliant on jump-scares than other horror titles. The game (thus far) has instead opted for a slower, more sinister feeling as you explore its dark corridors.
The game is very limited in its options and the save system seems checkpoint-based, with no user determination of when it saves (or where it loads) other than a vague "continue" option at the start. Also, the heavy video effect is either set to on or off, with the off option looking quite bland. The character models during cutscenes also clearly show their limited complexity, with textures and model complexity resembling more of a PS2 era level of detail. Its hard not to find some of the cutscenes as comical when the models of the characters are so simplistic, such as one where a character's bones and joints are popping out of place but the model looks more like a doll than anything super realistic.

While this game's pace, effects, and somewhat simplistic / vague cutscenes may turn off many players, I am enjoying the experience and think it's a good game in the Horror / Walking Simulator genres.

When people hear the term "games as art" they generally make the mistake of lumping everything into the same visual category. Sometimes art is in the form of a concept or idea and not just an optical quality, and it's in this sense that I highly regard Hatoful Boyfriend as a work of art. It takes a tired and cliched concept and reworks it into a thought provoking and never before seen idea that manages to be both humorously satirical and affectingly sentimental, causing the general public to reconsider and ponder the meaning of a mostly mocked genre.

Some may discount the games merits based on the corny puns, and these people miss the point entirely. What makes Hatoful Boyfriend so damn funny, so artfully clever, and so hard to stop smiling at is the overall concept of what's happening and the way the emotionally driven story is delivered. The idea of seeing such seriously toned dialogue combined with the strange and surreal imagery of a school of pigeons is wildly outside of the box, and to anyone with an imagination is at first incredibly entertaining. What really takes the player by surprise is the emotional draw the story has on you in the end for what at first was such a seemingly laughable and satirical plot.
Hatoful Boyfriend isn't just a satire or a mockery, it's not just one big comedic joke like some might intially believe. The characters are written well and manage to shine with more personality and.. humanity(?) than what we're used to seeing in the generally shallow world of anime dating sims, which is what makes the experience feel even more bizarre, strange, yet memorable given it's subject matter. It manages to feel more real and authentic than even the most sensible or conventional games in this form of interactive storytelling.
The strange feeling evoked by Hatoful Boyfriend of feeling a growing emotional attachment towards something so seemingly overlooked as a pigeon or bird in a video game is one I'll remember. People with no connection or empathy for the animal kingdom my find it hard to swallow the ongoings of St. Pigeonation and won't take away anything of value from this quirky change of pace needed in gaming, but those with an open mind and heart to the topic will come away with a new found respect and admiration for a species generally viewed as insignificant or often misunderstood.
If you're the type who isn't too concerned with artistic and strange new takes on old genres, or you're one of those gamer types who enjoys the same-old-same-old while fearing changes to the industry then by all means skip this and play what you usually play. For people who want something new in the medium and want to see differences to gaming that allow a wider variety of people into the world of interactive experiences we call games then Hatoful Boyfriend is something you'll want to check out.

In the first TDU game we had Hawaii/Oahu Island already, which is more or less a copy of the real Oahu Island! It is big, nice detailed, and the graphics are really not bad, it will take you a while to see everything! In TDU2 we have an updated version of the same Oahu Island map, plus Ibiza! Ibiza is even more detailed and really nice for slow exploring, while Hawaii is nicer for lot of fast racing and cruising with friends!
CAREER & ONLINE
The career is implented to the online game (where you can play single player if you change your setting to not "allow online interactions!", start your game online and after that you can play it single player whenever you want) If the server is really not available, you still can play your online account offline!
You'll have a lot to do to progress in level, win races and championship against the computer, race online against others, both has different race modes (race, time race, knockout race, offroad, street, bike)! Also you progress the game by all kind of other things, make friends, buy cars, buy houses, buy clothes, or a new hairstyle for your character, everything gets you up in level! Yes, i know.. it is a racing game and some people don't like such things in a racing game, people always find a reason to cry!
- online & offline play (cruise with up to 8 player in one session)
while you cruise around the island the game puts you in 'sessions' with people close to you, you can lock yourself to another player so while the game changes the session, you will stay in one session with the player you locked to!
- two huge and detailed islands (Hawaii is even 4 times bigger than Ibiza)
What can i say, it will take you ages until you have seen all roads, and offroads!
- cars and (dlc) bikes
Bikes are only available as DLC, and only 3 of them, some more cars you can get as DLC too! Some cars you unlock by finding wrecks of them around the two islands! Also, the Casino is a DLC, you can win money or cars at slot machines or play Poker Texas Hold'Em with other players!
- race, create races, challanges..
A lot to do! Of course it is more fun to race against other players, but be carefull, don't bet too much money! The single player races are really (too) easy, a good way to make money for cars and houses and progress in level!
-make friends, invite them to you home, race them, create a club, club racing, even have your friends with you in your car as Co-driver! Or just cruise with them, or alone.. there are different type of players, you will find the hardcore driver who only cruise with class A cars and burn their tires on oahu all time, some player prefer driving a real style.. even using indicator! And of course we have the noobies who crash you as a way of saying hi - i love you too but stop scratching my damn car!
- Day/Night cycle, weather
Damn, driving offroad in a thunderstorm looks really good!
If you like cars, open world, online gaming, huge game worlds, and spending lot of time in a game, TDU2 is really for you! The game is not perfect, but still awesome! No real handling like other leading racing games, but more freedom than every other racing game! And no, the handling is not that bad.. i think its still better than most other racing games, as i said somewhere between arcade and real!
The only game i have played more than TDU2 was the first TDU (and back a decade, operation flashpoint!)
I am sure i forgot to mention something, but let me tell you if you are thinking about buying the game and having daubts, leave the daubts aside and give it a go, if you are interested in this game then it wont disapoint you!

Full Review:
Ubisoft have had a bit of a troubled past for me. The Assassins Creed series took a nose dive after the first few titles, and it seems they are absolutely flooding the market with game after game and to be honest I can't keep up (nor do I want to anymore).
And while I've played a few of the Tom Clancy titles, I wasn't holding out much hope for Wildlands after reading a significant number of people talking about the famous "rinse and repeat". Then came the play free weekend, topped with a 20% discount if you buy direct from Uplay, and I now own a copy of the game.
It's true, if you play the game mission after mission, I can see why it would feel like the old rinse and repeat is coming back, but that's only seems true to me if you rush through the missions/side missions one after the other eager to complete the game in record time.
I've spent countless hours (19) just wandering around the streets looking at stuff, driving around, collecting items you need to unlock weapons and skills, and I've been in awe of the views and landscapes this has to offer. I've tried all the different settings, and this is packed full of them - from easy/normal/hard/extreme difficulty to a highly customisable HUD (or no HUD at all if you want complete emersion).
The characters are often amusing and your squad cracks jokes when you aren't in combat or just hanging around. The whole feel of the game for me is superb, and a credit to the Ubisoft franchise. And what day doesn't feel a bit rinse and repeat... we do something different to make each day different and I see no reason why this shouldn't be applied here.
If you see this on sale again and appreciate 3rd person shooters (1st person when right mouse button held) then grab yourself a decent shooter. It's definitely one of my more recent favs of Ubisoft's
Thanks for reading - Enjoy!

Costume Quest is another wonderfully comedic game from Tim Schafer's Double Fine.
You start the game playing as one of the two twins: the brother Reynold, or the sister Wren. On your quest for trick or treating and making friends in your new town, you discover monsters called Repugians, who kidnap the sibling that you didn't pick. Equipped with only your home-made Halloween costumes, battle stamps, and the candy you collect, you and your new friends battle the Repugians to get your twin back.
This has to be one of the more original games that I've come across in a long time. Each costume that you collect has different abilities in and out of battles. When in battles, the abilites are either healing, defensive, or offensive, and out of battle they help you navigate the various puzzles you'll find within the neighbourhoods you visit.
The battles are turn based, and the animations themselves are wonderful. At the start of each battle, a small cutscene shows your lead character transforming from a simple costumed child, into the actual monster their costume represents. Each monster's special move also has a cutscene whereafter you must complete a quick-time-event to maximize it's power. The battles do get a little repetitive by the time you finish the game, but the overworld puzzles, exploration, and humour should keep you going just fine.
If you're a fan of Double Fine's games and Halloween, you really can't go wrong with buying this game (and it's sequel!), even for full price.

Have kept an eye on this game since it first appeared on steam, and when the opportunity came to play the Beta, I grabbed a Soldier Edition right then and there. This was before any issues started with limited Beta keys.
Even then, this was access to a partial game, people knew that going in. The campaign mode, the main section of Numantian's concept was not yet realized and still in developement. This was a way to peak your interest in something replayable while you waited, aka Survival Mode,
Don't get me wrong, it may sound like something simple but it is not. Survival mode is hard, no matter your difficulty setting, and I love it for this. You constantly have to learn and adjust your play style throughout to deal with map terrain, zombies and random Town of Doom spawns. Your units can patrol all they like, but if you yourself are not paying attention   , it will spell your own doom. Units get hung up on attacking nearby enemies, but this means that while there busy at one end, some zombies may be getting through on the other, and all it takes is one to bring down your empire.
People have been comparing this game to Dark Souls, I've never played it despite owning the game, so I can't confirm or deny that statement. Personally, this reminds me more of Darkest Dungeon in some ways; luck does play a factor and RNG can kick your teeth in if you haven't spent hours learning to adjust for it, even then you come away with internal bleeding. It is hard and despite how much you think you've prepared for imminent waves and attacks, Murphy's Law will play it's part, if something can go wrong it will go wrong. You need to micromanage your troops and economy, building up levels upon levels of defences.
It's not for everyone, but it fills a nice niche, It's addicting, agravating, curse inducing lunacy, replaying over and over trying to reach perfection. It comes easier to some than most. Love it for what is currently is, and know that the main portion has yet to be implemented, for the campaign has not yet had it's chance to reign.

Got this game for free and thought I'd give it a try. Visual novels usually aren't my thing, not because I dislike them, but because I'm a speedreader who reads, on average, about one million words per day, and most VNs are just too short for me to appreciate.
However, this one, whilst extremely short, was actually quite a nice read. There was no real plot, or development, or point of any kind, instead it's a sweet little sort of 'moment in time' situation. More specifically the kind of time at the end of your life. It's sad, and painful to read, but also bittersweet.
There are no surprises in the storyline. You know what's going to happen, because of what has already happened, instead of a mental journey, it's a purely emotional one.
The art is lovely, the music gentle, and the ending gives you ambivalent feelings. It was nice to play it, reach the end, and close the (metaphorical) book.
I would give this game 7/10, and I recommend getting this game on sale, or as part of an offer, since it is over very, very fast.

A two-dollar VN that you can finish between 30 minutes and 1 hour, depending on how fast you can read. It involves no choices, so the replayability is questionable.
It takes some risks which are quite appreciated. Playing as an older, confused person not aware of what is real and what's just a memory is a touching experience, even if the general "message" of the game differs a lot from what I personally believe, it's coherent and decently written. Some problems with English grammar are annoying, but forgivable.
However, the game also struggles with some budget limitations and / or slight laziness. Visual Novels can be made in many ways, and this current production doesn't use its medium to the full advantage. Most images are repetitive and we spend about 90% of the game looking at the very same room, only with slightly changing shadowing suggesting the passing time. The amount of character sprites (expressing emotions) is very limited. The music is serviceable and loops well, but its generic taste doesn't help the game stand out. Very often we see an empty room and just read one textbox of narration after another, which would be much more powerful with additional pictures and more text-free narrative.
Whenever the game actually uses some scene-specific fullscreen pictures, it makes a great impact. I wish it would be use more often, though.
TL;DR - It's cute, it's emotional, but it's not great. If you feel like the dementia-related synopsis could resonate with you, you should be satisfied.

A beautifully written and touching story about love, loss and reunion. Tells the story from the point of view of an elderly man losing his memories, family and health as he ages. For anyone who has lived with dementia in whatever form, be it friends, family, patients, or neighbors, this story will tug at your heartstrings. If you're one of the few lucky enough to have never had to deal with it, the story is still something to be touched by and learn from. It's a truely sad disease process for everyone involved and this story does a good job of showing some of the emotion involved.
As to the game itself, it's a short (~1 hour for me), engaging, kinetic (no choices) visual novel. The piano score accompanying the play is well suited to bring out the most in the story. It's well written, with a lot of feeling. The art is nice, and while nothing spectacular, it has well designed sprites and backgrounds. I'm only recalling one CG. No voice acting involved, and really with the beauty of the music, would probably detract rather than add to the story. No issues with crashing or bugs. For those interested, there are steam achievements that are earned with just the play through. Trading cards are listed as being available for the game, but I haven't played long enough for them to start dropping at this point.
Highly recommended to any who enjoy visual novels, especially those that deal with emotions and feelings.

I really enjoyed The Bureau: XCOM Declassified.
It's a tactical cover-based shooter in a thirdperson view.
You're playing one of the agents of XCOM, fighting back an alien invasion on the earth.
It has a pretty nice '50s/'60s style which fits the game perfectly and looks pretty neat (sure, no high-end graphic but it has still some nice and atmospheric visuals).
It's very linear and you'll always see when a fight is going to happen (you'll spot the covers you can use).
I found the gameplay and fights to be quite enjoyable. Though, the A.I. has some flaws (and i just played on a low difficulty, so maybe it might be worse on higher difficulties).
It plays like every other cover-based shooter, with the exception that you can give your 2 companions orders (there are maximum 2 you can take on missions with you). Opening up this menu will trigger a super slow-motion, giving you time to activate skills, place your companions on specific points on the map or heal yourself.
You also have to be careful/tactical as the characters won't take too much damage, so run&gun isn't the best option here.
Between missions you're always going back to the underground base of XCOM, where you can find some people to talk with, read some notes and do some smaller side-missions, which was a nice idea in my opinion.
You can also recruit different soldiers which have different classes and therefor different skills they will use, e.g. one can use a shield, another one can place a turret and the next one can make himself invisible.
If you're a die-hard fan of the old XCOM games, you might be dissappointed, as it is not the typical turn-based strategy game, but apart from that i found it to be pretty enjoyable.
Worth a look if you like SciFi and tactical third-person shooters.

The Bureau is a tactical third person shooter, exploring the origins of the xcom. The xcom being the alien defence force, protecting the world for total destruction! Very dramatic. You'll be playing as agent Carter or Deadpan Mc Shooty as he’s better known. When he has an accident with some kind of brief case all hell breaks loose and aliens invade. You are then tasked with defending the earth with various interchangeable allies. The plot is not that amazing with one twist in the end that you don't see coming because it does really make a huge amount of sense, it just sorta comes out of nowhere and changes everything. But don’t fear, you'll still be shooting aliens.
The game play is fun for, mostly, the guns feel alright but nothing special. You'll begin with the terrible rifles and surprising quickly move up to lasers then plasma weapons. You'd thing that researching new weapons and then being able to manufacture them to then use on the battlefield would be the way to go (like every other xcom I might add) but no, you just pick them up and use them, because you know how to use strange alien weaponry right off the bat.
As for your team mates you can move them around when going into your tactical slow down vision and tell them to use their abilities on different targets. The whole thing works well and is very stream lined in fact. But the AI is dumb, if you put them into cover they sometimes stay there or sometime they move to the wrong side of cover and get shot, which means you need to go and revive them. Or if you don't feel like having holes blown in you can send a team mate, but that usually ends with you needing to go revive two people. On more than one instance I have had my team mate’s role out of cover because a grenade has been thrown over then get back into the cover before it has gone off and being killed. Also like other xcom game there is perma-death so when an agent dies you can't get them back, so you need to level another agent, trying not to let his weak♥♥♥♥♥get killed in the process.
The gameplay is fun and controlling your agents is satisfying when everything goes to plan. But the AI is still dumb it will be a deal breaker for a lot of people. When the mission report come in and I have killed 70 alien and my agents have killed 13 and 7 then you begin to see the problem. But even more astounding is that the enemy AI isn't that bad (mostly) they can flank and Ihave only seen a few occasions when they have gone to the wrong side of cover and I have beaten them up as a result.
This game may only be for people who enjoy tactical game and can put up with the bad AI, as well as the very strange fact that the per-rendered cut scenes look worse, a lot worse than the in engine ones, take that as you will. Oh and one last thing, the back pack are useless, completely.

To be honest this isn't the kind of game I would normally even look twice at, the premise seemed plain bizarre to me and I'm not generally a fan of the genre anyway, so when a letsplayer I follow decided to play it, I was very sceptical and had low expectations. As I watched however my opinion changed to the point I decided to buy and play the game for myself.
It's really more interactive novel than game, and the premise IS odd and just slightly silly, but the game is deliberately tongue in cheek and playfully makes fun of it's own insanity. That said don't play this expecting complete lightheartedness , humour and pure parody (although that side is definitely part of it), if you follow certain routes and get into the back-story of the world and characters it can get surprisingly dark, and the story is better and surprisingly has more depth than you'd think at first glance, it even manages to be sad in places. Depending on the route you take, some parts can even cause the game to switch genres (into an rpg fighting game for example). It's definitely a niche type of game, but still a surprisingly good one, and one that's much better than I initially gave it credit for.

So I bought the game and started on a single player planet. Played around for an hour and wasn't very excited.

What I've found was a very crowded starting zone with tons of abandoned starter bases by at least 30 different people.

After something around an hour, I decided to try to get in contact with the other Player on the Server and met a really friendly pal showing me around while I was looking for rubber and carbon, and yes, the game doesn't give you any hint about where to find them until you notice there are some very sparse nodes of them.

To be honest. This game has potential. I really want to give it the same love I give Space Engineers or 7 Days to Die, but in it's current state it's unfortunately nither not worth my time nor the 18€ I've spent on it.

Well,
is an indie horror game with not much variety or intrigue into it. It's not horrendously bad like most indie horror games made in Unity here around, but it's nothing especially worthy of your time either. Aside a basic charm and some potential, it ends up being tedious anyhow. So, this will be mostly an informative review rather than a genuine upvote or a direct downvote. Decide for your own self.
It should be safe to assume that it's sometime between 60s and 80s in America. We are taking the brief role of a detective who searches for a missing young girl in a rural area. The introduction cinematic presents us a brief phone call between the mother of the girl and our detective in somewhat okay English - it might be important to note that the developer is not a native English speaker, so we'll encounter some problems with the narrative. Luckily, there is not much dialogue or written anecdotes within the game anyhow. After the phone call, we somehow arrive to our destination: a two-story abandoned house at the middle of nowhere. Our brief search is constantly recorded through a camera, I suppose - thus, the title of the game - explaining the constant darkness and flashing white static when you move the camera. Throughout our brief search, we'll go through the house, the dungeon beneath, a series of haunted hallways, a dark water level and finally, a forest. At the end, we'll be given the opportunity to run away with our lives or seek for answers. Neither of the endings are interesting or satisfying, and this will be it.
So... let's begin with display options, shall we? Aside the basic Unity horror environment in pure black and white, the main feature of the game is the camera mode which is presented for the purpose of augmenting the effect of the atmosphere. It is claustrophobic and quite disorienting, sure. But it serves to be a headache rather than being actually effective as a horror element. So, after trying to do this thing in the right way for 5 minutes, you give up and turn the camera mode off anyhow. After that point, there is nothing fundamentally scary. Well, this might be a bonus point actually. Most games in the indie horror genre end up abusing jump scares and screeching sound effects. Here, we'll have none of those. The game takes on a slow pace, heavily relying on atmosphere only and the sound effects are mostly appropriately unnerving. Is the atmosphere really scary? Nah, not really. It's the Unity version of a satanic cult settled under a big house and some haunting occurrences.
The main problem is that nothing you do or discover within the game is actually entertaining or intriguing. You keep walking around, go through a pathetically easy stealth portion to be caught by our not so neighborhood friendly cultists. After that point, whatever happens might be explained as either an actual haunting or a heavy drugging case, where you get to live through some nightmares. Whichever explanation you take. You end up in a pretty effectively haunted hallway, where our demonic victim resides, get a warm (?) welcome from her and start running. You get to light three candles and leave the hallway, then... the really frustrating and annoying part of the game begins. In a dark semi-flooded area, you are expected to run around and get near some light orbs, so the gigantic demon head wouldn't end up swallowing you. There is no saying when and where the thing will spawn, so you mostly rely on luck in this part. After that, you are back to the forest. This time you are chased by cultists in the woods, so you get to pick a direction (and an ending) to go, all the while trying to avoid getting stuck on branches. After that, well done. You beat the game.
Now you can either be done with it all, or if you are completionist like me, you can try for the bonus levels - which will give you some achievements when completed. One bonus level is the dark-flooded level with the demon head all over again, in which you are supposed to survive for 5 minutes. This was pathetically tedious and annoying. Another asks for you to switch between cameras until you collect 20 notes. Lights go out sometimes, so you gotta collect fuel to reactivate them to keep the demon girl away. Easily done. The last one - The Forest - is seriously annoying, where you are to walk around in the forest to again collect some notes. You are supposed to be chased by a monster there, yet I've encountered nothing in that level. It was the most boring walking simulator ever for me.
In and all, the main scenario presents barely an hour of gameplay - even with the frustration for the demon head. Bonus levels included, you would be done with all this game presents within 2 hours. Another hour is required to drop all Steam cards. Well done. Seriously. You are done now. The story? What story? You've encountered some cool satanic enactments, and you survived. Isn't this enough already? Joke aside, there is really no story. The whole thing is mostly an excuse to present an environment experience wrapped in really annoying camera features.
When this game first came to Steam, the original price was 5 dollars. Now, that was a huge exaggeration for whatever you'll be getting yourself into here. Now, the base price is dropped to a dollar, so it should be a safe bet to go for. You might try it without actually losing much here. Worst case scenario, you'll get some achievements and Steam cards. It is somewhat sad really, because I do believe that the game holds some potential. I especially liked the cultists themselves. With some actual story, or at least an epilogue stuck at the end, it would be an okay game. As it is, it is a "meh, why the hell not for a dollar" title. Enjoy, I guess.

This game is very simple, and in some ways feels like a cheaper, off-brand version of a bigger JRPG, namely one of the Persona series, given that you fight with the powers of a swappable costume.
But it's got a lot of charm, delightfully cohesive theming, good writing that allows the kids to be kids, and sprawling level design with slightly retro area access puzzles that fit into the Hallowe'en theme very well.
There are turn-based battles with quick time events to maximize your damage and reduce the enemies'. They aren't always easy. There is also a two layered strategic system of costume specific special abilities and 'battle stamp' special abilities that can be used with any costume. There are quite a lot of ways to build effective combinations, and in some difficult battles, you will have to adapt your strategy to the circumstances to succeed.
Downsides? Well, the camera angle is fixed and with levels so sprawling and complex, it can be easy to miss things hidden behind the foreground that are mandatory for story progression and to have to search for them.
Some of the puzzle solving is quite silly, and the player characters' unprompted hints to solve them can be annoying as often as they are helpful.
If a baddie wandering on the overworld map initiates combat with you and you lose, you get spat back out in exactly the same place, and the baddie will immediately initiate combat again, giving you no time to switch up your strategy before being launched into exactly the same battle; that can be a bit frustrating.
And finally, the lack of complexity can mean that the simple mechanics get a little bit dull even over the short playtime.
So its JRPG lite, but I recommend it for the charm alone. This game has actually made me question my disillusionment with the corporatization of Hallowe'en by showing me the cuter costumes and candy in a more wholesome and fun light. If you have kids, invite them to play it too. It seems like a very child-friendly game.

I can't bring myself to dislike this game. It's so incredibly, endearingly dumb.
Not only is it mostly stock assets from unity, every single element in the game is a road-weary stock horror trope. It reads like an edgy short story for a 7'th grade creative writing class. The environment is so delirious and changes so frequently, instead of being disoriented you think "oh, he's trying to disorient me, that's precious." The enemies' movement isn't even completely animated for god's sake. A good one third of the objects in the game don't have collision.
Despite all that, it has a good rhythm and it keeps a good pace. Some unintentionally funny moments (a lot of them actually.) It's got a few tense moments too, and the end in particular is actually a pretty original and cool boss fight (a rare thing in a walking simulator). I recommend it to the same type of person I would recommend a Uwe Boll film to.
I paid sixty cents for it though. If you pay too much more than that you'll feel like you got ripped off, I think. I've got just under an hour in it and I finished it. I could go back for the other ending, but even then that's an hour and ten minutes maybe.

The Tape is one of the weirdest horror games I have ever played and it's bizarre nature is not good.
In The Tape you play as a detective who is tasked to find a missing girl in a US suburb. He explores a house where she was kept and the more you venture the more the messed up the situation becomes.
The Tape is a really weird horror game as it's split into segments which all have different play styles, so I'll break it all down how each segment plays.
In general the game is a stealth game, where you have to hide from cultists while you try to get to your goal. But in later segments the game throws a lot more hazards making it harder to explore the environments around you, but all the environments are barren there's no point in exploring any of them.
The Atmosphere and some of the cultists designs are the only good things I can find about this game, nothing else.
The game has this really annoying film grain and I have no idea why it's there. Even though the game is called The Tape the game looks like any other horror game. Adding a really terrible film grain doesn't make it feel like found footage.
The game is also incredibly buggy, some of the bugs are also game breaking. The dream sequence with the candles I had to repeat multiple times since most of them the game bugged out and didn't let me progress. The first time the enemy that kills you on the spot was stuck in the only door which leads to the exit and if you go back to the starting door and pass it the game doesn't let you go back.
The Tape is also incredibly short, it took me 40 minutes to finish it, but it has a bit of replay value. The game has two endings and a few other game modes in the bonus tab, so you can a solid two hours of play time, but the game is also really bad so I doubt you will want to go back,
Overall The Tape is not very good game, I payed 50 cents for it which I got from selling Trading Cards, but in general I don't think this game is very good and with that 50 cents I could have gotten another, better game on sale. Just skip this and just get something else.
Final Rating:
3/10
Pros:
+ Good Atmosphere
Cons:
- That film grain ( I know you can turn it off, but it's how it was meant to be played, so I'm deducting points for it)
- Short
- Game Breaking bugs

World War II (often abbreviated to WWII or WW2), also known as the Second World War, was a global war that lasted from 1939 to 1945, although related conflicts began earlier. It involved the vast majority of the world's countries—including all of the great powers—eventually forming two opposing military alliances: the Allies and the Axis. It was the most widespread war in history, and directly involved more than 100 million people from over 30 countries. In a state of "total war", the major participants threw their entire economic, industrial, and scientific capabilities behind the war effort, erasing the distinction between civilian and military resources. Marked by mass deaths of civilians, including the Holocaust (in which approximately 11 million people were killed) and the strategic bombing of industrial and population centres (in which approximately one million were killed, and which included the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki), it resulted in an estimated 50 million to 85 million fatalities. These made World War II the deadliest conflict in human history.

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II Chaos Rising is a real-time strategy / tactical role-playing video game developed by Relic Entertainment and published by THQ for Microsoft Windows based on the fictional Warhammer 40,000 universe. It is the sequel to the Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War video game series.  Dawn of War II features a non-linear interplanetary campaign, as the Space Marines. The campaign can be played either as single-player or cooperatively with another player through an online connection.
The game's campaign departs from those of its predecessors in several key features. One of the most notable departures is that there are no base-building elements, unlike in previous Dawn of War titles. Instead, the player chooses the units to be used prior to beginning a mission, cannot build new units once the mission begins, and has only limited reinforcement options.
Has serveral multiplayer modes of play.  Adds Chaos Marine, Elves, and Tyranid avatars.
Chaos Rising is set one year after the events of Dawn of War II and the defeat of the Tyranid invasion (as well as the Eldar and Ork forces) of sub-sector Aurelia. My heart goes out to the people who made this game. It was clearly a bad idea to make it with the X-Com title, but someone somewhere made the decision to put it out, and everyone else had to go with it. And clearly, they put a lot of work into it.
As it goes, I think a 1950's X-COM is a really awesome idea. The game rips off Mass Effect's combat system, and I'm really ok with that. It's a good system, and it doesn't really hurt to have it in more than one game.
Now, with that out of the way, let me tell you, this game is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥how.
The storyline is boring and poorly-written, and the main character is unsympathetic and, at some point, becomes actively hostile to the player in a way that is not at all interesting. At some point you can make the dialoge choice not to be a horrible person, and he disobeys that and does the thing you just chose not to do.
Gameplay-wise, it's Mass Effect, but really poorly made. The "sprint" button is the same as the "stick to cover" button, which really was the worst design. It's easy to pop out of cover and get killed, and even easier to stick to a wall when you're trying to escape gunfire. The game has a really good engine for figuring out where cover is and what it covers, which your companions will completely disregard, rushing into open terrain frequently, and allowing them to be completely mowed down by enemy fire (enemies who, by the way, do not have similar problems finding cover). Playing with this AI is about as much fun as a giant long escort quest.
Finally, the game doesn't deliver half the strange alien horror that the initial preview footage promised. I'd be interested in a director's cut version that would basically be a finished version of what they originally showed E3. Not that that'll ever happen.
This is a great concept and a lot of hard work ruined by a few glaring problems. The tactical system is well-made, and could be fixed easily. The writing is usually the easiest thing to replace before the addition of voice-overs. I wish this game was better. DON'T BUY it for more than $5.

I feel bad giving this a thumbs down as the story was sweet but nothing amazing and the rest sort of falls short.
Art:
The art is good. Not amazing, but good.
Gameplay:
Kinetic novels don't really have gameplay, it's just a story, which is fine, and they are often short but this only took me 25 minutes to get through and there is no reason to play it twice. That was only enough time to accrue one of the three trading cards the game provides so if you wish to collect them be prepared to leave this running in the background for a while.
Story:
The story of an old man with dementia. I appreciate any story which has themes which raise awareness of important things but I actually expected a little more. It started out with promise, he couldn't remember that his daughter was long dead, forgot how to use his knife and it was very poignant but suddenly it's all about ghosts and his impending death and the main theme of the novel gets kind of lost in the shuffle.
SPOILERS AHEAD
It is obvious what's happening from the get-go, when the spirits of his wife and daughter arrive. Not that that's necessarily a bad thing, I just don't think it was done as well as it could have been. I have to say, his daughter wearing a tomato costume was weird, it was meant to be cute and had a little story behind it but I can't help think that literally anything else would have been better because she was dressed as a frikkin' tomato and it made it hard to take it seriously. I also wasn't keen on the fact that the town was called Memoria because that is way too on the nose. It's poor writing.
I'm a sucker for tragedy and normally someone going out to find out that their wife has fallen down a hill and died in the night would be gold but in this story it's just pointlessly brutal. The story is meant to be about the man and his life and his dementia and it seemed totally unnecessary to have that as the plot. It's like the story couldn't decide what it wanted to be and so it chose to be everything.
+ Hearing about his past and the stories of how he met his wife and the end when they promise they'll be in heaven waiting and he finally passes on and meets them are quite well-done and did make me smile.
Writing:
+ The writing was good. You won't be blown away but it was very good. I noticed only a single mistake, a missing full stop near the end on one of Maribel's lines.
Value For Money:
For the price it's not worth it as a good rule of thumb for any game of any genre is £1 per hour of gameplay. If you can get this for £0.50 or less, that's fine, but I wouldn't spend more.
Bottom Line:
Don't buy it unless you can get it for less than 50p. If you can, expect a half hour of a cute story with many flaws which will make you smile by the end but then be forgotten pretty soon.

First of all, I played the game in its original release, so don't let my play time fool you. I've put far more hours into this game than most.
It sounds like a bizarre combination at first- a dating game with pigeons. No doubt, Hatoful Boyfriend creates a world where a healthy dose of belief-suspension is in order. But beneath that silly exterior is a tale that's sweet, funny, dramatic, endearing, and very cute.
If you're a bird lover like I am, you'll find the world and its characters particularly charming, but you don't have to be one to connect with the cast. It's easy to forget the species of your schoolmates when you want to see how each of their stories unfold. Only the most shallow will let the fact they're pigeons get in the way of their emotional tales, which are spun to make the player laugh, love, and maybe even shed a tear here and there (anyone who watched me stream this game knows I sure did). It leans on the short side of duration, including all potential paths, but just like how it takes itself just seriously enough, the game gives you just enough to accomplish its goal without overstaying its welcome. It's succinct, hitting all the key points necessary to develop a world, tell a story, and make you interested in the characters, which is really all one can ask of it.
Hatoful Boyfriend is a quirky little game that was made with love and is worth checking out, even if just to explore a dating sim from a different angle. And if you're a bird lover, then it's a must. As Oko-san would say, it's "coo!"

I really like this game, A LOT. Warning up front, you'll need patience if you want to play this game, read on. Played it for about 17 hours now since I bought it a couple of days ago. It's beautiful, the graphics are cool, it has a nostalgic kind of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. / Unreal feeling to it. Creatures at night scare the s* out of me, I really don't scare easily so this is great. Some creatures are easy to kill, some are hard. All creatures have weak points where you can hit them to increase your chances of doing more damage. Can't wait to get to outer space and find out what's there. The health/suit combo is a really nice one, where you have to maintain your suits' integrity. Eating and drinking is well balanced.
There are however a couple of things I'd like to suggest/mention to the developers:
- Increase the agility and stamina from the start: It's really annoying to walk. Walking a bit, then standing still to recharge stamina/oxygen. Walking again a little bit, recharging AGAIN... I found this run/jump/hover/repeat move so I don't have to wait, but it's frustrating. It gets boring really fast, to the point where I'm just autowalking (great function for this) and watching American Dad or Family Guy while "playing"/listening if I get attacked or walk into pin-bushes.
- Increase the walking speed. It's like he's taking a stroll in the park. Or make it so we can make sort of an early starting mobile/car kind of thing to get around, running on raw plutonium or something. We need to go faster!
- Inventory items should auto-stack. I find myself throwing away, or not even picking stuff off of creatures anymore, just because it's such a hassle to manually f****** sort everything. I need to buy a new mouse pad, the table underneath it is wearing. Please consider doing this as a priority. It almost made me quit the game a couple of times.
- Bug. There are still some bugs with the tech tree, but I'm sure you're aware of that (since a lot of people have mentioned it)
- Bug. There's a sound issue where a creature on the left has it's sound on the right side, this makes me turn my back to creatures, I see nothing and suddenly I get attacked.
- I would really like to be able to break free from interacting with a building just by walking away with the movement keys and/or using the 'f' key, could you consider doing this? I find I need to lift my left hand to the esc key a lot. Usability is important.
- Can you make it so I can leave the "customize" option on a building/pannel? I have to move my hand to the esc key a lot while refurbisihing my habitat or other buildings (usability).
- Could you add an auto-sort button which organises inventories? Sometimes there's still a spot left but I have to search for it. (usability)
- Please increase the scroll speed inside of containers, I need to scroll like my life depends on it when moving up or down in inventories. It would be a lot easier if it moved up and down one or two rows.
- I'm missing water (in game, not the bottled water), is this on the to do list? Can't remember.
- The time it takes to recover from an enemy attack might be reduced. When fighting more than 3 monsters I find I can't orientate myself / get in a shot myself, especially early in the game. It's frustrating just watching and waiting until you die, I need to have a feeling I can do something against mobs.
I think that's all for now, maybe I'll add some points later.

Don't believe the reviews saying it takes long time to gather resources (of course depends what you consider long).
In 12-14 hours of gameplay you should be able to have a close to fully equipped base with some vehicles (gotta love the mecha crab).
Of course when you play for the first time it will probably take more, but just make sure your base is in the right spot so your droid can mine all night for you. That's the important part - to not waste time at nights or when building you can send your droid to mine resources for you.
Now the review:
The good:
Game has great atmosphere -  it really makes you feel a bit on edge all the time. The music and sound effects are really good, what I have a feeling that still needs work is positional audio, though maybe it's realistic to lose sence of sound direction when wearing a helmet. When you play alone you get a real sense of being alone on a planet.
Visuals - they are stunning, absolutely amazing.
Gameplay - it's fun, sure there's a bit of repetition like in every survival which depends on mining resources, but it's fun to go on expeditions looking for those more rare resources. Now there's another moon to visit too!
The development so far seems to have the right direction and good speed which is important in early access games.
The bad:
AI - droids trying to shoot enemies through your buildings, etc.
Some building clipping - both player and enemies.
There are bugs that will cause you to die and basically lose all progress (freezing on ice planet's orbit for example).
Most of the bad things are early access problems, so that's fine for now.
Looking forward to see this game grow. It's off to a great start.

"The Tape" is an example of indie horror done really well, without going overboard.
=====
CONS:
- Lack of terror: I didn't find this game necessarily very frightening, though I did find it was good for a little bit of added anxiety, at points, regarding "getting away', etc. For a horror game, I would've preferred it to have been a little bit more frightening.
- Lack of story: The story really didn't do it for me.. what little there is. But, in a way, I suppose its refreshing to know that a game doesn't need a whole lot of story to tell a creepy, unsettling, well... narrative, of sorts. The events make sense, though the overall story was a little lacking as a whole, and didn't really find a way to tie everything together in a fulfilling way.
NEUTRAL (+/-):
+/- Visual effect settings: The "Heavy" visual effects setting makes the game hard to see at time, and for people with sensitive eyes, or who are prone to headaches, I don't recommend it. For those people that have a hard time with it, set the visuals to "low", and the game becomes monochrome, and ditches the heavy, fuzzy, visuals. Though, at times, even though it was a little straining to look at, I did find myself turning them back on. They really do add a unique touch to the game, and make it something more interesting than your average horror in terms of style.
+/- Puzzles: They aren't really difficult, yet they don't really tell you anything, and aren't exactly straight forward either... if you've played horror games as much as someone like me has, you'll have no problem figuring them out. But for those who aren't used to using their brains as much for puzzle-type activities, this could stump you for a good few minutes. It's worth the effort, but it's not really difficult. It's kinda.. in the middle for me.
PROS:
+ Atmosphere: The atmosphere in this game is well done. There isn't any extra fanciness added to make the game seem like its spoon-feeding you eye-candy, and it introduces any and all "horror" elements with a reason, and with good taste. Its not trying to jump scare you and phone in some cheap excitement for Youtube Screechers to pretend they're frightened by. Its atmosphere is really well put in place. The visual style, granted, could be considered "extra fanciness"; however, it's possible to turn it off, and truly does add to the experience overall (for those who can withstand the eye-strain).
+ Sound effects/BGM: The sound effects and background music really add to the tension that the developer was trying to put forth in this game, and really help to tie the experience into a(n) (almost) complete package (barring a shallow story). Though, the lack of story elements don't really detract from the overall gameplay here, as all you need to know about the environment to 'feel' what the developer was trying to convey is the visual aspects, and the sound effects/BGM.
=====
Do I recommend "The Tape"?
Yes~! Absolutely~
It's an interesting, and short experience that neatly combines unique elements with tastefully placed stereotypical ones, to craft an interesting experience.
And now to go watch some "tapes" of my own before work~
