One of the great things about PC gaming being a truly global community is that I get the chance to play games developed around the globe. Part of what attracted me to E.T. Armies is that it was developed by an Iranian studio, which is extremely rare to find even in this environment of wide-reaching internet and digital distribution. I can't actually name any other Iranian developers. Even more interesting is that it's seemingly developed for a Western audience; it's a sci-fi military FPS all spoken in English and evoking a lot of the tropes of the genre. At the time of review, it doesn't even have an option for Persian dialog or subtitles. So how does it compare to its contemporaries? Not well.
E.T. Armies is a sci-fi military FPS, set in a post-Earth world. War and energy greed have ravaged Earth to the point that it had to be abandoned. Not everyone made it off the planet, separating humanity into the Parsis and the Forsaken. You are Aria, a Parsis soldier whose dropship has been shot down over an unnamed planet. You and your squad must fight off a resurgent, invading Forsaken force.
E.T. Armies is an indie FPS built on the Unreal engine. Its design is not particularly inspired, but it works and it looks okay. A bit dated and bit too much colored lighting and effects, but it's got a consistent look. Weaponry is strictly your military FPS standards: three flavors of assault rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle. There are weapon turrets and a situational fire support that you can use against bigger flying enemies. It's all perfectly functional.

If perfectly functional doesn't sound exciting, though, it's because it's not. The game is a lot of running down overly colorful, but still dark, corridors and shooting mostly brainless enemies in an utterly linear fashion. There's a jump button, but I never found a use for it because I couldn't even clear seemingly waist-high obstacles. The story is pretty nonexistent with the exception of a couple cutscenes, so there's not much driving you forward except to get to the end of it. It all feels very 2000's era FPS.
However, where it commits its worst offenses is in the sound department. The weapon sounds are weak, the music is uninspired, and voice work is all dreadfully bad. I would chalk up it up to the language difference, but there is no option to hear the voiceovers in Persian. They're all in awfully delivered English. This is an instance in which I would rather hear the lines delivered in the developer's native language, even if it means I couldn't tell whether or not the voicework is any better in another language.
E.T. Armies appears to be Raspina's first FPS, and it feels like it was a learning experience. They got a lot accomplished emulating older FPS games. Now they have to fix the sound quality, and spice up the gameplay to make something really enjoyable for 2016. Unfortunately, as it stands, E.T. Armies isn't very good and it has a lot to improve upon.

Kinetic Novels, I don’t have a hate for them, I just can not love them. They are falsely billed as RPG’s or as an adventure games, key word here is ‘GAMES’.
These are novels, not games and as novels, ‘Forgotten, Not Lost’ is a well written journey of an elderly gentleman, suffering from dementia and recovering from the recent loss of his loving wife.
Graphics is the standard Anime style with nice background music. Any interaction is limited to just flipping the pages.
Again, I will re-iterate, this is a novel, NOT a game. If you love Novels and hate paying $10 for a standard paperback then get ‘Forgotten, Not Lost’. If you love Games, walk away, just don’t stand on the bookworms on your way out.

The Bureau has suffered a lot of criticism - mostly justified for breaking away from its strategy game roots - but the game that has seen multiple rebuilds over many years came out on the other end a decent-enough game that is at least worthy of a sequel or a major update.
This game takes place amidst the Communist Scare of the 1960's, where an alien invasion turns our country's defenses on their heads and forces the The Bureau to come into its own as the nation's (and world's) defense against aliens.
What I personally liked about the game was that its style and themes made it feel original, but its characters felt forcefully placed in 1962, with dialogue forcing issues like women in the workplace and military, Communist scares and questions of loyalty and security. I think these themes could have been better written to blend with the story and events in the base, and the time spent developing the base combined with better expanding on the characters, which all felt somewhat flat.
The gameplay is directly inspired from Mass Effect, but the AI lacks the intelligence to make safe decisions for itself, making your squadmates a frustrating liability. The choices in weaponry and equipment are as barebones as Mass Effect, but I suppose there are worse things you could rip off. I would hope a sequal or major update would expand on your equipment and abilities developing as you develop XCOM itself as a key member.
To wrap this up - this game was obviously (and famously) rushed to completion, but is nonetheless a worthy play provided it's on sale. I think the game deserves a sequel provided more time is put into making the game original and deep while improving on its many weaknesses and failures.

This game is pretty awesome. It has many pros, and few cons.
First, the fact that any piece of hardware can run it is nice, and even the highest-end PCs get a kick out of the best settings. There are many little things to get sidetracked with, from special events to higher level bosses. If you're anything like me, you'll appreciate the chance to show off on a special boss, or one of the many raids. But the best part for myself were the classes.
You choose a side, a race, and one of four basic classes. Depending on the class you choose, from the cleric, the warrior, the wizard, and the (rogue?), you then choose what type of class you are. You could be a rogue tank if you wanted, with no regards to stereotypes, although it definitely changes the playstyle. All of it helps to define you, and determine your soul trees. You can change them later, but the soul trees help to really define you. I'll add that even though most of the abilities seem overpowered in most games, they scale well in this one. Enemies and players have very notable differences in their power between levels. Most MMOs give you the ability to fight enemies many levels higher than you if you're skilled enough. Not this one. Walking near enemies who are even 2 or 3 levels higher spells death for a solo or duo party.
As with anything, there are cons. First, scaling is extreme. You can't expect to compete with people 10 levels higher, and enemies that high are out of the question for the casual adventurer. Second, and probably the only thing that made me stop playing, is the quest system. The quests are very repetitive, and if they aren't, the likelihood is that you're running for 10 minutes to where you need to go. Lastly, the story/lore is very long. If you don't like reading, this game is NOT for you. Most quests are on average several pages long of information you don't need unless you want lore.
tl;dr
Pros:
Very optimized for any hardware, many events to partake in, and lots of character development.
Cons:
Extreme scaling of enemies and players and very repetitive and semi-boring quests.
Give it a try. You can't lose much other than time and memory with this.

I won this game in a giveaway on Steamgifts, so I got it for free.
I enjoy horror games that are widely considered "bad", and often I find something good in those games. There are not many games that I feel I have to warn others (not even Chernobyl Commando or Manhunter).
I really tried to like The Tape, but I can't.
That said, I cannot recommend a purchase of this product.
The game is divided into a main game and three bonus levels. Upon completion of each, an achievement can be earned.
Spoilers ahead. You have been warned.
The main game starts out okay-ish: a police detective looks for a missing girl. Alone. We find that kind of premise in a lot of horror games, so I won't criticize that. But upon
, the
becomes highly illogical:
The whole storyline told by the game does not make sense at all when summarized. And it's short. Depending on your pace, you can finish it in 45-90 minutes.
Let's get to the bonus levels. I'll tag them as spoilers.
Dungeons of Terror:

Forest:

Dark Waters:
The worst one, and the reason for my relatively high playtime.

So we have a short game with a dubious plot and underwhelming and even annoying bonus levels.
The game description states: "Some of the scenes you are witnessing (sic!) in this game are the most disturbing in horror game history.", and "...reveals things so horrifying, that it make (sic!) him question his own sanity." Those superlatives are highly exaggerated, none of this is true. The Tape is relatively harmless.
The game had potential, but as this is a finished product and the developer has been aware of the issues for about a year, it seems that nothing will change.
If you're considering a purchase of this game, watch HarshlyCritical's playthrough on YouTube. He pretty much sums up the experience I had when playing it.

(mini-review)
An interesting, polished, well-conceptualized and executed first-person shooter.  Armed with weapons, melee, subterfuge and a variety of far-out powers at your disposal, you can either exact vengeance on your enemies or dishonor them to produce a more horrifyingly shameful end.  The graphics look great, the game runs reasonably well and the gameplay has several layers of depth as you control how you infiltrate a variety of strongholds or secured facilities.  Still, without multiplayer, a wide array of unlocks or other "sweeteners" the game would likely lose its appeal after 2-3 playthroughs.  That simply isn't a ton of value, in my estimation.  Additionally, the plot isn't phenomenally deep, nor does the game have uniquely memorable characterization, motivations or surprising plot twists.  Finally, the game rewards evil, malicious and dark-power bargainers by proffering them not only a greater level of power more quickly but far more useful and effective powers.  In short, you're hobbled by your desire to hinder or control your own inner demons/dark desires and at times, even punished.  While that may have been a conscious choice by the developer Arkane, truth be told, I find it a bit hypocritical.
So often you hear about players being denied the ability to play an evil character within a game and yet now, here we have quite the opposite.  It's not impossible to play a righteous character in this game but it is more difficult and due to the lack of powers/variety...also less fun.
Still the game is a worthwhile diversion if you can afford it.

Wow.  Having just finished this, it was fun and familiar, (being a great fan of Mass Effect 2!) but with a blend of the XCOM history and a little splash of Men In Black.  This game made me realize I like first/third tactical cover squad combat games very much.  In short, it was worth a play through, especially if you can get the title on a sale.  I don't know if the title is worth being a completionist for all the achievements as compared to XCOM:Enemy Unknown.  It plays almost like an action-adventure game.
I played through on Veteran and only the main campaign, and except for a very difficult Rosemont mission where I was not yet accustom to the ebb and flow of the battles, the only major difficulty was the very last battle.  That took 4 tries to finally get a tactic that kept me stable in the battle until the most unreasonable and crazy release of opponents at the end (I won't spoil it for those who want to know, just realize it will get worse, MUCH worse before it ends...).   I am working on the Hangar 6 R&D DLC at commander difficulty to see how that works with the rest of the game story.  I will also try a play through on commander difficulty with the main campaign just to see how much difference not restoring your squaddies to combat will be.
I enjoyed the story, and yes, it was kind of predictable as I noticed others have mentioned in their reviews.  However, because there were only a few major twists, it made for a pretty straight through game.  It greatly shortened the time it took to complete the story so I really did not loose  interest and have to revisit it over several months.  The linear story made it like playing an older science fiction novel in it's form. I enjoyed that very much.  The graphics were par for the usual excellence of the Unreal Engine used in the game, with a few cool particle effects that helped it out a bit.  I personally liked the cliche 60's acting and viewpoint writing for the plot and characters, however this was not at all Emmy winning material.  The dialogs added to the nostalgic flair of the period presentation.  Some of the over presented images of the era added to the effect, even if they were not fully realistic (I know, realism in an aliens game, right?) like the clouds of smoke and the ashtrays everywhere, and the clothing, the stylized electronic and computer items.  I enjoyed the not so crazy ending that was somewhat plausible given the XCOM storyline and was sad to see the last battle occur, even though I was very happy to have it over!
However, I will say that several factors reduced the game to be more interesting as a secondary title to the XCOM series, instead of a gem in it's own right.  No, I don't think that this game had even spiritual succession qualifications to the XCOM series, any of them.  To me, The Bureau is like a supporting novel to a game series, you don't really miss much if you didn't read it, but it has entertainment value if you should happen to try it.  I had two glitches that made life miserable on several occasions, further detracting from my desire to play through more than one more time.  First, the number of times that I would hit space instead of R-ctrl, and thereby miss out on the timing of things like a grenade landing next to me was too numerous.  Often, the return from the tactics system would not allow the R-ctrl to be acknowledged in a timely fashion. ( I know remapping might have helped me here, but I like to play through using the default controls to see how they lay out. )  I will be re-mapping for my next play through so I can break cover far easier.  Second, I had 3 separate missions where the trigger for the mission end overlapped with a different event, and caused the ending not to occur.  Specifically, on a manufacturing plant mission that takes place on a farm, where the end event was supposed to be the helicopter landing at a pad after the last alien was taken out.  Well, some event message over-rode the end condition event, and I wandered around the available complex for about 20 minutes before resetting to the last checkpoint out of frustration.  I redid the battle only to get the same thing again.  On the third try, I used a different tactic, and finally heard the "all clear" message and saw the helicopter set down.  I still have no idea what happened.  Certain missions are flawless, others really do cause the computer to pause for brief and unexpected areas.  These just broke the flow enough that it almost felt like the game was dragging in these areas.
I will restate that I liked the game, I would say it is worth playing through if you can get it on sale.  I will update this after I have played the DLC through.  This is not XCOM, nor should it be compared with XCOM:EU, and especially not with the original XCOMs.  The only relationship to the XCOM universe is the use of it's prequel storyline.  The Bureau is a different type of game, and I did have fun with it, for the couple dozen hours I have into it.
A cheap, poorly constructed Mass Effect clone. I totally regret this purchase. Awful.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a 3rd-person tactical shooter that takes place during the 1960's and absolutely nails its setting. The graphics and art design are fantastic, as long as you get the game running well on your machine. In The Bureau, aliens invade Earth and the XCOM group sends their best to take on the aliens.
Combat is very similar to that of Mass Effect 2 + 3 - but combat here is much more tactical, since you have way more control of your party members. In fact, it's pretty much essential to survive that you must use the tactical "slow-down" to survive. It's not a BioWare-style tactical pause here - it only slow-down time a bit for you to make orders. You may create, randomize, and recruit agents and their actual looks, class, and everything at your own will and desire. Though, the down-side is that you'll never really feel attached to your teammates - since they do not have personal "Loyalty" missions, to make you care about them; this isn't Mass Effect here. If there's anything besides the excellent art direction and setting that 2K Marin gets absolutely right with this game, it's the excellent tactical combat. One thing that is never dull here is the tactical combat - and this is certainly the best reason to play this game. If you liked the combat in Mass Effect 2 + 3 but wanted something a bit more tactical and have more control over your party members when in combat - this is the game for you.
Even on Squaddie (difficulty #2 out of 4), this game is tough - and this is coming from someone who plays a lot of games - especially shooters. The game actually suggests difficulty #3 by default - which given how tough Squaddie often is, given the number of times my party died, had to reload a save, or lost a party member to "perma-death"; I'm not sure if the 3rd difficulty should be suggested as its default! "Perma-death" is in effect here - so if you survive a mission and one of your party members doesn't, they're gone from your game entirely.
2K Marin did a fantastic job with storytelling & character development in Bioshock 2: Minerva's Den DLC, but doesn't do so as much here. Storytelling events that occur either are quite obvious as to what's going happen next (predictable!); and/or the big pay-off moments just aren't well put-together or is under-developed. By the time the game's story gets very interesting & has an excellent twist, which is somewhere closer to the back 1/4th of the game - it makes the gamer wonder why this sort of execution also didn't happen earlier, as well.
But, once this plot-twist happens, the game drops the ball again in another regard: by spreading out auto-save points, which can lead to moments of complete frustration when players have to replay long-winded shootouts. There's nothing wrong w/ grand, long-winded epic shootouts like these - but it could've used an auto-save, somewhere in the middle or before the game brings out the really tough moment - since the game does have difficulty spikes within some of these sections.
What it all comes down to, is this: if you want a game with excellent art direction; an excellent setting; looks great in DX11 mode (if your PC can handle it); you enjoy 3rd-person shooting similar to Mass Effect 2 + 3; but you also want a shooter more tactical than Mass Effect 2 + 3 - then this game is for you and it shouldn't be missed. If you're looking for a game with great story and characters, most of the time - this is not that game. It doesn't always execute that stuff consistently. The Bureau could've been elevated to a much greater status, if it actually delivered more consistently on its character + story elements, since it actually does often try to emphasize these elements. Overall, when it's all said and done - The Bureau is a solid and worthwhile 3rd-person tactical shooter.
Final Grade: C+

So, Evolve Stage 2, lets jump into it.
Initially I had avoided Evolve, like always I waited until a while had passed after the initial hype died down and sadly I was not surprised to see that it did not work out so well. (The gaming industry has made me a cynical little ♥♥♥♥)
So recently I log into steam and a friend invites me to play Stage 2 and seeing as how its free to play I said to myself why the ♥♥♥♥ not and I joined him. Now I went to thank that friend later because I had an absolute blast playing this game. after enjoying myself (haha) for a while I thought to myself, well, this game isnt so bad, why were people so negative about it?
A few google searches later I found that in Stage 2 (pretty much) everything that people complained about in the original games had been tweaked, changed or flat out removed. This ended up in a much more enjoyable experience. Now I feel like this review is going to be long as ♥♥♥♥ if I keep formatting it like this so Im gonna throw some pros and cons at you.
(DISCLAIMER: As you can see I dont have a lot of hours in this game (38 as of writing this review) so Im not going to even pretend to know anything about the balance of this game, some say monsters are ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥OP ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and some people say its harder to steal candy from a baby than it is to kill them. Personally I think it has to do with the huge difference in player skill right now but whatever, not my expertise. ALSO: I have based these pros and cons largely on my own opinion, these are not facts per se, but they showcase my experience with the game.)
Pros:
- Free to play (♥♥♥♥ing why are you reading my review its free go see for yourself! (But thanks for reading it anyway))
- Fights feel intense, both as the monster and hunter
- Roles are well defined and each make you feel important to the team (Even if sometimes people do--- HEY SHEPARD THATS A CON GTFO, okay okay)
- You get to play as a huge badass monster capable of roflstomping entire teams of hunters in convienient bite sized groups of 4
- Game changing perks have to be earned, so no paying users at level 1 getting a massive advantage (Except for founders, who get a small amount of level 1 perks available to them)
- MOST people are pretty nice in this game, cant make any promises though
- Queue times are quite short
- Characters are unique and interesting
- Dialog at the start of the game is charming and will often get a chuckle out of you
- Gunplay feels smooth and well refined, as well as monster control and abilities
Cons:
- People dont always know their roles, and seeing as how every role is rather essential to the team, this can result in some quick losses as the hunters (Or some really quick wins as the monster, *evil monster chuckle*)
- Gameplay can feel a bit inconsistent, sometimes youll kill the opponent(s) with ease, sometimes you can get roflstomped
- Learning curve is a bit steep, I highly recommend you watch some videos and read some guides if you want to get into Evolve
- Though I did say most people are nice, there are people out there that will nitpick every mistake you make (Not really a problem of the game itself but do be advized, if you cant take that this game might not be for you.)
- More difficult monsters to beat can be very overwhelming at the start of your Evolve carreer and this can be very demoralizing, but dont listen to anyone saying theyre flat out OP, every monster has a strategy to beat it
- The currency system in this game revolves around grinding out keys, and the grind is real. Expect to have to play a lot of games before you get to buy the stuff you want to buy
- After a game the lobby is immediately disbanded and there is no way to get a recently played with list in this game, its not integrated with Steam. This makes making friends in this game very, VERY hard, especially so if your newfound would be friend has a very common username.
Some kind of neutral closing statements:
- This game is pretty competetive, even in casual play. If you want to play this game to just♥♥♥♥♥♥around, get some friends to do it with because you are not going to receive a lot of appreciation
- Do note that playing with friends is a LOT more fun than playing solo most of the time, and I highly recommend getting your friends to play with you
- The system requirements for this game are pretty steep so check beforehand and possibly save yourself some time downloading it, that being said, my potato that barely has minimum can run it decently at the very minimal graphics
- There is the occasional crashes that get reported, while not everyone will have this problem this might happen
Well, time for me to wrap up the review, I love this game, and I hope you will too, the more the merrier.

You play for 75 days. You've dealt with hordes, and the occasional Harpy showing up and jumping a wall, causing panic for a short while. You might think you've carved out a little haven where your filthy steampunk peasants can toil for you, and eek out a miserable existance for themselves while you ride high as the Honorable Mayor.
Then...day 90 happens.
It starts like any other day; you upgrade some walls, build turrets where you think you might need them, and back them up with some garrisoned towers. You make a few more units, and build an advanced farm for more food. "Life is good", you say to yourself, sipping what is probably wine mixed with some form of oil; because steampunk.
Then a warning. A horde approaches. "Let them come", you think. Well let me just say that this game doesn't care about your carefully placed walls for symmetry; or your finely organized stone houses that your people live in. It will throw a literal wave of infected flesh at you so dense that even triple thick stone walls can't compete with.
You fall back to another wall, then another. You watch the infected tear through the streets like a bull in a steampunk china shop, causing exponential problems as they infect more citizens. You hear the last of your units die in agony as the infected swarm your Command Center. Game Over.
TL;DR

This game is bad beyond reason.
Mahjong Solitaire should be, one would think, a relative hard thing to get wrong. You match tiles, there's an element of randomness to it, so you don't always expect to win but as long as you can find two matching tiles the game is pretty simple. Right?
Wrong.
So, first the game introduces all these crap tiles which I guess are supposed to make the game interesting but just wind up confusing the rules and making everything terrible. You've got brick walls, AKA tiles you can't clear. Which any person with a room temperature IQ would say, "That's a bad idea and antithetical to the idea of Mahjong Solitaire", but then they graciously add dynamite, which you can use to clear brick walls. Except there's 3 types of walls and 3 corresponding types of dynamite, so it's possible to have dynamite but not the right TYPE of dynamite and on boards where the brick walls are used there's usually more walls than dynamite anyway so the odds are good you're going to wind up pinned on your first couple attempts.
That's just the beginning of the bad bonus tile nonsense. You've got typhoon tiles, swap tiles, copy tiles, magnet tiles... and that's just in the part of the game I could be arsed to suffer through.
The boards in story mode aren't random either. Another thing that a decently intelligent person would be like, "That's bad. Don't do that." But no. The main mode of the game uses the same configurations for every single level the whole way through. Which brings us to....
The point of the game is not matching tiles quickly. Which, AGAIN, anyone who didn't have their head lodged firmly in their colon might opine, "This isn't even Mahjong Solitaire any more, what is the point?"
Instead, you complete levels by matching two SPECIFIC tiles. Or sometimes three. Because if you can't make things interesting, make them stupid. So generally what you tend to do is match the fewest number of tiles possible to carve away the board around the magical plothole tiles and when you match those everything else gets matched automatically.
Fortunately, if that seething pile of stupid is too much for you to handle, there are two additional game modes; Free play and Tournament.
Free Play is basically the game you expected to get when you bought a Mahjong Solitaire game, and the challenge level is even decently good. There are double-sized boards where you really have to work quickly if you want to clear them in the time limit if you want to test your skills.
Tournament Mode is where the game ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed again and then rolls around in it for good measure.
See, Mahjong Solitaire isn't really supposed to be competitive. Hence the 'Solitaire' bit. But the game gives you the option to play against other people. A reasonable person might conclude then, that between two players, the player that matches the most tiles the fastest would be declared the winner. But that doesn't happen, because again they decide to ruin everything with the addition of special tiles.
In addition to the regular runs, there are Bronze, Silver, and Gold 'Yin Yang Coins' that give you a score multiplier, 1x, 2x, and 3x respectively. The way to win is to match as many of these coins as possible first, pumping up your multiplier, so each match you make is worth more. However, the boards in tournament mode ARE completely random, which means you could out match your opponent 10:1 but it won't count for anything if they got more coins than you at the start of the game. Which means tournament mode isn't based around skill so much as dumb luck. So what is the point?

After trying Stacking and being disappointed, I wasn't sure if I'd like Costume Quest. Psychonauts was good - if not limited by platforming - and Costume Quest is right up there with it.
The style is a charming, delightfully-quirky one that puts you in the role of a child on Halloween, trick or treating with their sibling. The pace spirals beautifully until you're facing off against giant monsters in a twisted maze, firing rockets.
One of this game's seeling points is its fantastic humour; like Psychonauts it puts you in the position of a child and throws referential and meta humour at you, barrelling on whether you get the jokes or not. This is one of its strongest aspects as it's funny to those who get it and doesn't slow down those who don't.
The combat is surprisingly deep considering the simple controls and is very balanced...except for the final boss in the extra adventure, Grubbins On Ice. The final boss of that doesn't follow the rules established in all the rest of the combat.
Despite this little hiccough, it is a easy to grasp, QTE-based combat with scope for personal preference.
One last thing to note is that it isn't very long; 9 hours to 100% it with all the achievements. There are shorter games out there and there are certainly longer games, but this is one of the funniest.

The game oozes charm. It has child characters that are actually likable, funny, and clever, which is pretty rare in video games. The monsters and villians are pretty funny. Basically, it's just so fun!

Because in my backward country, we use AZERTY keyboards instead of QWERTY. See, the game won't allow you to re-bind keyboard keys and the keys are set for WASD. Now, I don't have a problem with WASD in itself but I do have a problem when controls are stubbornly fixed to those
(input) and
, meaning for example that the W for 'forward' is located in the bottom row of the keyboard, the spot where Z is on QWERTY keyboards. As you can imagine, this makes the game practically unplayable.
So I can hardly recommend a game I can't really play. Also, I wanted to send out a warning to other AZERTY users and possibly even QWERTZ users, too. Should they fix this problem, I'll be sure to upgrade my review to an actual review of the game.

Singleplayer quickly puts you up to task, teaching you how the system works: get licenses, complete races, get cars, customize cars, complete championships, buy houses, buy furniture, get bigger garages and then buy more cars. The map is huge, its fun to explore, Hell!, its fun to just pick a random car and drive around the island, for some it's even therapy and it works just fine!...at least the singleplayer.
Multiplayer mode is not so multiplayer, constant connection problems logs you out of the game, some players might have their cars shaking on your screen due to connection issues, and 'clubs' which are the "guilds" in this racing game, as mostly not used by anyone, believe me... I've tried.
After learning not to mind the bad physic system and buying an Xbox Controller so I could play it not so terribly, I find myself enjoying this game very much, there is even a chasing mode which reminded me of the old need for speed games.Once again, It's a fine game, despite its flaws, I do recommend Test Drive Unlimited 2 for any racing games lover.
tl;dr
+ Great amount of vehicles
+ Huge map, fun to explore
+ Immserive Atmosphere
+ Plenty of things to do
- Bikes are DLC only
- Connection and launcher problems
- Driving physics feel clumsy
- Menus for social interactions are not user-friendly

I might as well review this now, because I'm really not the type of person that finishes games like these. This game is a simple, fun, run around and take things in type of game with a light mmo feel. Huge map, things to find, and they seemed to take notes from Just Cause 3 and make sure the reason for people doing things wasn't "Just Cause" This game gives me a real army of two feeling. where you can run amok and hang out, while getting things done.
Ghost recon wildlands is about the only open world co op third person game that exists with some semblance of character creation. It's pretty bare honestly, and like most games with terrible creation, you'll probably be hard pressed to change your clothes, as most clothing options do nothing for your silhouette, so in terms of style, there isn't much. the textures are nice, options are good, and the game runs smoothly.
Gunplay is actually pretty intuitive. Bullet drop as a factor is really a fun thing to see visually and it really contributes to the guns you choose moving forward. Ammo capacity and handling also play a big part in how much you can do in a single down sight sitting, and how confident you can be trying to run and gun. Guns that have more ammo are harder to move about, but great at doing things like killing helicopters in a single clip. (Early on, skills may make it obsolete.)
Enemy AI is bittersweet honestly, Foes are mostly difficult because of sheer numbers, vantage points, weapons, backup, helicopters, etc. They seem like they know how much health you have, and gun for you pretty hard. (Might also be because I don't use any suppressors) There might be some sort of hidden aggro system in it. Which is great for multiplayer.
Ally AI is probably the most blatantly irritating thing I've ever experienced. Unless you're forcing them to sync shot like a cheat, or telling them to fire, they just amble around. But even when they're told to fire, something seems slow about them, as if the game doesn't want to expose how bad they are by having enemies seek you like an impurity. Watching the AI revive me in front of enemies with no consequence whatsoever. I almost never see them throwing grenades. They're more effective than a terrible team who can't keep one survivor, but otherwise, the AI allies are useless for anything aside from cheesing shots with sync.
The cars in this game make grand theft auto San Andreas look like a driving simulator. But, it's actually a good thing. Hitting turns and cornering around cars is about as easy as using a bike in the typical open world city type shooter. The bikes are somewhat worse, as falling off at any type of decent speed and hitting anything will kill you. I don't wear a helmet, it would actually be kind of funny if wearing a helmet remidied that.
Helicopters are absolutely a blast to use however, and planes are fun, but only because they are pretty hard to manipulate properly, watching my friend crash it into a mountian immediately after liftoff was worth every penny. And landing a plane in the wrong spot, only to sit around bumping rocks until you get where you need to be is pretty funny too.
-As a side note, sometimes if you make a vehicle unusable, (Break helicopter blades but not the vehicle) Other players can still use it but not you, and it looks pretty funny lol.
Dying in an exploding vehicle is something I wish would be dealt with better. I would have imagined people would have the option to rip the body from the vehicle and then revive, but as far as I've seen, if you die in a vehicle about to explode, it's pretty much over.
I really can't find anything I truly dislike about the game. Most of the things this game gets wrong is cheesy mechanical mistakes and weird vehicle movement. Fast travelling exists and closes most gaps that are way out of reach, The one or two revives per shootout thing doesn't happen when online, and unless whoever you're playing with isn't there, or just runs in and gets no kills, they're better than the ai. I can really recommend this to anyone who likes co op, and wants to have a game that doesn't feel extremely hard without friends, or empty.
Unless you have no one to play with... it's definitely worth a sale price, maybe even full price if you already have three other people who want to play.

Osiris is another survival, crafting, building, exploring, fighting/defend yourself type of game.  You start out very much like you would in a game like Ark;  You have the bare essentials to get yourself started and have to build up from there.  Also like Ark, you have aggressive creatures all around trying to kill you as you attempt to build yourself a base and so on.   If you like to play multiplayer, this game has that as well.  Where this game sepparates itself from games like Ark is that once you progress far enough, you can build ships and leave the starting planet for another.   According to the developers, they are going to create an entire solar system to explore before they are finished.  Apparently, there is only the one planet at the moment but there are space stations orbiting the planet so you will have places to visit right now once you do get off the ground.
Bottom line is if you are familiar with Empyrion, just figure this game as being very similar.  I like the graphics of this game much better than Empyrion but the Minecraft style "block" building system in Empyrion offers more options for creationism at the moment.   Still, I believe that this game is much more ambitious than Empyrion but Im happy to own both.
UPDATE:  Cranked the game up again after not having played in awhile.  Went to one of my save games and discovered that the base that I had built is now located in the center of a massive hillside.  I cant even get out of the base now.  Im pretty disappointed since that save game is the only one where I had played long enough to have built a space ship and several other vehicles.  Now I have to start all over again.  Oh well, thats early access for you.  Im just happy the devs are actively working on things.
UPDATE 9/16/2017 Logged in again after having not played in quite awhile and am VERY happy to see how this game is doing and where it is going!  I dont know why the reviews are now "mixed", this is a great survival/crafting/exploring game.  Im thinking that many of the negative reviewers just dont understand the concept of EA games.  Sure, there are some glitches on occassion but Ive encountered FAR fewer glitches this time around than I did when I first bought and played this.  Ive read where a few negative reviewers want to blame this game for the fact that their old, outdated toasters cant run it.  Runs pretty much flawlessly for me and many other people so I doubt its the game thats causing your problem guys lol!  So, yeah!  Im happy with the game and where it seems to be heading!  Ignore the clueless negative reviews and give this one a try.  Better yet, read the negative reviews and see if there is anything in them that the classification of "EA" doesnt pretty much void out.  Have fun!

Did you know that in 1997 Microsoft created a game named Age of Empires with randomized maps? They were balanced, never started without a spot of gold, stone or without berries or room to build my base.
So how come that TAB is UNABLE to do it right in 2017?
You will restart a game again and again because you don't have room to build, no access to enough wood, have zombies cities near you or way too much ground to cover to make defense. Or without randomized loots near you. Or with way too many zombies everywhere.
-Way too many ressources to care for. Seriously, citizens, workers, food, energy, gold, wood, iron, stone, oil, buildable tiles, energy coverage.
It's just too much crap to manage and feel really artificial ( and redundant, I mean citizen plus workers? The♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ )
To build something you need to build it in the energy coverage of the town, provide material then workers. Workers also need houses, energy coverage, food and materials. All these things also need a load of others things. So in the end to build one ranger you need half a dozen things to construct. I don't whant to play factorio with zombies -_-
To build a little sawmill you need 2 houses, one tesla and at least one mill and one fishery/hunting lodge, it's just crazy. Sure a part of the food from the fishery and a part of the energy for the mill can support a bit more peoples but damn it's insane to have to build so much crap.
-No campaign/No tutorials. When you get the game you only get the survival mode. Which is the hard mode of the game, the one that should only be played when you mastered the game. A really dubious choice, especially with the ironman mode and no way to customize the game ( can only change the starting quantity of zeds from "too much" to "computer crashing" and the number of days before last huge zeds wave ).
-When a building reach 0 HP it get contamined and all the workers are transformed into fast zombies that rush the nearest building and so on until you lose. The main issue is the insane number of building you need to have, the fact that the buildings have enough HP to tank ONE sneeze from a dying zed before getting destroyed and the fact that you get no warning when zeds are spotted. You need to carefully watch the MINIMAP ( emphasize on the MINI part, a half pixel sized red dot is hard to see on that map ) and hope that the zeds aren't going to exploit invisible breach ( especially border near forest/water ) in your defenses. The moment the icon saying that your base is under attack appear, it's already too late unless you get troops really near the breach.
-It seems ( according to ALL the guides and comments from "veterans" ) that the troops and defenses aren't balanced or usefull at all. Hard to say, but I agree that the rangers are way more powerful and useful than the soldiers you can make from start.
There's a couple others flaws but for me theses ones are the most fun-breaking. This game isn't the Darksoul of RTS. Darksoul is about skills, TAB is about lucky RNG mainly.
And Darksoul was popular because of the blood and flashy 3D. You don't have that on TAB.
That's the main things here, a core of players do everything to make this game as hard as possible and the creator listen to them. I think the game need to be more accessible to the average player ( by having lots of things to customize each games ).

This needs work, full stop. Although the game's premise isn't exactly original - being a blend of Stunt Playground, a freeware classic of old, Trackmania, and Clustertruck - it is fairly interesting! You're racing on tracks with obstacles and competition, but being that it's early access, you're dealing with a limited amount of unique assets on the tracks - I hope you like swinging hammers - and you're dealing with a lack of actual real stakes. If you crash, your weightless-feeling car careens off the track and you start again. Your placement relative to your opponents doesn't matter, finish first, finish last, just finish. Considering it seems to want to be physics-based damage-emphasized car game, it's not actually that satisfying or useful to hit opponents, you simply don't have enough control to recoveer properly, and all the cars are flimsy and easily broken. You're better off just staying away from everyone.
So it's not bad - it's definitely a good start - but the physics, the tracks, the driving, all need development. I'm excited to see where it goes, and hope that it has a successful development.

Dear devs, as you said, you people are going to develop this game based on the feedback of players. I'm really happy you guys do, because I've got a lot of suggestions to do with this awesome game.
This game is really awesome! I want to let you know, as a person who has been playing a lot of racing games for more than 10 years long, that this game, which seems to be in Early Access, is heading in the right direction.
The idea of making an arcade racing game with damage physics similar to Next Car Game or BeamNG.drive is an amazing idea! And it works surprisingly well.
The driving is pretty decent. The car controls with WASD and brakes with Space. Very simple, very decent.
The soundtrack is very enjoyable to listen to. It fits the game well.
Graphically, not the best thing I've saw, but honestly, graphics don't matter much if the gameplay is good.
The gameplay is VERY addictive. It's so fun to race with many other AI cars with damage physics similar to Next Car Game. It leads to unique crashes, saves and race moments that are totally epic. The tracks are short, but the level design of these tracks is excellent.
Crash Wheels is heading to the right direction. However, the only problem of the game is the lack of content.
However, there are a lot of ways Crash Wheels can obtain much more content.
Devs, consider adding/fixing/improving these:
---Add a level creator. Since the main tracks are quite simple, it should also be simple to do a custom level. Have workshop support if it's possible
---Add more cars. Having the possibility of driving only one car isn't good. Or at least, make that car customisable. Let players change the colors of the car.
---The racing is hard. I'm not sure if there is a drafting system, but if there is, make the drafting more effective. If there's no drafting, add drafting. Or else, it's hard to outrun some AI cars.
---If I'm not the first car to reach the finish line, the game still says that I've won. While it might be a reference to Big Rigs, I think it shouldn't say that I've won.
---If I try to crash an AI car while driving, I will very easily lose control of my car. While it kind of works, I think the intensity of the loss of control should be toned down a bit.
---Add more options, such as a way to change the controls, mute the music or sounds, etc.
---Add multiplayer. Both Local and Online multiplayer will work.
---Add different camera views, such as a view in the interior of the car, on the hood, etc.
---Make the suspension slightly softer. Right now, the suspension is too hard.
---Improve the interface of the menus. While there is nothing wrong with simplicity, it would be prettier to have a better looking interface, making the game more professional-looking.
---The collision between the sledgehammers and the cars can be quite glitchy. Fix this issue ASAP.
In conclusion, you should definitely buy Crash Wheels. It's a very simple game, but it has a bright future and a lot of potential.

I know what everyone who hasn't played this is thinking; "A dating sim for BIRDS, are you crazy?" I've already seen remarks like "Why does this even exist?"
Well, I'm here to tell you why. It's wonderful, hilarious, uplifting yet simultaneously heart-wrenching, and sometimes even TERRIFYING. No one takes it seriously at first glance, but they /learn/. It's a carefree experience where you pursue a pigeon boy of your choice and everything is sunshine and rainbows. But, you quickly start to realise that Something Isn't Right. There's something going on at this school, and it's not just Okosan's search for the perfect pudding...
So here's my recommendation. Play this game. Play through every route. Start a new game, and then, then you will understand why this game is amazing.
Trust me, I dated birds before it was cool.
Edit: I forgot to add, this game is also hilariously self aware.

First and foremost for those that fail to read the information above this is a visual novel. That means the majority of the content is reading. If you dislike reading turn back now.
Alright. For those of you still here yes this game is satire, but it can also take itself quite seriously. While playing this you have the amusing routes(which can overlap), the tear-jerking routes(which can overlap), the childhood friend route, the jerkwad routes, the senpai route, the sensei route, and the reformed thug/female route. Additionally there's the secret plot-heavy route that will not be spoken of for the sake of spoilers. The gameplay is much like you'd expect from a visual novel. Make a few choices. If you select the correct ones and have the proper stats congrats. You just landed yourself a good ending. Speaking of stats they aren't used as much as the other games of the same read-and-select format. An amusing game at the core for the most part.
Now what this rerelease was mainly supposed to fix was the engine. You see the previous engine back before the steam version was riddled with bugs and made playing it rather difficult. While this engine does run much more smoothly than Famous Writer did it does, in fact, have some bugs too. There have been reports of freezing on a white screen during the loading process before getting to the menu, crashing when loading human portraits, and likely more that have yet to be reported. Thankfully these aren't as numerous as the previous iteration. Still annoying, but some have reported fixing it by restarting the game. As per the others... Well this is a custom engine. Perhaps there will be patches in the future to fix the problems.
As per double the original price... Moa used a lot of open sourse content to make the game as cheap as possible at first, and this remake gave the game its own look background-wise as well as replacing that outdated freeware engine. The music is the same and the birds are higher resolution, but more or less the same. That said some of the birds are higher resolution than the other birds.
All in all I still do recommend it since it is less likely to backfire on you than the original and does provide a good deal of amusement.
Edit: It slipped my mind earlier, but the collector's edition does hold true on its claim. The original game is included if you feel like owning both renditions.

Here is a game as joyous and painful, as mysterious and memorable, as high school itself.
Hatoful Boyfriend captures the longing of the lonely, the brute insult of bigotry, and the wonder of even the most simplistic actions making the world feel right again in post-apocalyptic dystopian future. Compassionate, dramatic, this is writing that always knows when to take a moment for humor AND pathos. Let the deep and highly metaphoric story sink in over multiple playthroughs or you will be missing out on some of the best divergent storytelling of the generation.
As you click through interaction after interaction just know that others are out there are taking time to do the same. Slowly begin to realize that some people can be trusted. It was people that made this game, after all, people finally aware of the  consumer fatigue of space marines and dragons. You may never fully rehabilitate into a properly functioning member of human society by their standards but you understand, just as I understand, that it is people that we do NOT understand. Remember, birds can be trusted, birds always come back. Some people are meant to be with people, and others, like us, are just different. We may not have the shiniest of neck feathers and our ultimate failing is to be aware that we are not aware. But we have finally found somewhere we can live in peace.
Let us never forget the healing power of columbidae society but let us always try to remember to wash our berries before we eat them. Our digestive and respiratory systems may be different but blood is pumped into the heart from the body through the veins, the blood then enters the right atrium, then gets transported through the right ventricle and then is moved to into the lungs and oxygenated just the same.
"In some things they shame us, by and large. Once mated, they are wed for life, unless forcibly separated. When set to the task, such as a long race, they will persevere and endure through measures of hell that only the best of men will willingly undertake. It might be argued that they are simply, dumbly, following the programming of instinct, that they can do nothing differently.
Perhaps that can be said of us as well."
- Where Pigeons Go to Die.

I avoided Dishonored when it was being advertised, years ago, because by one look at it I knew it would be "Half Life 2 meets Bioshock". The art by Victor Antonov was very clearly 'butthurt because they didn't use my ideas in HL2 so I'll take it over here'.
I was not off the mark there, in any way. In fact, many lines of dialog, all the vehiclular designs, color schemes, and whole battles, arenas, events, and visual constructions of levels are blatantly Half Life 2. (let's see, 'you were in the wrong place at the right time', the entire 'strider battle' with tall boys, 'nova prospekt', 'captive in the metal transport cage/battle at the top of a tower', every single combine-i mean sokolov- vehicle's appearance, the blue metal structure walls blocking off streets.... I could go on?) Throw in the visually steampunk Bioshock aspects, and add in the Plasmid use... Toss a pile of Thief stealth aspects, and you have Dishonored.
Oh yeah, I was kind of expecting Corvo to have a voice actor? I guess they wised up in 2 and gave him one. Yet Another Mute Protagonist. While Corvo can be pretty amazing, when you look at him he's absolutely the blankest of blank slates, and has zero personality aside from the clear adoration of Emily. All the rest of the characters in the game - and specifically the DLC with Daud - have far more attachment and engagement with what's actually going on. I find it hard to believe that Corvo himself isn't dumb as a bag of hammers, given that he, as the Lord Protector and lover of Jessamine... *went out for months* while the clearly devious Spymaster was busy engineering the Empress' demise. I mean, how about "no, sir, this is my post and it would be completely insane to leave it" comes to mind. With the flimsiness of that plot however, it also seems like the rest of the city is exactly as vapid as the protagonist.
There is so much potential in this game's world for story telling. So much, completely wasted with this game. However all that said:
It was an enjoyable game, fun to play, and fun to play again. While the quirky specifics of the achievements are indeed pretty weird (i'm going through a second time trying for clean hands, but not ghost and definitely not flesh and steel) I like exploration and definitely like the stealth aspects. I only wish that they'd allowed for more of a non-lethal Corvo! Playing the DLC as Daud at least you get the ability to increase the number of sleep darts you can use, but Corvo cannot?! Well, at least that still plays well enough with being able to use takedowns.
Even though visually the game is shamelessly HL2+Bioshock, it's at least internally consistent. However the art itself is garbage, undetailed, might as well be low-rez in many cases because they don't stand up to close inspection. If I look at it as 'they're all paintings', that's not bad at all, because the character design and lighting supports that pretty decently.
The clunky UI is clunky, the radial menu difficult to use at best, and the lack of hotkeys for certain things was dismaying.
I think my biggest beef with it is that you just don't get one straightforward story even though there's a shockingly linear progression through the game. There are hints in all the books and notes you find that there's something much more deep and entertaining, but *none* of it surfaces, ever.
The DLC and challenge levels are actually far more engaging than the main game, though the level design of Daud's story is far less clever and much more limited than the main game. I wish that the level design had kept up in terms of exploration and complexity, but that the main game had the personality of Daud's dlc.
Anyway - I do recommend the game, but don't expect anything other than highly derived locations and visuals, and if you've played either Bioshock or Half Life 2 understand that this game WAS designed by the same guy doing HL2's work... and it showed.

Wildlands is an interesting open world take on the Ghost Recon franchise. It is similar to The Division and the FarCry series. It feels easier, more "casual" than the old GR games, but on higher difficulty you are better off sticking to stealth.
The shooting mechanics are well done, gravity is actually affecting bullets, so you need to compensate in long distance shots. The open world feels authentic, living. With cars traveling the roads, people living in towns. The environments and scenery are beautiful and varied, from swamplands, mountains, deserts and so on. The graphics are good, weather effects are pretty. Locations are well designed, they do not feel as a level in a game, they feel like farms, towns, factories, etc. As it should be. You have a good variety of vehicles (cars, boats, helicopters) to get around the fictionalized Bolivia,
but driving and flying feels a bit off. It is usable, but not as well done as it could be. There are lots of weapons to find, and the customization is definitely a highlight. You can change almost any component of a weapon to tailor it to your play-style with silencers, scopes, magazines etc. There is a lot of attention to detail, like that enemy vehicles act as disguise, the paint job of your guns will scratch and wear over time, guards have different behavior in day and night etc.
Although it works as a single player game, Wildlands really shines in co-op, it is meant to be played with a group of friends. Especially on higher difficulty levels, where squad communication and coordination is essential. You can play drop-in-drop-out coop with random people, but the results is as you would expect...
After a while it does get repetitive, but this is the characteristic of open world games like this. There are some small bugs, like climbing on rocks and your squad members freezing up, enemy soldiers spawning from nowhere, but I did not encounter any game-breaking ones.
If you have a group of friends to play with, or you just like open world games with a bit more tactical and stealthy game-play, I can recommend it.

Lets come to the most important statement right at the start:
Its hard, its brutal, but its so damn good.
First time I ever played a colony builder game was back in the early 2000s, when I discovered the Settlers 1.
Shortly after I discovered the Settlers 3 which was for ages the only really great colony builder I out there and I played it a ton. And now finally there is a great one again!
They Are Billions is different in many ways, but shares enough similarities to be, for me, worthy of taking the rank the Settlers 3 held for so long.
Lets take a closer look at some aspects of the game.
Pros:
Cons:
I'll just make one list that covers both the pros and the cons that slighly overshadow them. I said slightly.
Overall, this game is just brilliant and its brutal. It is quite annoying that you have to beat the first map on 100% in order to get access to another map type, but even putting this aside, this game is addicting and has a massive replayability due to the randomly generated maps that offer you great positions at times, but could also put your citadel right next to a zombie village.

Welcome Soldier to the most generic shooter on the market.
E.T. Armies is one game that I was looking forward to playing when I got it as a gift from a friend. The game looked fun and for an Indie game looked like it had tons of potential and boy I'm disappointed.
E.T. Armies story is a very generic story. Earth becomes ruined and the population splits into to factions and then they go to war. It's nothing special and it's a boring story. The characters are one dimensional figures which you don't care for and the voice acting ruins the entire game. The ending is also really bad so don't expect anything amazing.
The gameplay is generic fps stuff (notice the pattern here ?). Nothing really stands out. Shoot your way through to the next objective and repeat until the game is done. I would at least give the game points for having decent shooting mechanics, but those don't exist in this game. The shooting is very stiff and the aiming is abysmal, it get's really annoying having to aim for a headshot, but the mouse just veers off to the side.
The graphics are alright for the most part. Even though the environments are generic all of them look nice and vibrant. While there's not much to look at in the first act, the facility chapter looks decent enough and the rain effects are great and I don't know if this a gloating thing, but the game even remarks the rain effects in the character dialogue.
The game is also incredibly easy, I played on Normal before the game broke and got to the final section of the game when the game wiped my save file. My journey was easy, but to breeze through it faster, I decided to do on easy mode cause I didn't care at all by the start of my second playthrough.
Now for the technical issues. The game crashes constantly and one time it wiped my save file and it forced me to start from the beginning. Bugs like enemies phasing through walls, items falling through the level are also present during the entire time of playing. Really hope that the developer patches these things out.
The game took me 2 hours to finish and after that there's no replay value, it's a very linear game and there's not much to do in the first place. Now there is a multiplayer mode, but I didn't get the chance to play it.
Overall E.T. Armies is as generic as it can get, now I know this is an Indie developer and I quite admire the work that they put into this game, but the stiff shooting and the story just ruin the entire experience and if they came out with a redux or a remaster of the original game which fixed all of the problems, I would gladly check it out, but as for now, it's not worth your time or your money.

First Impressions: E.T. Armies
I got this out of bundle fairly cheaply from Bundle Stars (Pick & Mix bundle, 3 games for £2.29), it's currently part of the Steam Summer Sale (ends July 4th) so if you've read this review and want to pick it up cheaply you can do so using the link below.
Made by an Iranian developer, Raspina, E.T. (Extra-Terrestrial) Armies is a first person shooter. With a rather cheesy plot, sub-par voice acting and a clunky controller port, frankly I'd only recommend this if you like being tortured frantically by aimless robots, or like bad games.
Controls:
Rather clunky, aiming with a mouse is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor, let alone with a controller! Instead of the usual 'hold to zoom' most games have, you're stuck with a toggle zoom. Which you can't change at all.
2/10
Sound:
Whatever you think a game with guns and vehicles should sound like, it sounds nothing like it. Bad meshing of sounds, leading to desynchronized audio whenever you make an action or when the characters speak. Hell, every single gun has the same sound coming out of it!
2/10
Graphics:
This wasn't that much of let down to be honest on Ultra-High. However, it is badly optimized, with lag and framerate drops during cutscenes, (before you think it's due to the computer, I far exceed the recommended specs - see Test System specs below) during gameplay, it ain't half bad. The game is based on Unreal Engine 3.
6/10
AI/Difficulty:
I played this on 'Normal' difficulty, which is the highest difficulty you can play on if this is your first try. 'Brutal' difficulty can be unlocked once you complete the game. The enemies were either quite predictable or erratic in their behaviour depending on which part of the game you are on. I found it easier to walk past, get shot a couple of times and leave the enemies in their patrol path, or stuck in their position. For Normal difficulty, I felt that the game was quite easy. You could run through the whole missions without dying or reloading a magazine in some cases.
3/10
Overall, I give this a 3/10. If you like bad games, this may be for you.

has a lot of good things going on for it.  The game takes you on a journey of the imagination as some children’s quest for candy on one Halloween night quickly turns into something much more.  Ultimately, this game is just very well done and has a “soul” that should easily appeal to a vast audience.
The level design is charming and exploring the maps is fun.  The whole concept of “trick-or-treating” being a fundamental part of the gameplay is brilliantly done.  The story is basically one giant trope, but the way it is told is delightful.  The characters are likeable and the humor is clean but entertaining.  Even the style in which you warp into old-school, turn-based battles is executed well and synergizes perfectly with the atmosphere of the game.  This game is a quintessential example of how several good things can work together to create something great.
As I alluded to, one of the most charming aspects of
is the way “trick-or-treating” in the game world is a central part of progressing the game.  You knock on doors and are either given candy (treat) or have to fight a battle (trick).  This leads to another splendidly charming feature of the game, which I also alluded to earlier: the battle warp-ins.  Depending on what costumes your characters are wearing, they change from little kids into various gallant warriors with nothing but the power of their imagination.  From there, the battles play out in the old-school, turn-based RPG style that was prevalent in the 90s.
Aside from that, you may also want to explore the levels, find secret areas, meet characters, and do side-quests and mini-games to gather more candy and collect the trading cards.  There is plenty to do!

Forgotten, Not Lost is a kinetic visual novel by Afterthought Studios (A More Beautiful World), and it’s available on Windows, Mac OSX and Linux via Steam for $1.99. It includes Steam trading card, but no achievements to collect.
Who are you?
In this visual novel, the reader takes the role of an old farmer who is suffering from dementia, and is slowly losing more and more of the memories of his wife and child. Due to the shortness of the novel, it’s really hard to go much more into the details in order not to spoil it all, but it’s easy to say that this is one emotionally loaded novel. Depending on one’s reading speed, it will take a little over or under one hour to go through Forgotten, Not Lost. There is no replay value at all.
Occasionally it’s easy to lose track of the characters due to the similarity in all of their names, making for some confusing scenarios. One could go and assume that the confusion with the names of the characters happens on purpose, but it can easily sway the reader from the verge of tears to confusion, really eating out the immersion that was being built. But since the author of the story has based it in their own, actual experiences, this could very well be something that just escapes me since I have not had to deal with any sort of memory loss in life – this is to say, the story might resonate more with those who have actual experience with the matter.
The art of the game is quite simplistic, but it fits the sorrowful theme very nicely – same can also be said for the music, which complements the whole package neatly. And while I do feel that there could’ve been some more sound effects in some scenes to bring even more life to the experience, it’s not a major downfall.
In conclusion
Forgotten, Not Lost is definitely a decent visual novel, and while it is very short and even quite confusing at times, overall it manages to make itself worthwhile. The price of $1.99 is already not too bad, but later down the road when discounts start to hit it, it can easily be recommended for a short bedtime story.

I came across this game after playing the A More Beautiful World demo made by the same studios.
First of all, I wanted to say that I like the art style. Especially the backgrounds, well done. I also like the music as well, it fits the moods well(though it gets kind of sporadic and repetitive, still good).
I also admit that it's a tough and noble thing to tackle the issues of mental illness and trying to fit the reader into the shoes of such a person. I think we need more stories like this in that manner.
Having said that, I can't recommend you pay any sort of money for this novel, for the following reasons:
1. The story does not do the topic justice. It's confusing, goes nowhere, nothing happens, nobody changes or learns, and the ending is predictable and boring.
2. The charatcers are confusing as all get-out. And boring. Not fleshed out at all.
3. The story was definitely padded with the same thing over and over again (i.e., character recalls something, character's wife reminds him that so and so died, character accepts as the truth, pats daughter's head). This happens ad nauseum throughout the story.
4. The music and audio inconsistencies. Music randomly cuts in and out, sound effects are random.
5. Spelling and grammar. Did you proof-read this? And is it Madaline or Madeline? It keeps changing in the story making it quite discombobulating.
6. Some of your character prompts were broken (i.e., lines spoken by the wife not displaying their name, meaning that it looks like the main character is speaking it.)
In the end, this is a noble freshman effort which lacks polish or any decent story. There are bits where it does shine, but it beats you over the head with them so many time you wish you didn't bother.
I would recommend to Afterthought Studios that you up your writing game, or get another writer. I think you could have great potential, but until you have a good story, it will be difficult to ewach that potential.

I never read a review of this game until after I had beaten it.  I wasn't terribly interested in buying it based on the poor review scores it received.  I decided to pick it up on a weekend sale based on a friend telling me they enjoyed playing it.  All I can say is that I'm glad I did.  While I understand where a lot of the reviews are coming from, the story at the end goes batshit very quickly, especially with unexpected and uncharacteristic responses from the main character due to what's happening in the story.  Also the mechanic where you get punished more for partial success than for failure in that if an agent dies and you succeed, he stays dead.  But if he dies and you fail, you start up at the last checkpoint.
That being said, the combat is pretty awesome.  It feels like it's taking a page from Mass Effect 2/3 combat but also combining it with a bunch of X-COM: Enemy Unknown's tactics/aesthetics.  It's a pretty game, although my computer struggled with DX11 a little bit, so I ran standard.
I plan on playing it again on a more difficult setting.  On normal it was an alright challenge.  I managed to finish the game without losing any agents, though there were times that I'd fail encounters outright multiple times before completing them due to managing my team better.
SPOILER(ish)
The one thing I did and also very much did not like about the story, all at the same time is that very near the end they give a very good explanation for the 3rd person perspective and the slow down time mechanic of battle tactics.  If you played it, you'll definitely understand what I'm getting at.
I definitely recommend this game to fans of Mass Effect 2/3 combat.  For X-COM purists, I hear it's a tough pill to swallow regarding canon, so take it with a grain of salt perhaps?

Dawn of War II was a nice surprise. Breaking away from the regular mold of RTS games to create something more action oriented was a bold move that paid off. The campaign had a lot of hectic moments and offered some interesting RPG elements to help build a sense of progression throughout it's missions.
Chaos Rising takes that RPG-lite system a step further and introduces some branching paths to the games various missions. Doing certain objectives (or failing to do them) may "corrupt" your squad, which can unlock more Chaos oriented abilities. You also have the reverse, which is Redemption points. It brings a further level of depth to how you can tackle missions, as well as introducing slight alterations to the story based on your choices.
The story is also dramatically improved over what the base game had. It deals with the uprising of the Chaos Space Marines and how one of your own may be a traitor. While you can't directly fail a mission, some of the scenarios are out of your control, in terms of victory. You fight unending odds and need to retreat, which ramps up the tension quite a bit.
It all ends with a twist that you shape based on your choices, but it's never directly stated how that works. It makes for a far more realistic take on the morality systems usually in place of RPG systems. Losing one of your finest squadmates to Chaos can be a devastating blow and knowing you could have prevented it makes it more agonizing.
As far as the general gameplay goes, there aren't really any new additions (aside from Corruption/Redemption). Everything functions the same and you still can collect gear to improve your squads. You have a new Hero in the form of The Librarian. He acts has a healer and a ranged caster, which can help tremendously in the more closed off environments in the campaign.
There are some missions reminiscent of the atmosphere that the Alien films made famous. You will be traversing through derelict vessels looking for Bio-samples and other materials. Ambushes are frequent and your squad is often outnumbered, so a strong emphasis is put on tactical manuevers more so than brute force.
The campaign is about half the length of the main game, which is a plus and a negative. While the main game became a bit repetitive towards the end, Chaos Rising seems to teter between being excellent and being bland. While the Corruption/Redemption mechanic does allow for different approaches to certain objectives, they almost always culminate in a boss battle.
The general difficulty is also much higher than the main game. It makes for certain missions that feel a bit cheap, as you often just don't have the manpower to overcome the odds. Since you can't build units on the fly, you're often forced to retreat and wait for reinforcements. It makes some missions take upwards of 30 minutes to complete, which just drags out the pacing.
Overall, I think the campaign is better, but it does have more problems. It's not a bad attempt at expanding the groundwork set in Dawn of War II, but more could have been done to keep the consistency of quality at a high level. Still, more of the same would have been sufficient, so I admire Relic for attempting to mix things up.
As I said in my review for the base game, the multiplayer is practically non-existent. I believe that is more down to the second expansion, Retribution, being the first Dawn of War II title on Steamworks. Chaos Rising and the base game were added to Steamworks only 2 years ago, but that was 3 years after Retribution released.
While I couldn't find any games for co-op or competitive, the functionality is present. That means the co-op campaign is an option for people who want to bring a friend along. It would probably mitigate some of the difficulty concerns I had, but it would also be cool to tinker with the morality system with a buddy.
Regardless, I would call this expansion unessential. It isn't bad, but it's mostly for the more hardcore of fans. Dawn of War II provides basically everything this game has, save for the Chaos Space Marines. If you really want, you could just get Retribution, which includes a campaign for every race.
You could do much worse, though.

TDU2 had its multiplayer peak in 2011 [2,000 average number of players online each day] and was excellent and seamless join from singleplay and support was good. Since then Atari went broke, sacked its Eden devs and try to maintain and code and 'update' it by themselves and they have failed  breaking much of the multi and have even broken some of the login process and Uplauncher. Support is not much after 3 years.  Many forum posts complain about not being able to get past the uplauncher into the multi game. If you do manage to set router firewall exceptions for port 8889 and 3478 [not so simple] then you will mostly get into multi ok and all will be good.
Backup your Savegame every day.. that's Documents\Eden Games. Copy the whole folder, find a safe place on other drive, create a new folder, name it as e.g. 'May12-ellie-lev22' Open it, and Paste in there. Ok. Do that every day, make new folder each time with new name, e.g. 'May13-ellie....etc. after a week you have 7 backups of your Eden Games, you can delete the oldest one, you still got 6. My backup folder, if it gets more than 50 in it I delete a few, but I always keep the most recent 5.  If your Tdu2 gives error or crashes, go Documents, Cut the Eden Games folder, Paste it to Desktop, Open the recent backup folder you made, Copy  (not Cut) that Eden Games folder and Paste it in Documents. Run Uplauncher all good say Hurray for backup, delete that bad Eden from Desktop, go Play. If still fail ask for helps.
Thanks for reading. Have fun!
