So far, it's been a pretty fun game. I'm a huge fan of the Far Cry series, so naturally, I came to enjoy Wildlands. The graphics are great, runs smoothly  (with the right graphic tweaks), and the gameplay can keep you playing for several hours. The co-op is incredibly fun with a friend or even a random person. I hate to use Far Cry in comparison, but it plays just like Far Cry 3 & 4.
The graphic are excellent. I'm able to get 60-80FPS on medium-high settings on an XFX RX 480 8GB paired with a Ryzen 7 1700x. Even at lower settings, the game looks great. It's hard to complain about something in this area.
The audio is pretty nice. I play with my Apple earbuds and sometimes with my Turtle Beach headset and the sounds are great. You can hear explosions in the distance, the direction of gun shots, and not to mention Ubisoft did an excelent job on the audio for the weapons. The dialogue seems a bit half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's irrelevant in most situations outside of the main story. I'm not even sure if every member of the squad that follows you around has their own voice actor, it's always the same guy it seems.
The overall gameplay is pretty solid. The gun mechanics are great, the bullet drop makes distant kills satisfying, and the sound the guns make feel real and varied. The customization of each weapon is pretty awesome, though, it takes a bit of time and effort to unlock the things you would like to have for your gun. Unfortunately, due to time contraints of my life, I had to spend about $5 to get the weapon unlocks in a timely manner. You do not have to spend money to acquire weapon attachments and the base-game skins are readily available.
The content of this game is pretty interesting. It's similar to that of Far Cry where you go to a base and essentially take it over by taking out bad guys using whatever method you desire. Want to run in and guns-a-blaze? Go ahead, but you'll probably get outnumbered if you're not quick enough or have proper gear/skill points. There's plenty to do in Wildlands. There are side missions, collectables, and bases to attack. Though, the missions do get repetitive, but there is more than one way to play each mission. You could try different tactics, there is no "right" way to play this game. There's not a lot of variety to the enemies, either, There is the Santa Blanca cartetl and the Unidad, each faction with their own set of soliders, snipers, and armored guys. The AI, however, is becomes more challenging as the game progresses and awards stealth over run 'n gun in most situations.
There's a lot to do to finish the story. I'm about 25 hours in and I have yet to make it to 50%. The story, at this point, seems a bit uninteresting and the interactions with the underbosses are anti-climatic. Plus, they seem very easy to manipulate for a drug cartel. Each underboss (sort of like a mini boss, sorta) has their own set of missions designed around their weaknesses in order to take them down to get to the final boss. These missions do add some variety to the game, but  most of the stuff outside of the main story missions get repetative very quickly. If it wasn't for the great gameplay, the missions wouldn't be very interesting.
The vehicle mechanics are pretty terrible, especially with a keyboard and mouse, but this is to be expected as most things are generally better with a controller (with the exception of shooter games). Most of the vehicles handle very strangely. The dirtbikes are pretty fun off-road, if you can manage to stay alive when you're flying down a massive hill.
One thing that I really like about this game is the ability to change how your character looks throughout the game. I'm not really sure if your apparel makes a difference when it comes to visibilty to the enemy or whatever. But, you do look pretty snazzy in an all-black attire with a ski mask. You also have the option for gilly suits, which is neat.
Not worth writing about. The PvE and story mode is where it's at and it's even better with a friend.
I know, it's like word vomit to a lot of gamers, but I think Ubisoft does it right here. There are no loot crates, instead, you can either choose to buy the guns for the story through the store with real money, or, find them in weapon crates hidden throughout the game. I don't have a lot of time to play video games these days and I really wanted the M4A1, so I ended up spending about $5 to get the things that I wanted. The rest is just cosmetics. And honestly, I think the base-game has some really nice character customization options.
Overall, I think Ubisoft did a great job with this game. It's worth the $60 price tag and could easily suck you into its endless gameplay and gun mechanics. Though, with repetitive missions and difficult AI, frustration could soon be an issue if you play for long periods of time.
If you're a fan of the Far Cry series, I'm sure you'll enjoy this game.

Early Access inital reaction review:
Current EA Score: 6/10
This game has a ton of potential. A ton. However there needs to be growth in a few areas that I've seen already within the first 3 hours of gameplay:
1. The drone bot needs an AI optimization. It seriously gets stuck on absolutely everything.
2. Magnesium is a really unnecessary grind ATM for a material that's required to start building anything.
3. Base/colony building needs to be seriously increased in the flexibility dept. Multiple buildings of the same type should be allowed. Colony minimum distance from one another should be configurable for those of us who want to build with a buddy as a neighbor.
4. If you want to meet up with a friend, you should have some method of meeting up at the beginning of the game; currently far too hard for one player to trek across the planet with starting drops in hand. Which brings me to #5....
5. Would be nice if you could hold off on the sandstorms for the first day or two. Let a new player figure out their surroundings, keys, menus, and gameplay before you toss them into a sandstorm/hurricane/nighttime misery. Sitting in your inflatible dome for a half hour isn't "challenging", it's a timesink and a reason to go make a sandwich.
If 1 though 5 were addressed, I'd adjust my scoring of this game to at least an 8/10.
Even though I have these suggestions, I feel this game has a major potential to compete with other extremely popular survival games. Keep the updates coming, keep the bugfixes coming, keep showing love to the base building engineers  out there (Hi!) with new structures and more flexibility in colony planning... and you've got a winner!

STORY:
In Dishonored, you play as the former royal protector, Corvo, who has been framed for the murder of Jessamine Kaldwin, the empress and for the abduction of her daughter, Emily. You get thrown into prison, tortured, but a mysterious "friend" helps you out.
8/10
GAMEPLAY:
There are many ways of playing Dishonored, and almost every way of playing is supported by an ability or gadget. You can play as a ghost, who doesn't kill anyone nor knocks them out, only sneaking his way through Dunwall. You can play as the predator, who hunts his enemies down from the shadows, and so on. The gameplay is very smooth, the stealth kills look awesome, the animations are not choppy. The game doesn't get boring nor repetitive, even if you keep playing the same way. In various quests and missions you can explore the map for collectibles and resources.
10/10
THE CHAOS SYSTEM:
There is a so called "chaos" system is the game, that determines your reputation, the number of enemies on the map, the amount of weepers (zombie-like creatures who were infected by the rat plauge), and the paranoia (ergo perception of the guards) There are many ways to alter the chaos:
INCREASING THE CHAOS:
-Killing enemies
-Killing assasination targets
-Killing civilians
-Doing frontal attacks on the enemy guards
-Letting dead bodies be found
DECREASING CHAOS
-Knocking out enemies
-Helping out civilians
-Hiding dead/unconscious bodies (really important)
-Doing the non-lethal way of eliminating the assasination targets.
GRAPHICS/WORLD BUILDING:
Don't expect 4k textures and extremely immersive shaders, but it does pretty well considering the fact that it is a 2012 game. The color palette is the fifty shades of slate and ash, (it is dark and gray AF) due to the fact that most of the game is played in the night, but when it is daytime, it looks prettier. And those HUGE HANDS THO
9/10
DLC:
Buy these DLCs:

-The Brigmore Witches
Awesome DLCs. Totally worth it.
10/10
OVERALL:
Definetly worth the 10 bucks, or the 20 bucks with all the DLCs. I recommend you pick it up if you want to experience an interesting world and great gameplay.
RATING: 9/10

E.T. Armies is a sci-fi themed military First Person Shooter by a small Iranian studio, made in Unreal Engine 3. It's clearly not a triple-A title, but does show a solid degree of polish and professionalism; there are actual production values behind it, and it's not just a student programming project made by one or two dudes in their bedrooms (like a lot of First Person games on Steam these days). I'd say it's comparable in quality to other studio-developed "Euro" FPS games on Steam, like Alien Rage, Alpha Prime, Chaser, Chrome, Bet on Soldier, Exodus from the Earth, S.T.A.L.K.E.R., Ubersoldier, etc (although the graphics are more modern than most of those games, which were made in the late 2000's).
Generally, the game plays like a typical modern shooter; you have regenerating health and can survive a reasonable but not overwhelming amount of gunfire, can carry 2 swappable weapons plus a backup pistol, can throw grenades, enemies generally take 4 to 6 bullets of automatic weapons fire to kill depending on weapon, etc. The one caveat is that movement speed feels somewhat slow (if anyone remembers Unreal 2, that's how slow you move in this game), although you can sprint to move somewhat faster. There's no inventory management; your ammo is restored to full at ammo boxes spaced periodically throughout the levels, although if you're using enemy weapons you need to pick up dropped weapons to refill ammo instead. Overall, the gameplay and animations are a little stiff compared to an AAA release (or even something like the Metro series), but there are no glaring bugs or  major frustrations.
The Unreal Engine 3 graphics are very nice and up to modern standards (though not quite the bleeding edge photorealism of a AAA title), as previously stated the game has actual production values behind it and the graphics are a lot better than other UDK games on Steam that were made by one or two people. The only thing that looks a few years dated are the character faces, and even those are OK. However most of the levels after the first one are somewhat disappointing in terms of art style, as they all take place inside a generic sci-fi factory-type setting.
Level progression is very linear (no sidepaths and no exploration), although the levels themselves can be very large in scale. The game has about 6 levels, with each level taking about 20-30 minutes to finish. Overall, the game can be finished in a little over 2 hours, which combined with the very basic small-scale plot and abrupt ending are probably the biggest weakness of the game.

The story is surprisingly small-scale, and focuses on a single mission (to retake/destroy a power plant taken over by enemy soldiers) during a larger war between the Parsis (colonists who fled Earth after a global nuclear war) and the Forsaken (humans who were left behind on post-apocalyptic Earth). There are a couple hints of a larger plot (your character makes note of strange ruins in the desert, abnormal weather, and the Forsaken being more technologically advanced than they should be), but these plot threads never add up to anything concrete, and the game ends abruptly with you simply blowing up the enemy base. Overall the plot feels like the first act in a 3 act storyline (i.e. the Modern Warfare games), which makes it seem the Devs ran out of time/money and could only put out the first act.
The cutscenes and dialogue are probably the weakest part of the overall presentation. Characters are reasonably animated in cutscenes, although animation appears non-mocapped and seems on par with a mid-2000's game. However, dialogue isn't lip-synced well and the dialogue itself is pretty poor (you can tell it was translated from a non-English script, if you've played games like Chaser, Alpha Prime, or Bet on Soldier you'll be familiar with this). It's not "Master of Unlocking" bad, the dialogue IS coherent, but there's just something "off" about it that makes it clear it was translated. Still, since the plot itself is so basic this doesn't really hurt that much.
Weapon variety is pretty basic. There are 3 assault rifles (the Parsis assault rifle, the Forsaken assault rifle, and a stronger elite Forsaken assault rifle that can be picked up in the later levels), a high-caliber pistol, a shotgun, and a sniper rifle. Guns have a decent amount of recoil and your aim jumps when firing, so you don't have laser-like accuracy even when Aiming Down Sights; at the same time you're still pretty accurate when hip-firing or running-and-gunning, unlike say Call of Duty. Hip fire is accurate enough for normal combat, though you do need to aim to be accurate enough to get headshots.
Enemy variety is also basic; you have a standard soldier, an elite soldier with a better rifle and more health (who looks EXACTLY like the regular soldier except for a slightly different-color uniform; camo grey instead of black), a close-range shotgunner, and a sniper. There are also wall turrets, 2 different types of flying drone (one type has somewhat more health than the other), and an enemy aircraft that can only be killed with mounted turrets or special laser-targeter binoculars that take time to recharge. Enemy durability is on par with games like Killzone or the F.E.A.R. series, with enemies dying after 6 shots from the Parsis rifle, 4 shots from the Forsaken rifle, or 3 shots from the heavy assault rifle or pistol. Headshots from any weapon are an instant kill.
Generally, the enemy A.I. and animations are also very basic. Enemies often stand or crouch in one spot while firing, they do slowly strafe left or right when shot at, and do make some usage of cover. I'd say the A.I. and animation quality is comparable to other "Euro" FPS games (Bet On Soldier, Chaser, Chrome, Ubersoldier, etc). The enemy animations are functional, though they do have a certain stiffness to them (I'd say it's comparable to the animations of the human enemies in the first Borderlands game). Enemies have a fairly basic animation/move set and aren't as fluid as in games like Call of Duty, F.E.A.R., Rage, Far Cry, Borderlands 2, etc. There are a couple nice touches though, such as enemies stumbling or doubling over when shot.
I've heard there were some issues with rebinding keys, invert mouse, etc, but all of that seems to have been addressed and the game now has all the standard options you'd expect in a professional studio release.
Overall, if you play budget/Indie FPS titles and don't mind the basic, even truncated plot, you might give E.T. Armies a try.  It's pretty generic and basic, but it's also competently made. If you generally stick to AAA releases, though, you might want to skip it.

Costume Quest is a simple but well put together party based RPG game. You play the role of a child who is obsessed with halloween, and spends the night going around the neighborhood trick or treating to get his candy. At the beginning of the game, your twin sister is kidnapped and you embark on your journey to rescue her. Along the way you make friends with other trick or treaters who join your party.
While you are walking around the world, you are able to pick up extra candy, talk to the residents of the town and start battles with the bad guys. The combat system in Costume Quest is turn based, each of your characters will have their own costume which all have different powers. The combat is also primarily quick time events, which is normally not something I am a fan of, but it works quite well here.
The graphics are nothing special, but they do look pleasing and the cartoon style is something which fits the story and setting nicely. Sadly the audio in Costume Quest lets it down, there isn't any voice acting, and very little sound effects when you are walking around the world.
The game is set across four different levels, each of them has their own theme and style, with lots of different items and hidden locations to find in each of the levels, they feel plumped out and interesting to explore. I didn't find there to be any difficulty, you can complete the game without being beaten once, so maybe a New Game+ mode would of fixed that. I'm not sure why Steam has counted me having sixteen hours, as the game took me about five hours to complete along with the majority of all the side missions and achievements.
I only really ran into one technical issue, and that was frame rate, the Steam in game counter shows it running at 30 fps while walking around the world, while in the combat phases, this jumps up to 60 fps. I noticed some screen tearing with v-sync off, but this also may be an issue with my rig (I don't think it is considering the specs I run), but it was nothing major.
I can recommend Costume Quest, because I had a really good time playing, and it has a different take on the party based games, and for the full price of £6,99, you can't go wrong with the amount of content that is included.
If you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. You can also find more reviews over at

Indie horror game that hard core horror fans will appreciate. It has it's flaws but makes up for it in atmosphere.
There is very little in the way of backstory as you quickly find out that you are investigating a dissappearance of a young girl. There was such a seamless transition from cut scene to game mode that I didn't even realize that I was supposed to do anything. Once I started pushing keys I was quickly on my way to the abandoned house at the end of the road and my investigation had begun.
The camera effects mode... well intentioned but just didn't do it for me and I had to turn it off after about 10 minutes as it was leading to a headache for sure. I found the basic monchromatic view so much better and a perfect fit for a story of this nature, almost with a Silent Hill vibe to it.
You make progress in the game primarily from exploration and use of logic. There is very little in the way of object interaction beyond just going through doors and such but the surroundings and backdrops are so nicely crafted that I found myself admiring the game from an aesthetic viewpoint.
One suggestion I would like to make to the developer (and many other developers who does not speak english as their native language) is that if you are looking for widespread acceptance of your game from people in the West, you should collaborate with someone who speaks/writes english well in order ensure proper grammer and pronunciation of spoken dialogue and subtitled content. On several of the games that I have reviewed recently I have noticed grammatical errors that are not a huge deal, but correcting these would provide the polish it needs to give it a more professional appeal. Like I said this isn't a deal breaker... just a suggestion.
For such a short game I'm sure many could not justify the price but for a fan of the genre like myself I'm ok with it and it is a welcome addition to my horror collection. Recommended for those who like story driven games and the horror genre!

tells a story of an old farmer who's suffering from poor memory, aka dementia, all the way from his perspective, so delivering an interesting twist of narration. As it's kinetic novel, there are no choices.
Story is only one hour long but it goes through both happy and sad parts. While I have no experience of working with people with dementia, to myself the presentation seems alright and realistic (well, except for the spiritual-religious part). Man goes through states of clarity and foggy, yet the narration is adequate enough not to confuse the reader. Except when it's meant to. :) I liked this aspect a lot.
Visuals are simple, with just a couple of scenes and a few characters with various expressions. Sometimes the character expressions didn't seem to fit the dialogue but it was unclear whether this was due to hidden information (as everything was narrated from the perspective of the old man) or limited presentation. Otherwise I liked them and they were quite good.
Soundtrack consists of a few simple tunes of piano, flute and the occasional string instruments. They've been chosen to fit each scene well.
In my opinion the price of 2 € is just perfect for a snack like this. At the very least it is ridiculously easy to "complete". Get it for a short charming story!

Warhammer 40K Dawn of War 2 Chaos Rising is the standalone expansion to Dawn of War 2 and it shows in quite a lot of ways that THQ is not only capable of taking criticism, they can take that criticism and turn it into game fixes and improvements.
Perhaps most notably and most importantly, the single-player campaign. No longer will you be fighting the same battles on the same maps over and over again. Now every single map is a unique entity, properly designed filled with story and gameplay triggers. Although this does mean the campaign is a good deal shorter than in Dawn of War 2 the trade-off is well worth it. Instead of getting only a couple of good missions and a ton of generic ones you now only get good quality missions. This also makes the storyline more condensed as you no longer have 5 generic missions in between every revelation and it keeps your interest up much more efficiently.
The campaign meta-game continues to use the RPG elements from Dawn of War but introduces a new one, corruption. As you play through the game you will find corrupted artifacts and face gameplay choices that result in your heroes slowly turning towards Chaos if you give in to temptation. Although this mechanic is not fully realized, you can't join the forces of chaos, it does give you some interesting choices along the way and a fairly significant storyline consequence towards the end of the game.
Perhaps the most immediate impact of the corrupt mechanic is the various abilities your heroes can unlock as they give in the dark influences. Although many of the abilities feel like just filler a few of them are actually powerful enough that you might opt for corrupting one of your men just to grasp that power. The corrupted weapons work much the same way, some of them being immensely superior to their regular counterparts.
In terms of multi-player the situation is much as the same as in the main game, nothing has really changed except for the addition of a couple of new heroes in Last Stand. GFWL is still present as are the heavy duty matchmaking and connection issues.
Graphically and sound-wise nothing has really changed either, the game still maintains a high quality in both albeit some of that might come from my infatuation with the general art and sound style of the WH40K universe.
When it comes right down to it Chaos Rising is an expansion that improves significantly upon the main game and has taken several steps to correct mistakes made in the original. Although it is an expansion that focuses mostly on the single-player aspects of the game it still manages to feel like a total revival and come out looking superior in every way.

Atari broke my Steam Tdu2 last July 23rd 2013. no support atari said tell Steam, Steam said go tell Atari. So I had to buy it again, I now play in retail Tdu2, same game but play hours are not recorded.
Tdu2 single player is [imho] 95% at super excellent; more after my word on multiplayer.
TDU2 had its multiplayer peak in 2011 [2,000 average number of players online each day] and was excellent and seamless join from singleplay and support was good. Since then Atari went broke, sacked its Eden devs and try to maintain and code and 'update' it by themselves and they have failed  breaking much of the multi and have even broken some of the login process and Uplauncher. Support is not much after 3 years.  Many forum posts complain about not being able to get past the uplauncher into the multi game. If you do manage to set router firewall exceptions for port 8889 and 3478 [not so simple] then you will mostly get into multi ok and all will be good.
Backup your Savegame every day.. that's Documents\Eden Games. Copy the whole folder, find a safe place on other drive, create a new folder, name it as e.g. 'May12-ellie-lev22' Open it, and Paste in there. Ok. Do that every day, make new folder each time with new name, e.g. 'May13-ellie....etc. after a week you have 7 backups of your Eden Games, you can delete the oldest one, you still got 6. My backup folder, if it gets more than 50 in it I delete a few, but I always keep the most recent 5.  If your Tdu2 gives error or crashes, go Documents, Cut the Eden Games folder, Paste it to Desktop, Open the recent backup folder you made, Copy  (not Cut) that Eden Games folder and Paste it in Documents. Run Uplauncher all good say Hurray for backup, delete that bad Eden from Desktop, go Play. If still fail ask for helps.
Thanks for reading. Have fun!

115 HOURS PLAYTIME XBOX 360. It's a driving RPG/sandbox. The driving mechanics aren't the best, nor is the game bug-free. But it's a complete package. Nothing here is of a high standard or has a quality feel, but at least it's not boring. If you want pure racing, look elsewhere. If you want an enjoyable experience, this is fairly good. It sure is addictive. What this game tries to do, and how well it does it, cannot be commended enough. It's such a shame that the game had so many bugs and exploits when it was first released. The achievements for this game are also pretty terrible. Sure, if you have them all, you have done absolutely everything there is to do in the game, but most of them are pretty silly and pointless. Chievos aside, TDU2 is the most complete driving RPG experience you can find. The quantity is here. The quality? That's personal preference. I think it's pretty average. However, if you consider what this game actually has done, you'll begin to see why it's one of the most underrated and underappreciated games EVER! Not only does it connect everyone playing the game seemlesly in a free-roam MMO Racing RPG environment in two beautiful islands with simply breathtaking sights all round, but the whole customisation of your cars (of which there is great variety - old and new - supercars to hot hatches and 4x4s) both performance-wise and visually, as well as customising your character, you houses and also the ability to challenge anyone on a huge variety of events and location at the flash of a headlight is just remarkable. The challenge creator gives you infinite possibilities, and the multiplayer races are not only innovative events such as having highest combined speed through cameras but also there are co-operative ones too. Don't see that anywhere else. The single player content is pretty good with again nice variety and makes use of both islands, all vehicle types and very satisfying. AI isn't a problem at all either. The driving physics are solid both off-road and on the road without assists; although you can enable them to suit your needs. You do get manual transmission, you get collectibles too. I can't see how this game could be improved other than a few finishing touches to make it less glitchy at points. It really is driving nirvana, which gives you ultimate freedom wrapped up in an MMORPG environment.

I play a lot of driving games across many platforms, and very few legitimately anger me like this one does. The physics are horrible, each group of cars feels the same. Whether it's the uncontrollable spinning nature of the Classics, the incredibly light and floaty steering of the Off-Roaders, or the go-anywhere-but-around-corners Exotics.
And the challenges, oh man the challenges. You'll find yourself exclusively playing the car loan challenges only because A: The ygive you an incredibly unbalanced amount of cash, and B: because it keeps you away from the other challenges that will make you drive your mouse and keyboard (and gamepad if you own one) into the monitor as hard as you can. Like the challenge that requires you to drive a drunk woman home, where first gear alone will fill the meter by half, and the turns will take the rest.
It wouldn't be so bad if the game had some variety, some sort of life to it, like it's predecessor did. But in this it just feels like they carbon copied the last game and then poorly redid the main functions of it. Hell, it has the island from the last game, but having two islands causes them both to feel empty, due to spreading out the game across the two, and lazy, due to the two islands not really having much to diffferentiate in terms of scenery and road design. (You would think that Hawaii and Ibiza would be a little bit more diffrent, if only to justify having both islands)
In the end, the game will frustrate you and make you wish you'd just bought something else with your £15. I've played a lot of driving games, and this is honestly one of the very worst.

Rift is a fun to play MMO. Especially for a title that had made the move to a free to play game. I think Trion has done well with the store integration and the game it still very playable to the level cap even if you don’t pay for a thing. I have played many MMO titles free and paid and have found Rift to be one of the more enjoyable.
I have seen complaints from others of how Rift has become a pay to win game, they have broken the PVP system or the game is full of bugs. I personally have seen nothing in these regards that would cause me to have any complaint. Yes, the store is full of items and such that I would call “stupid expensive.” I remind myself that the people who buy these items are helping to make the game free and I can just work for something for a bit and still get good and powerful items if I have a little patience. As for people complaining about PVP all I have to say in response is I suck at PVP so it is broken in every game for me, I am missing nothing on this front, lol. As far as bugs go, I have experienced a few crashes and glitches in the game but no more so than many other games I have played. I have not had a glitch or crash that has caused me anything more than the minor annoyance of waiting for about a minute to get back to doing what I was doing.
Over all I find my experience of Rift to be quite enjoyable. Before starting to play Rift when it became a free to play game I had considered going back to WOW, but I am glad I gave Rift the chance. In this case, it's the "found footage" gimmick and VHS-style atmosphere that tricked people into voting this for greenlight. The models are some of the lowest quality I've ever seen, there are severe clipping and lighting issues, and the A.I. is so pathetically dumb that you essentially have to run straight up to them in order for them to see you. Mind you, I played this game for a grand total of 9 minutes before I rolled my eyes and quit. I'm amazed that there are people who managed to endure it longer than I did.
Steam is asking me if I recommend this game. No. Hell no. Not even for the 99 cents I bought it for. (At the time of this review, it's $4, which is way too expensive. The Tape is a short horror experience crafted in Unity. While that sentence will put off many people, including myself, I must say that this game is the very first Unity horror title that has run at a stable 60 FPS with no frame drops on my high-end rig. I should also mention that the developer also brought us Putrefaction, which was well received in general.
The story line within The Tape is perplexing and mild at best, you're a detective out to solve a murder. Your investigation takes you through two "haunted" houses, a cultist infested dungeon, a strange water level and a forest. I must say, the only part that I found at all intriguing was when blood began dripping from the walls. The entire experience will last about 30-40 minutes at best, and there are two endings to choose from. Luckily, there's a save point at the last part of the game, so you can replay the area and get the other ending if you wish.
The Tape's main graphic feature, which is a heavy "camera" filter setting, actually bothered my eyes more than it did to help my experience within the game. I turned it off, and what I was left with was a black and white game. While I'm not adverse to black and white movies and such, I must say I just do not feel that a pure black and white setting works here. Sure, it helps the faint shadows that are cast to stand out a little more, but other than that the title could stand to have some color added.
Aside from the extremely short main game, the player will have the chance to play three "bonus levels", which act a bit as challenge maps. The Forest mode is basically a Slenderman simulator; you walk around a forest until you've found 8 pages. I didn't run into any foes in this area, it seems to be just tedious walking. Dark Waters is a recreation of the water level within the main story, where you simply turn from left to right, gather up light and survive as long as you can against the demon head. Lastly, during Dungeons of Terror you will flip between 4 cameras with the aim to gather 20 pages and collect fuel to keep torches lit to keep the demon at bay. The pages show up randomly over time. All of these levels are rather easy and generic, and will not tack much time on to the overall game.
Though the game originally sold for $4.49 CAD, the new asking price of $1.09 CAD is more justified for the half hour of gameplay that one may get out of it. I ended up getting this on sale for around $1.50, but you can luck out and grab it for around $0.65 CAD now, which is a price I can recommend this game at, if I were to recommend it at all. Alas, I do not, as a seasoned horror veteran The Tape will flee from the vaults of my mind by the time I wake from my next sleep.

The Tape, developed by Kazakov Oleg, is a first person horror game based in the rural outskirts of American suburbia. You play as a nameless detective, on the lookout for a girl who had recently gone missing. He had compiled enough clues to pinpoint the girl’s last known location; an abandoned home nestled in the forest. It is your job to investigate the house and gather whatever information is available. Armed with nothing but your camcorder, you unwillingly uncover the presence of a mysterious cult operating in the area. Through them, you hope to find the girl and escape with your life.
Right off the bat, I want to make something clear; I really didn’t want to give this game a thumb down. The atmosphere is spectacular, the mystery is intriguing, it’s got some awesome concepts, and it’s creepy as ♥♥♥♥.  But sadly, every time The Tape managed to scare me or do something brilliant, it does something equally stupid and unappealing.
First, let’s talk gameplay. There is none. You walk and doors open automatically as you approach them. I have no problem with this. In fact, I’ve played quite a few games with limited mechanics that still entertained me from start to finish. I mean, it’s the atmosphere and suspense that counts in these types of games, so I was willing to forgive it for that. And let me tell you, the first few minutes of this game are great! The crappy camcorder effects were really appealing to me and added to the environment, and exploring the first level’s abandoned house was straight up creepy.
But… like I said earlier, the game took a step back shortly afterwards. You see, about midway through the second level, you have to make your way past some cultists, who patrol down a series of pathways. If one sees you, he runs at full speed, torch raised high, and proceeds to bonk you on the head in an overdramatic fashion. I laughed my head off when this first happened, and due to your painfully slow speed, there’s no way of outrunning them. So I was totally sucked from the experience thanks to The Tape’s horrible stealth section.
The Tape has some truly good moments, but a handful of bugs, a stupid maze puzzle, and an unsatisfying ending just don’t make up for them. You can easily beat this game in under an hour, and seeing as how the bonus levels are uninspired and boring, I just can’t find it in myself to recommend this game.

Costume Quest is a game about capitalism and the futility of fighting the system. You play as Wren or Reynold, fraternal twins locked into a system in which happiness is always kept at arm's length. Your twin, the object of your worldly fulfillment, is taken from you, and you are forced to incorporate yourself into the capitalist consumer machine in order to free them from bondage - i.e. willfully enslaving yourself even deeper in order to cast off perceived oppression.
The erstwhile heroes are indoctrinated into consumerism through perceived need. Costumes and battle stamps are tools by which they can defeat their perceived oppressors, and candy and creepy treats are the currency by which they can obtain them. The creepy treats only award a special costume upon completing a full set, forcing the consumer-hero to seek out other members of their in-group to trade with and developing a reliance upon victimizing the out-group in order to obtain more. The same is true for candy, but on a much larger scale: widescale destruction and abuse of natural resources is encouraged, and upon reentering a zone the supply magically replenishes itself. Candy is ultimately spent on battle stamps, an entirely extraneous commodity that the game can be won without, but is marketed as invaluable and a means by which to constantly sink the children's personal supply of wealth.
The true capitalist hero of this story is Sadie, a brave young entrepeneur with a monopoly on the battle stamps market who is happy to aid the heroes in their fight against the villainous 'monsters.' She allows her customers to develop a dependence upon her product before beginning to dramatically ramp up the price to obtain newer and better versions of the same - designed obselescence at its finest. By the end of the game the player is lucky if they have several hundred pieces of candy in their bucket, while Sadie sits on thousands that the player spent to constantly upgrade their battle stamps. The 'monsters' of the game are cast as villains bent on hoarding all the world's candy for themselves, when in reality they are collecting it in order to save their own lives. Sadie, on the other hand, is motivated purely by profit - lying, expanding, and price-gouging to drive it ever higher.
The harsh reality is that this game is designed to indoctrinate the player into heedlessly reaping the world's resources and victimizing their competition in the name of achieving fulfillment. They are taught to at the same time fear and trust the two heads of the capitalist serpent, sybomically mirrored by the twin heads of the Doublefine logo: the Repugians, who are the face of foreign investments, and Sadie, the friendly face who is always there to help.
10/10 illuminati confirmed.

Costume Quest is an interesting RPG with a few minor flaws that keep it on just the wrong side of the greatness.
Pros
-Amazing Art Style, very cartoony and friendly.
-Halloween Theme is awesome.
-Manages to be appealing to kids but enjoyable for adults.
Cons
-A little too simple in certain areas.
-Lack of combat and customization variety
-Rediculous difficulty curve
So firstly as I said the style is amazing, a lot of greens, oranges and blacks mix well to give the game a nostalgic feeling of halloween's past. You use different kids halloween costumes to have different powers and they change form between the overworld and the battles, both of which look great, almost cell shaded and comic like in places.
The story is similarly charming and cartoon-like with a lot of effort put into appealing to the child in you and the nostalgia that part of you holds. I won't give out details but needles to say it is certainly interesting and although it doesn't take you to many 'new' places it will probably give you a fair few chuckles while playing it.
However gameplay wise is were problems start to happen. It has solid enough combat, basically lifted directly from super mario RPG, with an extra damage/extra defence mechanic which has you playing very brief mini-games with each hit. Although the combat is solid it is also a little same-y, you'll find yourself doing the same thing over and over again but as you constantly get new costumes and abilites it doesn't really get boring.
A big plus that helps remove some of the repetative nature of the game is a lack of grinding. Although you have to fight a certain number of fights in each area (sort of) you don't usually find yourself grinding to gain XP as you will rarley find yourself outstripped by enemies...until the ending.
Okay so I'm not going to give the ending away or anything but between the last normal enemies you fight, groups of 3 level 10 enemes, and the final boss there is a 10 level difference. Meaning that although you can blitz through most of the game up until this point (completeing all quests is seriously not even a chore if you keep your eyes peeled) you will have to go back to previous areas to grind up at least 5 levels before you are even remotely ready to take on the final fight. This isn't helped by the final boss' ability to clone itself into 3, although that is the least of the issues.
One final annoying point is that the ability to hold a button to go fast in the overworld is tied to a specific costume which means your main character has to wear it the entire game if you want to be able to move with any decent amount of speed, a very poor decision.
Overall not a bad game, a little short and a huuuuuge difficulty/grin wall right at the very end but it has a lot of charm and if you can get past the issues you will find a great little experience. Worth picking up for such a low price and sure to be someones nostalgic memory in the future.

This game is not a satirical parody of visual novels in any way whatsoever, contrary to how it appears.
Going into Hatoful Boyfriend you can't help but think "Damn, this is going to be one hell of a weird game" and although you're right in saying that, it's much, much more. Although it's hard to review this game without spoiling nearly everything I can truthfully tell you that it's well worth your time and that you'd be missing out if you passed Hatoful Boyfriend up.
Despite each playthrough being short (around 45 minutes to an hour and a half per route) there are fourteen total endings, following the usual visual novel fashion of ranging from happy, lovely fairy tale-esque endings to extremely dark, likely traumatic endings. Things escalate QUICKLY. Eventually you'll reach the point where you can experience the true ending, which lasts a fair bit longer than usual and is actually an incredibly suspenseful and fascinating mystery/thriller. It alone is worth the price of admission.
The characters, although they're well.. birds are actually fairly well designed albeit a little basic due to the short, concise nature of the game itself. Artistically the characters are beautifully drawn and are, admittedly, very good looking.
The soundtrack is solid, fairly run-of-the-mill for the most part with a few tracks that really stand out.
All in all, despite being mediocre as far as visual novel gameplay and writing goes, the game's charm makes it entirely worthwhile, and hey, who doesn't want to tell their friends that they've been playing a bird dating simulator?

Well worth $1.99, a bit maudlin, but for anyone who doesn't understand what a person with dementia goes through, this would be an excellent intro.  This is totally not my genre, but I picked it up for the topic.  Not my art-style.  Not my choice of general sentiment.  But it's so profoundly praiseworthy for the natural characterization of the main character.
Hands down the best first person portrayal of dementia I've seen in any media.
A lot of people seem to think that there isn't a person inside the shell of the person with dementia any more because the interfaces are broken.  And for all that this is a treacle-y love story, it really gives you a notion that there is a person inside the broken memory.
I took care of my own mother for years after my dad died, in my home.  I'm a rather ancient gamer grrl as such things go -- pushing 60, and in our ethnic culture, it's the youngest daughter's job, and a loving duty.
Mom had times where she'd have issues of thinking Dad would come by, particularly before they got her on l-dopa for Lewy Body dementia -- she would set table and cook dinner for the two of them, and then be terribly upset he wouldn't show up and be worried something had happened to him.
This story puts something like that into a magical realism/fantasy setting.
Generally, we infantilize and disrespect our elders in general American culture (if there is one), but even more our elders with dementia.  We dehumanize them.  They require our compassion doubled and more.  Any one of us could be there in some number of years, and that should drive us to care more, not drive us away.
There is something very amazing about old marrieds who are best friends, quite literally forever.  I have a few friends and family that I will never give up on even if I don't see them ever again in this life, whether or not they are still with us.  And those relationships really are the last things that stay with us.
And perhaps at some point, when I'm too tight wound and can't let go, this will be the thing I'll come to, to take a wrench to the faucet.  Fair warning.

As for the story itself, I found it to be compelling. It is both sad and hopeful at the same time. The focus isn't so much on what is happening, but how the protagonist experiences it. The lines between memory, dream, and reality get intentionally blurry.
The visuals and audio were simple, but appropriately expressive.
Overall, I'd recommend the experience. It got a tear or two out of me, and got me to go hug my parents afterward, so it definitely affected me.

An excellent expansion to an excellent game. The campign picks up the story where the first ended, and this time it's chaos forces you are up against with your Blood Ravens squad.
There is an excellent corruption mechanism that really makes you fight chaos's corruption on a personal level - there are various sideobjectives that you can choose to do for usually a big item reward, for example choose to destroy the statue of a space marine hero. It also comes with corruption points, and those will slowly but surely take away your soul: your corrupting heroes and his fellow squad members will slowly lose their abilities (your saves carry over from vanilla DoW2 by the way!) and gather new demonic ones instead, along with their looks (chaos items have a corruption level requirement) and even their personality in conversations. Other side activities that are sometimes difficult, also come with corruption points - such as defending a temple the chaos forces want to destroy, and at the same time you are on a time limited objective in the other corner of the map. May you fail to defend the temple, your corruption level increases, so you are really fighting to stay pure and also constantly tempted by the power chaos offers. Because of this, there are 6 different ending to the campign that vary based on your corruption level, and the story can slightly change depending on which squad member of yours is the most pushed to the dark side.
The campign is way more linear, the endlessly generated sidemissions are also gone, the open maps are gone and you are usually given one or two way of approach, though your tactics with the added corruption changes add another layer to the already big pool of tactical and character build options. There is a new "support mage" type of hero joining you, the buffing fireball throwing Jorah. Personally I didn't like him at all, but it's always nice to have additional characters.
For multiplayer, you obviously get a new faction in the form of Chaos. Existing factions also got new units (free for all players who own DoW2 only and not this expansion), and obviously new maps with a new chaos hero for Last Stand.
WHAT TO BUY CHAOS RISING FOR?
If you liked vanilla Dawn of War II's campign, this is a fantastic campign expansion for it definitly worth even full price. The corruption mechanism that lingers above every mission, every man, really makes you personally fight the temping chaos that offers great power, but costs yourself.
WHAT NOT TO BUY CHAOS RISING FOR?
Multiplayer and Last Stand. The game's multiplayer is entirely played in the last expansion, Retribution, and because vanilla DoW2 and Chaos Rising used Games for Windows Live ( it got removed years after relase, don't worry it's full steamworks title now, just like Retribution ), the multiplayer players are separated from each other (DoW+CR and Retri are the 2 groups). Also Retribution includes everything for multiplayer, including it's new faction, and Chaos aswell without the need to own Chaos Rising.

>Buy for additional stuff in skirmishes and last stand.
>Discover one of best coop campaigns in all of gaming history.
Definitly worth the campagin experience if it's on sale, but the multiplayer based aspect is a bit too simple for me to actually ever want to play it with anyone

After nearly 10 hours with XCOM:D I've come to several important conclusions. 1) The XCOM universe is absolutely interesting enough to warrant spin offs. B) A tactical FPS could be interesting, if they'd bothered to make it work. IV) Even though this game is a shiny turd I'm going to finish it.
Story: From the start, the plot is pretty cliche. Standard alien invasion bit, inexplicable super powers imbued in the main character from the get go.... felt like I was playing a knock off of Resistance, which isn't bad in itself but it's played over territory. There are steps taken to add some depth, little notes and records scattered around which help the world feel immersive, but the overall plot is so 'meh' I've started skipping over them because I no longer care.
Gameplay: So damned broken. In any situation where you're to be responsible for the actions of multiple characters in a real-time environment, you should be able to manage their commands quickly, cleanly, and intuitively. The Bureau fails all three. Everything in the not-quite-paused command mode feels just a bit off, and absolutely optimized for a controller rather than a mouse and keyboard (seems a shame in an FPS). Move your mouse too close to a different team member's control prompt and *whoop* you're managing a new guy before finishing the last set of orders. Not that they listen to your orders anyhow. Sure, immediate actions take place, but much of the game is based around tactical placement of the crew and these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s just won't stay in place... until they do, and then they don't leave when they should. Giving the AI team members a little skill couldn't be that hard, they seemed to do alright with the enemy, but the idiots with you seem to want to die. I find my teams constantly manuevering into the line of fire when I've sent them to flank, running in front of my field of fire for no apparent reason, or standing up in cover watching an enemy shoot them in the face instead of withdrawing. It seems I spend more time trying to keep them alive than I do killing, which isn't to imply they help much in the firefights. The game gives you a kill count at the end of each mission, listing by squaddie. It's not unusual to see the AI put up a combined 8 kills to my 60. If they'd left this as a simple one man army kind of FPS, I'd be onboard. As it stand, I want to slap someone.
Graphics: With all settings cranked to max, things come out fine, I guess. The environments again bring to mind Resistance or Half-Life. I'm slowly becoming convinced these titles are all developed by our future alien overlords who want to familiarize us with the world to come. Oooh, a big tower emitting light into the sky? I bet I'll climb it and it'll be all metallic and LED lights! SO UNIQUE!
Fun: Yeah, this is it's own damned category. In spite of the terrible squad combat and hum-drum plot and graphical choices, I still find myself enjoying The Bureau. It may be the joy of finally getting to take down a muton myself, rather than watching from the 3rd person view in XCOM: EU. Or the glee I get when stomping a sectoid and recalling my disasterous first forays into the tac. genre and having them wipe out my whole squad. It is satisfying to put a bullet between the eyes of a sectopod pilot. So, yeah, still fun... just occasionally wanttopunchthings-frustrating fun.
TLDR? For $10, it's entertaining. At $50, you'd be better off lighting your head on fire... fewer regrets, better stories.

The concept of the game is alright, throw gravity nodes and roll around to navigate a level filled with obstacles. But there are countless flaws and bugs in the game and it is basically abandonware at this point.
Bugs: The biggest bug you could imagine. The game freezes after the last level. There's supposed to be a final confrontation but it won't actually load the last section of the game.
Many achievements are described poorly (saying the achievement is on a different level than it is), one seems to be actually impossible to get. The discussions are full of bug reports and the devs haven't responded in years or apparently fixed any. The level collectibles dont update properly so I've collected over 100 so far and the game only has 40 levels (I also still don't have the achievement for that either)
Gameplay: The concept is fine but poorly executed in some critical areas:
For a platformer where precise movements are fairly important, Gravi (you) slide all over the level at will. Precision jumping sections are a huge pain and will come down to a fair amount of luck and grinding several dozen deaths at just one section. Difficulty curves are all over the place as precision landing is incredibly difficult while some of the final levels aren't particularly challenging.
Abandonware: The devs have left this game as is. It isn't coming out of early access any time soon if it ever does. The devs have actually been posting more about some other games they are working on instead of fixing one they already had customers pay for.
Verdict: Buy a better platformer. Find a better gravity based game. There are many games that outclass this installment in every way. And those games probably also work right.

I'll start off this small review stating that I don't usually play kinetic novels, I'm more into the "choose your own adventure" type of VN, but as this one was short (and not expensive at all, especially for the quality it delivers), I decided to give it a go.
I was pleasantly surprised by the fact that the developpers were able to throw me (and, for what I can tell from the other reviews, not only me) into the shoes of a character that suffers from such a sad and detrimental illness as dementia is.
I could really relate to the character and feel for him, especially because, as a reader, you KNOW what is happening before he does... and you can't help feeling helpless for what is about to come. Luckily, it all ends as it must, with a very touching and happy ending, despìte everything that goes by.
I'm not going to spoil it for you, but if you're into touching stories and relatable characters, or even if you just have a little time to read a sweet story (just an hour or two of gameplay, depending on your reading speed) then this is for you. You won't be disappointed.
The music fits this  VN perfectly, and the art is also very soft on the eyes and fitting, gives you some sort of nice, cozy feeling when meshed altogether :)
It's just 2 dollars...and for what it gives you, it's more  than worth it.

My grandmother died because of a mix of dementia and old age last summer, I only visited her twice in the span of four- to six years. Now it's too late for me to visit her.
I love this game, it made me feel like a horrible person, but I simply didn't have the heart to see my grandmother in such a terrible state. I'm so sorry.
The novel's full of simplistic, but still good, symbolism. Such as the different emperors of Memoria (pretty obvious ...), and of course, the characters that the main character interacts with through the story.
I recommend this novel if you want to think while reading it, maybe about the past, just like the main character. It can be finished in an hour, maybe even less, but it will be worth it.

Too many people dismiss video games as “mindless entertainment” and assume they’re all for kids. But then games like
are released showing how the medium can be used to deliver strong stories. While this title is more of a story than a game, with no choices to be made, it is still none the less an enjoyable experience with lovely artwork and music tying the tale together.
The story is about an old man named Reynard who is suffering from memory loss, perhaps dementia or Alzheimer's, the game itself never says. He lives with his loving wife who helps take care of him and their home as the two enjoy their golden years. The story follows Reynard as he tries to recapture faded memories and prepare himself for the inevitable. The story is short but revealing much else might spoil things, I will say it is
The artwork in the game is soft and gentle, matching very well with the tone of the story. There aren’t many characters in the game but each one has a lovely model to fit them. The game also has a few cutscenes which are of the same quality. The background music fits very well, relaxing and soothing as you follow along through the journey of memories. I found the game very aesthetically pleasing and found no issues with it.
, actually, especially seeing more illustrations of the old stories Reynard was telling.
It’s a visual novel and all you have to do is sit back and read since it is the kinetic kind that doesn’t require any interactions. You can use your mouse to click through the lines of dialogue or set the game on autoplay if you’d rather just read and use your hands for other things, like I personally enjoy eating while reading a good visual novel. You can save you progress, adjust the text speed and many other basic options one would expect. The text is easy to read and the menus are very easy to maneuver through.
I fully recommend
, as a heartwarming story that brought me to tears. It’s a very short experience, maybe an hour or two but it’s well worth it.
that are easily obtained through the course of the story. I honestly have nothing negative to say about this game, I do wish it was longer however it accomplished its goals either way and I was left with a satisfying experience.

This little VN is amazing. Last time I cried this hard was when I played “A Bird Story”, but I think that “Forgotten, Not Lost” takes the prize. My grandmother suffers from Alzheimer, and learning how the MC of this game sees and remembers the world around him… It’s painful in a way. A quite accurate description of this terrible illness.
∞/10, would cry again. I’m really enjoying all the works from these developers, I hope to see more works from them soon.

So basically this is not a game in the traditional sense, and if you're looking to play something with a gameplay element, then forget about it. The only interaction here consists of clicking the left mouse button, or pressing spacebar from the start to the end of the story. I'd generally categorize this under the 'kinetic novel' category instead of a game. It would be nice too if there's some element of choice in the story, but I understand that would probably blow the budget beyond the cheap price of this game.
Being aware of that however, if what you want is an EXPERIENCE, a nice story of how an old couple live together at the end of their lives (and beyond), then by all means, get this kinetic novel. I guarantee that this product comes with tons of chopping onions and will touch you deeply as tears flow -- especially if the characters in the story are people you can relate to. Arts is okay-ish and does the job, the music is excellent! Writing is decent. The nearest equivalent to this would be those $1 indie self-published books in the kindle store, but this one comes with a full multimedia experience of graphics and music too. I play it at night and managed to go through the story in about 30 minutes, and for what I paid, I consider it worth the money. It's also something I will definitely recommend to other people whom I know share the same taste as myself.

once you add Chaos Rising to your game library, if you had the base Dawn of War 2, it will become Chaos Rising too. Both games will share the same campaign and Last Stand levels, but multiplayer stats and achievements will be different.
Bought this DLC a long time ago, because I was excited whenever I was watching the others playing the Sorcerer in The Last Stand.
And I'm not disappointed, at all. I'm litteraly bursting every loyalists in my path in the name of the Dark Gods, and I love it.
You have 2 ways to start a Chaos Rising campaign : either use the "New campaign" button to create a predefined lvl 18 Force Commander, or load the Dawn of War II finished campaign to keep some of your wargears and your hero levels. You can now reach level 30 (in the Dawn of War II campaign, max level was 20), and thus new hero skills have been added too.
But the campaign itself is really short. You can easily finish it in a day, as there's only about 15 missions or so, even if you do the few optional ones (whilst in the original Dawn of War II campaign, at the pretty end, you were flooded with optional missions). By the time your characters reach level 30, you're more than likely about to win the campaign already.
If you want to buy this DLC, I suggest to buy it only for the 2 extra heros you can take on The Last Stand (Hive Tyrant and Chaos Sorcerer).

This DLC add a bit more content to the base game, which is nice with one more squad type, a new "chaos" mechanic and more weapons/equipments.
The campaign is shorter than the base game: the base game lasted for last than 20 hours for me, and this one lasted for about 10 hours for me (Note: I sometimes play the DLC through the base game, so the playing time for me is not accurate). But given it's a DLC I think it's acceptable.
Recommend to buy the Master collection if you are interested in the game (which is what I did).

THE TAPE is a pretty appropriate title for this one because it feels like about halfway through, somebody recorded something else over the top of it. It's a bizarre mess of stealth levels and seeker maze quests and there's even a water-based boss battle to get involved in but it's all mashed together into a forty minute campaign without anything in the way of cohesion.
The loose plot hangs on the back of a detective searching for a missing girl in 1960s rural America with the gameplay conducted through the nauseous jitter-laden lens of a camcorder. I won't even get into how many feet of film you'd need to be carrying around with you to run one of those beasts back in the day but at no point does the game ever indicate that we NEED to be viewing this through a camera. It's a gimmick to sell a disjointed collection of stage designs rather than a game.
There's a 'Use' button mapped and you'll press it four times. Once to pick up a key. Three to light some candles. I used the jump button more than that. And there's nothing to jump on.

It has a really great and spooky as ♥♥♥♥ atmosphere. Plus I'm really digging the mini games.

I'm not entirely sure that it makes much sense for a "detective" character to go around investigating spooky, cultist-and-demon-infested locales with nothing but an extremely damaged and/or astonishingly low quality video camera to guide his way, especially when he seems incapable of RUNNING at any given time, but I can safely say that it makes for an amazing atmosphere.  The sound in this game is equally impressive/oppressive, so these two factors already put The Tape yards ahead of the vast majority of alleged "first person horror games" released onto Steam in the past couple of years.  The "story" - what little there is of it - is furthermore highly intriguing, and the scenery is suitably compelling.  There's even a tiny bit of what one might conventionally term "gameplay" on offer:  A tiny bit of "stealthing" and/or other enemy evading, and even a "boss battle" of sorts near the end.  That's the good stuff.
Now onto the not-so-good stuff.  The price is possibly a tad on the steep side, considering that the main game/campaign itself is probably under an hour, although there are some simplistic mini-games included as extras for those who can find pleasure in such petty things (including one where you time-manage some different camera angles to ensure things don't get dark for too long or you get jump-scared - sound familiar? - and another one where you wander around in a gloomy forest looking for pages of a book - also sound familiar?)!  There's also more than a touch of the "what the ♥♥♥♥ am I supposed to be doing here?"s in a few bits, though one could certainly argue that this fact adds a little to both the mystery of the piece AND the length of the gameplay, so it's perhaps not an absolute detriment to the game overall.
So yes, it's DEFINITELY scary and disturbing, DEFINITELY short, DEFINITELY not extraordinary value for money, but DEFINITELY worth a look if you're a die-hard horror fan, especially if you can grab it on sale.  By all means, if you keep your expectations fairly low, you may be pleasantly surprised.  Expect another Outlast - a game which it owes a small amount to, if not THAT much - then, well, you're clearly a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot and DESERVE to be disappointed.  I will be looking out for other releases from this Kazakov Olag character, though, as it's due time one of these Euro dudes churning out cheap horror games turned out to be one with a noteworthy TALENT (and while we're at it, more than just a fly-by-night scam artist).  Oh, look, he DOES have another game out already...hello, Putrefaction...Kazakov, don't fail me now...
Verdict: 7.5/10.

This game isn't bad. Actually, in a few areas it excels rather nicely in, while not scary it is a bit creepy and a few of the scenes and moments are nice twists on some old-timey horror convention, and it isn't riddled with jump scares, with attention focused on to build a sort of slow-burn or atmospheric experience. However, the game as of the time I played and write this does have a few bugs, the developer doesn't appear to be native English and the dialogue comes off as a bit broken (it's only really noticeable in the endings, however), but the biggest deal breaker for many will be its length; The main game is about 35-45 minutes long. There's some bonus stages I'll get to in a bit, but the time might sell some off the title.
Which is a shame since it actually isn't a half-bad game. While the pacing is decent, it does feel the game could be fleshed out more and there's more to explore here. I actually found the game quite interesting; It's hard to talk about specific moments of the game in part due to the game's briefness, but the basic aesthetic is well-handled (and some screen artifacting and effects used to give it and old film sort of feel are well-done, though if you don't like it the options allows you to turn it off), the game isn't repetitive and despite its shortness does mix-up the variety and threat multiple times, though isn't hugely challenging. But what the game excels at is giving the feel of something like an old black-and-white horror film in game form. The audio is very minimalistic and somewhat washed out, but worked with the old film aesthetic. And some of the imagery is tad creepy... But not of the sort it happens suddenly or catches you off-guard, the sort of slow-burn where the camera stays fixated on a piece of imagery for an extended period of time as it sort of ingrains a sort of deeper feeling to the scene. As a big horror enthusiast, I did find the interesting scenarios and imagery to be enough to make the experience worthwhile. And for those weary of crappy indie horror games; this isn't one of them. It's not bad, or badly made, or using assets badly, or not understanding horror, or anything like that. It's solid, and you can tell the creator both knew what they were doing and understand the horror they were going for.
But not flawless. Outside of length concerns, the way doors opened were a bit awkward, the game has a few bugs... I didn't encounter anything game breaking, but a couple objects I could walk through, and the way doors open in this was a bit janky (they kind of open automatically when you get close to them, which is a bit odd in how they do as such). Really, just some small janky things like doors or the cultists in the first scene you're in danger being blind as a bat almost, but thankfully it didn't take away too much from the experience.
There's some bonus levels in the game, at the time of writing three in total (the the developer has said he wants to make and release more post-release), but I'm hoping future levels end up more like levels from the actual game than the sort of mini-games the three currently available are. The mini-games are a bit finicky, more than the main game, but fine. Two of the mini-games also have obvious inspiration, one more than the other, which I'm happy they kept out of the main game, but questions if we need it in game at all. Regardless, what I think is the best of the bunch is a minigame that's kind of Five Nights at Freddy's inspired, but also it's own thing. You have four cameras you switch between in a dungeon, there are torches on each camera feed (two torches on each camera feed I believe), you need to collect fuel that appears randomly and locate pages to make more pages to appear you need to pick up, all while avoiding a demon that will appear and disappear; make sure you keep at least one torch lit on a camera screen and don't hover or linger on cameras with the demon on it, all while locating and picking up pages (the objective is to pick up 20 pages on the feed). I had a bit of fun with this mini-game all things considered, was worth a play. The other two were passable though; One is kind of a 'keep-away' mini-game based off of a certain moment in the main game where
and you keep them away with light, but honestly you turn so slow and it was a bit dull (the section in the main game which is a twist off this was better done in my opinion). The last mini-game is the worst, in my opinion, it's a Slender clone, but not an especially good one. The extra mini-games are fun, but pale to the main campaign and I kind of hope if/when more bonus levels are added in the future, they build more off the main game than as little mini-game diversions. I'd be more interested in content more like the main game than little, "inspired by," mini-game sets.
Which brings me to my core point: I like what the main game has going for it. It's not especially scary, but I found it enjoyable, creepy, and interesting. I think a few scenes from the game are memorable, and honestly would like to see more of it. Which highlights to me it was worth experiencing on my side, but also underlines the game is short and could go on for much longer than it does; flesh itself out more. However, if the length doesn't bother you and a slow, little atmospheric dive into a creepy little horror game with some nice style going for it sounds appealing, I think the dive is worth it, but do hope the developer expands on the game if it does well for him rather than abandoning it. What's there is good, if needing a little polish. As is, I'd give it a solid 7-7.5/10, but with some expansion/extended content and added polish I would easily raise that score. While a bit lacking in some areas, it's not bad, not bad at all, and some scenes I feel are worth experiencing, especially for any horror buffs than may enjoy interesting and somewhat creepy scenes that aren't necessarily  scary, but interesting.

I'm writing this without having yet beaten the game. While this game had a lot of promise coming from a franchise I've thoroughly enjoyed, it has a few VERY major problems.
1. Incredibly linear storyline. Choices don't seem to matter, if they come up at all.
2. "Customization" and "Skill Trees" are nearly laughable if they weren't so inconsequential.
3. Movement is incredibly clunky, everything is done with the shift key including running, leaping obstacles, and also entering cover. When you have cover, it's ridiculously easy to break, which is nice to not feel "stuck". However, it also makes you ridiculously easy to kill, as an errant turn of the mouse-controlled camera can turn your wallslide into a "turn your back and slowly run away from the aliens as they blast you with high-accuracy efficiency" sort of moment.
LAST BUT NOT LEAST:
4. The AI in this game is VITAL to game progression. Too bad they forget to put some AI into this game, then, right? Your squadmates are more helpless than children, and if you don't constantly micro-manage them, they will run full tilt across a battlefield with no cover and get shot by as much as dozens of aliens at once. Once the aliens make short work of your idio... er, friends, you have to save them or they will die. And if you try to save them from their idiotic lunge full tilt into an area with no cover, YOU will die. Also, even if they only take one or two hits, or seem safe under cover and being fired heavily upon, they'll complain and cry and ask for guidance, because why the hell would they have any kind of battlefield capability on their own? They're only the [MINOR spoiler alert] handpicked best the world has to offer as far as special forces, recon, and the like.
While I'm enjoying the writing of the game to some degree (specifically the level of humanity they throw into the mix via interactions with survivors) I'll probably only be completing it to complete it.  The game itself is not enjoyable for me. :(

An interesting concept for a game is marred by poor execution and some questionable design decisions. The Bureau gets more intriguing the further you play into it but a dreadfully boring start and some very stale characters may cause you to give up before the story gets kinda-sorta interesting. The combat is generally fun and certainly more tactical (flanked enemies take triple damage for instance) than your average third person cover-based shooter but is tempered by some clunky controls and design decisions. For instance: You cannot place an allied area of effect ability freely, you must walk it around barriers and obstacles as if you were moving a character. This can be especially aggravating because the tactical mode doesn't pause the game completely, so while you're attempting to place an artillery strike on the ledge below you, you're getting shot and killed. Trying to move the artillery strike out of its effective range for a moment to get around a barrier to attack the enemy literally ten feet from you?♥♥♥♥♥♥out of luck. Some enemies take absolutely enormous amounts of damage and do not react whatsoever to your fire, that's not fun.
Overall, while it has some serious problems and there are certainly slicker 3rd person shooters out there, none attempt to be this tactical and for that, The Bureau is somewhat unique.

If there was ever a reason to not trust game reviews, this is it. What a great game!  I'm so glad I didn't miss out on it after reading all the negativity over it. It was not deserved. The graphics are beautiful, the sound is amazing, the voice work is great and the gameplay... well, do you like Mass Effect or Gears of War? It's almost exactly like those two except commanding your two squadmates is much more important.
I played the first half with KB/Mouse on my main rig and the second half with an Xbox controller on my less powerful media PC. It ran well on both machines. I could max everything on my 660Ti but had to lower the physics on my 550Ti to keep it running smoothly. I had to remap the squad commands from F1 and F2 to buttons 4 and 5 on my mouse. After that, controlling and commanding was a breeze. Things got even better with the Xbox controller. The game switches to a more controller friendly UI and for what little speed and precision I gave up, I was able to whiz through the rotary command menus with even greater efficiency.
The stylized 1950's graphics are nice but it's not until you reach the more alien levels that it really starts to look seriously, eyeball-melting beautiful. Unreal 3 still shines after all this time. You start out feeling a bit weak but you will see your team become stronger and enemies that were once pretty tough become a breeze. That's when it starts dropping Mutons on top of you and then the Elites show up. It keeps the challenge up all the way to the end and that final battle is a doozy.
There are 4 possible endings and l'm very happy with the ending I chose. It pleases me greatly that this was not another turn-based strategy game. I really enjoyed The Bureau.  It might not be in the traditional spirit of previous Xcom games.. and feels like a mashup between Mass Effect and Gears Of Wars, but it really seemed to deliver.
The Burearu is a game about the struggle of a classy detective and his squadmates against inhuman odds.  The action is live and every order you make counts.  The combat is full of tension and adrenaline, and I enjoyed every minute of it.  If you're a fan of the Xcom lore and don't mind a deviation in gameplay style I'd definately recommend XCOM declassified.
If you are in it for the turn based mechanic however, I plead with you to wait for the next xcom title, as the active third person shooter gameplay may not be up your alley. It is quite polished and I can not think of a single complaint to make, but it does not follow the gameplay tradition of the games of the series that game before it.
That said, I have played all of The Bureau main campaign before writing this review (save for the post final boss content) and am 100% satisfied with the game save that I wish it was a little longer.

Yep, characters weir cool fedoras, but it's not enough to create the feeling of an era.
The best thing about the game was its dialogue -- not the storyline ones, but those little 3-4-liners NPCs exchange when they think you're not listening. I've beat it once and will hardly ever return.

Secondhand Lands is a game that an individual will have to invest some time in to fully enjoy its unique features. At around level 200, you unlock all of the PvP and faction-based features, which make the game incredibly enjoyable. At around level 180 scrapper, you'll probably have enough skill-points invested in the Constitution build to make some pretty unique and awesome items for your character. I say give it a try and see if you can make it to lvl 180. There are plenty of older community members who'd be more than willing to assist you in leveling your character (a Mystician-based wolf can level you to 100 in about an hour.) I recommend starting with a wolf geared for PVP (just focus on the Strength build in your skill-tree.)
