“Forgotten, Not Lost – A Kinetic Novel” is a dream I pray to have one day, and a can’t imagine a finer one. It’s a dream of a happy family sharing profound and eternal love. So does it even matter how much of it is true, and how much takes place in the forgetful mind of an old, possibly dying man who often forgets his own wife’s face and name, and the death of an only child? This story is a reminder of how true forgetfulness isn’t in the old, but in those young people who have forgotten that true love can never really end. After all, where would it go that we cannot follow, someday? (And the music is exceptionally nice.)
There may be no shortage of those saying that FNLAKN (which is by no means a game, but simply a story that moves at the reader’s own pace) is contrived, designed simply to provoke deep emotion. And it might be hard to argue to some extent, since it does do that very well. But it’s more than that. No doubt the meaning and value of this story resides largely in the heart of each reader, and will be interpreted very differently based on age and life experience. But for one ageing male gamer who married for the right reasons, however mistakenly and briefly, this is a story about the hope that even the simplest memories of love can be eternally (and eventually) redeeming. And that goodness and kindness can be those stepping stones we need to cross that last river. But mostly Forgotten, Not Lost – A Kinetic Novel is a reminder that no matter the number of powerful and sustaining memories age and dementia may take from our daily awareness, in whatever remaining part of our minds we continue to dwell those memories also reside, undiminished.
If readers wish to feel the heartbreak of dementia, and understand how too many people currently experience each day of their lives, FNLAKN is an excellent experience. As well, if you wish to understand caretaking of your own elderly family members, now or in the future, and this more regrettable possibility of your own future, again, this is a simple, short and inexpensive way to preview those prospects, in a hopeful manner. Or if you’ve simply lost love, and wish for the reassurance of its possible return, this may prove a very pleasant way to spend some time while warming your heart.
Thank you.

Forgotten, Not Lost - A Kinetic Novel was developed and released by Afterthought Studios. Forgotten, Not Lost released on 2nd April 2016. The game costs £1.59 and the game is available for Steam. A press review copy was provided for The Hidden Levels.
Forgotten, Not Lost is a visual novel game which touches upon the difficulties of dementia and old age. You play as a farmer in the game who is simply forgetting more and more things and feeling the effects of dementia more and more as time progresses on. I don’t want to touch too much on the story because it is short and I do not want to spoil the pleasant experience I had with the game.
Positives:
Art Style and Direction – The art and backdrops to the game provide a good image to work around mentally. I loved the unique style of the characters (which fell more into an anime style) and found the art style to be well done and very consistent. I really enjoyed that the music backed up and really complimented the scenes.
Price – The price of the game is really low. For the price I cannot think of another alternative visual novel.
Save slots – A lot of VN’s I have played have lacked spots to save the game. This game comes with a total of 38 save slots which is way more than what you’d need.
Touching and emotionally packed – The game hit me right in the feels and this is where the game excels. If you can let your  barrier down and put yourself in the characters place you will find real emotions, confusion and happiness hit you many times.
Negatives:
Longevity – The game is short and not very long. This could be a downfall for a gamer searching for a visual novel of length. One play through was enough for me but it was enough and I felt satisfied after.
Name bars – Sometimes the names of the people speaking do not appear over the text box. When you character speaks there is no text box to indicate who is speaking which can get a bit confusing when it swaps to them speaking and there is no name indicator.
Confusion – The game temporarily hit me with confusion, making me feel that I missed something. This was resolved however and I really feel this is not so much a negative. Just made me feel temporarily out of place.
After seeing someone in my own family go through dementia this game for me was always going to be a touchy subject. The author of the story also based it off actual experiences caring for someone with dementia. I hope that this game raises a lot more awareness for Dementia and the difficulties people face going through it.
The game was short but I believe it was for the better, I really enjoyed it from start to finish and one of the quotes from the game page was “a visual novel that hopes to bring tears into our readers' eyes, especially those who have gone through similar situations when dementia or Alzheimer's has claimed the memory of a loved one.” – I would gladly say that this is backed up by me playing the game and around halfway through having tears flow from my eyes. This game may not be for everyone but if you are a fan of visual novels or wanting to find out more about the effects of dementia I wholeheartedly recommend this game. I had a great experience from playing the game and it will leave its mark on me for a while as a really good eye opener to ageing and dementia.
If you find it hard to connect emotionally to games or don’t really like Visual Novels or games where you don’t get any choices then I would not recommend. For everyone else though this to me is worthy of a purchase.
Score: Buy it now!

This game is very short, and it's lack in interaction/"gameplay" is made up for heavily in atmosphere. The plot is not very elaborate or intricate, but in my view, this kind of game doesn't need to be. The atmosphere is quite terrifying, and the camera effects are *perfect*. You can turn them off in the menu, but I would recommend leaving them on as they really give you the  full experience. There is an extremely  basic form of stealth in this game, and honestly, for what it is, it's all it needs to be. The game isn't about stealth, it's about showing you an extremely creepy and dark atmosphere. The levels are minimalist, and this fits with the abstract nature of the game. It doesn't need lots of models or props, and I think while some of the level design seemed to be lacking in content (tunnels), this is probably more seemly so due to the speed at which your character moves for the first half of the game. But I think this game is really well done, and I do however wish that there were more to it. If the same sort of design, camera effects, locations (the forest reminds me of something from Blair Witch Project), and atmospheric attention were given to other horror games that give more in terms of interaction and gameplay, I believe that horror games would be far more tense. I would definitely hope to see another installemant, maybe with more interaction as well, and possibly more subtle music to add even furthur to the atmosphere. Overall, this game is exceptional when it comes to atmosphere, and I would love to see more like it.

These two open world race titles have much together, but also much differences. And will The Crew be as good as Test Drive? Find it out in this review.
________MAP_________
In TDU 2 you have two maps: Hawaii and Ibiza. You unlock Hawaii after 10 levels. What I have to say about the maps in TDU 2 is: They are vacationish. More about that in the Graphics comparision, but let me say one thing: garish colors all over the map.
In TDU you also have pretty much the same look everywhere. In The Crew you will be able to drive through several stuff like (real big) cities, deserts, mountains etc... So that is a point that The Crew wins.
Both games have huge maps. In Test Drive the map is a bit smaller though and, as I said, splitted in two pieces, so The Crew wins in general.
The Crew 1 : 0 TDU 2
______STICKERSHOP_______
The Sticker shop of TDU 2 is great. You can choose different stickers (like out of 150!) and turn and place them whereever you wish. Choose colors by yourself, this is just a great content of TDU. The only bad thing I know about it, and it is very bad, is that the car and older sticker become more and more fuzzy when you add more stickers.
THe Sticker shop of The Crew is not completely finished, but you can test the pre-alpha at their website and I have to say: Wow, good job already, Ubisoft! It has pretty much the same functions as the TDU one, though not so many stickers yet, and some nice "import" functions.
All in all these two games are most probably the games with the best stickershops until now.
Draw!
The Crew 1 : 0 TDU 2
______TUNING______
TDU 2 has to stand back in the Tuning category though. The only things you can do are: Level 1-3 Brakes, level 1-3 Speed, level 1-3 acceleration and some different wheels.
In The Crew you can tune everything, every little bit of your car. Look at these preorder boni:
There are tunings avaiable for interior, tencers, skirts, motor hood, rear wings and even side mirrors. Not to speak of the whole in-car techniques. Motor, Tires, Suspers, weight, chasis etc etc. And the car looks completly different depending on in which mode you drive it.
This is a completly clear win for The Crew!
The Crew 2 : 0 TDU 2
____MULTIPLAYER_____
Both of these games are multiplayer games. In both you mainly drive online, but also have the opportunity to drive offline. But in The Crew it works out better. As the name of the game already says: "The Crew". You drive in a crew, hopefully out of friends, otherwise out of AIs. But the options to play with your friends (that I could test out at Gamescom already) are just much better in The Crew. Though both games do not have any loading screens it is slightly easier to handle the menues for online play in The Crew.
Moreover the servers of The Crew will most likely be online longer. Take a look at other Ubisoft games: still a good connection. Take a look at Test Drive: Servers already offline! And the best thing about that: the game still tries to connect with Atari, so many people can not play their game anymore at all. Because of that bug I would even like to give a minus point to TDU (guess whose copy does not run anymore), but I do not know how many people actually have that issue, so I am just going to call it a Draw again.

In both games you can use your keyboard, a Controller or a Racing wheel. And I have to praise TDU, because you can even use an H-Shifter as controller, but Ubisoft did not give me any information than the ones I found out myself, so I think I am going to call it a Draw again.

As a hesitant consumer, and all around lover of complexity, I am wary of 'streamlined' games which I and other regulars often conflate with 'dumbed-down' versions of ADHD-inspired design and marketing focus.
HOI 3, though, was a game badly in need of serious re-organization and focus on gameplay, not accountancy for everything from distance to the commander's comander's commander, to manually placing and ordering in some cases down to specific companies and battalions where they constantly should go for the entirety of the war becuase the AI was totally incompetent if left to its own devices for more than 3 minutes.
While I miss some of the trade games one might play with resource stockpiles, this is  now transformed into stockpile games with the finished products the resources make (resources are now only 'flows').  Gone are the endless chains of commander level which some may miss, but also gone are the endles complications and useless orders which the AI would incompetently ignore or execute as if programmed in another language whether or not you had properly constantly (and manually) reorganized your units to meet the arcane commander restrictions of which group was where.
While the AI is still incomepetent, it is less so. If this sounds like damning with faint praise, to some extent that is fair, however, it is VASTLY less incomepetent. :)   One can give a number of orders and - assuming one has kept up with supply, equipment and the proper number and type of units needed, the AI will give a passable workmanlike performance.  This is useful if one needs to look at a half dozen places at once, which, I can say one still need do if playing at any upper level of responsibility in an alliance of any weight.
Don't worry, a lot of what you liked in the earlier games is still here, and some things that were masked by all the accountant's red tape is now exposed for fun and games which is what the series was supposed to be about in the early versions.  Yes, some historical specificity of particular units is lost.  You will have to use mods for that, but the good news is mods are emminently available and easily made and used thanks to Steam Workshop, as are all your fav flag and what if mods.
DLCs are another matter.  No one denies that Paradox has made a rather mess of that with EU4 and CK, and the first DLC performance for HoI4 both in cost and underwhelming content is not encouraging.  It may be the message has finally been received in Sweden, and a less expensive and more meaningfull effort for DLC #2 will shortly be available (tomorrow).  In the meantime - the base game IS worth it, is very reasonably priced in the EU and US and on sale from time to time when keeping a wary eye out.  If you aren't in Russia, many of the recent negative reviews are misleadig the witness - meaning you! - becausee they are about  price change in Russia, not about the gameplay.  Have a look at a let's play/playthrough.  If you find yourself thinking you want to watch another one- come on man, just get the wallet out.  :)

I rate the game Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War II: Chaos Rising 3/5. OK.
If you want more of the same campaign with the same characters as the original Dawn of War II game you should definitely give this add-on a try. However, there really isn't a lot else to this game except it lets you play as Chaos forces in the multiplayer modes and has multiple endings.
The single player campaign is nifty in that you can easily pick up your characters and their various customized skills and many of their items pretty much where the main campaign of Dawn of War 2 left off. On the downside though the final boss fight of this add-on's final mission is needlessly frustrating and very poorly designed. On the easiest difficulty, playing it twice I must admit I was unable to beat the game's final boss. The ending mission's boss fight is a LOT harder than any of the boss fights leading up to it (those I had absolutely no trouble with but fighting against Ulkair himself is ludicrously frustrating).
Perhaps the signle best thing about this game is how the single player campaign also has several endings and which ending you get seems to depend heavily on how you did and what choices you made in most of the previous missions of the add-on leading right through to the ending. These endings range from your main character being executed to you and your squad being proclaimed heroes (an excellent variety of endings). These multiple endings and the manner in which you must arrive at them (through the decisions you make over the course of the entire add-on) are a very welcome change from how most games tend to work, and the manner in which this game executes its multiple-ending structure well done even when compared to many other games which do have multiple endings. Getting one ending versus another in Chaos Rising is not so simple or easy as deciding between flipping one switch after the final boss fight versus another (as was true in Deus Es: Human Revolution). in Chaos Rising, which ending you get depends on what objectives you fulfill or not and what items you choose to use and not all along the way, almost from beginning to end.
Although the multiple-ending structure adds some potential replayability to this game, although the game itself, its story and which missions you have access to and what order they are arranged in is, for the most part, arranged in a fairly linear fashion and the frustrating final boss fight serves as a bit too much of a counterweight to this game's various strengths. Also, there are still no single-player campaigns which let you play as any force other than that of the Blood Ravens Space Marines from the original Dawn of War 2 and endings in the Warhammer 40K universe can be predictable due to the sheer implacability of the game's setting. Regardless of what you do, war is going to continue (and so sequels are going to happen) but this is true to the franchise.

Early Access review.
Solid RTS where you struggle against a literal horde of zombies in a world that is post-apocalyptic... with steam powered tech.
Pros: Fun little RTS, cool setting with interesting mechanics. Zombies are predictable in small groups but in larger packs can surprise you! Large maps with varying terrain are randomly generated vary up the gameplay but still manage to be generally beatable (i.e. generally you won't be gimped by not having some resource at your start point; though it can happen occasionally). Having a big army of walking steam war walkers is damn fun! There are top hats and monocles! Steampunk needs more love!
Cons: Most cons atm are just that it is simply unfinished (duh, early access); there's only one game mode, balance issues abound (though they adjust balance often) and generally... if you can survive the initial onslaught and aren't too aggressive in your expansion it can be hard to lose until the final wave. Some restrictions to building placement combined with map randomisation can frustrate. Bugs can be annoying but this game is generally better than most in early access. No multiplayer atm; not sure if they're planning it and I personally don't mind but it could be fun.
I'll update my review if anything significantly changes or when the game is released. Looking forward to the single player campaign! Lot's of potential here...
Definitely buy if you're looking for a RTS that's a little different.

Costume Quest is a good game and definitely worth $10. This game reminded me A LOT of South Park Stick of Truth to the point that I actually wondered if the South Park team had used Costume Quest as an influence when they created their game. That being said, obviously the actual story and dialogue is very different to Stick of Truth. For one, the kids aren't swearing constantly, for two nobody is getting anything shoved up the rear region and for three there is no
dialogue. I was really on the fence about there being no voice actors in this game. What I enjoy about Double Fine Production games is that their characters are really likeable and they take the time to show you a little bit about everyone in your world, even the guy that you see for one second will have a funny line and a nice costume. Here I felt that was not necessarily absent but not as prevelent when compared to other Double Fine games like Psychonauts. I wanted to hear the kids voices especially in cut scenes where the dialogue is bouncing between 5 different people. It just would have made it easier to follow. Obviously it's not like you're constantly reading, this isn't a visual novel, it's just something that I would change. The characters are still likable and the story keeps you motivated to continue to the end.
What I liked the most about this game is that it's funny! It's fun! It's lighthearted! The art style is great. The world is detailed and immersive. The turn-based fighting avoids becoming repetitive because every now and then you get a new costume and a new set of awesome moves that come with it. Everytime I got a new costume I would call my boyfriend over so we could watch it's ultimate ability and high 5 afterwards because 90% of the time it was FREAKIN AWESOME! Heck I even took one of the ultimates and put in on 9GAG because it rocked my world.
What's more, you get Grubbins on Ice which is about an extra 1 - 2 hours of gameplay after you've completed Costume Quest. It's equally as fun and provides a great ending leaving you wanting to purchase Costume Quest 2 so you can see what happens. To complete both Costume Quest and Grubbins on Ice should take 7 - 10 hours depending on how into unlocking achievements you are. It's also the type of game that you can play again after a year or two. Oh and also, if anyone from Double Fine reads this: Thanks for adding the Psychonauts music in the Camping Store at the Mall. It made me smile <3

I have been playing SHL for 9 years and I've made some pretty great friends, some of who I'm still friends with to this day and I wouldn't trade what I have with them for the world.
Some little pointers, because I'm quite biased when it comes to this game haah;
- The community is a tight knit group of people; we're friendly and willing to help, we've been around long enough to give pointers and whatnot.
- Fun and eventful quest line; they can get quite tiresome but they're worth it to see what the game is all about.
- There are many items on this game and then you have crafting to make your own the way you want them.
- The skill tree can be clunky but it's easy once you get the hang of it and know what skills go best together. You are only limited by the four trees but other than that, you can mix them up however you want. Older members can give you advice on the best skills for PvP if needed.
- Factions such as bo peep and little red riding hood for things like PvP and events; contests are also quite fun to do.
- Tokens can be bought with real money and they give you access to things like pets, combat monkies etc.
- Game Masters are quite friendly and always willing to help, they like to go afk but they return...eventually.
- Guilds are a neat way to team up with friends or simply use for PvP, plus the guild vault is handy for sharing things between the guild.
- Its an open world concept, there's lots to do to keep you occupied.
- You can have your own land if you buy a land deed, you can decorate it with certain items and invite people to it by making them guests.
SHL has had some ups and downs throughout the years but Bobby has worked so hard this year to make it what it was again, and now it's thriving on steam, please try not to judge a book by it's cover (graphics :p) and give the game a chance, it's very enjoyable with a group of people or even by yourself. I've enjoyed this game for many years and I hope to enjoy it for many more to come.

One of the most generic shooters I've ever played.... but also one of the most SOLID shooters of the last five years. A simple, standard FPS with a normal "War Sucks" message, regenerating health, and guns with genuine feedback. Using cover is required, but instead of a pre-rendered cover system, you must actually use POSITIONING and TERRAIN.
While there are a few problems with invisible walls over low obstacles, generally the game is good about making the staircases easily visible. For an indie-game on sale for $12? More than worth the price. As an added bonus, the translated voice acting lends a sense of charm to the entire game, and the visual designs, while pretty generic, are generally colorful enough to prevent boredom, and the environments, while bland, typically make sure everything important is vibrantly colored. All in all, I'd say this is an above average game, and that I look forward to more from this developer.

Think dating sims are for the birds? Well ignore that kind of chickenscratch because this game's a feather in the cap of any player!
Romance! Mystery! Birdseed! I'm not just squawking here! Hatoful Boyfriend will have you flying high on the wings of dove!
But enough of me parroting the opinions of others, try it for yourself and you'll agree that when it comes to the dating sim game Hatoful Boyfriend is a real coo!

Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
I'm going to level with you: I'm not exactly the dating simulator's target demographic. I'm a 20-something man in college, in a committed relationship, with a PC and too much time on my hands - oh my God I AM the target demographic, aren't I? “Hatoful Boyfriend” is one of the latest titles released belonging to this proud, illustrious genre. It's also cringey, groan-inducing, and unpleasant to play (like many dating sims!). It is, to use the parlance from the game, not going to be (ugh) everybirdie's cup of seed. Are you laughing at my clever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of a classic idiom? Laughing so hard that you're starting to see spots and people on the subway are asking you if you're alright? If so, stop right there and buy this game immediately. If not, welcome! I will be your sanity Sherpa, guiding you safely down from the mountains of madness. If you can see past the singular, selling point gimmick of “Hatoful Boyfriend” you'll find yourself staring at an unimpressive, run-of-the-mill visual novel.
You are a human in a world dominated by intelligent birds that range from pigeons to parakeets (it is WEIRDLY derivative of “Rise of the Planet of the Apes”). You are attending the prestigious St. Pigeonation's Institute, the first and only human to do so (despite claims of a multitude of curricula there appears to be three regular classes – math, gym, and music – likely because every other classroom is filled with bird♥♥♥♥♥♥. Also attending the school are several suitors, all male pigeons. That is the premise. How zany and quirky! There's one obsessed with pudding (how strange and charming!), one that's an aristocrat (I bet I can change him!), a childhood friend (but we're just friends... aren't we Ryouta san?), and so much more! Plenty of options for you and many branching paths, though you will find yourself seeing the same conversations over and over again. Level up your stats by attending classes, and depending on where you choose to go and how you spend your time you'll see and interact with different characters (i.e., superimposed bird pictures against static art backgrounds with dialogue bubbles). Some story paths are downright strange and out of left field – which is a feat considering the game is essentially the definition of left field.
But is it good? Is it fun to play? Not for me. Think “The Walking Dead Season 2” or “Long Live the Queen” with even less interactivity. Lame bird puns? Yes, flocks of them. Tedious to slog through every conversation? Yes, especially after your second and third flythrough (you can fast forward, thankfully). It's a visual novel and thus has LOTS of reading, which is fine. But the periods between your brief choices and talks are long and tend to be... just not all that engaging. What about lazy mistakes? Yes, “Hatoful” has it all! Plenty of them – typos, mislabeled dialogue, and music randomly cutting in and out.
“Hatoful” came out originally in 2012 but this HD release feels like an attempt to catch some of that “Goat Simulator,” one-note-funny fever. I laughed... once. A guffaw at my character's dwelling. That was it. The rest of this just left me bewildered. The story is nonsensical. Strange for strange's sake isn't funny; it's just arbitrary. It's a chore to replay this multiple times just to see the many different, unfunny outcomes. “Ah, if I had chosen to get a job so-and-so would have liked me more and thus I would have gotten a different, jarring ending.” There is an element of psychological horror you'll uncover through subsequent playthroughs but it does little to save the game. It will likely be defended as "satire" and "deeper than first, second, and third glance," but after the sixth glance I felt little compulsion to return to St. Pigeonation's.
“Hatoful Boyfriend” tries too hard. It's that friend we all have, the one who jabs you after telling a terrible joke, smiling open-mouthed and staring unblinkingly into your eyes until you awkwardly laugh or else he will kill your entire family. It feels cheep (good, I met my bird pun quota and can die happy), like something you could download for free at any number of sites. Some people will like “Hatoful Boyfriend,” find it charming – but if you're having any doubts, heed them. If you like dating sims, visual novels, and beating-a-dead-horse concepts, give it a shot. If not... fly, you fool.

This game... I started playing it when my buddy started WoW, I chose this one instead because it was F2P. I almost immediately began spending money on it. Level 60 boost was awesome, patron bonuses are handy, and if you're planning on raiding most classes will eventually need both soul packs (mage being the exception, they only need one of them)
That said, every single one of those things can be purchased through in-game currency, oftentimes at a very reasonable price and especially so if you have nice guildmates. Once you hit the level cap you should be able to farm enough plat by doing your dailies, chronicles, and soloing the old 10 and 20 man raids that you won't know what to do with it, and some of the most expensive essence drops in the game are worth twice as much platinum as both soul packs, an instant 60, and 30 days of patron combined. Having a fat wallet or a gift card will certainly be a boon, but it is not necessary at all, and there is plenty of other content to be had here.
The most important thing I want to stress is about the soul system and how incredibly versatile it is. You can choose to be a Warrior, Rogue, Cleric, or Mage, and each of these callings has 9 unique souls. You pick three of those souls to build a Role, which is like your current class. You can have up to 20 Role slots, and they can be swapped on the fly anytime you're not in combat. This means that, in practice, one character has to be able to fulfill the duties of any member of a raid. In WoW, you might roll a DPS character, and all you do is DPS, but in this game literally anyone can DPS, Heal, Tank, OR Support and each different spec of each different calling has its own situational uses. As a mage, the raid requirements of my guild mean you have to be able to play the following specs:
Stormcaller/Necromancer hybrid - DPS
Chloromancer - Heals
Stormcaller/Archon - Ranged Turret Support/DPS
Harbringer/Archon - Melee movement-friendly Support/DPS
Stormcaller - AoE DPS
Each one of these has its own priority list, its own nuances, and its own applications. Not to mention that there are two variants on harbringer/archon depending on if you need to purge, and if you need to burn an add down or simply DPS the boss. There is also Stormcaller/Harbringer, which is arguably the fastest and most difficult spec in the game and yet yields incredible numbers. Not to mention Pyromancer if you need good target-swap burst DPS. And you'll notice, I've only mentioned 6 of the souls, and a handful of the ways they can be combined. As continual adjustments and tweaks to gear and abilities are made, new souls and hybrids will become viable, and others obsolete.
This game is very competitive, and if you enjoy learning in-depth skill trees and experimenting with cutting-edge hybrids to min-max your DPS in any situation, you will find all you could ever hope for and more. On the other hand, if you are very casual, there are always guides out there a few weeks after the top guilds discover a new build or when a soul recieves a large buff. Not only that, but you will never be restricted by your choice of character (ugh, im so sick of healing, i guess i better roll a dps toon and start over from level one.... hah!) and you will never have difficulties finding dungeon groups when any mass of five people can fulfill all 4 roles (tank, dps, heal, support) and have one extra dps.
Bottom line is that this game is extremely deep and rewarding at the end game, and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an MMO to occupy their time.

You never have enough time to analyze any situation in order to solve the issues before you, so it results in you bashing your little blue self against the traps over and over in a desperate attempt to manage these unwieldy obstacles. I really wanted to like this game, and even accounting for it being "Early Access", but I keep finding myself irritated and wanting to play anything else.
To begin with, the idea sounds awesome.  Roll around, fire out your little gravity bender, get pulled to it.  You can "resist" the pull, and use that to your advantage.  However, where this whole mechanism falls apart is in both the control scheme and the implementation.
Your projectile also has to follow the standard parabolic path any first year physics student would be familiar with.  Trying to accurately aim this parabolic projectile with the mouse, while also controlling Gravi with your keyboard, seems to be entirely an exercise in frustration.   If this is where the developers were getting the "puzzle" part of "Puzzle platformer", I think they should revisit what that means.  There weren't times where I was trying to find my own path through a level, or trying to figure out which switch to pull when.  They levels were incredibly linear, and the only puzzles I could find were the mechanics.
For instance, there are areas near the end of chapter 1 that require you to "swing" from the ceiling, while avoiding the fire jets above, and the spikes below.  This turned into pure frustration for me- minor changes to the angle of my projectile caused it to miss the ceiling pillars entirely, or catch the side instead of the bottom and pull me into the flames.  When I could successfully hit the first pillar, transitioning to the next one seemed to be "how fast can you slightly adjust the mouse and fire again so that the projectile hits the pillar before you fall to the spikes below", not "can you make a good plan through this gauntlet".  Super Meat Boy was fun because of the precision required and how exact the control felt.  Gravi is not, because it requires similar levels of precision but has controls that feel much less exact.
Perhaps it would be better with a controller, but I feel that the problem is not solely to blame on the control system, but instead lies in the combination of cramped quarters and need to exact responses with pixel-perfect precision.
Control issues aside, the levels looked rather blah.  Graphically they are detailed enough to have some character, but the limited palette leads to some visual confusion at times.  It also felt at times like the detail of the background fights with the important information about dangers in the level itself.
The audio wasn't bad, but wasn't great, either.  I would consider the sound and music to be a wash, all told.
Overall, I cannot recommend this.  There are better platformers out there, and I didn't really find the "puzzle" aspect to this.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified
The game feels like they wanted to make a Mass Effect game, but put to the XCOM setting, in the 60's. The companion AI works not unlike an RTS AI in terms of movement, so they tend to run on the most direct route for move or attack orders. Though the companion system is a little more interesting than the Mass Effect one, since they knew that fans wanted more strategy; so be ready to micro manage your companions in every battle.
Lip sync is sub-par, graphics look like some elements are in beta still while others are finished. Sound is good, bring in a nice tone of atmosphere. Plot is very generic on the early cold war era alien invasion plot. First half of the game was enjoyable, but the last half had me wishing it was over; everything became pretty boring.
All the nods off to XCOM are a nice touch, yet the story and setting just blow Enemy Unknown's entire structure full of gaping plot holes, that are patch worked in with the Enemy Within expansion; even then, it isn't enough.
In the end, I'm glad I got the game on sale, and I do not recommend it, unless you really like the cold war era alien invasion setting.

I'm a huge fan of the original series. I wanted to like this game. The 60s setting is original and fitting. But that's about the only good thing one can say. By mixing real time and tactical combat the way this game does you end up with the worst of both worlds. The real time interface is horribly convoluted and cumbersome so it doesn't play well as a regular shooter. The tactical interface is so bad it's essentially unusable. Level design is shallow, bland and illogical (how did the aliens get into locked rooms?). Graphics are mediocre at best. The characters are unbelievable and clichee.
But worst of all this game is 100% linear. You progress on rails with no choice or agency. To the extreme that you cannot open doors until one of the scripted dudes finishes saying his piece and then it suddenly magically unlocks. This is total blasphemy to the original spirit of the series which was all about an open world to play in as you please. The original gameplay was about hide and seek, clever tactical maneuvers and resource management. This on the other hand is an excercise in frustration and pressing random buttons at the time the game tells you to.
Even at a 75% markdown this game is a complete waste of money and time. It's brain dead at the level of ancient arcade shooters where you point your gun at heads that randomly pop up.
Would not play again.

♥♥♥♥♥Tracy meets the best of the X-Com franchise and fails miserably.  The environment they create is excellent until the characters speak.  Dialog tends to run on about less than important information.  Base management is virtually non-existant and the gameplay itself in tactical mode is mostly redundant and boring.  This game fails to create strategic value or tactical tension that is the hallmark of the X-Com series.  This is indie developer quality at best and worse, indie games tend to be more fun! Nothing about this game is great other than the environment and I would argue the gameplay actually takes away from that heavily.  The other thing is the game runs heavy on even high end systems for no discernable reason.  It is likely that the time to properly optimize this game was never made.  The best correlation to system demand is X-Rebirth which is simulating an entire universe of things happening per frame.  How The Bureau requires and equal amount of processing power is beyond me.  The AI isn't good at all.  Bypass this title entirely.  Even on sale for 10$ it isn't worth it.  Buy some DLC for XCom: Enemy Unknown or Within and have hours of entertainment.  Even the original release of Sword of the Stars II didn't have me wishing for a return policy with STEAM so badly.

So I finally finished this game, and decided to do a review on it after I'm actually done with it. I must say, this game is amazing; I've waited so long for this game to be on sale, and now I'm really tempted to buy Dishonored 2.
This game has a rich storyline, with a lot of plot twists and leave you wanting more. Of course, a game this good is bound to have tons of bugs etc. One of them being a glitch where I think I attempted the mission wrongly, and was not given the subsequent missions even though I've completed it and had to restart just so that I could continue the game; and there are certain parts where it is really glitchy, like for example I tried to toss the body, and it glitched at the fence instead of being tossed over the fence. However, this game provide a lot of action (basically you can kill anyone) and puzzles to solve. The decision you make (be it killing someone, doing a favor for them etc) will actually affect how the game will be played (but the ending will be the same). I didn't know about the hagfish & weepers until they attacked me, which should have been hinted to us, as well as the River Krusts which I never knew was a thing until I heard it's creepy noises and then it started firing at me.
Overall, a really good game; something similar to Thief, and a must have for anyone who is interested or have played Assasins' Creed before. I'm rating it 8/10

So far this game is very enjoyable. I will update this reveiw over the next few days as i play more.
(edit) After playing for a few more hours the "beta" part of the game is showing itself more. It could certainly use some quality of life changes like multiple profiles, a zoom in on minimap, and a few adjustments to where you spawn (I spawned on the opposite side of the river as a zombie settlement and it made the beginning of the game way to grindy) With this said, the startegy of the game is quickly becoming endearing and the various zombie types are interesting. The "small force defeating a massive horde" feel of the game makes you feel like you are overcoming during a horde. As oppose to a basic gameplay mechanic. I really would like to see this game grow.
Finally, I would say that some balancing changes are needed. Workers and power in particular see to constantly be in low reserves. Most of the mobile units arent good on defense making the emplaced turrets vastly better then staffed towers. A large part of this has to do with AoE damage being vastly better. Therefore the fire rate of snipers, soldiers, rangers, ext...needs to be increased. That combined with a change to stone houses giving them more workers on less energy would make this game mostly balanced i think.

I should mention here that I have been playing this game for years and my review might be a bit bias but still I’ve seen the game grow and know quite a bit about it, so perhaps it might be biased but its throughout.
I was just going to do a short review then I thought, eh why not do something long and formal.
Pros:
Long quirky split questline, you can do both parts on the same character if you want as well.
Factions, groups, and guilds.
Player market and personal/guild vault system.
Trading system.
Multiple, customizable chat logs.
Multiple races with different skills.
In game purchases. (Tokens represent real life cash).
Daily grind where you have a chance to win tokens.
Contests and other events that you can do with a team or try out solo.
Lots of achievements.
Crafting, enchanting and collection system.
PvP is optional (but beneficial). [enable to pvp you must drink juice, this is called ‘juicing’]
Dueling.
Helpful community.
Large map.
Combat and vanity pets.
Player color, pattern and size customization.
Player instances (land/home) and objects to place there.
Options for role players like animations, emoting and player biographies.
There’s a skill build for pretty much anyone.
Lots of skills from each race help the other so it’s great for team play.
Been playing for years and am still learning/finding new things.
Cons:
The questline can get a bit difficult when searching for certain items, sometimes you can find these items on the market however or by trading.
Juicing can cause drama if you complain about being killed, if you are not interested in pvp(player versus player), please do not juice. Also, if you’re going to be AFK step into a safe zone. Someone might accidently AFK kill you doing a stealth attack not realizing you’re afk. (or they did it on purpose –shrugs-). Either way you’re vulnerable to other players while juiced and members of the opposite faction may attack you.
It is nearly impossible to 100% this game. Some of the achievements can only be given by game masters, it may be impossible to get all of them, but you could sure try! (You’ll be a legend.)
Tips:
If you’re going to be juiced it’s easier to play with those of the same faction.
Go through the questline at least once, it’s really fun, quirky and helps you understand the game better.
If you’re having trouble with a quest ask for help, if you’re looking for a resource check the market.
Make multiple characters of multiple races, each race is unique in its own way.
Participate in events and contests.
Buy a collection album, it makes the game so much more organized.
The player base:
The player base is pretty close with each other for the most part. As with any pack there is an omega who turns their back on the rest but that’s a tale for another time. They’re very helpful to newbies so if you have a question, don’t be afraid to ask someone.
The game masters and administrators:
Great people, these guys. Even if they’re afk they’ll still send you a message and answer any questions when they’re available. If you have any bug reports you can let them know.
I recommend this game 10/10. There’s something in it for everyone and it’s free to play!

Costume Quest is a child's fantasy turned into a real game. You follow the protagonists as they have to fight a menacing threat on Halloween and their costumes will help them. I will give a short explanation concerning several aspects of the game.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is pretty solid, though it can get repetitive after a while. Each costume brings with it a certain power or ability that can be used to get past certain obstacles (Such as entering a location, passing an object and more). This means that every new costume you unlock will be used, one way or the other, to acquire new adventures, enemies, candy and secrets.
The combat is turn based, but it works. The idea behind it is simple. You have to press the attack button (E for keyboard) and then time the same button again at the right moment (A small bar appears) to gain an effective attack.  After you have attacked, the enemies will attack your group. Defense works the same. The enemy goes into slow-motion, you get a chance to press the right button to defend yourself. Succeed and you get less damage, fail and you get more damage. On the third turn of the battle you unlock your costume's special abilities. And last, but not least, you can augment your costumes to enhance your performance in battle or cause status effects to your enemies by battle stamps, which you can purchase. Candy is the currency in the game.
Story:
The story is simple, but fun. As I wrote at the beginning of this review, it's pretty much a child's fantasy turned into a game. You have to fight monsters, your Halloween costumes give you super powers and you get to save the world. There's not really much to tell in this part.
Sound:
Same as with the story, the music is simple, but it works. It's not the type of soundtrack that starts to get annoying after a while and it does give you the proper atmosphere for the game.
Style:
The game has a very colourful appearance and you'll see this in-game as well. From the small houses in the comfy neighbourhood to the big, shiny, blasting super costumes, everything just screams fantasy.
Total:
If you're looking for a fun game and you don't mind a bit of repetitive combat, a simple story with a rich fantasy style attached and you can miss a few bucks/ euros, then go ahead, you'll probably enjoy it. However, if you're looking for a game with engaging gameplay, a rich story, a good challenge, this game won't be for you.
Personal:

[This review is based on only 3 days of gameplay during the Free Weekend.]
During the three days I managed to play the game 33 hours.

I don't know what game the people in the other reviews are playing but this is nowhere near being a "great" game. There is definitely passion and a concept but the execution leaves me wanting to play better shooters. And I think that's the one thing this game does so wrong, it's presentation just feels cheap.
The sound effects sound muffled or that they came from an early 2000's shooter. The voice acting is hilarious and your character's catchphrase seems to be "Yes Boss." Just the things the characters say in this game are uncomfortable and unnatural. For example, HQ or headquarters is called headquarter in this game and responses to questions don't sound right. Now the voice acting can probably be attributed to the script which I don't believe has translated very well from the original language to English. You'll also notice that there are grammatical errors all over the place ingame.

Furthermore, he gameplay feels slow and a bit uncomfortable. A good comparison would be how the Starship Troopers shooter was, it feels out of date despite the fact that it's a new game. It's almost like the whole game is just missing that fine polish that one would expect from a modern day shooter. Maybe I'm just spoiled by all the big budget shooters we have now-a-days but there are still indie shooters I would recommend over this one. Insurgency, for example. Control is tight, guns feel meaty and effective in that game. They don't here.
On the plus side, the graphics aren't half bad. There is some tearing here or there with a really weird haze that surrounds items sometimes but for the most part the game looks competent.
In summation, save your cash. While not a terrible shooter, it's not a very good one and there are far better games on the market for the same price or less.

This is a review of Hearts of Iron 4

This game somehow got even more casualized than EU4 with the lack of content and depth. There is little to nothing to do in the game other than spaming troop types and war. Combat or planning battles results in the game playing itself with the click of a button while manully commanding troops means you have none of the bonuses. The trade, supply, and command system of HOI3 or HOI2 has been gutted in favor of a non-existent one. AI divisions are willingly deploying deep in the frozen and sandy wastelands to starve to death. The colors or terrain of the world map is jarring to the eyes but at least you can turn off the epileptic night-and-day cycle. Air and naval combat has been dumbed down to abstract regions where they offer almost no effectivness, not to mention submarines are useless now. One of the few good things about this game is the existance of a non-abstract economic system where you can see how much of certin equitment is producted. The Fouse Trees are also a nice touch of giving opitions to nations compared to the railroading of HOI3 through events. Overall, if a products is the sum of all it's parts, this game doesn't have enough good parts.

Chaos Rising continues the story of Dawn of War II. This time instead of the tyrannids the main enemy is the forces of chaos. The orks and eldar are present but they aren't really important at all. Two new locations are added; a frozen planet lost in the warp for one thousand years and a warp corrupted battle-barge. Corruption has made its way within the Blood Angels and it is up to you to find out who are the traitors. Unlike the original Dawn of War II, Chaos Rising's campaign actually features multiple endings and missions based on how corrupted the player's force commander and other squads are. Choices within missions and equiping chaos war gear will cause your squads to become more corrupted. However Corrupted wargear is much stronger than regular wargear and "redeeming" wargear (wargear that reduces corruption) is even worse than regular wargear. This actually makes trying to deal with corruption a very compelling game mechanic if you are trying to stay pure and loyal to the emperor. If you still have your save file for Dawn of War II you have the option to continue using it to keep your levels and gear in Chaos Rising.
Multiplayer is pretty much dead but Retribution, the last expansion pack of Dawn of War II, still has an active multiplayer community.

An expansion that refines the best parts of the core game, and gives you more options on how to play. More squads to choose from and a corruption system that affects which of the endings you can get.  Adds in cinegraphic cutscenes and more dialogue from your squad leaders.. All in all makes DoWII into a 4 star game.

I have a bit of a bone to pick with video games that rely on ball physics. For various reasons the act of rolling a spherical object around in a digital world almost always proves extremely frustrating to me, as there is a fine line between overt realism and cartoon looseness that is often stepped over one way or the other to make for an unsatisfying experience. Gravi personifies the bulk of my gripes with this style of game, a hodgepodge of bad design decisions, uninspired art and music, and soulless level design.
Gravi functions around a core mechanic: creating temporary gravity fields which suck you toward them, by which you make your way around the levels, flipping switches, avoiding traps, and getting to the end pipe. Actually creating these fields is not nearly as intuitive as it should be however, and the controls leave a great deal on the table with regards to movement and precision (whether using a controller or keyboard and mouse). Your ball is either rolling sluggishly or far too fast and shooting gravity fields is almost trial and error like with how quickly and erratically you have to place them to survive.
This is worsened by the almost instant difficulty spike which only grows higher with each passing level. Checkpoints are placed annoyingly far apart, certain switches are timed which calls for even faster movement than usual (and yet there is no distinction between timed and normal switches), and the developers even try to work in multiplane levels (ala LittleBigPlanet) which more often than not winds up breaking and glitching you into spikes or other hazards (I also experienced at least one glitch that put me inside a piece of the environment). Some will defend these problems because the game is listed as being "Early Access", but with how long it has been available elsewhere without a beta or otherwise incomplete label, I find it rather inexcusable and just inherent to the poor design.
I played about halfway through the game before deciding to quit, and was bored well before I reached that point. The art direction is so bland and the music so generic, that the whole experience feels lifeless and disconnected. Even had the gameplay been better (or even good, which I would certainly not consider it) nothing about the way it plays or is presented is at all compelling and although I didn't expect a to actually become attached or care about a little glowing ball, I found it impossible to become even somewhat interested in anything the game offered.
Gravi is derivative, at times almost broken, and just not fun. Despite my prejudice against ball physics and games that utilize them, I feel I gave it more than a fair chance to prove me wrong, and yet all it did was further affirm my original thoughts while disappointing me all the same with its own form of mediocrity.

I've played this for about 15 minutes in early access, completing 25% of the levels, and I'm surprised at how disappointing the experience has been.
I bought it because the core mechanic seemed interesting. You basically throw a projectile against a surface and, if you're within range, you're drawn to it like a magnet. I figured this would allow for some clever level design, but the ten stages I finished were short, cramped, straightforward, and filled with generic hazards like spikes. Level 11 introduced reverse-gravity spots as you would find in some Super Mario Galaxy stages, but I couldn't progress because they made me clip into the ceiling, making it nigh impossible to avoid a spike hazard. Maybe later stages are more interesting, but what I've seen so far makes me wary regardless.
I also feel like left/right movement has too much momentum, especially when you're required to land neatly in between two spike hazards, or something of that nature. I'm fine with high difficulty, but I don't like when games ask me to do precise things with imprecise movement.
I would watch a gameplay video or two before committing to this one. Maybe the game will improve upon full release, but I've lost interest.

I was never a fan of the XCom series, mainly because of games like Fallout, Baldur's Gate, Torment, and just about any other FPS back in the day.
When I first heard about The Bureau, I checked it out and saw some game where the setting was old and the idea was XCom, so I passed it by. I was so wrong.
This is not the isometric, turn-based RPG game that I thought it would be, like the previous XComs; instead it's an amazing 3rd person game that combines the tactical challenge of games like XCom, Torment and Icewind Dale, but combined with the action of truly fun games like Mass Effect 3 (gameplay; we're not here to discuss the SP storyline or tout the amazing MP fun).
Graphically it's great: high-end visuals with a great style that utilizes the oldschool look in a great way to introduce the invading beings from afar.
The story is also very good. Yes, we've heard and seen everything before so supposedly there's nothing new but the approach to the situation presented in this game is absolutely spot on and it will keep you hooked and entertained.
The audio fits perfectly to this game. Nowadays audio isn't as important, it seems, unless it's a game about stealth or silence, where the sound is paramount to gameplay. Screw that! The sounds from the weapons firing to the abilities being used, to the menu, fit well and draw you into the world.
Finally, there comes the multiplayer... Just kidding.

I have had a lot of fun in Osiris so far, however, I would recommend you hold onto your cash until release. If you're the sort of person who really enjoys the standard update cycle of Early Access games then this may definitely be worth your money now. Whilst the game has a lot of features already in place (and working somewhat well) it's just missing content at the moment.
At the moment I would give it these pros and cons for buying:
Pros:
- Incredible atmosphere. Requiring resources at night is terrifying task, made more so by the real danger of having to go out and mine when it's dark and you can't see scaly animal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s sneaking up on you.
- Fair build/resources system. Building is expensive but the resources are by no means unachievable, and encourage you to explore and find better ways to claim the resources you need.
- Beautiful. I'm amazed at what they've been able to pull out of Unity's graphics capabilities. In some ways it sets Osiris apart from other obviously Unity games, other than some UI choices.
Cons:
- Combat. It just feels clunky. The pistol is by far a more reliable weapon than the assault rifle, which is needlessly expensive to buy ammo for an insuperior gun. It's innaccurate with the animal movement, does less damage than the pistol, and unlike the pistol requires expensive ammo to be made for it. I could honestly say a lot about how the combat isn't quite how I'd like it to be, but this is trying to be a short list.
- Content. As soon as I was able to manufacture vehicles I realised how small the world feels at the moment. It took away from my sense of awe a little, as at first the feeling of having to plan out the day ahead was great. Not getting shredded in the dark meant you had to think about which resources you'd need carefully, and also where they were and how to get to them. The vehicles upset this balance because they're kind of the end game at the moment. The space ship allows you to cross the entire map in about 20s, which makes it feel tiny when both the G.A.V. and on foot would do the time spent on the world justice. There's not really a lot of alien types, or especially interesting and useful areas that have function at the moment.
- Performance.

[This review is based on only 3 days of gameplay during the Free Weekend.]
During the three days I managed to play the game 33 hours.
The game looks beautiful, but I did not manage to play it smoothly on 8GB RAM (The reccomended) in Co-op, single-player and 4v4 was fine. The game at first did not seem that interesting, but after a couple hours and learning the controls I was hooked. It is really fun and addictive, and I didn't even get to experience it with friends. The first two days of the weekend I only played Solo Campaign mode, which I finished about 40% of. Meaning you get a good 50 hours out of the Single-player alone! On the last day I tested the Co-op campaign with strangers which was also alot of fun, it's basically just like the regular campaign, but instead of AI bots you have three squadmates. Then I went on to test out the Ghost War (4vs4) which at first did not seem like fun, as I just got owned the first few matches I played, but as I played more I went on to liking it alot, it had alot of tactics and skill involved, which was very interesting to watch, all the different gadgets and classes. You could almost never just rush in and attack the enemy, there was alot of waiting involved, to see which side messes up first and reveals their position or intention.
In conclusion I would reccomend the game. It is pricy (60€ also the reason I do not have it bought) , but it will keep you occupied for a good while, if you like it even the slightest bit you should get a good 100+ hours out of it, with alot of hours adding ontop of that if you also enjoy the competitive 4v4 and climbing ladders.

Chaos Rising is much better than DOW II. Compared to DOW II, it's as if Relic sold you an unfinished beta and then proceeded to sell you a full game.
1. Corruption System
Great idea. It melds very nicely into the game. Getting to choose who becomes corrupted is great, since they allow you to pick the highest corrupted member of the Blood Ravens as the traitor. I would have preferred a totally random one instead.
It lets you weigh the pros and cons of balancing super powers with the risk of corruption within.
2. Less "Dhaka, Dhaka, Dhaka" missions
DOW II sucked. It was just move to Point A, B, C. Kill everything there. Rinse, repeat. You captured shrines and astronomic arrays (telecom towers) for no real reason beyond achievement, intelligence and
In Chaos Rising, at least you have stealth missions where you avoid killing your fellow Blood Ravens, battles aboard the Judgement of Carrion where you gather gene-seed.
These examples make the game more immersive rather than the bland "shoot here, here and here and we're done" in DOW II.
3. Choices
I like how you can plan and choose. E.g. Like killing Captain Diomedes. I used an orbital bombardment to destroy the platform instead of killing the Captain.
4. Predator Tank Combat
Very, very good. Nice smooth movement. You reverse and turn nicely.
Note : While I know that Relic Entertainment also did Company of Heroes 2, COH 2's tank movement was horrendous. To mimic World War 2 tanks in reality, they made tank movements slow, clunky and boring.
5. Vox Chat in the Orbital Control
I liked how you could talk to each character and get information. I liked how you could ignore some of the heroes and cause them to get corrupted.
1. Intelligence
Not really useful. It should be default as such data can be gleaned from Google, thereby weakening its value.
2. Bugs
Few but annoying.
3. Capture Points in Multiplayer
Very dull. No narrative or objective. I would suggest using a minor benefit beyond the plain Requisition and Power. You have Shrines, Gates, Astronomic Arrays and Turret Generators. Why not make use of them to make it interesting?
a. Charging
E.g. Captain Thule (Dreadnought) can't charge up a slope. He can walk up, but he can't charge up. He gets stuck at the bottom.
E.g. Both the Force Commander and Captain Thule will charge right into a wall/friendly unit and freeze. It is most silly.
3. Silly AI
Same problem in DOW II. Melee units just stand around getting shot. Happens a lot with melee Force Commander and Captain Davian Thule.
4. Vehicles
Sometimes, I find it quite odd that vehicles don't have good firepower. E.g. Lehman Russ Land Raider can't take down buildings. It only has a machine gun and flame throwers. For a large T3 unit costing over 600 requisition points, it can't take down buildings well.
5. Logical Inconsistencies
a. Fighting only 1 side of the Planet
You only ever fight on one side of the planet. What about the other end? Or the North or South Pole?
How about underground? Do you ever see anyone fight only on one side?
b. Land Battles only
Everyone loves to fight on land for some reason. No water ever.
c. Living Conditions
There's always enough oxygen to breathe with no viruses, there's always just enough gravity to walk like you're on Earth (Terra), everything just looks like home.
6. Silly Powers
Tendrils for the Tyranids just break apart so easily. E.g. Carnifex could get stomp a tendril.
1. Random Traitor
A random traitor would have made the game more interesting rather than allowing you to choose who the traitor is. Then the player would be on edge as he would never be able to trust his units. Making Captain Thule and the Force Commander immune to being the traitor spoils the whole traitor mechanic. The higher your corruption, the higher the probability that you are the traitor.
2. More Hero Combinations
Missing the Apothecary, Techmarine and Land Raider. It would have been interesting to play these heroes. I know that you can find them in the Multiplayer but it's odd that they can't be used in the campaign.
3. Overlap Experience from Multiplayer with Last Stand
Last Stand Experience will also unlock Multiplayer Experience and vice versa. This way you incentivise players when they play both games, instead of separate experiences.
4. Last Stand Heroes into Multiplayer
I believe it might be very interesting for the commander of the army to vary according to playstyle. Rather than the 3 standard Attacker, Defender and Support commanders, let the players decide how they want to play.
Do they want a hero-centric army with an OP hero or do they prefer the power of the mass army ganging up on smaller sized armies? Do you like playing a Khorne strategy with big vlada-boom? Do you like Tzeentch instead, where speed, stealth and mobility are your trademarks? Or you do prefer Nurgle with a fortress like demeanour, capable of withstanding any siege? Or maybe it's Slaneesh, where you can stimulate your forces against overwhelming odds or demoralize your enemies with ease?
DOW is not a competitive multiplayer strategy by far. So, why not make it fun to play?
It's also closer to the table top board game in this manner, where you balance a 2000 point army.
4. Balance Issues
If you want, you could even add population cost to Wargear. In Chaos terms, that would be the equivalent of ritual sacrifice for better equipment from Khorne, Nurgle, Slaneesh or Tzeentch.
5. 3 Buildings
I think you need 3 different buildings in this game. 1 for T1, 1 for T2 and 1 for T3. Building all your units from one single building creates a major choke point. It makes sense that your production should double then triple. No need for 4 buildings.
Lets say your strategy is massing T1 units. Having the same production capability (of 1 unit factory) from start to T3 is just gravely against this strategy.
Additionally, you could even add in fancy animations for how each tiered unit is constructed or produced.
6. Special Strategic Capture Points
Related to CON 3. In a multiplayer game, you could make capturing strategic points more interesting. E.g. You could capture an Astronomic Array that shows you where the enemy troops are.  A Gate that prevents the enemy from assaulting you directly, causing him to switch tactics to teleporters and jump jets. Shrines which gives you Blood  Points for your global abilities. Safe Points that let you reinforce units. Forges that doubles your production speed.
Rather than a boring circle on the floor, it makes sense that you would capture a point for strategic reasons. In reality, no one would take a point that has little or no strategic value. You shouldn't need to specifically click on the circle too, just standing within the vicinity of the strategic point should be enough.
Look at it this way, it is part of the Warhammer Lore, it accelerates the game and it makes it more logical and real.
7. Tactical Grass
I enjoyed the campaign where you had to kill the Lictor Alpha hiding in the grass. A thought came to me where you could implement strategic grass into the game. I am thinking of the same type of grass in the MOBA League of Legends, where units instantly become invisible/inflitrated when they run into foliage.
8. Tactical Woods / Swamp
To differentiate between the benefits of infantry and vehicles. I thought of creating wooded terrain or swamps where only infantry could enter and shoot from. Vehicles can't move through.
This way vehicles could be buffed up (they don't seem to be very explosive, no impact) as they are restricted from moving in certain terrain.
Refer to a game called Etherium for more details.
9. Weather Conditions
I know that other Relic Entertainment games have weather effects. It would be nice to have some weather effects in the Dawn of War series.
10. Envisioning DOW III

More than just competitive racing. Two huge open worlds where you can explore almost anywhere, even drive to the mountain peaks if you are so inclined, pun intended. Not much to complain about this game except the traffic and keyboard control. Traffic can be a pain in the rear - erm i mean front, mostly front. They can appear and disappear at will as if  thrown in front of you for no other reason than to aggravate you but what driving or racing games has perfect traffic behaviour? Keyboard control is not smooth on asphalt for cars but for bikes it's perfect. On dirt tracks, keyboard control feels natural on almost any vehicle except for sports cars.

So what's so good about this game? Well there are 2 huge open free-roam worlds, that feels alive with day and night cycles, random weather with thunderstorms, birds and airplanes flying, airplane landings but i've never seen birds land on anything. No NPC ai walking about which is a good thing since my driving is all over the place.
There are NPCs in the buildings though that serve as interaction points for shops. There are different kinds of shops for customizing your avatar and vehicles such clothing shops and paint shops to name a few. Showrooms and real estate agencies are also available for you to expand your car collection and buy more properties to house all your vehicles. Having many properties means you can park at any convenient location before logging off. It doesn't matter if your garage is full. Or if you're really in a hurry, you can simply logoff from anywhere in the game world.
While a lot of these customizing options and services may seem like fluff, it does add to the sense of immersion and of being in a vibrant world. What sets this game apart from all other driving games are 3 things:
- You can invite friends into your house
- You can drive a friend around in your car or if you prefer - a stranger.
- You can drive almost anywhere where there are no visible physical barriers in place.
So yeah get this game, 'coz there's nothing like it, even TDU1 falls a little short. What TDU1 does better is smoother keyboard control and the ability to set a completely private session with your friends in the game world. Everything else is better in TDU2. Last but not least, it's low in price, high in content and it can be played offline. So even if the server is down you can still have your cake (game) and eat (play) it, just not the same savegame, which is more than can be said for the likes of The Crew or Elite Dangerous.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the Third-Person shooter which places you in the shoes of Agent Carter. A CIA Agent turned X-COM Agent. The game's start is well paced, it isn't an hour long mission which gives you the details in one whole package, instead, it is phased in little cutscenes throughout major missions and through your own exploration of the surroundings. The game is very similar to Bioshock Infinite in the way your companions behave, the gunplay and also the collectable notes, audio logs and the image which appears on the right hand side of the screen, similar to the way the audio logs do in Infinite.
The collectables are easilly noticable and have little actual challenge to them, however there are a lot you can miss if you just run and gun through the missions. The AI support you have are actually quite good from my experience, I had read many reviews claiming the AI were bullet sponges etc, but for me they were well placed during combat and only got injured through my own fault in dealing with enemies. The game uses a system which allows you to control what you and your teammates do during combat. For example, moving them behind cover and marking a specific target. The game also has customisation for your character and teammates, so you can get attatched to your team and then watch them die... But, luckily that didn't happen to me. And if you want to break away from the immersion of a full scale alien invasion... if you can really get immersed in that... and customise your teammates to have 'fabulous' (for lack of a word) colour schemes such as Pink, Purple, White and more Pink!
The gunplay is great, each weapon has a different leve of damage or recoil and the sound isn't just reused throughout. The only issue I have with the guns is that later on, picking up a laser weapon is the easy way out, as it is just running around after the enemy collecting ammo afterwards, without that fear of running out and having to push back to collect more.
The maps for each level is also a brilliant feature, as far as I saw each map is unique and has lots of different routes and ranges of cover to make each fight unique and to also really allow each player to have his own tactics played out just perfectly, in my case that was send a sniper to flank whilst myself and my other teammate stuck behind cover keeping them distracted. The enemy AI is at times silly but they do take cover and pose a threat should a teammate down and need reviving, the capatilize on errors such as a lack of ammo too, pushing forwards when you don't expect it. This being my first XCOM game I can't really say if the enemies are the same but I can only assume so. In addition to this being my first XCOM game, I would recommend watching or playing Enemy Unknown before saying it isn't as good as Declassified, as from some gameplay I have seen, they look quite different.
The Bureau doesn't follow the usual turn-based style which other XCOM games do, which allows for much better, flowing combat and tactics. However, this takes away time to think  about what is happening as sometimes I found myself going off my plan to cope with enemies.
The game features quite a few cutscenes, some of which are in HD, some are in SD, which at times can be quite confusing and annoying as it doesn't look and sound as good. But I managed to get used to the cinematics in the lower definition, the game itself has brilliant high quality level, gun and character designs, with nice little touches on things like hats, ties and cloth which sway in the wind, get shot off in the case of hats and also get knocked around when you pass by or shoot through.
Overall, The Bureau for me is a huge success, thoroughly enjoyable and exciting at all times. I never found myself bored and found the story gripping and suprisingly well written. The multiple choice system allows for a unique knowledge of each character, (If you go through all the options in dialogue with them.) and the games ending is well done as well. I would say behind GTA 5 on console, (Hopefully PC soon!), The Bureau is my favourite game I have played in this year, and last since we are very early into 2014!
I would recommend this to anyone who liked the Mass Effect or Bioshock series and to anyone looking for something else to play.

Massively disappointed in this game. Your ability to "control the battlefield" is marred by the idiocy of your NPC colleagues who I am convinced are sleeper agents for the enemy or under permanent mind control given their uncanny ability to get shot repeatedly while behind cover, sit on explosives and grenades thrown at them with the express purpose of killing them and generally run in the exact opposite or most compromising direction possible when asked.
You WILL have to personally oversee every encounter and will inflict at least 98% of the battlefield damage yourself. Fine, no problem with that, if you want to be a hero, but then please at least give him decent weapons, armour and lose the whiny "buddies" who need so much micro-management that you feel more like a babysitter than a commander.
And what gives with the base? The graphics and scenery in this game are great. The detail is brilliant and the atmosphere outstanding, so why make me rush from semi-circular battlefield to semi-circular battlefield and ignore everything in the middle? This is especially apparent in the base. Mind-numbing, non-developmental discussions with the cardboard characters, divided up by corridors to run between to achieve the simplest tasks that even in 1950 you could get done with a radio and large-buttoned tape-computer; …why? What’s the point? I constantly felt like the game was hiding the best bits from me and corralling me through set pieces in order to point my tinfoil-hat wearing team at the danger and then use them as the most ineffective distraction since Roswell’s weather balloon factory.
My final issue was with the “give you everything then take it away” bit at the very beginning. Without ruining the game, you start as a fully loaded badass. Everything is unlocked and you learn the ropes by kicking alien♥♥♥♥♥and taking names. Then you reach the base. You get access to your tinfoil-hat team armed with water pistols and flashy suits. Where did those other guys go!?! You know, the two bad asses you were working with 3 minutes ago? And what’s this? I suddenly contracted amnesia and forgot how to do loads of cool things? And tech tree is suddenly locked until me, the saviour of the modern world apparently who is working in isolation with the most inept government agency since the Bush administration, is forced to go after the invasion fleet with a tray of tea and crumpets? I despise games that give you early “educational power” and then take it all away once you stop walking into walls and jumping instead of crouching, as if trying to say, “Look how cool you will be later! We know the (many, many) glitches are irritating and the story line ludicrous, and the majority of the people you are working with have been lobotomised, but please don’t stop playing! Please?!?”
