This review is written cause I don´t think the reviews give enough credit for this.
This game is best approached as a sideproject of x-com. I. If x-com enemy unknown (the new version) was diamond then this game would be gold. Don't expect a copy paste x-com game and you will be fine. Think x-com but more action orientated. While i do recommend the other x-com enemy unknown over this game, i can also recommend this one if you finished that one. Especially while its on sale. I think its worth the price.
Story (8/10)
The story is actually pretty good. Voice acting is spot on. The story pulls you in. If you have played x-com u might be familiar with a couple of terms like skyranger, sectoids and certain names. I feel the 60's feeling works. While playing this game, I think the game felt like x-com. It also reminded me a bit about the new "xenonauts". The game has a bit of an eery feeling, like something isn't right. But that's the right feeling, as the world is under alien attack. You can feel the despair. The story felt like a movie, which is a good thing in my eyes. This game also has a lot of lore hidden inside it. Lots of short notes, letters , audio tapes during missions. Its a nice bonus during gameplay and promotes discovering the area.
Graphics (8/10)
The graphics get their work done. The game shows a lot of movies during gameplay, which is nice as it keeps you into the story. Overall I thought the game was pretty good looking, playing at 1920x1080 with mostly max settings. Don't expect the most beautiful graphics and you will be fine. The motions of the enemy and of your soldiers feel natural. While running the camera can shake a bit, so if you are responsive for motion sickness be a little careful with this game. Personally I didn't have problems with it. The graphics are a medium to get you into the world of x-com at which it succeeds. First I wanted to give the graphics a 7, but because I really liked playing into this world and graphics are a part of it, i give it 1 point higher.
Gameplay (7,5/10)
The game consists of walking around the base and doing missions. It feels a bit of mass effect, but i take that as a good thing.
I think the gameplay gives enough tactical freedom to make strategy count. You can allmost pauze the game during playing and select different abilities of each of your soldiers. Comparision with mass effect is the right choice. While much of the strategy is being lend from this game, keep in mind that mass effect was a really good game. The third person view actually give me more a feeling about being into the world. If you walk around your base, you actually feel being inside it. I played this game on veteran, early reviews complained about keeping to ressurect your men. What they don't tell you, is that your men can also ressurect themself. During a heavy gunfight you may expect your men to go down, but then again i gave my men offensive abilities. It was not more bothersome than "gears of war" on higher difficulty levels. I gave my men mostly orders which abilities to use, but never really bothered with orders where to stand. I do think this game might be harder if you play like rambo, as your men want to stay close to you. Keep your distance to your enemy and you will be fine.
I played this game mostly as a sniper and had a lot of fun with it. Headshots feel like satisfaction! Your commander can "taunt" the enemy and I finish it off. The game starts a little more difficult cause of lack of abilities, but the further you go the stronger you become. I can also recommend finishing the minor missions cause of leveling reasons. It's also easy to train your agents cause of special missions made just for them. The max rank is 5 and you should be able to get them that high as early as 25% of the game. Yourself can become as high as rank 10 and you will only be seeing that, at the end of the game.
Overall
I give this game an 8. Buy this game if you like x-com and action orientated games. If u want an exact copy of the tactical x-com with bird view, you might want to stay away from it. Also if you like shooters and are open for a little more tactical gameplay with abilities, you might want to give this game a go. It might suprise you.

I found this game to be incredibly drawn out and boring.  You are given very few bullets to start out, and are required to mine hundreds of times just to make a storage chest.  Each time you begin mining you are going to get attacked in the back by one of the local monsters, who are overpowered, and will kill you because you ran out of ammo after fighting the first two creatures.  Resources are unbalanced and hard to find what you need to complete the first few missions.  After 10 minutes of game play I could see that this was going to be a big time suck of searching and mining for resources, and getting very little reward for your efforts.  The game looks nice, but got boring after the first few minutes of gameplay.  Everything seems unbalanced at this point in the game.  Creatures that should be able to be killed in a few shots, take an entire clip of ammo to kill, which means you will have little to no ammo within a minute or two of spawning in the game.  You are given a pistol with unlimited ammo, but it takes an entire day to kill a small creature with it, because it is so underpowered.  You will find yourself constantly attacked, and trying to scramble to fix your exosuit without any resources to actually accomplish anything.  There is nothing new in this game compared to other survival based games, except that the graphics are decent.  I however, had major frame drops on my i7 rig with a 980ti.  This game might be ok in the distant future, but I'm talking years down the road.  These developers have bit off way more than they can chew.    If you want a more polished game experience, that has everything and more this game has, I recommend Empyrion Galactic Survival over this game.  I returned this game after about 40 minutes to an hour of gameplay.

Costume Quest will bring out old memories in you, even if you live in a region where Halloween is not that big of a festival/event. All those childhood fantasies of wearing a make-do costume and pretending to be a bigger robot/ninja/whatever-you-liked is what forms the premise of this game. Evil monsters are here with a sinister plan to rob the world of all its candy!! Your sister, who dressed up as a candy for halloween is abducted by them too. Hence starts your quest to rescue her. You get many costumes along the way, which turn into their big sized fantasy counterparts when you are in battle mode. Some of the fun ones include a burning fire attack Scarecrow, a Pirate that can summon ghost ships and even a glowing Unicorn to heal! You also meet friends along the way to help you in the quests, eventually increasing to a party of 3.
Though this game is short, but it does not feel so as it has adequate amount of quests and in game story to keep you attracted for a lazy weekend of playing. There is the main story to follow, the addon DLC, trading cards (in game not steam) to be collected and even battle stamps to be bought with all that cany you collect ! Last but not the least. it rewards you as well with not that difficult to get achievements.
The game is open world, with a linear flow, yet is not pushy at all. Humour is present and its of the pleasant kind, not the very obvious or cheesy just-for-kids type. So full marks there too. Battle system is turn based with a system of quick key presses to get the most optimum attack once u have selected your options. Battles are easy for the most part. Later bosses require a little strategy, which while keeping you sufficently involved in the story, are easy enough not to deter the calm flow of the game.
In all, a recommended buy. Do not hesitate if you get it on sale.

Games are supposed to be entertainment, right? Have we forgotten that? Well the folks at Valve still know what's going on. Portal is just so much fun and very cerebral, high-minded fun. Tough puzzles and complex obstacle courses are combined with a cutesy, droning robotic voice that guides you through the strange, Science Compound-esque environment to create a game atmopshere that is delightful.
The portal gun, the tool you use throughout the game, is used to create "in" and "out" portals that whisk you from one room to another. You can dive into them, shimmy through them, use them to toss blocks here and there. The possibilities are endless really, and you must tap all of the options to figure out how to get through each level.
The voice is also a trademark of the game. The droning, high-pitched female robotic voice is sarcastic and innocent sounding. Is it hiding something sinister under its cutesy guise? You don't know for sure. But the real scene stealer here is the voice, and it echoes in your head long after playing.
Overall a very very fun experience.

(..for my full review, look for the heading "Rager's Review of DoW1&2&Ch.-Rising"..)
DoW 2 Chaos Rising is an interesting expansion for Dawn of War 2. I played FPS games, and to a lesser extent third-person games, all my life and I never gave strategy games much of a chance because they did not suite me well. But the Dawn of War series appealed to me with its art work, story explanation, and user written reviews. I gave the series a good try and to say I'm 'just amazed' would not fully describe how much I enjoyed this! I find that because this is a standalone, you might want to purchase the original game first/along side this, but either way they both come with the co op game mode 'The Final Stand,' multiplayer (not very active), and an awesome campaign. I got to enjoy this and the original DoW 2 all day and all night during a free weekend. I fell in love with the game series <3 and planned on picking it up while on sale but I overslept after playing all night and missed it ;(
v-v-v-__ (Rager's Review of DoW1 & DoW2 && DoW2: Chaos Rising) __-v-v-v
( I wrote my reviews of DoW 1 // 2 // C.R. over the course of an hour, mostly nonstop typing. It may not be the best review of the series but it is an honest review and might convince you that the DoW series might be for you. Enjoy! )
[[-_ DoW #1 _-]]
-DoW1 is what you would think of a strategy game, meaning you build an HQ, barracks, generators, etc and then dominate your opponent (with the exception of some missions based on command one squad and infiltrate the enemy's territory)
---The multiplayer was hardly alive, and I was unable to join a match the first and last attempt I made.
[[-_ DoW #2 _-]]
-DoW2's campaign is mostly command the Force Commander (the main character which you get to name) and 3 other squads and dominate the enemy orks, farseer, chaos, tyranid. Did I mention it is co op?
---That isn't the only great part of #2 though! It also has a co op survival game mode called "The Final Stand" where you and 2 others work together to survive and progress through the increasingly difficult waves of enemy A.I. You get to choose your race and also level up each individually, earning new abilities, armor, and weapons. This game mode is still partially alive with players.
[[-_ DoW #2 Chaos Rising (standalone sequel) _-]]
- DoW2 Chaos Rising's campaign is based on an encounter with the Chaos Space Marines (for those who don't know; the Chaos S.M.s are "heretic rebels" to put it quickly). It was quite interesting but I did not make it very far into the story so I won't give it a full opinion. For me it was more appealing than the original DoW2's story because I had an experienced friend play co op with me.
---A few features of Chaos Rising - Corruption meter (scroll to the bottom of the review for explanation), corrupted armor/gear useable by your corrupted space marine squads, and the same goes for those who go the way of purity
---Chaos Rising is sometimes said to be dull or predictable; I cannot agree or deny this as I did not get too far into it
----Thanks for reading/skimming through my review!! ;)
-Chaos Rising - Purity vs. Corruption skill points
---Purity; viewed as space marine devoted to his emperor; earned by completing the mission and no corrupted objectives
( (10/10) - Would play all weekend long again (Except next time I'll remember to purchase it earlier!) )

I waited for this to download. I waited for Glyph to install. I waited for the e-mail from Glyph that told me I had to do it because I was using a different computer. I waited for Glyph to update. I waited for Glyph to tell me the current version of my game needed to be completely re-installed. I waited for it to install it all again. I waited and waited, all so I could play this game and you know what? I have no FREAKIN' idea why I did!
I got to the fabled Customization menu. I figured since so many people were saying such great and grand things about it that I'd love it to death. You see I have this problem with loving to customize my characters too much that I spend hours in it. After picking a side and a character type I finally saw the options it gave. Really? That's it? I've seen better customization in Vindictus or APB. It's literally ever so slightly better than SWTOR's customization but it leaves a lot of room for improvement. Oh, wait, you have to buy those improvements... with real money. Great. So I get one set of options and everything else possible is something I have to buy. Nothing I haven't seen before. So I ignored it.
My character looked about as generic as a Skyrim character by the end of it. And you know what else? It looked worse In-game than it did in the character creation screen. I figured it was my settings. I noticed that it was set to Custom and that everything looked terrible. I did what any smart gamer would do and put it to Ultra. It looked the exact freakin' same. I put it to Custom and maxed out everything slowly, checking for differences in between. No changes that greatly improved the game's look. Wow, so everything looks like a dated 2000's MMO game. Awesome! -_-
So my character's head looked well modeled but the body didn't. I could clearly see a low texture just under the neck line as everything there looked like pixels. Burry, crappy, pixels. This was all with everything on Maximum settings. Sure, the hair looked nice and shinny and never changed but my character's arms looked off, either too long or too pixeled. I blamed the textures.
I figured, maybe the gameplay is better than it looks since the menu selecting my class type looked very promising. HA! Big fat nothing there. It's basically a mish-mash of talents used to create a supposed new class. I ended up getting two skills that are almost 100% exactly the same. The "build guide" used for the Tanky Tank just placed points into both Tanking trees and gave whatever double ups there were. The talents in general are either meh or interesting but there just so damn many of them. The trees also go in two directions. I hadn't seen split points since Titan Quest and at least there it did it right. Alright, so were the skills at least good? Nope. Basically exactly the same as WoW with possibly better looking icons and Action Bar animations. The XP bar looked great but leveling up was pretty lackluster.
So, I played the damn game. I accepted quests and did as they asked. Normal stupid fetch this, or wack that 4 times. None of them were interesting or challenging. I continued, I used my skills like they were intended but I must be too low a level to feel the real greatness of the game because after leveling a few times on the most boring enemies period, It was just tiresome. Enemies that did attack you, didn't pose an actual threat. Enemies you attacked, barely could defend themselves. I stopped attacking to see if one could kill me and it took so long just to get me CLOSE to half health that I killed it. The combat never improved enough to stop me from being bored of it as a whole. My skills weren't interesting to use nor were they fun.
The animations looked like a good start but the actual skills were just copy-pastes. The skill effects were as you expected up until the fact that the Tank is basically playing as a Rogue. Instead of Combo Points I have... Attack Points. Like WoW, I get the little icon and improve damage.
The areas looked less fantasy like and more generic MMO trying its hardest to be realistic looking. For me, it looked bland, boring and useless. Nothing was unique about it. Nothing I haven't seen a million times in lesser games already.
I couldn't get past how worse than WoW it looked and felt. For a WoW clone you'd think they'd get this down.
Anyway, I've moaned enough about this game.

Will definitely be playing this more, because it shows massive potential. Graphics feel really fun and clean--puts me right back into being a kid. Weapons feel satisfying, gameplay ideas seem solid. Because this is Early Access, I want to put my most immediate things that turn me off, hoping they will fix these:
1. MOVEMENT. Especially--dear God--JUMPING. Feels slow and clunky, especially when fighting something fast like the spinners. I don't know what it is about the double-jump, but it's really hard to nail down compared to so many shooters. Trying to double-jump up the side of a box to replace the battery in something while your defenses are failing...and repeatedly dry-humping the box instead of scaling it...is the most frustrating feeling in the world.
2. WEAPONS - the default weapon can switch between Assault Rifle and Shotgun modes--not that you can tell the difference. When you flip from one to the other, they don't look significantly different, so it's easy to forget in the heat of a fight which one you've got equipped...and reloading takes so long you don't want to mix them up.
3. RELOADING - does it have to take this long? And if it does, we need a way cooler animation that a spinny loading icon.
4. DEAD BATTERIES - Some kind of charge indicator on the side of batteries would be super helpful, even if it's just in the helpful special vision mode--because of the way they pile up at the bottom of your energy pylons, it's damn near impossible to cycle through the used ones to get to one relatively fresh. Playing "Which battery's got juice?" in the middle of a toy invasion isn't my idea of fun difficulty.
Other than those UI tweaks, having  great time! But those small frustrations add up, and can seriously dampen enthusiasm for a game.

This game is all about the charm. The story isn't the same ol' derivative RPG story. The characters & setting are very enjoyable. I especially enjoyed playing this during Halloween, It put me in the holiday spirit.
As an RPG there's nothing truely ground breaking here. The combat is ok, It's a class based system. Classes are selected through a series of costumes. Some costumes have healing abilities, some are damage/crowd control & others are defensive. It may sound unique & interesting, but the battles generally all go the same way due to the fact that your abilities are not able to be activated till the 3rd round. Damage for 3 rounds, if the enemy is still up, stun heal & damage battle over.
I'm a fan of Tim Schafer's work, but I'm going to rate his work on it's own merits. This game is fun & charming & I would recommend it, but I would say wishlist it & wait for a sale.

This is a new review as i have taken the time to think about my feelings since this game from the BETA, to the EA (now that it is available on steam). I have over 80 hours into this game now.
In summary: I currently do not recommend this game, both because it is unbalanced and also because it is essentially like an RTS version of dark souls.
Pros:
+some cool units (Titans-long range armoured damage dealer) and Thanatos (mid range AOE), Soldier-short/mid range dmg, Rangers (silent and deadly).
+units can now gain one level of veterancy
+graphics are amazing! great attention to detail with steampunk style and everything appears crisp
+things work in a mostly logical way (stone walls are better than wood, upgrading makes sense *too a point (more on that later)
+animations for units is very well done, voiceovers are pretty well done as well
Cons:
-game has gotten progressively more difficult with successive patches: such as removing the ability for the player to disable turrets (to save energy/workers and  lower upkeep for gold while it was disabled). This was huge as it really made the game that much more difficult.
-game seems designed to be relatively difficult (which is ok to a point) but dying repeatedly after dozens of hours in is made worse by the fact that economy (i.e. upkeep) was nerfed while the game was still in BETA (making it harder to get your economy going (its like playing RTS/Tower defence colony management sim with an emphasis on the colongy management and the other two suffer because of it.
-This game is billed as a tower defence game...but it actively punishes you for using towers with really high upkeep (making the higher tiered towers (exectors) pretty much not being used until near the last wave).
-Billed as an RTS game but it costs a lot of resources to set up unit production facilities (making it hard to make more than one early/mid game and even later game it can be an issue as you are always strapped for resources since the upkeep of everything was increased.
-special units like the Titan are basically not used anymore (it costs so much gold just to unlock them it makes more sense to just skip them, oh and their upkeep is very high too. Thanatos are still expensive and high upkeep but they are easier to get than titans..even so, they are used sparingly.
-pretty much a very specific way to play the game every time (spam rangers bc they are quiet for early/mid game..then soldiers/snipers with some thanatos towards the end...all the while expanding as much as possible.
-advance buildings are a joke..upkeep costs are way to high and provided you have the space, it makes way more sense to just spam the lower tech buildings
-unit pathing is annoying, grouped units go every which way and aggro zombies like crazy
-one zombie hits a building 2-4 times...the building spawns a bunch of zombies and you are overrun
- no saving (ironmode only) so you can leave and come back to the game ok, but you can't restart if you die (i.e. zombies overrun you).
-each match takes 3-5 hours (yes it's pausable but you can't speed up time
-you can't build on resource tiles (build near them only..making you use 2 quarries when you could just use one (if you could place on the resource)..this is made worse by the fact that buildings have higher upkeep.
-you can only unlock the next map (4 in total) by completing the previous map at increasing difficulty levels (20/60/100 percent respectively). It used to be 100/110/130 so it has gotten better...but really there are only 4 maps... you should be able to play whichever one you want woithout having a difficulty cap locking you out of the other maps (i have 80 hours in and have only unlocked the second map ffs....)
-a community full of gatekeepers who rage at anyone who questions the difficulty/balance or even asks for additional options to tweak difficulty settings (which would not affect them in any way as this is a single player only game). Check the forums for this game to see people asking to make the game harder..raging that the devs lowerd the difficulty requirements to unlock the other maps etc).
-enemies now aggro weirdly...you can be using rangers (silent) and still aggro tons of special infected or villages of doom (VOD) sometimes for no apparent reason either (which is very frustrating).
-smaller resource tiles than there used  to be (sometimes right at the edge of the map where you either can't build on them, or can't defent them properly.
-essentially the difficulty ruins this game for me at the moment...and it keeps getting more difficult. It is hard to get excited to get wiped out because the zombies randomly chose your weakest point or a spitter shoots over a goddamn mountain, and infects your building (which then kills your colony). Many of your units are slow so it's not always possible to move units around fast (as your base becomes pretty big via necessity as you need a layered defence)
-random map generation-but no map seeds to pick maps you like again or to replay the exact same map to find out what you should do differently
Overall, there are some great aspects to this game. Unfortunately, the difficulty/heavy focus on colony management (i.e. resources/people/energy can sometimes lose you the game, as you need to bulid a tower but can't because you need more workers (but you can't get more workers till you make more farms but you can't make a farm till you get more energy...see where i am going? Hours of playing can be wiped out because your economy hits a crunch, and since you can't save the game, you have to start all over again on another random map.
because there is a very specific approach to winning a match, you end up playing the same way  (albeit on different randomly generated matches) so much that it just gets super repetetive...especially since most of the high end units rarely get used due to cost/upkeep and the fact they just wreck your economy.
Anyway, that is my thoughts after 80 hours spent playing this game. It was fun, but the shift towards increasing the difficulty further, being locked out of the other 2 maps, having hours of gameplay ruined by one zombie or bad economy (around the time a wave comes, without any saves) is just a lesson in frustration. I have spent more time being annoyed/frustrated with this game than i have had fun while  playing it. I have been playing RTS/Strategy games since the genre was invented, and it's one of my all time favourite genres. That said however, They are Billions (TAB) is just way more frustrating than fun at the moment. Hopefully it gets better, but as is, i just can't recommend it until they give us way more options to adjust difficulty, unlock all maps, and come up with some options for economy/upkeep as well as give us some additional units/towers and balance the units/towers currently in game.
Buyer beware here...at least i warned you what you are getting into.

As a fan of horde/tower defense, this was a game that caught my eye and immediately delivered. Plays like a AoE/Starcraft 1 UMS hybrid with villagers that you do not control.
-You start off with a command center(town hall) and slowly expand via a Protoss pylon type system while trying to keep infected from destroying your town hall.
-Most buildings have upgrades, but it is this reviewer's opinion that the time to get to those upgrades takes a little too long.
-There are a total of 5 controllable units, all ranged, 2 wall types, 2 trap types, and 2 defensive tower types. Some more variety would be nice, but right now this works fine.
-Average game length can range from 5 minutes to 3 hours. Depending on where your base starts in relation to hordes or infected towns will typically decide the length of your game. If you play on anything but the easiest mode most of your early games will be over quickly.
-Things I did not like :This game could still use some early warning systems for infected. A few of my losses were simply because I did not know that I had been under attack. The upgrade system could use tweaking, defensive upgrades for villagers and the command center would be useful. the area management is a little janky, upgrades to the pylons to increase their AoE would be great.
-Still obviously a work in progress but has time to elevate itself from a great early access game to excellent full release with its already polished ideas and gameplay.
-I could eventually see this game having multiplayer Vs/CoOp that would be incredibly fun, fighting an enemy and trying to use the infected against them.
Overall very good game and I look forward to its full release.

The on the fence people. So if you are looking at the 4 bad reviews, most of them are because of the "non save" feature in the survival mode or wanting to be a "save scummer". There is NO save during a game unless you save and exit back to the menu. The game is like this for a reason. If you ever played XCOM 2 (Ironman Mode) or SC2 Campaign without a "Quick Save" or "Save" mode and enjoyed it, you will probably like this. I understand one is a turn based strategy game and one is a real time strategy game, but the concept is the same, just faster. That is why I also compared it to SC2. Let me just say and reiterate "S U R V I V A L" mode, not "save and revert to a previous save because now you know where the wave is coming from and beat it that time" mode.

TL;DR: Portal is a great game with near-perfect level design and lots of enjoyable mechanics. The modes outside of the main mode aren't very good, but if you're looking for a solid game that will take you a few hours to beat, this is the game for you.
Portal is a game where you try to get from point A to point B by using different mechanics such as portals and cubes. The game does an outstanding job introducing its mechanics gradually, so that way the player isn't confused nor bored. The game's story, level design, mechanics, art design, and progression are amazing, however the alternate game modes (namely being the steps and time challenges) are a bit lackluster.
The levels in Portal are simply amazing with everything in each level working together to bring the player a great experience. Everywhere the player needs to go is highlighted by an object or an art asset, so the player never feels lost. Even though this may seem hand-holding or too easy, the game will still leave enough puzzles to the player to add enjoyable gameplay with a large sense of satisfaction at the end of each puzzle. Some of the levels in the game have different shortcuts that only experience players will find. These shortcuts add replayability to the later few levels of the game, as the player will most likely not find all of the shortcuts in his or her first playthrough of the game.
Portal's mechanics are very consistent throughout the game, and compliment the level design. Portal does a great job of keeping the mechanics consistent so the player knows exactly what to do. For example, you cannot place portals on dark surfaces or metal throughout the entire game. All of the games mechanics interact with the level design to create a cohesive puzzle that is extremely entertaining. In the game, every time you see a large button, you know that there is a cube nearby, and the level does a nice job of explaining where the cube is. Also, in the earlier levels where momentum is needed to solve a puzzle, there is always an extended piston so the player knows where to place his or her's portal. The piston tells the player that momentum will be involved, so the level design and mechanics work well together.
The art design in Portal is very simplistic, which puts emphasis on the different aspects of each puzzle. It's very hard to get lost in Portal, because the puzzles stand out so much against their environment. In Portal, because everything is so simple, it gives the player a sense of "Everything is here for a purpose." The art style also does a great job of telling a story. In the game, certain areas opt-out of using standard lights, and instead use these small rooms hidden behind opaque windows to give the player a feeling of being watched. The art design in Portal works really well with the gameplay and the theme.
The advanced maps in Portal add a little bit more to the game, but I don't think they're anything to write home about. The advanced maps in Portal add obstacles, and remove shortcuts to the already existing levels to make them harder. I didn't spend much time with the advanced levels, as they're built on the same maps from the main game, because I feel the main game's maps are a lot more open with what way you solve the puzzle. Each advanced map has only one or two ways to solve the puzzle, whereas the main game of Portal has lots of different ways to solve each puzzle. Overall, I prefer when there are lots of ways to solve a puzzle as opposed to just having one way, so I didn't enjoy the advanced maps as much.
In Portal, there is a separate mode called "Challenges." The challenge maps are the exact same maps from the main game, however you have a second goal, such as using the least number of portals, taking the least amount of steps, and completing the level as fast as possible. Completing each one of the later levels with the least amount of portals I found pretty clever and fun, but the other challenges have lots of problems. I found the least number of steps challenge to be ridiculous and unenjoyable. The mechanics needed to complete the level with a gold rating, I found to be pretty frustrating and irritating to pull off. Another issue with the steps challenge is Chamber 17. In Chamber 17, most of the level has nowhere to put a portal. Having nowhere to put a portal completely takes away from the challenge, and becomes an annoying game of timing each jump. The final challenge is the time challenge. In theory, this challenge should be pretty fun as it let's anybody try to be a speedrunner. However, for a few of the challenges, the time given to get gold is extremely low, and turns the challenge into constantly saving and reloading. This problem could easily be solved by giving the player a few more seconds to get gold. Overall, most of the challenges are not fun, but they do add lots of replay value as the player must try each challenge over and over again until he or she gets gold.
The Developer Commentary in Portal is put together well, and is pretty interesting. If you're interested in the development of games, including art design, voice acting, and level design, then I recommend playing through the Developer Commentary.
Portal as a whole is an amazing game, that has incredible level design. The game does have some problems in its other game modes, but the main game is still great. If you are even remotely into first-person games or puzzle games I strongly recommend this game.

Cards on the table, this game has problems. The biggest of which is you'll keep wishing for co-op that just isn't happening. Also the voice clips get annoying pretty fast.
But I want to say that this game is a pretty good time. Each of the heroes has a distinctly different flavor, the cards as powerup system is wonderful and opens this game up to a lot of interesting strategy, and the game handles very well.
Think of this as an action RPG that trims the fat of a typical Diablo game (exploring a largely empty map, busting open every barrel you see for a few pennies, constantly swapping equipment for slight benefits) and gets to the good stuff in a hurry. The good stuff being using your wits and your items wisely to blow mobs of mooks to red mist and taking on bosses with challenging patterns.
There are some things to warn you about though. Cards are everything and the only way to get more is getting gold through the rounds (win or lose) and feeding said gold into a slot machine. Thankfully that costs in-game money, but know that the process of getting your deck into solid shape will take time. Early game tip, keep the card "Paranoia" in your deck, since a one hit shield that keeps coming back each round is more valuable than you'd think.
Try it yourself and I think you'll know right away if this is your jam or not. Because if this is up your alley, it scratches very specific itches and it does it pretty well.

Forced Showdown combines action and collectable card game into one. The end result is pretty incredible.
Players select one of five characters to go through staged battles. Each character uses a deck of cards which players can modify in order to provide upgrades/consumables for use in battle. Cards are limited by a mana system which increases as players advance through the stages. Most stages are altered by one or more mods which makes this game fun and challenging. Coupled with different combinations from the cards, every playthrough is something refreshing and new.
The game does have certain areas that require improvements. As many others have pointed out, this game is extremely grindy. You get one card for every card pull, two in very rare cases. This feels unnecessarily stingy especially for a single player game. The challenge does not come from the limitation of card choices, so I feel it's missed opportunity for allowing players to experience more card combos. I was also disappointed to find that there's no co op mode for this game as I had a lot of fun playing Forced with my friend.
Overall, following the huge enjoyment I got from Forced, BetaDwarf has done it again. This game is nothing short of excitement. Be warned that it is very challenging.

This is not the type of game that appeals to everyone.  As many reviews have stated, it is a game that attempts to incorporate many different features such as cards, but does not do so particularly well.  There is a definite grind that will become very annoying to casual gamers, and having to unlock cards and characters can be frustrating as well.  There doesn't seem to be any real cohesive theme to the game, which can make it rather confusing at times.
Nonethless, it CAN be fun at times, and I do recommend the game and DLC, but only if purchased during a sale.  If you prefer "pay to own" games such as myself, and are looking for something a bit different, I highly recommend giving this game a try.  However, if you are a fan of "Free To Play" games and prefer in-game transactions, you are likely to be displeased.  Like all games, it comes down to personal preference.  Being a more casual older gamer, the whole "Free To Play" model doesn't appeal to me whatsoever, it just ends up being a money sink.
In the end, I like the game, and feel it is worth the money when it is at least 50% off the original price.  I find myself returning to it every now and then, enough that I'm glad I made the purchase.  Though I'd like to see more content, I'm pleased with what is there.

The premise of the game is interesting but the way it's been carried out is just extremely unenjoyable.
First of all, there's only five characters. Was expecting at least ten to twenty considering how simple each is and how grindy the gameplay is. But no, there's only five to pick from. That alone is a huge immediate stunt to the entire game is that there's barely any player choice, you have to just pick from one of five generic characters and if you don't like any of them then that's your problem.
The gameplay itself is literally grinding. Players fight through randomly generated, inconsequentially designed maps and kill fodder enemies who often only deal damage by hitting players when they aren't looking or with their overbearing capabilities. That is the whole game, is killing fodder in a box, over and over. Alright, you made the boring grind mode players have to endure if they want more currency; now where is the actual game.
The world design itself is generic but the maps are just unappealing. Flying pirate rat place, floating human medieval garden place. They look so stupid and abrasive to the eyes it's like one of those bad three dimensional cartoon childrens games, badly thought out fantasy that just isn't cool as a concept.
The difficulty is not there, as said it mostly comes from arbitrary things; there's little real challenge. In the end, defeat is decided by the player gradually losing pieces of their health overtime across all the stages; and then if they don't have enough to defeat the boss then game over restart it all again. Which wouldn't be a problem if the gameplay wasn't so generally boring and grindy. There's no challenge or strategy or structure at all.
And as a side note, certain allies players can spawn are actually capable of hurting them. There's one-way friendly fire between the player and mob type ally enemies they conjure up. So you can die because your mob ally decided to fire out a wave of missles while standing beside you, and that literally happened one time and reset the entire thirty minute run.
Game doesn't even have multiplayer, which not only is what the game looks like it was entirely designed for but in its current state multiplayer is the only thing that would make it remotely playable.
Game should have been a free competitive and cooperative arena fighter and wave survival game with purchasable currency to buy more cards or one of more then five characters. What this is feels like a couple good mechanical concepts mashed into multiple different gameplay settings they don't belong in at all coupled with unstructured boring gameplay and little character diversity. This literally felt like a chore to play.

I really like the concept of this game. It has some great ideas powering it and I enjoyed playing it for a week, however in its current state I can't recommend it.
I appreciate that it is an early access game, but even for early access it is lacking in content. In 20hours i'd completed the game. I'd build all the structures and all the vechiles. Been to space, which had nothing in it.
There are also a few elements letting the game down. It's buggy, again understandable for early access but i don't expect to be pushed below the terrian, teleported out of buildings or getting completely stuck on stuff, to the point i can't even change whats in my hand. Oh and crafted items can sometimes disappear. If you don't place your lab(vechile construction) right, vechiles space underground or at the least clipping through the ground.
Actual game mechanics which is fustrating; no auto stacking and if you craft something it goes into the inventory of the machine not your  inventory, if inventory is full it spits them out, which is fine but items disappear somethings(I assume go under the terrain). Both these just feel like common sense features and and possibly should have been sorted before release.
The vechile controls are a bit off in places too, the hoover bike is supreme, it feels great the drive, the spaceship is completely the opposite, and G.A.V and rover are ok, but can do some weird stuff when hitting objects, like bouncing off players if you hit them(And I mean bouncing +10meters), which considering your in a massive 6 wheeled vechile just doesn't compute.
I think this game has a lot of potential, However stacked up against simular games that were released in early access like ARK, this game in hopelessly lacking in content and is extremely buggy. I will have another play through in a few months and I may change my review then, but until then I say this is a game to watch not buy. Hopefully the developers will do some good work and turn this diamond in the ruff in to a pure gem.

First Impressions:
Impressive amount of depth for a squad-based third person shooter - clearly built with a lot of love.
It's the first in what hopefully becomes a very successful spin-off of the much beloved XCOM series.  In traditional XCOM, the entire game is played from a tactical point of view, giving orders to a unit of soldiers fighting against the alien menace. In the Bureau, you play as the commander of a squad, participating in combat as well as using a pretty unique "Battle Focus" system to issue orders.
The actual issuing of orders is a bit tricky at times - the soldiers don't always do what you want them to do.  However, once you get used to the goofy little nuances, it easily becomes the most compelling and interesting feature of the game.
A lot of people will tell you that this game isn't XCOM or it's some kind of abomination.  Those people are known as idiots.  This game was always intended to be a spinoff - If you're looking for something truer to the original experience, you're looking for XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  It has all the flavor and intrigue of XCOM, but again, it's a spinoff - it has a non-traditional gameplay style.
It's my opinion that this is good. Others can disagree, but I don't actually care what they think.

Having only played through the free weekend and with a total of around 10 hours some may say that I am not qualified to write a review for this game.

Pros and cons?
Like with every other Ubisoft game out there, graphics and sound are never the problem. It's the content.
Having to basically do almost the same thing a hundred times gets really boring, really fast.
Completionists aside, even a speed-player will have to spend hours grinding or finish the game with starting gear - and that's another thing about this game - I'm usually a sucker for getting new, more powerful guns (but I love precision, tuning, not raw firepower) and upgrading them to perfection - having gone through the entire list of weapons in this game - I maybe found 2 others (besides the starting one) that I wanted to try. There were honestly too many brute assault weapons (that don't really fit the gameplay) and boatloads of freak (called signature these days) weapons - a.k.a. copied from Far Cry. Which brings me to my point - this game is basically a content copy-and-adapt from other (mostly Ubisoft) games.
There is absolutely NOTHING original here. The story, apart from "briefings", is just basic cutscenes with poor dialogue (which is becoming a Ubisoft signature feature) that simply tell you what is going on. And that's it. There's no "real" story in there. Far Cry 3 had 10 times the amount of story in it. Story-wise I'd compare this to Red Faction: Guerilla.
As for bugs I haven't encountered any yet, except teleporting AI teammates but that's just the usual AI programming laziness of Ubisoft, so no shocker there.
It amazes me that people would actually pay 60 EUR for a game like this. I wouldn't pay 30, I wouldn't pay 20. At 15 I'd think about it and 10 EUR or below is about the mark that I'd consider "worth the price". I think it's safe to say that after the weekend trial (during which I basically got the whole experience), I won't be buying this game any time soon...

Currently, as it stands on early access, the game is extremely promising and has the key features to become THE space game everyone wants after the No Man's Sky Fiasco, it has the atmosphere of a survival game with elements of horror embedded nicely into it, theres a lot of work to be done though, currently you can enjoy if for about 5-8 hours that you will spend mostly gathering materials and surviving against giant crabs, and then build the currently available structures with the hard earned ores you got, and then realize it needs more content because theres nothing else to do than to explore the caves filled with creeps that resemble necromorphs (also the only way to get diamond ores) or get lost on the vast desert that surrounds your oasis, the basis of a great game is there, time will tell how amazing it'l become,
Also, duly noted the XP system and the proto-MMO elements on this early access, its clearly meant to be played in Multiplayer for the full experience, but indeed, theres a LOT of work to do on almost every field, however there doesnt seem to be any catastrophic glitches or problems that would destroy your gameplay. Looking forward to see more, and heres a wish, the ability to create your own custom ships (just like space engineers) may pretty much attract a lot of people.

tbh.. this is the game i feel NMS should have been. I'll be the first to admit it, I'm a sore loser.
I've played games in the past for less than an hour and never looked their way again due to them being too hard or complicated for me.
But this? This is a whole new kind of frustrating.
In 2 hours I've had 4 different games, each one getting progressively further, but ultimately failing just as hard as the previous one.
I'm struggling to manage my resources, my units, my defence, basically I'm just struggling.
And yet, I'm writing this review just before going to sleep and I'm already excited to get back at it tomorrow.
I'm not angry that I keep losing, I'm excited to try again. I'm already planning different defence tactics, already debating which research to prioritise.
This game has me expecting defeat, which would normally be a turn off for me (Dark Souls etc), but yet I carry on.
I can't quite put my finger on the reason why this game evokes a different reaction from me, but I'm not going to complain.
If you like losing, if you like watching your colony overrun by zombies (which is oddly incredibly satisfying), if you like the whole "one more turn/one more try" kinda games with the hope that the next one will be THE one, then I strongly suggest you buy this game.

Wow! amazing game! Basically, it plays like Gauntlet but with lots of micro arenas.
Here's how it works, you play to win a battle. A battle is 8 separate fights (arenas). For each arena, you can choose which power ups (cards) you want to use. The power ups carrry over to the next arena until you die or complete the battle. The game lets you get ridiculously powerful because the powerups stack and stack and stack. When you kill a big boss (or die), your buffs reset.
You only level up in the sense that you unlock/earn more cards (powerups) that you can use when you retry the battles.
The game is just incredible in the way the powerups make you feel like a God. After a short learning curve, the game gets really hard and starts to really challenge you.
The in-game acheivements "quests" are significant too as by achieving them you can permanantly increase your health, your companion health, unlock boons (powerups) get gold (used to unlock cards) which in turn make you more powerful.
The other thing that I absolutely love about this game is the way friendly fire works. Your enemies hurt each other. In-game traps hurt them. Everything seems to hurt them. Sometimes you don't even have to attack them; just avoid the traps and let them die from the friendly fire. Another cool thing. One of the bosses is a necromancer. He can raise any enemy from the dead. One of the stages gives you necromancer powers. There's no way they'd let you raise everything from the dead right? Like - the Necromancer boss? Wrong. The game lets you raise a summoned boss from the dead (if you play your cards right *wink wink*)
TLDR: This game is fun. Buy it.

Calibre 10 has all of the ingredients for a very, very entertaining game. It's like Trackmania with turrets, where a gunner and driver are paired together. Four drivers speed down the track included with the Alpha as they race to grab power-ups and avoid gunfire from turrets. The teammates can swap between any available turret locations on the map. Is a turret occupied by an opponent? Take it out and steal it from the enemy. Drivers can grab missile turret upgrades or debuff enemy turrets, as well as grab Nitro and Shield pickups. It's a fairly simplistic formula that keeps things balanced and straightforward. Unfortunately, I could only play against the AI so it's tough to tell how the whole game will pan out. If memory serves me correctly, the Live Arcade had a smiliar entry from the same team. From what I can tell, however, Alpha 1 has a bit of interesting content, a teaser, if you will. If they can iron out some of the loose car handling and reign in turret damage, this could be a fantastic title.

I was an original Rifter, and have left off an on over the years, but I keep coming back. The latest expansion pack, Nightmare Tides, has been such a blast to play. I was a little worn out during the last expansion, because the new continents (new then) of Brevane and Dusken were so huge, and the carnage quests too big (go kill 12 of X). Now, in the Planes of Water area, the carnage quests are reasonable (6 or 8 mobs), plus the story quests are fantastic.
Besides quests and leveling, the game has a TON of content. Like to craft? Lots of that. Like fishing, or building your own dimension (house)? Rift has that. Like huge raids you can join at a moment's notice out in the open world? Or private pre-arranged affairs? how about quick Instant Adventures, where you join a smaller raid of 8-10 or so, and gallivant around the countryside doing speedy quests together. Then there are the traditional dungeons, expert dungeons, and PVP warfronts. There's even a collectible "card" game you can play, like a casual game. Besides the one in-game, there's another in a mobile app. You like special holiday events? How about being able to wear costumes while still wearing your gear? How about puzzles and unique achievements? Collectible artifacts in game to find throughout the world? Yes, all of the above are in Rift.
Plus, the landscapes are gorgeous. So are the faces and realistic bodies of the characters -- the females, at least (so glad I could make one without balloon boobs.) My avatar is currently wearing a holiday sweater, and I can see the individual stitches in it! Oh, and if you're tired of your look -- or even your race (species) -- just visit the barber and change it!
Yes, some things cost a bit, but even a measly $5 will get you pretty much everything you need to get started, and it's an incredibly reasonable price for hours and hours of exploration and fun.

While the Art Direction is often admirable, one's left with the impression that 2K had no clear vision for the game throughout production. The graphics seem dated, but on the bright side, the game runs fairly smooth.
Unfortunately, the same can't be said of the gameplay, which is often that of a clunky and overall dissatisfying cover-based third-person shooter. It’s reminiscent of Mass Effect with a focus on tactics and “magic” abilities, but while the game is playable with Gamepad or Mouse + Keyboard, neither option feels optimal when guiding one’s squad in the slowed-down but all too narrow tactical view. Neither abilities nor weapons (even Alien ones) feels particularly good or seem all that interesting. Last but not least, the overall storytelling seems broken, with too much poorly written dialogue and bad sound design.
I would love to recommend the game, mostly because I found the setting intriguing with Cold War Agents running around dressed in fancy suits in cigarette smoke stenched interiors fighting Advanced High Tech Aliens, but there’s just so many signs of a messy production with no clear vision it’s impossible to do so.

EDIT: The developers speedy response made me change my mind. I will leave this review as recommended for the time being. Let's see how it progresses. My points still stand though.
This MIGHT be a good game someday, but its being held back by questionable design choices.
This game has batteries which powers up your turrets.
Why have them at all if they're just going to spawn right next to the core?
Gameplay-wise this makes the batteries completely pointless, might as well have just a regular 'press F to repair/recharge' feature.
You gain credits every round, but after the first few you have enough to buy out everything, there's no upgrading or repairing. The walls are destroyed very quickly, only for you to spend 20 out of your 4000 credits to rebuild it.
There are pre-placed areas where you can build. This isn't an issue in many tower defense games that does this, because they usually have a lot of them, with a variety of stuff you can build on them. This game only has a few, the only ones you can build any different structures on are the foundations (of which there aren't a lot of) and even then there are only a few turrets. This removes any and all tactical aspect to the game, and in my opinion the most fun part of tower defense games.
Sanctum does what this game aims to do much better, and that game was released in 2011 and costs 8 dollars. When you pay 10 dollars you expect more, even if it is early access.
This game runs on the unreal 4 engine, so it looks gorgeous, it runs smoothly and they've nailed the toy-store aesthetic.

I will be adding occasional, concise updates regarding changes significant enough to mention in the comments on this review to keep information up to date without making this review a multi-page essay.
HYPERCHARGE: Unboxed is a pleasant surprise. I absolutely love Co-Op wave based survival games and tower defense games so seeing this pop up on Steam's Upcoming was exciting. I decided to just go for it with semi-low expectations and pick it up on release for $15 and I'm honestly glad I did. In it's current state, an early pre-alpha, it doesn't offer a lot in terms of content or replayability but what it has in copious amounts is potential. The visuals are incredible, mechanically it's very solid, combat and movement is polished and fluid, has a great and fitting soundtrack and overall the audio is pretty good. Digital Cybercherries have also heavily emphasized community interaction and personally working with them to make HYPERCHARGE the best it can be. The foundation for an incredible game is here and what you'd be primarily paying for currently is an investment and support in the development team as well as a chance to watch this game and its community grow. I have owned my fair share of Early Access games and a lot of them have been abandoned or failed to become a worthwhile game but based on what HYPERCHARGE has and the commitment promised from the developers I have a lot of faith and excitement for this games future.
-----------------------------------------------

* Visuals are impressive, almost a bit surreal. They really nailed the toy store aesthetic between the plastics, toy boxes, visual effects, sounds, and overal scale.
* Though you are usually confined to the isle of a toy store, there's a whole new level of freedom when you're the size of an action figure. You're able to climb up through all the boxes, racks, and hangars making the toy store feel more like a jungle, adding an unexepected depth to the isles.
* A lot of little easter eggs and comedic design hidden throughout the game. Exploring the map and checking out all the various toys on the shelves is pretty entertaining.
* The mechanics, movement, and gunplay are really solid and surprisngly well polished. Overall the game feels great to play.
* There's a fair amount of customization for your player model and they executed it very well. The models are very well done, from the color schemes to the general design and you can have the color scheme persist to your weapons and turrets.
* It runs well. Rarely dip below 60 FPS max settings @1440p with a GTX 780.
* Comprehensive settings menu for graphics, controls, audio, and some gameplay.
-----------------------------------------------
* There's not a lot of content or replayability at the moment. There's
also not a lot of progression yet, mainly consists of upgrading defenses but there is an inactive exp system for future updates. Currently there is only 4 maps with 5 weapons and 5 mostly cosmetic attatchments to choose from.

* There are some bugs.

* Multiplayer can be a bit laggy. Not unplayable by any means but it's inconvenient at times.
-----------------------------------------------
Should you buy it? Short answer, Yes, if you don't mind the typical Early Access investment of buying an incomplete in development game. HYPERCHARGE does what it sets out to do very well so far and if a Co-Op survival tower defense game is up your alley then this is the game for you. If none of the above applies to you I recommend either skipping this one or keeping an eye on it as it recieves more updates. However, you can tell easily within the first two hours if it's something you'd want to keep, giving you the option to pick it up and refund it if you don't want it.

Enjoyable racing game. Features the islands of Ibiza and Hawaii, which means plenty of roads to race on! Or instead of racing the races you could of course just do some relaxing sightseeing, test drive the cars you can't afford (yet), replace the furniture in your house or get cosmetically adjusted. Yes, this game also has some Sims-like aspects lol, but fortunately these are, as far I can tell with only 9 hours in, only aesthetic. Oh and you play online 'by default', making the game kind of MMO. This makes it easy to play races vs other players, since (in non-race mode) they are always driving around in the same world anyway.

My observations;
"Bullet Hell Brawling"
I hate bullet hell. this isn't bullet hell. it's good - all enemy attacks are avoidable, there is almost always an escape, or somewhere to go if you play well.
"Roguelike/Roguelite"
Mostly Roguelike. As you play (and win arenas) you unlock coins that unlock cards; its a little bit RNG what you can get. It's 'truely' roguelike in that when you die, you start at level 1, no special permanent unlocks that give you any advantage over your first run (OK you might get an extra card or two here and there - and a different pet to assist you, but they are not really game changers) -
The Card system;
Cards add abilities / skills (think of them as items that make you stronger like in moba's). You can build a deck of 30 cards, once you've used a card in game, it's no longer available to reuse for that arena (aka until you beat a boss - this is esecially important when considering when to use healing cards).
Side note; each arena goes like this; Area1: 1 mana to spend. Area 2: 2 mana, area 3.... etc etc. if you don't spend it, at the start of the round, you lose it, you can't save it for the next round. use it or lose it.
The Unlocks System.
Fortune uses gold won (collect gold during 9 arenas, beat the miniboss to keep the gold, spend the gold on Wheel of fortune spins to win cards), doubleups can be interesting, in the unlock system. but triples go toward a gem currency which guarantee unlocks of new / unique cards. So you will unlock everything, eventually. You can also unlock helpers, and other Champions (Contestants) through Quests... which I don't much like, especially as many of the quests remain 'hidden' until you either complete them or partially do so.
Arenas;
Procedurally generated? I think so? each arena follows a theme for the 9 battles you'll have there. Each has it's own hazards; spikes, spitting acid, exploding barrels.... Each one gets harder until the boss. Beat enough mini arenas, face the Gate Guardian. I have yet to beat the first one; I may do so now that I've figured him out. (I'm 3h into the game). The trick is that you get 4 arenas to choose from in a leadup to a gate guardian; the trick is that it can be any combination of arena, miniboss, and Hazard.... Oh Hazards. You might have to fight with acid clouds, meteor showers, increased enemies, Rage (Less health = more damage dealt)... or perks that help, (start with extra mana, extra consumables, etc) but are balanced by having more enemies.
Bosses
there are always the same minibosses to beat; but they are made interesting becuase depending on the miniboss you choose to fight... they actaully throw an obsticle at you periodically through the arenas before you meet them in the bossfight on the last arena - the piraterat throws mines down all match, undeadfred throws turrets, and so forth.
Gameplay
twinstick (WASD to move, mouse aim). It would be nice if the courser was easier to see. That's about that, really.
Champions.
The starting champ, is the best champ - at least for my playstyle. each champ has abilities that synergise pretty well. some are ranged combatants, some are midrange, some are melee-ish. They seem to work well, but atarting guy = best guy. which is nice, it means all the good stuff doesn't take forever to grind to getting.
DLC
Mostly cosmetic; i bought the one that changes gameplay (Drone invasion) as it gives another character, arena, boss and obsticle, or something. Nothing really P2W in there, but it is added content.
Overall;
A good game for doing like 20 minute runs, a casual drop-in type roguelike that you can pickup again in a few weeks or months and not feel punished by for not having mastered everything about it (Don't Starve, anyone?). Totalbuiscuit does a nice review of the game if you want a let's play or whatever. It's a perfect game for when you want a light break from your normal, hardcore games that you play the rest of the time.

I played the original Forced and I totally loved it, both because of the co-op and because of the brilliant combination of WASD action and smart level design.
I was first hesitant with Forced Showdown as it's only singleplayer, but boy was I mistaken to delay playing it. I had never played a rogue like game before, nor had I played a deck building game before. The rogue like part brings suspense and a rewarding feeling to every battle, and I totally love the way Beta Dwarf implemented the deck building part in Showdown. I personally like the RNG of the cards as it brings flavor and variety to every single battle, and the sheer number of cards means that you can play each character in multiple ways simply by switching to a totally different deck.
If you decide to go for it, I recommend being both focused and patient in the first few hours until you get a good grasp of how the card draw works. Also, roll the Fortune wheel each time you get gold as you have a ton of cards to unlock.
Before confronting some of the higher end bosses (for example the last boss of Frontline and higher), I'd recommend doing a bit of reading beforehand. A quick google search will make you understand some mechanics and will spare you a lot of lost time (remember, this is a rogue like game, so if you die you start over).
All in all, a brilliant game which I see myself playing well over the 100 hour mark to get all the cards and complete all the quests.

I would allllllmost recommend this game, but I can't quite bring myself to fully endorse it. The basic concept is that you get put in an arena for eight rounds and need to kill all the enemies. The cool part is that each round you get to play cards that boost your character in various ways, some temporary and some for the whole eight rounds.
There are two really annoying features that keep me from endorsing the game. First, one or two of the quests are bugged and do not register properly as completed. This includes the absolutely most annoying quest in the game, which involves being lucky enough to have your partner turn evil, the enemies be smart enough (hah!) to not kill themselves, and you to finish off every single one with the weakest attack in the game.
Two, it is more luck-based than it should be. Those eight arenas I mentioned? A "program" is several of those in a row, topping out at, as far as I can see, eight in a row. If you lose a single one of them, you're kicked back to the beginning. This can be a huge problem as some characters are at an extreme disadvantage against certain bosses.
If this game gets a little more love I would probably change my review, but it isn't quite there yet.

Things you CAN'T do:
- no moving, hiding, or searching bodies (and they disappear)
- no bases to capture and defend (enemy presence gets lower but they are always randomly around)
- no sharing a motorcyle with a teammate
- no switching from pilot to passenger in a helecopter that's hovering
- no secret passages, no hidden items, no reason to explore
- no yaw (rudder) control in airplanes
- no trip mines or claymores or other anti-personell traps (just anti-vehicle mines)
- no starting fires for area denial or fun
- no interaction with the trains that go around the map (besides getting run over by them)
- no sitting or laying on a teammate's vehicle while they drive (other than the contextual seats)
- no climbing or parkour or team boost areas (the ghosts can vault some walls up to ~7 feet but that's it)
- no shooting through chain fences or camo nets, but the enemy can (this happens occasionaly)
- no environment or building destructability (besides a few props)
- no bandages, medpacks, or adreniline or anything health related
- no 'knocked down' or 'last stand' states, ony 'alive' or 'incapp'ed'
Other disappointments:
- all gear is cosmetic only
- enemy AI: somehow worse than Farcry's
- the drone magically returns to you anytime you stop controlling it and it can't be left hovering or landed anywhere
- the random npc rebels and civilians have very little character
- night/thermal vision: no animations or models on the player when activated
- they added a few more HUD options but they are still severely lacking (can't disable 3d enemy markers w/o disabling them from minimap, also other players and rebels)
- variety of missions: there are only a few diffirent mission types, mostly it's the locations that change
- not very good peformance for the quality of the graphics
- friendly AI: worthless in all situations (except 'sync shot' which let's them shoot through buildings/terrain)
- some of 'side' mission scenarios feel like they were made in fifteen minutes with no consideration for gameplay at all (put the objective here, put some enemy spawns here, done!)
- in all of the area to explore there's very little 'environmental storytelling' or details that you find in carefully created games

halloween-themed rpg with simple turn-based combat. gave me billy and mandy vibes at times. felt like an rpg for kids with its simple quests and directions, but i love halloween too much to feel any shame. not that i don't think adults won't enjoy this.
the story doesn't take itself seriously and was good enough to make me want to find out what happens next, the funny dialogue and cute cartoon artstyle mix well to create a comfortable halloween feel.
the combat has quick-time events for offense and defense. classes (attack, defense, support, and special) are determined by the costume the character wears. costumes are changeable and each has its own stats (health and attack) and unique special attack that is charged every 3 turns. there are also equipable "battle stamps" that modify health and attack. the battle stamps can also give a unique ability such as resurrection, poison, or dodge chance. the combat was easy enough to where i rarely felt the threat of defeat. the camera is impressively cinematic in battle with pans, zooms, and letterboxing.
gameplay outside of combat has literal trick-or-treating, fetch quests, bobbing for apples, playing hide-and-seek, defeating specific enemies, and doing-this-to-be-able-to-go-there's to progress in the story and collect items. some costumes have an ability outside of combat that allow you to access otherwise inaccessible areas. the dialogue and atmosphere keep the overworld entertaining despite the simplicity. there is a quest log to help you keep track, but there is no map. however, the areas were not so complex to where i felt lost.
there are three levels that you can teleport between, so don't worry about missables. you also can't jump. this is frustrating when something you want to get is just out of reach, but look around enough and you will find a way to get to it.
Really funny dialogues, original idea. Totally recommend it.

As a HoI3 veteran, I felt obliged to buy this game and try give it a try, HoI3 was and still is a very good game, perhaps a little on the clunky side but still manageable. I was expecting HoI4 to be as good if not better, but boy was I in for a ride.
It is very obvious that Paradox has tried catering to a different, wider audience with HoI4. Every single aspect of the game, which is also present in HoI3 in some way or another is very much dumbed down or downright completely alienated. After HoI3 and seeing how much trouble people are having with it's complexity, it was probably a good idea to try and make sure HoI4 was an easier to control game, with a little less complexity but staying true to the kind of game paradox tries to make. Paradox however, hit the nail completely wrong when it comes to HoI4. The game is so extremely simplified that a 5 year old could play the game and mop up the USSR by 1940. Let me explain why.
Let's start off with aerial and naval combat. In HoI3, naval and aerial combat was quite important, not only it being necessary to weaken enemy troopt, but also to mess with supply lines, bomb ports, bomb stockpiles and resources. In HoI4, aerial and naval units do none of these. Air and naval units exist solely to bomb factories and provide 'air superiority' or 'naval superiority' to give your units a slight buff in combat effectiveness or enable you to stage naval invasions. You also do not have any control over these units. You build the units, assign them to a sea or air zone and that's that. Nothing else. It's almost completely irrelevant and a game mechanic that is so dumbed and watered down that it is essentially a waste putting it in the game like this. Maybe paradox will release a dlc in the future that fixes this, but aerial and naval combat, compared to HoI3, is something out of a kids game.
And I haven't gotten to the land combat yet.
One could argue that the recruitment and production mechanics in HoI4 are quite good, and a definitive improvement over HoI3 and I would agree with you. Sadly, these are the only two parts of the game which are actually good. In HoI3 you carefully needed to manage and set up your army structure to prevent it from it turning into a chaotic unworkable mess as soon as the war started. It was also important to be able to utilize the AI. The OOB system allowed you to name your units, create your corps and armies as you saw fit and keep situational awareness that way. HoI4 did away with it completely. The days of carefully crafting your armies are over, now all you need to do is make an army group, throw all your units in it, draw a line and an arrow, and off your units go. There is no strategy or careful thinking involved. Sure, you could split up your units into different smaller armies, but it soon turns into a unworkable mess of arrows. Try finding a specific group of armored units you want to go to a certain point on the frontline. In HoI3, these would be under a corps somewhere, easily findable. In HoI4? Not so much.
It's pretty obvious that with HoI4 paradox tries to make the AI play the game for you. You're just there to manage the AI, and provide it with units and technology. It's a shame that the HoI4 AI is many, many, many times worse than the AI in HoI3.
So what about diplomacy, trade and intelligence?
Intelligence wasn't really that big of a factor in HoI3, maybe a slight nuisance when someone would reduce your national unity or steal a big tech but not really something to worry about. In HoI4 however, it's turned into a frustrating mess of who can coup the other the fastest. The mechanic is so bad that most multiplayer games outright ban you from 'boosting popularity' in other countries. It's a plain ridiculous and honestly stupid mechanic.
Resources are important. Especially for the Axis. Most of the game revolves around going after resource hotspots to help you to inevitable victory. Careful stockpiling was necessary in HoI3 leading up to the war, as to make sure you wouldn't run out of them mid game. HoI4 completely eliminates this aspect from the game. Instead of having a fleshed out and quite well functioning trade mechanic, paradox did away with it completely and decided to replace it with a simplified abomination where you trade factories for resources. No more stockpiles, no more worrying about resources. All you need to do is either occupy the areas or have the factories to trade, as long as you aren't at war with the person owning that resource.
To conclude, if you're looking for an in-depth, fleshed out 'War Simulator', a title which HoI3 still wears, then I cannot under any circumstance recommend you this game. In almost every way, at least if you have an IQ consisting of at least 3 numbers, HoI3 is a better game. HoI4 is a dumbed down piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Do not buy.

I really like this game, but here's the reason I don't recommend this game.
It's poorly optimized, so the game lags quite bad about around 1943. I'm over the recommended requirements so it's not my pc. In fact HOI4 is only using 40% of my cpu and there's 50% of my cpu free (10% is used by other things). It's not my gpu either. So you may never finish WW2 because the game will slow to a crawl. Especially if Germany beats the Soviets and Japan beats China.
And this brings me to my second problem. There's no way out of a war except total victory. If you are playing as Turkey and the Soviet Union attacks you, well guess what? You have to conquer the entire country of the Soviet Union just to end the war. If you manage to beat them, are you going to just have a white peace with them, no you'll just take whatever you can/want because of all the trouble you went through just to defend yourself. Which is stupid, if the Soviets were losing to a minor country like Turkey they would sign a peace deal just like they did with Finland, not let the war drag on for over a decade with 20 million of their soldiers dead, over claims on the Turkish straits.
If you have a super computer and only plan to play total conquest then this game is for you. Hopefully this game improves. Europa Universalis IV, Crusader Kings II, and even Stellaris got performance improvements, so perhaps Hearts of Iron IV will be next. And maybe we will get better diplomatic options for peace and trade deals in future updates.

Forever I've been scorned  by Diablo 3 and their reluctance to give me gamepad support to the PC... not anymore since I started playing this about 23 hours ago and I'm yet to slow down.
To keep this to-the-point I'll simply highlight the reasons why you should buy it:
1. The gameplay is SMOOTH.
2. No microtransactions to stall progress.
3. The rogue-like elements are light and by no means feel like a burden.
4. The card mechanics add a REALLY REALLY neat mix to the gameplay.
5. The areas are short and you never feel like you're doing ANY kind of busy work, it's action action action non-stop.
6. This game has quite a bit of RNG in it but on every aspect it seems like you have some level of control and choice making the whole randomness feel much more manageable and giving us a very neat layer of strategy.
7. The difficulty seems fair and often times creates very clutch moments.
Now for what I don't like:
1. It's a indie title and looks like one, the graphics won't impress anyone.
2. I'd love some pre-built decks and/or an easy in-game access to suggestions, it's a bit annoying to build them as is and the deck building interface doesn't help AT ALL.
3. I’d like more of the commentator in-game, as it stands during matches he barely opens his mouth… I’d pay quite a bit of cash to see YouTubers lending their voice-overs and such. As it stands, it feels very dry on this regard.
Bottom line, pay full price if you must, this game is a must have for anyone that has even a passing interest in any of the parts that make it (namely ARPGs, card games and rogue-like), it takes the best of each and while not over simplifying any creates something trully unique and incredibly fun to play.
