Things you CAN'T do:
- no moving, hiding, or searching bodies (and they disappear)
- no bases to capture and defend (enemy presence gets lower but they are always randomly around)
- no sharing a motorcyle with a teammate
- no switching from pilot to passenger in a helecopter that's hovering
- no secret passages, no hidden items, no reason to explore
- no yaw (rudder) control in airplanes
- no trip mines or claymores or other anti-personell traps (just anti-vehicle mines)
- no starting fires for area denial or fun
- no interaction with the trains that go around the map (besides getting run over by them)
- no sitting or laying on a teammate's vehicle while they drive (other than the contextual seats)
- no climbing or parkour or team boost areas (the ghosts can vault some walls up to ~7 feet but that's it)
- no shooting through chain fences or camo nets, but the enemy can (this happens occasionaly)
- no environment or building destructability (besides a few props)
- no bandages, medpacks, or adreniline or anything health related
- no 'knocked down' or 'last stand' states, ony 'alive' or 'incapp'ed'
Other disappointments:
- all gear is cosmetic only
- enemy AI: somehow worse than Farcry's
- the drone magically returns to you anytime you stop controlling it and it can't be left hovering or landed anywhere
- the random npc rebels and civilians have very little character
- night/thermal vision: no animations or models on the player when activated
- they added a few more HUD options but they are still severely lacking (can't disable 3d enemy markers w/o disabling them from minimap, also other players and rebels)
- variety of missions: there are only a few diffirent mission types, mostly it's the locations that change
- not very good peformance for the quality of the graphics
- friendly AI: worthless in all situations (except 'sync shot' which let's them shoot through buildings/terrain)
- some of 'side' mission scenarios feel like they were made in fifteen minutes with no consideration for gameplay at all (put the objective here, put some enemy spawns here, done!)
- in all of the area to explore there's very little 'environmental storytelling' or details that you find in carefully created games
Open-World Goodnes

Bought this item on sale and even though im not a survival games fan this one really kept me playing. The game might not have as much to do as you would hope for in this type of genre but it is still undergoing development. Still has a lot of technical issues but I guess thats fair given that it is in alpha phase. Multiplayer is fun if it does not disconnect (sometimes it disconnects frequently which can ruin the experience). Crafting system is interesting with a lot of variety. The world needs a bit more features in terms of plant life, landscapes, caves with rare resources etc, feels a little empty which does not entice you to explore everything. There is rainfall almost everytime I play and I know its a dessert-like setting but there are no water masses like an oasis here and there with streams or rivers. Overall its an awesome terrain but I feel that it just needs a little more extra on what it has to offer to urge you to explore every bit of it. Would love it if they add more planets, each with it's own unique environments, life forms, plant life, vegetation and landscapes. I also feel that the game needs a bit more to do rather than gathering resources all the time, there could be mini quests or events which players can partake in that offer rewards such as valuable items or allow you to loot places such as ship wrecks which can hold rare weapons left by earlier advanced alien life forms. Lastly the hostile alien animals on the planet are interesting and their attack power and damage is based on their level, however it would be nice if there is a larger variety. I feel all these improvements together would encourage players to work together on PvE and PVP modes rather than each person trying to survive on their own. It would add to the growth of the community and also contribute to the longivity of the game's lifetime. Overall the game is fun and shows a lot of future potential. I hope they keep developing it and adding more content.

I played this game casually on console when it first came out, but with all the DLC and dead playerbase I quickly abandoned it. Once i saw it was f2p on PC I figured I'd give it another shot. And my review is mixed but leaning negative. The game looks pretty, has well designed monsters and character who have neat banter. There is plenty to like about the game. Sadly, all of that is ruined by the terrible balance issues. A wraith will sit at spawn and kill all the hunters at stage 1, some of the hunters are objectively trash tier and same for the monsters. This game remains a game with a really neat premise, but one which ultimately fails to bring that to bloom. I'll probably still play it more anyway.

I am thoroughly enjoying the changes made in Stage 2. Many of the die hard players that played when it was not f2p seem to dislike the loss of the extended hide and seek game play due to the dome and tracking changes but as someone that also owned this game then, that was the worst part of the game for me. Sometimes you'd do everything right but the monster would get lucky, sneak off and you'd never find them again until they are already evolving to the next stage.
The changes to Stage 2 make the game feel much more like a struggle between hunters and a giant, killer monster to me. People seem to be claiming the monsters struggle at level 1 but that's the point, you're supposed to start out weak, you should feel pressured to evolve. Normally I lose half of my health before I manage to get to stage 2. But once I'm there you can feel the tide start to turn.
And I still see room for stealth in this game. I've player roughly 10 games as the monster in the new version and I have no problems hiding for quite some time. Yes, they do eventually find me due to the planet tracker, which honestly probably could use a slightly longer cooldown. But it is very possible to put some distance between you and the hunters and use stealth to delay encounters.
You do, unfortunately, seem to lose those moments you used to have in the old game where you'd hide in a corner somewhere and catch a random guy by himself and just destroy him though. But those moments weren't that common anyway.
It's my opinion that the game is much improved from it's old version and the people complaining that they liked it the old way are just purists who liked an unpopular game that was unpopular for the very reasons they liked it. Definitely worth giving a shot considering it's f2p.

There is no other game that I've played for 600+ hours within the first year after release. And yes, there are still things that need to be improved. Well.. really only one thing. AI! The game is challenging on 'veteran' or against actual people, but the AI controlled nations will still make stupid attack moves or just leave some of their borders open for invasion. So I agree with everyone saying that the AI needs to be fixed. Is it bad enough to give this game a bad review? No way! I love this game, and here is why.
Just a quick summary on HOI IV.
You start by picking a nation. It can be any nation in the world, and thanks to the amazing mod support, that is common with paradox games, you're not restricted to world war II. It can be world war I, cold war era, modern times or even alternative history. Every nation has a wide variety of political advisors, resources and national focuses. Once you start the game you'll expand and improve your nation. You do this via military expansion/intervention, diplomatic relations, constructing buildings (factories, infrastructure, dockyards, airfields and more) and research that involves land, naval, air, industrial and various other improvements.
Now why is it so good?
To me it is the fact that no campaign is ever the same. There are so many variables that influence the course of the game. You'll go from the German Reich completely destroying Europe, to Hitler being assassinated and the Soviet Union taking over the World. While this is happening you the player try to see the end of the conflict in the best way possible. When fighting the war you can use over 40 units and support companies to make all sorts of combinations in division templates. The war is fought in land, air and sea regions. When you plan and combine everything just right, the game is so satisfying. Perfectly executing a D-day invasion, simultaneously conquering dozens of islands in the pacific or cutting the enemy lines with paratroopers and air support.. they are some of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.
Are you interested in the great wars of the 20th century and do you like grand strategy games? Buy this game!
As always, a Paradox gem. Buy, play, enjoy, makes you smarter! :)

A pretty OK jigsaw game with the gimmick being that the puzzle is a looping animation.
The movement of pieces is not as tight as the Pixel Puzzle Ultimate game and there are no help functions whatsoever except for separating edge and regular pieces, but the largest puzzle sizes, 350 pieces are still pretty easy to solve.
The only gripe I really have, is that the subject animations are really awkward looking. You would think it would be possible to either make clips or pick some publick domain scenes where the actor/woman in the scene could look a bit more natural, and it really started to annoy me way more than it should for a casual puzzle game.

Ten puzzles in three sizes (60, 240, 350 pieces) and you must solve each puzzle in every size to complete the game. Some puzzle/size combinations are unavailable at the start, unlocked as you solve the others. A nice twist is that the unlocking unlocks both easier and harder puzzles; it's nice to race through a 60 after spending an hour or two on a 350! The game will separate edge pieces for you, so you can get those out of the way quickly. Rotation is not necessary, all the pieces are right side up.

I'm a sucker for puzzle games, especially these new "animated" puzzles. It's honestly a great idea and I'm looking forward to seeing more like this.
This specific iteration, the "Japanese women", seems easier than it's counterpart, "Beautiful Japanese Scenery". Each game in this new-ish series is extremely relaxing. I often watch a YouTube video or listen to a podcast/music on my second screen while I piece together these puzzles. I'd be lying to you if I said that when I first read the title "Japanese women" I was expecting them to be clothed, but I bought the game nevertheless (on sale) and I'm happy about it. There are 10 puzzles in all, with each puzzle split into three identical puzzles based on the number of pieces in each--60, 240, 350. If you take your time with it, you can easily get anywhere from 12-18 hours out of this game.
In summation, I'd recommend this game to anyone who, like me, is a puzzle junkie. I'm looking forward to seeing what the devs do in the future.

This game feels like it should have good potential to become a great game if some areas are buffed and tuned.
while this game is just 2 months from its initial release on steam, it is still in early access, and as such has the usual bugs and glitches that go with EA titles.
base building.
like other survival type games, you need to collect resources to build. the recipes are not too complicated, but the gathering of resources is just too much of a grind to enjoy.
lack of customization also adds to the tedium of resource gathering. while you can add a splash of paint to your walls, and place connector halls from one building (habitat) to the next. there just isnt any unique features to the build system that make you feel like you constructed something from your own imagination.
you are given cookie cutter buildings, and finite possiblities of how they function together.
i feel like resources should be more abundant or recipes less demanding to relieve the grindyness of cookie cutter base building.
aliens.
while there are a few different types of aliens that spawn, they are not diverse at all, you are basically presented with 5 types that will attack you, each with a slightly meaner variant of different grades. and there are 2 types of neutral species that wont attack you unless provoked.
one major annoyance is that the npc aliens will just spawn into an area even after you've cleansed it. so you're constantly having to fend of baddies, with no real reason for them to just appear. (albeit you may have 10 minutes of freedom).
alien ai is absurd. if they spawn close they will just rush and attack you. if you shoot at one from a mid range to long distance, they will just turn and head straight for you. oh and when you get the common aliens down to one or two shots from a kill they will then turn around and run away, potentially robbing you of wasted time trying to glean XP from the kill.
once you have killed an alien baddie you have to be fast enough to harvest the body, and the loot isnt much of a reward: you are given typically 1 unit of alien meat. which is another strike against the current alien enemy system. there really isnt much point in killing them other than to protect yourself and your repair droid.
current enemy ai behavior is 2/10 (abysmally stupid), and needs a huge overhaul to how aliens spawn into the map, just appearing in cleared areas is a disgrace.
the dune inspired sand worms are epic, but once you see them, you, your gear and your carried inventory are sometimes converted into worm poop.
missing and odd animations.
while the option of switching between 3rd and 1st person has become somewhat of a staple in survival games, there are missing animations in 3rd person, that leave you to wonder what your avatar is doing (repairing, customizing.)
oddly the 3rd person mode is set with your character in the lower left of the screen with no current way to adjust the 3rd person positioning. while this is fairly unique, it makes for a rather unnatural cursur/crosshair movement and placement.
your character looks fairly goofy with your chisel in 3rd person, and looks more like someone trying to fence with an epee sword.
personal assistant repair droid.
while i find the personal repair droid companion a fantastic idea, it has its short commings in current form.
the particular areas that need attention is navigation and remote commands. currently the personal assitant bot will get stuck trying to climb steep inclines such as the lip of a crater or very steep hills. and as such will cease to move until you provide it with a new path or instruction.  (again navigation of npcs in this game needs work)
and secondly there is no way to remotely call or command the bot to your current location, you have to run to it and tell it to follow you, or catch it running by on a mining run.
i am enjoying this game at the moment, but base building is way too grindy in regards to resource gathering. the current formula kills the fun. the constantly spawning aliens is also disappointing. the game as you would expect just lacks polish that accompanies a fully released title. plebs will say "hey its early access, how dare you criticize the only game ive ever been good at." and i say, i know its early access, take my criticism and make it better, pleb.

A little rough around the edges (owing to a long and turbulent development cycle) but overall a decent tactical shooter.
The core gameplay of moving between cover, issuing squad commands, and deploying special powers on the battlefield is fun. Loadout customization and team management systems offer some options for adapting your playstyle, but aren't so heavy as to bog down the player with brain-bending optimization choices. The Bureau occasionally stumbles over forced RPG and puzzle elements, but these are rare and typically couched by solid action sequences.
Where The Bureau really shines is its ability to convey setting and theme through the art and level design. The retro-future art style is unique and often refreshing. Without giving away any spoilers, I'll say I was legitmately surprised and impressed by some of the eye candy in the later missions.
Through clever set pieces, prop placement, and various notes and signs littering the environment, most of The Bureau's levels tell a story of their own. In fact, I'd be willing to bet some missions would be improved by simply removing the ever-present radio chatter and letting the player piece together the story for themselves.
Bottom Line: Ignore anyone comparing this game to the other XCOM titles - it's closer to Mass Effect Lite, set within the XCOM franchise. If you want a more traditional XCOM experience, Enemy Unknown is fantastic. If you want a straightforward cover shooter with light strategy elements and a lot of character, give The Bureau a shot. (Just, maybe wait for a sale.)

The atmosphere is very much intact, but it misses a lot of what Enemy Unknown did well, such as character customization. They let you get attached to your characters, giving them medals and accolades, watching them go through the ranks, while in this game it's very hard to feel anything for your fellow characters, to the point where it doesn't feel like a big deal when they die.
A lot of the game is unexplained. The abilities that Agent Carter has, like the pull and lift abilities, just seem to have been ripped from BioWare's KOTOR and Mass Effect without any explanation as to why he has them. Except for the one thing that grants you these abilities, every tech has to be figured out (with no in-game research, dammit), and this thing is just kind of written off. Plot holes of this magnitude can be found in a few places, and it's very frustrating to witness.

I played this game casually on console when it first came out, but with all the DLC and dead playerbase I quickly abandoned it. Once i saw it was f2p on PC I figured I'd give it another shot. And my review is mixed but leaning negative. The game looks pretty, has well designed monsters and character who have neat banter. There is plenty to like about the game. Sadly, all of that is ruined by the terrible balance issues. A wraith will sit at spawn and kill all the hunters at stage 1, some of the hunters are objectively trash tier and same for the monsters. This game remains a game with a really neat premise, but one which ultimately fails to bring that to bloom. I'll probably still play it more anyway.

I am thoroughly enjoying the changes made in Stage 2. Many of the die hard players that played when it was not f2p seem to dislike the loss of the extended hide and seek game play due to the dome and tracking changes but as someone that also owned this game then, that was the worst part of the game for me. Sometimes you'd do everything right but the monster would get lucky, sneak off and you'd never find them again until they are already evolving to the next stage.
The changes to Stage 2 make the game feel much more like a struggle between hunters and a giant, killer monster to me. People seem to be claiming the monsters struggle at level 1 but that's the point, you're supposed to start out weak, you should feel pressured to evolve. Normally I lose half of my health before I manage to get to stage 2. But once I'm there you can feel the tide start to turn.
And I still see room for stealth in this game. I've player roughly 10 games as the monster in the new version and I have no problems hiding for quite some time. Yes, they do eventually find me due to the planet tracker, which honestly probably could use a slightly longer cooldown. But it is very possible to put some distance between you and the hunters and use stealth to delay encounters.
You do, unfortunately, seem to lose those moments you used to have in the old game where you'd hide in a corner somewhere and catch a random guy by himself and just destroy him though. But those moments weren't that common anyway.
It's my opinion that the game is much improved from it's old version and the people complaining that they liked it the old way are just purists who liked an unpopular game that was unpopular for the very reasons they liked it. Definitely worth giving a shot considering it's f2p.

Dishonored, an oldie but a goodie.
First off, let's start with the pros -which there are a lot of-
The Stealth:
This game has stealth, and it does it GOOD. The suspense of listening and watching for guards walking past doors, tallboys roaming, making those dreadful noises. It's incredible. Sneaking up on a man standing on a balcony, teleporting up buildings. It's well done, no, fantastically done.
The Design:
Each level is designed with care, and passion, and TONS of effort. Arkane did a terrific job making sure each target was well placed, the levels weren't too long, too short. Everything is balanced, and it's great. There are so many side objectives, like runes, bone charms, side missions, and the like. It'll keep you coming back, doing so many different runs, just to grab every small little thing in the game. Through the game, you'll encounter excellently written characters, whether it be side characters, main protagonists, or even antagonists.
The Story:
You are Corvo, Lord Protector of The Empress. After returning to the Empress with bad news, she is assassinated, and her heir to the throne, Emily, is kidnapped. You are framed, and as the title implies, are "Dishonored." After escaping prison and coming to the Loyalist Conspiracy, you are confronted by the Outsider in a dream, and are given magical powers to take revenge on those who helped wrong you. Incredible setup, and even better execution. Never once through this game did I ever stop to think about why or how this is happening, because the writers have intricately and delicately crafted an amazing story about a man seeking retribution for the loss of the Empress, and the heir to her throne, Emily.
Now onto the cons.
Game can bug:
I haven't had this happen to me personally, but the game can bug. Like say, the screen going black, or a guard spazzing out when thrown down.
Can be a bit boring:
With all the unskippable cutscenes, I felt like I was watching a movie more than playing a game.
But, that's mainly all I've got, hopefully this helps some people who are buying this game to prepare for Dishonored 2.

Played the free weekend 10/13-10/15 2017.
I was able to clear the first zone purely in singleplayer mode. While the gunplay and gameplay was pretty good, I can't justify spending 29.99 for this as a full title. There just isn't enough here.
My strategy was largely as a sniper and true ghost. I prepped the area of interest by observing guard numbers and movements. If necessary, I thinned them out with long range suppressed shots. Which...in this game...is cartoonish. No supersonic round is going to be totally silent. At the very least, the other guards would hear the supersonic crack of the round as it went over their head and into their buddies' noggin. They just stand there as though nothing happened. But I digress. After a recon, I would park my team outside and go in solo, get the intel, object, or lieutenant solo, and get out. This worked fine for a while. It was like playing a more pretty version of Far Cry, which I am experienced.
Though after the first section, the difficulty ramps considerably. You have to park your NPC allies further and further away. Before long THEY get spotted which instantly puts the whole compound on alert. As far as I can tell, there's no way to disable alarms either. And there's nothing more infuriating to stealth masterfully through a section of bad guys for 20 minutes only to see "Murray spotted" on your screen and have to settle in to the certain death you will face, through no fault of your own. I just wish I could send my allies back to base, with a box of slim jims and just...MGS my way through the campaign.
Though you can't do that. That's a problem. Also this game has UBISOFT-itis. Inflammation of the map area. Communication towers, and boxes you have to dig through. For some reason, you went into a fortified area filled with some of the most dangerous enemies in the region, and only brought a 4x acog with you...
Everything else has to be scouted and ground out, in regions where you may not be high enough level for yet. You just have to OSP them. It's like come on. You had a helicopter. Load the gear. I get it. It's an unlock system for players to slowly be exposed to the game and progress with increasing difficulty but decreasing overall challenge. Well, Rainbow Six Vegas gave you a full arsenal of weapons and scopes from the start. It ramped up by giving you more complex terrain to navigate. Giving you more fortified enemies, and giving you less options to traverse. That was good. We want those days back again.
The regions get to be very VERY repetitive.
The story, what I've seen, is not good. Bad guy is bad. Good guys are good. Here's a bunch of collectables that add to the shock value. Thanks Ubisoft.
Bottom line--wait for a sale. A deep sale.

This title had a lot of potential. It delivered very little.
"As agent Carter, call the shots, pull the trigger and lead your squad in a gripping third-person tactical shooter set within a covert war to protect humanity from an otherworldly enemy. "
In terms of setting it could have been one of the more interesting ones of recent memory, but it fails to leverage this and instead challenges your ability to suspend your disbelief for its ridiculous plot and happenings.
Gameplay-wise, there is very little to it beyond a third-person shooter with some abilities to fire off from time to time. There is nothing tactical about it, your squadmates have more difficulty killing foes with a rifle than you do with a pistol outside of their active abilities. Enemy waves spawning in close to you on the battlefield means making tactical manuevers like flanking extremely risky with very little potential payoff.
The squad mechanic becomes more of a burden and you are constantly required to babysit your squadmates by telling them to move out of enemy LoS and heal them up when they get seriously hurt. You will have more success putting all your squadmates far and out of danger, and combining their abilities to set up easy kills - you know that the commander in full cover will reveal himself just because your Commando is taunting him from a mile away, only to be sniped off by your Recon EVERY SINGLE TIME. All this while they have trouble taking out a single Sectoid or Drone. You do want your agents alive if only just to keep ability unlocks for more means to clear out threats more quickly and efficiently.
Activating abilities off cooldown between third-person shooting? You're better off with Mass Effect. This game does have long elevator rides (and decontamination chambers), if you are into that sort of thing.

I would recommend it, the plot is entertaining at times, but not for the price of 49.99 USD. This game is easily worth 15, maybe 20 USD, but you've got to love luke warm cover-shooter-hot-bar-magic strategy and a superficial morality system (Think watered down Mass Effect).

I wanted to give this game a proper chance, I really did. Even as a serious X-COM nut I know the plotlines have always been 'meh' and after FiraXCOM was announced I was more accepting of this as a spinoff (like Command and Conquer: Renegade, which I liked). It was still a daft move to make the first XCOM game announced for years the one that closest resembles X-COM: Enforcer, the lowest point of the series.
This game however is a perfect example of what happens when you force a franchise into somthing unrelated. I like the 1960's and I like the Men in Black angle but by cramming in lacklustre combat and a horribly broken squad command interface into a game that was not designed from the start to be something different has hampered the game horribly.
I said 'lacklustre combat' but I suspect that is being generous. 'Broken' is more like it. To squeeze as much as possible from the squad command gimmick the only way to do serious damage is by flanking the enemy. That in itself wouldn't be too bad if a) you weren't being constantly forced down linear pathways with little chance to spread your tactical wings and b) most importantly, the squad AI wasn't atrocious. I even tried getting them to stay in place while I flanked as they kept with the lemming act when I gave them the move command. What did they do? The followed me. There is no 'halt' command, before you ask. Add to all that bugger all ammo capacity and you'll spend the game running for a thousand guns just to take care of a handful of mooks.
The graphics are mediocre at best, the base command is even less than what you got from Mass Effect 2 (at least you could choose your research there) but the worst crime in my eyes is the plot. The 1960's was a troublesome time with not just the Cold War but rights movements for women and people of colour. Does any of this get to the game? There's one Soviet agent which is nothing more than 'you can recruit this dude to be a generic squad mate,' only a handful (2 on my admittedly amateurish count) of comments about one of the star agents being a woman and not a single sausage about the amount of black agents and scientists (Again, this is the sixties, that would have been huge and quite interesting). I keep thinking they missed an opportunity by not doing something like Expeditions: Conquistador; imagine if your squaddies had personalities. Likes and hates and all that jazz. Some are progressive and some are more traditional. Do you stick by your guns and rely on women and coloured folk despite the anger you'll recieve or will you bow down to social pressure and prejudice?
Between the lack of care for anything happening in the 60's and all the sci fi weaponry there is no reason this couldn't have been set in modern day, the eighties, or even in World War 2. It takes effort to make one of the most interesting decades in the last century that generic.
Add to that the most generic hero character ever (seriously, the guy is every bland hero trope imaginable; WW2 veteran, dead family, alcoholic, tortured past, gravelly voice, etc) and a plot that makes Independence Day seem high brow and it's a total loss on story as well as gameplay.
The tragic thing is when I look back at the original vids (the ones which sparked the public outcry) it looked really good; the old 'man in black' conspiracies mixed in with the Stepford Wives. That could have lead to some interesting investigative angles and could have created a properly eerie alien plot. If it was allowed to be it's own thing instead of having a brand name forced on it (a brand name not unfamiliar with being abused, admittedly) and not reworked time and time again for stupid reasons we would have had a much better game. For those who whine about the Devil May Cry reboot (which I say was solid), that was at least in the spirit of the originals. The Bureau reeks of the sort of soulless boardroom mandates that I would have expected from EA.
Would I recommend it? It's better than the Syndicate Reboot, but then very little isn't. The word 'generic' appears in the above text a lot. That should tell you everything you need to know.
Quick edit: Yes I know this is a 2K Games published title and not EA, that was a stab at the people who could turn Syndicate into a FPS far worse than Goldeneye: Rogue Agent (which had the excuse of being unfinished and rushed and was still reasonably fun) and the sort of people who looked at the Divine Comedy, social, theological and political commentary that it was and say to themselves, "Yes, this is perfect God of War clone material!" That's right; I am comparing the Bureau to EA's Dante's Inferno.

This game is rock-solid. A rogue-like arena brawler with short intervals between each arena. It's difficulty may vary but it isnt too hard to pick up and play. It is soo much fun to play and its definiately worth the price it is asking for. But if you feel like the price is too much then grab it on a sale definiately as it drops to 40-50% off.
So as far as gameplay goes:
Pros:
+ The deck building makes the gameplay unique and varied from every arena session
+ The varied gameplay with each arena having passive effects make each one different
+ The AI mobs are not brain dead and don't just soak up damage all the time and actually fight
+ Can vary from normal roguelike to bullet hell depending on the mobs
+ The amount of classes make the gameplay Unique
+ Pets are not as useless and can be very helpful in both damage or tanking
+ The boss variety in skills make it an enjoyable experience
+ Short burst of arena sessions makes this a game to play off and on or for long hours.
+ The boon system which rewards a buff after each completed arena makes some future sessions start off better (reduce some of the rogue-like start off flaws)
+ Daily missions with some fun conditions is always a plus (ex: Every kill revives them as an ally)
Cons
- It seems like most of the classes feel a bit weak (in  terms of skillwise) with the exception of the first class you play at the start
- Like most rogue-like games the start of every session of arena feels a bit dull with no upgrades to start
- You AI companion/Companions you need to save may sometimes have bad AI (stand on fire traps or run towards mobs)
- Difficulty in terms of damage is outrageous on traps and mobs sometimes (some mob charges me to 2-3 fire trap and I die cause I'm stunlocked in the fire trap. Health from 120 to 0 in 2 seconds or I kill a mob and it explodes with a huge radius and kills off another mob which chain explodes into another mob that does the same and i go from 200 to 30 just for that)
- Your companion has limited to no skills and just has an auto attack ( wish they gave them skills or even a skill tree to make them more customizable)
- One of the stage passive with damages you by 10 for each unused Mana point spend needs to be nerfed (End game can be a pain if you dont have any more cards and end up taking a large portion of the damage for something your not really too in control of in terms of what you draw for the mana cost)
- Melee classes needs a bit of a tweak for buffs as melee in early and later levels feels a bit weak with having to take alot of damgage just to go close up to even attack compared to the range classes. (maybe buff its defense or hp pool or chance to block [as in most games melee has parry but there is no parry so block would be better] )
- The respawning of dead mobs as a special summon makes it a bit difficult on some levels to force you to rush on killing all the real mobs on the level as quick as you can before this happens.
- Some of the enemy's Card consumsables are a bit hard (Meteors fall on you, excess of bomb traps all over the place, a plane that comes out of no where and literally does a ton of damage)
- Uncontrollable Lag during Snake boss (Occurs when the boss is spawning mass minions) and there is no way to reduce the lag at all as I have set everything to low or off to try and test it but with no change.
Overall this game is really fun despite the long list of cons you may have seen. It just makes the gameplay that much difficult but makes you want to play and try to overcome them to feel like it was worth it (Beat a boss with literally 1 hp throughout the entire match due to arena passive of dealing  10 dmg per non spend mana and 80 damage cause i had no cards leading me to start with 1hp). I play a lot of rogue-like games and this one feels like a mix of gauntlet legends (the asthetics + and quick pick up and play) mixed with binding of isaac (Movement to have to dodge + difficulty)  mixed with Hand of fate (Deck System) all in one. I bought the game on a sale for $24 for the complete bundle and I have not regretted it. I know I will spend a ton more hours on this game and its replayability is no questioned there with each playthrough being different. Feel free to buy this on a sale or not because despite not having alot of advetisement to get this game known, it is certainly a hidden gem for any one into rogue-like games. A must buy and not one you should look over.

First off, it is IMPOSSIBLE to tell you how much bloody FUN this game is!  So stop reading and BUY it!  But this is a review... so....
Well, how to describe the game?  It's part card collection game, part Role Playing\Leveling up game, part Rouge\Diablo style combat game, and ALL awesome gamepad bashing extacy!
You begin by selecting your character - or Avatar - 1 of 5 (the fifth is a DLC), and then you make a deck of cards with the individual you have selected.  Certain cards or only for certain Avatars, while others are for all classes of people.  For example, you can start off as a "Squire of Light" - and bring flames to your enemies!  But you don't fight alone - you have a companion who ALSO levels up with you, and you can change what kind of companion fighter you want, along with what cards you have in between rounds.  You fight numerous dungeons untill you reach a boss - and once you've beaten the boss you go BACK to the pause in the game where you can level up, select buffs, spells, attacks, and such.  The game is very addictive, VERY replayable, and well worth a 50$ price tag - and considering right now it's selling (not on sale) for 19.99$, it's a no brainer.
If you have played it's prequel, you will feel at ease with the combat style - its easy to pick up, but it has nuances that are a joy to master.  The previous one - while feeling like it, is a COMPLETELY different experience.  But in my opinion, the sequel is even better then the first.
And by the way... they have just announced the title to the NEXT entry in the "Forced" saga - "Forced to Duel - Minion Masters'".  So if I were you, I'd ship myself (me) a whole lotta cash.  Or catch up in the series to get ready for the next addition in this highly addictive, creative, fun, and unique experience.  An easy 10 out of 10!  Way to go Beta Dwarf!  AGAIN!

Forced Showdown is a singleplayer arena action roguelike card game. A goddamn mouthful if I say so.
You fight through multiple arenas to get to the boss while buffing yourself to be stronger.
In this game you can make insane amount of decks, but they can fall pretty much to the same type of decks. Going just upgrade decks with some healing consumables, full-on consumable decks, class card decks and spell decks.
There are 4 different heroes (1 dlc hero extra) with like 2-3 abilities and most of them have a passive. All heroes also have their own class specific cards. Spin move with fireballs. Volcanic Strike that splits in to 2 or 3 and even a card that makes the range infinite. 2 of those cards and it'll loops once again. Those examples were for Volco, but he's probably my least favorite hero.
I probaby don't like him as much because he gets locked in place when you use his Volcanic strike or auto-attack. I've got hit too many times, ♥♥♥♥ him. Some characters like Stormbringer and Squire of Light then have really op class cards. You can basically just pick them and automatically win.
Ravager is my favorite hero but his class cards are butt. Like really weak, but he's hella strong with pure damage cards. His only weakness is the new dlc boss because Ravagers strong point is staying on the boss and using invulnerability frames to stay alive. The dlc robot ninja boss keeps teleporting away making it hard to chip away his health.
My interest in the game came back strong with the new dlc and it added the needed enemy variety. More cards and a Maze making the game very interesting again.
I finally got the 100% achievements in the game but one of them were bugged until a recent game update. So they are still fixing the game. Which is a good thing, I at least didn't see that many bugs until I was almost done with the game.
I do recommend the main game and the dlc even with full price. A goddamn good roguelike card game whatever.

I played this game casually on console when it first came out, but with all the DLC and dead playerbase I quickly abandoned it. Once i saw it was f2p on PC I figured I'd give it another shot. And my review is mixed but leaning negative. The game looks pretty, has well designed monsters and character who have neat banter. There is plenty to like about the game. Sadly, all of that is ruined by the terrible balance issues. A wraith will sit at spawn and kill all the hunters at stage 1, some of the hunters are objectively trash tier and same for the monsters. This game remains a game with a really neat premise, but one which ultimately fails to bring that to bloom. I'll probably still play it more anyway.

I am thoroughly enjoying the changes made in Stage 2. Many of the die hard players that played when it was not f2p seem to dislike the loss of the extended hide and seek game play due to the dome and tracking changes but as someone that also owned this game then, that was the worst part of the game for me. Sometimes you'd do everything right but the monster would get lucky, sneak off and you'd never find them again until they are already evolving to the next stage.
The changes to Stage 2 make the game feel much more like a struggle between hunters and a giant, killer monster to me. People seem to be claiming the monsters struggle at level 1 but that's the point, you're supposed to start out weak, you should feel pressured to evolve. Normally I lose half of my health before I manage to get to stage 2. But once I'm there you can feel the tide start to turn.
And I still see room for stealth in this game. I've player roughly 10 games as the monster in the new version and I have no problems hiding for quite some time. Yes, they do eventually find me due to the planet tracker, which honestly probably could use a slightly longer cooldown. But it is very possible to put some distance between you and the hunters and use stealth to delay encounters.
You do, unfortunately, seem to lose those moments you used to have in the old game where you'd hide in a corner somewhere and catch a random guy by himself and just destroy him though. But those moments weren't that common anyway.
It's my opinion that the game is much improved from it's old version and the people complaining that they liked it the old way are just purists who liked an unpopular game that was unpopular for the very reasons they liked it. Definitely worth giving a shot considering it's f2p.

The Bureau is an uninspired, and standardised third-person shooter in the vein of Gears of War, with little hints of the 'tactical' play of Mass Effect thrown in for flavour. Set in a parallel 1950s america, with many levels seeming to take place in the stereotypical midwest small towns popularised in so many UFO abduction stories, the player takes the role of a Secret Service agent tasked with delivering a mysterious artefact to the head of 'The Bureau', an unknown and oft-ridiculed section of the US government.
Attempting to provide history for the X-COM project as present in the firaxis game, The Bureau toys with themes of sexism in organisations, loyalty, and the importance of self...all with the ham-fisted bashing on a keyboard one would expect of most popular shooters. It takes itself and it's cheesy encironment with far too much seriousness and not enough self-awareness to really make the slightly B-movie plotline work.
I was actually impressed with the announce trailers for the original 'XCOM' first person shooter, and thought that while not an 'X-COM' game, it could have been an entertaining and uniue exploration of clandestine UFO investigation from the point of view of a squaddie or corporal. The numerous rewrites and alterations of the project's lifespan, and the apparent dusting under the rug after the success of Firaxis' 'XCOM; Enemy Unknown' have hurt this title.
If the pre-order bonuses were still available, I would suggest buying this game only for the X-Com complete pack as a pre-order bonus. Unfortunately, without that particular enticement, I can only suggest to avoid this game unless you feel an unhealthy urge to open plot holes and experience painfully obvious twists in storytelling.

There is no other game that I've played for 600+ hours within the first year after release. And yes, there are still things that need to be improved. Well.. really only one thing. AI! The game is challenging on 'veteran' or against actual people, but the AI controlled nations will still make stupid attack moves or just leave some of their borders open for invasion. So I agree with everyone saying that the AI needs to be fixed. Is it bad enough to give this game a bad review? No way! I love this game, and here is why.
Just a quick summary on HOI IV.
You start by picking a nation. It can be any nation in the world, and thanks to the amazing mod support, that is common with paradox games, you're not restricted to world war II. It can be world war I, cold war era, modern times or even alternative history. Every nation has a wide variety of political advisors, resources and national focuses. Once you start the game you'll expand and improve your nation. You do this via military expansion/intervention, diplomatic relations, constructing buildings (factories, infrastructure, dockyards, airfields and more) and research that involves land, naval, air, industrial and various other improvements.
Now why is it so good?
To me it is the fact that no campaign is ever the same. There are so many variables that influence the course of the game. You'll go from the German Reich completely destroying Europe, to Hitler being assassinated and the Soviet Union taking over the World. While this is happening you the player try to see the end of the conflict in the best way possible. When fighting the war you can use over 40 units and support companies to make all sorts of combinations in division templates. The war is fought in land, air and sea regions. When you plan and combine everything just right, the game is so satisfying. Perfectly executing a D-day invasion, simultaneously conquering dozens of islands in the pacific or cutting the enemy lines with paratroopers and air support.. they are some of the best gaming experiences I've ever had.
Are you interested in the great wars of the 20th century and do you like grand strategy games? Buy this game!
As always, a Paradox gem. Buy, play, enjoy, makes you smarter! :)

When I bought the first Forced game, I was hooked for many days. So naturally, when its sequel was announced I became very excited about it. However, my thirst was quenched quickly due to my expectations.
Don’t get me wrong, Forced Showdown certainly is an enjoyable game. It’s an arena brawler like its predecessor, and certainly provides a good – and fair – challenge. While it certainly can be hard at times, you won’t feel like the game cheated on you to raise the level. Everything can be dodged, and projectiles and explosion areas are indicated. And everything is fast-paced action. Bosses also provide for random effects throughout the area which you have to deal with, and from the second level they will also get cards to make things a lot harder.
The game has huge amounts of customizability with its trading cards, which you can use for building decks, which in turn you use to grow stronger throughout each level in an arena – though you lose it after beating the boss. It is random, so your plan won’t work out every time, and you won’t always get the cards you hope for – and with mana rising each level you might not be able to play a card for a few levels if you’re out of luck.
It’s replay value is high – due to multiple characters you can master, but also due to the enormous amounts of customizability you get by collecting cards and building your own decks. Also, when you grow more confident in your abilities, you can provide yourself with additional challenges – which you can choose yourself from a list you get provided by the game. There are also daily challenges, in which you can compete for the top score so that adds a lot of replay value too.
The graphics are ok. They serve their purpose of setting a more comical mood, but I don’t feel like they are really gorgeous or something. The sound, however, is really nice. Both the voice acting and the music set the tone really well for a fun experience.
Forced Showdown also has a few cons. The first that could be considered is the lack of checkpoints. You can spend a long time to hack your path through 9 arenas, but if you die you have to do everything over again, which can be a bit frustrating – especially when you die at the end. However, BetaDwarf has done a decent job in making it so that you don’t have to follow the exact path and fight the exact same enemies so it won’t feel as much of a grind. You also get gold after completing challenges for trading cards so your time wasn’t completely useless.
The game also relies heavily on grinding gold and cards. You get gold after arena’s, which you can trade into random prices (cards, shards, more gold…) for it. You can only own every card twice, so they get turned into shards too afterwards – for which you can buy cards you don’t own. Getting cards is very random, and you’ll find yourself playing a lot to get them. Maybe to get that one card that would make your deck complete, or maybe to get all of them. This is the part that can get quite annoying at times.
I’ve also encountered a lot of bugs, especially at the time the game was just released. I even dropped the game out of frustration because I was getting a lot of CTD’s during battles. However, most of them seemed to be patched and nowadays I haven’t encountered a CTD or a frozen game after I started playing again.
Now, for the things I long for when thinking of the first instalment of the franchise. Forced was a game that provided you with some basic puzzles throughout its arenas, which is one the reasons why I rate it above Showdown. Also, while you have customizable decks, you don’t get the customizable characters you had in Forced. With less and fixed abilities characters feel the same much more quickly, and decks aren't as reliable as abilities and passives due to their randomness. Card decks are quite fun, but I’m not sure it’s worth losing the ability and passive customization for. Maybe a combination of the two was possible, but maybe that would’ve made it a bit too complex.
And of course there is the multiplayer which Forced was famous for. This game would also be so much fun in a multiplayer setup. Lesser so because of the lack of puzzles but still a lot of fun. I certainly hope BetaDwarf will implement this in the future.
So in conclusion, this certainly is a game worth playing and I've enjoyed it quite a lot, but if you want to buy it because you've enjoyed Forced, you should be warned that Showdown is quite a different experience.

Do NOT play this game until they fix the GLYPH launcher issues. Otherwise you will be stuck as I am (and thousands of others apparently) with a high level character in a game you can't even log in to. I've never had a game actively prevent me from playing (or spending money for that matter), but that is what RIFT has become. Great game ruined by the worst launcher in the business.

What can I say? If you've never played an MMO before--especially of the whack-a-mole variety--then RIFT is as good of a place to start as any. It's F2P (with the usual silly restrictions, but not too bad) and there is always something going on, regardless of whether you're into massive raids in PvE, comparing sword sizes in PvP, or even actual role-playing. It is also one of the best-looking MMOs in my ever-so-humble opinion, which helps to draw one in regardless of what some might have to say on the matter. The crafting is a bit weak at the moment, but the devs say that there are some changes coming soon.
In a nutshell: RIFT is FUN to play. Check it out.
Edit: The population tends to swell and recede across all servers, especially in the low- and mid-level areas. The majority of players tend to have at least one charcter at the level-cap of 65, and if you do join a guild, most will push you to just grind away until you're able to join the endgame club. So, it can be more than a little tedious if you follow that path. My advice: ignore them, play how you want, doing whatever you want at your own pace. Or--create another character for having fun, and leave one as the grind-ready min-max boredom generator that so many seem to love.

Rift called by many a WoW clone is (regardless if it's true or not) a great game. Great F2P Model, good gameplay, goo story and overall very engaging.
Like all MMORPGs you start off with a specific combat type, however, unlike many other MMORPG this combat type is highly dynamic offering you countless types of classes.
You are set in a world interacting with multiple worlds, in the sense that the world where you do your regular actions is frequently invaded by planar creatures, creating a good atmosphere where regular global events to fend off attackers take place. These events are called rifts  (tears in the fabric of your universe).
I'm still in the beginning of this game so I will update this review as I progress through it, but so far I'd highly recommend this game for its fair model, and hell, it's free. Give it a shot!
If you are a fan of MMORPG you won't regret downloading it!

Setting aside the style change from tactical top down to first person shooter, this game is a mess.
The first issue to strike most is the that code is not optimized, and places a strain well beyond what should be required to run what is at heart a relatively simple game (from the perspective of a major studio production).
Secondly, the play style is a poor rip off of Mass Effect style, but instead of giving you teammates who can almost function, the developers here have given you two berserkering mentally deficient man-children as partners.
Third, the plot structure is awful. It's almost as if written by a a gang of 12 year olds who weren't allowed to communicate. This lack of plot structure becomes readily apparent when you first arrive at the Xcom base, where you are told that the location has to be ultra secret, or the aliens will just blitzkrieg it like they did the other bases. After that tidbit, you'll told that the Major (or whoever, I don't remember) has an urgent mission for you, while at the same time being told you should just wander around the base and acclimate yourself. When you finally decide to check this mission out, it turns out an alien has snuck into the base and is trying to plant a bomb. Seems like that would have been mildly urgent, but naw, not a big deal. Plus, this doesn't blow your base's hidden location for, um, some reason?
Fourth, the game will only appeal to arcade-style folks, anyone looking for a remotely indepth game play will be disappointed. Random alien weapons are left laying around for you to basically run over and pick up, destroying any hope of making an indepth game.
Between the terrible performance issues, god awful teammate AI, poor plot structure, and simplistic play style results in a game that should never have gotten 66/100 from the critic average. I think they got blinded by the pretty graphics, which only really work on a great machine.
Oh, and the studio closed, so don't expect patches. Don't buy it. Ever. Even on sale.

I don't see what is wrong with this game.
I played the strategy equivalent, XCOM: Enemy Unknown (which is also pretty awesome) and this is like the prequel to that. There isn't as much strategy, but the command mode makes up for it. It basically slows down time (but doesn't stop it) and allows you to make moves such as making your guys move, use special abilities depending on their class, and focus fire. Leave this mode and everything plays out in seconds, which I find really cool. Customize your squad, chose your weapons, and kick some alien butt. The lipsyncing is off, though. It is kinda annoying, but gameplay makes up for that. My only complaint is that the camera and character movement is a bit jerky.

Interroga ali, pega aqui, pega esse veículo e vamos pra tal lugar pegar um tal alguém, matar ou recuperar algo. E é só isso.

Cons:

Dishonored in quite possibly the most innovative and enjoyable single player game I've played since I was a kid. Why?
Corvo, the empresses bodyguard turned "Assassin" by a group of loyalists that wish to put Emily, the late empresses daughter, in charge of the kingdom. How you do that however is compleatly up to you.
You will get missions to go Eliminate targets and you can do this by Killing them or "Removing" them if you are the "I can't be bothered to use stealth!" type of person you can run in there willy nilly and stab your target or you can be more creative. Poison, choking them out and throwing them into a pack of hungry rats, or using your magic to send them to the moon Or on the flipside, you're the type of person that likes stealth and to be as non-leathel as possible you can find alternitive means to eliminating your targets.
The way you play greatly affects the outcome of the story
This game is increadibly innovative. Good line of sight on guards, fun and interesting ways to kill and neutrilize people, amazing story with charaters you get attached to, combat that makes you think of how you're going to tackle groups of enemies, whilst still being a challenge to the player.
So far I've played this game through to the end 3 times and every playthrough has been different.
If you're browsing through steam for a good game to play at a reasonable price, £7.99 at the time of writing this, I highly recomend this game.

This game was one of my favorite hidden gems on the Xbox Live Arcade, so I was delighted to see it get a PC port. The PC port is basically the same game with more levels and campaign options, so if you bought the 360 version you won't be disappointed.
It's a charming and simple game where you blow up things with a rocket launcher, and the entire game uses pixelated characters and terrain (which is also destructible) in a unique enough way to make it interesting. Some of the levels are legit challenging but the game is not especially difficult. There's plenty of replayability with its additional campaigns and game modes, and the soundtrack is pretty cool too (though I much prefer the Xbox 360 version's menu theme to this one.) I find myself quoting the lyrics to the song (Rocket Riot Rocket Riot) from time to time around a good friend who also played this game.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. So, this is going to be a bit of an "early impressions" review, which I dont normally do, but... this game has impressed me so much that I feel like adding to the thumbs-upness that it already has.  Not to mention that while complex, the mechanics are easy enough to grasp that I feel I've got a good handle on things here.   And to explain a bit about myself, I'm a huge fan of three things:  1, bullet hell games, 2, roguelikes/rogue-lites, and 3, CCGs (or TCGs, whatever you want to call them; games played with collectible cards).  Very, very familiar with and fond of all three.
Imagine my surprise when I found a game that smashes all of those three things together.
Imagine even more surprise when I found out that said game actually does it RIGHT.
That's the really interesting thing about this game:  It takes all of these different ideas and squashes them together, but locks them into place alongside one another that it all just works.
In this game, you start out by choosing one of four hero characters (five if you have the expansion).  That doesnt sound like many?  There's a good reason for that, which I'll get to in a bit.  You can also choose a "pet" to accompany you into battle, each having it's own abilities/stats and unique ways of helping you out.  When you're in battle, you have a few abilities you can activate, each crucial to your success, and each having a cooldown; there's no mana costs here, just the cooldown.  Mastery of your abilities is key, and learning enemy behaviors and patterns is another key.  While this game may look a bit like a Diablo clone when just viewed by those that have never really seen it, it definitely isnt.  This game is not just about attacking your enemies as Diablo is (where you often just stand in one spot and fire spells and such), instead it's about fighting and actually DODGING things; every attack is fully dodgable, and you MUST do this if you are to win.  This is where the "bullet hell" label comes from, as enemies are going to fling dangerous explody death balls or whatever all over the place.  Many things to dodge.
Each "battle" VS a particular boss consists of 8 arenas, with you teleporting to the next one after clearing the current one of non-summoned enemies. These get harder and harder up until you hit number 8, at which point you'll fight the boss itself (pretty much always with some of his minions tagging along).  Enemies have all sorts of varied and dangerous attacks, bosses can be very dangerous with their own ability to fill the screen with pain, and what's worse, there are traps, and throughout all of those arenas (including the 7 where the boss isnt physically present) the boss has an ability that they can trigger (on a cooldown, like yours) that just makes your job harder.  Each run through the game consists of a series of many different battles, so you have much to overcome before you can win a run.
Fortunately, you arent going into this lunacy unprepared.  This is where the CCG aspect comes into play.  When you select a hero, you also select a deck of cards to bring into battle.  You assemble these decks in a seperate interface; once you've actually started a run with a hero, you cannot alter your deck in any way (which is as you'd expect, right?).  But the point is, you build a deck filled with various types of cards; spells (one-shot effects), consumables (which when activated give you consumable items of some sort that can be activated during combat) and upgrades (permanent effects, lasting until the end of the battle, through all arenas up till the boss is beaten).  There's all sorts of fun and crazy cards here, and they're just as complicated and varied as you might expect from something like this.  Assembling a good deck is not easy, either, which is good.   When you're in a battle, at the start of each arena you're given the chance to play cards from your current hand.  You have a mana pool, which works similarly to Hearthstone in that you start with 1 max mana, and at each new arena, this goes up by 1.  As you might expect there's ways to manipulate this or do things like change the costs on cards or... well, you'll see for yourself the things you can do.  Card synergies are important, of course, but it's up to you to figure out what to use, and what fits the deck idea you're going for and your playstyle.
But dont think that these cards are an almighty advantage for you.  Bosses have their own decks, and a steadily increasing mana max like you do, and will play their own cards just before you play yours (meaning you can see what they do, and respond to them).  Their cards can do all sorts of really loopy things, which really add alot to each fight, yet never really feel unfair or anything.  They'll do their best to put an end to your run, but if you use your own tools right, and keep dodging all that chaos... you can win.
That's not all though!  There's a long list of modifiers that can be applied to each battle, and during a run, you select from different possible battles that have their own small list of modifiers.  Modifiers can be beneficial (though this also increases the enemy count in each arena) or negative (which also lowers the enemy count).  Learning what these are and selecting the right battles is tough, but something you'll need to do.  Choose the wrong battle with modifiers that go against your deck, and you're putting yourself at a disadvantage.
Between battles you also level-up and select "boons", or perks.  None of this is carried over between runs, naturally.  This game is stuffed full of roguelike elements, after all.  There's plenty of RNG here to keep things interesting, but without ever feeling like a total mess.
As for the heroes?  There's only a few of them because of the card mechanic; some cards are geared towards a specific hero only, affecting their abilities in various interesting ways.  These are important, as you'd expect, and using them properly is important.  If there were too many heroes, the total card count would be stupidly high.  The really good thing though is that because of the card system, you get a ton of variance in how you can play each hero and how they'll work.  They're not always going to feel/play exactly the same.  They all work out well and are great fun to use, and you'll make individual decks for each hero.
All in all, these many mechanics combine to form a very deep, satisfying, and very challenging game that can keep you coming back just as often as many roguelikes do.  And keep in mind, I only discussed the game's main mode here... there's more modes than just that.  There's a LOT to do here.  And even more if you get the expansion, which I can already recommend.
Overall, this is a fantastic game with great execution, mechanics, and tons of difficulty that's going to keep me coming back over and over.  I'm loving it, and I highly recommend it.  Just be aware of how hard it is.  It WILL beat you over the head with your own face.  It'll laugh while it does this.

Ask yourself two questions
1: Do you like deckbuilding games?
2: Do you like action games
If yes, then Forced showdown is a game for you!
Forced Showdown is a spinoff from Forced that was a splendd Co-op game, where Forced Showdown is a single-player game ATM. The game lets you make a deck consisting of 30 cards. No more than 2 of same cards is allowed.
You choose 4 champions (5 with expansion) that either is meele oriented or ranged. Each champions have a diffrent aproach regarding active and passive skills. It takes skills to master them all.
A similar game idea is Hand of Fate that also is action-based with deckbuilding feature. The diffrence between them is that in Hand of Fate you could randomly start with the BiS cards in the beginning (after you have collected them of course) making the game really easy. Where in Forced Showdown each card has a manacost. Each new arena in a battle gives you more and more mana to spend on those awsome late-game cards. But until you reach late arenas you har stuck on relying on early cards and skill, wich is a good thing =). You also get a pet companion that help you in each arena. You can chose one from three companions once unlocked
Aquire new cards is done by spending gold that you earn in-game. You get a random card that is divided between 3 raritys. You can have max 2 of each. If you get a third copy, that card will automaticly be converted to shards that is spent on making new cards that is guaranteed to be a new card.
The game have many achivments. Each achivment is part of a quest. When a quest is completed you get in-game rewards. Be it more gold, shards or a special boost, that is up to you to find out =)
All in all. This is a very good game that provides deckbuilidng, action, achivment hunting and grinding.

TL;DR: Mostly straightforward puzzles with just a couple that will throw you, interesting if somewhat overdone and predictable largely on-rails story, some replay value (such as with optional puzzle rooms), using UE4 when it could have been done in UE3/Unity and it wouldn't have mattered.
Tentatively recommended.
Long version:-
The puzzles are, for the most part, not taxing (with the exception of two puzzle rooms in the main story and the optional puzzle rooms) which does mean it is likely that players will finish the game, but it left me feeling unsatisfied somehow. As a frame of reference: I always found The Riddler to be my archnemesis in the Arkham games and taken great delight in solving all of his (also straightforward) puzzles and riddles. So if you played the Arkham games and couldn't stand The Riddler's puzzles and riddles, then this isn't the game for you.
The story is one that's been done many times before and better (intelligent AI...yes we all know what's going to happen next!), with the philisophical questions trying to be more intellectual and high brow than they actually are and it falls short.
Indeed the style of the story and storytelling reminds me strongly of Gone Home. In both you follow a linear path and you hear audio recordings as though they were chapters in an audiobook. In both you can pick up and examine miscellaneous objects that neither move the story on nor the game. Unlike Gone Home, the puzzles here are blatant and numerous; you actually have to work out what to do; and you learn about the different energy spheres mechanic that you can harness through actually playing the game. However, it comes across that these puzzles are more padding between story bits than integral to the story after the first few.
The final puzzle room in the game I actually solved by being silly and it felt as though I was cheating than legitimately solving it.
A sidenote about the audio logs: some will be located in the "reward room" at the end of optional puzzle rooms. If you're blasting through as I did, then this won't be so much of a problem for you. If you find yourself stumped by the main puzzles constantly (being stumped by Sector 36 is understandable though), then you're not going to get all the details to make your final and more informed decision.
More criticism can be had with the graphical side of things. I find it hard to justify the use of UE4 except for prestige as we have very basic rooms (90 degree orthoganal cubes) for the most part which, whilst are appropriate for the story and setting, get tiresome fast. The areas at the end of chapters actually allows for creativity in the design, although the outdoor areas are hardly ground breaking, and the worst sin of all: there are only two times you see your main character's face in-game. One time is the menu and the other is as a portrait on a monitor.
Personally I thought I'd be seeing at least a reflection in an occasional mirror, however there aren't any mirrors and it'd only show Ava's spacesuit with the completely opaque and cheap looking helmet visor down. Given the graphical capabilities of UE4; I place the blame at the developers for going to all that effort to pre-render the character for the game cover artwork, only to then not bother in-game when the engine is more than capable.
This brings me to my final bugbear and that's - in this instance - using a female protagonist comes across here as a gimmick. We don't get to choose how she responds (which itself could easily blend in to the story) until the very end of the game, which for me means we don't get to learn about our character and bond via a common goal (e.g. without spoiling, do we accept or reject what we're being told? And will we be allowed to?).
All this said, whilst the listed shortcomings may be enough for some to not bother, I bought my copy on sale so for a few quid I got my money's worth - which is no bad thing.  I also felt as though I was going through the last section of the original Deus Ex (if stretched out quite a bit more) which is mostly a good thing in my book.
As it stands? I can't hate The Turing Test as it isn't terrible, but it is - if only just at times - enjoyable. Play it for the puzzles first, story second.

The Turing Test is a shallow, disappointing experience. Neither the puzzles nor the story are worth the hours you'd spend to see them through.
A handful of the puzzles are good, but many of them (especially in the latter half) are artificially convoluted. In many cases, the solution feels obscured due to the distance and barriers between switches and objects being switched. It takes a lot of running around just to be able to reason about the space, and oftentimes by the time I finally figured out what the point of the puzzle was, the solution became startlingly simple.
The story is pretty thin. The context for the puzzles is very shallow and not very believable. That's not always a problem for every game, but it's especially a problem for this game because it takes its story so seriously. The barrier between gameplay and story is sky high; there's a brief moment about 2/3 through the game (and another pale echo during the ending) where an interesting story event occurs during play, but neither of them justify the co-existence of these puzzles with this story. In the end, the puzzles feel like something that was put in the game just so that this wouldn't be labeled a "walking simulator". (For the record, I do enjoy some walking simulators. I almost believe this game would have been better if it had attempted to be one.)
The game's story tries to tackle some deep philosophical questions, such as strong AI (human-level thinking), free will and determinism, and utilitarian ethics. However, if you've spent more than a few moments researching or pondering these questions yourself, you've probably explored them to a greater depth than The Turing Test has. The questions are explained in an "Intro to Philosophy" level, which makes sense, since not everyone has considered or researched these topics before. But it never goes any further than that. The protagonist has some banter with the in-game AI about these questions, and some hidden rooms have documents and audio logs from other characters, but it never gets any deeper than, "<Human> I think I have free will. <Robot> No, you don't. <Human> Well, you're not a conscious being. <Robot> Yes, I am."
If you're looking for an interesting exploration of these philosophical topics, you are better served picking up a copy of Isaac Asimov's short story collection "I, Robot". You'll find the experience more engaging and thought-provoking, and you won't have to suffer through mediocre puzzles to get through it.
Alternatively, if you're looking for a deep, rewarding first-person puzzle game whose puzzles
feel like they were shoehorned into the experience, and whose narrative context
feel congruent with the gameplay, check out The Witness, if you haven't already.

I am both pleased and humbled by a response from the developer, thank you very much!
In light of this I wish to be more detailed in exactly what I loved so much about Osiris.
The world you created for us was the closest I have ever encountered in any game like this, to what I could imagine an exoplanet to be like. The mineral distibution was dead on realistic for what we know about our universe. We can estimate that habital planets in the universe could have up to 60 Be Minerals, but most will have much less.  Your world had a very realistic amount. And there was room to add some more later without going anywhere near the unrealistic stage of quantity. And although I know a lot more about planetary science than I do chemistry, the combines for creating materials seemed spot on too. I loved it!
These two aspects allowed me to immerse myself into the gameplay very well. Add in the fact that the world is absolutely gorgeous and full of danger really set the mood right. The only thing I found at this point lacking in realism was a source of water, which is a requirement for life to exist. I found no lakes or streams of any kind. And yet the planet has plants and monsters. Then one night there was a thunderstorm and I smiled bright as rain pelted off my greenhouse. (I figured at this point, they got this, they'll probably just add in a standing body of water at a later point of development).
Then the mining change occurred. The addition of the basic and advance mineral node completely shattered the feeling of a real exoplanet. To say it is statistically Improbable for so many unique minerals to be compacted into the same rock is being generous.
I do agree that material farming needed to be tweaked and adjusted to a slower rate than it was. I believe this could have been done easily by removing some of the mineral nodes in each grouping around the planet. As well as adjusting the rate of return when using our pick on the nodes themselves.
Personally a grind doesn't bother me when the feeling of completion is rewarding enough. Realism however is very important to me in a game like this. I've spent my life studying planetary science and I just can't stop thinking about the lack of scientific realism everytime i see one of these new nodes.

Soup is a simple game, but it has fun gameplay. The aim of the game is to win from the Virus, this as Bacteria or Nanobots atm.
Gameplay
You have your collectors, mines and fighters (and you can shoot these torpedoes). These all you can spawn with one single button Z, while holding down the Z button you can see the different units and select them like this. So your collectors collect and grow bigger and on some point you might want to recall them using the X button before they get wiped out by the enemy fighters. You also have mines that circle around your "base" for defensive purposes mostly.  Then you have fighters, these attack enemies anywhere in the playing field by bumping in them (this eventually kills them as well). As the last unit you can use there is the torpedo, well looks like a kamikazerun.. but anyway you can use this to directly attack the virus. Depending on the size of you main body the units you have can be smaller or larger too.
Updates
Looks like we will get updates quite frequently.. Last update changed the fighters and mines behaviour. Mines play more friendly as in letting you collectors through to be reabsorbed by your main body. The fighters gotten smarter, which makes winning a bit more challenging.
Verdict
I'll be keeping my eye on this game, as I've played it for a few hours now and it was fun to do so (only won twice). I'll be looking forward to things like maybe: being able to change difficulty settings, sound options, opponents, able to be the virus instead of a bacteria. For now I recommend this game, the price is right and it's fun to play.
