The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a third-person tactical shooter set in the 1960's and allows the player to take control of Agent William Carter, a washed up agent with a haunted past. This game is different to the other entries in the XCOM series in that the game does not play like an RTS game or feature an isometric view, and is instead played as a standard cover shooter with an over the shoulder view. Does this make it a good game? Yes.
While hardcore fans will of XCOM will find this change of formula jarring, I personally found this formula to be a unique technique and a fresh flavour specific to the XCOM series. While the game plays a bit more like Mass Effect this time around (you can pause the game and command your team mates via a command screen, such as ordering them to move or use special abilities, etc) , it still feels like XCOM, as you still have to take strategic care in how you enter combat situations. I liked how you had to be strategic in how you placed your team mates, and how you must constantly adapt to combat as enemies flank you and draw you out of cover. This made for a tense and enjoyable gameplay experience, and is definitely a must on the harder difficulties. Unfortunately, the AI of your squadmates leaves a lot to be desired, and you will definitely get frustrated by their lack of competence.
You will also get frustrated by the generic and often boring characters as well as the lacklustre plotline; this is standard alien-invasion fare, and anyone else looking for a riveting science fiction story will need to look elsewhere. I rarely find moments of the plot interesting, except for the rare dialogue encounters with the aliens themselves, which were a joy to behold. However, none of the other characters offered much in the way of development and voice acting, and I found them bland and uninteresting.
The graphics are quite nice, and lots of love and care have been dedicated to the lighting and detailed environments in the game. Many of the details in this game are quite nice, and this game looks extremely good when cranked up to max settings whilst running on DX11.
In short? The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a unique yet unusual entry in the XCOM franchise, and is a reward to fans of tactical shooters in general. Despite the occassional stumble in gameplay, incompetent team-mate AI and a lacklustre story, The Bureau is a solid game and I recommend it highly despite its flaws. I give this game a 7.5 / 10.

After all the bad press surrounding slapping the famous XCOM (sic.) brand on a TPS there is a surprising decent game left behind.  You are Agent Carter, a cynical broken man thrust into the limelight after an Alien invasion now tasked as the tip of the spear against this new threat.
There are many elements and ideas drawn from the previous games but it is a strictly linear and pre determined experience.  You operate out of XCOM headquarters between the main story missions.  You have free run of the base and are able to go on minor side missions, perform investigations inside the base and sent agents out on missions on their own to gain experience and new equipment.  Sadly even though the base has vast Engineering and Lab sections, they are cosmetic.  You can't perform research on new equipment or ideas or perform autopsies.  The only way to get new equipment is to find it during a mission and the only way to learn about various elements is to click on one of the copious clickables in the world.
Carter can bring two additional henchmen with him on a mission from one of the four classes.  They are all pretty standard tropes from other games but do add an interesting element to the game.  Do you go all out attack with commandos and snipers, sit back and dig in with engineers and support specialists or a combination of the four.  You can move henchmen around the battleground, conveniently littered with waist high walls, flank enemies and use the various abilities in conjunction with Carter's unique ones for a multitude of strategies. But...
A warning: The friendly henchmen AI is some of the worst you'll ever see.  They'll jump out of cover, run left, run right, turn a full circle, jump over another wall landing right next the nearest enemy before coming back to you.  They need to be babysat at all times or they will be useless.
Where the game shines is in the fantastic recreation of cold-war early sixties America and the digital acting.  The influence of Mass Effect is obvious but still welcome and the story?  Well, let's just say it takes quite the left turn near the end!

If you liked Angry Birds but found that the aspect of smashing things made it too exciting, then this coma-inducing clone might be up your alley. Gravity Badgers is very literally a version of Angry Birds Space where instead of smashing through structures to pop pigs, you merely need to slingshot from point A to point B. Obstacles and the gravity fields of planets scattered throughout the levels complicate the task, but the same banal trial and error flinging that got you through Angry Birds will get you through Gravity Badgers. If your brain injuries are somehow so severe that you can't handle this menial objective, the game actually allows you to skip the level you're on, provided you're willing to wait long enough for the meter that allows you to perform this function to recharge. To its credit, Gravity Badgers has a ton of levels, but you'll get bored long before you've seen all of the samey content the game has to offer.

Fast paced rogue-lite arena brawler / "twin-stick shooter" with interesting setting (as a TV show).
You can choose between 4 different heroes - each with totally different playstyle (AoE focused caster, glass cannon, combo "enrage" fighter and melee heavy hitter) + one of 3 companions to aid you.
Main meat of the game is you fight in multiple rounds of small arenas (2-5 mins each) until you reach a boss. Rince and repeat until you reach the final boss of the show (in like an hour).
Twist of the game is, that you also build a deck of cards (permanent buffs, spells, etc.) that you play throughout your run and become stronger and gain new modifiers to your abilities - thus getting that "leveling up a new character" vibe.
After each run you get random new cards that can improve your deck (so there is permanent progression) and you start over (later even with optional challenges).
Easy to jump into, hard to master, lots of fun in between...

FORCED SHOWDOWN is a rogue-like arena-based combat game with lots of diversity, extremely engaging gameplay and tons or replayability. In many aspects, it looks like what DOTA would have looked if it was played by one character, on a small arena, and with WASD instead. The gameplay is very fast-paced and intense, it always keeps you on your toes, and winning a level is extremely rewarding.
And before someone starts bashing the game for not launching, the devs are hard at work at it. I can tell - untill yesterday's beta patch launched, I could not start the game myself, and now it runs flawlessly.
Allrighty, let's take a look at the good and at the bad.
THE GOOD:
1. Extremely engaging gameplay - as I pointed out in other reviews, to me, this outweighs everything else. You will be glued to your seat and will readily want to beat the current level just to see what the game has in store for you next. I haven't felt such an urge in a PC game for a good while.
2. Extremely responsive controls, be it whether you play with the mouse and keyboard, or with a controller. I love it when a game transcends the twin stick controls and allows the player to feel just as comfortable when using a keyboard and mouse, like I usually play my games.
3. Arena-style combat: every level is comprised of a number of small arenas that can be beaten in a few minutes, or even less than a minute. At first I thought I would hate this, but it actually ends up working for the better. This is the way to do it - fast paced, quick and engaging fights that never let up. It wants you to get to the final battle that features a boss toon that much more!
4. Selectable levels - it is entirely up to you to decide what kind of boons or setbacks are you going to have on a level, which is a great touch and furthers the replayability by a whole lot.
5. A deck of cards for skills - another very interesting design decision, that furthers the replayability even more. For each of the 4 heroes you can build up to 5 decks of 30 cards. At the start of the battle, you get 4 random cards from your deck of various magnitudes of 1 to 7 (or more under special conditions), from which you can discard, or keep as is. Throughout the levels, you get to play the cards from your hand as skills or consumable items (items with number of charges for the whole battle). On arenas 1-8 you get respective 1-8 mana points that you can use to play cards with, with each card having a mana requirement. This can be further influenced by boons (e.g. extra mana point on arena 1) and cards. There is a plethora of possible combinations that you can set for yourself - which lets you get very creative.
6. The game is very atmospheric - you really feel like a part of the show, with an announcer, small flying drones that take pictures of you, and even spectators around the arena who cheer.
7. Amazing musical score - the main theme of the game will finally succeed XCOM2's ready for battle as my pump-up song. It is so cool. It even made me buy the deluxe edition as to keep the OST and listen to it during my daily routines as well.
8. Unlockable heroes, quests, dailies,  achievements and all that good jazz that make you come back to the game over and over.
9. There is real progression in this game, even when you lose. You get to keep your coins and spend them unlocking cards of various rarities, which makes losses feel less impactful. You still feel as you are progressing, unlike other rogue-likes that simply wipe your progress and say "now play me for another 5 hours to get to where you were" - like the grindy WASTED, for example.
10. And last but not least - the replayability. You will never get bored even if you played the same Hero for 5 or 50 hours, and no two games are ever the same. At present, I have unlocked all of them, and I can sure as hell say that they all play completely differently, which is always a great thing to see. You get a max range, mid-range, close AOE and a very fast attacker. Take your pick, or master tham all.
And now the ba... Wait, wait. Let's just add the OK first.
1. DOTA style graphics. While this is not necessarily a bad thing and it is more than serviceable, I can't help but wonder what would such a game look on a better engine... That would have been totally epic.
2. The game tells (and expects) you to "git gud" before you can enjoy a huge part of its content. Yeah, you need to beat the Crucible before you can do pretty much anything else. While this is not necessarily bad, it does lock you out of content that you might enjoy right from the start.
And now, the BAD:
1. Having a deck also means you are playing an RNG game. You may get cards that will easily win you the level, but more often than not, you won't and be forced to play with what you are given. This can be off-putting to some players, and for a good reason.
2. Having a number of mana points per round can also be a problem. You can have a hand that is completely unplayable for a few rounds, which is always bad for your hero. You may still win, of course, that doesn't mean that luck will lose you the game.
The conclusion:
Yesterday I was this close to refund the game because it never launched for me, and after reading up the forums and patching it, I am so glad I didn't. You owe it to yourself to experience what this game has to offer. Every concept of it ties together perfectly to allow for hours of enjoyment. It is not the type of game to say "hey, sit down now, and spend 10 hours playing me or you won't have fun at all". NO! It is quite the opposite - it says "look, I know your time is precious, so how about you play me for a while, have a real blast and go back to your life". When such type of game shows up and is executed as well as FORCED SHOWDOWN is, it deserves a thumbs up and you owe it to yourself to try it.
P.S. And it still rocks :)

Gravity Badgers had the potential to be a good Angry Birds alternative, but it fell flat.
In Gravity Badgers you are a badger with a rocket-pack. You start as Pup and as play progresses you unlock more characters. Each level consists of launching yourself through space on a path which will hopefully collect all the "energy cores" on the map. Unless there is ice involved you launch once and let gravity handle the rest.
Each puzzle has different things which can influence your motion. As I already mentioned ice freezes you in place and lets you re-launch. There are planets which can either push or pull you and a handful of other things as well.
Though this game has interesting mechanics, moving obstacles and even a plot, those strengths did not make up for the fact it simply wasn't fun. In general the puzzles seemed repetitive and the correct path was too precise. The menu could use a revamp as well, it consists entirely of icons which you may or may not recognize.
Its not all bad, the "boss" I fought to save Grandpa was creative and according to the videos it looks like there are other interesting challenges as well. The tutorial is crystal clear in how to play and even has brief moments of humor. It also has achievements and cards.
The achievements tell an interesting story though, they are completely linear and tell you exactly how many people finish the game and where most people quit. Only a third of the players play more than an hour and even fewer fight the first boss.
If you are a huge fan of gravity / Angry Birds type games give it a go. Everyone else should just pass it by.

Fun, fast-paced gameplay in digestable sections, mixed with an engaging progression system that requires adaptive decision making.
The combat is a mix between Diablo and Dota, where heroes have a set number of attacks and abilities that are augmented with various cards. The game avoids button-mashy combat by providing benefits to utilizing a character's basic attack in different ways--one character, for example, has a damaging beam that slowly ramps up in damage the longer it is held down, but also restricts the player's movement.
Earning cards and creating decks provides an addictive experience, allowing a player to make decisions to reduce the randomness of each run. The decision making process is similar to Binding of Isaac, where risk and reward need to be balanced in order to overcome each stage.
Highly recommended for players that enjoy roguelikes similar to Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon. FORCED SHOWDOWN provides enough of a unique spin on the genre to stand strong next to the competition.

Davyria is a solid experience so far that gets the job done in terms of gameplay.
The game feels very much like it took inspiration from the Souls series. The general loop is nearly exact in that you go from area to area taking out enemies, avoiding their strikes and using dodge or block strategies against each foe. You eventually reach a boss that uses a few different attack patterns that you need to learn in order to effectively fight them. Dying will result in loading at the last bonfire (I mean shrine) and having to go through the respawned enemies.
The top down perspective works fine, there isn't anything that it gets in the way of gameplay-wise.
Playing the game feels a bit slow at times, even slower than what I was used to in Dark Souls. It also doesn't feel quite as smooth.
The artstyle works fine, it's not the best looker out there but the shading effects work to its advantage.
I didn't run into any performance issues while playing. There isn't a main menu or options menu in the game though, which is fairly annoying.
Overall it might be something you would enjoy if you like boss fights and strategic combat, again similar to the Souls games. For $10 or less you should be able to get your money's worth out of it.

I approached the creator of the game and said if I got a free copy of it I will publish a review and promotion on my website.
Now while the game is great, especially for a single developer, there are some thing that need to be said.
Let's start with the map, character movement and exploration. It is obvious you have spent time creating intricate level design to make it fun to explore, but it isn't. This is why. The character moves slower than a snail, even with significant buffs to agility. And exploration, is completely unrewarding. The only thing I got for exploration, was extra enemies, a healing item which I used for the enemies I encountered for exploring, a useless NPC that sells overpriced fish, and greatsword that is just as slow. The maps in this game feel HUGE for a game that has been developed by one person, and exploring them feels punishing, and dull.
You can't even sprint, so you're constantly moving at a turtle's speed which makes it boring to explore. The combat feels good, but when I dig deep down, it's all concentrated on patience and a broken roll mechanic. When you go up against a boss, they are constantly spamming a flurry of blows but it's impossible to dodge because it's broken. You dodge once, but then another hit is coming your way, and then when you try to doge again it just doesn't register, because your character is being forced to finish the rolling animation.
You are advertising a game that is HARD but FAIR. It doesn't feel fair. When a boss is spamming attacks faster than the speed of light, what chance do we have when we constantly take damage because dodging doesn't work and shields might as well be ineffective? And how is it fair, when you have positioned two archers guarding a doorway which you have to try to break, and if you get past that, there is another 3 archers shooting at you? Are you telling me, that trying to avoid 4 simultaneous arrows targeting me with pixel-perfect accuracy, a broken roll mechanic and a health bar that diminishes in two hits is FAIR?
I don't think so.
Conclusion: The game is extremely difficult and has great and awesome graphics, but I only recommend this, if the creator implements missing and simple mechanics into the game. If he made the character a bit faster, added a sprint mechanic, and more rewards scattered here and there along with a fix for the roll, that is when this game is worth a buy.
Hell, even now it's worth a buy, £5? This is a masterpiece and pure art at its core and has great potential to becoming one of the most memorable indie games anyone could ever play. But it's just those little details that matter.
Until the game is fixed I will give it a 7/10.

Yes, the levels look nice. but did the original really in need of a face lift? The game plays well, but the difficulty is way easieer than the original so you have to crank it to the highest difficulty just to have a challenge. (Unless you play the solo survival mississions. which are borderline impossible and were created just to be hard and not fun it seems.)
I guess the selling point was the multiplayer and the the co-op, but multiplayer is a ghost town and co-op only works if you know someone who is willing to play with you.
Also, why in god's name is the story a sequel? Yes the story is a sequel to the original Painkiller but the game is a remake. It makes no sense. Especially when you are going through levels you already played through in the original and are fighting bosses that should be dead from the original. You don't add a sequal storyline to a remake. This game was a disappointment for me. I am hardcore into both sci-fi games and adventure games, but this just didn't measure up to stuff like Shardlight or Technobabylon. It falls more into the realm of JULIA or STASIS, so if you liked those games you might like this one.
My biggest problem is that there is no motivation. There is no one to talk to. There is nothing to care about. You are just a floating head who listens to radio logs and does busywork. There are no narrative puzzles and no creative solutions. There is no opportunity to combine the wrong stuff for comedic result. It feels more like a hidden object game than an adventure to me, except even hidden object games tend to have some kind of compelling (if cliché) story.
The lack of story might be forgivable to fans of this sort of puzzling, if it weren't for the absolutely abysmal control mechanism. I have honestly never played an adventure game with such poor controls. It looks like it's a first-person game, but you can't move around with WASD. In fact, you can't move around at all. You are stuck in one spot and you need to very slowly rotate the camera till you find a magic hotspot that lets you click to move to the next corner of the room. There is no freedom to move anywhere. It feels incredibly restrictive and is very tiresome on your wrist.
The best part about this game was the walkthrough. It's well-written and adds a lot to the experience, because the in-game mechanics are so bad. But overall the game just isn't very entertaining.

Prominence is a very nice adventure game.
The graphics and sound are decent, the voice acting impressive and the puzzles are well integrated into the environment.
Movement is node-based with 360° rotation at any location.
The game is especially suited for beginners (or casual players) because there are no hard puzzles. Being observant and looking carefully at the environment is enough to complete the game without getting stuck.
So, thumbs up!

This is an enjoyable nod to classic point-and-click adventure games with a high attention to detailed graphics, excellent voice acting, and engaging storyline. In some situations (particularly right at the start of the game, when you're locked in a small area), it is difficult to visually distinguish betewen items which you can or can't use on the screen, but overall once you get the hang of it, the game flows very well.
I liked how they added some interactive puzzles in the game, like assembling parts in the correct order, or allocating power without overloading the circuit, etc. I also liked that there are two ways to end the game, so you get a little bit of choice on how you want to progress. It would have been cool to see even more options like this.
Fun game, definitely recommended if you enjoy unraveling a mystery where you spend most of the game isolated from other characters and trying to understand who you are and how you got here.

Prominence is more than just a game.  It's whole new sci fi arena. After you get through the game, your wondering when the movie is coming out.   You have these people, and this technology, and this history, and its all woven together and introduced in the game.  And it's complete - you have relationships between people and leaders and workers and hopes and dreams, and technology failures, and work arounds, and all of it centers around a certain star, and all of that is revealed one peice at a time as you play.  The art in the game is excellent artwork, and it works with background story.  You have the drab look of the lower level, and the pristine look of the upper levels.  The chipped yellow paint on the ladder in the elevater shaft, the natural beauty of the hydroponics lab with the large open window looking into space, the large brown CO2 tanks, and the awkard round thing that turns them on...the entire game has so much detail in the artwork - I dont know how the designers knew how to make it seem so real.  All the characters have different personalities that fit their jobs so well.  All of it reminds me of the way that different people worked together when I was serving on a ship in the US Navy.  The girl in waste processing who is tired of getting reminded of how to do her job when someone forgets to open the valve outside of the main room.  The security personell who stir their drinks with the stun batons, and break them, and the guy in the engine room who gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥becasue he has to fix them.  There is so much stuff like that going on.  And that's just the background.  The actual game plays great.  Even on my 13 year old single core machine.  Figuring out stuff is a challange, there is a lot of items and rooms and things to keep track of and sort through.  I've gone back and played through many times.  I write down names and notes to better understand the story, and the people.  Some of the tech in it is raw, basic stuff that is fun to work with, like the terminal computer, or like the card reader / encoder.  The music and sound effects are excellent.  I like turning up the volume on my 200 watt / per channel system, and clicking on a locked door over and over again to here the sound effect.  The locked CO2 absorbers have a really good sound too.  The voices of the characters are awesome.  The voices, and the way they say stuff, you can tell that the developers hired a bunch of different actors to get it right.  The medic, who has to tell someone that they have a day to live due to a lethal radation dose, but seems to get excited in the next sentence when she's explaing the technology, and that guy who is dying, OMG, you get to hear him giving updates as he runs around the ship trying to fix it, running into a hopeless situation that gets worse and worse, but he's pushing through the pain with an inredible sense of duty...I just keep on playing the game and listening to all of these lines over and over again.  I highly recommend this game.

A pretty good sci-fi puzzle game with an interesting story. Unfortunately it's too short. Took me 6 hours to play through it, including the optional puzzles.
As others have said, if you liked Portal and The Talos Principle, you'll most likely like this. It's clearly very inspired from those two games.
+ Good sci-fi story kind of in the vain of Portal and 2001: A Space Odyssey
+ Not as good as Portal and Talos Principle but still pretty good! Has a lot of potential in my opinion, it's a shame that they didn't do more with it
+ Fairly difficult levels with new mechanics being introduced pretty much every chapter
+ Interesting puzzle mechanics
+ The bonus levels are challenging as they usually require you to think outside of the box and will help you find more about the story
+ Quite a few audio logs and details that you can find through the game that let you find out more about the characters
- Way too short. Only took me 6 hours to play through 100%. Only 7 chapters and an Epilogue which has no puzzles in it which is a shame because
- No replayability
- Sometimes the difficulty is a bit all over the place. The levels get harder with each chapter as they introduce new mechanics but within each chapters sometimes you'll have really easy levels and sometimes really hard ones
- The ending is a bit anti-climatic and although you technically have 2 different choices at the end, they really don't make a difference
- Although the story is interesting, I didn't really find myself that interested in the characters. The main character is fairly interesting but the others I found easily forgettable
- The quality of the audio logs that you can find through the game is really bad. At first I listened to them anyway because I wanted to know more about the story but after a while I just didn't even bother because the audio quality was too bad
I would recommend this game but only on sale. I don't think it's worth the full price unless they suddenly decide to update it with new content.
Hopefully they will make a sequel or add more content via either free updates or DLC.
Adding workshop support and the ability to create and share custom maps would be really great.

Very good puzzle game mirroring the play style of the Talos Principle and godgame Portal. While I notice some people are frustrated at an aparent copy, I was pleased that the developers seemed aware of and played on the similarities in order to mess with the player's head.
The story is very motivating, the bonus levels add to the atmosphere. But I will say I have one caveat to my enjoyment of the game. The Turing Test is a method in order to distinguish a computer to a real person. Throughout the playthrough, there is reference to computer's reliance on binary computation. Midway through the game, I had already thought of a tertiary option to the aparant moral dilemma posed within the story. Yet, the human characters never address this. Therefore, the end credits should not read "You passed the Turing Test" but "You failed the Turing Test" as every character sticks to the obvious dichotomy and does not utilize human creativity (the key element of the game) to problem solve and think outside the box.
But perhaps I am nit picking.

Wow, this was a really wonderful game.  I've played a few in a similar vein (The Talos Principle etc), but imo this stood out as a superior example of this kind of puzzle solving while philosophizing experience.
Pros:
+Visuals are very pleasant, nicely rendered, and really help create an appropriate atmosphere.
+The story, while fairly simple and predictable was very engaging, raising questions about the free will and the value of the individual.
+The characters.  While I found Ava a bit grating at times (although this was probably because
, I really loved T.O.M., and found all the background players well-explored and believable through various recordings and in-game material.  It helped explain a lot of character actions and attitudes towards T.O.M. and the other members of the crew.
+The music, like the visuals, were atmospheric and engaging.
+The puzzle design, while implementing repetitive elements never FELT repetitive with enough variation and new elements being introduced throughout that it was continually challenging (although not TOO challenging) right to the end.  By comparison, while I enjoyed the Talos Principle, I did find the puzzles there a little tedious.
Cons:
-At times I felt the motivation of Ava to be a little thin and selfish.
Bottom line: if you like puzzle games, definitely add this game to your collection.
10/10 would question my humanity again.

It's great to walk around the XCOM underground base, you feel like you're part of something. The story is a tad cheesy, but all-in-all the pros outweigh the cons, but not by much.

It requires good timing and patience with the slow pace of your character, but thanks to infinite lives and relatively frequent checkpoints, it never gets too frustrating.
Where the game stands out are the atmosphere and the soundtrack, which are amazing. The game also tries to capture the graphic style of the old ZX Spectrum, with bright, popping colours against a dark background. If you like traditional platformers and don't get frustrated easily, give this game a shot.

I was intrigued by this game's premise of combining retro platforming with Lovecraft, but Deep Ones is just not a good game. Controls feel just awful, with movement being painfully slow yet still imprecise and jumping barely clearing the many obstacles in the game. Many times, I would jump toward the next ledge and get stuck on the side due to the character's arm clipping into the environment. Internal consistency also presents an issue: At some points you are required to drop into a pit to progress, though pits throughout the rest of the game serve as instant deaths. Enemies present little risk other than by providing more obstacles to jump over, and getting rid of them requires firing the equivalent of Megaman's lemons at roughly 1/20th the rate. The one part of this game that could be considered any fun at all would be the chase scenes, which do add some tension (though only for a small while).
If you want a comparison, it feels similar to the videogame adaptation of MANOS, but even MANOS manages to be more satisfying.

Pretty good game for $5, even better if you can get it on sale.  I mostly play Tradewinds Classic (the first and simplest one), but I've played a fair amount of Tradewinds 2, as well.  It's sort of a trade simulator, I guess -- each game has you take control of a captain with one or more ships under your control, and you sail around a historically significant trade sea buying and selling goods, fighting off pirates, and maybe engaging in some little quests or tomfoolery depending on the game.  Nothing super complex or groundbreaking, but it's a lot of fun to build your trade empire/privateer armada from nothing.
The first game's simplicity makes it an ideal choice if you just want to throw on a game for an hour or two and see how you fare, but once you master the fairly simple "buy low, sell high" mechanics, you'll inevitably cruise towards millionaire status as long as RNGesus doesn't take a dump on you (which does happen, with either stagnant prices for goods or a dearth of affordable ships for sale, but that just made me want to start over and hope for better luck).  Once you get really rich and you build up your perfect fleet, the game stops being very challenging, and thus you'll probably lose interest.  But it's good for a while, and you can always start over and see if your luck changes.
The sequel definitely has some welcome improvements, such as a story mode that gives the game some much-needed longevity, but I found it to be a bit buggier -- dunno if anyone else had problems with their saves, but whenever I would save and reload, it'd set me back to about five or ten minutes before I made the save, effectively erasing that progress and forcing me to retread some ground.  Also, I haven't finished the story mode, because it's really more just a string of sidequests that I think are eventually supposed to lead towards your character's goal -- I dunno, I saw progress in terms of islands unlocked and more powerful ships, but I never got to the point where I thought I was close to achieving my character's lifetime mission; she just kinda got caught up in politics and trading.  It does entice you with replayability, though, by offering new character unlocks, custom character options (unlocked by beating the main story once, I think) and a couple other game modes that I have yet to try.  Definitely the best from a technical standpoint of the three, and good if you want something more complex than Classic.  Plus it's got a cheeky sense of humor that I found quite endearing, something that sets it apart from the former game, which was largely devoid of personality.
Didn't really play more than thirty minutes of Tradewinds Legends -- it felt like it had too much going on and threw too much at you in the beginning, whereas Tradewinds 2 gradually introduced all the deviations and upgrades from Tradewinds Classic.  Kinda felt like it was heavily aimed towards little kids.  You might have more fun with it than I did, though.
Overall, it's a fun little bundle of games at an affordable price -- they're not masterpieces of innovation, and they don't have the shiniest or most realistic graphics (although I really like the art in them), but they're simple and fun (and at times addictive), and better yet, each game offers something a little different, so even if you don't like the playstyle of one of them, then you haven't necessarily wasted your money.  I had a lot of fond memories playing Tradewinds Classic on my family's desktop years ago, and I was happy to see this little gem pop up on Steam along with sequels I had never heard of.  If you ever wanted to life the life of a historical merchant or privateer, or if you need something simple an distracting as a break from your latest story-driven, action-heavy game, then maybe give one of these a try!

Relatively old games, I used to play these a few years ago and am enjoying them again for the nostalgia of it.
Tradewinds Classic is the most simplistic of these three games.  Set in the far east (China, Japan, Burma), you buy and sell five types of merchandise at five different ports, trying to make a profit.  Fight pirates, collect bounties, etc.  This one has the cleanest interface in my opinion, but also the least amount of game content.
Tradewinds 2 is not nearly as good as Tradewinds Classic or Legends.  Though several additions were made when compared to Tradewinds Classic, what is probably the most important part of the game was removed: the ability to build a fleet.  In this game, you're limited to a single ship.  I'm also of the opinion that the graphics are generally an eyesore compared to the other two, and being set in the Caribbean just didn't fit the style of the game series overall (again, in my opinion).
Tradewinds Legends is the most content-heavy (and humorous) one of these three.  Set in the Middle East and India, it takes the best parts of the previous two games, and adds interesting storylines as well as other completely new features.  It is actually worthwhile to read the dialogue in this one, simply because of the humor of several of the quests.  It's also not very realistic, but it isn't meant to be.  You can replace your sea-bound fleet with dirigibles, fight magical creatures, the mediterranean and red seas are somehow connected, and pirates tend to capture every other port every couple months in free trade mode.
There might be occasional problems trying to run these on newer computers.  I run them on Windows 10, and they do work, but I've experienced issues with the sound/mouse/screen aspect ratio.  The broken sound only occurs occasionally at game startup (and only on Tradewinds Classic thus far).  The issues with the mouse and aspect ratio only occur when you use full screen (though not consistently, Legends seems to work fine on full screen).
Overall, great games and definitely worth the $5 I spent.

Big Action Mega Fight is a very simple beat-em-up, but it's still fairly enjoyable, mainly due to the fun cartoony style, cheesy humour, and the classic feel that the music and sound effects bring. Oh, and it works well with an Xbox style controller - I used an 8Bitdo FC-30 Pro in xinput mode.
There's a lot of short stages in Big Action Mega Fight, which start out incredibly easy but slowly get... less easy. Most stages simply have the objective of "kill all the goons" but every now and then you'll get a stage where you have to "kill all the goons within a time limit". I attempted to get a three star rating on every level, but the final level just felt impossible to achieve this, though it's not hard to beat - it's just hard to beat with the high score they expect of you to get three stars.
My major gripes with this game are:
1) No interesting combos to string together, mostly just jab, jab, uppercut, and sometimes maybe you throw something (or someone) at someone (or something).
2) No multiplayer (not even local) with the developer stating there is no intention of ever adding multiplayer.
3) You're randomly given a special attack for each stage you play instead of being able to select it. Honestly the first special attack you get is the best, so why are the others even there?
4) I might have missed something, or blacked out, but I don't recall any boss fights. I get the feeling that there might be something more if I got 3 stars on all levels, but since I saved the guy and got all the achievements, I'm done here.
Despite those gripes I still had a reasonably good time playing Big Action Mega Fight, there's just a lot of room for improvement. Go in expecting a very elementary beat-em-up and you might enjoy yourself too.
5.5 out of 10, would FISTNADO, but only just. Buy it on sale if you do.

Played the game for the first few bosses and areas and gotta say it's actually really good.
- Mechanics / Controls:
The controls feel tight after you get used to them and timing-based combat like this is always fun to get used to/master.
The weapons have mostly differnent moves and ALL of them have different properties like swing speed and weight, which makes hunting for your own "favourite" weapon pretty fun, as well as changing them up based on the situation at hand.
(i.e. I'm using daggers a lot to stunlock smaller enemies without shields, but use a battle-axe against shielded enemies).
Also armor feels like it has some actual use apart from aesthetics (looking at you Dark Souls 3). Each piece slows you down but offers considerable damage reduction. So you really can decide if you want to be a quick, nimble fighter or a rather bulky slow brute. (or you know, somewhere in between).
Only downside for me would be a missing sprint option or something but someone else already mentioned it and i think it might get patched.
- Enemies / Bosses:
So far the few bosses I encountered were pretty well done, they have distinct styles (artistically and mechanically) to them.
It's the usual cycle if you experienced games like Dark Souls before:
At first the boss is intimidating and you die pretty quickly, then you learn the pattern until you think it's actually really easy, but then you got to play it out without errors until the boss finally dies ;)
As for the enemies they are also pretty varied up until now, ranging from savage fire-ball-throwing beasts to humanoid archers, knights and thiefs. Having seen the trailers there seems to be alot more enemy types later on (like spiders etc.)
All in all pretty fun, each enemy requires a different tactical approach/timing and (as i said before) you might want to switch up weapons depending on enemy type.
- Graphics / Visuals:
Not much to say here, as I generally don't care THAT much about graphics. Gotta say that the artistic style with the rather comic-like look fits the game well. So far the areas are mainly castle-like and forests but I have seen a crypt as well and I'm sure there will be more variety in areas to come.
To sum it up: the game is pretty good. Even more so considering it was done by a single guy!
I'm having fun so far and hope there will be more to come in patches/updates etc.

If you're unlucky enough to have to walk around a large mountain or mesa to find the basic resources you need to get going, you'll spend the entire 20 minute slog back to your inflatable hab wondering what other, much more entertaining things you could be doing with your time. Every time I've played, I've found myself wishing that the "sprint" speed (which your character can't keep up for long without overheating or suffocating) was the default walking speed, and that sprinting was actually fast enough to be worth the cost your character pays.

A well-crafted science fiction adventure.  This game is especially commendable because of its attention to detail and the authors' expert writing.  By the end of the game you will know the map of the Laeril, details about the crew
, and have a small inventory of tricks to solve the various puzzles with.  The story is plausible and original.
I was frustrated by several hidden hotspots -- a regression from otherwise excellent, plot-integrated puzzles.  Once you are aware that you spent 10 minutes trying to figure something out, only to discover that you simply weren't aware you could open some container, you spend the rest of the game wondering if the same will be true about each new puzzle.
The interface felt old-fashioned at times.  The ability to look around in three dimensions, but only stand in one spot seemed awkward.  The transitions should probably just be turned off for all they add to the game, although several cutscenes were well-done, if short, including a glorious compilation of sun surface video (which I think were taken from real videos of Sol!).
Overall, a strong recommendation, especially for science fiction fans.  Certainly not ground-breaking from an interace or graphics standpoint, but this is made up for by the care taken by the authors in crafting a narrative and world to take part in for a few hours.

Bought Dishonored a few years ago, and I admit that it didn't "grab" me right away. However after firing it up again a few months ago, I could not get enough of this game. The INSANE amount of detail placed into this game really makes it for me. This is a game that actually allows you to play HOW you want to play. You are not forced into a certain playstyle with a game like Dishonored. Play as a bloodthirsty maniac, a peaceful protector, a black magic wielding assassin, or just trust the blade at your side and stab everyone you meet. Finally, a game where you can TRULY decide how to play. The only tidbit to this, is that your objectives are somewhat linear in a way.
"This guy is bad. Kill them. Or, find a way to neutralize them so you don't get blood on your hands."
"This lady is bad. Kill them. Or, find a way to neutralize them so you don't get blood on your hands."
"Hey, guess what? This guy is bad too. But more bad than the last bad guy. Kill them. Or, find a way to neutralize them so you don't get blood on your hands."
However, the story and overall experience to this game is still one of my all time favorites. I would recommend this game to almost anyone that enjoys gaming beyond Tetris and Pong.
Pros:
Customise your character how you want to play,
Various endings based on your actions,
Choice of playstyles. Stealth, Guns Blazing, Combination of the two, etc.
Multiple pathways to your objectives. You are not limited to one narrow route.
As soon as the story ends, you want to already start over and play again.
Con(s):
Story could change a bit beyond each level only being to kill someone. Expand on the objectives!!

Liked this game a lot. It's easy to ruin a point and click adventure game (unfortunately), but this one pretty much nails it. Reminds me of what the best point and click games of the late nineties had to offer (think of the Myst series, 7th Guest, 11th Hour, Journeyman Project series etc.). It has good looking graphics, an interesting story that's slowly revealed, an intuitive interface and well integrated puzzles. None of those - I guess I'll just lock my safe with a sliding puzzle - type of puzzles. And also no puzzles that require some heavy lateral thinking in many, many complex steps (remember the puzzles from Day of the Tentacle or Monkey Island?). Some achievements can be tricky to get, but they are fun to find and there's plenty of hints in the forum. I've encountered no bugs, no glitches and no crashes, so the ones that have contributed to the negative reviews have aparantly been fixed. I'm also very glad they included the momentum slider. When I first started to play the game I felt seasick and had trouble clicking things until I turned the momentum WAY down. The only other negatives I can think of is the fact that the enhanced view mode you receive later on in the game has to be actived with the F2 key, which is all way on top of the keyboard. It would have been nice if it had been bound to either the space bar, the middle mouse button or if you could have turned this mode on and off from the inventory screen. Also the cursor changes to an upwards pointing arrow when you can climb up or down a ladder or something similar. It confused me several times having to click with an upwards pointing arrow in order to move down, but I got used to it in the end. Some of the screens could've done with a bit more animation, especially the one in the cockpit. But these are minor irritations which only serves to indicate that there is very little room for improvement. Bottom line: If you like scifi themed point and click adventure games, get this, you won't be disappointed. And even if you're not a fan of scifi themed games you might still enjoy it because it is well made.

One of the most enjoyable, unique, and memorable gaming experiences I've ever had. I played Stage 2 from the start and I'll keep doing it until there's no one to play. No computer game has ever made my heart pound and my breath short like this one. The frantic rage of the monster you control is communicated almost effortlessly by the mechanics, and playing as a hunter is an exercise in cunning and teamwork that is truly rewarding. Of the hundreds of hours I've spent on hundreds of games, my short time with Evolve will always stand out in my memory with games like Diablo II, Halo CE, and Portal as stunning examples of the multifaceted art that video games can be and the emotions and experiences they can communicate and generate.

An arena rogue-like 'game-show' that truelly lives up to what it offers. I saw Forced (the first game) and was very tempted by it for a long time, but then I waited for this game instead when I heard of it... I then waited very patiently for the summer sale and VOILA!! I'd just purhcased one of the best games in my library!
This rogue-like includes deck building, which you then take in with you into games. Each round (arena) you get a card or two and get mana to cast on them - Simple really. But it is done fantasticly so! The variation in the cards is noticable, which makes each one generally unique and useful in it's own way + (as is expected really) each different character gets their own unique upgrade cards, which affect abilities in various ways. 10/10 on this part of the game, the deck building is smooth, easy and beautiful. The artwork of the cards is very nice. And each card feels unique - Everything you could want.
The gameplay is AMAZINGLY smooth, even on ultra settings. I'm extremely impressed with the optimisation + zero bugs discovered. Entire 'game shows' (start to finish) can take anywhere between 10-40 minutes, depending on difficulty and if you die... But of course, you can hop out and jump back in at any point, so no need to do the entire thing in one session! Bonus points from me for this! Each character is completely different, and each playstyle stays true to what it says it is. 10/10 for the gameplay aspects from me, I couldn't ask for anything more from this! Perhaps a few more characters, but it is early days I guess so who knows!
Music... The music and ambience sounds are great, but it can get a liiiiiitlle repetative. It's not the end of the world though as they don't occur too often, and it's the gameplay itself that counts! The sounds and special affects of abilities/creatures etc are spot on. No lags or misleading noises that confuse the player - It's all exactly as it should be. 8/10 for this - As said some things can get a little repetative, and I wish there was a little more variation in dialogue. Not game changing though.
So I highly recommend this game. It's very unique in it's own way, and with a good community going on, 4 different types of daily runs that even the pros seem to struggle with means it ain't an easy game either and there's constantly plenty to dig into! Each battle has different combinations of battle enhancements (good & bad) meaning variation is in abundance too ;) Do enjoy if you pick it up, I'm sure you will!

English developer Stainless Software's "antidote to racing games" was originally intended to be a demolition derby type of game. Both the Mad Max and Death Race 2000 licenses were considered, but fell through, and what emerged from that was Carmageddon.
Breaking from British racing game tradition, Carmageddon isn't about finishing first. I don't even think the opponents can actually finish the race at all. They just drive around, crashing into each other. It's more like Twisted Metal, but without weaponry. Each stage is set in a sandbox-type level filled with hundreds of pedestrians and a few armoured police vehicles. There are three ways to complete a stage. Either you do all the laps, but like I mentioned you get no competition from the opponents; you destroy your opponents by crashing into them, which can be a little tricky at times because it seems like you have to hit them at the right angle to do damage; or you run down and kill all the pedestrians, which can take quite a while.
To progress in the game you have to increase your rank. You start at number 99 and have to work your way up to number 1 to unlock the last stage. In order to increase your rank you have to get a certain amount of credits on each stage, depending on which difficulty you're playing on. You get credits for running people over, crashing into your opponents, going through checkpoints, etc. You lose credits if you reset or repair your car, which is done by the press of a button while driving. The car kind of buckles out like in the John Carpenter film Christine, which is cool. There's a time limit on each race, which at first may seem kind of low, but you easily gain time in the same way you gain credits, except you won't get any time for actually racing.
Controlling your car in Carmageddon isn't the easiest thing to do. I can't really think of a game with similar steering. When you're driving slowly you have decent control, but when you get up to speed and try to turn it's like the car understeers, or a slight turn could make you lose grip and spin out. I usually use the handbrake for cornering, drifting tens of meters completely sideways before gaining traction again. It could be that the lower than normal gravity impacts the steering. At least it effects the way you jump, which is quite cool and makes the game more unique. It's sort of like racing on the Moon.
The game's biggest draw is being able to run people down and being awarded for it. It's not a very challenging game, but it's a relaxing one where you can just sit back and have fun. If you destroy your opponents cars you sometimes unlock them and can use them yourself. They all have a unique cockpit view, if you're into first person racing. Some of them have better steering, some are more powerful, and some are faster, especially a drag racing car which goes insanely fast but can barely steer. My favorite car is the one you start with, because it's the most balanced one, plus it's modelled after David Carradine's car in Death Race 2000.
There's a handful of locations in the game, from the big city to the coast, a chemical plant, a winter resort, etc. You'll have to revisit these places a number of times, racing different routes. This gets a bit repetitious because the routes often cross previous routes, and if you drive around trying to destroy your opponents or kill pedestrians, it's basically just like playing the same stages over and over again, considering they take place in the same sandboxes. The game is a little too long for its own good, but if you play it a little here and there instead of plowing through it in a couple of seatings, it's great fun!
----------
Carmageddon Splat Pack, which is also included in the Max Pack, is an expansion for the original Carmageddon, containing a bunch of new levels and a number of new cars. There are new pedestrians as well, and some new power-ups, but since the levels are the main thing I'll give some short comments on those.
Mayan Magnificence Hotels: Set in a Central or South American hotel resort with architecture resembling the ancient local civilizations. Well-designed map that is fun to play.
MagnaChem Rural Developments Inc.: Rocky and green prison island surrounded by mountains. Not that exciting. Lots of fluffy sheep though.
MagnaChem Abandoned Ice Station: Snowy industrial roads with gaps you have to jump every now and again. Nothing special.
Craggy Isle Dam Complex: This map consists of two islands: one is bright and colorful, with palm trees and a small nice town, and the other is dull and gray, with a boring dam in the middle.
MagnaChem Environmental Disaster: Kind of lackluster. A bunch of high bridges binding together a bunch of small dusty islands.
Nerdberksring Race Circuit: Actually a proper race track. Adds some variation to the mayhem, but it would be nice if the level had some stunt jumps as well.
Musty Ramparts Theme Castle: A large medieval castle filled with hallways. Good for smashing into the other cars. There's also a gravel road that goes through a decently sized outdoor area.
And last but not least, and possibly spoiler alert since you only get to play this map at the very end:
Hell: A big and confusing map that takes place in the underworld, complete with a graveyard, lava pits and burning demons, a flaming bar, Eskimos on ice, and the Devil himself. Takes some time to learn, but once you know how to get around the level is pretty fun.
----------

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a story about the struggles A Good Game encounters while it desperately tries to escape the clutches of its evil stepmother, A Bad Game.
The Bureau is a tactical third person, cover based shooter that takes place during the 1960s in the United States.  You play as William Carter, an agent with the CIA, and command 2 other soldiers as you fight off an alien invasion.  The main draw of the tactical portion is the "Battle Focus" where you slow down time to give orders to your agents, executing movements and plans. There's some light RPG elements that accompany it, where you maintain a small roster of fellow agents and level them up, picking up abilities as they progress through the levels.
Let's talk about the evil stepmother!
Even when you ignore the XCOM stuff, the story is a mess (XCOM fans, read below, but spoilers beware).  It's very generic sc-fi stuff, but it suffers from some weird pacing and organization issues.  The characters have no personality to them, they're just scarecrows with voiceboxes.  Obviously, the bulk of the game is spent fighting, but even that has its issues.  The squad AI can act pretty wonky, and they require a fair bit of micromanagement.  Multiple times, especially towards the end of the game, I would watch one of my squadmembers try and fire at something below him and achieve nothing more than hammer the window ledge for a minute straight.  Enemy grenades are aplenty, and your squad members do a good job of diving out of the way, but this leads to issues whenever they dive into the corner right next to the grenade or decide to charge through enemy fire to get another piece of cover.  I was pretty active with assigning targets and using abilities, but in the beginning I was still scoring 95% of the kills myself.  As your agents advance through the ranks, they get more abilities which help them carry their own weight, but they don't become much handier with a gun.
The squad management stuff is also frustratingly vague- when you recruit a new agent, you can pick a background for them that gives some sort of passive bonus, but the game doesn't give any hard figures as to what it does.  You get a blurb, so maybe you'll get a vague idea of what the bonus confers, but sometimes you don't even get that.  This is also a problem with equipment.  Your agents get two pieces of equipment, a weapon and a backpack, and the backpack features a description of what it does but never gives hard values, and a lot of them seem to do the same thing.  For example, you'll find mulitple backpacks that reduce incoming damage, but a lot of these offer bonuses on top of reducing damage, but there's one backpack that only reduces damage.  Does it reduce more damage?  Who knows!
All this aside, there is a shiny nugget of Good Game underneath it all.  There's a small bright spot in the story that probably lasts for about 20 minutes or so towards the end that was waaaaay more interesting than anything else that had happened so far, but then they decide to throw it away and keep on marching ahead.  The Battle Focus portion has some control issues, but overall I was really impressed with the way plans were executed.  The agent creation system was really interesting, as well, and it was a shame that it didn't offer much more depth or give you much of a reason to use more agents.  I'm convinced that there's good ideas sprinkled about the game like breadcrumbs, and if someone could follow it, there'd be something beautiful at the end.
I still had fun with the game, despite a long list of complaints.  At its core, it's a solid, if unremarkable, third person cover shooter.  While I have no desire to ever replay the game, and I'm going to uninstall it after this, I certainly don't feel as it was a waste of my time.  I would never encourage something to buy it, but I'd never discourage someone from buying it, either.
What I paid for it: 12.50
What I would pay for it: 10.00
Everything in the review is based off of playing it on Veteran difficulty.
FOR XCOM FANS:
As an XCOM title, the game fails miserably, both from a narrative and mechanical sense.  From a narrative sense, my first complaint is that XCOM is an international effort. I get that the game is a tie in, but I don't think I ever heard once the justification of why the organization is called XCOM.  The actual name of the organization is "Bureau of Operations and Command", and then they just start calling it XCOM.  There's also the timeline issue.  The game takes place in 1962, and during the course of the game you get all sorts of crazy, alien technology.  In 1999/2015, when the aliens come back, instead of just shipping over the technology/knowledge on how to beat them, I have to watch my Squaddies die brutal deaths all over the globe because the Air Force lost a Laser SMG in warehouse?  The Council only gets the barest of nods- if you have subtitles on, during the ending scene, someone with the name "Councilman" speaks.  Which, honestly, could just be a happy accident.
Granted, a lot of this can be handwaved away with the word "Spin-off", which is fine.  They pretty obviously co-opted Sectoids into this, but if you were to remove them and all instances of the word XCOM, this would be unrecognizable as an XCOM title.  Which takes us to how the game fails XCOM mechanically.
XCOM, for the most part, has been a game about overcoming insurmountable odds and crafting your own stories as you play through a game.  Yes, there may have been a Squaddie O'Malley in other people's games, but only
Squaddie O'Malley managed to kill two Chryssalids in a warehouse by himself before meeting his untimely end to panic induced friendly fire during the next mission.
The Bureau strips all that out.  Between the fact that soldiers are incredibly hard to lose- once they go down, there's a bleed out period where they die if they're not revived but you have plenty of time to bring them up. Between that, and the game focusing on characters that already exist, you just don't care about your agents. I still know the name of the 6 soldiers who went on my last Temple Ship Assault, but I couldn't even tell you the name of one of my agents from the game.  They were just "Level 5 Sniper I" and "Level 5 Engineer II".  By removing any tension, and making the player character a tough, disaffected badass who growls more than talks, it just turns into a shootbang gallery where fancy special effects happen sometimes rather than a tense, careful advance against enemies who are far more powerful than you.
If you came here for an XCOM title, I'd advise you to keep looking.

Forced Showdown is not your regular twin stick shooter.
It combines the best elements of twin-sticks, hero-abilities and collectible card game into one cohesive game.
You can pick between different heroes each with their vastly different skillset and a companion that helps you. You progress through multiple arenas which consist of 2 phases.
The first phase is the card phase where you can play cards from your hand that either improve your character, or give you short time benefits.
After that you play the arena where the shooting happens. Each arena takes ~1-2minutes after which you transfer into a new arena and start the process anew.
After 7 arenas you will meet a boss that has a high health pool and multiple unique abilities to defeat. If you defeat it you will end this arena set(called battle) and pick from a set of new battles.
Each Battle has up to 5 permanent modifiers that change the flow of the battle and your strategy. They range from simple ones like “meteors fly around the place” to crazy ones like “when your companion gets hit, it attacks you until you kill another dude”.
The combination of those modifiers can lead to depending on your specific deck very difficult scenarios or make you incredibly powerful. To offset a bit of the beneficial modifiers, the arenas in the battle will have more enemies.
When you die or are victorious after several battles you get awarded Gold depending on how far you got for your efforts which you can spend to get more cards.
Important to know: unlike many card-games in Forced Showdown there are no microtransactions and thus the frequency of getting new cards is pretty high. ( iirc i completed my collection after 30 hours of play).
Most of the obtainable cards are very creative mixed with good staple cards. There are not many cards that feel uninspired. They drastically change your abilities without being the boring “5% dmg yay”. They are more along the lines of “when you take dmg, you deal more dmg for a while”. Of course there are some plain stat upgrades in there, but not as much. They inspire you to build a wide variety of decks to try them all out.
Last but not least there are Daily challenges which are very hard, but lets you compare yourself with your friends and requires specific deckbuilding depending on the modifiers present.
With all these switching variables the game always feels fresh and i still log on pretty much every day to play a few rounds.

Timing, they say, is everything. Whether it is music, movies or video-game, the pacing can make or break the experience. "The Bureau XCom Declassified" has horrible pacing.
Take, for instance, the combat. It is an unexciting blend of tactical and first-person shooting. The levels are fairly extensive but are exceedingly linear and at least half of each map are dull, empty stretches where there are neither foes to fight nor secrets to discover. The fights themselves are overlong, made tedious by respawning enemies or slow-moving bullet-sinks. The AI - on both sides - is exceedingly poor and I was forced to kill most of the enemies myself. The best I could hope of my teammates is that they wouldn't get themselves killed while I did all the work. There was a dearth of enemy types as well, with the latter half of the game featuring up-powered versions of the same enemies seen in the first half. Exciting it was not.
Outside of combat, the game had little else to offer. As mentioned, the linear levels hardly rewarded exploration, with few secrets to discover and virtually no interaction with the gameworld. Between-mission, the opportunity to wander through the XCom base was a welcome diversion ruined - again - by the lack of anything worthwhile to do. The story was poorly paced and featured with three boss battles, not one of which had any climatic punch. I also can't help but feel as if the game would have done better if it hadn't been saddled with the XCom franchise; not only would people have had less expectation of it, but its attempts to work around the XCom mythos made the story unnecessarily convoluted.
Graphically, the game was a mixed bag, with some decent texturing and colorful level design marred by unimpressive, stilted animations. Weapons were plentiful (even if ammo was not), and the guns in the late-game packed suitable kick. The powers and abilities, on the other hand, were unimpressive and I rarely used them, although that may have had more to do with the poor interface  and controls.
There were traces of genius in "The Bureau" but on the whole the game was a mess of ideas clumped together into an unappealing whole.

TLDR: An arena brawler rogue-like with a tight, difficult-yet-fair combat system with collectible cards replacing typical rogue-like progression in a very well-executed and interesting way.
The game plays and feels like a roguelike where you progress through randomly generated arenas. Character progression though is done by collectible cards. You build your deck and play upgrade cards from it in between levels. Works great!
What I love most though is how the combat is done - very challenging, and yet so very fair! Every attack is properly telegraphed, there's no bool♥♥♥♥♥♥ no unavoidable hits. And yet the best players in the world still die to endgame daily content :-)
Each of the 4 chars plays COMPLETELY different, with multiple unique attacks and upgrades.
Dailies are very well designed and will keep you engaged for MONTHS!
One of the best games I ever played.

My first review for a fighting game and while I’m not a self-declared fan, I have to say the game was quite fun and it does prove to be a welcome break from the ever-increasing number of platformers that populate Steam’s indie game library. Big Action Mega Fight! is hard to give a binary grade for. I would grade it as a C-, but with the capability of improving its score with balance tweaks. Some things, however, can't be fixed.
If you enjoy Final Fight-style games, this will be up your alley. The levels are bite-sized, and you can upgrade your stats, item drops, and special attacks between levels.
One fixable complaint is the difficulty curve. Enemy reaction times are very slow to start out, and I was not damaged at all until level 15 when a motorcycle snagged me. I did not even know I was supposed to avoid damage to keep my multiplier up because no enemy was coming close to landing a hit. Enemies also go down really easily at the beginning, and it's very difficult not to three-star most levels through the first half of the game. Some HP and reaction time tweaks would solve this issue.
What's not so simple are the difficiencies when held up to the games it pays homage to. Mega Fight sticks to a plain left to right path through largely the same enemies for the majority of the game. There are no bosses. The game simply lacks some of the variety that you need from an arcade beat-em-up to keep things from getting repetitive. A lot of brawlers will switch things up with an elevator level, or introducing hazards/traps, isometric segments, boss encounters, set pieces in places like bars or a boxing ring, etc. Mega Fight does not have any of that. It's left to right, left to right, left to right, the entire time.
Combat could also use some improvement. There is no jump or jumpkick, and combo-ing is not really a thing. I'm honestly surprised there isn't a combo system in here, just the multiplier for damage without getting hit.
The game is still enjoyable though, and has a fun sense of humor and nice artwork and animation. That's what makes the game difficult to give a simple Yes/No to. I enjoyed it enough to play from start to finish. But I see a lot of places that could be improved either by patches or for a potential sequel.

So I loved evolve when it first game out, I enjoyed it alot and I would of even have recommended the game back on its release, however, After playing quite a few games and committing a good chunk of hours to the game to get a feel for it now, I simply can not recommend it any longer.
Lets start off with whats good about the game, It's quick, the matches are 10 to maybe 15 mins long, you get into matches fairly quickly, you dont really have to wait at all, and the players in the game are actually surprisingly good with communication, they tend to use voice more, they use pings, and they use their abilities not just spam their primary gun. The monsters are fun as well, a little less hassle to play as them, feel like you have some kinda chance at lvl 1, and you actually do have some pretty interesting tactics you have to use now inorder to survive the early game. Gameplay wise I would give the game an 8/10, its exciting, its constant, and you really dont feel like your just running around mindlessly like you did in the release version, which in the end does make the game loads of fun.
However now we come to the reason I can't recommend the game at all, Imbalance out the wazzu. Simply put the game is so horribly balanced that its near impossible to win as the hunters unless you fit an exact counter to the monster your fighting, now this is a little easier to do since all anyone plays is either the elder kraken or the wraith, but then you get that one person that randomly tosses in a goliath, and your entire team is ♥♥♥♥ed now because none of you picked a counter to him.
Outside of that you barely have to even be slightly compitant with the monster to take advantage of bad hunter choices, and if you are stuck on a team with bad hunter picks, you better kill the monster within the first 5 mins before it gets to lvl 2, or its over, you can not win the game unless the monster makes a really dumb overconfident mistake, and the game is basically a garenteed loss if they hit lvl 3, most of the time they can basically just ignore the hunters by this point, and just wack the generator till its dead, or if they want to just 3 hit your medic and then pick the rest of you off one by one till your all dead.
That doesn't mean though that the hunters aren't broken too, oh no quite the contrary, if anything actually thats part of the problem, the hunters are so geared towards countering a single monster, that they are basically useless against anything else. Lets use Sunny for example, she uses a mini nuke that inflicts LARGE amounts of damage, places a shield generator for their team, and boosts a single team members jetpack regen speed, and of course the normal support shield boost.
Against pretty much any monster other then one of the larger, bulkier slower moving ones like the goliath, or the behemoth she pretty much can't hit anyone with those nukes, unless they are making the huge mistake, of not moving around. Her shield is great, but aside from the less manuverable monsters like... the behemoth or the goliath, it gets taken out faster then it can be of any real use, and FINALY her boost to a single persons jumpjets is again, only useful to teams who get pinned by the less quick, less manuverable monsters like.... I think you get the picture. However don't get me wrong, it's not like the nuke launcher wont hurt a wraith, or the shield boost wont help your team, but if you fight a kraken as Sunny, your going to be kinda useless in the fight, aside from the occasionaly hit from your launcher, and the shield boost every few seconds, but aside from that... thats about it.

Basically what this boils down to is that they made the game far to counter pick balance heavy, you can't just willy nilly pick a hunter, or even the monster because it might turn out to be extremely unbalanaced choice, and since aside from voice and chat you cant even tell what your team is picking till you pick your hunter first. I dont entirely know why but I get the feeling that Turtle Rock didn't even realize they had made the hunters and monsters so heavily countered by one another. Whats worse is I don't think there is anyway to fix this issue, not off the top of my head anyway.
Needless to say, imbalance is my problem with the game, if they can ever find a way to get the imbalance fixed, so I can pick lennox and go against a kraken and still kick a lot of♥♥♥♥♥with her, then hell yea I say get this game immediatly, but till then, I think im gonna stick to just playing this extremely casually if at all and not recommend anyone who is looking for a less then frustrating time in game play it.

One of the better "Beat'em up" games I've played.  Crisp cartoon'y graphics with well-designed characters.  The reward/upgrade/challenge ramp feels about right, with many different items to upgrade.  The stages change quickly enough to stay fresh and the little bit of story doesn't drag on, but rather adds short humorous banter between stages for a few seconds.
On the down-side, I'm missing two things I enjoy about this genre:
Bosses:  While some harder enemies are introduced every couple stages, and usually first show up as the last enemy of a stage, they don't feel very epic or boss'y.  I've probably only progressed through half the story progression, but in that time, there were no comic-style intros or large health bars, arising out of the explosion that brought a huge boss onto the battlefield.  None of that stuff, but maybe the games saves boss stuff for the end?
Interactive Environments:  Sure, there's the generic stuff:  trash cans, barricades, mall kiosks, cars... but they're all a single frame images, outlined with a black line, as if to say "destroy me for a couple coins".  If items could be damaged (3 - 6 frames) or used on the battlefield (i.e. projectiles to hit towards enemies), that would add a lot of fun to this game.  There's just not a lot to do, other than "Beat 'em up", whereas games like Turtles in Time and the SNES Bevis and Butthead game (among dozens of other good examples, I'm sure) had plenty of fun things to play with while you were doing the beating up.
Overall, a fun game which I'll probably put another couple hours into, to complete and three-star all the levels.  (which makes me want to add "too easy?")

The Turing Test is a first-person puzzle game set on Jupiter’s moon, Europa. You are Ava Turing, an engineer for the International Space Agency (ISA) sent to discover the cause behind the disappearance of the ground crew stationed there.
If you think this looks a lot like Portal or Talos Principle then you're not mistaken. You might say that The Turing Test is a little brother to both of aforementioned titles. Its main mechanic is a sort of energy manipulation, your gun can store up to three energy charges and charges are used for opening doors, manipulating machinery, etc. The puzzles are not very hard albeit a few of the later levels might require some mind bending. I'd say as much as it's Portal-like on the mechanics side, with one main mechanic, it's Talos-like when it comes to serious story. The game is enjoyable even if it doesn't last long, it took me less than 7hrs to finish everything.
It would be a straight recommendation for everyone that liked Portal or Talos Principle, but the crashes. OH TEH CRASHES. The Turing Test crashed consistently on every level load, requiring restart, or in extreme cases hard reset. That means every time I started new level - level means set of 10 rooms here - I had to start the game, wait for it to freeze the pc, force close and restart, on force reboot my pc. Only then I could load the new level. Very annoying. Without technical difficulties it's a clear recommendation, with difficulties... depends on your patience.
