Carmageddon is a vehicular combat 'racing' game by UK developer Stainless Software released in 1997 to much acclaim for its advanced car damage model and sandbox style freedom and plenty of controversy for its depictions of gory carnage against defenseless pedestrians. This lead to an initially censored release for the UK version with zombies that bled green, the only way it was allowed to be sold until a patch was released later on to restore the original palette. The German version didn't fare much better however and was given robots instead that bled oil. Carmageddon's main inspiration comes from the 1975 film Death Race 2000 and was originally going to be a tie-in game but licensing fell through on more than one occasion, to the point Stainless said stuff it let's just get it out.
Carmageddon's a free-for-all race where you're encouraged to do whatever you want whenever you like and there is no restrictions on where you can go or what is considered fair or cheating. Your opponents will often be boring enough to race around the circuit and collect their weak paychecks from the checkpoints scattered about. Your opponents can't actually win anything however and there is no position of your standing in the race on your HUD. That's because you don't have one, and it doesn't matter anyway. What does matter is causing as much chaos as possible by either running down pedestrians, and in creative and gorier ways to net additional credits, and ramming the other cars. Wasting an opponent will give you a lot of credits, and more time than any other activity.
There's a timer that counts down at the beginning of each event and all manner of shenanigans will give you extra to allow you to explore the environment at your heart's content. For all manner of juicy bonuses and hidden bonus dosh/time and various PUPs (power-ups in Carma slang) litter the circuit and the outskirts of the race. These can be pretty gosh darned handy, for example complete invulnerability, acme damage magnifier for really putting a dent in your opponents, or pedestrian electro ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ray for 30 seconds. The wacky power-downs however come in a sizable variety and are usually harmless enough, but make your vehicle harder to drive for a short period of time. Pinball mode though is a worthy mention as its especially nasty and you'll want to recover ASAP if you're flung into orbit to prevent reparing serious damage.
You cannot actually be wasted yourself (at least in this first installment) but credits earned during the race are often used to repair your car, and repairing and recovering when you're on your roof or side will be happening a lot. So it's crucial to scouring and looting the race as much as possible to get more money to have enough left over at the end of a race. If you lose more than you make during a race and you didn't have much left over to begin with when you began the race your bank will go into a screaming fit and pull the plug, and this constitutes as 'game over' here. Failing a race by running out of time isn't penalizing though and you can simply jump back in and try again. You use credits earned between races to upgrade your car's abilities via APO (armor, power, offensive), which are bare-bones as upgrades come and simply make you more resistant to impacts, more horsepower, and dish out extra abuse when colliding into your opponents.
All races are won in three Carma fashions: Kill all pedestrians, waste all opponents, or complete all laps. The latter is reserved for ponces however and won't really give you a whole lot of credits but it's there to sate your particular needs, you weirdo. Murdering every ped is no easy feat however, but most levels usually have a Pedestrian Respawn or two (or three) somewhere and memorizing the locations of these after you wipe out a quarter or two of the population and going back for it can give you an extra edge. Participating in races is also done by a ranking system (which was brought back in Reincarnation/Max Damage) and you start at a lowly 99 with three races to choose from and the penultimate goal is to be number one, along the way will be more challenging environments with more unhinged opponents (and cops in APCs who just refuse to get out of the way). Getting hundreds of thousands of credits an event will move the rank much more (up to 5 increases max or none whatsoever if you're absolute tripe).
The player can choose between two drivers at the start and a difficulty determining starting time in a race, credits and bonus time earned from activities and how aggressive your opponents are. It's best to start on 'normal' and see how you fare, and if you're the kind of person who hides under the table during thunderstorms then easy mode should be right up your alley. Max Damage and Die Anna are the main 'heroes' of the Death Race and drive a similar model of car. Max's all-round great Eagle is better suited to rammin' and slammin' however whereas Anna's Hawk is a faster but less strong car. Nevertheless Carmageddon is an early supporter of equality, and all manner of men and women are subjected to the same treatment. Be it behind the wheel or roadkill in the street. Sometimes when you waste a specific opponent you have a chance of stealing and adding it to your collection. Some of these can be very powerful, others not so much. Beating the game will unlock every single one, including those labeled as 'cheat', your reward for being the baddest dude.
Visually the game is competent, with adequate detail for the environments, early 3D models for vehicles and props that are well designed and pedestrians are rendered as 2D sprites via digitized actors. Their deaths are often extremely gruesome, easily making this the goriest entry of the series even with later installments featuring 3D peds that can lose their limbs. Sound design is loud and crunchy, and impacts with the environment and opponents feel very raw, and the peds incredibly nasty and satisfying. The soundtrack also features four tracks from Fear Factory's 1995 album Demanufacture in instrumental only form, most fitting choice given the game's militant gameplay in a pseudo-apocalyptic near future world.
I have very few complaints with the way this game plays, maybe that it goes on for far too long (36 races) especially if you're trying to do the best you can on each race which can run anywhere from 45 minutes to an hour on average. Late game opponents become real damage sponges if you don't nick a better set of wheels (the Eagle/Hawk just won't cut it even at max stats) and cops are extremely difficult to waste and become very common near the end but if you manage to steal an especially hard to acquire ride in the event 'Blood on the Rooftops' you will know sweet, sweet revenge for all the trouble they were giving you early on and finish the last handful of events with pure bloody malice.
Carmageddon is decidedly British in its portrayal of humor, with plenty of tongue-in-cheek jokes, British slang, and raunchiness suited for a mature audience. Which only makes sense given the dev is UK based. There's plenty of pop culture references from the era, akin to games like Duke Nukem 3D (even has a reference to OJ Simpson here too!). This should've been more than enough proof that Carmageddon's intentions were never meant to be mean-spirited or shock jockery (a suggestion to add pregnant women peds was flat out no'd), just the kind of things that make the devs♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves laughing. And you can tell they had a great time putting this game together, a real labor of love. Carmageddon also has an equally humorous and interesting development history if you look into it more. If you think most racing games are too dull and traditional and you want to insert more mayhem in to your driving experience than this game comes as highly recommended! And if you still can't get enough the Splat Pack expansion has even more content to offer. The antidote to all racers.

Unfortunately, the game suffers from major balance issues, and it's not simply a matter of damage numbers.  The enemy AI is incredibly aggressive, and armed with a seemingly endless number of one-hit-kill grenades.  This by itself would be fine, laudable even, except that your squadmates' AI is horrendously inept and their combat value is entirely minimal.  You have to hold their hand at every single step, tell them exactly where to move, who to attack and what ability to use or they will sit there and do nothing.  But the game doesn't fully pause when you give commands, so every microsecond you spend issuing orders is time you could have spent killing more guys than your squadmates ever will.  Or, you'll return to your maincharacter's body, to realize you're sitting on a grenade.

Old Review:
Ignore what people are saying about pay-to-win here. BiS gear is still only avalible through Raiding and PvP progression and will stay like that.
As of this review the game has entered it's second expansion and this will be based off of 3000+ hours of gametime since I have stopped playing RIFT through steam.
First and foremost, RIFT offers an insane amount of customizability compared to other MMOs on the Market. There are the four basic classes, Clerics, Mages, Rogues and Warriors. Each of these classes can perform EVERY major role (tanking, healing, support and DPS). As a warning though, in order to get every role avalible for every class, you need to purchase two packs that launched with their respective expansions (so unless you pay for the expack souls, mages can't tank, warriors can't heal, rogues can't heal, clerics can't support). Aside from this howewer, the game is still very functional and you can still fill a majority of roles with the exception of one. Another interesting feature is that you can mix and match souls (specs) together to make unique playstyles to suit how you want to play the game.
Second, RIFT offers some entertaining large scale zone events. You could be wandering around in one of the game's leveling zones collecting items, completing quests, etc and suddenly you get a notice on your screen that something is going on in the zone. 2 minutes later dimensional portals (Rifts) open up and start spewing out mobs into your leveling zone and player areas. At this time it is tasked to the players to close those Rifts and go ham on the raid boss that had the bad luck to be leading the invasion. These events provide both a fun way to level and boast a wide variety of objectives, thereby keeping the game fresh.
Third, RIFT features excellent graphics compared to other MMOs (as long as you're not playing on a toaster). RIFT is a game that both plays good and looks good. Character models look good, the enviorments look great and the fantasy world is a prime example of how you design an MMO. Telara feels alive and this is one of the things that keeps me hooked to RIFT.
In regards to the combat, it plays like WoW, but RIFT's customization allows for consistent changes to the flow of combat.
In essence, if you're looking for a MMO to play or have yet to try one, I'd recommend RIFT.

I was relatively excited to try this game after seeing and grabbing it in a bundle. The quick blurb it gave about the gameplay grabbed my attention easily. I love the idea of a fun physics mechanic puzzle or game, because you can take it decently far in a creative manner through careful gameplay development, level design, etc. However, this game disappointed me extremely.
The gameplay was mind-blowingly simple. Drag, release, and watch the "Puzzle" play out. (It's like The Incredible Machine but with a single goal throughout every single level (Get to the portal,) and without the creation/building part, and with only 3 or 4 static tools/machines/variables that affect how the puzzle plays out. Comparing this game to a prime example of a good physics puzzle game really highlights it's bare-bones approach and lack of creativity.
The audio was annoyingly repetitive, and was too dynamic in volume for its own good,
The difficulty was incredibly easy for the levels I played, except for a few which clearly demanded a very precise angle (Not arrived by any other conclusion than trial and error. Not fun. Not considered puzzle-solving in my book.)
I feel like the difficulty or complexity of level design could have improved further down the line, but if a game is so boring as to lose its audience in the first 20 levels or so, then something has gone wrong in the development.
Mostly I feel like this game was a huge missed opportunity. Not trying to slam it or the creators too hard, it's not terrible. It's just, in my opinion, not good.
It is cheap though, and if you get it in a bundle or on really cheap sale, you might like fiddling around with it. I'm not sure, everybody's different, right?

I'm ~30 hours in, and I'm really enjoying this so far.  The combat is a fun, fast-paced, Diablo-style slaughterfest, and the addition of strategic elements really makes the game much more enjoyable and gives a sense of progression in a very fun and unique way.  The difficulty is certainly high, especially once you complete the first show, but a little determination, a little luck, and a few new cards can be all you need to turn it around.  It's a big pile of fun that I've had difficulty pulling myself away from.
There are warts, however:  I've run into some crashing issues, and situations where the game will simply hang the entire machine for a few seconds, but these seem to be getting better with each patch, and BetaDwarf is pushing patches very quickly so far.  The only other issue I have isn't with the game itself, but rather with dicumentation:  It's almost impossible to find good information about the game online.  There is a wikia page, but it has outdated versions of cards, lots of incorrect information, and a new ad on every page (at least on mobile).  Some of it is that the game is so new it hasn't yet built up a community, but BetaDwarf has not done a good job up to now of seeding this information to the players & potential community-builders.  Hopefully, this is just another symptom of small team with a brand-new product; They're probably working like mad right now, and these kinds of niceties will come later.
Maybe once they're done with that, they might work on a multi-player component, or Linux/OS X/SteamOS compatibility??  Pretty please??
Despite these things, I still couldn't not recommend this game.  It's just that much fun.

A sci-fi puzzle game that gives you a pseudo-gun with which to work through a load of puzzle rooms while the over-arching story about an AI gone wrong plays out. So, yeah, it's basically Portal. The story is presented straight rather than with any kind of comedy and the central mechanics contain nothing as mind-bending as a portal gun but still, it's clear where it's inspiration came from. That said, it's definitely A Good Game. It looks lovely, doesn't outstay it's welcome and smoothly accomplishes the trick of introducing simple mechanics then ramping up the complexity. It even manages a mid-game reveal that's not only a pretty sweet plot twist but suddenly changes how you look at and interact with the test chambers. The plot itself starts off strong but kind of falls apart at the end--and is mostly told through ♥♥♥♥ing audio logs because of course it is--but it does the job of framing everything. My only real criticism is that if you've played the Portal games you might find it a bit too easy. It's got a few mechanics in common (light bridges, buttons, etc) but more so because playing Portal just trains your brain so well to parse these kind of challenges. If you just fancy some engaging puzzling, or are usually put off by the difficulty of stuff like Portal, this comes highly recommended. It's also out on all the major platforms so accessible by all.

Meh, it's decent for what it is... has many a flaws but what do you expect for a cell phone quality game?
That being said, there are no microtransactions in this game, every upgrade is earned through game play... It's very grindy like a cell phone game though. You need coins to buy upgrades and if you're lucky you'll get about 50 - 100 coins per stage after stage 10 with most upgrades costing hundreds of coins.
Things you should know before buying this:
- Controls are very clunky and it has an auto targetting system that can actually screw you up and put you in danger.
- Character / object hit detection is horrible, I've been snagged on some debris and it seems the bottom of the screen is really bad for your character getting stuck on invisible walls.
- Upgrade your attack power as soon as possible, this game is meant for you to NOT get hit during stages as you have to keep a score multiplyer running to get 3 star rankings on each stage.
- Fistnado (the first special you unlock) is the most OP attack in the game, it makes you invulnerable to all damage, attacks foes with a D.O.T. the longer you stand on top of them, and once fully upgraded it lasts 8 seconds... With enough luck you can use it on every screen and clear a stage without incident.
Pros:
+ Cool retro references, not just limited to beat 'em up games.
+ Addicting and casual game play.
+ Upgrade system is fun.
+ Star rating system makes you want to perfect levels.
Cons:
- Need to replay levels without getting hit and keeping a high multiplier, can get frustrating at times.
- Not enough variety in battle mechanics. Punch, Uppercut, Roll and Throw... that's it.
- Clunky game design, lots of hit detection bugs.
- Too simple, challenge and mechanics wise, not enough depth to the upgrades / game play.
- Redundent roulette system implemented as a money sink.
- Gets boring quickly, almost seems like too long of a game for such a simple design.
It's a quick cash grab for the developer who's objective was to target a niche, dead genre and target those individuals craving this style of game. It's not a bad game, it's just not very innovative or worth your money / time. There's far better beat 'em up games on horizon, it just seems like the timing of this was perfect. It came out right before the release of some really killer beat 'em up games such as RCRU and Mother Russia Bleeds. It worked on me, I'm here to warn you not to fall in to the trap.
If you must play it, wait for it to go on sale for a dollar or buy it in a humble bundle pack. Again, not a bad game, just really mediocre over all.

Big Action Mega Fight is a brawler/beat ’em up that was originally made for smart phone devices, and it shows, but should be given a chance. The short story is that it’s actually pretty good, and I can recommend the pickup, though there are some design decisions that were made for the smart phone that don’t translate well on PC.
The combat is pretty good; it has a Guacamelee feel with the throwing of units into other units, while mixing it up with some power-ups that include magical uppercuts, spin to win and more. The problem comes from the level design, levels are incredibly short (1—2minutes) and this at times leaves you feeling unsatisfied at times.
The game has some RPG elements, at the end of levels you collect money and you can use it to upgrade your brawler. Very basic stuff, increase HP, increase dmg, increase skill damage, it seems pretty balanced for the PC version, I never felt I had to ‘grind’ to get any levels up. One of the poorer elements copied over from the smart phone is how you choose your abilities. You are only allowed one awesome ability per a level, but instead of choosing what you want it goes to a random roll system, now you can reroll it but it cost you money, money that can (and should) be used to upgrade your character.
Now it may sound like I’m bashing the game a lot, but really I had a lot of fun with the game. It has funny pop culture humour, a nice looking art style, solid gameplay and good replay value through a score system. It’s just a shame there’s small things, which were obviously intended for smart phone that don’t translate well to PC. It’s a great first PC game for ‘Double Stallion Games’, and hopefully we see them bring more titles catered towards PC gamers.
Gameplay, about half an hour in -

Big Action Mega Fight! Is a linear beat-em up game where you play as a character called ‘Brick’ who has to rescue his friend who got beat up and kidnapped from the Gym.  You will be beating down many enemies who try and beat you down.
Positives:
+ Lot's of achievements
+ Lot's of perks and powers to choose and upgrade
+ Graphics are really good
+ Lots of humour sprinkled in
Negatives:
- No windowed support
- No volume sliders
- Only one character to play
- Short stages
I personally enjoyed the game and played it for a few hours. The game revolves around keeping up your multiplier to get a high score to then three star the levels. The game has an abundance of achievements to keep you going through and a lot of levels. My only complaint is some of the stages feel very short and for two hours I have three stared roughly 26/35 levels.
I would’ve loved windowed support as I like to chat on Skype whilst I play games. You only get to play as one character; more characters would’ve been amazing.
Overall though, I had a great time and would recommend this game to most people. I am not a big fan of beat-em ups as I normally suck at them but found this game playable and easy to beat.
Score: Buy.

But if you're looking for a casual beat em up, or want to be introduced to the genre, then Big Action Mega Fight will fill that need for you. The simple mechanics of gameplay are easy to pick up, and easy to play out with simple dodging and a special meter that may charge a little too fast, but allows for you to throw specials around willy nilly. The game gets repetitive quickly, as there's not a good amount of variety in the gameplay. But from a simple visual standpoint, the game works as great characters and animation bring life to battles. The difficulty is too easy for my tastes as I prefer games like Phantom Breaker and Double Dragon Neon, but for those who want something a little more simple, a 5 dollar price tag seems to fit the game in question.

I think it would be amazing to play this game with friends or strangers and see all the rats killing each other!
That said, I think this game is very well-made, and the creator is talented and very kind. He responds to all messages and is open to suggestions. It's really worth 1 euro/dollar, at least at the moment, if other features, like multiplayer, will be added in future, I think it can be sold for more!
Give it a try. It deserves it!

This game is one of those rare gems of an indy title with a lot of potential. Whats in currently (A Skirmish mode on a large randomly generated map between two rat kingdoms) is extremely enjoyable. I can only hope this is built upon and expanded.
The concept of the game is something i find to be rather unique and pretty awesome. The atmosphere of being underground is very much built through the games visual style and soundtrack- the former being customisible to a ridiculous degree as you can pretty much change every colour and shade to how you'd like the game to be portrayed. Small touches added to this, like the zone of light around your cursor that contrasts with the dark, and the fact that the level of darkness can be customized to the point that the small zone around your cursor is all you can see, lends to a very visually pleasing and 'real' experience (This is my view though, i quite like to get properly immersed in what i'm playing!).
The lack of direct control too is something i feel is a pretty good direction, you give overall 'comamnds' and let the wee rats go about their business fulfilling them. Not only does this make for some very interesting gameplay, but also gives a sense of how i'd imagine a rat colony to function (lots of scurrying).
The ability to customize your soldiers in armour and arms is awesome, as is the use of both range and melee weapons. Its small touches of detail like this that make this title shine. The economy aspect is also pretty nice, being complex but easy to get to grips with (a lot of resources, but a simpligied hands-off means of collection).
I've by no means got to grips with this game yet (Indeed i get getting absolutely trounced by the AI- another positive being its difficulty and ability to fight effectively against a player) and look forward to getting back to trying to get my first victory.
Things i would like to see improved upon would be the ability to perhaps have more than two kingdoms fight it out on a map, as well as more content (maybe a campaign or a few different game modes?). Basically just MOAR! :).
Would thourghly recommend. And as of 1/2/17 its still being updated, achievements and trading cards- so my favourite past time of achievement hunting is a go- still getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked though.. so that's the 'defeat' one easy enough :P

What I like so far:
1. The aesthetic.
The idea of rats waging medieval war on each other via tunnel system is amazing. I love everything about that.
2. The art.
It's not a materpiece, but the spites look good and it looks like a lot of work went into them.
3. The music.
I didn't listen intently, but there are 7 tracks. I don't have strong opinions about music, but they are functional. They seemed to fit the theme quite well and I thought they sounded good.
4. The price.
At this point the game is early access. It certainly isn't complete but the bones are there and assuming the game gets finished, $5 is a steal.
What could use some improvement:
1. The UI.
The game has a very Dwarf Fortress feel to it, especially in that commands are given via menu for the most part, but it also shares a similar learning curve. When you hover over an option, a description is shown in the top dialogue box, however that description isn't always clear and you're left not knowing what a lot of buttons do. Building workshops is easy enough, but whether or not they cost anything isn't clear. Resources seem to be spent or created at regular intervals, however there is no timer or window to see where your resources are going or coming from. I was out of food at one point, so I began producing it as fast as possible to no avail. I figured out that I needed additional storage rooms, but nothing indicated that to me.
2. The combat.
Building hordes took some trial and error. There is a helpful menu for creating unit types but I didn't see why not to max the stats of every unit besides a bit of a cost increase. Resources seem unlimited provided you wait for them.
There is also mention of "unit type" which isn't explained. I think it's for creating your own templates, but they have pre-assigned images which makes me think their type implies something about them. Weapon and armor choices don't feel meaningful, but I might attribute that to my lack of experience.
Moving hordes didn't seem to actually work. The only options that made them move were "attack the enemy king" and "go home". I have since figured out how to move hordes.
Things I liked but could also use improvement:
1. Trading.
I like the idea of trading and it really helped me out a few times, but I think it would be better if I knew who I was trading with and if I couldn't trade whenever I wanted to. As it is now, you can trade any resource for any other resource if you wait for the trader's inventory to change every couple of minutes, essentially giving you 4 kinds of currency. I would like it more if either coins were the only currency and you had to buy or sell from the trader or if there was a bartering system where you made an offer and the trader made a counter offer.
2. Color palettes.
I love that there are pre-made color palettes and they look really good. There are several color palettes that are blank white. I didn't look at it too long, but I think those are for making your own. It might be better if player-made palettes are listed seperately from the rest in the interest of removing those blank ones.
Potential bugs:
1. Digging/Building.
Apparently there are 3-ish undefined "lanes" in which you can build structures. I don't know if that was intended, but I think it would be better if you could build wherever you wanted.
2. Unit action.
It might be a bug or user error, but sometimes seemingly randomly, one of my miners would just walk over to the enemy base and get himself killed. I couldn't figure out if there was a way to tell him to stop. He would even dig through walls to get there if he had to.
3. Glitched walls.
This only ever happened with a single wall, but I could not tell my miners to get rid of it. I just had to build around it.
4. Horde movement.
Sometimes units get temporarily stuck on each other in tight areas and take a while to move.
Summary:
Overall I think this game has amazing potential. I wish it didn't have as steep of a learning curve as it does. I think it would benefit greatly from a soft tutorial. Maybe introduce buildings over time as they become necessary rather than having everything available from the start. The game is listed as strategy, which seemed absent. I just built some hordes and sent them in to claim victory with very little resistance and was never attacked while I built up my own base. I was very much hoping to explore the pre-existing caves to find neutral monsters and loot that would give me an advantage over the enemy. I wish there was a way to achieve smaller victories without completely steamrolling the enemy in a single battle. I look forward to playing more of this game with more updates and hope that the community gets behind this one because it could be a real gem if we give the devs enough support.
Edit: After playing a few more skirmishes, I realized what happened to me the first time was not common. Enemies did attack me in my base and I had difficulty taking the enemy base (Actually I was defeated).

Dead on arrival. This game, supposedly "made by people who don't like survival games", is called by some the game that "No Man's Sky" should have been.
No.
Not even close.
Think of NMS what you will, but this game, made in Unity, is essentially a big boring map, with your standard crafting and "survival" mechanics thrown in. It looks good, runs poorly, is buggy, has clunky controls, broken AI, pathfinding and collision detection.
The devs made the decision to "handcraft" the map rather than make use of procedural generation (even though in this case, it would have made perfect sense), because they wanted players to be in a world that "feels designed". They wanted to place landmarks. What you get is a map that is rather boring and ugly (in some parts of the map you can see seams and holes in the geometry, grass are amateurish looking billboards, etc). Especially if you compare it to other games, like GRAV, which use procedural generation to generate equally, if not better maps.
Speaking of GRAV (it's also on Steam, look it up), Osiris is essentially GRAV, only "edgier".
I have serious doubts this game will ever be fully realized, especially considering that the devs announced the switch to Unreal 4 for their other project, because they were displeased with Unity 5.
They will either switch engines along the road, which will end up in delays and further issues, or end this game prematurely, like most EA titles.
Now, i've been harsh thus far. Some positives are atmosphere and music. The aforementioned GRAV lacked one key ingredient: survial.
Osiris made a good first impression upon running it the first time. I was thrown into this Mars-like environment, Spacesuit already broken and before i could even get my wits about me, a giant alien crab emerged and hunted me down. That was good.
But once you get into the game, you realize you're stuck with yet another Minecraft-like game, that will have you grind for materials to combine them into other materials in order to craft storage boxes and buildings.
I whish they went the whole nine yards and made this game more realistic. You know, dispense with all the "gamey" mechanics and be more brutal, sort of like DayZ in space....
Ok, wether the game will fail or actually become better with time i don't know. Just trust me that 22 bucks, at this point of time, will leave you severely disappointed. Get it on sale or just wait and see how it develops.

You can send them to catch the bad guys in a crossfire, or tell them to revive you when you take too much damage. It offers some intriguing possibilities, but the control scheme can be a little bit too finicky. More than once I've accidentally activated the wrong ability by having selected onto the wrong person without intending to.
If you can get it cheaply on Steam sale, go for it. Not sure I'd pay full price, though.

After downloading it I began to play, I immediately fell in love with the graphics, which felt just like a fantasy world, almost FF (final fantasy) like. The combat was very similar to other MMOs I had played, which if that floats your boat then thats fine. In the similar style to other MMOs, you pick between four classes. At first I was a bit bummed by this, but when I started the game I quickly discovered that each of the four classes had about 8+ different skill trees, and you can mix and match three of your choice to find a play style you enjoy. Another great feature is that you can 'save' specfic combinations/roles and have multiple saved roles that you can switch to anytime you aren't in combat, allowing you to easily change your role depending on the situation ahead of you. This was absolutely amazing, and I loved it. I spent many hours just trying out different combinations, and finding the ones I liked best for questing, dungeons, raids, and pvp. Do I want a cleric who summons creatures to help him fight, while also being able to heal my friends? Or do you want a rouge who can tank hits for his allies while throwing bombs onto his enemies?
After creating your character, it can seem that the world is quite linear, as pre-level 50 there aren't very many options for low level characters when it comes to "Where should I got questing??" but even so, within these areas there are a huge amount of quests and unlockables. Post level 50 the game opens up and becomes massive, the amount of content, whichw as already massive, triples. I once spent about 5 hours simply collecting squirrel tears to get a title 'Heartless'. I then spent another 50hours or so trying to find all these hidden creatures that were very rare. I found some cool puzzles to solve along the way as well. The amount of stuff to do was just too much, and I'm not even close to having done 1/4 of the things you can do and complete in the game, maybe I'm at like 1/8.
Another great feature of RIFT is that every so often these random portals will appear in the sky near you, these are called Rifts. You can then randomly team up with others near by to fight the waves of monsters and try to seal the rift and recieve rewards for it. This is huge fun and it really brings people together, instead of just having loads of people ignoring each other and questing. In one area sometimes a special event will happen where it seems that the entire area is underthreat by these Rifts. All the players in the entire area will recieve a warning about this and then can participate in sealing/doing what ever the event tells them to do, and this ultimately ends in everyone fighting a massive raid-like boss for loot. It's an awesome and amazing feature, as you can be simply by yourself questing and suddenly you and a good 20-30 other people are blasting fireballs and smacking the planar dust outta some massive fish or other type of monster. There are many other features that help players come together, one of these is adventures (think that's what they are called). In these you are randomly given to a group of players and you and those players complete all kinds of tasks within an area to recieve different rewards, and occasionally you fight a miny boss. These are also huge amounts of fun and can earn you a great deal of exp.
PvP is also great fun, and is another option for easy/fun exp and rewards. PvP is even rewarding at low levels, as all levels can unlock different tiers of PvP equipment. This PvP equipment can give you a slight edge in the fights during your specific level group (10-19, 20-29, 30-39, etc.). One of the problems with PvP that I felt is that there are certain classes/roles that if one were to use them, you basically dominate the PvP batteground. Of course it should be obvious that some class are better than others at pvp, but it gets to the point where if that class is on the other team, and you don't have it, you just give up, or you know it's going to be an extremely tough fight. One thing I really like about the PvP is how impressive healers are, especially at low levels. I always play healers in MMOs, and Rift was the first MMO that I have played where I felt like I was an absolutely invaluable part of the team during PvP.
There is so much more to this game, and honestly I'm getting kind of tired of writing this review, so I'll just add the things I didn't say into the TL;DR part.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR
Pros:
+Graphics
+Flexibility in leveling/questing/dungeons
+Huge amount of content- achievements, exploration, titles, pets, quests, dungeons, raids, costumes, etc.
+100% FREE, some things that can be bought in a store but one can use ingame money to purchase these if desired, the things that can be bought do not change or make another player more strong than someone who doesn't buy things from the store, with ingame or non ingame cahse.
+The joy of a random rift coming down/invading an entire area and you are some random people group up to defeat it.
+The mentoring system that allows high levels to play with lower level characters, and it will still be a challenge for them and they will still get decent rewards from it.
+The ease of entering into a group for questing, dungeons, pvp, adventuring, etc.
+The sheer amount of endgame content, I reached the highest level and then it still took me another 100hrs to actually have some high level end game gear in PvP and raids.
+One can level up consistently in PvP and dungeons, making them an enjoybale break from other tasks.
+New content is added often.
Cons:
-PvP can feel quite unbalanced at times, due to certain classes/roles being extremely strong.
-Quests can sometimes feel repetitive.
-Can be hard for someone to finaly reach endgame content.
-Depending on what shard you are on, some people can be extremely negative.
-Only limited areas to go to pre-level 50
A final warning to you all.... This game can, and has, sucked away hours, nay years, from peoples lives. Beware!

Edit: My views haven't changed, but I've rewritten the second half to give some clarity to some common complaints I've heard about this review.
Well, this isn't the easiest review to write. Rather than a "thumbs up" or "thumbs down", this is sort of "thumbs horizontal" I guess? There are very strong positive aspects to this game and very negative ones as well.
Typically, anything that markets itself as "discount [game]", is pretty much going to be "horrible [game]". So, Titan Quest is discount Diablo II, Demigod is discount Dota, etc. In this case, Rift is not so much "discount WoW", but "alternative WoW". Now, I've played WoW for a very extensive amount of time from the vanilla to Cataclysm, so I'm pretty familiar with both by now. From what I've seen, there aren't actually any "downgrades".  What WoW players complained about lacking for a very long time were pretty much stocked to begin with, if not pillars of the game itself. These included:
Regional events that keep areas changing and make it more interesting to live in, which includes their gimmick, rifts (portals from another realm that launch invasions on nearby towns).
1-2 player dungeons and easier match-making for full five player dungeons. In fact, because of how build classification works (tank, DPS, heals, support), you are assured that every party will be pretty balanced for what you encounter, since every party must have a tank, a healer, a support, and two DPS.
Guild quests and better guild management.
Mentor level - You can scale your power down to a lower level if, for example, you have a friend join the game and don't want to be grossly overpowered when you play with them.
Sidekick (which I don't agree with) - If you are the lowest level in your guild (which is the only explanation I can imagine) and everyone but you is doing some dungeon, you can temporarily raise your level to the party's rather than being left out of the event.
Instant Adventure - particularly useful if you are just going to be on for ten minutes and don't want to get into the game too deep.
Better UI elements like selling grey items and auction house price trends.
Change classification on the fly - Basically, the skill points that you first chose that got you to whatever level you are can be changed, easily. There's a huge amount of flexibility when it comes to how you play your character. A rogue can be played how you expect it to, relying on range or pets, or it can be turned into an assassin, it can be made into a make-shift tank, or it can be a healer.  Even when it comes to a make, which is typically a glass cannon, there's flexibility about whether you want a nuker-pyro or an AoE damage like stormcaller or AoE heal like chloromancer, you can even have a melee mage. The way you play your character has huge amounts of flexibility with both how you play and how you look, I may never see another game with this range of possibilities. Even though this strategy really only works once you've reached level 60 and unlocked all of your skill points, this is where Rift draws a lot of its strength and it's an awesome dynamic.
Warfronts (medium scale PvP) used to be broken and not match players up very well based on class and gear, but now they seem to be doing better, a few more tweaks with healing and I think I won't have anything to make note of there. The games are pretty good.
Conquest (large scale PvP) is a cluster. And honestly, I don't think a lot people enjoy it because you kinda have to play with your leader holding a gun to your head saying "move when I say move, ♥♥♥♥♥". Well, no one enjoys that, but most people do it because the rewards are high enough to justify it. It's more about leader strategy and numbers than anything you do, personally.
The theming for the original game is great. It definitely loses it and goes off in strange directions when you get into the first and second expansion pack, and that's mildly disappointing, but hey, don't let it get to you.
As has been described elsewhere, the only thing you cannot do without spending money is using the auction house and all of your potential bag slots - and as little as five dollars unlocks those. This is ridiculously cheaper than the $15/mo WoW charges for the privilege of the same service. That said, the devs still need to pay rent, so a real money store is available in-game. 90% of the items are cosmetic; the other 10% are basically broken into two categories: Spend a small amount of money to get a slight boost to gold, exp rates, etc. Spend an exorbitant amount of money to get significant boosts or an item outright. In, literally, all cases, you may not purchase any item in the store that you cannot get some other way in the game.
I donno, how can you work at a job for ten years, say you like the work but simultaneously hate working there?
The players suck. No really, they honestly do. I would take Dota people over these guys in a heartbeat. I have never in my life seen such a hostile group of folks in a game. It's kinda hard to get immersed in the environment and experience that I just described when there are fifty people at any given time complaining about how much they dislike the latest patch changes or the expansion systems or how their support ticket wasn't answered in the same day they submitted it...every single thing that the devs do is just a life-threatening crisis. Over a period of time, this really starts to affect your mood. But it's an MMO, a platform that is supposed to be around social constructs, communication, and collaboration. It's possible to turn off the chat and play completely alone, but dear god why should I have to do that?
On the free hours I'm so ungreatful for: Like I said, I support some sort of substitute for a subscription requirement in order to bring new players in and pay the dev to continuously add new content, since they continuously need food. I've supported substantively in that regard to the tune of about $60, which I find to be reasonably fair for the time I've gotten out of it. To say that I'm shooting down this game without chipping anything in is factually false and irritating to hear.
Ultimately? You should NEVER log in out of a sense of duty or sunk-time fallacy. There's a difference between "logging into relax and have a good time" to "logging into a stressful environment of conflict because of your virtual obligations". It seems like the hostile environment originated by the development team allowing themselves to be treated as punching bags, but changing their mind and punching back. Hard. So, the forums are dev/gamer flame wars, and the in-game world is nothing but passive aggressive condescending tones and internet♥♥♥♥♥kickings to the minority of people who agree with the devs.
I think where I differ from most people (unpopularly) is that I'm willing to say that the developers are equally as bad as the consumer.
Running a game you've created for a hundreds of thousands of people is challenging and every machine and gaming instance will be different. People will find bugs and as a dev, there's no hintbook or place you can just google that says how to fix it. Problems take time and experimentation and there's no promise of success. However, allowing a hostile and combative atmosphere serves no one and just lets people feed off of each other's hate. But adopting the same combative attitude as a dev? Is simply abhorrent.
As a player who has no stake in the matter: I got my 400 hours, the devs got their money, and now it is time for us to part ways. If I had known what I do now, I would not have enjoyed it nearly as much originally, which is why I can't enjoy it now. Those two sentences may be the most reasonable justification for a review decision you're going to find.

This is an awesome game! (If you're into rougelike games with a card game on top)
The challenging gameplay keeps you frustrated and addicted at the same time. The game has a decent introduction to the mechanics and overall rules of the game. When they are mastered it is off to do arena after arena to earn gold to buy cards to ultimately better your chances of winning more gold and more cards in the arenas. So an infinite loop of fun.
However it can get repetitive to run arena after arena to get more cards and thereby grow stronger as a character. Since there is no end goal in the game, other than getting better at the game and growing your card stack.
This is the strongest and weakest point of the game. You get stronger for every card you earn, but if you lose sight of your progression you might lose interest in the game. This is not to say that the gameplay is not fun, challenging or exciting, because it is.... It definitely is. Every match is a new beginning and the frustration of getting a bad card or the relief of getting a good one has an emotional impact on you every time.
It is a game you can play for a short periods of time and still get something out of, which is a nice change of pace compared to longer games. You can boot-up the game and play for 10 minutes and have a blast in those 10 minutes. That makes this game a nice "let-me-just-clear-my-head" game. The only "downside" is that you might get hooked in those 10 minutes and unable to stop for the next hour or two. ( This happens to me all the time)
To recap: A really addicting and challenging game with a nice touch of randomness to it. You might lose track of the main goal in the game, but you will soon forget that when you are blasting your way through enemies and earning cards.

"Among the Innocent: A Stricken Tale" is a walking simulator set on a farm in the Free State, South Africa. Some of the puzzles are abstract since the relationship between objects and the environment is not always clear. Thankfully, optional online hints assist the player in solving the puzzles. With clever cultural references (especially within the South African context), "Among the Innocent: A Stricken Tale" is an enjoyable game worthy of the current competitors in the walking simulator genre.

Exploration Adventure
Standard mouse and WASD in first person
Single Player
You start out trapped on a farmstead in the Free State province of South Africa, and have to figure out a way to get rescued.  There are items that you can interact with and puzzles to solve along the way.
If you enjoy games like CSI where you have to explore scenes and combine items in your inventory to solve problems, then you will love this game.  I generally avoid these types of games (I prefer the RPG survival genre), but I picked up a copy of it at the Rage gaming festival in 2016 when I saw it was set in South Africa (how cool!).  Despite the fact that it is not my proverbial cup of tea, I would still recommend this game. Particularly if you are South African, you need to support this game - it is high quality and inexpensive.  I'm proud that this was produced in my country.

Surprisingly good.  The game feels a bit like what you'd get if "Scratches" and "Dear Esther" had a love child.  The game marries the best features of both to create a rare style of exploration-based adventure game that you don't see very often.  (I wish we saw games like this constantly).
The first half of the game is very, very strong.  Fantastic atmosphere, a real sense of exploration and wonder, an excellent union of beauty with a sense of the decrepit, and an impied mystery left entirely to your own imagination -- you'll most likely start to ask yourself, "What the hell happened here?"  Answering that question is arguably the main plot, but is left entirely to the player.  In terms of finishing the game, you can completely ignore that aspect of the game and focus only on the puzzles instead.  This gives a true touch of realism to the game, as you're FAR from hit over the head with the story.  It's fantastically there, but the option exists to go about your business nearly oblivious to it.
Puzzle design is also excellent.  Difficulty is usually exctly right, and most are rigorously grounded in logic.  This does begin to break down towards the end though, as the game features two puzzles that are arguably far more difficult than they should be for tenuous reasons.  [Update 2/19/17: The game has been updated to make these puzzles far more fair to the player.]
That leads to the game's only real negative: the second half of the game is less strong than the first.  I don't want to get into spoilers in a game review, so suffice it to say that, eventually, "an appearance of supernatural elements" bubbles up.  As the game was managing to be a near-perfect example of realism-based atmospheric horror before then, this change actually feels unwelcome when it comes.  The ending, however, puts a renewed ambiguity on even that which makes up for it.
That said, the only REAL flaw I care to highlight is the two not-exactly-sensical puzzles that will likely grind your firstplaythough to a long, abrupt halt where you'd least enjoy that.   [Update 2/19/17: The game has been updated to make these puzzles far more fair to the player.]  However, if you have a gentle walkthrough to fall back on for just those two moments, this is definitely forgivable for the rest of the experiece.
Highly recommended.  You want this game.

Ah, Carmageddon, a game where you don't just race other opponents, but also try to destroy them, and run over hundreds of innocent pedestrians in the process. Wicked fun. And you are rewarded for all of this, which makes it even more fun. The game even lets you know how many pedestrians there are on each level, so you can make sure every single one is mangled.
There are some old games that I think have really good looking graphics, even though they aren't very realistic like modern games. Carmageddon is one of them. There's a grittiness and personallity to the graphics that new games don't have. The lower detail of the graphics also gives the game a little more challenge, as it can be hard to see things coming up at times (at least before you get used to the graphics}.
The game can be annoying at times though. I found the vehicle handling/controls hard to get used to as first. At least with one car, you can easily get stuck to walls, and have to steer into the wall to get free. That doesn't really stop being annoying. Also if you go too fast up a steep hill, you can end up launching off and flying way too far, and will end up needing to be recovered. These minor things don't detract from the fun though.
The game has some good music that goes good with the game. There some rock songs and some electronic songs. But if you don't like them or get tired of them, you can always turn on some Metal. Metal goes great with this game.
Carmageddon is a lot of fun. If you like games like Postal or GTA. If you like running over people, wrecking cars, and causing chaos, then you will like this game. If you haven't already played it and don't own it, then you should get it now. Or when it's on sale.

"Beauty is only skin deep." That is how this game felt like.
Seeking for a new MMORPG to play, I saw this game's trailer and was attracted to it. I started to download it and was surprised that it was over 18GB and thought that it must be really awesome. After the download, there was a patch that was over 13GB so I became impatient and was like, "This better be good." Then after gruesome hours of waiting, I was able to enter the character creation (which was unimpressive), and was finally in-game.
So first look, the game is visually good (just visually though). I ran around, explored and quested for several hours and this is what I have observed:
1.) The game is too passive and lacking
- I can't believe this was released in 2011 and it still plays out like an incomplete game today with little to no scenario and AI. It feels like those custom made warcraft maps in the works where only the terrain and units were layed out and has nothing much else to offer. Mobs are just standing all over the place or roaming all over the place with almost no purpose. There are a lot of things you can see and interact with that seems to have no significance at all.
2.) Poor mechanics and balance
-Special mobs or bosses, don't seem any different from the regular ones, just higher hp. Character's normal attacks are almost negligible, skills suck, your hp goes down almost the same rate as whatever it is your fighting then you regen everything so quickly after being out of combat for some time. Potions felt so irrelevant, you get mobbed by two enemies of same level, you use one, not so much hp recovered and the cooldown is so slow you just die unless you run, good thing the system is so undeveloped that if you just run with low hp you'll survive somehow because all of the nearby mobs just ignore you. They say dynamic battles in their site, but i don't see anything dynamic at all even in their videos.
3.) The interface and controls are not so user friendly
- This is the first time in my whole gaming history where it took me quite a lot of time to figure out how to navigate and use the interfaces. Equipping, buying, selling, etc. everything was just ugh.. not so convenient and the game heavily relied on right-clicking for no good reason.
4.) Unattractive and unamusing character 3D models
- For a game that looks so grandiose with a folder size of 37.5GB, it is just so sad that the character model's designs and movement are so mediocre and generic. Aside from the disappointing character creation options, I went in to battle just to find out how lame these models move. I can't believe that I was already using or chaining skills with what I was seeing, as they were not so far off from looking like a normal attack.
5.) Lots of features and game elements
- This game has a lot of content: multiclass characters, mounts, fishing, crafting, cooking, alchemy, blacksmithing, rifts, bigass bosses, etc. Aside from the visuals, this was the only other good thing about it. The system was just so bad despite being a non-beta game that I spent most of my gaming hours just fishing instead.
In conclusion, this game is such a waste. It has a lot of good concepts thrown into it that you just don't see or feel being projected in-game. If they can rework and improve their system, then it can probably be one of those games with ultra large communities that last for years.

*What is Forced Showdown?*
Forced Showdown is a strategic top down, twin stick, rouge-like shooter with card elements. Gameplay closely resembles Gauntlet, or a much differently themed Binding of Isaac. It feels fluid and fast paced. The rouge-like strategy comes in the form of the in game card system. You will feel right at home if you ever played Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering. If you haven't its not incredibly complicated, but provides many options and strategies. Now, BetaDwarf delivers a game which blends a in-depth card game and an easy to pick up but difficult to master rouge-like twin stick shooter.
*What do I think of Forced Showdown?*
I love this game! I have played many hours of The Binding of Isaac, Terraria, Ziggarut, Rouge Legacy, RIsk of Rain and other rouge-likes you probably havent heard of. I have to say this game is among my favorites and its brand new. If the in-game season mode is implemented correctly I have no doubts this will be my favorite!
*Why do you like this game?*
Mainly, the card deck customization is so great because it makes this rouge-like feel more like its in my control instead of "I hope I grab the right items so I can play the way I want". Getting new cards is not as grindy as Hearthstone and is paced excellently. This way, the replayablility, theory crafing and experiences are all fresh every time. Next, this game is challenging, but not unfair. This is a very hard thing to get right in a game and Forced Showdown delivers. Most rougelikes become very easy for me once I learn the mechanics, this game tests me at every step. Of course, none of this would matter if the gameplay wasnt fun or interesting, its great.
*Any problems with the game?*
I havent had any issues at all with this game since I bought it and put about 15 hours into so far (very strong by todays releases). The game has some slowdown in between rounds (1-2 seconds), but it never effects the actual gameplay.
*Other thoughts?*
If you like any of these games I would seriously consider at least trying this game:
The Binding of Isaac
Hearthstone
Magic the Gathering
The Diablo Franchise
Path of Exile
Gauntlet
Rouge Legacy
*Overall*

Mechanics 9/10 - Game flat out nails combat and the card system. Game isnt bare but would love more content.
Replayability 9.5/10 - With the new cards you earn, new ways to play. Keeps me coming back.
Reliabilty 9/10 - Game doesn't crash, haven't seen any bugs. Though, I have a monster computer and it stutters when rounds are over.

It feels weird doing this for a game which I've actually gone through and completely beaten/gotten 100% of the achievements for, but I can't really recommend Gravity Badgers.
Gravity Badgers is a simple puzzle game where you choose initial direction and velocity of your character, and then their trajectory will change based off of the type of planets you're near (some attracting, some repelling). You're attempting to direct your character to a warp at the end of the level, optionally picking up 3 items along the way.
It's very simple, and I suppose accomplishes that initial goal well enough, but in a lot of ways it just felt lacking. The character graphics are very static - at times feeling like it's a cut out sheet of a character moving around, but without the graphic design to make it seem like that. A large majority of the levels are actually VERY easy, with a few levels that are extremely finicky - there doesn't seem to be much of a middle ground for a pleasing challenge. And finally, there's boss levels, where your character starts shooting lasers at an enemy while they're going at you, and which has pretty much nothing mechanically which relates to the rest of the game. They feel weird, very out of place, and don't really "work."
This is very obviously a budget phone/tablet game, and probably better suited to that medium. If these sorts of games appeal to you, sure, go ahead and pick it up - it's competent enough in its own right, aside from minor other technical issues (a little bit of sloppy edge detection for some of the hazards, primarily), but ultimately the game is pretty rough around its edges. It worked well enough for a mindless distraction while I was also doing another activity (TV, work, etc), but there's not a whole lot there, and I doubt most people would enjoy it.

One Shot takes a tries its fur-hands at modern Adventure games, giving you control of the pregnant-with-a-light bulb main character Niko--a non-gender specific cat person a'la Undertale--tasked with restoring the sun to the world.
The game's biggest flaw: the writing. It's important to point this out first, as not to end on a note the suggests this is a bad game. It's easily better than any episode of Car Talk you might listen to, and by sheer aesthetic beauty alone, is worth playing through as one of the few adventures that doesn't require an Arc'teryx jacket or Hydroflask. The writing has moments of wit and irreverence. When the writing's good, it's great. There's a man who's reading in the library: "Third cup of coffee...can't stop reading...curse the author and his beautiful cliffhangers." Too often NPCs are a game of telephone, passing down vague boring Messiah talk. A common conversation goes something like, "You will be the one to save our world from eternal darkness" or "OMG, You're the Chosen One" or "Muad'dib! Muad'dib!" (I'm 68% sure about the latter quote). The characters mostly exist to interact with you, not to live a quotidian life the way one would.
The biggest problem with traditional adventure games has been the obtuse puzzles. In the worst cases the right item to use is what the designers intended, and not a mere logical answer. Some of the later meta-puzzles in One Shot take some extra head scratching, but thanks to an oiled hint system, don't slow the pace down much. One Shot keeps the old school puzzle solving logical, rewarding experimentation and letting the players get lost inside the atmosphere rather than have their minds wandering off to an FAQ.
And atmosphere this game has in baskets. The score is a reverb-heavy, sustain-filled synth composition by Nightmargin. It's a sobering OST that would fit in at the finest Cancer wards of California. Looking to cry? Looking to feel nostalgic while smoking a cigarette? My friend, you've come to the right game. The music pairs with the despairing landscape like a cheese does with the perfectly chosen Trader Joe's flax seed cracker. The Gas Fields are a digital Gregorian chant. The Abandoned Factory whispers with a staccato pipes. The sprite work forms beautiful high cityscapes, lush forests, and a foggy land worth diving into and just living with through moving meditation.
At around the four hour mark One Shot's not long, doesn't need to be (we all got sh*t to do) but makes every minute a pleasure. A full sensory experience. Something one could show their baby boomer parents and wouldn't immediately be told to stop wasting their time, as all baby boomers have money to make, as time is money, so get to work and lose the childish hobbies now as their still may be time to apply to the bank--they're hiring, you know.

When I first heard about "The Bureau: X-COM" I was both happy and sad, I was excited that it was going to be set in the 60's, I'm a sucker for old timer stuff (L.A. Noire, Mad Men etc.) but I also found out it wasn't a strategy game like "X-COM: Ememy Unknown"... I was very skeptical at first, however after playing it for a couple of days now, I have to say I'm thoroughly impressed and my earlier skepticism was completely wrong, this truely is a great game!
The visuals are absolutly marvelous, so much detail put into almost everything, the games style really captures the 60's era beautifully, as well as the sci-fi elements, all executed perfectly, beatiful and surreal at the same time. The sounds were also top notch, from the perfectly tuned soundtrack to the subtle ambiance of computers humming in the background, distant battles and leaky pipes, gun fire and explosions, the pew pew pews of laser cannons and the screams of Grey's being splattered on the battlefield, it all truely sucks you into the gameworld.
The combat is much better then I expected, a great merger of 3rd person shooting and tactical strategy feel very comfortable, lots of skills/perks and 2 partners to issue orders to at any time, a little bit of management thrown in for good measure and lots and lots of skillful headshots and well placed grenades fill the action quite nicely, I was never bored, the difficulty was just right, unlike "Enemy Within" which could be hellish at times.
Lastly is the story, overall it was quite good, had a great start, good pace, very strong arc.... then sadly fizzled at the end, I was a bit confused on the complete 180 the main character pulls in the last 30 minutes of the game, didn't make sense to me, besides that tho, it was quite good, lots of notes, photos, recordings and characters to interact with to enrich the backstory.
In the end, I had a great time with "The Bureau" not quite sure why all the negativity towards it, I was a little skeptical at first but I'm glad I gave it a chance, one of the better games I've played all year, a great little mix of X-COM meets L.A. Noire meets Mass Effect, three games I absolutely love!

FORCED SHOWDOWN is a rogue-like action RPG mixed with strategical gameplay elements.
When you start a game for a first time you should a pass a tutorial campaign and only after this you will get the access to the "real" game. Here you will find a three campaign , all have a different difficulty levels, so to the unlock a next one you should beat a previous.
Here you will find four playable characters with different game style and skills, but at the start you can use only one, others you will unlock later.
All leves in a game have 8 different arenas, in first seven you should kill only minions and at the last you should defeat a boss. All levels has his own rule, also arenas always are random generated, so every time when you start play that again you will find a different environment, traps and monsters. Also you have a companion, what help for you in a battle with enemies. One thing maybe can be annoying for you, and this is that: if you die you should star all from the beginning. Only two things you will not lost after death. The coins what you can spend in a market to get random new card to our decks and the "quest" progress. The quests just just some tasks as kill 6 monsters in a 6 second , kill 200 monsters, etc.
The tactical part of this game: cards. You start a level at the first arena with 4 cards what you can use before start a battle if you have enough points to the chosen card. At the first arena you have one point, at second two, and this amount grow till eight point when you reach a boss battle arena, so you should think before use the cards, because sometimes maybe better to use two or three cheaper cards than one expensive. Also a cards has more types, some do instant action, some add a buff for little time and some are upgrades to your stats.
The game graphic looks nice, well fit to the game style. This can say also for the music, this well fit to the action-packed gameplay.
So my verdict
+ nice graphic style
+ addictive gameplay
+ random generated levels
+ good music what well fit to the game action
+ great atmosphere
+ interesting mix of RPG, rouge-like and strategy
+ steam achivements
- optimization problem
- bugs and crashes
- long loading time
- the companions AI can be better
- not to much various bosses
- when you die you should start all from beginning
- no trading cards

The concept of the game is nice, but the other aspects are what ruin it. Well, the concept can get a little boring and repetitive after a while too.
Almost every surface in the game is white. Pure white. It's not nice. Maybe in first sight. But after a while it starts to hurt your eyes a little bit and get on your nerves. Almost everything you see is white. It's like being in an isolate room in an insane asylum. Pure white is all you can see.
The physics or game mechanics or whatever you want to call it is not well made and broken half the time. In the game you use red movable blocks to boost yourself a jump. From my personal experience, about 9/10 of the times when I wanted to boost myself with a red block, I would either end up clipped inside the block or if the block was moving horizontally I would end up on top of it instead of being pushed (boosted) by it. So this really breaks the game. Even if I was the pro master in the game, my no-death speedrun would be ruined just because of the broken game mechanics. Something that I have no control over.
Level designs are meant for you to die at least once in them. Not specifically because they are challenging, but because you have no idea what's gonna happen when you shoot a red block. It can just make a small platform infront of you or just extend 50 meters and shove you off the platform you're standing on. And you'd be staring at the screen thinking "Seriously?". So you have no idea what's gonna happen when you shoot a red block unless you've played the map before or it's plain obvious.
The crouching feels unnecessary. And you can't quite tell if you're crouched or standing up because there is only a slightl change in perspective and nothing else but your speed to make you realize that you are crouching and not running.
But even the slower speed can kind of take a while for you to realize. Since almost all the surfaces are complete pure white, you don't really have a point on a surface where you can measure your distance from. Kind of feels like running in a void with everything you see being white. You can run but you don't know if you're running or just thinking that you're running. (excuse my bad English, this paragraph was not wrote with the best English skills)
Dying feels cheap. You die a lot. From both broken game mechanics and bad level design. And when you do, it's not like "Damn, I messed up." it's more like "God damn stupid block!" cause you either got shoved off by it or clipped inside it or etc.
The game does not feel fluid for a speed-running game. Controls are uncomfortable, game feels laggy and if you overcome all of that, the game mechanics can simply get you and stop your run. Yes, I am mentioning the broken game mechanics for the third time because it is simply game breaking and the most annoying thing I have ever encountered.
The game was fun in the first few minutes until the above started to show themselves. I get that this is a project a student made for his university project but that is exactly why it shouldn't be here on Steam. You're just now learning to make actual games and you decide to throw your broken first-game into Steam without polishing it or fixing its bugs?
I did not enjoy this game and do not recommend it. You may think your experience may differ completely, but believe me, you will be in the same situation as me but with a different amount of tolerance than I. So you can either get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of more quickly or tolerate all the problems until the end. That simply depends on who you are and does not mean that my statements are completely wrong.

Turing Test is similar to games like Q. U. B. E.   I know people have compared it to Portal, but the comparison is limited, as Portal is a really novel and unique puzzle game with a major new mechanic, Turing Test falls short of that.  It's a VERY good puzzler with some great puzzles, but never has the uniqueness or depth as Portal.
But the puzzles in this game are solid. The game does a good job showing the player something new in a clever manner, letting them learn it and then using/playing with that concept for 10 levels or so before introducing another new concept.    The core game here is excellent, and the gameplay loop is fun.
On the other hand if a player is looking for something off the beaten path, there is 7 "secret rooms".  Though each is a very obvious door in the corridor.  Each secret rooms adds something new to the formula only for itself.  Most of them are rather well done, though I found them to require some odd thinking the game barely hints at.  One of them was hard to do on a controller, and when I found out the answer, it was mostly something that I had never considered.  Another one required a move that I thought was a cheat but found out to be correct.   Honestly I liked those secret rooms a lot, and appreciated their uniqueness.
However the puzzles in the main rooms of Turing Test are nothing to really challenge the player, they're interesting and fun but it takes small hurdles and just increases their height almost in time with the player.   In fact the longer I played Turing Test the shorter I felt rooms were taking me.  One of the only rooms that took me a long time was more due to the act of doing rather than figuring out the puzzle.
On the other hand the final room being one of the only ones on the main line I needed to look up a solution for, but mostly due to poor signage/visibility of a feature that was only used in one other puzzle.   A real shame, because it was one of the best puzzles, it just is near impossible to solve if you missed that one feature.
At the same time the game includes a story, and at first the story is a bit odd, about half way through the game there's a turning point for the story, and then nothing happens with it until the final minutes of the game.  It's as if they felt a big reveal needed to happen.  The problem is the reveal hurts the suspense, and doesn't really explain a great deal of the story of the game.
Without spoiling, it's a story that the more I think about it, the more it doesn't work.  But even with that the story did keep me engaged because it talked about a variety of interesting topics as I ran between rooms.  This kept my interest in a way I wasn't expecting.  It just isn't very good in the long run and bad in retrospective.
Still I came for the puzzles, and got a very solid 5 hours out of this game.  The game IS 20 dollars, and that's entirely too much for a relatively standard 3d puzzler, but at 10 bucks this would be a strong recommendation.
I recommend this game based on the strength of puzzles, not on the story, though the story will be strong enough to keep you hooked, it let me down at the end, however the gameplay was tight enough I'd consider running through it again after I've forgotten a few of the solutions.

is a puzzle game very reminiscient of the
series. Chances are if you enjoyed those, you'll enjoy this one.
Mechanically, the key difference between the two is that here, instead of portals your gun manipulates energy sources that are hooked up to doors and other objects with cables.
The game introduces new energy sources, consumers, and circuitry at a reasonable pace, allowing the player to get comfortable with the currently new element before throwing the next complication at them. The elements are introduced intuitively and unceremoniously. A completely new set of gameplay mechanics is introduced about halfway through the game, refreshing the gameplay and expanding the variety of the puzzles.
Optional rooms provide a bit more of a challenge, but each of the seven chapters only contains one of them, making them a somewhat rare and easy-to-miss treat.
Visually, the game is very appealing, thanks to the power of UE4. There's not really a whole lot to say about the graphics other than that. The lighting is appropriate and the puzzle design is constant without any "reskinning". The screenshots and trailer on the store page represent the graphics quite well.
The story, unfortunately, is the weak part of the game (spoiler tags not just for decoration).
Borrowing from
HAL9000, T.O.M. is an AI system sent along to support a long-term exploration mission and unsurprisingly
. Other than the completely predictable plotline, the game brings up some interesting thought experiments around AI, most prominently
.
The other crewmembers are not particularly memorable or deep, but
that doesn't really matter too much.
Audio logs and notes scattered throughout the world provide background details. I found myself abandoning these about halfway through the game because some audio terminals will contain four or five different recordings, requiring you to sit through them to click the next one.
Overall, the game is a decent puzzle game that should take you anywhere between four to five hours, depending on how much of the background stuff you pick up and listen to/read. The story isn't particularly riveting or inventive, but I came here for the puzzling, anyway.

The Good:
+Easy to get into.
+Good story.
+Good sneaking mechanics.
+Multiple paths to complete a mission.
+Interesting powers.
The Bad:
-Feels too short, the ending leaves you wanting for more.
-Dialog options feels meaningless.
-No Mod Support
I cannot think of anything else.
Overall:
I would recommend it, it's worth the experience which is very unique.
