Well, I've only played about 16 hours or so, but I feel like I've already done most there is to do in this game.
I know it's still a work in progress, but in my opinion they should have waited until it was more of a game. In it's current state if feels more like a feature test of selected features than a game. So at this point I can not recommend this game, but I will keep my eyes on it and change my review accordingly as it progress towards the end product.
A little annoyance I find is that the description of the game is written as if planned content is already implemented and should probably be rephraced so that potential buyers know what they buy.
The graphics is very nice, with decent vehicles, player avatars, droids and buildings. The monsters however feels out of place, as if they are taken from some zombie themed shooter game and the environment itself is rather bland and featureless. The terrain seem to be built from a bunch of craters and hills with occational patches och vegetation, huge trees or boulders. And the far too frequent storms and long night obscures all scenery most of the time.
The wildlife variation is currently quite small. Ive only seen seven different types, which all wants to eat you the moment they spot you. Different types can even attack you simultaneously while ignoring each other, which really hurts the beatial feel of them. Logically larger monsters should eat smaller ones and so smaller ones should avoid the larger ones, yet here they all ignore each other. The A.I. is much better than the general "run to straight to target and attack" script that is common in games these days, but it still need some work. The creatures can still get be tricked into corners below cliffs and such. They do however seem to dodge shots, retreat between attacks and flee when low they are close to death.
While the crab monsters have lots of hit points, are difficult to hit and causes a lot of damage per hit, I can not classify them as being difficult, and they are the toughest enemies except for that gigant worm that just comes and eat those who are slow to move, which is a nice touch. :)
The script that keep spawning monsters at the player's location every X minutes and the trigger than spawns monsters while mining are just just major anoyances, they add nothing to the game more than meaningless fights which makes an already long walk to far away resources feel much more of a chore than an expedition. And monsters in spawnng pits respawns a tad bit quick. All in all, I don't want to see any creatures drop from the sky as they do now, unless they where capable of flying and just landed from flight.
The building are bare minimum, and most of it has no purpose besides decoration yet. And the crafting is just as limited.
There are five different vehicles craftable at the moment, A hover bike, two different sized rovers, a mech and a space ship. The bike, the smaller rover and the mech comes with guns, while the larger rover and space ship are only good for carrying goods. I've only tested the smaller rover myself, and it handles well and was even fun to drive around, even though there currently are no power consumption and from what I can tell, it seems to be invulnerable to damage as well. The space ship however seems like a waste as there are nowhere to go beyond the starting planet yet. There's currently no droid crafting either, nor any form of research. And I've not found any way to get ridable monsters either.
The third person camera has it's aim off from the cross hair it seems, like the vast majority of similar games.
The caves I've found are really just large tunnels with a few monsters and a lot of resource nodes.
That's all I could think of.
As stated above, I'll change my review according to changes to the game.

Oneshot will inevitably draw comparison to Undertale due to its perspective, pixel artstyle and emphasis on story, but similarities stop about there; plus, I wouldn't want to dissuade people from this game because "It's like Undertale". That's reductive and does not do this game any justice.
Don't get me wrong, I've played both games and (spoiler alert) have enjoyed them immensely, but Oneshot takes a subtly different approach to its gameplay. Oneshot omits any sort of combat and focuses on its character interactions and puzzles. Some of these puzzles are fairly simple affairs - the kind you'd find in a point-and-click adventure game. The greatest puzzles in this game however, require you to quite literally think outside the box. I'll keep details light here since they're worth going into blind, but as a hint: the game encourages you to play in windowed mode because of these puzzles.
Also a fundamental difference between the two is the relationship between characters, in that YOU are one of them. No, you're not imposing yourself on the protagonist, you are a seperate character altogether, just as the protagonist is also their own character. This becomes one of the main focuses of the story - the relationship between you and the protagonist. Niko is a young and innocent child and will frequently turn to you for guidance, or just simply ask you about yourself, and you can respond in kind through dialogue options.
It's getting hard to say much more about this game without spoiling something big, so just to quickly wrap up here: If you're looking for an
, Oneshot will provide a memorable one. Nothing in this will rush you, you can take things entirely at your own pace and the game is wholeheartedly suited to those who will take their time to explore and immerse themselves in the world. The writing is strong, and ensures an entertaining and emotional journey through Oneshot's world.

Carmageddon isn't just an awesome game because it's essentially the playable version of the movie Death Race 2000 (
), it's a great game because the hard difficulty turns the game from a bloody yet loose open-world pedestrian masher into an actual racing game that requires quick thinking and huge balls.
I personally think Carmageddon plays it too loose with its formula. You get huge, huge amounts of time to actually complete the race, and every car you destroy or every civilian you run down adds a not insignificant amount to it. I wanted it to be more like an actual race, one where you have to quickly explore and find the secrets in order to get enough time to either finish or kill your opponents. Something quicker and snappier. I found out that Hard mode solves all of my complaints - you start out with 30 seconds, which means you need to start driving on the sidewalk immediately to turn wholesome North American guts into fuel for your hell vehicle. It encourages breaking off from the "track" to see the city and find new exciting pedestrians to murder. It is tough as♥♥♥♥♥♥but it is well worth it to see all the cool hidden areas the developers thoughtfully put in. It's that or wander around the track until you decide that killing every pedestrian is a ♥♥♥♥ing tedious exercise and end up destroying the other combatants. Or finishing the race, because you are 50 years old and you need to get back to filling out your Old People Forms.
Anyway, Carmageddon is one of the greats and despite my moaning about it it's still goddamn fun to play after all these years.

Im torn by this game... But overall, I really enjoyed it.
On the one hand, I love all things XCOM, ever since the Amiga Days I have been playing this franchise and loving it, in fact, some of my favorite gaming memories have come from XCOM.
That said this is NOT your normal XCOM game.  Its an over the shoulder FPS like Gears of War.  Gone is the research and base building, you play the part of an XCOM agent, a damn good one, but not the man in charge, just the man in charge of getting things done.
First the good things.  The story is quite good, I found myself immersed and wanted to know what would happen next, for me at least, it was a game where I could suddenly have that "oh crap" moment when I realized I had played all night and the sun was coming up.  Although you aren't making all the biggest decisions in the game, you do have several "choices" you make during gameplay that can affect the game somewhat, although, to what extent im not sure as I have only played through it once so far.
The characters are all believeable and well done, you can run around the base and talk to several of them, getting little mini quests or more backstory.  I found myself doing this quite a bit, I can tend to be a completionist, and beyond that, I was genuinely interested in fleshing out the storyline and the missions you can unlock can help you to recover alien weapons and artifacts that then become available for future missions.
I had some gripes with the game as well, sometimes the controls can seem a little clunky in the heat of combat, it has a slow motion "bullet time" like mode in which you can order your squad mates (max 2 at a time) to get under cover or use their abilities, which actually works quite well, but sometimes in the middle of running for cover its difficult to hit the left shift button or the C button to dive/roll/jump over obstacles.  It seems like it was never optimised for mouse and keyboard. Another complaint I had was the levelling, I found my squad mates at max level within the first quarter of the game, which left me feeling like I was wasting a lot of levels, especially considering there seemed to be more room for upgrades (and for some special characters there is) I also was semi-frustrated by the lack of options for some of my soldiers.  Want your support/engineer guy to use a rifle?  Too bad, he has to use a Shotgun or a SMG.   That said, there is a lot of variety in how you can put together your squads, even with only 4 different "agent" types.  Support/Commando/Sniper/Engineer.
All in all these are minor gripes, and really didn't lessen my enjoyment, I played the heck out of this game an beat it in about a week.   I frequently lamented that I didn't get to use some of the more high profile characters in my agent selection, but found the interactions between them and the main character quite interesting and quite easy to get invested in.  I truly feel the story of this game is quite strong and had me more involved than normally in games, although its pretty linear when it comes down to it.  You aren't the one designing a strategy and developing the resources to defeat an enemy from beyond our imaginations.  Yours is not to wonder why, yours is but to do or die.  Thrust into that scenario, I found I really enjoyed the setting and characters populating this game, and most of my enjoyment honestly came from them and the atmosphere you can only get from a 1940's/50's style "War of the Worlds"

Back in 2010, 2k Marin decided that it wanted to develop its own cheap knockoff of Mass Effect, but "Cheap Knockoff of Mass Effect" was not a very popular title in focus testing, so they licensed the XCOM name to apply on top like a smiley face sticker might be applied next to the "F" on your child's report card.  It bears almost no resemblance to the beloved franchise, with no research or base building, tiny squad sizes, very little squad management, and a plot that is incongruous with the original games as well as Firaxis' recent release.
In the course of development, it was then determined that creating additional missions or even coming up with a form of randomization would be too costly, and besides, what people really loved most about Mass Effect was running around the Citadel over and over and over.  So with The Bureau 2k Marin adopted the philosophy of Twice the Fedexing, Twice the Fun, and you'll find approximately 90% of your time in game is spent shuffling at a slow pace, unable to sprint or run or jog or walk briskly, up the stairs, down the hall, up some more stairs, down another hall just to talk to someone, and then back down again because even though you have a plasma pistol and laser rifle, nobody has yet invented the walkie talkie and everyone wants to talk to you.
Unfortunately you will occasionally be accosted by actual gameplay, forcing you to briefly abandon your quest for a new world record in Most Stairs Climbed in a Video Game and shoot some aliens, but luckily these missions are short, incredibly easy, and entirely forgettable.
In summation, I highly recommend picking up this game if you intend to play it only while honing your real-life drinking skills, though don't mistakenly assume that your in-game character's past drinking problem will make him more identifiable to you or provide any sort of character depth to make you at all invested in the backstory to the game, because 2k Marin thinks "character development" is a reference to the linear upgrade system available in the extremely limited RPG element of the game.

I'm re-writing my review for this game, after giving it another shot. My first impression of this game was really bad, though I had a pretty bad set of arenas and I didnt like the starting character. CGamer commented on my review as seen here:
Massive props to him for going out of his way to get me another coupon (though refunding it did actually return it to me but its that he went out of his way to actually do it that counts). After reinstalling and conceding the first game to unlock a second character, the game became A LOT more enjoyable.
So first off let me explain why I didnt like the game the first time:
The squire of light is the character you start with. He's pretty basic and really easy to play. I'd first bought the game thinking it was multiplayer (Which was bad on my part) so I then started treating it as a single player game and wanted to see if I'd like it before the 2 hour refund time. The Squire of light was just boring to play to me. The game was so that I didnt know if I'd be challenged at all, I barely got hit after I'd played the first 2 arenas, everything died incredibly fast and the characters playstyle just didnt apeal to me. On top of all of that, I randomly selected the same 2 templates multiple times and didnt have any fun fights in them anyways.
The second time I played:
I played Volcar (I think is his name, the hammer guy). He's melee, he's got a melee attack that you can chargre rather than just aiming a laser at people, his starting deck is really fun, and most importantly his playstyle was alot more what I was looking for. I never played him in the original FORCED because my friends would pick him, so I intially went in thinking I'd try to make myself really tanky, because that's what I enjoy normally. But I quickly found that stacking as much offense and playing like a berserker was what I really enjoyed about him. Not only that but I got different tile sets this time and actually had some close counters in combat that made me really enjoy it alot more. As well as encountering new, harder enemies on tile sets I'd seen before.
Aside from my personal experiences of the game, I've always thought that the whole concept of the game is awesome. I love roguelikes, and if you do too, you'll most likely like this game as well. There's heavy replayability in the way you can build your character between each game. You've got your deck which you can customize, you get delt different cards each individual arena fight. Across a single campaign you'll basically 'level up' and get a set of boons to pick from that can give you different buffs. So as per your typical roguelike, you can be delt a very bad hand that can make your run very hard. Luckily in this game you can most likely just outskill everything despite being weak from what cards/boons you're offered. Which is something I love. Challenge and replayability is important in roguelikes.
Anyways, I just wanted to update my review so this game has the rating it deserves. I'll probably update it as updates for the game come out and as I get further in the game.

I've heard "Angry Birds" thrown around when describing Gravity Badgers, but it really isn't. The similarities end at the slightshot pullback that you do to start every level (and gravity fields, in the case of Angry Birds Space).
Gravity Badgers mostly involves you flinging your badger to the exit, picking up to 3 energy cores along the way which decides how many stars you get for the level, after deducting one for each failed attempt. This makes it that there is often very little you can do fix a failed first shot and it usually boils down to making a shot and hoping that it grabs all 3 pickups and successfully makes its way to the exit. In essence, lives are irrelevant and most levels are fling and pray. There is little actual gameplay to speak of, if any.
Levels are mind-numbingly dull. Between every frustrating "GAH ALMOST THAT LAST GRAVITY FIELD UGH" level lies maybe 5 that involve flinging your badger in a straight line. There are multiple characters to unlock, but as far as I can tell there is no difference besides the slight visual changes on the character.
There is some nice art in the game that they use to move the story as you progress through the zones, but the in-game visuals are just hilariously underwhelming. Between the S-shaped space worms that lack all actual animation and squash and stretch on the spot and the way the protagonist flips like a piece of paper after speaking with his granddad, you'd just wish they'd put maybe a bit more effort into the visuals.
I might not enjoy Angry Birds, but I can strongly recommend that over Gravity Badgers any day. I doubt even mobile gamers can be engaged with this title.

TL;DR Even if the market for puzzle games was ten times the size it is (there's really only Portal and the Talos Principle to compete with), this would still be an outstanding game, with interesting puzzles and deep meaningful philosophical questions to ponder on.
Shortly after being awakened from stasis by an AI, you get dropped on the Jupiter moon Europa. The ground crew has discovered an alien organism and has broken all contact. Upon arrival on the surface, it quickly becomes clear that the whole station has been rearranged into puzzle rooms, a Turing test which can only be solved by a human and not an artificial intelligence. While parts of the developing story are predictable, I always found the philosophical questions about Consciousness in AIs, human behaviour and other moral choices (which I will not detail for story reasons) quite interesting and found myself repeatedly opening up wikipedia for further reading on the topics raised. That said though, if those don't sound like the kind of topics you'd find interesting, then a lot of the story would turn out boring for you and if you're hoping for the type of witty humour you'd see in Portal, you'll be equally disappointed.
Puzzles were interesting and steadily increase in challenge. Armed with a gun which can take up and fire a variety of differently coloured energy baubles, you have to mindfully power a number of different devices (such as magnets, platforms, switches, doors) to successfully make your way deeper into the facility and find whatever happened to the original crew.
The game looks beautiful and is clearly build with love, however the look of some parts of the station can sometimes feel somewhat repetitive between new sections, especially if you get stuck in some areas for longer.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend the game and sincerely hope for a sequel.

This game looks nice and has some decent puzzles, along with good voice acting, but the story is so lame and heavy-handed that I just can't recommend it. After six chapters of being beaten over the head with the terrible, mind-numbing, faux-philosophical back-and-forth between the main characters, I used a walkthrough for most of the last chapter so I could get the game over with. I have 25 hours in it, but that's because I kept getting bored in the middle and pausing it to watch videos or work on something else.
Mild, general spoilers:
--the character moments, the setting, etc.--has to be memorable and interesting. I didn't really feel that's the case here. The characters are awfully one-note.
The puzzles require plenty of backtracking. I definitely did enjoy some of them, and most rooms took me some time to figure out, but overall I didn't get as much satisfaction from solving them as some other action puzzle games because of said backtracking and because there are so many elements in play by the end of the game. When there are levers and moving walkways and beams and conveyer belts and magnets to move around, I started to feel like the room was doing all the work and not me, if that makes sense.
I will say that the optional secret puzzles and the audio logs/notes/items you can inspect do a much better job of telling the story than the main dialogue does. I went back to 100% the secret rooms after completing the game and I liked those a lot more than most of the rest of the game.
I recommend the game on sale to people who like puzzles, but don't get this if you're in it for the story.

Dishonored is a paradox. It's most satisfying mechanics are extremely violent, but the game punishes that indulgence with a negative ending. Yet it's in the DLCs of Knife of Dunwall and Brigmore Witches that the game takes full flight. Corvo is replaced with the grim figure of Daud. Finally, killing or the more pacifist angle makes sense from the view of an assassin pondering a career change.
Highly recommended, violent and fun.

So Dishonored 2 came about, lots of people had been praising Dishonored, so since it's on sale on steam, why not give it a try.

There is Chaos, which is a pure evil alignment. There is also "Order" which is Lawful Good. The Order fights you, since you are deemed "Evil" by the Order. Order also keeps Chaos in check, so if you kill Order, more Chaos wil occur. Chaos would be certain events that is not good, obviously. I won't spoil anything.
Due to the nature of the game, that is "play the game your way" nonlethal & lethal playthroughs, you can replay the game twice, just to experience both outcomes.
Play time:
Took me 14 hours to complete the story, I attempted to explore everything. That was only 1 playthrough, you have an option to play diffrently if you want. I went for a mostly nonlethal.
The Good:
+Easy to get into.
+Good story.
+Good sneaking mechanics.
+Multiple paths to complete a mission.
+Interesting powers.
The Bad:
-Feels too short, the ending leaves you wanting for more.
-Dialog options feels meaningless.
-No Mod Support
I cannot think of anything else.
Overall:
I would recommend it, it's worth the experience which is very unique.

Now that I have had a decent amount of time exploring this game I can give a decent and honest review of the current build.
Osiris is a game to keep an eye on going foward.  A shout out to the developers.  This team is pretty responsive to the player base and have been giving updates on up future updates.  I hope this continues as the game progresses.
In the games current build it is playable and fun.  That being said do not expect a large amount of depth to the game just yet because there is a long road ahead of adding more content.  I am not going to go into specific bugs because after all this is Early Alpha and bugs are expected.  I want to be clear though, in its current build Osiris is very playable.
The last major update did a bit more to balanace resource gathering.  At first I was not a fan of the change in Resource Nods to Base and Precious.  After playing I undertand why they did this.  Before you could gather resources a little too quickly.  This made it a bit more challenging as it slowed your speed of progress down.
The visual scenary in this game is very enjoyable.  I am sure better resolutions will come in the future as well.  For single player its very entertaining to explore a harsh, Mars like world with some creepy crawlers.  Beware, exploring caves can be horrifying, take lots of ammo, & medical aid when going into harvest rare resources.  Cave exploration will keep you glued to the screen for sure!
I do miss the ability to turn off the aliens in single player on a current saved game.  This gave players and chance to just explore without be viscsouly attacked every few minutes.  So far this is my largest complaint, the creatures behavior and agression rest time.  The respawn time for enemies needs to be turned down and the render distance for enemies needs to be increased to at least 200 meters.  It is annoying to have enemies spawn directly over top of you & when enemies actively spawn to hunt you down every few minutes even when you are just standing in your HAB minding your own business.  Hopefully this is adjusted in the future only time will tell.
Sound wise, not expect the best quality in the current build.  Sound transitions are rather misleading and often annoying.  Do not turn off the music, this will be your soul indication if enemies have targeted you.  The wind effect does get on your nerves after about an hour of game play.
I will not give this game an offical rating on a scale of 1 to 10 yet because it is far too early to do so.  For $24.99 on the steam market it seems a bit pricey in its current condition but I feel I am getting my moneys worth so far.  Osiris will hinge on the developers of this game to keep positive momentum, which is what they have been doing since the release date.  The Developers are correct when they stated Osiris is "Really big & ambitious" hopefully they can deliver :)

For players unfamiliar with PK, I'm gonna keep it short and simple since it's been 13 years. It's a fast-paced old-school FPS, akin to Doom or Serious Sam. You take on the role of Daniel Garner, a man who is trying to reunite with his wife Catherine after suffering a fatal car accident. Your beloved wife ends up in Heaven, but you're stuck in a Purgatory that's  undergoing an invasion plotted by Lucifer and his army. So you're on a mission to take out the lord of Hell's generals (and eventually himself) while blasting away his minions to a heavy metal soundtrack.
Hell and Damnation is essentially an HD "remake" of the original game, which follows the storyline I just described. It is technically a sequel, because it branches off of the original game's "bad" ending, but you play through the same levels again. Well, some of them.
So if you've never played H&D but you're familiar with the original, is it worth getting its high definition counterpart?
.
.
.
.
.
.
No, it isn't.
Keep in mind that this review is mostly intended for fans of the original. I'm gonna be making A LOT of comparisons with it. If you're new to the series, you've just read that H&D isn't worth it. So just get the Black Edition.
The graphics may be fantastic and the nostalgia might be there for long-time Painkiller fans like me, but this game suffers primarily because it's a cesspool for glitches. More often than not, monsters will get stuck on the map and you'll have to find them yourself. You might think you can just use the compass to navigate your way to them. But most of the time, they're inside parts that are almost unreachable without skilled bunnyhopping. It's especially frustrating when you're trying to obtain a Black Tarot on a level you must beat under a time limit. Moreover, the developers just so happened to take away the most memorable levels from the original game such as the Asylum and the Military Base. What's that? Oh, they're in the game?
Yes, they are. If you can afford almost $50 worth of DLC. Let that sink in for a moment.
Fortunately, the gameplay is still fun and the soundtrack kicks♥♥♥♥♥just like in the original (but WHY did they have to remove the Loony Park battle theme). All of the levels are still diverse and unique in their own terms. The enhanced graphics make the environments look amazing (I mean, Jesus Christ. Look at the remade Oriental Castle). But if you're familiar with the original PK, you'll find that a lot of key features are missing and/or tweaked in H&D. The checkpoints do not "heartbeat" when you're close to them, Painkiller-jumping is impossible, enemies are not visible through walls in Demon Morph mode, there's no autosave feature (might be wrong but I swear it was not in the keyboard config menu) and the Stake Gun's arc is a straight line that loses its height exponentially after travelling some distance. These are just to name a few, but the game suffers from these problems because it forces us to take some time to adjust to these changes. I would've preferred if some of these changes were simply identical to their original mechanics. Other than that, the ported levels have slightly new layouts and some secrets and enemy placements are a little different, but I have little to no complaints about these.
There's also more multiplayer game modes, a coop mission, and survival, but since I haven't tried these yet, I won't make my judgments yet.
Overall, I do not recommend this game to PK fans OR PK newbies, but the game does have its moments and like I said, very nostalgic. Do note that I did not play this game to find flaws; the ones I listed stuck out to me the most as a long-time fan of the series. You can still find some enjoyment out of H&D ignoring all of its flaws, but expect to encounter some frustrating moments at the same time.

I'm a new player who's never played any of the alphas or betas and have never watched any full youtube gameplays before.
I bought this for Christmas to play with my younger brother since he's always wanted to play it, but wow was this an utter frustration and disappointment for so many reasons.
(1) First off, the amount of bugs and troubleshooting I ran into just trying to START the game. I have 1920x1080 monitor and EVERY TIME I start up the game, it flickers this horribe and eye-soring green and pink overlay. It's apparently a bug that still hasn't been fixed, and you're supposed to press F11 to force the game into window mode, but this only works 3/4 times, so I end up having to constnatly restart the game sometimes until it works. Occasionally, it'll just freeze on the main menu for me. It also froze on the main menu when I was looking at the settings. Also, during the first cut scene, my character was just absolutely frozen and I couldn't look around or move at all, even as objects in the background (the rolling ball) was clearly animating and still working. These were just some of the first bugs I ran into, and I also ran into some more as I kept playing.
(2) A lot of the gameplay and puzzles are unintuitive for new players. There's no clear objectives or goals; you're just dropped into the world and left to figure out what to do. I usually don't mind being left to learn what I'm supposed to do, but this was just ridicously frustrating since what the game expected from you (aka how to complete the puzzles) is so bizzare. I eventually had to just give up trying to figure it out on my own and just look up a guide, since I had no idea what I was supposed to do, like in Act 2 when
despite having little indication that that's what you're supposed to do.
(3) Bad key binds and inability to rebind keys. Why do I have to hold E to pick up items? Why do I have to tap E to open doors or hide in closets? Why do I have to tap right click to drop an item, but hold right click and then let it go to throw it??? Why can't I just have different keybinds for this stuff??? Why did you make them share the same keybindings???
(4) Lack of animation. For a $30 game, the lack of animation was so disappointing. I've only seen small snippets of the alpha version when my brother used to watch it, but it seems as though the company didn't add in any new animations either. When you use a key on a lock, the lock just falls off and that's it. When the neighbor catches you, he just runs up to your face and that's it. When you pick up a chair that's blocking a door, it just pops up in your hands, and that's it. If this was a $5 or $10 game, I wouldn't mind this, but for its price, I expected a lot more.
Overall, this game is NOT WORTH $30. If it was maybe $5 or $10, I might be fine giving it a pass, but as of right now, no. Especially with so many bugs still present in the game too, it's lack of intuitive puzzles, it's lack of commands like rebinding keys or playing in window mode, I really don't feel like enough effort was put into this game. I would NOT RECCOMEND THIS at all, especially to any new players, and you're seriously better off spending $30 on any other game.

Being a game collector and having a soft spot for badgers (don't we all??) I just had to pick this title up.
Gameplay is simple but with a ton of levels (140) and the 'puzzles' getting progressively harder, you will soon start scratching your head a little for those perfect scores. Each different colour planet has certain gravity effects (like magnets). The idea is to collect all the stars and land in the portal via one click of the mouse. Easier said then done. ;)
Graphically speaking it's built on unity so easily scales up for higher resolution setups. While the game is built to probably resemble Angry Birds in some ways it most certainly has it's own charm. Controls are simple to match the gameplay so keyboard/mouse work just fine. Click and drag to set your launch arc and acceleration level. The game has a decent electronica based soundtrack and while there is no voiced dialog the 'story' is driven along via lovely artwork done in a comic book style.
Enjoyable little game you have here Wales Interactive. I'm honestly quite surprised.
Maybe wait for a sale but I can recommend this title. Only 5bucks afterall. :)

In brief this is a lovely little puzzle game. Provides a good challenge in a gorgeous environment and an engaging little story. All the controls work well and the game mechanisms are all smooth, a credit to the work of developers. I originally encountered The Turning Test at EGX a couple of years ago. Hadn't heard about it before, nor was it on my list of things to see. It was just a happy coincidence that I was walking by and the demo was available without having to wait for anyone else to finish. So I sat down and gave it a go. Ever since then I put it on my wishlist and waited for the full release.
The Turing Test is a clever little game about a woman, Ava Turing, solving puzzles which were designed to keep the artificial intelligence out of areas. (Essentially demanding that only a human could make it through.) It's flooded with a real passion for the question of whether robots and artificial intelligences can ever truly hold consciousness or whether this is an exclusively human trait. This game is probably aimed at the gamer who isn't just a puzzle solver but probably a professional scientist too (or at least has some kind of significant interest in various scientific areas.) The attention to detail on this along with the writing is very good and keeps the whole thing very engaging. I won't spoil the rather clever twist revealed at the end, but it is a moment to think and reflect upon the whole story.
The only cons to this game are that it came across to me as a little too easy. Then again I stormed through the Portal games in 2 or 3 sittings so perhaps that's just me. This leads on to my other con which is I felt it was a bit too short. (Whole thing lasts 4-5 hours if you're not taking any breaks.) As a result of this I'd suggest getting it when it's on sale. £10 seems a reasonable price to me and the regular price of £14.99 isn't a million miles away so a 20-30% off sale is probably the time to grab a copy.
All this considered, I've got to strongly recommend this one. A very enjoyable play and I'll keeping an eye out for the next  release from these devs.

Alright then.
4 hours in, and I can already tell you that this game is amazing. Not good, not great, but amazing!
And here's why:
1. The combat is enjoyable the way you would expect from an action rpg like torchlight. It is fast paced, but you have the time to think about your actions at the same time. It is simple, yet skillbased.
2. 4 heroes, who feel different. They are different enough to make sure, that there is a character for every type of player. And on top of that, you can customize each one of them with a unique deck.
3. Speaking of decks! This is not just a gimmick. Fans of deckbuilding games will have an incredibly enjoyable time with this part of the game. You can play each character in an unlimited number of ways depending on the deck you choose to take into the arena.
4. Random stuff. If you like the randomness of Binding of Isaac, you will love this too. There are random arenas with random enemies with random buffs. The boss has a random effect on the arena, and you will get random boons along the way. There are so much random stuff that I couldn't write all of it here. The great thing is - You never feel helpless in the same way, Isaac makes you feel. The random stuff is there to help you (mostly), and it feels great.
5. Cards... Come on - you get to spend ingame gold to buy a ticket for the  card-lottery machine. I imagine spending 100s of hours earning gold and spending it on more rolls in the lottery. Its like opening boosters, but with INGAME GOLD!!!!
6. Cute pets. I don't need to say more about this... but I will - Some of them are called puffs, who give you a bonus if you make it through an arena without it getting killed.
7. Interesting bosses. These guys are like vanilla WOW bosses. They are challenging and rewarding at the same time.
8. Difficulty. The first hour of the game, I was like "Man, this game is too easy". Boy, was I wrong. At the second level of difficulty, the bosses also start drawing random cards against you. I got curbstomped haaard. And I loved it.
There are a few cons to the game though.
The servers aren't very responsive. I got kicked out in the middle of doing a daily, and couldn't connect back up to the server again :( This will no doubt get fixed, but its still annoying.
There seems to be a slight issue where the game almost crashes. Sometimes the game freezes in a loading screen and windows tells me that the program has stopped responding. It comes right back up a few moments later, but apparently windows detects a freeze which isn't good.
As you can probably read, I am already a fan. I will keep playing this for a long time to come (hopefully), and if I find more stuff worth mentioning, I will update this.

First things first,before I say anything, I want to say that this is an incredible game. Now this game casts you as Corvo, the body guard of the royal empress of Dunwall. After tradgedy strikes the city Corvo is forced to become an assassin and lead the fight to free the city from it's new oppresive leader. This game features primarily stealth gameplay though it is optional, you don't have to sneak if you want. It's fully possible to beat the game running and gunning and murdering everyone that stands in your way. It's also possible to complete the entire game without killing a single person. There are side quests you can complete within each level and many collectibles that can allow you to upgrade your sneaky assassin powers. The gameplay is incredibly smooth and addicting, the game's graphics aren't the best so it doesn't take a powerful PC to run it. Thankfully, the graphics don't hinder the overall experience. The music is great and the overall atmosphere is incredible. I would fully reccomend this game to any gamer who likes great games.

The noblest pursuit of all gamers and petrol heads is encompassed by this masterpiece of digital entertainment.
A timeless classic has been brought back from near extinction. The cumbersome obstacles such mastering the reverse-engineered DOSbox and the long outdated supported Operating Systems and 3DFX cards of yester year are no longer the illuminating beacons holding the guiding light toward vast citiscapes of twisted metal and burning rubber.
Here, today, on this mighty platform we can share the elation of blazing through crowds of gormless pedestrians and wildstock, the exhilaration of t-boning your adversaries with an oversized dump truck and the exhaustion of being rammed all night long, unrestricted, uncensored and untainted by the passage of time.
Do I recommend this game? Yes.
Was my childhood a bright one? Yes.
Will you be forever ruined as an upstanding citizen of your country? It goes without saying, but... YES.

This is the classic that paved the way for many racing games to come.
This is a game that in 1997 created the racing game sandbox experience that would become a staple for the genre only many years after.
The way cities are sectioned into multiple tracks, and the way it doesn't impose a single objective, the way you can change focus between doing checkpoints, running over pedestrians, wrecking your opponents or just exploring the sandboxes is so ahead of it's time that even now, almost 20 years after it's release and after the mist of controversy has dissipated, it still feels fresh and an achievement in videogame design.
That it's gameplay and it's itch can still be scratched only by itself even now, so many years after it's release and so many clones in between says much more than anything that has probably been written.

I've been interested in evolve ever since it came out. I never had the money to buy it and when i did the game "died".
Since it became F2P i expected the game to have a lot of microtransactions but it doesn't, which is already a positive aspect for me. They have updated the game and added more hunters and monsters, deleted a game mode and some other small updates. Overall the game is fun, it's kind of balanced depending on how good you communicate with your team if playing hunter or how good you are at playing monster at the first few hours of this game it might seem really unbalanced. It's best to play it with at least one friend always makes a game more fun :).
Now the pros are :
- Requires 80-90h to get to max level (50) after that you'll be able to play for a lot longer leveling the hunters
- They added ranked (Would wait till you are at level 40-50 to play ranked to have fun in it)
- Various of different hunters and monsters you can choose to find one that matches your style of playing the game
- Game actually looks pretty good
- Community is quite good, a few trolls *cough* mainly a funny community as far as i know.
- No microtransactions
- Has a good balance there isn't a better or worse hunter, some just take more time to understand and actually be good at them.
Cons :
- Players don't exactly communicate if you are in a lobby with randoms which might result in higher loss rate of matches and less fun (this is why it's best to play with a few friends).
- The silver keys (game balance) ratio after a game is low, you'll need to play a lot of games to unlock hunters or monsters and skins. Don't forget the perks that also cost a lot of silver keys (also available trough leveling hunters up).
- People leaving the lobby if they don't get the role they want without any penalty, must admit i have done this myself too if i got the monster which i don't like to play when in queue with a friend.
- Still has some bugs (like a hand full) but hey it's free and beta stage 2 don't expect it to be flawless yet
- Sadly there are hackers i have only seen 1 so far, a support shooting the monster through the wall saying it was an ability of his ( first few hours i played this game, guy is probably banned already).

From my experience in the two weeks since the F2P switch (which is when I started):
- Consistently lost so many times (my win rate is bad)
- Won only once as Meteor Goliath and deserved it (the other one time they sacrificed themselves)
- Never got a win streak of 3 or more
- Experienced so much frustration about players or spectators resetting the lobby timer
- Other not so great stuff

Despite all the balancing issues (which are being rectified quite quickly) and bad press, it actually manages to keep me logging in everyday for one match and another. It pushes me to keep playing to keep improving, to learn from my fatal mistakes, and get some sweet satisfaction when I eventually do win. It is a work-in-progress (since the switch) after all, for both the game and myself. I have hopes it will eventually be the great game I saw it would've been.
